Updated review July 2017
"The Easy Game Maker"?
Well, yes and no. Very easy to get started, very easy map/level editor, drag and drop map making, and several demo games included which you can use as templates for your own games.
Shaping up pretty good  now with 64bit conversion and DX11, a good map editor, nice community, plenty of assets and lots of free assets available.
Very easy to make a basic shooter, let down by the AI if you try anything more complicated in its present state. Lua scripting is pretty easy to pick up and will be useful once the AI situation is fixed.
It is a one man development team and it is being worked on consistently.
Generous licensing terms, no royalties, and game assets can be used in any commercial or personal project in other game engines etc.

GameGuru now comes with a massive, free DLC, and a new Building/prefab Editor (called the EBE, = easy building editor), new shaders have been added, and cubemap shaders are in progress. It has made good improvements in FPS since it's steam release, as well as steady tweaks and improvements to the core engine.
There are over 50 hours of tutorial videos now for you to catch up on.
The software has improved steadily since it's first steam release and some games, mostly with poor reviews, have now been released on steam using previous and current versions of the engine.
There are a huge amount of free assets available, including scripts, and a very active forum where users help each other out, swap ideas, scripts and 3D models etc.   It is in continual development largely driven by a community voting system where new features are added alongside the developers' regular updates and engine improvements.
--------------------------------------------------------------
Original review  (still all relevant)
GameGuru is an intuitive map editor coupled with a very robust DirectX game engine all in one package.
Good for the casual or aspiring game maker with quick results, simple interface, and budget price, with the possibility of making something special if you delve into the lua scripting which isn't that difficult.
Probably the easiest game-maker on the market, and has had frequent updates and new features weekly since its steam release. it is just improving all the time.
At this price on steam its a complete steal
A great community, one of the best on Steam.
Active developers with a good track record who engage with the community and deliver on what the community asks for.
Lots of free assets and a good store full of very sensibly priced paid add-ons and content.
Very easy to use and understand, get started right away.
It is possible to easily throw together a playable FPS multiplayer map in half an hour or roll up your sleeves spend hundreds of hours on a project.
The steam multi player works well.
One click makes a standalone game from your project that anyone can play without owning GameGuru.

Tested with 1.0.0.1, on March 1st 2015, while it is still in early access.
"Now anyone can make a professional game thanks to GameGuru" they say on their website. I would definately not buy any games made with this. Feels too much like something that should be on console.
Pros:
1. You will get many assets with this, so you should be able to make something within 1 hour.
2. Very easy to use.
3. Test your game anytime.
4. Users can upload their own assets to the store.
5. You get premade "games" to learn what you can do with this software.
6. Multiplayer. Even if I didn't try it.
Cons:
1. Everything reminds me of something you would use on a console. Or on a pc in 2002.
2. Graphics aren't very good. Ok, but not good.
3. So far I think you can use LUA for scripting only.
4. Most stuff on the store costs money. Just like in the assetstore for Unity.
5. Editing is in 2d, except if you build your game and _then_edit_it.
6. I didn't find a way to edit multiple objects, only one at a time.
If you want to make your own game, just get the free version of Unity. You can make FPS games in Unity almost as fast as in GameGuru (provided you have the assets).
As of today, I can't recommend GameGuru to anyone but kids. I might change that later as this is early access. You are welcome to comment on this, but I will delete any comment that I find not serious.

Alan Wake is a psychological thriller/action game (notice I didn't say horror) about a man fighting darkness itself to rescue his wife. Simple, right? You'd think so.
The game is really cool at first. I mean, the combat isn't annoying, and the story isn't too bad from the start. However as you get into the game things change...
Game Mechanics: The game's combat revolves around the fact that light obliterates darkness and leaves controlled objects/beings vulnerable. Flashlights and other light sources are going to be your friend, as they are required for combat and saving your progress as checkpoints.
There is a small pool of weapons, but there's no need for any extensive armory to best enjoy the combat. Your tools do use consumables, but they are plentiful and should last a long while as long as you aren't a total dumbass and waste everything.
Puzzles are present but aren't hard. Just think and you win.
Driving sequences are not fun. The handling of the vehicles is horrible, and frankly they have no actual purpose besides "hey look you can drive. isnt that coooooolllll?"
That's all though. It's that same throughout. It gets VERY tedious later on in the game. Granted though, it's bearble. You won't exactly wish for death or anything of the sort.
Visuals: The graphics are a bit dated, but you really shouldn't be caring about that.
Atmosphere: Pretty ♥♥♥♥ing spoopy. The sound design, soundtrack, and environment really pulls you in, and makes the experience adrenilene pumping. That's what makes this game. There are jump scares in the game, but don't expect a scarefest. They aren't that scary, and you can see them coming from LIGHTYEARS away.
Characters/Story: Uggghhh. The characters have almost no depth, react to shadow people murdering their friends like it's just routine, are sometimes just thrown in (AND ARE NEVER EXPLAINED IN ANY CAPACITY). The voice acting is not that bad however.
The story seems cool at first...but is just boring. It falls flat not that far into the game. Then at the end, it just has a ♥♥♥♥ing heart attack. It was simply disappointing.
I would like to say something before you stop reading, and decide this game isn't worth it (you can't buy it on Steam anymore, but I'm sure you can find copies of the console version still, which is a better fit for this game anyway). This IS an enjoyable experience. It IS easy to look past the scars of this game and find fun. This isn't Bad Rats, Ride to Hell: Retribution, or Fallout 4. It isn't a peice of♥♥♥♥♥♥game. Yes, it had so MUCH potential, but what is there can be enough. Just open your mind, and try to find the good things.
In the end, I'm going to recommend this game, as I did end up enjoying the experience. On the surface, the flaws make the game ugly, but it's only skin deep...in my opinion.

As a graphic designer, fonts are critical to my job. Everyone knows the cliche of using comic sans; being a horrible representation of almost anything other than an actual comic strip. Fonts ilicit different emotions, and if you use them correctly you will be successful in what you are trying to achieve with your audience. So it is completely fascinating to see the history behind a typeface. What emotions were behind the creation of each one, and what kind of reaction they were trying to achieve. Honestly, I haven't played this game in a long time, but it still sticks out vividly in my memory. Even if you aren't thrilled by the game's history lessons, the gameplay is still very entertaining in my opinion. If you currently, or aspiring to be a graphic designer I recommend playing this game. I did take classes on fonts in school, and did a research paper and presentation on one, but this was a much more enjoyable way to learn about multiple fonts.

Type:Rider is a really unique game, in that while you play you learn about the history of typography. Each level we learn something about font families, technologies and the atmosphere of the levels reflect that. At first the game looks like the usual, very trendy monochrome or too blackish platformer, but the individual levels are much more colorful and really different from each other
The gameplay itself is a simple plaftformer, we control two unseparable balls and we can also jump with them. The game is better with a gamepad (as usually for platform games).
Typre:Rider is a short game, and well worth the money, if you are interested in typography. The game is simple and beautiful and can be completed in one sitting.

I am writing this review after my 5th playthrough of the game (3 on XBOX 360 and 2 on the PC).
First, the atmosphere of the game is fantastic. I had a wonderful time becoming emersed in the world created in Alan Wake. The way the context of the world around Alan grows as the story unfolds is wonderful. The episodic nature allows for play in segments and typically each episode is set up to make you anticipate the next chapter. At the time of its release (2010) I believe it changed interactive storytelling, and it is evident in the success of TellTale Games' episodic games.
While many did not enjoy the way the story does not clearly answer all of your questions, I found the plot, pacing, and conclusion satisfying enough to play the game several times. It is good enough to make one want to play the DLC and the small follow-up American Nightmare.
As for the gamey parts of this release, the mechanics of light and the flashlight for aiming work well. It contributes to the atmosphere, the tension, and is neatly wrapped in the plot of the game. It isn't as smooth as other shooters, but that may be intentional - the panic caused by this helps the tension in the game. I play on a controller mostly, but I did one playthrough with a keyboard and mouse. Both work just fine.
Graphically the game was fantastic and holds up quite well even in 2017. It isn't as stunning as it once was, but it doesn't feel like a retro game either.
The sound is excellent. Music flows right with the mood of the game and the narrative. The atmospheric sounds fit right in. The production level of this game is very high.
The only downside is that a sequel never got off the ground. It seems the game is meant to be the first act in a much larger story arc, where Wake is involved in a much broader conflict between the light and the dark. The last line of the plot seems to suggest this quite clearly.
The DLC fleshed out the narrative even further and is highly recommended. This game has held up over time and is certainly a classic in my eyes. I hope this review helps you out!

Like playing in the mud? Enjoy amazing graphics satisfying sounds and a whole range of vehicles? Then you'll love Spintires, but it does have its flaws. Spintires is a driving adventure game with lots of things to do.
Firstly lets cover the maps: As of 19/11/15 there are 7 maps with unlimited posiblities. In the maps you have multiple different types of terrains which some cars/trucks can handle but some can't. You can drive in water but it does increase your damage level. Pretty much all the maps are based in Russia and you can unlock multiple garages to store your trucks. Many people disliked this game at first due to its lack of updates but now the developers have seemingly come back to life and added about 5 more trucks/cars with loads of different mods.
Now, onto the gameplay: Driving in this game is quite fun, you can do it with friends also. Driving through the mud is a tricky buisness, whilst driving through it your tires can dig into the mud, which makes the game a lot harder, but wheres the fun without difficulty right, RIGHT? There are unfortunatley only two camera angles for driving in this game (Main 3rd person camera and rooftop camera) but both are nice and you can have your own custom view settings which save when you exit the game?! And when you log back into your save, it carrys on from that exact location.
Now: Objectives: There are multiple objectives in this game, such as a forestry delivery. In the forestry objective you have do deliver wood logs from one side of the map to the other. Also you can unlock garages by delivering "garage points" to them, every map has about 3 garages and when you quit the game saves your trucks there!
So in conclusion a massive Russian map with true mud trucks, deliver logs, tow trucks and have a Russian swear at you when toggling diferential lock and all wheel drive. Just buy this game (Find it on the Steam Store £20, Bundle Stars Sales around £6,66,♥♥♥♥♥approx £3,75+) Prices may vary.

First off, don't buy this game if you're looking for a fast-paced adventure experience, because you will not find that here. Instead, you'll find a visual novel with a boatload of symbolism and some interesting concepts. The story is slow-paced, but it's deep if you can read between the lines, and even more so when you reach the end of the game.
I love Journal. There's a LOT I can say about it, but not so much without spoilers. So I'll talk about the aspects I liked about the game briefly and generally.
You make decisions on the protagonist's attitude towards other characters in the game. Now, that on it's own might now seem like much. There are tons of games that let you do that. These decisions don't even have much affect on the game in the long run. It's a linear storyline. Still, that was just something I liked about it.
Some decisions do affect the game, and these are probably the biggest reason I love Journal. In one part of the game, the protagonist faces a challenge that she can choose to accept assistance in facing. I think that's a lot deeper than it may seem. Really, it says a lot about human nature. We don't like to reach out for help sometimes, but in reality, it would make the situation so much better. Then, immediately following that choice, you get to choose whether or not to let your mother know that you had trouble completing the task, and whether or not you seeked help for it. That's another interesting tidbit on our nature. Even if we choose to accept help on things, often times, we don't want it to be known that we did so. I suppose we just want to make ourselves look better by making it seem as if we've done everything on our own.
The thing that impacted me the most in this game was the choice of whether or not to fess up to something you have done. I played through this part twice, and I know both of the ways the story could go from there. Of course, I'm not going to say it for respect for those who do not appreciate spoilers, but I thought it was a very deep decision, and it really impacted me and really made me love Journal even more.
I also love the soundtrack to Journal. I just find it to be beautiful. The art style is attractive as well, featuring a hand-drawn feel to the graphics. It suits the game well as it is supposed to be inside of a Journal.
By now, if you've read this far, you can see pretty clearly that I'm a huge fan of symbolism. So another thing that I really appreciated in the game was the shadow puppet shows after each chapter. At first, I was confused, and I didn't like the shadow puppet shows. I thought they were fillers with no meaning and no input to the developing story. They just seemed meaningless and unnecessary. However, as I progressed through the story and thought deeply about what each character may have been thinking or feeling based on their actions in the game, I realized that the shadow puppet shows were symbolically linked to the main story. In fact, if you really think about the stories presented, they're surprisingly easy to link the symbolism. I realized that, really, the shadow puppet shows are a brilliant addition to the experience.
If you are patient enough to get through the slow story, you will not be disappointed.

I usually have sceptical feelings towards games that are overpromoted and with Alan Wake this is the case: its previously overpraised story is a total mess. It was probably the (5 years) long production time that took its toll: they had to cut out many things and the game became linear (as opposed to previous open world plans).
But what is the game really about? We play as the titular hero, Alan Wake who - after an in medias res prologue, that introduces the gameplay elements and some parts of the story - arrives to Bright Falls, a fictional rural town somewhere in Washington (state near the Canadian border, not the city) with his wife, Alice. He is a successful author of many detective novels and they expect this vacation to resolve Alan's writer's block.
Soon after they set foot in the idyllic, peaceful little town and reach the cabin on an island in the middle of a lake where they are supposed to stay, Alice disappears under mysterious circumstances. Alan wakes up in a wrecked car and only remembers a few things about what and how it happened.
Not too far in the game (I refuse using the spoiler tag here) it is revealed, that Cauldron Lake is the source of all troubles where the Dark Presence resides, that's responsible for turning the folks into twisted beings, called 'taken'. However it needs someone with enough creativity to manifest, or rather materialize its creations: a writer, Alan Wake.
On his journey to find his wife we control Alan from a third person view, (in a slightly averted view, which is handy at jumping parts ;)) through 6 TV-series-like episodes. Our main weapon against the possessed 'taken', who once were (not so) normal townfolks is light, primarily our flashlight, along with flares and stationary electric lamps. The light is required to burn away the dark aura that protects these beings and after doing so we must kill them the ordinary way - by conventional firearms. There's an issue here, since Alan can't carry much ammunition at once and he is unable to perform any melee attacks, so we have to make every shot count. Fortunately aiming is quite easy - we'll shoot at where our flashlight points.
With the flashlight we won't have such problems, batteries are plentiful and if we don't use our lamp, it 'regenerates' power (very player friendly feature, but unnecessary) plus it only consumes battery, when focused (this way it's more effective and can also stun our enemies for a brief moment (they can protect themselves with their arms, so we can't keep them at bay for long this way. By using flare guns and flash grenades we can instantly kill our opponents, thus avoiding the use of firearms altogether.
The 'taken' are stronger and faster than us, fortunately we can dodge their attacks, which the game refers to as "cinematic dodge" (in these moments the game switches into slow motion, as some kind of a reward, so we can plan our next move). There isn't a large variety of these enemies, but it didn't really bother me, since they were just townfolks so I wasn't expecting anything extraordinary (in fact there was one type which I didn't find fitting: a black guy wearing tracksuit and sport shoes, with switchblades... this is the kind of person I wouldn't expect to meet in the forests of Washington state :)). In fact I liked how the game introduced us posessed police officers and rangers, after a fight between law enforcement and the taken. There are archenemies ("bosses") as well who vary from large chainsaw wielding woodmen to supernatural phenomena, but they usually offer less challenge than situations when we are surrounded by multiple ordinary foes (who often respawn at certain locations).
The game is completely linear but does a good job creating the illusion that we can go anywhere. There's a little indicator which shows us in which direction we have to proceed. There are plenty of collectibles ranging from completely useless coffee thermoses to manuscript pages which - according to the story - are necessary to find, but we can still finish the game by not picking up all of them. They also help, or at least they should help understanding the plot, but they usually just foreshadow 'future' events and increase the atmoshpere. We can also find TVs at certain locations and watch episodic horror shows, titled Night Springs, which are very simlar to The Twilight Zone series.
The atmosphere, which is already great and probably the strongest point of Alan Wake. The dark, gloomy, eerie forests we get to spend lots of time in is one of the best experience in video gaming: such creepy, menacing and more importantly large woodlands are hard to come by. The game was palpably inspired by Twin Peaks, the famous TV show from the 90s. The Town of Bright Falls - just like Twin Peaks - takes place in a (seemingly) peaceful countryside with its strange inhabitants (one person for example, the Lamp Lady is a direct reference to the Log Lady or the lovely barmaid).
Almost all of the NPCs are well made, Alan's agent, Barry is especially great, who adds to the humour factor (with all the horror movie references and using the same animation over and over :P). As a matter of fact most of them are much better than the protagonist himself, who seemed too average and somehow distant.
And that is the point of the review where I've arrived to the biggest problem: the plot (which is a pretty bad sign in the case of a story driven game). It makes no sense, we'll never know which portion is reality and which isn't. The story looks compelling at first, mostly because it tells us so many things instead of being overly mistified. We can get over the fact that the core of the story
is not the most original one, even the jumps between past and present aren't annoying, but where the story 'develops' is inexcusable. The game leaves us with too many questions. What's the role of the totally pointless FBI agent? Who was real, Wake or Zane? Who created whom? What was even real?
It seems even the developers themselves got confused with the story and seemingly they just gave up on it and figured that everyone should guess and deduce whatever they want from the plot. Well, there's certainly a lot one can come up with the story the way it is, but personally I found it lackluster and lame, an easy way to get by without creating a really smashing one.
The PC version came with 2 DLCs (The Signal & The Writer) and while each provides ~2 hours long challenging gameplay they won't clear up anything, they manage to make the plot even worse (Barry?).
The graphics is truly something, even today, the environment looks absolutely fantastic: the town, the mountainside makes us wish we were there. The lightning effects are also superb. On the contrary some of the characters, especially Alan looks creepy and lifeless, mainly because of the weird facial animations.
The environmental audio is even more amazing, the echos, the trees creaking and mysterious clatters in the forest will creep out anyone. It is one of those games that will justify having a serious 5.1 or 7.1 sound system.
After failing miserably to deliver a well put together story, Alan Wake still deserves to be recommended, simply because everything else is done right. The effort clearly shows and altough it's far from being a cult- or even a very good game, its great atmosphere, polished appearance and the amazing locations it takes place in make it an enjoyable one.
PROS
+ amazing atmosphere
+ fantastic environments
+ superb environmental audio
+ pleasantly scary
+ good supporting characters
CONS
- plot holes, nonsensical story
- uninteresting main character
- the DLCs reuse some locations from the base game
RATING
6.5/10

Okay, so when I heard there was a new OMD in developement I was fairly excited because I loved the first two. Then I find out Gameforge is publishing it in Europe; my excitement goes straight out the window. But of course I still had to give the game a chance (even if I now regret that decision).
Basically what has happened is; Robot has hopped on the "sub-par, everyday MOBA train" in an attempt to hitch a ride to "Money Town".
After a very brief time playing I found the game to be repetitive and boring but, don't worry, if you're not a fan of grinding you can unlock EVERYTHING in the game by throwing your money at it.
Now, you may think a game that offers 5 player co-op would be fun, but you'd be wrong. Having 5 players drops the difficulty level to zero, again adding to the boredom of grinding. And while the idea of having a selection of characters also sounds good, it is poorly executed.
All-in-all Orcs Must Die! Unchained had everything it needed to be a great Tower Defense game, maybe even a decent MOBA, but it was completely ruined by the reliance on a HUGE "pay-to-win" scheme (seriously, if you think the £50 of DLC advertised on steam is a lot - it's nothing compared to the in-game store) and an incredibly poor choice of publisher.
If you're looking for the true Orcs Must Die experience (or even just a good tower defense game) get OMD2.
If you're looking for a good MOBA play literally any other one you can find.
Only buy it if you are going to play it with your friends.

Journal is a very difficult game to understand and that is mostly due to the fact that the game is left open to interpretation, especially regarding your own feelings on certain subjects in life or in very specific situations. I've played games before, such as Serena, where you go through an emotional rollercoaster, based these interpretations but Journal was certainly the most difficult rollercoaster I have been on so far. I went from confused to sudden anger, not towards the game or the characters mind you, to confused again. Only to be met with a sudden calmness when you think you've figured it all out, just to be thrown back in this huge loop. At least that's how I felt and you might feel different emotions when playing the game.
The story is about a young girl who's trying her best to understand the hidden meanings in life, about the interactions with complete strangers and people who are dear to her. You, as the player, are given several choices to respond, giving you the illusion that the story is adapting based on your answers while it simply doesn't. Of course, there are some options that will make you lose a friend, or not, based on your answers but the overall story will never change its course. After the majority of interactions, the girl will write down her thoughts in her journal. While this gives you some knowledge of the adolescent, you're still left with a handful of questions. At some point, it feels like there are two separate stories, which only makes your confusion grown but the stories blend together at the very last day. Out of all the possible explanations I had in my head, there was no way I could have foreseen the ending. It left me with a mixture of feelings and I swear, I thought I felt a tear.
The graphics look far too immature, almost as if they were trying to weigh down the heaviness of the story itself with puerile artwork but I have to admit that I grew found of it. In fact, I started to miss being in the sketchbook every time the secondary story was explained in the form of a puppet-show. As far as the voice-acting goes, I didn't find any real issues except that certain words seemed to get lost. Mostly these were the first words of a sentence but this could also be due to the fact I am not a native English-speaker which made the puny British accent slightly more difficult to understand. Other than that, the voice-actors did an incredible job by making their raw emotions heard.
Final Conclusion
The best word to describe Journal has to be 'bizarre' because that's the first thought I had of the game when the credits rolled down my screen. However, beside being an odd game, Journal is truly amazing. It lets your explore emotions and situations you, and possibly many others, struggle with on a nearly daily base and that's what makes it a great down-to-earth storytelling game that you should play.

Duck Game is that rare competitive gem where I have just as much fun losing as I do winning. It's hilarious and absurd and doesn't take itself seriously. It's a lot like TF2 in that respect, right down to the crazy number of hats available. There are some bugs, and it can certainly be challenging for new people to get into it when playing multiplayer against more experienced people. But in my opinion it's worth it because of the sheer amount of fun I've had--certainly more than any other game I've played on Steam.
Controls are tight and responsive, right up there with 16 bit platformers like Mario, Megaman, or Sonic. You can see from the video clips above that the graphics and sounds are pretty solidly retro-inspired and fit the game well. Rounds are short, sometimes just a few seconds, There is, indeed, an irresponsible number of weapons, and their interactions with each other and with different setpieces lead to a lot of interesting gameplay. I'm a little more than 50 hours in and still learn something occasionally. The basics are easy to learn: pick up a weapon, aim it at a duck, hit the fire button. Yet all the interactions of the different mechanics make for a very high skill ceiling, and the vagaries of online play combined with all the different ways to kill a duck (or accidentally kill oneself!) lead to great replay value. Consider that a round lasting for a minute is a big deal, and there are people posting reviews with over a hundred hours in-game. That's a
of Duck Game.
I feel I would be remiss if I didn't mention that the community, so far, has very few toxic people that I've seen. Sure, every game has its share of jerks, but I just don't see them very often in Duck Game. I think a lot of it has to do with just how
the game is, and how easy it is to laugh off a loss. Sure, winning is cool, but Duck Game is just so damn fun I don't care if I win.
I have enjoyed my time with Duck Game more than I have any other game in many years. It is pure fun, pure joy.

The Last Tinker™: City of Colors is an extremely charming little 3D platforming puzzle game. Don't expect a platformer in the likes of Banjo Kazooie though - expect more of a simplified Assassin's Creed 'free-running' style of platforming. If you're fine with that though, this game has a lot to offer and is, as I said, an extremely charming game. It took me approximately 5 hours to complete, although I didn't collect every last thing there was to collect, so this time could be extended out a little. AND I used a gamepad, so keep that in mind too.
The most striking thing about this game is its visual appeal. A world made out of bright and colourful paper glued together sets the scene for a very enjoyable experience for all ages. The story really is quite good, and it does have those 'moral-of-the-story' elements that would be quite good for children and, at times, a wake-up call for adults. The soundtrack for the game is fantastic too - something that I was very pleased about!
Now, as I said in the intro, the platforming of this game is quite basic. Simply hold down the 'free-running' button and move your character in the direction you wish to go in. However, that's not to say that the overall gameplay is stale. The puzzle elements of the game are often tied into the platforming, which is what creates the challenge. And where there isn't a crossover between the two, the puzzles were really well-done!
Finally, without giving away too much of the story, I shall talk about the combat. As you progress through the game you will unlock more abilities that will coincide with meeting more challenging foes or coming across areas that require something new to happen. I never felt as though I was doing the same thing over and over like a grind. It's not an amazing combat system, but it is still seriously enjoyable. Simply put, you press a button that is tied to one of your abilities and you punch a guy. These abilities are 'colours', and so pressing A on a gamepad will turn the bad guy green, because, A on a gamepad... it's green... Anyway, this can often lead to some cool strategies for taking out your opponents. Thankfully there is also the ability to dodge enemy attacks!
So overall, this game is the type of game that should really stand out to people who are drawn to colour! It's a game that has lots of it - but unfortunately the bleakness is taking over, so you must defend Colourtown!! Apart from the story, there are collectables to collect... heh... and upgrades to buy through the gems you pick up by smashing crates and bad guys. I definitely recommend this game to fans of the platforming/puzzle genre, even if the platforming mechanics aren't what you might expect.
Enjoy! :D

Lets get the obvious out of the way, NS2 offers a unique multiplayer FPS/RTS experience that you will not find anywhere else. It's PC centric with none of the dumbed down console design plaguing 90% of games this last generation.
While the heart of its addictiveness and its frustrations is the competitive nature against other human players instead of vs AI. If there's a reason you will keep playing NS2, it will be because of the players you will be sharing this unique gameplay experience with.
But it also has two very major problems that everyone who has played NS2 has experienced at some point - Performance & Balance. Few people have a computer capable of running NS2 at a steady 60 FPS throughout an entire match; the Lua coding and the engine has had a long history of criticism. And the game requires hundreds of hours to master its mechanics, that were majorly changed as of build 250 requiring a renewed learning curve.
Balance however has always been a topic of debate since the beta, the main problem with the way the game is being balanced is UWE's obsession with trying to turn it into a competitive 6v6 e-sports rivaling that of SC2. The small crowds at events and the low amount of views can be defined as very niche, yet this is what the game is being balanced for; NOT for public play or for the majority of people that quickly join and leave NS2 throughout its sales.
My personal experience with NS2 is hard to define...the first 5 months I used a mic, tried 6v6 pugs, experienced a lot of a-holism from people and played on a 1280x720 resolution. It was stressful, I hated it and ended up quitting.
5 months after with a much better computer & mouse, I picked the game up again as build 250 came out. Performance and balance issues were still very frustrating, the game was basically an on-going beta. But playing with people I became very familiar with is the reason I kept sticking around, as well as the mastery we humans care deeply about.
Do I love or hate NS2? Some aspects I love, and some things about it I can't stand. It's a bittersweet experience, the game has stayed alive because UWE keeps it alive with constant updates. However it's obviously not financially viable for them. So sooner or later NS2 will fade into obscurity if it isn't already.
I think for me, NS2 might have been the pinnacle of anything coming out in the next 5-10 years that has made me invest as much time into it as I have. I think the only thing I might have spent more time playing, is StarCraft.
Edit: As far as clarifying how I feel about this game retrospectively, NS2 had an amazing concept, one-of-a-kind; but the execution of the public multiplayer, the balancing and the decision of UWE to code their own engine probably doomed this game. And having played NS2 for 10 months, public games are 90% frustration and 10% balanced teams; same complaint I've heard from many whom used to play NS2.
And it always had a small player base for a multiplayer game, exceptions were when thousands of players would be joining and then leaving within like 2 weeks of major updates or sales. Thus I'm pretty sure that the small size of the remaining active player-base, makes a match making system completely redundant considering you need to fill up 12-24 slots; and at down-times you're lucky to find one full server in EU.
I regret wasting a whole year on a game that mostly brought me stress and contempt, but I have no regrets about all the experiences I've had with the hundreds upon hundreds of players I've met throughout all my time spent with it. Whether it be good experiences or bad, I have learned from them all and as a result; I have grown both as a gamer and as a person.

In short: fantastic puzzle game.
Heavily inspired by Cyan games, but sacrificing little bit of immersion and atmosphere for superbly crafted puzzles and great flow through all 20+ hours of gameplay.
This game is good in almost every aspect. The graphics, technical stability, the controls (yes, finally some puzzle game with great controls), and of course the puzzles. There is 20 hours of top notch puzzles. I made big mistake, by looking twice in the walkthrough in the beginning phase of the game. :/ NEVER DO THIS! All puzzles are logical and just pay attention to every detail -- including sound, and all scattered objects around. Everything has some meaning. During the later phases of the game I already had trust to the authors, so I was never afraid of some garbage solution of any puzzle, so the urge to check the walkthourgh disappeared. Overall the difficulty of the puzzles is between medium and hard, but never reaches Riven level of difficulty.
If I would have to nit pick something, it would be the music while not horrible, it is forgettable and sounds "generic". Also the ending phase of the game is lengthened too much, for no reason, because the game is long anyway.
I will definitelly buy Quern 2 (or other puzzle game) by this team, even without reading reviews.
Overall: 9.5/10

This is not your average shooter. You don't sit in hallways and snipe, you don't lurk in corners or vents (unless you're an alien :D ), and you really can't lone wolf effectively. The different sides, alien and marines, require different mindsets and strategies to win. You normally can't just run as a solo skulk or marine and win.
The map designs are amazing and the atmosphere is very impressive. There are specific areas of each map that one side will excel at using and trying to take one of those areas as the other side is usually costly. The maps are also unique in layout and space use. Not every map is a tiny cluster**** or a giant open arena.
The game and its "classes" require a bit of learning. It isn't just who can shoot fastest or get kills most effectively. There is far more going on and the strategy side of commander mode can rapidly change the outcome of a battle. The hardest part was getting used to commander mode. I am a fan of the RTS style game but this was a whole new level of awesome. Players following orders you gave and seeing your upgrades or buildings change the tide is downright exciting.
I do have some problems with game optimization and mechanics but its nothing to cry about.
TL;DR
If you enjoy teamwork, strategic gameplay, and general awesomeness this is a fine game. It is absolutely worth the buy and worth practicing. It can be tough to learn and may even not be enjoyable at first. This is until you get some practice in and learn the ropes. FInd a newbie friendly server (marked on server browser) and get started!

Okay, first off take the negative reviews with a pinch of salt. Yes, I agree there are better, faster engines out there. All are more difficult to use and have been available for quite some time. Nothing offers the features and ease of use Gameguru supplies. I'm sure if you are here checking this product out, you may have already looked at the other engines available.
Now on to my thoughts on GameGuru. I think it is great. I have been using it from the start when it was called Reloaded and have had much fun in the process. No one who purchased Reloaded has been affected by the name change, that is all it is. All pledgers have access to this package so the one particular bad review I saw is basically nonsense. I am currently looking forward to the new model packs my backer status will give me :)
I think my time spent on GameGuru even at this early stage is testament to my approval of this program. I daren't think how many actual hours I have spent with this package over the last 2 years! Now it's on Steam I will see clearly just how many hours this can eat up!
There are issues. AI can be a little dumb and plain idiotic at times. Speed can be a problem with large maps. There are still a lot of commands and options still needed. Overall though, for this price, if you want to try your hand at making games and have no idea where to start, GameGuru is a great way to get going! I really enjoy the process of designing levels and checking them out, tweaking and refining as I go. There is a ton of media included by default and a whole heap of extra stuff on the gamestore. Really, GameGuru is a bargain. It's release price is exceptional and well worth bagging!
Multi-player is also a nice feature and I hope it will be expanded beyond it's simplistic roots considerably. It's not a biggie for me, but I am sure many will find it a blast!
If I have to give a score I would say 8/10. As AI and speed need to be improved for us to make really good games.
For entertainment value alone though, it gets a 10/10 as I have spent more time with this in the last 2 years than ANY other game or tool I own.
I have a host of videos on my youtube channel regarding Gameguru and Reloaded, so if you are unsure and want to see how it looks now and how it has progressed right from the start; go check it out. Just search for retrogamebloke.
If you don't expect the world. You will be pleased with GameGuru.

Gameguru is by far easier then every other engine out there. It is quite possible to have a running level in less then 30s. This makes it perfect for Hobbyists or as an entry game development software.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Before purchase I would recommend checking these links to see what people have done, or will do. They provide a visual indication of what is possible by GameGuru.
(Screenshots)
(WIP)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pros
-It does seem to have good Optimisation for multiple entities
-Lighting feature does make an easy way to improve the look of the level.
-Interaction with the community [the main developer of the engine has been giving everyone a day to day blog of the development and often bouncing ideas back at the community via it.] [Link:
]
-plug and play
-Ease of Use
-Open World support(in terms of terrain editing)
-Large amount of assets(Currently making most fps games possible)
-strong community who are willing to help understand modelling, coding, or engine use.
Cons
-As of 28/02/2015 You are unable to really customise the User interface, aka its very limited, and Menu Customisation is the same way.(If there is a menu)
-It isn't Multiplatform. The engine will not work on a console or a phone as of 28/02/2015
-Right now it is only really effective for a single person to use as team support is not implemented(Note it will come, but its not here yet)
-There is no support for driving vehicles, and while air craft can be added it is not intended and often buggy(Note this will come in time)
- does not support 3rd view
-Does not have an inventory system(it is possible, but will require coding and wont be very visual)
-AI is weak(The AI is alright. but it’s nothing special and health is really the only way to increase difficultly, they don't really take cover, etc. However there are AI scripts already made by the community which makes them better)
-Support for rooms and inside games is currently unavailable(This will soon be addressed in a few updates)
-lighting is quite poor at the moment(you don't have spotlights)
-Open world is limited(no questing system in place, no day night cycle, no weather, no swimming)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Final Verdict:
As of right now for the price I would buy it as an 'Early Access Software' if you’re looking to support the developers of the engine or get a good deal I would recommend it.
However as a functional engine which you could make a game to sell, it won’t work yet. Yes right now there are some nice WIP games out there that will sell for the same price as the engine costs, but this won’t be for at least 6 months to a year when the engine has improved.
Make no mistake. Even when GameGuru is finished you will still have to spend countless hours to make a really good game and the difference between someone who has spent time making their game and someone who has not will show. However that is not to say GameGuru isn’t easy to use. Remember GameGuru is focused towards new entries to gaming development or hobbyists. So take that into account before purchasing.

A surprisingly fun platformer that succeeds in what should be impossible: making you care about fonts. If you take the time to read as you go and notice the differences as you travel through the ages, it's interesting to see how the evolution of a single written language can parallel the evolution of an entire culture. Of course this wouldn't matter if the gameplay was awful, but thankfully the platforming is serviceable and often broken up by clever moments that integrate each level's theme.
Type:Rider was clearly made by a development team that's very passionate about a subject that most people take for granted, and a video game is as good a way to learn about it as any. This game is worth a fiver even despite that, but more games like this deserve to be noticed, played and discussed. Rock on, Ex Nihilo.

:: Summary
This is a solid PC port, plays well, and makes for a good creepy playthrough. It's easy to recommend.
--
I originally played through Alan Wake (but not American Nightmare) on Xbox 360 years ago. I picked up a fresh copy on sale for Steam and decided on an October playthrough. Nothing quite like horror games as we slowly approach Halloween, right?
:: Graphics
Medium felt like a good match for what I remembered on XB360. I'm running an i5270 with an nVidia 1070, so cranked everything up to Ultra; the game looked pretty but there was oddly some stuttering with certain models during the intro (with Alan and Alice on the ferry), so I wound up turning settings back down for the sake of smooth play. I had no trouble holding 60fps at 1920x1080, and given how much of this game happens in darkness, it's really not a big stressor on one's video card.
:: Control
I used an XB360 controller throughout and had no problem with control or aiming. I didn't have to perform any special configuration to make the controller work and the game switches seamlessly between kb/mouse control and controller support.
:: Sound
Nothing special here, with minor sound balance issues between the game (softer) and cutscenes (louder).
:: Gameplay
No bugs to report; the game played fine end to end without crashing, locking up, or dropping me through a map anywhere. This has been a solid PC port. Most of the game consists of movement and aiming your flashlight, along with occasionally firing guns. Gunplay's so-so because you can't really aim aside from in the general direction of where your flashlight is/was pointing, but it's simple enough to get the hang of. The game doesn't starve you for ammo through most sections so you will usually have a few options available even when dealing with large enemy groups. Difficulty feels pretty mild on Normal.
:: Story
The story's still a fun one and is creepy enough to be suitable for playing after dark.

Well, I certainly can't say I've gotten terribly far in this game (at least, I hope not), but thus far, the first chapter and Chapter Two have been nothing but pure, unadulterated delight.  I'm just immensely happy that a friend of mine got this title for me as a Steam gift, as currently I've been unemployed and I'm fairly certain my physical four US pennies wouldn't have otherwise afforded me this title.
Change the "terribly far in this game" to "beat the game".  It was worth the 25 hours it took me to do it, every step of the way.
Graphically, "Dust: An Elysian Tail" is absolutely remarkable; even on my low-ish end Toshiba Satellite L755 laptop (with my dinky on-board Intel HD 300 graphics "card"), all of the animation is smooth as silk, and the sound track nothing short of breathtaking.  While I managed to pay nothing at all for this title, having bought previous games before, this is easily worth the US$15 when not on sale.  Also, don't let the "furry" theme of the setting fool you; the voice work is top-notch, and I'm even starting to find Fidget cute, and she's supposed to be the "nagging worry-wort" as far as I've been able to see thus far.
What it comes down to is I can't possibly recommend this game enough.  If you like other games such as "Castlevania" (which this game has an early and direct reference to) or "Metroid" (especially with the feeling of having to explore and return to areas several times over the course of the game, I imagine) and liked either of the aforementioned titles, you will most likely love "Dust: An Elysian Tail".

*I play with a Logitech G27 Wheel and have only played singleplayer (so far)*
I love this game. I don't really know why, but I do. I'm not a gear head or car guy by any means, but I got crazy into a racing game that led to me buying a G27 wheel. All I end up playing is Spintires though! I'm hooked. The game doesn't hold your hand at all, but it gives you all the pieces to do what you want. Beyond the objective of delivering lumber there is no right or wrong way to play Spintires, just your way.
A playthrough of a map consists of some basic concepts;
-You start with certain vehicle(s) at a checkpoint of a “garage”. Vehicles can take damage and they burn fuel that needs refilling.
-A garage lets you change the attachments your vehicle has. In general they are attachments to carry garage parts, repair parts, log carriers, or fuel. But each vehicle's attachment options vary.
-Each map has other garage locations that can be unlocked by delivering garage parts. Fueling stations for refueling vehicles and fuel carrying attachments. Lumber pickup areas where lumber has been cut down. And finally the objective areas where you are suppose to deliver the lumber to.
And that's it. It's a simple game. You have to pickup and deliver a few loads of logs to one or more specified locations on a map. Simple! But... Not actually so simple. The terrain will make that a monumental undertaking. Mud mud and more mud! Hills, rocks, woods, raging rivers, open water, and more all are there to ruin your vehicle and day. It isn't a matter of IF you will get stuck or rollover its a matter of WHEN. And if it isn't the environs that get you, it'll be yourself. Progress is very slow and steady and can lull you in to a false sense of security. An hour or two of mistake free trudging in first gear and you get lazy and you make a mistake. A bad  turn, hit an object, try to cut a corner or cross a river at the wrong spot, take on deeper mud than you should with a heavier load, etc etc. You'll make mistakes no doubt. Throw in some strategic planning with which vehicles(s) you use for what and some side objectives/exploring... And you got yourself buried neck deep in the mud both literally and figuratively!

But you aren't on your own out there. The vehicles and their attachments keep you movin'. And with winches on every vehicle as long as you're near some trees or can get a second vehicle close you got a chance to get unstuck or right-side-up again. I am constantly amazed at what I can get myself in to, and out of, in this game. And boy is there so so so many ways to get stuck, but just as many inventive ways to get out. "Where there's a will there's a way". You can spend hours just getting out of a mess you could have avoided in the first place. But somehow you end up not caring. As of writing this review I have completed 4 of the (currently) 6 stock maps on “hardcore” and they've taken me 3.5 to 6hrs a piece thanks to the messes you invariably get in to.
Pros:
-Difficult but completely fair.
-A million mistakes to make and a million ways out of each one.
-Runs at 60fps 1080p 100% of the time on my FX 6300/R9 270 toaster.
-Fun as *blank* with G27!
Things you will have to overcome:
-The difficulty and your patience.
-The camera angles seem annoying and “wrong” at first but ultimately make sense for the visual information you need when trudging through the mud. And you get used to them quickly. But the optional mouse movement to swing the camera around is fairly clunky. Also no “cockpit” camera as of writing this which means using a wheel in “third person” 99% of the time. There is a “hood” camera for tight corners. But like I said, the default view ultimately makes sense in the end. You see everything you NEED to from that angle, especially the tires' positions.
-!!!Using a racing wheel like the G27 will not absolve you from still needing to use the mouse (and possibly keyboard)!!! Not all controls can be bound within the game but I used the Logitech Profiler software to bind keystrokes to buttons to eliminate my need for the keyboard 100%. There are crane controls for loading logs in “hardcore” mode that needs 9 buttons on its own. Without doing it my way you would still need to control that crane on the keyboard as well as some other controls. Then mouse will control menus, winch hookup placement, and manual looking around no matter what. So you WILL need your mouse no matter what. Not an issue with my desk setup but I know some people have “cockpits” for their wheels that don't accommodate a mouse and keyboard. So fair warning there!
Cons:
-Saving system is so-so. Its automatic and works fine. But twice I had save files corrupt when I Windows-key'd to minimize then re-maximized. Nothing tragic but the potential is there with how grueling a map can be. I can't imagine being 4hrs in and losing a save. I'd cry. And some on the forums have complained of losing in progress saves when the game has updated. I haven't needed it, but saves are in C:/Users/”your username”/AppDate/Roaming/SpinTires/UserSaves and if I exit in the middle of a long game I manually backup the file somewhere out of fear. But I have never had to use my backup.
-Weird community. I guess there was lots promised for the game that the long time players still want. But there was a long stall in the updates or something. Then the current updates aren't coming fast enough for the community or something. You'll notice a lot of the “negative” reviews are people that actually like the game but are mad with the developers. Its unfair of me to judge being a fresh face but the community has been pure cynicism and impatience in my experiences so far. Which has kept me from prodding towards MP.
The game is a great unique experience and words cannot explain it. I can't imagine keyboard and mouse controls being that much less of a great experience as a wheel. Because the game is just plain fun. But again this review is written by someone using a wheel. Which has been a great experience. The regular price is a bit steep but there are sales to be had. I personally got it in a bundle and that was an absolute steal. As of writing this the game is still being updated and worked on by the developer which is nice, always appreciate more! Supposedly Steam Workshop is coming which would be pretty neat. I guess a mod community already exists out on the web. Also, the MP looks like loads and loads of fun as well. But the stock, vanilla game is keeping me plenty busy for now and makes the game worth it on it's own. I am not a modern multitasker but this game lends itself well to watching TV/movies during it. Or having a phone/Skype convo during it. Very casual and methodical. But like I mentioned, don't get too distracted and lulled in to that false sense of security... You'll be spinning tires in the mud and cursing the heavens in no time! Enjoy!

Alan Wake.
A horror thriller book-themed story - made into a cinematic and atmospheric action game. This is a survival horror; action adventure game. The game is quite story driven.
Alan Wake has a distinct atmosphere and great immersive gameplay. An artistic style that plays around light and dark- especially darkness - and the fear of the night.
A remarkable gripping narrative style with a handful of likable characters.
The combat gameplay is largely great, and will keep you on the edge of your sit. Quite a thriller indeed.
The mostly darkened world is surprisingly beautiful even by night. With some levels in daylight - that offer some serenity and a better look at your surroundings - before night falls - and with it danger awakens. The scenery is a mix of pleasant and beautiful - with a sense of dread, suspense and eeriness.
The soundtrack is just awesome. Poets of the Fall - one of my favorite bands - have stepped up to make a few custom made songs that fit remarkably well into the game -as well as providing a song from their album. Super cool.
I recommend this game to those who really like unique survival horror games, action adventure games and especially story driven games.

To debate whether this game has artistic merit or if it is worth buying seems almost pointless. The game is currently 80 minutes, and even then it is where the game has you make all the choices you can achieve before proceeding. It is not a game like Gone Home, where the details to every little thing are incredible. The game has rough edges where the main character would often clip at edges or I would go through a door twice due to tapping it once and going to the left slightly. But...I feel like it is a game that needs to happen for the continuation of the medium of games.
The character goes by unamed, and the first few minutes are rather naively optimistic. You are exploring why the pages of your journal are missing! It will be a intriquing journey of mystery and investigation. But the game hides what your character did and did not do, thus leading to misenterpretations where you make a choice that you regret instantly.
But, the game benefits from these choices. It is a very truthful game where the main character is not a vessel or a blank slate for the player, but is truly a confused young girl who is unsure of what is the right or wrong thing to say or do. Gone Home is where you view the experiences of a confused girl, while Journal is more about BEING a confused girl. I am really glad that my character doesn't agree with my own stance on the matter, even when she makes a choice I would have made because I am a seperate person from what her life is.
The art, while getting a lot of praise from people, to me is very simplistic and helps achieve a children's story feel that betrays the true meaning of the game. You do not help people in this game, nor do you make lifes better. It is what a child would feel when going through such a painful moment in their life, and I really do respect and admire a game that can achieve such clarity on the subject of childhood innocence and even if it is possible.
I say that it is a important step in video games is because this is a really personal story for the writer and artist. It is not a game where there is any power trip nor any sense of accomplishment, and is really not about finding the truth or letting go of things. It's about a normal person dealing with things that can never be undone or fixed. To spoil the ending or even the moments within it would ruin the experience of actually going through it.
Would I recommend this: YES
It is a very close and personal game, where the length or technical lack of polish does not ruin or even bring down the honesty and bluntness Journal has brought. I wish I could say specifics, but to do that would ruin your own experience with it.
Suggestion for developer: I believe more polish to the game would be benefical, and more stories from the writer and artist would be greatly appreciated.

The game provides us with some interesting situations, ranging from the social interactions with peers, to conversations with a priest, the deceased and a homeless person. We get a more or less subtle view into each of their lives, which adds up to a bigger picture. A bigger picture of life as a hardship. The human condition, if you will. Especially in the time as a teenager. Insecurity, stress, insufferable amounts of complexes and general frailty - when it comes to the need of being accepted by the people around you - are things which are prominent in the years of being a teenager; in the years of being at all, to be honest. Where the desperate attention seeking can spring into action actions which in retrospect can be seen as abhorrent. But with a little bit of care, consideration, empathy, with a little bit of knowledge and insight into a persons motivations, WITH A LITTLE BIT OF THESE THINGS, understanding these idiosyncrasies can be much easier. The person being a "♥♥♥♥♥" can at the same time at home deal with angry parents, destructive parents, alcoholic parents, whatever concoction of behaviorism you can imagine and thereby themselves become a person like their parent, for the simple reason of learning behavior from your surrounding.
A depressed, absent-minded mother who blames you for her stress and angst, and a father who left you stranded with her will surely make you desperate for attention, in whatever way possible, especially when you're falling out with your friends, or the people you assumed were your friends. This is the case of our protagonist. Making her actions understandable, as I've seen people think otherwise.
We follow our maincharacter through a hodgepodge of a timeline, where we often get to see the consequences of something she'd done wrong. As in cheating on a test, stealing a snow globe and breaking a window and blaming it on her friend. This is where we need to get the notion of what a game "SHOULD" be out of our head. We don't have a say in these things, we are merely a witness. Sure, we control everything but we're not really in control. We are watching everything unfold in front of us without any say. For once I find this positive. It's a personal story, why should the player interject their own personality, morality or will? Why plaster your face onto a character when it's clearly not meant to be that way? Why forcefully demand the relatability of everything any character does, that's why the personality of most gamecharacters are nonexistent. Why are we afraid of people not being like us? Let this game be an expansion of your view of people. Why not let a character be itself, and then the analysing could be of interest.
And this is where my point is to some critique I've seen for the game. This game is not about trying to let you choose how to handle a situation, it's showing you the situation of this particular teenage girl. It's showing you the aftermath of some regrettable actions. It's showing you how it affects a person, how guilty a person can feel because of a mistake they barely had any real reason behind. And how your peers and upper echelons shame you because of these mistakes. It show's you the protagonist being shunned by friends and family because of silly mistakes, and the fact that you feel the need to steer her actions lets you know that the game is doing what it intends to do.
The stereotypical feel of the characters in this game is because they are real characteristics of real people. They are very common issues, personality types, and very typical scenarios for people to be in. The thing about putting this in a game is to illustrate it somehow, and get an outlet for these things you think about, as you do. To get past things. To put things into perspective. It's all there, you just need to look close enough. The game doesn't hit you in the face with its messages, or it's insights. But it's all there. From the carnival stories, the distorted mirrors of better times, memories being forgotten of the people that passed, the lying lion who did anything just to get another bite of food - in reality a metaphor for attention? I need to play it again, you should play it, think about it. Discuss it. I wish I wasn't as tired as I am right now, I don't think I can do the game justice. It's not the most beautiful game, not the most intricate, not the most interesting, but it has its moments. It's a game that tries to give us something, more than just a couple hours of time spent. I will always pay for a game with a good concept, a game that tries to do something interesting. This game certainly did, even though it may have been too much to actually get across in the best way possible. But I think most of it is already there, the teenage hardships, the tragedy of selfishness, the selfish social interaction, the shallowness of sociality, the subtle character motivations which can be parallelled with our lives. It did what it set out to do, a shame it didn't get more leeway to express this in a much grander and more beautiful way, but what we see is what we get, and what we got was good enough for a purchase, also for probably more than one playthrough.
I think I got across what I wanted to say, albeit clumsily and badly, but I did it.

I am a fan of Mafia and Mafia 2 and I like how both of those games achieved what they wanted to achieve, in my book anyway. Deciding whether Mafia 3 is or isn't worth your money is not easy and - as it is often with games - depends a lot on if what you get out of the game is what you want out of the game. After close to 50 hours I think Mafia 3 was well worth my money and I'm looking forward to get all the Season Pass DLCs. But is it for you?
At release Mafia 3 had a lot of technical issues, many of them who have been fixed or seem to be fixed at least. But the game still has some issues that I want to point out. The most obvious one is that the lighting and weather is still broken as hell sometimes. One moment you're driving a car through dense rain with the most blue sky and sunshine you can imagine only to witness a blood red sky heralding the apocalypse 5 minutes later.
Something really annoying is that sometimes points of interest just don't appear on the map. This can become a slog, especially when searching for the last $2000 damage to cause or looking for the one junction box that just will not appear.
As most of you have probably read or heard by now: the mission design is mostly uninspired and the same all the time: extort some bad guys to find other bad guys. Kill them and destroy stuff until the bigger bad guy appears and kill then kill that one. Repeat until the credits roll. The game tries to give you more to do by hiding different types of magazines and other collectibles, but this will remind most players of the feathers and chests in Assassins Creed 2 and they wouldn't be wrong.
The game's story and characters are so well depicted I actually tried to prolong the end of the game with side missions because I did not want the ride to end. The atmosphere - while sometimes impeded by the technical problems mentioned earlier - is also superb. The Hollow Speaks and Native Son are just two of the little details that make this world come to life and I spent a lot of time just driving around, listening to the radio and searching for collectibles or just wandering around and looking for interesting spots. The shooting and driving are also good, in my opinion way better than the shooting and driving in GTA5. It is true, that stealth is way to powereful especially with a silenced gun. But to me those are just options. A toolset and potential easy mode that you don't have to use but can if you just don't manage to complete that one mission or if you simply feel like dress up as Agent Lincoln (the latest patch introduced several clothing options for Lincoln) :)
I would totally recommend this game, if you are ok with some repetitive gameplay and if you can spread the gametime a little bit wider and don't try to force your way through the game in just a few sessions. That way, the game becomes a lot more digestible and the story, characters and atmosphere get enough breathing space to shine.
If what you want is an open world packed with lots of different activities and funny, sometimes ludicrous, situations: go get GTAV. Mafia 3 is not that. Mafia 3 is a game about telling a serious and dark story, set in an interesting but inimical version of the 1960s New Orleans. It's a shame that the gameplay is not put to better use, but this doesn't mean you should avoid the game, particularly if you can get it for a low budget price.
Update: I still play Mafia III from time to time and I am still enjoying it. Some of the technical issues are still there but most have been patched.

Journals are personal things; housing our thoughts, experiences, and deepest secrets as we pour our hearts out into their pages. In a similar way Journal the game is also deeply personal to its developer, Richard Perrin, being kicked around for nearly a decade and only just coming to fruition after passing through numerous different forms and surviving setback after setback. It's a passion project that needed to see the light of day regardless of how long it took to do so, but as any artist should know, after spending so long with your creation it's easy to lose sight of where it's headed and what it has become. For all the time and devotion put into it, Journal is not the masterpiece its creator no doubt envisioned it to be, unfortunately materializing as something far less profound and memorable.
Journal is the story of a girl. A girl having a very hard time attempting to come to terms with the recent upheaval of her life, as well as the general pains of youth attempting to find who she is in the world. It's a melancholy tale that attempts to deal with heavy problems in a realistic, relatable manner, but for all its endeavors to tell a more down-to-earth story than you often see in games, it overplays its hand by throwing its character through far too many hardships without ever elaborating on any of them. It comes off as disingenuous and almost exploitative, like an outsider trying to explain someone else's troubles without anything more than a surface knowledge of what someone experiencing them actually feels like. It's hard to feel empathetic when events unfold like those of a soap opera; without any explanation or justification, only serving to move the narrative onto yet another contrived moment.
The cliches extend to the characters themselves, all of which encompass some form of clique or extreme to better fit into their role of providing the protagonist with a wall to bounce questions off of, with the answer being largely insignificance. One of my biggest issues with the characters and narrative on the whole is how it presents an illusion of choice with no real changes or consequences to speak of. Something you say may affect a handful of lines of dialog (usually not beyond the immediate scene) but the plot itself remains the same, with the most important moments being completely out of the player's control despite the dialog options continually alluding to something more, as if you actually have some control of the outcome.
The worst of these moments are those that retain pertinent information until after you've had to make seemingly important decisions, without being given the facts to do so. For example, early on a friend of your character is accused of breaking a window, an act she denies and you are inclined to agree with, only later finding out that you were the one who accused her in the first place (and as is soon revealed, actually broke the window and were hiding the blame). These revelations come too late though, as you are forced to choose a side prior to being made aware of what actually transpired. It's like walking into a play during the second act; you're expected to already know the characters, their motives, and the the events that have occurred.
By the end of the game I was thoroughly detached from the protagonist, as her actions became more selfish and out of character as the game progressed, and I was helpless to influence any of it or even be clued in as to WHY she was doing what she was. For what is essentially an adventure game with the puzzles and exploration removed, for the dialog and characters to be so uninteresting and half-baked made for an experience that felt hollow.
It might not seem it, but this was a hard review to write. I wanted so badly to be drawn into the beautiful artwork and somber soundtrack which seem so ready to compliment a deeper story than we've become accustomed to, but it all fell flat. Perhaps it's a side-effect of Journal's tumultuous development process, but something went awry and the end result is less than amazing. It's hard for me to pan something that was obviously close to its creator's heart, but when it is flawed at such a fundamental level I can't write it off as something that can be overlooked, but instead have to dismiss it as a whole. Like the journal from the title, it's almost as if large portions of the game simply vanished, leaving you with a shell of what might have once been.

In Witcher if you do not prepare to fight monsters like a Witcher you will fail miserably, and rightly so for thats what sets apart Witchers from just really juiced up monster slayers.

GameGuru is the spiritual successor to FPS Creator. It began life as FPS Reloaded but has since been re-tooled as a generic 3D game creation software with its roots still firmly in the first person shooter genre.
This project has been community driven with alpha and beta testing throughout which has really helped it deliver on a lot of the developers promises. Generally speaking every aspect of the engine has been improved with better graphics, physics, terrain, post processing effects and a genuinely fun multiplayer.
The addition of fully dynamic shadows has probably been the single most important feature to bring GameGuru into the modern world of gaming and it really works nicely. Unfortunately dynamic shadows do not extend to indoor environments and interior design in general is the weakest part of the product at this early stage.
There is certainly a place in the market for a product like this. It is very easy to use and users can implement their own custom content very quickly to make truly unique experiences. LUA support has been added to give proper scripting support for people that like to get into coding and you won't find a better product for the money being asked here.
Online multiplayer is probably the most exciting feature right now and the developers have already added the ability to load other peoples custom maps and content. It needs a few more game modes in the future but its quite solid and 8 player deathmatch can still get the adrenaline pumping.
The only question here is if the developers will continue giving the product the much needed improvements with indoor environment design and a lighting system which works equally well in both outdoor and indoor environments. It is a huge step in the right direction and I'm glad I backed the product.

Alan Wake is an episodic pschological thriller, with 6 episodes in total. The graphics are amazing, and the game was smooth, running on High quality for basically everything. The tiny details, such as the yellow writing on the walls, are one of the things that make this game special. The character development through the two main characters; Alan Wake and his agent, Barry; was phenonmenal. Everything from the way they grew individually, to the way the grew as friends and partners was incredibly well thought out. This making it extremely easy to get invested in the characters and what was happening to them. The music felt sinister enough in just the right places and the change of pace from slow, story time and lore learning to faster, more intense combat. The combat system alone was something that really drew me into this game. The Fight with Light style is a style I highly enjoyed, once I got the hang of it. All of the game mechanics were fairly easy to learn, and only slightly harder to master. All in all I highly enjoyed this game, and think that anyone into story games or thriller/suspense games would enjoy too!

The level design is original, stylish and will often surprise you. It's often quite tongue-in-cheek and takes neither itself nor the player too seriously.
Only the presentation of the educational texts is somewhat dry, although they are interesting and well written and tie in well with the sights and sounds of the levels.
The game can be finished in 2-4 hours depending on your degree of completionism and offers a lot of variety on the way. For five bucks, you can't go wrong.

I played this to completion because I thought that surely they wouldn't have made an entire game around three or rour repeated tasks. Unfortunately, that's exactly what they did. Following a promising if not buggy introduction, Mafia III devolves into an incredibly rushed mess of a game that utilizes the Assassin's Creed I approach to gameplay- unlock the ability to take out targets by choosing the same few options to create opportunity over and over until the game ends. As enticing as a plot centered around revenge may be, this is not enough to maintain player interest. This is a shame, because Mafia III does have potential.
Having spent time in Louisiana I can tell you that the world does a good job of creating the odd and unique feel of the state in a lot of areas. The soundtrack is incredible. There are a few mechanics, such as the rearview mirror, that work wonderfully.
Overall, though, this game would have benefited from at least another six months or development and essentially feels like a bunch of pieces slapped together in order to create an experience longer than a few hours. I can’t help but feel that this game is a victim of a marketing team given to much power and say in development and release.

Dust is a game of preference. The biggest thing that people will notice is the whole “Furry” debate. Now if you could care less if you are in a world of animals, have watched any cartoon or game as a child that used animals, or just have common sense, Dust is for you. Gameplay wise, it’s a hack and slash/RPG/puzzler/adventure. If you enjoy hitting things with a sword, this is a good game for you. If you like combining powers for devastating results, this game is for you. If you like puzzles, but don’t want to rip your own hair out due to difficulty, this game is for you. If you like exploring, plundering, and/or simply hanging out in a hub, this game is for you.
This game’s story is also a matter of preference. I don’t want to ruin anything for you, so if your iffy on story lines, know that the side quests will fill whatever void within you. What more, the many Easter eggs that you can find will really make any gamer smile.
All in all, Dust isn’t a long game, but what it does have is hours of entertainment. If you are at all interested in this game, I would recommend buying it. And if you’re still on the fence, just wait for a sale, because this game is worth it.
