I completed the first game yesterday and I enjoyed it a fair bit.
I loved its variety, story, character building and level design.
But I also hated the cover mechanics, gunplay and just overall gameplay stuff.
Well, this time around, this game did it all kind of opposite.
I'll start off with mentioning that the style of graphics/filters that this game has is pretty damn awesome. It looks like a documentary that had been filmed about the adventure of our protagonists. There are even things like rendering bugs, timers and best of all: censoring. Yup. When you see Lynch's flobby♥♥♥♥♥♥ you'll be spared the details. Same goes with a mob boss's daughter's ♥♥♥♥♥.
The shooting is great and feels very responsive. All gunsounds also sound amazing. Although later on in the game, enemies become slightly bulletspongey, which I don't approve. An early game enemy can take 2-3 bullets max. While at the same time, a late game enemy will most likely take 5-8 bodyshots or 1-3 headshots.
The sound design is... fitting. I personally didn't like the idea of excluding music and adding some weird noises to be played every few minutes, but at the same time, the lack of music introduces loud gunshots that were truly powerful thanks to the lack of tunes. I would've preferred a lack of music in the key points of the game, but that's mostly a personal preference and what they did was still executed well.
The story is less interesting than the first K&L, but this story will instead make you care about the characters a bit more and maybe have you even root for them. The ending, while hated by most, felt ok to me. It was pretty abrupt, but looking at the game's tone, it made sense. Same went with transitioning between levels and the upright skipping of filler content, like pointless running. It made sense in this documentary format and I'm fine with it ending like it did. I would've preferred a quick 2 minute cutscene of what happened next, but it doesn't really matter. The characters are pretty boring now compared to the predecessor, but since they were built up, there was no reason to just keep adding stuff there.
The length of the game has been its criticism. But... why? This game was short, but sweet. It never really had a dull moment, except for the last mission. If you want a long game, then just play Minecraft and WoW and stay there. Those are people that don't understand the idea of quality hours vs. random game hours.
The tone that this game has is gritty... really gritty. There is death and violence, sure, but the way that it's presented is what really impacted me. It does the gritty stuff without ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue, without bad graphic filters or anything like that. At one point in the game, it even felt more like a horror game than anything, even though I was shooting at enemies and there were no scares there. What scared me was the idea of all of that happening and looking realistic enough to be considered plausible.
The spectacle that the game offers in the game is really damn great. It's like an indie action flick that knows its audience. There are no moments of downtime really and that's just perfect. Seeing random character development is not what this game should focus on and they understood that.
And for my last point: Variety. It's... I mean... Hmm.. It's weird to talk about this one. There's variety, but it's nothing compared to the first game. You're mostly running around on the streets of Shanghai or in the buildings of Shanghai, but the variety comes in in the locations you're in. There's never a point, where something feels familiar or similar to something before. So, while it doesn't excel in this, it doesn't really fail at it either.
Overall:
Objective grade: 6/10
Above average
Subjective grade: 8/10
A truly great game
(All games start at a 5/10 and move upwards/downwards based on the pros and cons presented in the review)
P.S. All of this is from single-player. I didn't play in co-op. We all know co-op is better, so take that into consideration.

is a tough sequel to discuss and furthermore justifies its name.
Immediately from the opening intro, as the entire game presents itself as a realistic documentary, it doesn't restrain itself from being shameless as it follows the original two main characters on their very twisted and violent journey to survive the grotesque depths of Shanghai. Their adventure unexpectedly descends into mysterious paths that are rather clever and unsettling in some memorable sequences.
Some particular improvements are major upgrades to previous elements from its predecessor in terms of controls and execution. Unfortunately, as its predecessor upon completing the story, the content provided isn't nearly enough to retain replay value aside from optional difficulty settings, achievements, arcade challenges, and gaming cooperation with selective partners. Eventually the tedious segments become rehashed along with less surprising outcomes when played frequently.
The story itself, though not exactly
epic or ambitious as advertised, still delivered a gripping experience that captured the horrific shallowness of crime syndicates and deception among partnerships and greed. Though not a perfect game, this chapter in the franchise shouldn't be missed even by newcomers with low expectations.

Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae is Musou with just the combat or Devil May Cry without the exploration or complex combo system. What is left is an arena brawler that has surprising depth, since you unlock new moves as you play that encourages you to explore what combos you can make. The game throws stronger versions of the enemies you fight over time, so you are encouraged to strengthen your character as you play. The lack of variety in enemy movesets and models is unfortunate, but the limited scope of the game makes sense in that context. Character models look great and the overall system and memory cost is almost a non issue. Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae lacks the depth of other games, but it offers decent gameplay for what you are getting. I would like to see a port of this on VITA, but since a PS4 game has been out for over a year I don't expect that would happen.

Type Rider isn't for everyone, it's a somewhat educational platformer/puzzle (along the lines of Super Meat Boy, but far more family friendly, and not as hard).  Honestly, had I not picked it up for "free" in a bundle I probably wouldn't have purchased it based on the the "cover".  However, having played it, I'm glad I got it, and that I gave it a try.  I would absolutely pay up to a few dollars for it (I'm cheap with games, that translates to about $5, MAYBE $10 for most people), had I not already played through it, and for most people there's virtually no replay value.
If you're looking for something that you can safely put your kids down in front of and let them have at it, without having to worry about what they might see or hear, this is perfect, and like I said, it's somewhat educational; teaching about the history of writing in the prologue, then little tidbits about several fonts throughout.  If you're looking for a casual game, that will at times make you want to scream at your monitor, this is good for that as well.
The game is very creative, and although the first... probably 75% of the game is incredibly easy, the creativity in the gameplay made it fun.  The music is very pleasant (save for the hidden level, you'll want to mute your speakers after the first attempt), and the artwork is well-done, IMO.
The unique physics made the game very interesting, by which I'm referring to the "character" being a colon; two round dots that are loosely attached, and can roll over each other, even going on separate sides of thin platforms at times, and slightly rubber-banding at other times.  The same physics that make the gameplay intersting also make certain parts very challenging and frustrating, like when you're trying to balance on a narrow ledge and one dot keeps pulling the other off the side.
The entire game, including the very frustrating bonus level, took me a little under three hours, and that also included a trip to get food, so it's not very long, but ultimately it was entertaining, and even at the full $5 price, that means it was cheaper (for around the same length of entertainment) than going to a movie.  I'd probably pay that, although I'm sure you can pick it up for a dollar or two on sale.

I just couldn't bring myself to like this game no matter how hard I tried. I'm a huge fan of the Metroidvania genre, which includes games like Castlevania Symphony of the Night, Super Metroid, Cave Story, Muramasa The Demon Blade and so forth...
I approached Dust thinking it would be a bit like Muramasa because of its huge character sprites, similar anime-style art direction and also a big focus on melee combat. That's also what Dust is in essence, but when compared to Muramasa everything just seems very dull. The combat is floaty and I think there is not enough impact when you execute all your moves. The animations are very cool and flashy but the execution just feels wrong and rewardless. Your combo meter goes up into the hundreds, but there is just no feeling of impact. Also where Muramasa kind of had this alternation between combat and exploration, Dust is basically combat all the time, and the already average combat system becomes annoying after a few hours.
And that is basically my biggest problem in the gameplay of Dust, but then we get into the elephant in the room... The artstyle and the voice acting
There's nothing wrong with the execution and I know what they were going for, but the governing ideas behind it all rubbed me the wrong way. I just don't like the overly humanized furry design of the game. I know this is probably a reason why many people became interested about the game in the first place, but me as a fan of only the Metroidvania genre would not have wanted these characters to look that way.
Also a very personal nitpick is the voice acting for the two main leads. I found Dust and Fidget extremely annoying. I can hear that both the voice actors are very talented in their own right, but it just annoys me when Dust has to deliver all his lines with this annoying emo kid vibe and Fidget has this high pitched overly enthusiastic voice. As I sit here after finishing Dust: An Elysian Tail, I find myself having to fight back tears while thinking of the revelation-packed ending. It is not often that a game presents such a profound and gripping narrative, in this world of rushed to market cookie-cutter shooters and overblown RPGS. And yet here is a game, built in less than four years by a single driven individual. Dean "Noogy" Dodrill himself handled the programming, visuals, writing and animation, and only reached out for help with the music and voiceovers. And yet this seemingly simple metroidvania manages to surpass the production values of nearly any recent big budget blockbuster that can be named.
The gameplay in Dust is fast paced and compelling, with a combat system that takes the best parts of games like Castlevania SOTN and Devil May Cry. As in DMC, you can rack up insane combos for extra experience points (my personal best was just over 3500 hits). Upgradable abilities earned along the way keeps everything feeling fresh, and will open the way to previously inaccessible areas, a la Metroid. A continuously updating automap will keep you from ever getting lost in the game's vast world.
Dust certainly has a lot of stuff to do, with a number of sidequests nearly bordering on the excessive. There are countless secrets to be found, so be sure to explore every nook and cranny for destructible walls. If nothing else you will be rewarded with a Mysterious Wall Chicken. Noogy definitely packed the game to the brim with tributes to many classic games, both old and new (to get the "wall chicken" joke one simply needs to play Castlevania). Add to all that a blueprint-based crafting system, and Dust's adventure just keeps getting deeper and deeper.
When it comes down to the quality of the narrative and voice acting, Dust: An Elysian Tail is definitely no slouch. It is near impossible not to fall in love with the varied cast of characters and their often wacky hijinks (Dust's companion Fidget is one of the most endearing characters I have seen in years, and does well to break the "Navi" stereotype). That's not to say the whole game is a barrel of laughs, it gets incredibly serious towards the end with a major plot twist that will leave player's heads spinning. With an epic plotline that will last the average player at least 8 hours and with sidequests out the wazoo, players will definitely get their money's worth with this game. Dust: An Elysian Tail is simply too good to pass up!

The Binding of Isaac is a fun game. Diving into the game, I found the same satisfaction of playing, like I did with Demon's Souls on Playstation 3. You will die a lot, but that slow progression, and the satisfaction from defeating a boss for the first time is great.
The soundtrack get's a little repetitive after a while, although it is a short and good soundtrack.
For being a fairly short game, it still has a great system where it lays every new level map randomly + different bosses for each playthrough + all the loot.
Even though the game is depressing in many ways and there is an awful lot of blood and tears, there is a twisted and hilarious sense of humor in the game, and I found myself laughing at different bosses and loot I got.
So all in all this is a fun game, and definitely a must-buy if you are a fan of the roguelike genre, and since it is so dirt cheap I also strongly recommend it for newcomers and computer gamers alike.

A masterpiece. Only Cave Story is more of a marvel of individual achievement in video game development. Even if the gameplay was bad, the work that went into this game would be impressive. Fortunately, Dust is engrossing. I don't like crafting systems, yet I liked crafting in Dust. I don't usually attempt 100% completion, but I did in Dust. Amnesia as a plot device is usually bad, but Dust pulls it off.
Then there are the aspects that I knew I would like. Metroid-style exploration and upgrades. Hand-drawn cutscenes, environments, and character portraits. References to other indie games.
Half of Dust is exactly the kind of game I knew I wanted. The other half is the game that I didn't ask for, but ended up loving. Dust succeeds where lesser games fail.

The Last Tinker is, perhaps, one of THE best games I've played in the past few years. The entire game somehow managed to mix a bunch of different things -- the old quirky feeling of games like Banjo-Kazooie and Spyro, the free-range parkour of Prince of Persia, an almost whimsical setting/look, an utterly terrifying villain/force, and a serious plot -- while still feeling like something completely fresh and brand new rather than just rehashing old nostalgia. Everything about this game is good, and the mistakes it makes are few.
Let's start with the music. The music is amazing and well-made, and absolutely catchy at times. There is a point where the music goes utterly harsh and terrible (as in badly done), but that is a completely plot-related reason. All of the tracks fit their areas fairly well, and if there was any unfitting combinations, it was subtle enough that I never even came close to noticing it. In fact, the music is so important to the game that there are sections where you have to jump or move in time with the beat in order to progress, which makes you really feel immersed in it!
The graphics are absolutely amazing. They tie well together with each other, and they look unique. Unlike a lot of other realistically-styled games (which could almost be interchangable), the whimiscal, I'd say almost coloring-book-and-culturally-designed-look of this game stands out; it reminds me of designs and artwork used for things like pinatas almost, with every character and area having multiple patterns. Every stage and character looks unique (group-wise, if not individually) on its normal design... until the Bleakness runs through and makes it all monochrome and same-looking. However, rather than detract from the game, it
to it, showing you just how terrifying the force you're up against is and just what the world is when you strip away its individuality and destroy everything that made it unique.
The plot and writing is some of the best I've ever seen. Like any writing, it can hiccup a bit at times, but overall it's absolutely fantastic, the characters are amusing and quirky and tend to feel unique, and even though he never speaks a word your main character feels just as unique as the rest of them. The plot, itself, is actually quite terrifying, and deeper than it first appears to be. Without spoiling anything, it's just as good as the rest of the writing, but stands
it rather than
it despite all the differences.
Now for the negative parts.
Firstly, the game can be very confusing at times. While you do have a way to show where you're supposed to go, it can be outright unhelpful at times, leaving you without knowing where you're supposed to go or what you're supposed to do when you get there. Usually, a mix of that direction system, backtracking, and exploration can help you find your way, but it's definitely something that can be a bit frustrating at times.
Secondly, a few of the battles can be incredibly frustrating to outright unfair. Small platforms with shield-generating enemies and tons of normal enemies (that you can't hit until the shield-ones are gone) are not unknown, and a lot of the more difficult battles you can't actually run past and skip. Additionally, if you die, you have to start the entire battle over again. On top of all this, enemies can be placed very nastily and with far too many numbers, making just running through areas as fast as possible sometimes the best course of action, which detracts from the experience as you're missing out on the beautifully-crafted areas.
Thirdly, the Color Spirits' powers feel vastly underused. While it does give you more in-battle powers and even a small handful of out-of-battle-powers, the game hypes up Koru and the tinkers in general as some powerful, creative force, yet you so very rarely
like such a force when your powers are mostly just used in fighting enemies. This is especially true for the last Color Spirit that you get, which is only used for a single thing and only in the final boss fight.
Overall, I would say that The Last Tinker: City of Colors is an absolutely amazing game. They do so much RIGHT with it, and it feels like an amazing, enjoyable, and -- unlike many games --
experience which is sure to stand out against the crowd of samey-old-type games.
Pick it up. If you like platforming, or unique games, or fun plays, pick it up. Trust me: you won't be sorry.

I notice that The Last Tinker: City of Colors is often compared to Banjo-Kazooie and said to be a platformer. I don't think this is an accurate comparison. This isn't to say that The Last Tinker is bad. Only that other games bear a better comparison. I think that a better comparison is to a game like Beyond Good and Evil, or perhaps 3d Zelda titles. I hope the reason for this comparison will become clear through the review.
First of all the platforming in The Last Tinker is context based and not free. You cannot actually jump at will in this game. You run at edges and leap to the next designated spot.  The challenge is not based on jumping onto difficult platforms, but on timing your leaps between platforms. The platforming is more a puzzle than a test of dexterity. The platforms can be considered more a mode of transport than the main challenge.
What you do spend a lot of you time doing is fighting. The combat is basically puzzle based. You have a couple of unique strikes, which are useful against certain enemies. You often have to choose which enemy to defeat first, and use your skills to keep the other enemies off you. The combat feels a little strange. You can approach the same battle in slightly different ways, with one time earning your death and the next trouncing everyone quickly. I believe this may be the result of the puzzle emphasis on combat. If you abuse your somewhat very powerful abilities you will win. If you go in as a traditional brawler and don’t abuse your abilities, you won’t do well at all. What I mean is that the combat is not nuanced. You solve the combat, you don’t win through strength or dexterity. This would make it similar to the platforming in that the challenge is solving the situation. Enacting your solution is usually quite easy.
The checkpoint system is generous, and unlimited. So any frustrations that may be felt are reduced to very minimal levels.
Puzzles are the fundamental challenge of the game. This is experienced through both the above mentioned combat and platforming, and also normal puzzles you would normally encounter during an adventure game. Challenges are usually not highly dexterity based.  You quite often interact with other characters to solve puzzles. The puzzles are quite varied. While no puzzle is particularly difficult, each puzzle meshes very well with the universe. In a sense, you learn about the world through solving puzzles.
The overall story is very important to the structure of The Last Tinker. Every level feels like it advances the plot, and feels like a natural extension of the previous events. The exploration is linear. There is no hub and there are no levels that branch off. There is a continuous story. The levels are chapters in a story.  This means that the gameplay always feels wedded to the world you are exploring. I never felt like anything I was doing was game logic or ‘just because’ you needed something to be in the way.
You spend a lot of the game surrounded by other inhabitants, and this goes a long way towards making the world feel believable. You interact with, if not every inhabitant of the world, what feels like enough inhabitants to understand and care about the world. And the main character feels like his contribution to the world is defined by a heroism of spirit, and not of being the strongest person around. The other characters you interact with achieve a balance of being very defined, and in a sense extreme, but also being human and relatable.
The story is very well told. It has a fairy tale quality, which means that while the story is not complicated, it does demonstrate something fundamental about humanity.
I highly recommend this game to people interested in an adventure built on a fairy tale style story and immersion in a fantasy world. If you are looking for a intricate gameplay based game then it is better to look elsewhere.

Alan Wake is a third person shooter / horror game that follows the story of Alan Wake, a writer trying to take a relaxing break away from writing in a small town called "Bright Falls". Unbeknownst to him there is a sp00py evil shadow thing that lives beneath the lake plotting to take over the world or something. Now, Mr. Writer's Block must fight the shadow monster to rescue his wife. The game also has a very neat "storybook" feel to it since the main character narrates parts of the game, which does a great job tying in the "writer" part of the main character.
Gameplay consists of pretty basic third person shooting with a small twist, the scary shadow monsters you fight are invulnerable until you scare the shadows off of them by shining a light source on them for a few seconds (most of the time by pointing a flashlight in their face). After that, they become vulnerable to guns. The game doesn't get it's "horror" title for nothing. The game keeps you on edge by setting a very tense / dark atmosphere by making use of fog to obscure far away objects. Combine this with the very dark environment and enemies that can appear at any time from any direction end up making the player feel constantly on edge making this a very competent horror experience.
One other thing I will commend this game for is the "extra" bonus levels, which are sort of like an epilogue to the main story. Since they are sort of "dream" levels, they are really fun to play, since they don't have to follow the laws of nature and that boring crap. It really adds a unique twist on the gameplay and also ties the story over to the next game.
If there's one thing i'm going to criticize about this game, its going to be the cut scenes. While the game does do some of it's storytelling in-game, it does much of it's exposition and plot development through pre-rendered cut scenes. While I don't have a problem with pre-rendered cut scenes in general, Alan Wake does it wrong. They use the same game assets the game uses, which is, again, not bad
, but they don't look particularly great. First off, The resolution and framerate are very low, which might have been passable in 2010, but are not very pleasing to look at today. Not only that, but the characters movement and facial animations are very stiff and awkward. And I know they used pre-rendered cut scenes to hide loading screens but with all these things combined, the cut scenes end up looking worse than the actual game. Compare that to Bayonetta, which recently had a re-release on Steam. While they also used pre-rendered cut scenes using the same game assets that the game uses, the animations are nothing short of fantastic, and they take the opportunity to do some large scale cinematics that current hardware (and especially 2009 console hardware) aren't capable of doing at a decent framerate. Plus they appear to be at LEAST 1080p, if not higher. So aside from the lower-than-normal framerate, you might not even know that some parts of the game are pre-rendered.

I played this game a long time ago and never left a review for it, so I'm going to rectify that now.
That said, though, I'll be very brief about it.
You can tell my over-all time with it is just over 15 hours,
so that's more or less the total length of the game.
Alan Wake is just a fantastic story-telling experience.
It looks great, it sounds great, it has very solid voice acting.
Playing this game, I said to myself:  "This is what good story telling and pacing should be."
So I believe this game does set a certain standard for how to do it correctly.
But this is game you play entirely for the story.
The gameplay is extremely simplistic, and repetitive.
Often it's only "hard" because you're being overwhelmed or flat out "ganked".
There's only 2-3 enemy types in the game, and the bosses are just stronger versions of said enemies.
Personally, I'd recommend setting the game on easy, because all difficulty does (from what I remember), is change the number of bullets required to down an enemy and since taking more bullets to kill an enemy doesn't add anything to combat and just makes it more frustrating (note: frustrating, not challenging in my opinion), it's better to keep that to a minimum.
This is an amazing game if you play it for the story.
If you're looking for fun or engaging combat, you won't find it here.
The ending does kinda fall flat but isn't that how it always is with horror plots?
Really hypes things up and then the explanation isn't as complex as you hoped.
It's still well worth it if you can grab it on sale or something, for sure.

EDIT:
Robot Entertainment has decided to dump Gameforge as the EU publisher and publish the game themselves. I would like to applaud their decision. Better late (in this case quite late) than never. However, I will not change this review to recommended for the simple fact that they shouldn't have selected that publisher in the first place. This is what ultimately ruined the EU version of the game, and it should be a good example to any other developers who consider Gameforge as their publisher (although more are more developers are duming Gameforge nowadays). I am not going to edit any of the details below since I haven't played the game after I wrote the original review, but I will most certainly consider returning to the game after the migration of the servers is complete.
Here's the original review:
Part 1:
How To Kill A Potentially Good Game (For Dummies):
- Make a potentially good game.
- Give the publishing rights to Gameforge.
- Done!
I mean, let's take a look at some of the games that Gameforge ruined:
- Aion EU (utterly dead)
- Tera EU (completely dead)
- Soldier Front 2 EU (a.k.a. "S.K.I.L.L., although the only skill you need for that game is a wallet)
- Raiderz EU (shut down)
- Mythos (shut down)
- Katsuro: Path of Honor (shut down)
- Hellbreed (shut down)
... the list goes on ...
Why would ANYONE in their right mind allow Gameforge to publish their game?! Gameforge is known as the WORST European publisher. No one does business with them anymore and they're close to filing for bankruptcy. They already closed their location in Berlin. Why would you do that, Robot Entertainment?
It could have been a great game...
Part 2:
Since some lovely folks commented that they would REALLY (real-time executive realness) want me to review the game itself, and not its publisher, here you go:
Pros:
- Great voice acting. The way they went with it (overly sarcastic) could have ended up being cringy, like the one in Wildstar, but instead, they did a good job with it.
- Good animations. The game feels like it's polished and well executed.
- Short queues and loading screens.
- Interesting tower defence gameplay (as far as the Survival mode goes).
- Character development and a crafting system.
- Runs great on a high-end laptop.
Cons:
- Poorly optimized for computers that are supposed to be able to run the game on its minimal settings.
- Gets quite repetitive quite fast.
- Grinding for materials can be tedious.
- The Siege mode needs a lot of work. It is nowhere near as polished as the Survival mode.
- The Survival mode can be too short at the early levels.
- The developer decided to give the game to the worst publisher in Europe, and probably even the world. I mean, even EA isn't that bad anymore. I guess Gameforge could compete against Webzen for the first place.
- You are able to buy almost everything with real cash, and if you don't want to, you better prepare for a long grind.
- Did I mention how stupid the decision to give the publishing rights to Gameforge was? I think I did, but oh well...
- The game is basically a cash shop oriented version of OMD! 2.
There you go! You're welcome.
P.S.: Needless to say, I won't be spending a dime on this game, as long as Failforge gets a cut. I encourage everyone to do the same. Robot Entertainment might get their heads out of their... (you got the point) and change the publisher before it's too late for the game.

I was in the mood for a Third-Person-Shooter this weekend, so I loaded up this game, because I haven't played through it since it came out in August 2010 (man, over 6 six years ago already. time really flies...).
The first thing I turned off was the shaky camera, because I would get motion sick from that. So, thankfully it can be turned off in the options menu. I started the game and I have to say I was pleasently surprised by it. I really like the setting, it's not a space station or a futuristic planet or New York City for once, but instead dark and dirty back alleys in Shanghai, China. I really like that, because it feels fresh to me (haven't played Sleeping Dogs, though), but I can't tell if it's anything like the real Shanghai at all, because I haven't been there yet. The visual style of the game is also very unique: it has a weird filter all over it. For example, a light on the ceiling is not only there, it creates a bar of light all across the screen. And there are some other strange effects like that. It works here with the setting and all that, but I don't think it would work in many other games. The gunplay is pretty solid and satisfying, but nothing to stand out. The cover system is acceptable. It works most of the time, but it feels a bit clunky and unpolished.
The campaign is shockingly short, I've beaten it on normal difficulty in 3,5 hours. That's REALLY short, but then again, I personally don't mind playing a shorter game that I can beat in one sitting. The story starts out pretty interesting, but gets more confusing as it goes on. It's just not told very well at all. What really sucks is the ending, which is very abrupt and leaves a lot of questions unanswered and a lot of things unresolved. Also, the game is absolutely 100% linear, which again, is something I don't mind. There are enough open world third-person-shooters on the market. Besides, I think linear games keep the pace up better than open world games.
I haven't tried the coop mode or multiplayer because from what I've heard it's pretty much non-existent anymore.
So, would I recommend this game? Tough call. I enjoyed playing through it and liked the setting. But Space Marine, Splinter Cell Blacklist, Red Faction Armageddon, Tomb Raider, Sniper Elite V2 and Spec Ops The Line (especially that one) are all probably better third-person-shooters than this one. And Kane & Lynch 2 has some rough edges and shortcomings. But if you don't mind these and are looking for a few hours of mindless non-stop action, then (and only then) I would recommend that you play this game.

Great educational game for anyone who is remotely interested in the history of typography which might seem to be a very odd interest until you realize how fundamental these developements are not only for art history but for everyday life as well. It is a good game in that it is fun to play through occasionally and you feel like learning something too, the mechanics are solid enough, but not very finely tuned, which doesn't affect the overall experience but at very few times it can make the game challenging in a cheap way.
I can only recommend picking this up, especially when on sale. It clearly stands out in the mediocrity of educational games and is graphically quite artistic, though ironically not always typographically correct as there cases of wrong hyphenation, some odd linebreaks, and stretchings in the texts (might just be an issue with the german version though).
Looking at the potential that is there, it is a pity that the game only occasionally manages to transcend the "museum-experience" (i.e. looking at things, reading text about things, looking at things again) when it comes to informing the player about the background and a more playable approach would have been welcomed also as an inspiration for other games. There are some ideas for that, like, when you make your way through an offset printing machine.  But it is not elaborated enough to understand how it works, it still heavily relies on the player reading the corresponding text. One of the later stages is a bit more about playing with what you're supposed to learn, but imho gets a carried away into non-typographical territory. But this is somewhat of an unfair point to make here, as - as far as I am aware - nobody else has pulled that off on that scale of teaching so far.

This game is most definitely the purest space exploration simulator there is. If you have any interest in rocket science, space programs, astronomy, or just space in general, then give this game a look.
In Kerbal Space Program, you run your own space program on the planet Kerbin (which is not at all like Earth -- don't mind the continent that looks like Africa), which is populated by little green people called Kerbals. Anything you want to do in the Kerbin solar system can be done. Want to make a moon base? Build deep-space probes? Drive rovers on other planets? Maybe just get some cool pictures of foreign landscapes? This game has you covered. If you can think it, you can build it.
There are several game modes, the first being "career," where you have to run your space program's administration as well as your research to unlock new rocket tech. You'll have to manage your funds to buy parts, your reputation among the Kerbal public, and your science points that let you progress. Next is "science" mode, where you only have to worry about advancing your tech tree. Finally, there is "sandbox" mode, where you have access to everything, instantly.
Within the solar system, you can explore 6 other planets and their moons. But don't get too excited! Unless you cheat, you'll have to do some clever engineering to get to them. KSP's dynamics can be difficult to master, but as the saying goes, once you're in orbit, you're halfway to anywhere. Although, since you control your vessels manually, some practice will go into it.
Is the vanilla game too boring for you? Then don't fear - KSP has a great community that makes modded content all the time (and the devs continually update the game themselves). Even if you don't want mods, check out some of the players' own ideas. Truly, it is very difficult to run out of things to do in this game.
To sum up, Kerbal Space Program is an excellent game for anyone interested in space. With so much content and freedom, players will spend hour upon hour trying new ideas. KSP is 100% a recommend.

tl;dr It is not good. It's buggy, the UI is bad, the writing is bland and the puzzles are mediocre.
So the good:
The sound design and music stand out.
The game looks pretty good for a Kickstarter title.
The voice actors are quite good, I enjoyed listening to Maythorn speak.
There is some visual storytelling going on in the game that was interesting to see.
Manipulating objects in your inventory is novel.
The environments are nice.
Now the bad:
The worst is the game's stability. My first launch of the game met with a crash. The first time I flipped through my notebook I accidentally clicked "Previous Page" while zoomed into a note, and the game crashed.
I went through loading screens to find no textures then the game crashed. It crashed a lot for me.
And it was also really slow for the graphical quality. I don't have an amazing rig, it can only run Overwatch at about 90 FPS, but I could barely eke out 30 FPS average on this game, with middling settings.
The puzzles are OK, though there is not any real progression through them; every puzzle stands as an island with a few exceptions. The "Ah-Ha!" moments are few, the puzzles themselves feel more like busywork than anything else (Especially the puzzle in the Library and all the Alchemy puzzles). There's a few times when there is absolutely no indication on what you need to do next beside wandering around aimlessly.
The story is trite beyond measure. It is yet another rehash of "The power will consume you" storyline while providing poor evidence of it within the game.
I'm willing to forgive a cliche plot for characters, but there's no reason to like or hate the characters because they're so bland. One is your generic explorer who came to Quern to learn stuff, and learn stuff he did. The other is a generic
who is only interested in a "balance" and keeping people out of Quern because she sucked at her job.
What little is explained in the world is not explained well. You are told the story instead of shown it, culminating in a moment with one character taking 5 minutes to dismantle any reason why you would care about her or her entire argument by telling you her own backstory in a slow, plodding, predictable way, yet trying to frame it as though it were some great revelation.
If you want a cut-rate Myst game, Quern isn't bad. I just cannot recommend this game because it is aggressively mediocre in every respect.

This game is a beautiful gem, and one of my favorites. I keep looking for others like it. I think I hear people complain most about the story writing, but I really liked it and felt it moved very naturally. The voice acting is very good overall and feels out of place only rarely and very forgiveably. Combat for a button mashing kind of game is pretty clever besides looking very good. It is a somewhat short game and leveling is pretty quick, but it is surprisingly well balanced. If you play normal difficulty you won't find many skill-based threats, just ones you have to learn how to approach to reliably (and then perhaps easily) overcome. I found tough difficulty on a second playthrough occasionally lead me want to grind for a little more experience or items and die several times at cruxes, but there are never bull---- challenges, not one. This is also true of almost every secret in the game, and really only one I think I wouldn't have figured out without a guide. One really fun aspect of the game is the Cirelian Trial challenges so don't pass them up. There are relatively few side quests and fewer that lead you much out of your way. I don't know that that's a good or bad thing as much as just the way the game is put together, but it does give it a good feeling of cohesion to the story and I think the developer chose a very good scope for the gameplay overall. I will offer the following critique that I felt the ending was just kind of emotionally a miss. I think the developer had lots of good pieces and didn't put them together very well at the end, but I'm semi-detached from most stories anyway so maybe you'll disagree. I do truly love this game though. The characters are adorable. I bought the soundtrack (it is a good soundtrack!) and listened to it for a day straight after playing the game the first time because it left me with a sense of loss and heartbreak kind of like the Portal games did. Anyway buy it. You'll like it!

text:
The creators of The Last Tinker attempted to create a 3D-platformer like they were in the good old days about ten or fifteen years ago. The intentions are good, but unfortunately the creators must have thought the development of this genre during the last few years was a massive improvement. There certainly were improvements like ditching the classic live system or autosaving. But for me, on-rails-platforming is not an improvement.
On-rails-platforming means that the protagonist, Koru in the case of The Last Tinker, jumps automatically. You just walk around while holding a button and overcome the obstacles automatically. Some games like the AC series have an excuse for such a simplification: a lot of background stuff is going on which you have to keep track off, focussing on precise jumping all the time would be too hard. However, this excuse is not valid for The Last Tinker.
Even though he refers to something slightly different, I would like to quote Ben Croshaw here: "[...] there's no challenge to this! This is not platforming, this is just walking down a very unusually-shaped corridor."

Fortunately the developers of The Last Tinker made this observation as well and included timing sections to add
some challenge to the platforming. (For the record, the same holds for the developers of Enslaved.)
Enough about the "platforming", let us look at other aspects of the game. It is rich in variety after all.  There is some combat, of course, the common button-smashing combo-based combat. There are some railsliding sections, where you have to continuously switch between rails to not smash into obstacles. And there are many puzzles of various types which are usually nice, but not diffifcult.
What I really like about The Last Tinker is that it tells its story not exclusively by the means of cutscenes and dialogues, but also by the environment itself. You can literally see how the city is estranged and united again.
Conclusion: The Last Tinker has its weaknesses, but it shines in other aspects. It is not challenging, but also doesn't get boring easily. Overall The Last Tinker offers a very nice experience.

The further you get into the game the more inspirations you can see the developers adapted and put their own spin on it. If you like Psychonauts, Mario Sunshine, Banjo Kazooie, Jak and Daxter then this game is a must play. Everything feels nostalgic and really great.
The story itself is surprisingly good and it was enough to keep me interested throughout. There wasn't a point when the story got in the way or pushed it in your face, it was subtle and benefited strongly from that.
The visuals are super colourful and the art style is impressive also. The character and world designs never got boring. The game also supports colourblind mode in case you need that.
The only negative I can think of is the combat, the game kinda forces you to use certain moves to kill certain enemies. Some of them will be shielded, some will just kill you in 1 hit. While it adds a lot of variety in combat it sort of gets repetitive. It has a combo system that's hardly implemented which is a shame. And seeing as fighting is what you do 80% of the time it kinda slows the pace down.
You should highly consider playing this tho. It took me around 8 hours to finish on and off. Aside from the story there are collectibles to find also, you can go back to areas at anytime in case you missed them giving it more replay value.

So I've finally found some time to play this game and... it's perfectly fine. A fun action clicker that will eat up some of your time untill you get used to the difficulty.
By no means is it an AAA masterpiece and a Game of the Year material, but honestly, you could spend your money way worse. Fiery Dissaster delivers what it promisses - fast paced action with a pinch of strategy and resource management (in regards to your regular attack overheat metter, upgrades, or even unburnt ground that damages the enemies more the first time your lava plume lands on it, etc.).
I honestly don't know why somebody would find it not reccomenable for people who are into such games. One reviewer says he/she doesn't see the point of this game. Well, for the most part, the purpose of any game is to be fun for the player, and Fiery Dissaster is fun (again, if you like such games). Another one says it's not really tower defence and strategy. Well, while agree it's not a full blown strategy game, neither is Bejeweled and it still has the tag. There are different flavors of strategy, and this game is one of them. Also, it's not a tower defense game? Then what the hell is it? You have a tower (volcano), and you defend it. You don't build stuff apart from getting upgrades, but of course it's a tower defense game! Also, if you check the instructions box (or play long enough, which the negative reviewers didn't apparently), you'll see it's actually a bit more complex than meets the eye. Hell, it even has two player mode!
Ok, rant over.
In regards to technicalities, again, they're fine. Simple, but neat, 2D graphics and OK music and sounds (apart from the overheatting noise - goddamn, that's annoying. Fortunatelly, you can turn it of in options). You also get a well made intro and a dark-ish plot about everybody getting crazyier and crazyier as the story goes, that also serves the purpose of introducing new upgrades. Wickedly fun. Also, the game is polished. We all know what "gems" one can get from Greenlight, and this game shows that the creators at least gave a damn. I haven't had any critical errors, gamebreaking bugs or anything like that. In fact, I don't think I've had any trouble with the game whatsoever.
As far as I know, this is the studio's first game. This means not everything will be perfect, of course. Apart from the overheating sound (I know, I know, it's just... damn, I guess the creators and beta testers were good enough not to hear it constantly, like I did) and OK graphics and sound (again, enough, but nothing too fancy) there are some things that show their inexperience, but nothing too bad.
My issues/advice for the creators:
- why is it called Arcade mode when it's basically survival? You could avoid at least one negative review if you called it that, so that people don't click first to check gameplay.
- The color of unlocked missions and locked missions is the same on my monitor (the former should be white, the latter grey I guess, everything white-ish for me).
- Arcade mode has no description – the first thing that appears after clicking it is the choice between single- and multiplayer and then leaderboard. It just begs for an introduction like „Welcome to Arcade (coughcoughSurvivalcough) mode. Here, you have to try to survive for as long as possible. Note you should play Campaign first to get to know the mechanics etc. etc.”
And that's it. These are my biggest gripes with the game. Which can telly you one thing – the game is polished enough that I had to grasp at straws to find something bad to say about it thats not “derp, I haven't even checked the video introducing the game on store page and it's not what I thought, 0/10”, which, honestly, is silly.
All in all, I heartly recommend the game for people who like both action and tower defense. The game is fun, you can see the developers have potential and work hard to make it as good as it can be. I'll be looking forward to their next games, and so should you.

I played this game a long time ago and never left a review for it, so I'm going to rectify that now.
That said, though, I'll be very brief about it.
You can tell my over-all time with it is just over 15 hours,
so that's more or less the total length of the game.
Alan Wake is just a fantastic story-telling experience.
It looks great, it sounds great, it has very solid voice acting.
Playing this game, I said to myself:  "This is what good story telling and pacing should be."
So I believe this game does set a certain standard for how to do it correctly.
But this is game you play entirely for the story.
The gameplay is extremely simplistic, and repetitive.
Often it's only "hard" because you're being overwhelmed or flat out "ganked".
There's only 2-3 enemy types in the game, and the bosses are just stronger versions of said enemies.
Personally, I'd recommend setting the game on easy, because all difficulty does (from what I remember), is change the number of bullets required to down an enemy and since taking more bullets to kill an enemy doesn't add anything to combat and just makes it more frustrating (note: frustrating, not challenging in my opinion), it's better to keep that to a minimum.
This is an amazing game if you play it for the story.
If you're looking for fun or engaging combat, you won't find it here.
The ending does kinda fall flat but isn't that how it always is with horror plots?
Really hypes things up and then the explanation isn't as complex as you hoped.
It's still well worth it if you can grab it on sale or something, for sure.

Let me start by saying that this has one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard and going from place to place was never a chore with so many great classic era rock, jazz, and country music always playing on the radio.  There's so much great music to be had in this.  The characters, as well, solid.  Story is very involving and it drags you in to keep that constant want to play in there.
However, that's sort of where the good ends and the mediocre starts taking hold.  Missions to take over territory are very much the same thing over and over and over again.  The extra side missions are just more of the same, you don't really gain too much more by doing the little extra missions around the territories except maybe some extra backstories.  Just save yourself the time, get the boss to show up, and then assign it.  You don't need to worry too much about♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your cohorts, either.  You'll be able to unlock nearly all that you'll need and keep everybody equal, there's not too much of an urgency or nail biting situation.
Unfortunately though, the looks and performance matters are a drag.  I was wondering if maybe for a AAA title the graphics were a little more than sub-par especially by today's standards and there's some mechanics to the game that get annoying pretty quickly such as the retalliation squads that get sent out.  You'll have to wait for them to come to you, there's no going after them like everything else.  The "extra content" that's coming out as well seem to be more than a little lacking and stink more of scraped content to string along players so that they could push the unfinished product out the door quicker.
Wait for a good sale or try to pick it up cheap somewhere else.  Worth a playthrough, but not at full price and that's the real shame in it.  Even at a $1 per hour, it comes close, but falls short.

Maybe I'm not far enough into it, but it doesn't seem to be what it claims to be.  I didn't hate it enough to ask for a return.  If I manage to stomach it long enough to be surprised, I may edit.
When I see the Strategy tag, I expect it to be a major part of the gameplay from the start.  I don't see any in the first few levels.  It's not campaign-promise level false advertising, but it's certainly a major letdown for me.  Maybe they slip actual strategy in later, but so far I feel like I've been invited out for Indian and served a burger.  At no point will I feel less cheated if the deep-fried oreos for dessert are served with chai.
The ad claims "Epic cinematic music".  Shenanigans.  It's ok.  It doesn't detract from the gameplay.  It's far better than the tinny crap that makes some folks wax nostalgic.  But Epic and cinematic?  Don't compare yourself to Michael Giacchino if you're outclassed by Bon Jovi.
Enough about what it isn't.  Here's what it is:  Bad guys come out.  You throw manually aimed fireballs at the square you think they'll be in by the time it gets there.  You get doubly punished for missing, both on the score and because if you shoot too often, you overheat and can't fire for a few seconds.  The rate at which enemies spawn is faster than you can shoot w/o overheating.  You're going to take some damage without near perfect accuracy (maybe even with it).  That may change if you get farther in, but the first few levels are almost pure whack-a-mole.  Except whack-a-mole doesn't punish you for swinging too fast.  It's tough, fast-paced, and very early you find yourself fighing on multiple fronts.
If that appeals to you, great.  Give it a try.  For the price it seems like a good deal for folks who like what the mechanics acutally are.  Just don't expect "Strategy" or "Tower Defense", at least not in the first few levels.

Fallout Shelter is a time management game where you as the overseer trying to keep your happy dwellers alive. Crafting items or doing quest requires a lot of time, but that's the whole point of time management games. The ingame timer is still ticking while you are not playing the game.
What I like:
- It's free and not pay to win. You can easily complete the game without paying a cent.
- You can farm nuka cola and speed up the timer.
- Everything is obtainable without the need to pay real money.
- Interesting combat system while doing quest.
- It does not requires a lot of your time. You can run it on your background & do other stuff.
- The 2D art is refreshing and cute.
What I hate:
- One achievement is almost impossible to unlock unless you cheat. I only got 4/20 process while having over multiple hours of playtime. That's just a bad gamedesign choice imo. No one will be that crazy to keep playing for so long after completed the game without any new content.

I vaguely remember the original Kane & Lynch being something of a mediocre shooter, mostly written off for being uninspiring with unrelatable protagonists. So when "Dog Days" came out, and the reviews trashed it for being nauseatingly bad, I felt no strong urge to pick it up.
Then Eidos had that massive Steam-Bundle and both games were sort of shoved in there,which is how they ended up in my library. I feel like I specifically need to point this out, I did not go out of my way to get this game. It was essentially just a freebie that I decided to check out to see if it was as bad as everyone seemed to think it was.
I kept an open mind and fired it up. First thing that struck me was the absolutely nauseating camera. That's not hyperbole either, the god awful "found footage" style wobble was so bad I felt physically ill. This is the first and only game that has ever had that effect on me, by the way, I typically don't get nauseous from bad camera work. Second thing I noticed was the audio engineering was all sorts of broken. Bad repetitive gunshots, weird ambient noise and a cacophony of shouts and screams made every waking moment playing this feel like an assault on your ears. It never let up except during the loading screens, and then the effect was is so jarring you feel like you experienced whiplash.
The graphics are passable, for a PS3 port. There were minor issues of pop-ins and screen tearing, but otherwise it was fine. Overall the mood was they were aiming for was dark and grungy, and I suppose they did alright at that.
The gameplay is probably the worst aspect of the Dog Days. All you'll be doing, from the minute you start until the final cutscene is third person running and gunning, broken up in only one area where you're stuck in a fixed position shooting out of a vehicle. Occasionally they will insinuate that you are supposed to be engaging the enemy from stealth, but I never seemed to be able to sneak up on anyone, the enemy always seemed to detect you, no matter how slowly you moved past them.
When it comes to the cover based shooting mechanic, they manage to somehow mess up the two most fundamental aspects of the gameplay style. The shooting, and the cover.
Sticking to cover, never seems to really shield you all that much from enemy fire, and you can't aim your gun to save your life. The targeting reticle is always so massive, and the firearms so inaccurate it feels like you are constantly blind-firing from the hip. I swear at one point I unloaded an entire SMG on an enemy no more then 10 meters away from me without any effect.
Couple this with the fact that the enemies soak bullets like sponge does water and the main... no, check that, SOLE gameplay becomes an exercise in frustrating tedium.
The plot to this game is fairly threadbare as well. Kane and Lynch meet up in Shanghai to sell guns and murder people, only they murder the wrong people and now they are being hunted. Lynch has a girlfriend, she gets killed, he goes nuts, badguy gets killed, and the credits come rolling down in what was such a startling surprise I actually laughed out loud.
You can see that the time I spent playing this game was just over three and a half hours. That's how long it took me to complete the single player storyline. I didn't even consider checking out the multiplayer aspect.
So yeah, avoid this game, unless you are morbidly curious about just how bad it is.
If you've got a few minutes to waste everyday, I definitely recommend this game.

Helvetica, Times, and Comic Sans are all explored and the reasoning and history behind them is explored. For example, the Helvetica level brings up the Russian revolution and the new Americana feel without saying a word and the atmosphere is great from there. However, one big problem is there are literal text dumps which would have been nice as narration or something else. I don't want to read an essay.

This is a good first effort by a young team of Hungarian developers.
As others have noted, the developers are obviously inspired by the Myst series in aesthetics and puzzle design. There are some great, inventive puzzles that challenge (especially enjoyed the green crystal bits) and the best part is that they are completely fair. I did not need a walkthrough at any point. There is an inventory system, but the items are not used in obtuse ways (like, say, using an elephant tusk to remove an electrical panel a la The Dig). The puzzles are not always easy--there are head scratchers--but they do vary in scope and difficulty, and can be satisfying to solve, which is the hallmark of a good adventure title.
Reception has been mostly positive, but sober your decision to purchase this title with the knowledge this game was developed by a team of four. You will spend 3/4 of the game in the same small, drab brown area going back and forth, and back and forth. The environment gets a little more interesting past that. While there are nice puzzles, they often feel stitched together without logical justification, which doesnt help sell the world. The story is paper thin, and will do little to motivate you. Sound design is mostly good, but the soundtrack is forgetable, even grating at times (I played with the music turned off). The graphics are compentent, but generic in many spots.
If you like adventure games *and* are conscious of all the shortcomings, then I would say give Quern a chance. For a first game, the team has done some good work.

Did you enjoy Myst & Riven? Did you enjoy complex puzzles that require you to sit down and take time to process what the hell is going on with these weird characters and chemicals in front of you? Do you enjoy having a pen and notebook nearby to scribble down notes and clues? If you answered yes to any of these, buy this now. There have been many indie devs who attempt to capture the unique feeling of Myst, but few have ever managed to capture it on the dot like Quern has.
The puzzles and the logic behind them require a vast amount of processing. They will have you writing down things, expirementing like a child seeing something for the first time trying to figure out how things work. These aren't a bunch of random hard puzzles thrown together in a hastly manner. These puzzles took time and effort and affect the entire world around you each time you beat a puzzle is one of the most gratifying sensations I have had in gaming for quite some time. That feeling of being watched all the time is also in the game, which makes the game feel almost spooky, without actually feeling spooky.
The graphics & visuals are striking and unique in a very good way. Many developers have tried to make a unique looking world but end up with stereotypes that just make the world feel bland. In this game, the world feels very unique, buildings have a never before seen look to them, while throwing in some buildings that give it a Myst/Riven feel. The look and feel of the world just feels perfect yet unsettling all at the same time. I would personally recommend this higher than Obduction (Cyan studios new game), it feels like the original 2 games in the Cyan series, but managed to do it in such a unique way. It honestly feels like playing something Cyan Studios made back in 1998, but with a real game engine. This is a great game and should be ranked one of the highest in the puzzle solving genre. I am curious to follow the developers for their next enteries.
Just a warning, for those of us who have issues with Audio Tones, there is a puzzle that requires this in game.

Take on the roll of
, a writer trapped in his own story. Ironic, isn't it? The game offers a great story up front, follow along as you become
trying to write your way out of his own problems. The story is the biggest hook for me and one of the best things going for it. The game mechanics aren't as bad as you would think. At first I assumed that this game would have you rely on battery pickup and management, or face death and despair. However, that's not the case. You can manage to play through the game without running out of batteries or coming close (unless playing on Nightmare mode) but if you do, it's not the end of the world. The flashlight recharges over time anyways causing you to not have to rely on batteries through out the entire game. Lastly, another great thing the game has is an amazing back story and collectibles that are written right into the story. As you go through the game, find and collect the manuscript pages that help you get back story and Alan get information about what has happened and is to come.
For me, the game mechanics are a double edged sword in this game. Although the mechanics don't make you rely on batteries the entire game, it's not without flaws. The game feels and plays slow, which is meant to match the pace of the game. However, at some parts it almost feels too slow. On top of that, the controls seem a little unresponsive/delayed at times. You could hit the pick up button and sometimes it wouldn't go through, or you could hold it to switch weapons and end up waiting at least 10 seconds before switching for a weapon on the ground. Another thing that I dislike about the game is that it doesn't feel like a true horror game, especially for being tagged as a horror game. From time to time you may get a flash of a cut scene to try to jump scare you, but besides that the game plays more of a thriller then a horror game.
So would I recommend this game? Definitely! It has a great story and is fun to play through, you can even squeeze out a couple play throughs before getting too bored of it. Although this game is now off of Steam, if you can find a hard copy or even digital copy somewhere else, I would recommend grabbing it!

What is there to say about a game like this. One that apes nostalgia so much and one that really does bring back that feeling of classic PSX/N64 platforming? Anyone that knows me, knows that some of my favorite games growing up were Spyro, Gex, Sly Cooper, and Banjo Kazooie just to name a few. I absolutely adored 3D platformers when I was a kid. Seeing something like this pop up on steam out of the blue was a very real, very welcome surprise.
In a world of countless dark, edgy brown and grey, dirty games, Mimimi Productions picked the perfect time to put this game out there. It's strikingly bold color pallette was enough to catch my eye, and after not only watching the start of a live stream with the dev, but speaking to one of the devs herself/himself who was nice enough to answer my many questions on the game, I knew this was a company that deserved every penny.
Let's be extremely clear on this: This is a kid's game. There is no deep rooted meaning and the colorism "Seperating of colors being bad" undertone is about as subtle as a brick through a plate glass window. On the upside, it's not so overbearing that a young child could easily grasp it at first. There are plenty of references for long time gamers and a lot of enjoyment to be had with this title with little ones if for no other reason than it being a colorful distraction for a few hours.
THIS PART CONTAINS A SPOILER...
Now onto the one gripe that struck me right at the very end. Once you reach the end of the game, there's no going back to a fully united colortown to complete side objectives and such. To pick up all the brushes and "complete" the game. This is a pretty big gripe unfortunately because it kind of undermines all that you went through to get the town united. Not being able to see the fully realized colortown with all the districts means you don't really feel fulfillef at the very end. Sure you CAN go back to previous chapters and collect the brushes, but you'll be replaying the game essentially with the bleakness still around, again, undermining all the work you put in and the adventure you just went on. I don't know if this was a conscious decision or if it was a limitation, but it's the one gripe that I had to really dig down to see if it was worth mentioning, and I feel it is.
NO MORE SPOILERS...
So what are my final thoughts on the game? For the demographic it was made for, and for long time fans of classic 3D platformers I highly suggest picking it up if for no other reason than nostalgia. Unique character designs, bright and colorful color pallette, overall upbeat game with an interesting twist about halfway in. It's a really good game, and to hear that it's not only from an indie dev, but this being their FIRST indie game released? I fully support this group going forward and I can't wait to see what they make in the future!

Alan Wake is a thrilling TV serial in video game form.
Alan Wake is a prolific writer on vacation in the quaint but awe-inspiring Pacific Northwest area of Bright Falls, Washington with his wife; in an attempt to overcome a severe case of writer's block.  But after waking up in a car crash he doesn't remember having; he finds himself pursued by shadowy figures and something ominous lurks in the corners of his mind.  He can't find his wife, and the cabin he was staying in has vanished entirely.  On his journey he continues to stumble upon prophetic manuscript pages from a book Wake authored but has no recollection of ever writing.  What follows is a season of six episodes and two special features that dole out a very original thriller.  Watching the mysterious pieces fall under the light and put themselves together is gratifying even if the ending doesn't tie up every loose end.   Every facet of the world from character personality and design to the locale's history and layout are rich in detail and it really pays off.  When the shadows aren't conspiring to murder you, Bright Falls feels lived in and genuine.  When a doctor comes to check up on the gash on your head, he doesn't walk in with a white coat and name tag.  He shoves his fishing gear onto the table beside you after having been called in from what he thought would be a quiet afternoon by the river.  The little details like this elevate the people in Alan Wake from characters who are merely here to be part of a story, to real lives that have hobbies and jobs and do things when the player isn't around.  Alan Wake doesn't deliever a deep message or reveal a piece of human nature.  It tells a wildly page-turning tale in digital form.
A relatively simple third person shooter, Alan Wake arms players with a nothing but a flashlight, a few backwoods firearms like a revolver or hunting rifle, and a couple highly lethal and very unorthodox tools based on light.
At the heart of combat is the flashlight.  A darkness drapes itself over and consumes everything it can to stop Wake; from men and mine carts to birds and trains.  But Wake finds himself in an almost fantasical scenario where squeezing his torch in terror actually wills it to shine brighter than it should.  Draining the battery in seconds, this strips the shadows from foes far faster than merely pointing the light at them can.  Burning the juice from your batteries can also stall and then slow down whichever foe you've pointed it at; but you'll need to keep a fresh supply of lithiums loaded if you want to keep up the pressure.  Once stripped of their inky shield, Wake can open fire and finish them off for good.  Brandishing all manner of knives, scythes, sledge hammers, and saw blades; the Taken men of Bright Falls will do everything they can to close the distance and deliver staggering blows that easily knock Wake off balance.  A simple dodge mechanic is integrated into the spint button, allowing Wake to evade most blows but he tires incredibly easily.  Retaliating before you wind yourself is paramount.  Flares can be popped to ward crowds back in your moments of weakness, and flash bangs are instantly lethal.  Flare guns act as makeshift rocket launchers; turned from a marking tool to a tiny handheld genocide popper.  Mobs of aggresive crows can be burned from the sky with heavy pulses of your flashlight, and possessed objects can be whittled down as they hurl themselves at you; intent on crushing Wake to death.  Aiming and shooting is very responsive, and although simple; managing your constantly advancing opponents with dodges, flashlight batteries, and ammunition loading is a blast.  Mashing the reload button to insert cartridges faster is an excellent touch too.  It really conveys tension in a very special way.  Some occasional platforming is rare which is for the better.  Wake moves sluggishly and his jumps can be rather janky.
Along Wake's path, players will find scattered pages of a manuscript.  Serving as narrative beats that take place most often in the future; they can give players a grain of warning before they reach the page's turn.  Or make them dread the horrors to come.  Also hidden throughout Bright Falls are a collection of coffee thermoses, supply chests, and other knick knacks.  The chests can be a boon to Wake's flagging supplies, but outside of the radios and TV's that provide narrative information, comfy midnight broadcasts and tunes, and a goofy low budget thriller called Night Springs; the knick knacks serve no purpose than to be collected.
Beautiful.  The little town of Bright Falls can't be described any other way.  From the dense and foggy pine forests to the hiking trails like Lover's Peak; Alan Wake's take on the woods is simultaneously postcard worthy and oppressive.  The droning sound of horrors rolls in as fog chokes the branches around you; concealing ambushes and distorting the world in a smearing mess.  Character models have the look of real people, but not the graphical detail in close ups to hold that realism.
Soaring strings, combative percussion, and gentle key strokes comprise an excellent ambient soundtrack that's bolstered by excellent choices in a list of many liscensed songs.  Each chapter is book ended in an ALAN WAKE title drop and a musical interlude; television style.  And each chapter starts with "PREVIOUSLY ON" recapping of the events as though its been a week since you last played.  It's a very unique approach and it really gives the game a feeling of narrative rise and fall in the action.
Animation is another story, sadly.  Character's faces are so poorly animated that their mouths sometimes hang open even as they continue to speak.  Hands rarely grasp what they're touching or even flex their fingers for that matter, and outside of combat, which has an excellent weight to each movement; characters animate rather woodenly.
Lighting is voluminous, dense, and well-crafted as bright lights shape themselves around obstruction.  Flares slather the world in strikingly sharp shadow, and lamp posts welcome players to temporarily escape the darkness around them.  By and large, the game's visuals do far more good than bad.  Just... try not to watch those faces too closely.

A teamwork oriented extreme off-roading logistical puzzle exploration game that believably captures the mesmerizing subtlety of navigating treacherous paths.  It has thankfully evolved from the janky award winning tech demo in 2009 to what is now a polished complete experience.
Each vehicle causes you to read the landscape in wildly different ways which cascades down into different configurations of the vehicle.  Screenshots or videos don't quite capture the absolute fear or excitement that manifests as you test the limitations of the vehicles with increased ambition and discover that roads are suggestions.
You can travel a road 3 times and it will be different every time as the terrain becomes a custom sculpted mash signed by you.  In these moments, you feel your heaviness visualized by the scar it leaves behind.  It's like every foot of terrain is a mini-game where finessing your steering and acceleration reward you by permitting movement under the captivity of weight.
When the miracle of movement no longer graces you, the winch is the undead arm reaching out of the grave.  At times your winch makes you feel like a vehicular Bionic Commando or Spider-Man as you get pulled out of the mess you're in and you must employ strategy in selecting what to connect to lest it put you in a whole new mess.  Don't let this obvious scenario fool you, though, the winch is as versatile as it should be.
Winch to a friend to have them lower you down a cliff.  Attach to the right spot on an overturned truck to right it, or secure yourself to pre-emptively avoid overturning.  Pull debris out of the way.  Cross the uncrossable river.  Maybe even tow a truck that's damaged and out of fuel.  Your very own personal tractor beam is satisfying to use every time.
Each map has carefully placed vehicles, garages, fuel supplies, cloaking fields and obstacles which you must configure your trucks for and build a plan around in order to facilitate the completion of the map objective.  Positioning fuel trucks, maintenance trucks, cranes, lumber haulers, etc around the map to optimize a route proves to be satisfying.  The objective serves as a fairly standard carrot, but the real meal is the pursuit.
Even though Spintires is worth it just for the authenticity in the unique experience it provides, you can't help but realize it hasn't reached its full potential yet.  It is still under active development and while it does support modding, It could benefit from more maps, multiplayer saving, different climates, real-time weather, better use of verticality, more required uses for cranes, maps with unique coop-only challenges and a larger variety in objectives.
It looks good and it's better than it looks, but fully experiencing multiplayer requires patience and dedication since you can't save map progress.  As a workaround, you can decide to start with much better trucks which can reduce how long it takes to finish maps.

The enemies seem to have pinpoint accuracy with all their weapons, which is very irritating.
The cover system is bad. Enemies will still be able to hit you sometimes, and you will only be able to poke your head up for long enough for the animation to finish before being damaged enough that you have to retreat back into cover. You will need to wait 5 seconds before popping back up to fire off another bullet only for it to miss and have the cycle start again.

I did not find out until an hour in that these could be disabled because they are not labeled well in the options menu.
The game is around 4 hours long. I quit 5 minutes before the end because I could not handle anymore of the cheap deaths or bad gameplay. Do not buy. If you own it from a humble bundle, you can experience all the game has to offer from the first hour.

Yes, the Binding of Isaac is one of the deepest, heart touching and emotionful game about life of a little boy named Isaac. It has many Bible references, those make the game more mysterious and interesting. Not willing to spoil anything, but it's more like how Isaacs life turned into hell. He just lived a happy, joyful and simple life with his Mother in a small house on a hill. But one day Isaacs Mom heard a voice from above.. The God tells his Mother to prove her faith in him by sacrificing Isaac.
The gameplay reminded me a lot of Zelda games - Bombs: used to break rocks, kill enemies and cut Your way through closed doors if needed. Coins: Used to play slot machines, buy items and etc. Keys: Unlock treasure rooms and other locked doors. It is also a very random, no two runs are the same, random pick-ups and enemies. Variety of items - over 250 items! every collectible You pick will be shown on Your character. Make Your shots (tears) stronger by collecting those items to defeat more difficult bosses, make Your Character faster by collecting other types of items, to dodge enemy attacks and so on! I'm definitely recommending it! You won't regret! The soundtrack is also very nice and fits the game. Many endings will keep You satisfied to play more, even if You die (Death is permanent in game).
But the game has a deeper meaning to it, wayy deeper, it is what it makes so original and very different, from the other games, even games from the same creator. Yes, it is sad and You'll understand it once You've beaten the game 10th time..
Have a nice time playing this amazing game!
