Kayne &Lynch 2  is a third person shooter game with almost non-stop action where you have  to mostly cover and shoot using the "cover" mechanic that is implemented into the game.
The goods:
A well-crafted story and two pretty well done characters.
Great level aesthetics, It's simple yet well done.
The bad:
The placement of cover is pretty bad if you're trying to play a bit-more agressive every now and then. I also felt as if
most cover-objects where a little bit too small to actually hide behind, this on the other hand could and should've been
an easy fix for level artists.
Enemy HP/Cover Ai,
These two basically go hand in hand in my opinion: If you make the Ai take less cover you'll be better off giving it some more Hp and vice versa, but what I noticed in this game was the total opposite most of the time.
Also something that really stood up to me was the fact that some street-cops had more Hp / damage than some fully-armed millitairy men, which is  weird and makes it difficult to prioritise your next target.
The tweakable:
There are actually not that many things that have to be changed in order to make this game "great".
Let's start with a few basic things.
-The cover system
It's basically the exact same what I described earlier: Make the cover-objects larger or add something that makes you as a character able to crouch/lay down on the ground even further to avoid damage.
-Enemy spawning times
Sometimes you felt like you had to run through a certain room to the next because the room was very damaged( Mostly into the late game of the main campaign)
But then when you're running to the end of the room and reach the door to the next a whole wave of heavily armed soldiers spawn right on top of you, which isn't really fair level design considering one of the achievements is not to die during a mission.
To change this the developers/level designers could easy just move the event-trigger to the start of the room or add a sound-clue to make it sound that there is an actual trained militairy squad comming after you.
TL:DR:
All in all Kane & Lynch 2 isn't a bad/terrible game as many people claim it to be,sure it has it's flaws but from a story/gameplay perspective it's a fun tough little game that's just a bit different than all the other games out there.
If the developers just had a little bit more of a budget and or time they could've easily fixed most if not all flaws in the game.
If it's on sale you should definitely give it a shot.

The best description I have for this game is that it is pure.
There's no side quests, no dialogue treees, no moral dilemmas.
It's just you, a sword and an ever increasing, in both numbers and strength, opposition.
The developers wanted to make a game about a school girl killing men and demons with a sword, and that is undeniably what they delivered.
The closest thing to a plot is a couple of sentences at the start about someone from her school with another, demonic, sword, but this can all be safely ignored once the game starts.
And about that gameplay, it starts off simple enough, with some human opponents, also with swords that chase you around, but are easy to dodge, and progresses to enemies that can charge at you, and goes from there.
in your arsenal you have severral basic attacks, osme with the sword and some without, and a super move, all basic stuff, which by the way, really does need to be played with a controller.
How much enjoyment you get out this basic formula is up to you, as other have said midless button mashing can and will work, at least at the start, but there is depth for those willing to put in the time.
Aside the gameplay, two thing stand out, the first is the graphics, it looks like something from 2010, which meant that my PC ran it without even breathing hard, but also looked terrible. While I haven't tried a decent laptop from the past couple of years should be able to run this easily enough. But beyond that the arena is small, large enough to have a conga line of enemies chase after you, but only just, and it feels like a rather silly limitation, a larger space, maybe a hub of some sort between rounds could give the game a sense of place it currently lacks.
The second is the blatant, and rather off putting fanservice, obviously it's every man for himself, some people like it some people don't, consider me someone who doesn't and the panty shots are not something I want in this kind of game, to say nothing of the fact that the protagonist is (supposedly) a high school student.
As I said the game is pure, it set out to do one thing, and lo and behold, it does it. While the combat can drag, the graphics felt last gen and the fanservice was just off putting, the game does exactly what it should do and absoutely nothing else, whether that's a good or bad thing depends on how you view the core gameplay

I spent quite a number of hours on this just to actually wager on how bad people say it is. In the end, it’s not bad at all. Without a doubt, there are noticeable flaws in this game, so I’ll push them out of the way now. The annoying camcorder effects -- which thankfully can be turned off in the advanced settings, except the constant shaking when you run -- and the abysmal ending that was set for a sequel. When there is enough damage to the head (i.e. a buckshot from point-blank range) causes a censor effect. To me, this is questionable, but when you have that chance to see what it's censoring depends on the viewer. It does have detail, such as the bullet hole down to the blood streak coming from the eyes. I guess people really did want that gruesome detail. I can see why the shotgun is “accurate” due to the fact that it fires buckshots. But they don’t cause that much damage.
The introduction jumps you to how badly Kane & Lynch are involved in. Throughout the game, they are hit from practically everywhere they go, desperately trying to make it better. Character development is practically nonexistent in here, or rather, much of their character from the previous game. Lynch’s psychotic episode isn’t involved here, not like it was back in Dead Men. Disturbingly enough, they remind me of Michael and Trevor from GTA V, only one is keeping his issues under control now. Vague conversation is used between the two, unless it’s later in the story, where Lynch describes who or what is going on. Finally, the levels are incredibly linear, the story is pretty weak, and -- of course -- it's ending is unsatisfactory.

Erwin's Timewarp is about a dog that gets transported back into time by accident, and must find time machine parts in order to go back to the present.
After the main menu, you're thrown into the game's world with no explanation whatsoever. No cutscene, or text box. It's a bit disorienting, and I found myself quite lost, although after fidgeting around for a few minutes you figure out what you're meant to do.
You can interact with objects if you get close enough. Although this interaction isn't very reliable. Sometimes you need to get the correct angle and distance, and will need to twitch around until you get it right. Once you've found the position, a small menu pops up with a few interaction options. These all do nothing to really explain what exactly they do. Trial and error is the only way to find out.
After putting an object in your inventory, you'll most likely need to use it later on by interacting with something or someone. Most of the game consist of walking around relatively similar looking areas, with little variety in gameplay.
The graphics are decent. I like the slight mix between realistic and cartoony styled characters. They have goofy proportions, while their textures are decently realistic.
The absence of sounds and music in-game is a bit annoying. It adds to the generally unfinished feel of the game.
Overall, I felt like the game got stale pretty quickly. The lack of tutorial or help hurts your inital impression of the game, and after you figure it all out, there's little content to keep you gripped. I hope this improves in the future, considering it's in Early Access. However, I can't recommend it in its current state.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is an action role-playing hack and slash video game developed by Polish studio CD Projekt RED for Microsoft Windows, Xbox 360 and OS X. It is a sequel to the 2007 video game The Witcher, and was released internationally on May 17, 2011 for Microsoft Windows, and on April 17, 2012 for Xbox 360. Erwin’s Timewarp is an adventure game. You play as the pet dog of some scientist who built a time machine and sent you to the past, and you’re tasked with finding various pieces of this machine in order to return to the present.
Starting the game you’re able to put it in various resolutions of window mode, and you can also choose to play at full screen; this is something I usually really appreciate as I don’t always like to play certain games in full screen. However, there’s little else in the form of proper menu and options. The only sounds to be found in the game at its current stage were also only in this menu, and unfortunately, the music was completely awful to me. I could not click out of the menu fast enough.
Visually the game is kind of cartoony. It’s relatively good looking and the textures are nice, as well as the details on the areas; for an indie unity game in 3D/top-down/isometric view it ran surprisingly well on my computer, so kudos to the dev for that accomplishment. I usually have a lot of optimization issues with indie games on unity.
As I mentioned before, there’s little in the way of sounds or music outside the menu, and that is almost a blessing considering my dislike for the meny music.
You’re also tossed into the game with little in the form of tutorial, explanation, or back story. In fact you’re only told a couple times about what’s going on and what you’re supposed to do and find. If you didn’t read the description on the steam page, you’d have no idea what you’re supposed to do until you encounter that alien – which btw, I’m still wondering why there’s an alien there.
The puzzles are fairly easy to follow on what you need to get in order to do what, but the way of interacting with things is a bit uncomfortable. Sometimes objects will highlight but not pop up hints, the icons offered as menu aren’t clear on what they do until you click them and find out, and they won’t appear until you’re in some particular range and angle from the item. Still, the rest of the controls (mostly movement wise) are fairly good despite this.
What makes the game a bit harder is that you have to spend quite a bit of time trying to figure out what to do at the start, and you CAN die (and you can save, too, so be sure to save): some characters will hurt you, and you must also keep yourself fed through the game, which I guess is an interesting twist for an adventure/puzzle game, but frankly I’m still unsure if it works.
The character animations for the dog and companions are fairly good, but the human animations leave much to be desired. There were also some bugs in which, for instance, you’d get stuck against certain things.
All in all it seems like an ok game, and I can see some potential in it which is why I would recommend to keep a watch on it if it sounds interesting; but it really needs a proper introduction and a brief tutorial. I understand Early Access is expected to not be completely functional, but there’s “we’re still testing out things”  and then there’s “this shouldn’t really be open for sale and/or the public as a whole yet”.
If you like adventure games and want to support the dev, I’d recommend it, it’s an ok game with what it has so far. I can see potential in it, but currently it’s not something I’d recommend to just about everyone.
I'll keep a watch and might change my rating once the game is further fleshed out.
Overall: 4/10

Type: Rider is an interesting puzzle/platforming game, most similar in game play to something like Thomas was Alone, but completely different in style.
You play a colon (no faeces jokes, please!) which can roll and jump around the landscape, collecting letters of different type faces and occasionally an asterisk, thereby unlocking a page on the history of writing and typography. These history pages provide a reward of sorts, and I personally found them very interesting, but many people will skip them as they can be lengthy and are very dry. Unfortunately for me, I found the writing to be quite poor in many of these pages (especially the tutorial), with errors in layout and grammar scattered throughout. Given the topic of the game, this was a very big negative for me.
The music is calm and quite lovely, and the graphics are exceptional. Levels look, by and large, simple, and are made up of parts of font glyphs and other thematic elements, but some of them are actually quite tricky.
Overall I do recommend Type: Rider, but it is a bit of a weird mix. The puzzle component of the levels seems to mix quite well with the literary and somewhat intellectual topic, but this doesn't quite gel with the dexterity required to collect some of the letters in the more platform-ish parts. The game is mellow, but frustrating at the same time.
I plan to keep playing to completion, but I may rage quit a few times before then.

I hadn't expected much going in. It looked a little pretentious, but entertaining. A cute little game loosely about driving over letters.
I was impressed. The look and feel of the game is quite beautiful. Each level has a different feel, tied neatly into both a typographical theme and history, providing context for the fonts we use each day. Played correctly, this game could give someone a whole new perspective on words and the ways we write them. As your small colon-shaped avatar rolls over letters and symbolically knocks the serifs from them, you start to understand how much of a break with tradition sans-serif font is (because you've been rolling around serifs for three levels' worth of history at that point).
Playing the levels is simple enough. Finding all of the pickups is a little challenging. It's worth checking out, for word nerds definitely, or for anyone who wants to appreciate typography for its own merits. There are plenty who won't really get it. Perhaps I am just pretentious enough to understand and appreciate this game.

Alan is a famous writer of psychological horror books who goes with his wife to vacation in Washington, more precisely in a small town called Bright Falls. In this place the protagonist begins to experience episodes of its last book published and about which he does not remember to have it written. However, all the current events in your life are directly and indirectly related to this book. Here could be a lot more said, however they would be spoilers of the game.
Alan Wake's graphics are very beautiful, well rendered and polished. The detail levels of various objects are quite high. The light and shadow effects are exceptional and the textures are very well crafted. Details such as the reflections of light over the water and the light of the lantern illuminating the setting or even focusing on objects through a glass are excellent. Undoubtedly graphically the game is very well done. The fictitious and mountainous town of Bright Falls with its native forests, abandoned and old mills, empty houses and sheds made of wood and weathered are exceptionally well portrayed. When you are driving a car, a pick up or a jeep very fast pop-ins are present, but do not even bother.
Sound effects are very well applied to the circumstances the player is in. The noises of friction between objects are very convincing. The noise of the waters of the streams, the steps of the protagonists on the floor made of boards, the firing of weapons, vehicles and much more, are very well done and convince us. The voices of the characters combine with their physical types and personality, and the dialogues are also very cool. At the end of each episode plays a song whose lyrics makes a certain reference to what was experienced by the protagonist in the episode in question, and the songs are very good.
Gameplay: here, without a doubt, is one of the great points to emphasize in the game. Alan is an ordinary person, that is, he has no special power, he is not a soldier, he is not an athlete, he does not have any kind of military training, he did not even wear a white band in Judo. This means that Alan, when running off in a few meters, will tire and his gait will decrease considerably, his leap is the average of humans as well as his strength and endurance. To face the enemies (the Taken, mainly) Alan has a significant arsenal, but do not expect sophisticated weapons or rocket launchers, Alan uses a lot of flashlight, as well as flags, bombs with moral effect that explode when they emit a flash , A revolver beacon, a common revolver, or a shotgun, or a twelve-barreled twelve or a twelve-eight-shot. In addition to this arsenal he has an elusive and his greatest asset is to shoot well, as he will always shoot in the exact direction in which his flashlight is illuminating. Anyway, Alan's moves are quite realistic (for a sedentary person), whether walking, running or reloading weapons or even jumping over some object.
Alan Wake is a game that took a cut from Alone in the Dark the New Nightmare and combined with the atmosphere of Silent Hill (mainly SH 2 and 3), ie did not innovate, but knew how to take advantage of the idea of ​​others, And this may be his greatest merit. It is a game that certainly causes a bit of anxiety, since the absence of maps can, at certain times, make us a little disoriented especially when we are facing the Taken in the forests. It has an intriguing and complex history, because there are times when we do not know if what Alan is living is real or not, in addition to other elements that cross the story and increase its complexity.
Pros:
- It takes between 15 a.m. to 8 p.m. to close the game;
- Good story;
- Very good graphics.
Cons:
- The character could travel a greater distance before tiring.

I like it.
...I do. Is good, man.
I'll be honest, I decided to get it after finding out It had Poets of the Fall music in. Big fan of that band.
The fact I'm a horror fan helps too.
The story, I think was the main reason I played through. I kept getting more and more interested as I went on.
And the fact I can easily pick it up to go acheivment hunting on ''100%'' the game must count for something.
Graphically speaking it perfectly passable. Minor issues with the models but overall the enviroments were quite nice to look at. Both day and night parts. Character animations were well done (Think they used motion capture)
One minor thing is the difference between Alan Wakes face and Ikka Villi's. Something about his cheeks made him look a bit droopy compared the the actor he was based on. But again, that's very minor.
The lipsyncing was off. That's always a pet peeve with me.
The motion blur was obnoxious at first but after a while I got used to it. Though that hasn't stopped me from finding a way to turn it off. Honestly looks way better without it. My guess is they added it to make it look really dream-like. But honestly for something as motion intensive as a videogame it can just be annoying. Even disorientating for some.
Combat was... Interesting... At first I found it incredibly difficult. But after a while I found myself enjoying it. I wish Wake had more stamina, though. I mean, I know writers are probably not known for going out alot but even so, I can probably run longer then he and I hardly ever leave my desk :P
I played of normal (hard mode going by the achievments), and being a not paticularily good gamer I did die a few times. Mostly to big hordes of Taken... And Harvesters...
But it only ever frustrated me if the last checkpoint I got was a while away. Otherwise The combat was enjoyable enough to not make me wanna pull my hair out.
The collectables are... Well, there are alot of them. I got a fair amount of them first go around. And I will attempt to find the rest. Eventually tackle Nightmare mode. But goddamn, I think they went a little overboard.
I honestly did enjoy finding all the Night Springs TV shows. Fun little callback to the Twilight show which makes me wanna actually watch that show. Seeing as I've never seen it before.
Another minor problem is the fact that it records your statistics for thing, remembers what manuscripts and other such things you've gotten but doesn't remove them from the levels if you replay them to find the rest. I think they should only return if you start a new NEW game. But instead it just makes it a little confusing since you might not be able to remember which ones you've collected. meaning you could waste time searching in areas you've already searched.
[Edit] after replaying using the Episodes option I've found my last gripe wa inaccurate. So ignore me. I'm dumb...
I found the ending to be a little anti-climactic gameplay wish. Story wise it was quite intruiging (At this time I havn't played the specials). But honestly as a final ''boss' it was a little lackluster. I won't spoil it but it's mainly just topping up one weapon, and standing in one spot firing at a big thing that doesn't really damage you. Not overly epic. When before they had amazing standout moments. Like the Children of the Elder Gods segment and the War segment. They were most likley enhanced by the badass music, though :P
I found the ''Horde' segments more interesting, I guess.
Though overall I found the game fun. I'm honestly the kinda guy who likes 'sploration. So the overabundance of things to try and find kept me occupied. That and it drew out more Taken which forced me to improve at the combat :P
The story, I pretty much found interesting all the way through, so it wasn't hard for me to get into it everytime I opened the game. I am hoping the specials clears some things up, though. I can gather the basics of the ending but it is a little bit vague. Not really a big issue for me, just something I'd like to see explored more.
Overall, I really liked this game. Now I understand why people are desperate for a second game.
It has it's problems. But overall the characters, story and neat combat kept me coming back and enjoying myself.

I guess I liked this game because I was a heavy reader of Heavy Metal magazine in the 80s and 90s. Heavy Metal was mainly a science fiction and fantasy comic book which featured some fairly cool artwork, notably that of Italian cartoonist Paolo Eleuteri Serpieri, whose protagonist Druuna is fairly comparable to Sheyna in this game.
Growing up in the 70s and 80s I played arcade video games from the earliest incarnations of them and so Age of Barbarians feels very much like a joystick and 3 buttons game you'd find in some back alley quarter arcade. It definitely reaches back to that nostalgic era successfully in the same way other mediums have managed recently, notably Stranger Things.
Yes, there's nudity and sexually suggestive content, but high fantasy artwork has always had a tradition of sexploitation and so Age of Barbarians is not out of place. It's unapologetically cartoonish in dialogue, animation and storyline. It's meant for a laugh and so it succeeds on that level.
There are some drawbacks:
* Not being able to map the attack buttons to your mouse
* Landing in traps because of poor controls and not ability
* Graphical glitches and anomalies
* Checkpoint save system means you can't just stop whenever you want
The game is a 6/10 but it's worth $10.

The game starts off interesting. But quickly loses value.
The pros: The game is nice, not exactly a fallout game but its nice to be the overseer for once. In the early stages of a vault, you can fill up spaces rather quickly and you have to keep on it to harvest your resources. Staying on top of the game means logging in for at least an hour a day and playing his little game, which does keep you interested as it can be done while you do other things. Just keep it in windowed size and minimize when you need to focus on something else. You can build up to 30 dwellers in a few days without much effort and you can build rooms to train their attributes. The variety of junk, Weapons, armor, and incidents is entertaining at lower levels.
The cons: After you have 35 dwellers, you usually have 1-3 Mr Handies. SO now you dont have to worry about havesting your resources constantly, they do it for you. by now you have an established breeding pair(s), a pair of dedicated door guards, many people working in the resource departments, a fair amount of storage space, and have successfully fended off mole rats, Rad Roaches, and raiders to the point you dont even look any more except to collect the loot when they die. You likely also have realized that armor is ornamental and you can train your dwellers in specific atributes to function as specific things regardless of what their base line is.
By now you also know that you either go on quests constantly toget lunchboxes that often just overload your inventory with useless weapons and low grade armor (seriously. a rusty BB Gun does 0-1 damage and they are very common. you get one on every quest, even the higher level ones). Selling weapons becomes useless after a while because by the time you ahve 45 dwellers you hit the max caps because Bottle and Cappy come by 5 times or more in a single play run. Bottle drops Quantum rather often (usually betwen 1-5 every time you click his dancing animation. have gotten as high as 6 before), and Cappy drops a ton of caps every few seconds. WHen your vault reaches huge size, keeping up with them without zooming out is near impossible. And makes it hard to even click on them. At this point, forget finding the mysterious stranger when he pops up. Even if you have high end headphones and get directional pitch to the sound to guide you toward his general location, you wont get there fast enough to click on him.
Crafting is utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, because to upgrade the crafting rooms you have to find recipes in the quests (i have found duplicates before. 3 of the sme gun from the same quest. that was irritating) and armor does nothing but make your character look pretty. It has no effect on combat stats at all. you need 75+ dwellers to upgrade the crafting stations to make Legenday Armorand weapons. unfortunately you also need levenday junk which is about as easy to obtain as proper medical treatment for cancer.
Sending a wanderer into the wasteland is a great way to kill them. you cant reject ppl fast enough once you hit max dwellers because even with radio off, no breeders in the vault and you kicking 10ppl an hour you have a constant line of 10ppl waiting to get in.
By the time you have 120 dwellers you have max res production to the point you need about 1% of what you make and one mr handy can harvest it all for you no issue. your dwellers are so strong they kill deathclaw attack at the door and your quests are the only reason you keep returning in the vain hope of scoring something unique and new.
TO get pets, mr handy bots, etc you need to drop serious cash because just buying the specific crates will often generate the exact same ones as you already have with the sme abilities you no longer need.
In short, this game becomes very boring and unplayable after 10 hours. Even restarting with a new vault you end up with the same issues because you know how it works now and hit that brick wall even faster. SO unless you play 3 min, once a week you should have 3 max vaults in under 9 days. its not even a time waster at this point its just a waste of time and effort to find enjoyment in the game.

More Fun Than It Has Any Right to Be - The Fun B-Movie of Video Games
==========================
Is this a good game?  Objectively, no.  The gratuitous nudity, violence, character proportions, bugs, and sluggish controls would damn most games... but not this one.
This is the video game version of a fun B-movie.  It has no delusions of exactly what it is, and all its flaws only enhance the imersion of a B-movie.  The devs know EXACTLY how gratuitous everything is, and they've done it because it's an homage to what is essentially a gratiutious genre.  The classic barbarian fantasy game -- full of weird landscapes, inappropriate dinosaurs, and apparently warm enough that nobody ever needs to wear clothes.  Because of this, the poser models actually WORK -- they don't look out of place in the slightest, because they just blend in with the ham, cheese, cheesecake (and beefcake).
The controls feel sluggish because there's no animation cancel.  Characters stop running when their animation finishes, and move buffering means sometimes your character goes on auto-pilot for a few seconds.  Enemies strike at random rather than having any real semblence of AI.  The fighting isn't polished - parries usually but not always pay off, and enemies can be cheesed by the advanced commands.  Sometimes you have to switch to keyboard over the game pad in menus.  Your character's taunt may replace your item menu depending on range from an enemy.  Somtimes.  There are terrible escort missions.  Regular bosses are laughably easy; special bosses are cheesy and irrittating.  You can't skip cutscenes.
And you can impale yourself at will on trap spikes simply by jumping up.
None of it matters, it just piles on the ham and cheese and just ADDS to the ridiculousness of the game and consequently, usually makes it more fun (except the final boss).  Despite all its flaws, this is a game that has a lot of heart and love poured into it.  Plus, despite all the low production values... there's some real bits of clever design thrown in, just to throw you off guard.  Little bits.  Occasional bits.
This isn't a game for someone looking to have a serious, polished, awe-inspiring experience.  This is a game for someone who wants dumb fun, and for someone who enjoys a good bad B-movie, and wants to laugh at a game that's so bad but so simutaneously sincere about its badness that that it winds up kinda good.

Erwin's Timewarp is a charming puzzle game where you play as a dog who has gone back in time. The game is currently in Early Access and right now you can play in 1984. You roam around collecting items which will help you solve puzzles. One example is having to lure a police officer away so you can climb stairs on top of a building. If you have found the correct items, you can light a fire causing the police officer to investigate and allowing you to reach that otherwise inaccessable area.
This game doesn't hold your hand. You will have to explore and find everything on your own. This is not a bad thing at all as it makes each puzzle more satisfying when you complete them. I have come across no bugs at all and the game runs very smoothly.
I am impressed with the attention to detail of items throughout the level. (The sand pit looks great). I hope this level of attention to detail continues in all future levels.
Instead of having a timer counting down, you have a hunger meter which counts down. There are food bowls scattered around which will refill this meter. I thought this was much better than having a generic clock ticking down and it made me feel a lot less rushed having this system in place.
This game has a lot of potential and I look forward to playing future levels as they are released. If you are interested in puzzle games then this is one that should satisfy.

In short, I really enjoyed Type:Rider, but there are some points I would love to see... revisited?
GRAPHICS:
The graphics are nice, they fit on the style of game and yes it is undeniable that Limbo played a strong inspirational role here, which for me is only positive since the topic of the game makes it a whole new thing and I really enjoy this type of "ambient scrolling";
Don't even think they copied Limbo, because they sure didn't, it is just really the atmosphere that gets similar points!
THE "STORY":
As a graphic designer and typography lover, I HAD to have this game and give it a try. I had little difficulty understanding the game story and in my opinion everything was connected in a extremely smart fashion, but I do realize that people without "education" towards typography/printing history might not link the things as I do;
Now, to claim "historical" as a tag to describe the game, a little bit more of in-game action, other than reading the chapters about each Type, would also be requiered.
GAMEPLAY
Simple commands are okay, but sadly, very simple and short levels. But still they are very beautifull! Adding a little extra of content to each level and making it a little bit more challenging / long would be a perfect modification to the game!
THE SOUND:
It is okay.
My overhall thinking is that the game could:
a) have a major update;
b) have a TYPE:RIDER 2 to prove everyone how talented the devs are really ;)
Cheers

Ever since those of us who like exploration/puzzle adventures played Myst, we have been seeking its equal - and Quern is a contender to displace Myst and become the new standard.  There is an interesting story, some really ingenious puzzles that are fun to solve (and they fit into the story), the graphics are beautiful, the music haunting, and most of all, there is a lot to explore in a seemingly small space.  Like ROOM, the world of Quern unfolds into more and more levels as you solve puzzles, but you get there by just opening doors rather than using the Myst artifice of book linking.  A very nice touch that puzzles are re-used.  There are also a couple of endings to choose from.  All in all a solid effort and a fantastic contribution to the genre.  I will now be seeking Quern eqiuvalents!
Most of the puzzles can be figured out with some decent thought - it is nice being able to think "what would I really do in this situation" and have that work.  There are a few times I found myself a bit stumped about what next to do, and typically all I needed to do was visit everywhere I'd been, and think about what I had on hand in inventory and how it might be used, or things I had seen previously that seemed to have no immediate purpose.  Everything has a purpose.
My toughest times were figuring out where to aim the lighthouse light and with which crystal,  the inverse of the puzzle with the concentric circle segments, and figuring out how to get to the second story of the lab - I did need to get help a few times - but once I got underground below the tower I sailed on through without any issues.
This was fun in the purest exploration/puzzle adventure sense.  Highly recommended for fans of the genre.

Mafia 3 in my opinion is well worth the buy although many people would probably disagree, and I can understand why you might not like the game so im going to break this review into two parts. The first part will be a bullet point list of everything wrong and right they did and the second part will be going into more depth with some of the key pros and cons of the game.
Pros:
-Story rich (Amazing story)*
-Great graphics
-Great cutsences
-Great voice acting
- Extremely satisfying gun play*
-SOUND TRACK IS A 10/10!!*
-Full game will take you 30-60 hours*
-3 different endings*
-Underboss system*
Cons:
-Very poorly optimized*
-Repetitve missions*
-graphical bugs here and there
-CUTSCENCES DON'T LOOK LIKE THE REST OF GAME
-Open world felt pointless*
- Side missions were boring*
-No ending free roam*
In my opinion this game is a 8/10 being held back from a 10 because of the performance issues and it's repetitveness although it doesn't bother me, and I still love this game I tend to take strong storys over perfect gameplay. Speaking of which, every pro and con listed with a * next to it above will be put into more depth here.
The story- This story for the game was done PERFECTLY! It has a twist very early on in the game and it's very well paced, the story for this game was one of the biggest things that kept me going through to see what would happen. Since it is set in the 1960s many of the people are prejudice of one another and it fits really well in with the setting and story, needless to say it's done well and I liked it so much i'm probably going to play it again. (I don't want to spoil anything so i'll leave that there)
Gunplay- The gunplay in Mafia 3 is done extremley well. All of the guns in the game fell more realistic than in other 3rd person shooters and the vilence is extremley satisfying to watch and never gets old. There are also light stealth mechanics that I don't think work too well with the game but hey they're there and itkeeps your options open. You can also perform takedowns and brutal takedowns which I personally couldn't stop doing just because they were really cool to look at. Although its a very simplistic gamplay formula it works well and is satisfying as ♥♥♥♥!
Soundtrack- The soundtrack is a ♥♥♥♥ing 10/10 hands down! nearly every single song on this game's soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing perfect and they have so many instantly recongnizable clasiscs as well as some amazing unpopular songs too. If you don't believe me then go listen to the soundtrack on youtube or something you don't need the game to excperience the perfection of it.
The length of the game- The game will for the average person i'd say take around 40-50 hours but if you decided to pump a ton of extra time into the side missions, and how good you are at games in general then or not at all i'd say it would take you around 30-60 hours which is a damn good amount of time for a tripple a game if you ask me.
3 endings- There are 3 differen't endings to the game which I was pleasently suprised to see it wasn't linear to the end. All of the endings were fasinating and very unique which I feel is a plus considering I love a good choice ending even in a linear game.
Underboss system- In the game you progress in the story by getting new teritory and assigning it to your underbosses, which I thought was really fun and cool to see how they would all react depending on who you chose to give it to. Sometimes they'd be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥other times they'd love you and I believe although this didn't happen to me, if you♥♥♥♥♥♥one of them off enough they'll actually revolt and try to kill you which I also thought was an extremley cool feature in the game.
Now on to the cons
Very poorly optomized- The game although it looks pretty that doesn't mean♥♥♥♥♥♥if it can't run well which it doesn't. I have a pretty godamn beefy computer and I clock out around the optimal system requirements but im sitting here scratching my head as to why in the hell i'm getting 45-50 frames half the time on medium settings! and it didn't change if I put it on low either and I know i'm not the only onw with this issue. I can't underatand why componies think its ok to give us ♥♥♥♥♥♥ console ports it blows my ♥♥♥♥ing mind why we as pc gamers are treated like second thoughts and last minute plans its ♥♥♥♥ed and needs to stop. If you don't hit the reccomended system requirements don't even bother your game will probabaly crap out enven on the lowest settings.
Repetitve missions- This the one thing people always bring up when ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on mafia 3. THE REPETITVE MISSIONS. Look in my opinion it wasn't a big deal at all because the gameplay and story kept me from being bored at all while playing even if the missions were repetitve sometimes which yes they could feel that way. But it certaintly isn't a deal breaker or makes the game all that much worse to me.
The open world feels pointless- Mafia 3 is an open world game for almost no reason. The game is extremley linear there aren't really any random events or stores you can shop in, or anything worth going to visit or see and the game didn't have to be open world. It kind of feels like it was something on a checklist. And although there are side missions i'll get to that in a sec.
Side missions- The side missions are abosolutley AWFUL. they are one of the most useless ♥♥♥♥ing things in this game. All of them are just fetch missions to grab something and bring it back 3000 meters in a slow♥♥♥♥♥vehicle, and what they are supposed to do is earn you more money, and build trust with your underbosses but ♥♥♥♥ I barley did any and I always had more money then I knew what to do with and never had a problem with one of the underbosses getting furious it was just a sad attempt to make it look like there was more you can do in the game and I don't aprriate the attmept.
No ending free roam- Now in most open world games you would excpect a free roam at the end but no, you decide what happens at the end and that's that. No more its done. It just shows how much this game didn't need to be an open world because there's nothing to do once you get done with the story and it stands true even the creators agree because they didn't put a free roam at the end of the game.

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

The first half of this game is mostly an absolutely delightful joining of typography, education, and platforming. This half fosters exploration and replaying levels to learn more and get everything.
However, the Clarendon level contains a completely idiotic mechanic that runs counter to the calm, though hazardous, exploration of the first part of the game. While I understand including the stalking gunfire in the spirit of the "wild West", it detracts immensely from the game. From here, new mechanics involving floating, moving death spots, moving platforms, and crushing blocks, bring to the fore the uneven and unpredictable controls. Whilst trying to complete Pixel, I found that as I got past each stick point, I felt no sense of accomplishment, and merely swore at the next stick point, which I would discover just as I reached the bit of the map that was not on the screen yet.
While those with extreme skill at platforming might continue to enjoy the game at that point, the inability to feel any mastery of the controls killed the game for me, and I have had to change my rating from thumbs up to thumbs down. I began this game with joy and a desire to challenge myself to complete most of the achievements. I have ended it with anger and a determination that I would be better off picking up a textbook on typography.

First off, I just want to say it absolutely blows my mind that this game is reviewed as overall "Very Positive" on steam.
I bought this game when it was on sale right before it was removed from steam. I love narrative driven games, and so I was really looking forward to playing it. At first I did enjoy it quite a bit, but by about the third chapter I began to get very bored with it and now that I've finished the game I have to say I strongly dislike it.
Pros:
- The way the story is told is actually a pretty neat concept
- The combat is solid, and the way you have to use your gun and the flashlight together combined with the enemy design adds a nice level of strategy that was quite refreshing at first. The enemies are easy to handle in small numbers, but in larger groups they're very formidable to the point where it can feel like the player is on an almost even playing field with the enemies. At times it can actually feel a bit unfair, but this is not very often.
Cons:
- The level design is atrocious. Almost the entire game feels like one long boring level where you're constantly looking at the same dark and drab color scheme with almost no variation and its sickening after a while. If you're picking up Alan Wake, expect to trudge through a dreary forest and dark, featureless hallways in circles for 18ish hours.
- This is the basic structure of every chapter: run here and do this, only to find out you need to run there and do this first, so you can go all the way over there and do this afterwards, and so on and so forth, all the while stopping to fight the same enemies in copy pasted encounters every few minutes.
- The chapters are dragged out to add artificial length to the game. I don't know how many times I thought I was nearing the end of a chapter only to have a ski lift collapse or tree fall over and block my path, forcing me to go around and deal with more of the same repetitive enemy encounters. As a result, the narrative is streched thin and as the chapters drag on and on with little to no plot advancement it becomes increasingly difficult to stay engaged in the story. Which leads me to my next point;
- While the story is actually decent, its very difficult to stay engaged or interested since key plot points are spread few and far between amidst hours of walking through a dark forest. There are literally no significant moments in the story from the beginning of the second chapter until the end of the fourth chapter (several hours worth of gameplay) and at that point I was so annoyed by the game I didn't even care. I actually think the game could have been cut down to a fourth of its size and you could still fit the entire plot into it easily. It also becomes increasingly convoluted as it progresses, and it can be extremely cheesy at times. The character named Barry is the game's attempt at comic relief but he is anything but funny and is actually cringe worthy most of the time.
- The movement is abysmal. As if the game wasn't already long enough, it becomes even longer because your character crawls along at a snail's pace.
- The camera angle is AWFUL. I don't know what the devs were thinking with this one.
- The controls are pretty unresponsive and clunky
- The ending to this game is honestly god awful. Little to no closure and it does a horrible job of explaining anything. I had a hard time even understanding what was going on.
And that about sums up Alan Wake. When I bought this along with Alan Wake's American Nightmare I was excited to play both of them along with the two DLC chapters. Now that I have finished the base game, I will be playing neither the DLC nor American Nightmare.
TL;DR: Alan Wake has potential, but it is crippled by flaws such as poor level design and plot that is spread too thin to be thoroughly enjoyed. 5/10

This game is honestly the best Myst-like game I have ever played.  In fact, I hesitate to even compare this to Myst as it shines in its own way (and, in my opinion, is even better). Pros:
> Interactible objects
> Tying story pieces into the puzzles themselves
> An *amazing* narrative
> Stunning scenery, especially in high-res
> Puzzles are well-done and rack your brain without feeling repetitive or random

Cons:
> I did get stuck one or two times, unable to figure out how to continue.  This is a problem in almost every Myst-like game, and it's actually fairly minimal, but I felt it should be pointed out.

This could be a really good game, despite its graphics. It has everything you'd want from a barbarian game. I played the "non extended" version a lot, bought it before it was on Steam. It's just something you don't see often in video games nowadays, so I'm really glad someone made a game like this.
Unfortunately the unresponsive controls and glitches totally ruin the game. Like seriously half of the time the input doesn't register correctly, your character starts runing towards the enemy instead of doing a special move, combos don't work, blocking fails, etc. The delay between the input and the actual movement is also a real pain to play with, and even simple things like hitting A and X at once for a vertical attack doesn't work sometimes.
I got to the minotaur-thing kind of boss in the first zone by reaching the caves, then the slaughterhouse, then the dungeon, just to get matched against a level 9 boss ( I'm level 5 ) which could kill me in two hits because of several "glitches" :
- when the boss is about to hit you, you're pushed back, which makes the "scene" move to the left. During this time, blocking ( and roll/dodging ) doesn't work ( like if the game was paused during the camera movement ), meaning that if you try to block just at this moment, you're dead.
- the boss can push you to the edge of the screen and you can't even see your character then, making it pretty much impossible to fight back. He'll just keep hitting you until you die.
- sometimes the boss will kill you even if you're blocking, while normally blocking just puts you on the ground, but you don't take any damage. So you CAN kill the boss if you perfectly time your block ( he's pretty slow ), until the game just glitches and you die anyway.

On top of that, the game suffers from some terrible designs :
- you can't go back through some doors for some reason
- there is no map so you have to remember the exact layout of the levels to know where you went and where you're going, which is made pretty hard because a lot of rooms look the same.
- nothing is explained and the tutorial is extra poor.
- loot is random, and your character gets hungry. But sometimes you won't find anything to eat so... I don't even know the effect of hunger anyway, it's not explained. Maybe your stamina drains faster or something, I don't know.
- every time I level up, the "select" button appears and shows me the movement list. That's cool, but... why ? Do I unlock new moves when I level up ? It's not shown on the list, there is no "skill point" to spend or anything. New moves aren't highlighted either. Dunno how it works.

And so on, and so on.

I love this game.
The only reason I haven't played more of it to date is the same reason I'm giving it a thumbs down. It shouldn't have left Early Access.
When I started playing it (March '15) it was already out of it and therefore supposedly a full release.
I dipped my toes in every map and made some progress here and there, until one day they released an update and I found out my 20-something hours worth of advances had been wiped out with it.
Looking around in the forums, it soon became apparent that it wasn't just me nor was this the first time it happened. In fact it happened with every single update done before. Others had lost much more time than I did.
This would be excusable were the game in alpha/beta stage or even still Early Access and things were getting ironed out. Or if it was a 'rogue-like' or 'casual' game. Instead, this is the Dark Souls of truck driving games (set in some kind of deserted Russian Woodstock) and saving your progress is not something to dream about but a fundamental feature that is already there and works. Well, until they do another update.
To be clear, I'm speaking of the single player aspect of the game only, as multiplayer has no saving options to date.
Irked out, I forgot about it for some time, and came back a while later. This time I didn't split my attention on several maps, aware of the risk it would all go down the drain at any point. Soon enough came another update, and down the drain those extra few hours did go.
In the wake of complaints in the forums, I remember reading an announcement by Oovee stating they would be having a meeting with the developer (I paraphrase) and would 'explain to him how important maintaining the saved game progress across updates seemed to be to the players'. Which to me is nothing short of fascinating. That such a basic and obvious priority
to be told to a developer. Over a future meeting, no less.
Today, about half a year later, came another update and, unsurprisingly, another wipe. Wonder how that meeting went.
If you're on the fence and somehow stumble upon this, consider it a heads up that shouldn't get you out of the fence anyway, because I actually think the game is great, and it is perfectly playable as long as you don't wait too long to pick up where you left. The longer you wait, the higher the chance you'll have to start from scratch.
I'll update the direction my two cents are spinning if I ever become aware of this issue getting resolved. As it stands, Spintires suffers from a lack of respect for its players' time.

Kane & Lynch 2 is what the first game should have been. I played the first Kane & Lynch all the way to its conclusion and knew what the developers were going for, but they never really hit the high notes with their first effort. Kane & Lynch 2 is completely different in that respect as this game is raw, brutal and very violent...
It still has a host of missed opportunities gameplay wise regarding controls that could have been tighter; the cover mechanic work but only just and the weapons; while most feel good, there are a few that don't really feel under powered. The game also suffers from a very short story mode that severely hampers the overall product on offer.
The positives do make up for the negatives above in some respect. The story maybe short but what we have is two desperate men fighting their way out of China's criminal underbelly. From the first mission where Lynch needs to 'talk to someone’; the whole scene is turned on its head in seconds. What entails is a desperate struggle for survival for our two main men. Although the quality of dialogue varies it is still nice to hear Kane and Lynch communicate with one another. Lynch, who has deep lying mental problems, can be heard talking to himself more frequently over the course of the game. Kane tells him to pull it together has he knows what a loose cannon he can be but this fuels Lynch even more. Also, when the s**t does hit the fan, the characters sound like they are clearly fuelled by adrenaline when talking... This is a very nice touch and in some fire fights, it adds momentum to the scene. Graphically, this is where the game stands out to me! The handheld video effect is amazing and adds the grit that this story needs for player immersion. When you see naked people or shoot someone in the head, the camera goes blocky just on the 18+ parts. The brutality of the killings is better overall and I was pretty bored with other games that had gratified enemy’s heads exploding up walls. With this kind of game, this sort of graphical execution is great and differentiates it from the pack.
There is other stand out moments in the game but I wanted to just mention Arcade mode and multiplayer. On PC the multiplayer is dead which is a shame has the modes on offer where great and a lot of fun to play. However, if you and your friends have this game, you can do coop through arcade mode and story mode using HAMACHI (program that lets you connect to friends over the internet but tells the game you are playing it through LAN). Arcade mode is fragile alliance which is a great and it will keep you busy for a while. It's a bank heist with 8 other players, AI or friends and you; the mission? To escape with the money but friends can turn on you at any point in the level. It’s nice being on edge all game as an alliance in one round can be forged by helping a team mate out if they are caught in a sticky situation, however; due to the nature of the levels you can sometimes shoot a heist member accidently meaning you are labelled a traitor for the rest of the round. It is a stand out feature but is lacking further development as the 7 levels can be completed in around 5 hours. The only drawback to such a feature is the guns that you unlock as you gain new ranks.
In conclusion it is a package that should have been developed better as a single player game with the multiplayer additions adding weight to the product. Instead, what the game has is a under developed single player and good foundations for multiplayer. Combined it is a game that would be a good pick up from the bargain bin for under a tenner given that the online multiplayer is dead. The single player game is worth a run through twice if you like collecting achievements but a once through is suffice. I do like Kane and Lynch 2 I just wish the single player had a few more chapters and because of this, it gets a good 7/10.

One of  the  greatest games/simulations I  have ever played!
TLDR:
+++ If you have any interest into space, rockets and flying to other planetsand moons, this is the game for you!
+++ KSP is basicly a sandbox simulation with the entire solar system as your playground.
+++ You learn a lot about physics and the mechanics of our solar system.
+++ The Modding community is very active and has published thousands of really great  and complex mods for this game.
Full review:
The learn curve is very hard in the beginning and you do not know what you are doing. Over many many hours you learn the basics of rocketry and planetary physics. It takes a long time until something  really works or to just launch a rocket into orbit and cycle the planet  without crashing .
But then comes the revelation!
With every step you make: Launching a rocket and land on the mun was for me the greatest step of all. After nearly  1200 hours of  playtime you plan, construct and execute highly complex missions to the most distant plants and moons in the solar system. Building massive space stations and catching class E asteroids before they hit Kerbin (KSP Earth) , will also be on your list to do.
You always keep setting new goals for yourself  after you achieved soemthing.
The ability to just try something out and construct the weirest machines, robots and rockets is the most fun. I think I spend more time in the rocket assembly building, constructing ships, rovers and transfer stages, than actually flying around with my constructed ships. Watching what happens is  such  a  joy! Mostly it will explode and crash at some point...
But when it works and you landed on a distant planet like duna for the first time, it feels like you just have beat one of the harder bosses in dark souls!
And to mention the modding support! This has me hooked everytime when new mods (e.g. Chaka Monkey exploration) came out.  There are countless new parts for the editor, planets, moons and  many more mods available on a lot of webpages around  (e.g. Spacedock). You can basicly extend and adjust the gameplay to your liking. At some point I had a couple of thousand mods active at the same time, increasing loading times vastly. But when it launched it was so worth the wait!

T:R is a pretty good documentary [as you would expect from arte], and it is told in a nice platformer game which one can think of as 'limbo' meets 'wikipedia'.
The information is told through collectible objects, as you collect more, you reveal more information about the history of typography. The information isn't just a text-dump, it reads nice and easily and in such a way hat there's no information overload.
The game is pretty good. It has a sort of platformer style, similar to the game limbo, only perhaps a little more colourful. You roll through various levels relating to the typefaces being discussed, from wild west environments to modernist abstract areas. These provide interesting challenges, although I did find at times it got a bit frustrating trying to get past certain obstacles.
It goes without saying, if you don't like documentaries, don't play this game. If you are interested in learning more about typography, then you should play the game.

I came into this game expecting the messiah, considering the volume of praise it gets, and I found myself disappointed. I'd still recommend it, but I'd only rate it 6/10. Here's why:
1. I have no prior knowledge of the source material, and this game did not in any way interest me in it. Geralt may be the most badass character of all time in the stories/novels/whatever they are, but here he just seemed... aloof. No real interest in what he was doing. I had read in numerous places that playing the original Witcher is unnecessary, but without context to the world, I couldn't care at all about the political intrigue that was supposed to be the entire main story.
2. For a game lauded as "mature," nothing about it struck me as terribly adult.  Yes, there was sex in the game, but it came off as immature, lending itself more to spouts of people screaming "Ohh, boobies!" than any real character development.
3. The battle system had a really steep learning curve, resulting in an unevenly difficult start of the game compared to the easy end of it, though this is not a bad thing. The bad thing is that I never felt rewarded for overcoming difficult tasks. Without a sense of accomplishiment, diffiuclt victories felt hollow. Why didn't I feel accomplished? Because...
4. Quicktime events. QTEs are not intrisically bad, but they added nothing to the boss fights they were involved in, and only served as an unecessary wall to victory.  Not every boss fight had them, thankfully, but fights involving them marred my image of the game.
If you can get past those gripes there are plenty of postive qualities in the game.  Your choices did seem to matter, which is rare in RPGs these days, and the side quests were a lot of fun. Weapon modification and crafting/alchmey were great, even though I think I underutilized alchemy in my first playthough.  Replay value is huge due to a divergent story at the 1/3 marker, as well as three skill trees that cannot be filled in any one playthrough, resulting in a myriad of gameplay styles.
While the game disappointed me, I will probably buy Witcher 3 (on sale) to see how my actions play out in the long run.  Happy hunting.

The game gets compared a lot to the DMC series and I can see why, though I would say the combat is closer to MGR:Revengeance. Unarmed and weapon attacks can be links together fluently and more moves can be unlocked/bought as you progress through the game. There's also a blocking and counter system complete with Just Blocks and Just Counters, though these are near impossible to use when taking on a horde of enemies (atleast for someone of my skill level).
The game, I would say, suffers from repetitiveness when it comes to fighting the grunts. From stage to stage you'll be fighting similar enemies both in design and attacks.  In higher difficulties, there's simply more of them and they also do more damage. On the other hand, bosses are a lot of fun to fight against, especially Suzuka. It's during these that you can  actually use blocks and counters more effectively and stylishly. It's fun to learn the bosses' attack patterns and they also have a sort of "low health phase" where they'll use more powerful attacks and mix things up a bit. For someone like me though, I really enjoy the "stylish" aspect of these boss fights. It's rewarding when you perform Just Blocks and Counters and beat the boss with only these tools. The flashy effects compliment it too.
In short, a simple hack and slash game that's easy to learn but hard to master. The repetitiveness can get tiring, but in my opinion, the bosses more than make up for it.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game to which I have no bad words to say. It is a 2D hack-n-slash action RPG in which you play as Dust, a somewhat confused warrior with no memory of his past, as he journeys through the land of Falana in search of his identity. The story is well-written, moving, intriguing and exciting right to the end.
The combat in Dust is simple but effective, with a depth to it that keeps it from ever growing stale. The enemies, too, are delightfully varied, with many requiring different techniques if you want to fight them effectively.
The game is populated by many memorable characters, and all of them have their own superb voice actors and unique personalities. Some of them can seem two-dimensional, yet they are all believable characters, helping to make the vibrant world come to life. Most notable is your constant companion, Fidget - a cute, lovable and entertaining little creature who never annoys and is amazingly helpful, especially towards the end of the game.
But what really stands out about Dust is the beautiful environment. Each area has its own aesthetic, perfectly realised by the scenery and complemented by an excellent soundtrack. Moreover, you are encouraged to explore this world, with over twenty side-quests, XP bonuses just for talking to new people and dozens of little secrets littered around the world, some of which are very interesting in their own right.
If I had to make one criticism, it would be that the blacksmith is not as useful as she perhaps should be, since her fee for crafting an item is the same as you would get for selling it. However, this is a small complaint, and not one moment of gameplay is a disappointment. I count Dust among the best games I have ever played.

Where can I start...
Over the past year I've came across 4 great puzzle games that have kept me begging for more, The Witness, Anitchamber, Obduction, and now Quern. For me The Witness blew my mind and I caught the bug for puzzle games again. I couldn't remember playing a puzzle game that great since the days of playing Myst.
Then Quern came along, and after having just played Obduction (spiritual successor to Myst) I realised just how lacking Obduction was when compared to Myst. Quern in my eyes is the true spiritual successor to Myst.
The type of game I enjoy is certainly a game that makes me take notes without holding my hand at all, and currently I'm sat here with an A4 piece of paper covered with notes from the past few days. I'll admit there were a couple of occasions where I was stumped, but for me that just feeds my curiosity and motivates me to figure it out. It made me question certain solutions that I thought would be a stab in the dark, to the point where my mind was repeating "Clever girl".
It's content is not only huge for the price but the amount, quality, and variety of puzzles in Quern is astonishing, and the story unravels to a great finish. And to top it all off, the presentation of the game is simply beautiful.
I can't wait to see where Zadbox goes next.

I've been playing this game on and off ever since the tech demo first came out (the 8x8 train car on wheels mod* was amazing fun) and after having spent some time in the full game, this is here to stay.
The objective is fairly simple, namely pick up logs at location A and transport them to location B, but succeeding in that is anything but simple. Essentially any time you try to take a "shortcut", the result is drowned trucks, lost loads, stuck in quicksand, the list goes on. And given that there is no time limit, there really is no excuse not to take the long and safer route around. But it does make for discovering all that the maps have to offer, which is a lot.
There's a nice variety of trucks and trailers in the game, although they're all Russian. I think that's a plus, since there's not a lot of games that feature those. Great details on them too.
Final note: the ambient sounds (birds, crickets, owls, etc) are downright amazing. I sometimes just turn off the lights and the engine and leave the game running for the ambient sounds.
* At the time of writing, it looks like mods will, in some form or another, make it into the game eventually.

This is the last sentence in the "intro" section of the game which consists of a text explaining the background story. Apparently, we are the guinea pigs of a scientist and since we are inmates the doctor got special approval so that he can sacrifice the prisoners of the institution. The experiment is simple: we are chased by a demon and our job is to escape.
Again, the above is literally taken from the intro text. I picked a random sentence since most have typographical errors. We are only talking about a handful of sentences so you can guess how much time was spent with doing some quality check after the "development" was over. As for development: due to the typos and awfulness of the rest of the game I have to assume that this is one of those "lovely" Unity-asset-turned-into-video-game examples. Since another language selection is possible I assume the developers are not native English so they quickly used Google Translate to have the English translation from their mother tongue done for the "intro".
A mess. Nothing more, nothing less. We walk around looking for the exit. Occasionally a demon appears and runs towards us. The only thing we can do is to open cell doors and hide. Usually, the demon doesn't disappear so this option to hide is quite disappointing. Also, why are we unable to sprint? 3 hits and we are done. Back to main menu, hit play, watch the "cutscene" again, start over, rinse and repeat.
The demon's head often does some clipping as does our body when it comes to objects. Our protagonist constantly wants to climb over objects (desks, chairs, computer consoles, etc.). If he is unable to do so the clipping will suffice. At one point I managed to clip through the rusty objects in front of me to be able to find safe haven between 2 bunks. We have a flashlight but it usually works when we are close to walls i.e. the light appears only on them. Otherwise it is as if the light was constantly flickering.
Says the store page but running is not an option. In fact, the Unity start-up screen tells us we have "fire" as an action button along with jumping. Neither works - for the latter our character starts by making an effort then he quickly lands as if he hit his head. Several options are available for graphics (from the very low to ultra) but none of them show any difference.
Evade this game at any cost.

My personal rating -> 5.0 stars
I have been a long time fan of the NinjaKiwi's Bloons Tower Defense series from way back with the first one. They have come a long way since then and I must say, NinjaKiwi is one of the best companies for making addicting tower defense games that have enjoyment for the whole family, fun enough to play for days, and exciting enough to keep you playing for years.
The free version is for those who love to grind for days to slowly inch their way up the ladder to having all towers and all those tower's upgrades available in a match. You do get small amounts of currency for losing but 5x the amount for winning. But without investing some money it will take you quite a long time to achieve this. However, if money is no object a one time 50$ investment could net you all the towers with all their upgrades and still have some currency left over to put a few decales on your bloons if you so desire.
The game does have a practice mode (which I recommend using as much as possible) and is there to help you learn where to place your towers and when to upgrade them without any penalties of losing game currency.
The game seems to pair you with others that are of similar calibur using the battle ranking and for the most part seems pretty balanced. However, until you understand what the towers can do and where they are best placed and who they are best partnered with you can feel a little overwhelemed.
Bloons Battles is not for the faint of heart though. It is a pvp style tower defense game and a lot of the community are in it to win it and will not give you a moments rest. They will capitalize on any minor or major boo boo you do in the game and you could end up seeing the "Defeated" screen a few times more than you wish.
All in all I give the game a full 5 stars. Of course this could be biased because I feel NinjaKiwi is the best at making Tower Defense games fun, addicting with mega hours of replay, and a generous amount of DLC to purchase.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game to which I have no bad words to say. It is a 2D hack-n-slash action RPG in which you play as Dust, a somewhat confused warrior with no memory of his past, as he journeys through the land of Falana in search of his identity. The story is well-written, moving, intriguing and exciting right to the end.
The combat in Dust is simple but effective, with a depth to it that keeps it from ever growing stale. The enemies, too, are delightfully varied, with many requiring different techniques if you want to fight them effectively.
The game is populated by many memorable characters, and all of them have their own superb voice actors and unique personalities. Some of them can seem two-dimensional, yet they are all believable characters, helping to make the vibrant world come to life. Most notable is your constant companion, Fidget - a cute, lovable and entertaining little creature who never annoys and is amazingly helpful, especially towards the end of the game.
But what really stands out about Dust is the beautiful environment. Each area has its own aesthetic, perfectly realised by the scenery and complemented by an excellent soundtrack. Moreover, you are encouraged to explore this world, with over twenty side-quests, XP bonuses just for talking to new people and dozens of little secrets littered around the world, some of which are very interesting in their own right.
If I had to make one criticism, it would be that the blacksmith is not as useful as she perhaps should be, since her fee for crafting an item is the same as you would get for selling it. However, this is a small complaint, and not one moment of gameplay is a disappointment. I count Dust among the best games I have ever played.

Very rarely does a one-man game turn out so well. Correction: NEVER has a one-man game turned out so well. Aside from some voice acting and music, and a little bit of the story, this game is the work of one man. There are a couple downsides to this, but only a couple. The game as a whole is a masterpiece built on the work of others—failing to do much that's unique, but everything it does, it does well.
The first thing to notice about this game is the graphics. This is two-dimensional graphics at its finest. If I didn't know better, I'd say this game uses vectors instead of pixels. There is not a single pixel to be found anywhere in the game. Given that most indie games don't even try for beautiful graphics and instead content themselves with "retro" 8-bit graphics, this is a marvel. Graphically, I imagine this game will stand the test of time, which is something this author believes no game prior to the Xbox 360/PS3 will accomplish, and very few since. Light shines through forests and deer run along beside you, heat ripples of volcanic rock, and animations make it easy to keep track of the action, no matter how busy the screen becomes. The hand-drawn levels and characters only serve to accentuate the powerful story it tells.
The story itself is wonderful from beginning to end, although the end does become a little confusing with terms like Sen-Mithrarin being used, though I won't spoil what that with a definition or description of how esoteric the story becomes. Although fantastical, the story does not bother with traditional happy-ever-after endings for its quests, which is a welcome change given most stories which take place in such a vibrant and colorful world have Disney endings. Oh yes, and Fidget, your guide through much of the world is hilarious. "No! Mash the buttons!"
Which brings me to gameplay. At its core, the game is quite similar to Street Fighter with its combos. And contrary to what you are told by the in-game tutorial, button mashing is not a crime in this game, at least on the easy difficulty level. The list of combos is quite short... too short, but every combo in the game is useful, even critical in some parts of the game. Fidget serves as an additional source of combos, but at least in combat her contributions are much more optional, usually acting as devastating kill-all moves that must be built up to. The controls are responsive and it feels good to cut your way through masses of enemies while still requiring you to adapt your fighting style to the enemies you're facing
The game incorporates many RPG elements. Better armor and additions to your blade can be created from materials acquired from enemies, better healing items are found our purchased as your buying power increases from beating tougher enemies, and occasionally your level goes up, allowing you to increase one of several stats. But despite the inclusion of these gameplay elements it all feels very shallow. It's not bad at all, and I believe it's impossible to beat the game without it, but it feels rather meaningless since none of that unlocks anything other than increases in damage dealt or decreases in damage received.
Overall, Dust: An Elysian Tale is a wonderful romp that everyone remotely interested in fighting games should play through at least once. Here's hoping for a sequel!
