You remember the Alien vs. Predator frenchise back in the day? Before Half Life 2? This is it at it's core. And then, it isn't.
Natural Selection 2 is a competitive FPS-RTS mix that features asymmetrical gameplay. A team of Marines is put against a team of aliens that play entirely different while one player of each team serves as an overseeing commander from a top-down perspective. As commander you have to put down buildings like ressource extractors, armories, robotic facilities or buildings that provide upgrades for your little and ever complaining servants. This mode actually plays quite a lot like Starcraft or Command & Conquer for example. At least most of the times. You can even issue specific orders to individual team members. Following these orders and the way they are executing them is completely up them though.
While the commander and his skill is certainly critical to the success of your team, the personal skill of every soldier/alien matters almost as equally. But teamplay is objectively the most critical. A team that communicates a steady flow of information is already half way through the match.
There is quite a lot of maps shipped with the game and an almost infinite number of custom made maps as well as different game modes. The basic mode though puts you on a map with usually 5 locations where a command terminal or hive can be set up. These are needed for your commander to do his job. If you loose all of your Command terminals / Hives you loose the game. You start with one prebuild at a random location together with your first ressource extractor that provide a slow tick of ressources, both for the commander to spend on buildings, upgrades etc and for every player seperately to spend on personal equipment (Weapons, Armor, perks, ...). In case of the Marines you also start with a single Infantry Portal on which dead marines can respawn. Aliens hatch from eggs that spawn near a Hive at a slow rate.
So the immediate goal is to expand to other ressource nodes, build up you base and defend it and eventually destroy the enemie's bases. It's a game about map control like you would expect from a competitive RTS, so usually the team that holds the majority of ressource nodes for an extended period of time wins the game. Usually.
So much for the gameplay. What's it mechanically? It's a fast paced shooter that orientates itself along older titles like said Alien vs. Predator, Unreal Tournament, even Counter Strike for a certain degree. Weapons don't nessecarily act realistically. It is more important to keep the cursor on target than it is precisely aim or shoot in bursts to maintain a narrow spread. Aliens regenerate health at a slow rate but marines need medipacks that are dropped by the commander or an armory to get back up to full health. In addition they need a teammate with a welder to fix any armor points lost.
So, pretty old school but with an interesting twist and certainly a focus on teamplay.
Gameplay mechanics for the commander are deskribed in one word: Starcraft. It's an established formula and it works fine. Hotkeys, hotkeys, hotkeys. Every building and every equipment you may drop as commander is sorted in different categories (basic buildings, advanced buildings, etc.) and mapped to a specific key. (Controls are fully rebindable by the way). That's it. It's pretty easy to pick up although quite hard to be good at.
Technically and graphically the game is not really state of the art. It is not an ugly game and the texture quality is reasonably good. Animations work fine although they might look a bit silly from time to time. Where it really shines is it's dense, almost claustrophobic atmosphere and the ammount of adjustable game and graphics options as well as it featuring a good, old fashioned server browser and full mod support.
It's a PC game so why would you not want to pick a server based in your country with a low ping instead of being randomly assigned some server at the end of the world where not a single person speaks a language you recognise and you lag yourself through the map? Server browsers are your best friend in any FPS and Natural Selection 2 has one so... go for it.
If you like Counter Strike but would like to try something that puts two teams with entirely different strengthes and weaknesses against each other while maintaining a high degree of competitive gameplay then Natural Selection 2 is a thing you will most certainly enjoy.
If you already enjoyed it's predecessor or Alien vs. Predator back in the day but the graphics get a bit old for you then this is an absolute no-brainer. Buy it. Love it.
One thing to keep in mind though is that the developer pretty much ceased any support and further development to be able to concentrate on their current project. Although there are still frequent content updates and plenty of bugfixes provided by the community team that officially took over and so far the changes that were made by this team improved the game in many aspects.

Middle Earth Shadow of War is the sequel to 2014's surprisingly good game. Shadow of Mordor was a really neat little game where you play Talion, a ranger killed with his family but ending up as an immortal man with the help of a ghostly companion: the ghost of an elf which turns out to be Celebrimbor, the forger of the rings. The game was innovative with its nemesis system which led to many relations being made between the player and orcs, he would first be their ennemies and then be able to brand them in their army. The problem was that Shadow of Mordor didn't feel really big, there were a lot of missing mechanics which led to the game feeling a bit short on many aspects. First of, the story was pretty much Assassin's Creed with revenge being the center of Talion's attention. Many missing features like being able to unbrand orcs or having them as body guards made them feel more like slaves than companions. This is was a problem since they felt alive and free before you brand them but then their eyes turn blue and they just follow orders without actually stating that they now work for you, they don't say stuff like "I serve the lord of light" or "I'll destroy the lord of darkness". Finally Shadow of mordor was WAY to easy, it kinda removed the whole pupose of having a nemesis because I would have to force myself to die or let them run away if I liked them since they were way too weak. This was caused by the skill tree being way too generous and making you an unstopable beast. You could also easily cheese the battles and just jump above orcs and hit them in the back.
Now that we've got that out of the way, let's talk about Shadow of War and why its incredibly superior to Shadow of Mordor. The first thing that struck me was the story, it isn't about revenge anymore but more about Talion trying to save the Mordor from Sauron. Shadow of Mordor ended on a cliffhanger ending which Shadow of War happily follows which kinda make the first game necessary to play if you want to understand what happens in this game.
I was also very glad to see different difficulty settings which drasticly change how you play the game. Playing on easy will give you the same experience as Shadow of Mordor but playing on Hard like I did makes every orc captain a threat which gives way more impact on every battle and the overall feel of the game. Orcs don't just take damage anymore, now they adapt to your playstyle and will force you to use other technics instead of spamming the same one. Playing on harder difficulties will make orcs adapt pretty quickly so it really was hard, I died 79 times according to the stats page on the Warner Brothers forums.
The variety in orcs is spectacular, they are way more types of captains than before and they range from hilarious to nightmare fuel. It really makes you want to play more to meet more of them and maybe recruit them in your army. Because Monolith listened to us, we don't want orcs as slaves, many of us want them as friends and make them fight along side us on the battlefields. This is the biggest improvement to game has made over the original in my oppinion. You can now have a personal bodygard which will help you or even save you from an execution from times to times. However there is also a new mechanic: treason. Orcs that are on your side can now tell you that they don't need you anymore and will rejoin the Sauron. This is what makes the biggest difference on the battlefield: you are embushing someone, you are about to fight him and all of a sudden one of your orcs turns his back on you and manages to make you fail the mission. This is what makes orcs have a lot more personality and actually feel human which is one of the best experiences I've had this year.
Now let's talk about the big thing this game introduces: the sieges. The storyline wants you to capture 4 forts and make them yours to control the region. This is a huge change in focus from the first game and now the monarchy feels a lot more important. In Shadow of Mordor, the highest grade for an orc was "Warchief" which didn't do anything to be honnest, they just stopped roaming in the map. In Shadow of War, Warchiefs defend the fort during sieges which makes them way more important and honorable. You also have to put an orc at the very top which will lead the region and the fort. Both react to the commander and will change their look, the fort will have an industrial look if the commander is from the Machine tribe for example.
The story is dividen in 4 acts, the first one is some sort of prologue and is pretty boring, you should only play the story missions during this one. The second act is the meat of the game, its where you have story missions and side quests from the different factions which are actually pretty good (compared to the terrible ones the first game had). Act 3 is a big 30 minutes mission with a lot of story events going on. I love it and was really looking forward to see act 4. Act 4 is the worst thing I've played this year. There are no story events, not dialogues, no cutscenes, nothing. You just have to endure around 20 forts defenses in a row without any story between them. Your reward for that is a 3 minutes cutscene at the end which is actually the ending of the game. This is very disapointing, I expected act 4 to wrap things up in a big battle and end the game nicely. Instead, the ending of the game IS Act 3. This is very wrong, Act 3 feels like a turning point in the story but it just happens that this turning point is how to game ends.
It is obvious that Act 4 was added to make you have to choose between grinding to level up your orcs for the sieges or buying lootboxes to instantly get better orcs. This is not what I've done. I've 100% completed that game and haven't spent a cent on microtransactions or DLCs. They are not thrown in your face and are useles during the first 3 acts.
What I recomend you do is to simply skip act 4 and watch the ending cutscene on Youtube as soon as you've finished Act 3. I was told to do so and I didn't listen but I really should have. It took me 35 hours to complete Act 4, this wasn't fun.
Conclusion: Shadow of War is a great game, it improves on nearly every aspect of its predecessor but when you reach the ending it feels like there should be another Act based on narration. Most of it will probably be added by the DLCs but it still feels disapointing to end so abruplty. The game is still incredibly good and unique and I'd recommand it to anyone. You don't even need to know the Lord of The Ring well to like it. Is it worth 60 dollars ? Yes in my oppinion, it was a great experience and I'm looking forward to the future of the series.

This is a great game... For about 15 hours.  The storyline is pretty much nonexistant, the combat is ok, and killing orcs wholesale is pretty fun.  But after that 15 hour mark, a few glaring issues pop up:
Controls -  The controls in this game are♥♥♥♥♥♥  You will find yourself rolling into a wall repeatedly going "please just climb it... no... no just... just climb... sigh."  Capturing orc captains is nearly impossible, as you have to stand perfectly still for 3-5 seconds, and any kind of damage at all interrupts it.  In general the controls just feel super clunky, and you'll find yourself wondering why there wasn't more time spent developing the combat (its two buttons, fyi)
Gameplay - Beyond the 15 hour mark you enter the last act of the game, which is clearly a "oops we didn't design enough of a game, lets just replay the first part."  You'll find yourself forced into completing twenty (yes, 20) siege battles, which the game was not designed for.  Add to each of these 20 battles that you'll be encountering orc captains as well as losing some of your own.  "But of course!" you say, "why wouldn't I want those things?"  Well.... Every captain you encounter has between a 5 and 30 second monologue that you CAN NOT skip.  Every captain you lose is a 5-10 second slow motion animation that you CAN NOT skip.  You can try saving your captains, but you again will have to stand still.... for 3-5 seconds... with every bit of damage interrupting you.
Online pit fights are literally AI controlled random battles that you sit and watch for 3 minutes.  I'm not saying "you can kind of play but its only 3 minutes long", no, let me reiterate: the online arena battles are 3 minutes of your orc fighting another orc with zero player input or control.
Overall this game was worth the 30 bucks I paid for it on sale.  It is IN NO WAY worth the full sale price, and you should not buy it for anything more than 40 under any circumstances.

If this game ran properly, and it currently does not (abnormally high CPU usage, pop-ins, chrome overlay on things during transitions, graphics even when maxed hardly living up to their performance demands...) I think I'd have a much more positive view on things, but considering how much time I time spent trying to get this thing to run stable, it's hard for me to do so.
If you experience absurd FPS drops, it's probably CPU related, and I advise you go into task manager and set the games processing affinity or w/e to high. It helps, a lot. That being said, technical issues aside, it's still not at all what you'd expect in a Mafia game.
This feels very Saints Row and it's not a bad game by any means. Infact, if you disregard Mafia 1/2 and just want a time waster game, it has a Godfather 1/2 vibe in the racket takeover sense and I really do enjoy that regard of things.
Missions themselves are extremely repetitive for the most part, but the big story set pieces feel fantastic when they occur, and even the repetitive filler is usually pretty fun just because of the level of care and detail that went into gunplay. This has some of the most satisfying and cinematic gunfights I've had in a third person game in quite awhile. It's extremely satisfying to walk up to an enemy who's still alive, huddled up in a pool of blood, surrounded by his dead companions, and firing the final shot into him.
Driving is pretty decent as well. I find it fun. It's a Mafia game. You should rest easy knowing they maintained a high-standard for driving.
Music is fine. It's your usual fare for a game like this. The soundtrack has it's moments that can really amplify a set, but for the most part, it all just kind of blends into the background of the game. Maybe that works in favor of the game overall.
Story is definitely quality, rest assured, and I won't get too deep into it, as I have not finished, and I don't want to spoil what I have played, but it's enough to keep you engaged and it feels like a really goddamn classy gangster flick.
While vastly different from 1/2, 3 favors a more sandbox style approach akin to a Ubisoft title, and it's interesting to see in play. I cannot recommend the game at it's current price, or anything remotely close to it. 2k have been extremely lacking in their patching, and for a long time, the game was simply unplayable. It's unacceptable and until the game is moreso stabilized and optimized, I wouldn't bother. Maybe on sale for $30~

It’s a game about the obscure subject of typefaces..... and I enjoyed it! I’m as shocked as you would be, but Type:Rider is actually a competent physics-based platformer game that’s legitimately fun, and you don’t actually have to read the “educational” stuff if you don’t want to.
This game is similar to “NightSky,” which is also available on Steam (and is in no way educational). but for some reason I liked this better, even though I had no interest in the history of fonts. (But then again, who does???)  It turns out that learning about fonts was actually one of the best parts of the game! The compulsion to collect more chapters of the “history book” and learn more about fonts made this game strangely interesting.  You can skip the reading part if you want to, I suppose, and just enjoy the platforming, but I found the info intriguing.
As for the game itself, it’s a physics platformer that ingeniously uses fonts (of the historical period) as platforms and obstacles, with many interesting puzzles, treacherous jumps, and fast action.
Make no mistake, this isn’t a triple-A game, but it is fun, and I played it to completion. If you see this game during a “Steam sale” I would recommend considering it.

Another disappointment was the arbitrary way the plot unfolded: "This is the explanation! Wait,
is the explanation!" "I kidnapped your wife -- no,
did!" "You have to run here!" "Now you have to run there!" "It's a conspiracy!" "It's magic!" "It's all in your brain!" At some point, the "dream logic" of the game became just too much and I managed to finish my time in Bright Falls without a clue what was going on.
So as I said, I didn't hate the game. But when forced to decide whether I would recommend it, I would say "no" because the overall experience was just too uneven. It was like watching the rough cut of a movie that's interesting enough to sit through, but I was kind of glad when it was over.

The loot boxes I'm okay with.  It's not a big deal since it's very easy to get loot and the in-game currency.

A captain dies and I have to watch that happen.  A captain freaks out and has to do a scene. TBoI is an old-school sidescroller, with semi-randomly generated levels, items and bosses and that unpredictability makes every playthrough unique in its own right. Unfortunately it also means that it can often be quite frustrating - expect to rage quit a lot as you get the worst possible item combinations and hardest bosses. The items themselves don't have descriptions, nor do they display stats - it's all about exploring and experimenting with different combinations, slowly pushing forward past each of the game's milestones. It's all about trial and error, so expect to die. A lot. A full playthough of the game can be anywhere between 20-60 minutes, or you can die in 2 minutes flat.  Beating TBoI can take a whole lot of time, patience and luck, but it feels immensely satisfying.
The art style is cartoonishly grim and visceral and the soundtrack has a fantastic retro vibe to it. The tunes are memorable and catchy, and the visuals appropriate to the game's disturbing universe.

The Good:
1) Strong risk/reward design. The game is built around the premise of taking risks however being strongly rewarded for it. Do you use your item in the current room or save it for later? Do you fight the last boss of the level or continue exporing the level in hopes of finding a good item to help you? Do you take the super powerful item at the expense of your health? These types of decisions are present with every playthrough
2) Plenty of replayability due to the vast number of items and randomization. The fun comes from playing the game over and over again and seeing what new items your going to get.
3) Due do the vast randomization of items/levels/bosses there is something always new. 20 hours in and I just played against a new boss I haven't seen before. Things like this keeps you playing for hours.
4) Cute and dark humor  really lends itself to the atmoshpere
The Bad
1) It can be frustrating at times, due do the vast randomization, you may get a playthrough where you get really bad items.
2) No save, understandably, a save feature would break the game however it needs to be mentioned that you need a solid 45 minutes - 1 hour for a single playthrough. Longer with the DLC.
Final Verdict
A highly addicting game with lots of fun and replayability. Buy this game.

I can't remember the last time I had so much fun in a hack n slash. Though it is on sale now at only $2 bucks or so, i'd say it's definitely worth more than the $10 price tag its given.
Mechanics:
Looking at the game overall, it's pretty simple. The mechanics involve combos (and i'd definitely recommend using a controller for the full experience + vibration support) which chain up with other skills that you'll purchase along the way from skill points given (by killing enemies). The game doesn't have a bazillion combos as one would expect but rest assured there's something satisfying about how polished the attacks are on such a simple game.
I think the only downside for the game mechanics is that the arenas are all the same. You'll enter one arena, fight a few wave of enemies, a mini-boss, then move on to the next arena which looks pretty similar  to the previous one other than the last two.
Side note: It's not said in the tutorials but take note that when upgrading some of the skills you have beyond level 1, they will unlock new moves within that attack (which are awesome).
Story:
It's a cheesy story. I wouldn't expect one to critisize this game for having a simple one because it's such a simple game and I think it fits in nicely with the mechanics and scale of the story.
Overall:
9/10 - Great game for the price and it's extremely polished for such a simple game. Though it doesn't have the best story or game arena aesthetics, it makes up for mechanics that allow a lot of replayability.
TL;DR - It's about $2 right now, WHY NOT?

The Binding of Isaac is a roguelike. The game is difficult, but may be able to be overcome with sufficient practice. I think it just has a high learning curve. Through my experience with binding of Isaac, if you enjoy watching it, you won't necessarily enjoy playing it. With that said, it is still probably one of the better, more well produced games in the genre. If you're looking for a roguelike, you probably won't go wrong with Isaac, but if you're looking to enter into the genre, you might want to check out some of the free offerings to see if you even like these types of games. The game goes on sale for cheap fairly often so it might be a good entry point into the genre as well.
If you do end up picking up the game, I'd recommend buying the Wrath of the Lamb expansion as a gift and playing the game a bit before redeeming it so you can get a bit of the vanilla experience. Additionally, I'd recommend not watching any Let's Plays of the game before playing it as they really take out the mystery and charm that roguelikes are known for.

I got in a fistfight over whether the protagonist is an umlaut, a diaresis, or a sideways colon, and I'll fight you, too, if you pick the wrong side.
As a learning experience, Type:Rider is great: A nice, quick breeze through the history of typography and printing from cave paintings to universal desktop publishing. Each level covers an epoch in written language, and the visuals and music come together gorgeously to convey the feeling of the era.
Unfortunately, the game-ification of it all feels tacked on. Type:Rider would be better served without fatal platforming sections, traps, and 'puzzles' that are less about solving them than about making mechanics work correctly. Is it fair to expect players to weave through a deadly field of Tetris blocks when your jumping physics don't seem to have predictable, repeatable results? You can convey the excitement of the Helvetica level's ski-jump aesthetic without making players dodge icicles with a pair of dots subject to a bizarre, fickle sense of gravity.
It's also a shame that a game that is necessarily as much about publishing as it is about typography does so poorly in laying out its encyclopedia entries, missing the odd punctuation or word here and there and lacking any fine tuning in the letter kerning, leading to ugly spread-out lines to meet the full-justify layout.
So it's not perfect. But you'll learn something and be really impressed by the design work. Art and publishing nerds should definitely give it a go.

Amazing story but clunky combat
You play Alan Wake, and author with a serious case of writer's block. He and his wife, Alice, go on vacation where Alan becomes the center of his own horror story. Reality comes into question when Alice disappears and locals are consumed by darkness. Armed with a flashlight, flares, and some bullets, Alan has to battle the forces of evil, real or imagined.
Alan Wake is a 3rd person shooter horror survival game with a focus on story telling. The episodic nature of the levels and narration by the protagonist makes the player feel like they are in a book... written by Stephen King. Presented as a normal, rural setting while a malevolent force is hiding below the surface is just up the horror legend's ally. This is one of the most engaging well presented stories I've played in a game.
The sound is great with an excellent score to ratchet up the tension. The voice acting is excellent and the writing is on point particularly when talking with other characters. The levels are well put together, though some of the character models during cutscenes are rough.
However, the combat has frustrated me and, no doubt, others. Wake uses a light (typically from a flashlight) to burn the darkness off of NPCs before finishing them with a weapon of choice: revolver, 1 of 2 shotguns or a rifle. It's an interesting mechanic were the player is vulnerable for the start of every battle and one that I liked it's almost everything else that is annoying. Alan has almost no stamina as 10 seconds of running leaves him gasping for air. I understand it as a combat mechanic, but there is a large area to explore for items and collectibles all the while listening to Alan sounding winded. There is a dodge mechanic, which is bound to the same key as running, which means Alan will awkwardly squat and launch himself in a direction which looks like a new born drunken giraffe learning how to walk. When dodging attacks, there is a  slow-motion cinematic with a panning camera which interferes with movements. It's possible to get stun locked by NPCs and you simply die. Also, there are times enemies spawn directly on top of you (cue dramatic camera spin) and you can't evade them at all.
The controls can feel sluggish. Dodging isn't always on point. Vehicles are awful to drive as if they are constantly in mud (slow starts and wild skidding even at low speeds). When performing an activity, it is sometimes impossible to cancel out of it.
On harder difficulties, enemies deal more damage, take more bullets to kill, and even take more light before being vulnerable. Some conflicts can be avoided and strategic use of items or the environment goes a long way to surviving. I do have to give credit for ally NPC's not being hot garbage and actually being helpful in combat.
There is an absurd amount of collectibles (over 200). Now some are really cool like TV shows but it makes no sense that the manuscript pages are only available in nightmare mode which isn't even unlocked until you beat the game. And other collectibles, particularly thermoses, are out of the way and of course the low stamina makes picking them all up irksome (several take 8+ stamina drains to collect).
If you are looking for a strong, story telling gaming experience,  Alan Wake is a worthwhile experience. If you are looking for a 3rd person horror, survival shooter, there are better games on the market.
Edit: Post Nightmare run and DLC
Obviously, the only changes on this difficulty (aside from new pages) are the increase challenge of enemies. They take more light to weaken, more shots to kill, and hit a lot harder. The clunky dodging, cinematic slow motion, control locking issues are exacerbated.
The Signal DLC: is absurd brutal in its ambushes. Almost ever fight starts with Alan being full surrounded and is easy to be instantly killed even on easy mode. The church basement area was interesting and several of the set pieces look nice. It does pick up following the ending of the base game. Same enemies and items.
The Writer DLC: Even more elaborate set pieces than the other DLC but nothing else is new. Continues the story from where signal ended.

As someone who never played the predecessor, I can't comment on any similarities or improvements; what I can say, is that this game is one of the most enjoyable multiplayer shooty pew pew games I've played in years.
First off, it looks lovely. Whether you're playing Aliens or Marines, the game has a very nice polished look to it and while the standard map rotation isn't massive, they are well
, which is something I have found to be lacking in a lot of similar team based games. The balance is more impressive when you consider that these aren't typical teams, either. Playing as the basic Alien species, the Skulk, gives you the ability to wall walk and hang onto ceilings, making you a perfect ambush predator. Marines can develop jet packs later in the game, allowing them to fly, but both teams have very distinct differences which makes the need for balance more important.
NS2 is also a game which is very hard to 'carry'. Whereas in other games in a similar vein, you can have a random player join your team and absolutely face ♥♥♥♥ the opposite team with seemingly no help from you or your mates, who are in their minds probably sat with their heads up their arses. This is a game where teamwork is absolutely necessary to succeed, and when you do succeed, it is
. A win on this game on either team feels amazing, like you've worked your balls off to earn it.
As with every other multiplayer game in existence, you will sometimes get a♥♥♥♥♥♥team. Sometimes you will be on that team, it happens. Other times you will be on the murdering death squad team and feel like you're a god. A lot of the time this responsibility rests on the team Commander. The Commander will sit in the Hive/Command chair, depending on the team, and will take on a top down view of the map. They are in charge of deploying resources and upgrading abilities/equipment for their team; they also direct their team mates as to where they should push or where the commander thinks they should push. Team synergy between the troops and the commander is vital, and I've not seen that nailed so well before as in this game.
The NS2 community is also very friendly. The first time I decided to play Commander I was a nervous wreck, but I was guided and helped by my team mates and - shock horror -
screamed at for my lack of experience. I've been in the odd game where new players are given crap, but the vast majority of games I have played have been with very nice people who are endlessly helpful. Even starting out playing, other players will help if you ask and give you tips as to what to do.
One downside I've found to this game, and it's a major one, is that the player base appears to be dwindling. This means that relatively full games are getting harder to come by, especially later on at night. Many servers are empty and it's a real shame, because this game is a bundle of fun once you get to grips with it, which leads on to my next point.
NS2 has somewhat of a steep learning curve. When I say steep, I mean that it takes a while to get learn the benefits and playstyle of each Alien and also the Marine weaponry and equipment.
I've personally found that this isn't a game where you can just pick a class and play however the hell you want, you have to know what you're doing with certain things otherwise you can be a bit of a spare part. For example, when you play on the Alien team, initially you will spawn as a Skulk. To play the other 'classes', you have to Evolve into them and this is done through your own personal resources which increase as you play, push and kill. The most expensive class, the Onos, is an absolute beast, but new players (and old) can sometimes be seen playing them and just rushing into Marine bases because at first glance you see your massive health pool and think you're an immortal juggernaut. Tactical maneuvres, organised by and with your team, are the key to success in this game and the solo warrior approach simply will not work.
NS2 also offsets potential pitfalls presented by fellow players. Occasionally, you will get a complete and utter turd as your Commander - it happens. Thankfully, you can choose to Eject ♥♥♥♥♥♥ commanders, along with a plethora of other commands such as voting, signalling to your team mates and taunting, amongst others. Team communication is vital in this game so a mic goes a long way for those times when you're getting the♥♥♥♥♥♥shot out of you and can't type your predicament. Map pinging also helps brings sticky situations to your team mates' and commander's attention.
Overall, awesome game. I only hope that the playerbase gets a revival, because it is a shame that more people don't get to experience the brilliance that is Natural Selection 2.

NS2 could probably be most accurately compared to Planetside 2 and Team Fortress 2. Very heavy on team cooperation, ever escalating battles, however confined to smaller areas, with an overarching Hand of God watching your back (and judging you). Sitting in the command chair feels like you're no longer watching a struggle with your fellow players fight an enemy onslaught in a particular hallway, it turns into you watching every struggle in every hallway and feeling like you're not doing enough to help your team. Cooperation has probably never meant more to a FPS than this. Failure is assured if the commander is lax, or guaranteed if the grubs rely too heavily on him as well. But find the balance, win the day, and you'll find yourself coming back for more and more.

The Good:
1) Strong risk/reward design. The game is built around the premise of taking risks however being strongly rewarded for it. Do you use your item in the current room or save it for later? Do you fight the last boss of the level or continue exporing the level in hopes of finding a good item to help you? Do you take the super powerful item at the expense of your health? These types of decisions are present with every playthrough
2) Plenty of replayability due to the vast number of items and randomization. The fun comes from playing the game over and over again and seeing what new items your going to get.
3) Due do the vast randomization of items/levels/bosses there is something always new. 20 hours in and I just played against a new boss I haven't seen before. Things like this keeps you playing for hours.
4) Cute and dark humor  really lends itself to the atmoshpere
The Bad
1) It can be frustrating at times, due do the vast randomization, you may get a playthrough where you get really bad items.
2) No save, understandably, a save feature would break the game however it needs to be mentioned that you need a solid 45 minutes - 1 hour for a single playthrough. Longer with the DLC.
Final Verdict
A highly addicting game with lots of fun and replayability. Buy this game.

The Binding of Isaac is a roguelike. The game is difficult, but may be able to be overcome with sufficient practice. I think it just has a high learning curve. Through my experience with binding of Isaac, if you enjoy watching it, you won't necessarily enjoy playing it. With that said, it is still probably one of the better, more well produced games in the genre. If you're looking for a roguelike, you probably won't go wrong with Isaac, but if you're looking to enter into the genre, you might want to check out some of the free offerings to see if you even like these types of games. The game goes on sale for cheap fairly often so it might be a good entry point into the genre as well.
If you do end up picking up the game, I'd recommend buying the Wrath of the Lamb expansion as a gift and playing the game a bit before redeeming it so you can get a bit of the vanilla experience. Additionally, I'd recommend not watching any Let's Plays of the game before playing it as they really take out the mystery and charm that roguelikes are known for.

I really wanted to give this game a thumbs up but I just cannot. While it seems very atmospheric, has an educational element to it and seems like a relaxing experience with a casual platformer, there are several glaring issues that ruined the experience for me. First of all the game can be finished in a couple of hours if that much. I took the time to unlock everything, read through all the texts etc but even so it wasnt what I had hoped it to be. The info exerpts are fine but they in no way compell the player to read them aside from personal curiosity. That could have been done better if they enriched the game mechanics in some way for example. The levels are pretty distinct altough few and fairly short. The real problem of this game is the incredibly clunky controls. You play as two wheels which roll onward and can perform a slight jump. So far so good. However the rolling itself lacks the feeling of friction so you often find yourself simply sliding off slightly slanted surfaces despite being on full throttle so to speak. Add to that the affinity of the wheels to bounce repeatedly and your inabiltiy to jump while in the air and you're left with the exact opposite of a precision platformer. I have lost count of the times that after a long and well timed jump my front wheel would clear the platform but my back wheel would not and would promptly drag me back into the pit; or the times when I would try to make a simple jump onto a higher step but my front wheel will roll slightly up the wall changing my angle just enough that the jump which follows sends me backwards insted of the intended forward; or the aerial stunts (of which there are quite a few) when holding the forward key would send the wheels into a looping spin as if the air itself has some friction but only for one of the wheels. For someone like me who likes responsive, precise cotrols this was a frustrating experience. Granted, it's a casual game but the later levels require a good amount of precision in navigating wall jumps and vent glides - precision that simply isnt there with the controls as they are.
That being said the game has a good idea and aside from the bothersome control the price could be worth it if you're willing to put up with some clunky movement.

Overall: Overall I say this is a really good game for how much it is, keep in mind two does have a workshop now but for me one will always have a place in my heart.

This is one of the simplest games I ever played, yet it's still my favourite. The gameplay and mecanics are basically: Run, kill, die, repeat. That's pretty much it, going on a killing spree with diferent weapons against enemies with a one-shot dead difficulty that will make you restart a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of times. This kind of gameplay and the visuals might not be your cup of tea, but if it is, boy are you going to enjoy it.
What interests me the most about this game is it's narrative. It revolves around a bunch of murderers with animals masks that kill russian gangsters, following orders of mysterious people leaving messages on their phones. The game is brutal, and it showcases a massive amount of extreme graphic violence, like executions, decapitations, broken bones, mutilated parts of the body, etc.
And, both the character and the player, enjoy it. Why would you be playing this game otherwise? "Do you like hurting other people?". This phrase is presented at an early stage of the game, and everything is based around this. Hunger for violence. In the music during the slaughter, the adrenaline rush, the gore, and then the sudden music stopping while watching all the people you just brutaly murdered on the way out.
This game represents the most pure and hidden sadistic side of the people that play this kind of games. The desire to kill and destroy just by the pleasure of doing so. And I love it for being that way.

Natural Selction 2 is a real standout in the FPS-Genre. The two factions play very differently from one another without feeling imbalanced (even though you will meet some players who say differently). Though there is a rather high learning curve, Natural Selection 2 is worth the frustration and failure you may experience at the beginning. Just visit the "Rookie friendly servers" and you will find many players who are willing to help you and explain certain mechanics that will lead to victory for you and your teammates. To me Natural Selection 2 isn’t great only because it’s very different from all the other  FPS's out there, but because it does asymmetrical multiplayer so damn well, offering up a variety of experiences in one small game.

1. Fluid gameplay: No lag, smooth combat mechanics, and satisfying progression system
2. Nod to various other games in the form of easter eggs and quotes. These easter eggs come with benefits too!
3. A very decent story with likeable characters that you feel attached to as the story progress. Fidget is very cute. (I want a flying-puppy like it)

Animated Jigsaw Puzzles? Yes please!
So, what does this “animated” in the title mean? Is the whole puzzle a video instead of an image? Technically yes, but the game manages to achieve the perfect balance between movement and stillness in its themes, at least for the biggest part. It feels like you are dealing with both a classical static puzzle and an animated picture simultaneously! This is happening because while in most of the themes there is a static thing e.g. a big building, at the same time this is surrounded by moving things like clouds, water with reflections or even ducks moving in its surface! On a side note, it seems that this is the biggest difference with the other game of the series, Wild Animals, because due to its theme there is a significant higher amount of movement involved.
Thankfully there is no rotation involved with the pieces. While this might be a desirable function for some people, for me it would make most pc jigsaw puzzle games unplayable, as it would take all the relaxation part of the experience away.
There is a ‘group-all-pieces’ button that is extremely useful - especially at the very beginning - as it is shorting out together all the border pieces. Also you can close the game at any time and the progress for the current puzzle is left intact, which is nice.
The only negative thing that I can say about the game is the very repetitive music. You can choose between 3 short tracks and while the tracks are not bad, they will shortly become tedious to listen for the whole puzzle, let alone for hours (I am giving some extra points to the third track). Actually these 350 pieces puzzles can take more than an hour to complete, so it would be better if you are equiped with your own background music! Also I would like to suggest to the developers to save more space on the left part of the screen by allowing more pieces to be put there and turn some of these ‘constantly on the screen’ options a pop up button maybe.
Although every theme can be played with 3 different quantities of pieces, 60, 240 and 350 (with the 60 being obviously asymmetrically easy compared to the other 2), some people can be sceptical about the price VS the limited amount of different themes in the game - only 10. But let me tell you, if you plan on finishing all the themes in all the settings the game is guaranteed to offer you many hours of puzzle solving and while on discount you cannot go wrong with it if you like jigsaw puzzles!

What twisted minds did the developers of The Binding of Isaac have. How disturbing is a mother trying to kill her son who escaped to the basement, and can kill anything with his tears.
Exploring the basement, you come across all sorts of horrendous monsters, decapitated cats’ heads, piles of faeces lying around and of course, your mother’s pads...among many other disturbing things.
However once you become desensitized, this little game is pretty good. Going through each level, finding power-ups (or power-downs) to help you with the increasingly difficult monsters, ultimately fighting a boss to proceed to the next level of the basement.
There is no continuity, so once you die, you start again from the beginning. Everything is randomly generated, so you will never have the same experience twice.
It’s a really fun and interesting game, with alot of little references to other games -  You might find a pixelated pickaxe as a power-up, which of course, is Notch's pickaxe. You might come across a monster that spews toxic green acid, just like the one from Left for Dead 2 - and the list goes on.
For the price you should certainly try this game out.

Sometimes it will just make it skewed, or it will be top down or sometimes it will be riding inside pipes, or inside pipes that also move laterally or on pipes with a normal view, or on a pipe with a static view. It is a little hard to put into words, but the pictures in the store are not cinematic, the camera view actually changes in real time in-game.

Rarely do you see well done or even modern free roam games such as this. I can tell you that I thoroughly enjoy playing this game. Here is a short review and/or summary of this game.
First, the mud effects are great. Obviously I have never seen anything like it in a video game to date. Being a person who enjoys mudding in real life, this game was a must get. The ruts that appear after you dirve through an area just really make you feel as if you are there.
This game offers a real imersive feel. You can use a winch, you have to worry about fuel, you have to worry about not damaging your vehicle(which by the way, you can see the damage on the vehicle which is a great touch!)and if that isn't enough, there is another hardcore setttings which feature even more realistic additions to make your experience more immersive and of course difficult.
The graphics. The graphics are outstanding. They are very pleasing to the eye and definitely cater to the immersive feel and the physics are great.
Now you may be thinking that this is game with no objectives at all. Well if you thought that, you are mistaken, because there are logging missions which is another fine touch to this game.
There kind of is a short ammount of different vehicles, but said vehicles are customizable and also there are mods to fill your want for a new ride.
The multiplayer aspect of this game makes it really enjoyable. You can invite your friend to go along with you exploring and doing whatever you feel like in the large worlds. Be it forging new paths, playing in the mud, playing in the water, hill climbing, logging, or discovering the entire map and unlocking garages in the maps. There are limitless options to what you can do in this game.
There is a decent variety of maps for you to choose from allowing you to explore a lot of new land.
I truly love this game and got it around when it first came out and have enjoyed it all. Like I said, if you enjoy offroading, mudding, multiplayer, and free roam, this is the game for you. I hope you benefitted from my short review.

For a mobile dodging game, it has surprisingly pleasing aesthetics and good music. The gameplay comes down to just moving Left/Right without any other manual controls. This is not a speedrun game because you can only move out of the way at a set speed.
Perhaps this game is too simple in comparison to those that are made for PC but it does not stop it from beeing challenging. You can't switch directions very fast because it is done on purpose to create difficulty based on momentum. For me, the best part of the game are the stages that have all kinds of visual effects with trippy camera angles.
+35 story levels. 3 to 5 hour length if you have competent reflexes.
+Fair difficulty that progressively goes from casual to hard.
+Replay value in grinding skins, levels, achievements and high scores.
+Lots of cool looking visual effects.
+Great music.
+Gamepad support
+Interactive Story
-Lack of any other moves other than moving left/right. ( which is not a downside depending on how simple you like your games )
-Uncomfrtable controls in pipe levels.
-In endless modes there is a bit of a luck factor. Sometimes you just get screwed by combination of cameras and random obstacles .
The game is like 160MB and yet it is 10 times more appealing to look at than some of my 10GB games. I did not know you could fit so many effects into such a small package but I guess there is like no texture XD. Sometimes simply is better.  I really like that some levels even try to set the atmosphere by just having a long tunnel with a different sound distribution. There was not much copy/paste and most levels felt unique. Sandworms were my favorite ( reminds me good all Arrakis ) I think it would have been better if they separated each level theme into sections like Desert, City, Snow but they kind of mixed it.
Overall the game has a nice difficulty progression,good levels and enough single-player content to pick it up. It is a simple dodging game but enjoyable for what it is .

What interests me the most about this game is it's narrative. It revolves around a bunch of murderers with animals masks that kill russian gangsters, following orders of mysterious people leaving messages on their phones. The game is brutal, and it showcases a massive amount of extreme graphic violence, like executions, decapitations, broken bones, mutilated parts of the body, etc.
And, both the character and the player, enjoy it. Why would you be playing this game otherwise? "Do you like hurting other people?". This game represents the most pure and hidden sadistic side of the people that play this kind of games. The desire to kill and destroy just by the pleasure of doing so. And I love it for being that way.

Story : This game have a very shallow storyline. If you like a game with deep storyline this game is not for you.
Gameplay : This is a basic Hack & Slash game where you have to fight waves of enemies before you fight the boss. You will face several type of enemies with different abilities and gain SP points when you kill the enemies to buy upgrade for you character. It is repetitive as you fight wave after wave but the challenge and fun is still there . The combat system is I think the most enjoyable feature of this game. Start form basic attack from the beginning then you will get new attack/skill when you upgrade your character. This new skill will add new way and combo for you to defeat you enemy. Some of this skill are very straightforward & some will required skill & practice to master it. This may make you want to replay the game on harder difficulty (or probably the same) just to test this new skill/move you unlock. The boss of this game can be annoying if you not pay enough attention to its movement and pattern. Pay enough attention it will be walk in a park.
Music & Voice Acting : Average…
Overall : It is a very fun game to play. Especially when you manage to unlock all upgrade for you character. I really recommend this game if you want to play a simple yet fun beat em up game and my rating of this game is 7/10

Off-road driving simulator. In this game you drive Russian extreme terrain vehicles, made for transporting wood logs and vehicles supporting them.
Different size trucks for wood transport. Repair and refuel support vehicles. Game has vehicle damage and fuel consumption system, no actual truck model damage as of yet. Realistic water simulation physics, terrain deformation system, deep mud, tires sink into terrain after heavy wheel spin, or heavy cargo weight.
Great vehicle modification system, that allows you to chose a variety of different truck parts and accessories. Cargo beds, cranes (for operating claw to manually load in logs), trailers, fuel cisterns (for on the spot refueling), utility boxes (for on the spot repairs), etc.
At the moment the vehicle variety is small, but I'm sure they will be added in time. Great detail on actual trucks, good looking terrain, day and night cycle. Decent amount of maps, both for single and co-op play. Co-op play supports up to 4 people, and is very enjoyable. Be aware that this game requires careful driving and moderate navigation skills, because there are almost no roads to speak of. A unique driving experience never the less.

Type:Rider is a platformer where the levels are designed as the alphabet in a particular font, running the gamut from Didot to Helvetica to Comic Sans MS. Recommended, with a few caveats. You should buy this/add it to your wishlist if you're looking for:
-easy achievement acquisition
-you appreciate good graphic design and the history of aesthetic movements
-you like "quirky" games
That said, the physics are incredibly frustrating at times, more obviously so in the last few levels. Your player-character is a pair of dots, and jumping/rotating in mid-air can be nothing short of impossible in some instances, particularly if there's a time pressure and you find yourself freaking out the more you're unable to jump and land correctly between serif ledges. Beating it is doable, but the extraordinary patience and perserverance required is more of a design flaw than an intentional teaching-moment mechanic. Still, the feeling of satisfaction you get when you finish the Pixel typography "book" is just as rewarding as mastering a level of BIT.TRIP.

Powerhover is a simple yet challenging game in which you are a robot on a hoverboard. The only mechanic in the game is moving left or right. But this mechanic is compounded upon by tons of level hazards and challenges.
The 35 levels are very varied, and have a great and cohesive artistic direction. You won't be feeling like you've played the same level twice. The levels are enhanced by the awesome soundtrack, which is seriously amazing. Most levels are a sort of challenge requiring precision and memorization. Some levels called "boss levels"(a misnomer imo, there are no bosses) are procedurally generated and take out the "memorization" aspect and require good precision and fast reflexes.
Each level introduces a different mechanic, such as rail grinding, giant snake worms or rockets shooting at you. There is always something to hold your interst.
My major gripe with the game is the difficulty curve. Some levels you can breeze through and 100% on the first try, other might take 10-20 attempts. Though it doesn't ruin the game, it definitely hit me for a jolt when I thought I was getting the hang of the game and then I get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me.
Overall, a unique and fun experience that is full of challenge. The full game took me about 3 hours to beat, but there is also a challenge mode as well, which should add on another 45 minutes or so. I would not reccomend this game to people who don't like having to repeat a task to perfect it, or those who hate losing.

Story: 4/10
Starts really strong but then quickly turns generic and boring throughout the whole game. Even Vito offers nothing interesting.
Gameplay: 3/10
The missions are unfortunately VERY repetitive. There is no difference between the main missions and the optionals except for a very small number of unique and cinematic missions (like the steamboat or shooting up the KKK).
The guns are fun, but the horrible stupid AI (who is just so willing to be killed by you) make both stealth and combat super easy. I only died a couple of times because of the stupid, not-computer-friendly controls and the cover system.
You can just whistle to lure someone into your direction (they will go 1 at a time), kill him, repeat over and over again. The 7th guy won't be thinking "hmmm what happened to my 6 buddies?"...
Driving behaviour and physics are awful, but tbh I still had fun driving around. Altho there isn't much driving included in the missions (except for the optionial boring stuff), so wasted potential here.
And for some absurd reason they got rid of features that were in the previous games, like buying/changing clothes (or stores in general), car physics (demolition, destruction), cops that don't shoot you on the smallest delict (plus I want to note that the whole state knows about you the very second one bloody cop spots you - no matter how quickly you take him out), and many more.
Graphics: 4/10
People complain alot about the overall graphics but for me it's more on the technical side: Graphics glitch out or don't load properly at times, especially when you drive fast. The lighting, which can be very awful and points and then be really great in other moments. And second, the skyboxes... they are just... really effin weird.
There is also some really weird weather transitions at random points (not talking about quick transitions that are mission-related). The overall graphics like geometry and textures are totally fine to me and had some beautiful moments. Especially the cinematics and animations are really well done.
It seems like performance-wise the game is alot more demanding than it should be for this quality.
Sound: 8/10
Weapons and vehicles sound good, soundtrack is great (obviously, c'mon you know the songs!)
Tho, it's really annoying that your wheels are screaming the very second you hit the forward button.
Final words:
This game does not deserve the title "Mafia III"
The game can be fun and I played through it because of the great soundtrack and atmosphere. But there is also alot of frustrating and boring moments.
If you want to give this game a try, do it when it's on sale. Not worth the full price.

Power Hover was a fun albeit difficult ride. It’s just what you’ve come to expect from an indie hybrid between an endless runner and a racer on Steam. Its developer has literally hit the ground running since they made a more than decent debut for a title sporting Unity Engine 5 assets in a minimalist style. More and more devs seem to find new uses for that game engine and we should all be grateful indeed.
Surprisingly, this is a story-driven experience and not just a random succession of levels, even if the themes never repeat themselves a lot. You initially control just one robotic courier on a mission to restore electrical power to various parts of the game world. A task easier said than done since collecting the batteries needed to unlock different structures which produce electricity, will have you travelling at breakneck speed across desert plains, oceans, cityscapes or even purely abstract levels. And in order to make the challenge truly worthy for the veterans of this genre, obstacles either static or moving, will try to stop you constantly.
Why is the game that difficult? Well for starters, I found that the game progression requires that you max out on the numbers of batteries you should collect during each individual level, if you really wish to power-up as many structures as possible and thus reap the rewards. Powerful boons, that will include even the possibility to unlock new controllable avatars or at the very least provide you with more “lives” or chances to start a level section at a checkpoint instead of restarting from the beginning of the stage. It certainly adds to the overall difficulty, the fact that you have a limited amount of retries as it is, and quick reflexes will have to be complemented by nerves of steel. More often than not, you may skip on grabbing a battery since you were too focused on the obstacle in front of you.
Ironically almost, but for such a fast-paced game, patience is of far greater importance than the ability to quickly shift your hoverboard in the general direction of the scattered batteries. There are fortunately, many checkpoints along the routes you traverse. It won’t help by much but at least it gives you the chance to memorize some of the battery locations as well as the traps and occasional bombs which will instantly rob you of a precious life. Not even all obstacles can be learned by heart since in the “boss” levels, you have to quickly travel through elaborate laser beam patterns and vent blades for example. Not really something that you can rely on replicating with the same results, at a subsequent restart of the stage.
So at least some degree of luck might also be necessary. I’m open to any gaming genre even if the ones that constantly require quick reflexes, aren’t among my favorites. I will still try to improve myself and overcome the not so favorable odds since rage quitting isn’t a worthy practice for any type of gamer. So even if a particular level might seem harsh, rest assured that there is most certainly at least one that’s far worse, as you advance the story. Keep playing and you might get good enough at it.
The “Less is More” motto befits Power Hover wholeheartedly. The minimal looks are perfect for the type of gameplay that’s all about speed and precision. Game sounds are indeed repetitive, but considering  its legacy (initially a smartphone title), that is weak point we can safely overlook. I was expecting more achievements, but even as they are, I’m sure that collectors won’t be displeased. If you consider the game to be overpriced, then wait for a bundle or a Seasonal Sale. Other than that, Power Hover shows great promise, should its developers attempt a sequel.

TLDR: The game could have been great but the developers or the publishers made it super grindy and stupid. The betrayal rate is way too high, and the game does not give you enough resources to play through the game at a decent pace without buying loot boxes or xp multipliers. I'm about 40 hours in and I just got to the end game.
I really wanted to like this game, but there are a few things that absolutely ruin this game. Because the publisher wanted to make more money on loot crates there is a sh_t ton of grinding if you don't want to buy the loot boxes. There are quests that give out 2000 or 3000 or even 6000 xp at once but those are quite rare (at level 45 you need nearly 20000 xp to level up). Killing high ranking orc captains doesn't net you much xp, helpling other orcs on missions doesn't net you much xp (about 800 xp in the late game). In the late game the game seems to make it extra hard to capture forts and it costs a lot of resources to defend them later on, points that you probably can't get without loot boxes. Further more the invading orcs are at such a high level that you then have to switch out your commanding orcs to stand a chance without doing everything yourself. It's just a ton of grinding intended to encourge you to take the easy way out.
One of the good things is that the nemesis system has been improved, orcs seem to have more personality and the structure seems to be more complex which makes you feel more invested in the orcs. But the blood brother ties make it more difficult to keep high level orcs because they will betray you if you accidentally kill the wrong orc or they will betray you just because they feel like it. And when an orc betrays you there is practically no chance to get him back. The better nemesis system seems to encourage the play to become invested in their orc captains but the very high chance of betrayal disincentivizes attachment to individual orcs.
To assign an orc to a position of power in a fort requires that you send them into the pits to fight a challenger. Early on the fight system works ok, the AI is really stupid but usually the higher leveled orc will win. There are some weaknesses that can be exploited but usually the higher leveled orc will win. However later on the fights get really BU1♥♥♥♥♥♥ I once sent in a level 36 orc only to have him lose to a level 24 orc, a 12 level difference and the level 24 orc didn't even have anything to take advantage of any weaknesses. At this point I felt like the game was just cheating. There is also the problem that you can't recruit orcs higher than your level which would be fine if leveling up in the late game didn't take forever.
If you liked the first game and don't mind grinding then you will probably enjoy it, otherwise it might not be the sequel you expected.

Type:Rider is an elegant and humble platforming physics game with an emphasis on collection and only three inputs: left, right, and jump. You are a colon -- a grammatical one, thank goodness -- who must travel through the history of the written word, from beginning to quasi-modern times, one font face at a time, collecting letters and such as you go; perhaps to understand the meaning of your own existence. Fair warning: If you're not at least mildly interested in reading about typography, you won't be terribly happy with this game.
Type:Rider isn't complicated, as there isn't any combat or anything. You have infinite lives, and death from obstacles or falling down pits will just put you back a few seconds. It does however have puzzle segments, usually focusing on weight or game physics. As your character is composed of two wheels, more or less, you can stand on round things and move to spin them. Each level also introduces new gimmicks such as wind or water jets that will add significant velocity to you on touch.
This is at heart an educational, scholarly game - each time you pick up an asterisk, you receive a new article on another element of typography. They're not terribly long articles. A game like Spintires is one I have been hoping to see for a while, one that focuses on driving Soviet built off road vehicles in a off road environment. While it is a fairly well done game, especially for one which is almost entirely developed by one person, it isn't one I would recommend at the full price that it is sold on Steam ($30)... yet. If you can grab it on a sale, and one where it is sold for 15 dollars and under, then I would say you can definetly get your money's worth, especially if a game in which exploring maps and getting loads from one side to another with many obsticals like terrain, trees, mud, rivers is more your style.  Of course, I might change this review a little later when more is added to the game, but in its current state, it is a little overpriced for what you get out of the box and can do right away, not to mention other small issues which I'll summarize in the Pros/Cons section below.
Pros:
- Mud Physics which do take some challenge to get out of (and not much to get into). The whole aspect when your "tarmac" road becomes a muddy road, then becomes a river or small pond that just happened to look like a huge puddle is one of those neat things I just LOVE about this game! It sort of makes you plan accordingly and find ways around places that might be unnavigable.
-A wide selection of addons to vehicles, be it a toolkit (trunk) you can place on top of the A-469 to help repair some vehicles to a crane arm to lift and place logs onto trucks for most of the vehicle. Some even have attachments custom made for them, such as the D-7310's Utility attachments which make it into one awesome looking tow truck. Sometimes these are addons that help complete certain tasks, like unlocking garages, or transporting logs. Sometimes they change the behavior of the vehicle or even the look a little. Other times, can be used as things to support other vehicles, be it to refuel them, or to repair them or both.
-Other vehicles can be used to help get those stuck in a tough situation out.
-Various choices made, from tires to route, vehicle choice to even driving style can affect fuel burn. and even traction Also an added load or add on can weigh a vehicle down enough to make driving around very difficult (think the C-255 hauling a garage attachment and a garage cart in areas that are heavily muddy.)
-Not as demanding on many machines, but still looks quite acceptable graphically! Part of the reason from my understanding is that the "Active" world as we know it in the game exists in a world that is largely only 10m in radius or a player. This does reduce the amount of calcuations the computer needs to do, but it also does constrain the range of the winch too, which can become a frustration.
-Mod Support. Yeah, the game can be modded, you can change out various vehicles, and I think maps can be added (I haven't added any yet).  We now have the workshop that adds vehicles, but we're still missing ability to have map mods on it!
Cons:
-That damn camera. It isn't very easy to work with, and sometimes puts itself in a position where one can't see where their going. I'm not sure if it ever occured to Pavel that sometimes a view off a little to the left is a little useless when that side is completely obscured by trees or bushes. Thankfully, a fix is in the works. The choices of cameras are a little limited too, with a in truck view rejected since it seemed to induce nausea in their testers when it was tested. For the time behing, there is a camear that is mounted on the top of the truck's cab though, and for the time being, it gets some of the job that the normal camera can't do fixed up. Of anything, it's really the most broken thing about the game!
-Damage has some issues of being rather inconsistent. Take water damage for instance, sometimes getting some water up to your wheel arches does 35 damage, while being completely submerged might barely damage you! There are other wierd things. Also it doesn't seem to affect your vehicle's ability to get around until the last 20% or less of the damage bar, when you'll notice it just can't output the same amount of power and find itself stalling a little more. It also corresponds on how the visual damage model only lasts for that session. Reset and you'll see the truck still has the damage, but won't have much of hte visual deformation it may have had from a nasty meeting with a tree, or a botched attempt to turn it over with another truck.
-Diff Lock damage. Also, in a attempt to make it less Sim-ish and more "Game-ish" Oovee had forced the developer to add in Differential Lock damage in a very unrealistic way, which means keeping your diff lock on in Hardcore mode will cause your truck to stop violently and add a random amount of damage. In my opinion, there are other penalties already in place for keeping the Diff Lock on (like fuel burn), especially as it's already restricted  for use on Reverse, First and High First gears! Of course, Causal mode lets the user have it on whenever with no penalty to their truck in terms of damage.
- Multiplayer. While overall, the base funcationality of multiplayerworks, it seems there are a lot of problems as of now. Mod your game? Then you need to follow some ritual to make MP work again. Want to get everything done? Gotta do it on one sitting and PRAY that no one has any connection issues, else it completely resets that player, and totally resets for everyone if the host's connection craps out (no MP saves yet). Hopefully that should be fixed in a future update.
-Updates. For some reason, it takes Oovee a while to get updates. As of this writing (August 8, 2015), I think Oovee had finally noticed and let people know they notice it. Something they apparently can't tell us is preventing a release, hopefully we'll get it soon enough. I can't wait to drive around in a Zi... *ahem* C-131. Next to the camera issue, the wait for an update is really the most frustrating aspect of the game.
-Trucks could use more attachment points to help set them back on all fours (or sixes, or eights, or whatever). As it is now, you have to do a lot of guesswork and hope you get lucky when getting a truck back to an upright position.
Overall, Spintires is one of the games I myself enjoy a lot. But there are many issues that need to be adressed. Hearing that the game is continuously worked on is promising, but of course, the slow pace of updates from the Publisher (and the secret nature of why, which definetly doesn't help them), and the current Limitations with what can be done with the game thus far as an end user, plus the various issues above make me feel that the current full price is a little too much to ask for, but once in a more advance state I can realistically seeing that as the price. If camera fixed, and Mod Support added, this can easily make the game that much better, with the other issues being small things that can be worked on over time. For a game that has been developed largely by a single person, this has been overall pretty well done. Even though the Cons I listed feel much larger, the Pros of the game from my perspective as an end user largely outweigh them! I personally want to thank Oovee and Pavel for making a game I would have dreamt about come true, but I do hope they continue to improve upon this until it feels a little more complete. As it is now, it feels a little more than a very well developed Alpha with a high price tag, but with a little more here and there, it can easily start commanding that $30 price tag!
~EDIT: Apart from rewritin the mod support section, I also have changed my recommendation to Not Recommended. While I am a HUGE fan of the game, it has been recently found there have been parts of the code that cause the game to break after 300s of gameplay. Whether this was intentional or not for paying customers, it now makes the game unplayable. In its current state (2/27/2016), I say pass.

A strangely relaxing game. If you'd asked me if I'd like to chill out by driving Russian trucks through waist-deep mud, I probably would've looked at you funny, but there we are. In that sense I find it more similar to a game like Take On Mars than to another truck-themed game like Euro Truck Simulator. It also doesn't hurt if you think Russian military trucks are nifty.
But this game does not appear to be for everyone. If you are considering buying it, I'd advise waiting for a sale to bring it down to, say, the $15 range, and keep your finger on that refund button. It's also very interesting from a technical point of view, since, as far as I'm aware, there isn't another driving game that models offroad driving and terrain deformation in quite so much detail. As I've suggested earlier in the review, it's oddly relaxing watching your truck try to wade through fully deformable mud and water, and a small thrill when it manages to finally climb out the other side. Though, on the other hand, it's at first mildly frustrating getting bogged down in that same situation. I say at first because, like Kerbal Space Program, a short-term failure is merely an invitation to mount an elaborate rescue mission, and the scope of these rescue missions broadens when you introduce other players in co-op.
The developer and publisher have some issues with communication, and have suffered storms of drama in their relationship in the past, so the future of the game's development is far from bright. However, even with that, I think what's here (and what will be added in the upcoming, nearly-finished, update) is well worth the asking price when the game is discounted down to what I suggested.
