Power Hover is an adventure racing game which is a game essentially about robots with hoverboards and their quest. Does it stick to its route or falls down a cliff, let’s find out:
Power Hover puts you in the shoes of a Robot with a hoverboard who is tasked to collect batteries and bring back power to the world. The story revolves around a city whose power source has been stolen and it went into complete blackout. You were tasked to chase down the thief and in the process bring back the power to the town. The gameplay of Power Hover is extremely simple, you slide left and right trying to avoid obstacles and collect batteries. But don’t be fooled by its simple aesthetic, the game throws a lot of difficult sections where you have to really test your skills. After you have completed the first couple of levels, you will be introduced to the thief who stole the power from the town. The game then tasks you with chasing down the thief and take back what’s yours. It is not really a race as there is no time limit and you won’t overtake the thief throughout the game.
Then what purpose does he serve? Along the way, he drops batteries at difficult paths and you have to be on his trail if you want to collect them all. In between these batteries, he will sometimes drop a bomb or two in your way which bursts as soon as you pass through them. Initially it seems that the thief is merely more than another character on screen as his bombs are very easy to avoid. Slowly though he starts placing bombs right after a battery which makes it increasingly difficult to pass the levels.
The game introduces you to new sections and obstacles in a very subtle way. Before you come toe to toe with the real thing, the game will tell you in a visual way how the machines or beasts work. All of this is told through environmental cues and you have to be careful about the environment you’re cruising through. The game also changes camera angles at correct times to give you a top down view for sections which are designed like mazes. The checkpoints are placed so that you can continue your journey after you have died without any sort of frustration. After each level you are awarded with stars which give you a specific amount of electricity which in turn unlocks buildings in the town which gives you various upgrades.
After you unlock a specific amount of buildings with enough power you will unlock boss levels. Boss levels are endless levels which produce procedural generated machine madness in your way. They are much more difficult than the normal game and require you to accumulate a certain amount of points to unlock the next section of the city. Power Hover’s biggest challenge is not only passing through levels, but passing the levels while collecting the maximum amount of batteries.
Not all is good with Power Hover though, there are sections in levels which have nothing inside them which makes those parts feel incredibly bland and boring. The story while told in an interesting way lacks originality. There are a few characters available to be bought through power but they are purely cosmetic and do not have any gameplay or visual incentive to be bought. The hover board itself is a major pain to control sometimes as it will spin out of control and will do whatever it wants. The game also suffers from a certain amount of bugs and glitches which makes some levels really frustrating. But overall, Power Hover is a game which is easy to learn but hard to master.
Power Hover is very appealing and soothing to the eyes. The graphics have low polygon count but more than makes up for it with its gorgeous and varied world. The creatures of the world are created so that you will marvel at each and every sight. In fact, the game places a few puzzles just before something incredible happens on your screen which will leave you in awe and off guard. The game shows its world and tells its story through its visual design and it does a superb job at that. From sandworms to Giant spikes and mining monsters, everything is created so that you have a joy in exploring these levels. Truth be told, my main purpose for completing Power Hover’s levels were not about collecting batteries but to see what new wonders the game held next.
The sound design of Power Hover is amazing. It compliments its visual design very well and has a soothing effect on ears. The soundtrack of Power Hover makes traversing its marvellous worlds all the more better.
Power Hover is a simple game with a superb visual aesthetic and sound design. There are a few problems you will encounter here and there but nothing will distract you from exploring its world. It is a very relaxing game and very easy to pick up and play. For its price, you can’t go wrong with Power Hover.

When Mafia 3 was unveiled about a year ago I thought it looked like it was going to be a GTA V clone, which is something I probably wouldn't kick out of bed for eating cookies. Once it got close to release I heard rumors that it was repetitive and boring to play, but I didn't pay much attention. There have been so many instances where I've heard accusations that a game is boring and repetitive but I disagree. Assassins Creed 1 is the first example that comes to mind. No denying its progression cycle was repetitive, but it didn't bore me.
Mafia 3 started out well. The story seemed engrossing, the cut scenes were well done, the characters were interesting. The game play didn't fare as well. I started out with the driving set to "Simulation" and it didn't feel great. Difficult to pin down exactly what I didn't like about it, aside from the accelerator being way too sensitive. I tried setting it to "Normal" for a while, but I didn't notice much difference so I set it back to Simulation. Playing on Hard difficulty mode, the gun play and combat are just... meh. The only thing that feels at all satisfying is sneaking around from cover to cover and taking out enemies from around corners and such. Every mission feels the same. The only thing to do outside of missions is pick up collectibles which are mostly pointless (though I give them props for including some very cool Playboy interviews from the mid 60s e.g. the Beatles in 1964 and Stanley Kubrick talking about 2001 A Space Odyssey right after it released.)
I can't remember the last time I bought a new game but didn't finish it simply because it couldn't hold my interest. Normally I insist on finishing my games come hell or high water, but I just couldn't stick with this one. After about 15 hours or so I felt like I'd done it all multiple times and started putting it down to replay Watch Dogs instead (because I'm extremely hyped for WD2.) At first I was just taking short breaks from Mafia 3, but before long I just wasn't going to back to it at all. Kinda doubt I ever will again. The story wasn't ~that~ engrossing.
Mafia 3 left a bad taste in my mouth, and I'm hoping Watch Dogs 2 will be the perfect mouthwash. I'll know in exactly three weeks.

"Natural selection is the gradual process by which biological traits become either more or less common in a population as a function of the effect of inherited traits on the differential reproductive success of organisms interacting with their environment. It is a key mechanism of evolution. The term "natural selection" was popularized by Charles Darwin, who intended it to be compared with artificial selection, now more commonly referred to as selective breeding.
Variation exists within all populations of organisms. This occurs partly because random mutations occur in the genome of an individual organism, and these mutations can be passed to offspring. Throughout the individuals’ lives, their genomes interact with their environments to cause variations in traits. (The environment of a genome includes the molecular biology in the cell, other cells, other individuals, populations, species, as well as the abiotic environment.) Individuals with certain variants of the trait may survive and reproduce more than individuals with other, less successful, variants. Therefore the population evolves. Factors that affect reproductive success are also important, an issue that Charles Darwin developed in his ideas on sexual selection, for example.
Natural selection acts on the phenotype, or the observable characteristics of an organism, but the genetic (heritable) basis of any phenotype that gives a reproductive advantage may become more common in a population (see allele frequency). Over time, this process can result in populations that specialize for particular ecological niches and may eventually result in the emergence of new species. In other words, natural selection is an important process (though not the only process) by which evolution takes place within a population of organisms. Natural selection can be contrasted with artificial selection, in which humans intentionally choose specific traits (although they may not always get what they want). In natural selection there is no intentional choice. In other words, artificial selection is teleological and natural selection is not teleological.
Natural selection is one of the cornerstones of modern biology. The term was introduced by Darwin in his influential 1859 book On the Origin of Species,[1] in which natural selection was described as analogous to artificial selection, a process by which animals and plants with traits considered desirable by human breeders are systematically favored for reproduction. The concept of natural selection was originally developed in the absence of a valid theory of heredity; at the time of Darwin's writing, nothing was known of modern genetics. The union of traditional Darwinian evolution with subsequent discoveries in classical and molecular genetics is termed the modern evolutionary synthesis. Natural selection remains the primary explanation for adaptive evolution." - Wikipedia

-The "Analysing Roads" Dialog gets stuck open; Persists for duration of gameplay session.

is required to beat the game though it'd be nice to clear unused turrets)

enemy spawn point. I had between 5-6 at each of the three spawn points, and that was way overkill.
-100 Waves is a bit extreme since you only fight the same 8 enemies each wave making the
game feel tedious after wave 10. Enemy numbers should increase per wave. Maybe implement an option to set wave count?
-Advancing waves quickly will cause a glitch where enemies turn invisible; Turrets within range will fire until despawned enemy is deemed "Destroyed" by the game.

-No difficulty ramp despite session being 100 waves. The game should get more challenging with each wave propting the player to place more turrets, upgrade turrets, use different turrets, and possibly even alter the layout and placement of turrets.

This is a driving / offroad fan's dream game. Ten year old me would have been easily banned from the computer for playing too much while the adult in me has to remind myself I have work in the morning.
Spintires is an offroad open sandbox game complete with 5 maps and about 7-8 different trucks. Now, the idea of it being sandbox may throw some off - but oddly enough there is enough going in this game to keep you busy. The game concept follows around objectives and the process of driving up to garage's and trucks to unlock them. Some (or most) objectives require you to transport certain materials such as lumber. Not all trucks can carry lumber and not all trucks have the attachments to. When starting off at your main garage, players can modify their vehicles by adding utility carts, lights or such other accessories. The trucks that are put into this game are pretty cool and quite dynamic. Some are stuck without all wheel drive while some have differential locks as well as all wheel drive.
Trucks can be as small as a jeep, to as big as a heavy crane truck you would see helping unload construction material near a job site. Some trucks even come with cranes to load and unload lumber! There is, however a draw-back to this awesome inclusion. Typically, you load up your lumber automatically and only if you happen to get into an accident or logs fall out, then you can use your crane to load them up. So the crane does have a use, but can also be seen as useless to some. The driving experience itself is addicting. I'm not sure why, and I'm not sure how, but the challenge of ripping through dirt road, water, mud, even rolling over sticks or the occasional rock is amusing. Adding a cart to the back of the truck also makes the challenge that much harder as it's not only the truck you have to get across the river. The driving itself seems quite realistic to me. I have also seen a lot of reviews saying it is ridiculous how some trucks have the hardest time going over rocks or even loose tree branches.
Although it can be the case, typically the trucks shouldn't have too much of an issue going over the obstacles. Tree branches aren't too bad but the rocks will definitely set you back. I wish there was a bit more freedom within this realm to go over obstacles, but going through trees that haven't matured quite yet is pretty fun (disclaimer : I don't ride my Toyota through any tree, shrub or the sort. I love mother nature).  Sometimes where the is no path, a path can be made with a heavy truck pushing small trees aside. Most collisions feel right except one little thing that bugs me, why can't I drive into an exploding barrel that was put on the map? I know it's kind of silly to have such a thing next to a lumber yard, but why put it there if I can't "use" or hit it? The game has weird moments like this where it chooses to clip instead of let you collide. What I absolutely do love about this game is the winch. When I first started, I was extremely frightened to go at it alone as I would end up on my side or get stuck. I started learning how to use the winch efficiently and my experience with the game got a lot better. I'm glad I chose to play multiplayer first in lieu of single player. The community was a worldly and friendly one. Multiplayer WILL NOT save your  progress but single player WILL.
Graphics are quite nominal especially when it comes to the mud and water. Trees are there but I think could have been done a bit better. Back drops are nice, would have been nicer with some mountains or something else to fill some gaps. The game also features a night and day scheme. The sounds are actually on point, and when your vehicle is physically damaged, damaged sounds also follow.
I like this game, it could have been better with a bit more variation and a few more construction touches (crane's and the like... maybe even dirt diggers), none the less, pretty good game to some, decent for others. I would love to see more map additions and truck additions, and a little variations on objectives.
I have yet to try the mods but when I do, I will update the review.

I'm an admirer of fonts and typesetting, so the premise of this game has certainly had me interested in playing. Unfortunately, the game is riddled with bugs and the platforming-oriented gameplay itself is often frustrating. Probably a more exploratory rather than player-challenging would have suited this game better.
Gameplay and puzzles are physics-based, and this leads to obvious problems where you have to restart a section because you’re unable to get yourself or another ball to where you want it to be. Thankfully, the autosave points are aplenty. Or you might read another (often, interesting) font history blurb only to go back and see that the game has continued in the background, you have fallen into the abyss and will have to restart again.
Finally, I have found it very sad that a game about typefaces isn’t using pair kerning or even ligatures anywhere in the interface. Also, annoyingly, the audio volume is not preserved across restarts. The music itself is pretty good though and generally fits the theme of the current level very well.
Overall, the game is hard to recommend. If you’re interested in the theme, rather get the game on sale.

"Type:Rider" a self-proclaimed typographic puzzle platformer, in 2-D. Why typographic? Well, essentially, through it you're supposed to discover the history of typography moving from era to era. As someone who has a sort of interest in the subject matter, plus on the other side I like platformers also, this seemed like a no-brainer.
Well, as it happens, "Type:Rider" only looks great, but it's neither very educational nor it plays well.
You control two dots, a colon, which might've as well been a single dot for all it matters. And basically you roll your way through beautifully designed levels. And that's about it. The platforming is basic really, as you've no control over the colons jumping mechanic which is the only action they possess beside the aforementioned moving left and right. They can jump, and that's it. It will get you through the levels easily, but to gather all the collectibles - the letters of the alphabet in each level, plus additional info about the period - which require some actual platforming... it's pretty much all down to luck. Will the colon bounce as you want it or not? In the latter case you try again from a respawn point which is always rather close, but still... it doesn't feel that great when the platforming is mostly about luck rather than skill.
And the "education"? Well, it consists of finding a condensed article about various people and types, which you read as you would any other article in any encyclopedia. This is done when you collect an asterisk (*) that unlocks the new info section. Then you press ENTER and the gameplay pauses while you read what you've unlocked. No narration, nothing fancy or exciting. Just plain old text that is, ironically, not typo-proof and sometimes oddly formatted.
At the current price of 6,99€ (which is about 9.50$) this is definitely not worth it. In a sale or in a bundle, perhaps. If you have absolutely no interest in typography, skip it regardless.

When I first saw this game, I had to pick it up and see if it stood up to my expectations. I can certaintly say that this game has achieved and surpassed my expectations.
Power Hover is a game where you ride in a hoverboard and has a simplistic control system of just the left and right arrow keys. I made a claim in my video review of the game that the developers should add in a/d controls because it would feel more natural. I was shocked to say the least when I actually got a notification on twitter from them saying that they would immplement it right away! I really love to get games from the smaller developers because of interactions like this.
Then next point I want to get on is the soundtrack. I was stunned to hear it because It was both beautiful and stunning to hear. I never got tired of listening to the music as I was playing because It was so relaxing. The game itself isn't a rage game at all, It can be a bit challenging (especially if you want to 3 star everything) but the game was nevew meant to be rage inducing, but a game you can sit back, relax, and enjoy yourself.
Next I can go onto the graphics. The graphics are very beautiful to say the least. They are simplistic, but not in a way that will hinder the playing experience. When I first started playing the game, I noticed the graphics right away (as do everybody else) and payed close attention to the small details. They really put a lot of thought when creating the graphics for this game! They payed attention to small things like the light from the hoverboard and the look of the worms from the early levels!
Now that I got the most important positives of the game, I can now get into the only negative I have found in the game.
The game can be a little confusing at first. When I got this game, I wanted to read what it was about to decide weither it would be a good game for my channel, and inside the description of the game it states "Someone has stolen all the power from your robot village, but the track is still warm, hop on your hoverboard and get the energy back!" But when I first got into the game, I noticed there wasn't a cutscene explaining why I was on the hoverboard in the first place. The first level however states "The theif has dropped some batteries, follow the trail, collect the energy!" Other than that I felt like there needed to be a little bit more on the whole story aspect.
As you can see the Pros definitely outweigh the cons in this game. Needless to say is only $5.99 in the steam store as of the release sale ($7.99 off sale). If you have the extra $5 saved up, and are looking for a new game, Powewr Hover is the game for you.
TL;DR portion
Pros
+Easy to learn controls
+Beautiful Music
+Amazing simplistic graphics
Cons
-Story explaining

Having played the "flawed in everyway" frustrating first game I was not excited to play the second. Having purchased them together for $5 I felt obligated to play them both instead of them sitting there in my library never to be touched. When I started playing Dog Days it was like a completely different IP than the first.
Shooting was about the same but cover mechanics were vastly improved, with a dedicated into and out of cover button, and a whole array of new weapons, and most importantly a story you cared about... to the extent a game like this can have.  If this had been the first game in the series I'm sure it would have been much more successful. Although it was generally panned by most critics it improves over the first in everyway.  The pacing is tight and there is always the sense of "you have to keep moving" or the situation just gets worse.  Constant difficult battles, even on medium, challenge you to be frantic with your movements, and small amounts of ammo, combined with how innacurate most aiming is, constantly require you to go pick up dead enemies weapons or rush out into gunfire to collect ammo.
The "found footage" style of the camera movements (sometimes nauseatingly shakey :D) and the quality of the picture make it seem like a documentary of two men that just can't catch a break playing back on a vhs player.  There isn't some grand epic adventure unfolding before you a la uncharted or gears of war.  It's just 2 guys trying to escape the streets of Shanghai and it's all gone to hell.  For how cheap it is you should pick this up.  You can skip the first game and just play this one without being out of the loop on things for the most part.  If you can stomach the first one play it to get a little backstory.  Or just read the synopsis on wikipedia. I'd give it a 7/10.  Not amazing but a solid game worth the money and few hours of insanity.  I think it took me 6-8 hours to beat.

At first glance TBoI seems like a cheap and simple flash game. However, this is not the case. The game at a basic level is a shooter, with you clearing out rooms by dodging enemies and killing them with tears. But as you explore more you'll find hidden rooms, places to bomb, and little shops to spend hard earned coins. It almost resembles the original legend of Zelda on NES. These elements are all necessary as the game brings back the difficulty of retro games as well, also when you die its permanent.
The best part is that the game is random generated each time you play, so it never seems overly repetitive or stale. Sometimes this tricky as the better stuff you find, the better you'll do. But that's more interesting than it is annoying.
Overall a great effort for Team Meat and a challenging game everyone should have in their games list.

You know those god awful Japanese B-movies starring Japanese high school girls fighting grotesque monsters and you watch it anyway because it's campy and over-the-top?  Yeah, this is a lot like that only if it were put through the filter of Devil May Cry.  What I, personally, really liked was that all of these moves ort of cancelled nicely into each other allowing you to go from kick to sword to block to dodge to sword to super on the fly.  It really makes adjusting to whatever the chaotic hordes may throw at you intuitive and keeps the fights going at a brisk pace.
There are a couple of flaws that keep it from being pretty damn excellent, though.
For one thing, there's no lock on.  No lock on means you're going to end up swinging (or worse unloadin and wasting entire bars of Super) in the wrong direction every now and then and eating a sword to the face.  It also means the camera is VERY uncooperative once you start speeding up and moving all over the place.  I'm already busy enough as it is trying to keep combos going without getting hit, I don't want to have to worry about swivveling the camera an inch every other 10 seconds.  There IS a button that turns you around to face the nearest enemy, but again, a proper lock on function would have been better.  Another flaw is the lack of different attacks to buy.  Once you buy the flash kick launcher, the dive kick, and the counter there's nothing else to upgrade other than increasing their strength.  And then you have some of the enemy's attack's being a little janky.  Sometimes it's hard to tell whether a move should be dodged or blocked until you've already eaten the hit.  Allow me to give an example: the first boss has a  number of attacks to keep track of, right?  Two of which are a a pretty quick two swing move, and a back hand semi-spin attack.  The two-swing move is completely blockable, however the back hand semi-spin must be dodged.  Both are fairly similar looking attacks and for me it wasn't clear enough which one was unblockable.  Maybe I'm just bad at video games.  Who knows.
I get this is an indie game, and so it might be forgiven for a lack of polish.  However flaws are flaws, and when all is said and done these aren't game breaking.  In fact I'm very much impressed with what they were able to make given their limitations.  I'd love to see a sequel where they iron out the kinks and really explore their combat system to its fullest.

With only 5 stages, this is a short game that reminds me of older arcade titles.
There is barely any story to increase the length. That story is once again reminiscent of older arcade games, and is packed 100% with action anime tropes of course.
If you're good with brawlers you might finish it in two hours. Or even less.
However, beating the game unlocks harder difficulties which are so much harder, that it almost starts feeling like you're playing an entirely different game. (I am pretty sure I will not be able to beat the hardest setting actually XD).
There is also a grind quest to unlock new anime-classic costumes by earning points, it seems this quest seems to require around 10 game completions.
The conclusion is that these incentives to keep playing might be worthless to you, as they only matter if you like the game enough to keep playing after the first run.
So, would I recommend a two-hour-to-beat-once game?
Well, in this case, yes.
It's only two hours, but those are quite awesome and entertaining, especially if you're into anime.
The character, Misa, does't have a huge number of moves, but it's more about mastering them. All of the moves are useful and truly mandatory in harder difficulties. In my humble opinion, this is better design than having a huge moveset that you only use at 30% of its potential.
I know for sure that I had more fun with this game than with some hi-budget brawlers. I recommend it for anime and brawler fans especially. However, avoid like plague if you hate anime clichés.
And also : to truly enjoy this game, you NEED a controller. Preferably with twin analog sticks to have best control of Misa and the camera at the same time.

Type:Rider is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played.  If there is one best thing about it, it is the sheer beauty of it.  However, it has a number of good qualities.  I went into playing the game suspecting I'd not bother finishing more than a level.  Instead, I finished it (and most achievements, though I wasn't actively trying for them or aware of their requirements) in one sitting.
It is obviously a labor of love.  The passion it's developers had for the material is evident throughout.  Type:Rider is a game wrapped around a surprisingly interesting core: a summary of the history of fonts and typography.
The gameplay is primarily that of a physics-based platformer.  The controls are as simple as the analog stick and a jump button.  I strongly urge the use of a gamepad if one is available.  While this may sound overly simplistic, the joy is in the level design.  The integration of the subject material and the level design is where it really shines.  And that integration gets more impressive in latter levels.  Some segments were just marvels.
The platforming, separated from everything else, is decent.  It can occasionally feel a bit unfair and require trial and error.  And sometimes you may need to retry a section over and over.  Fortunately, with the exception of one optional nugget of masochism that isn't part of the main game, it saves your progress very frequently.  You will rarely have to redo anything you wouldn't consider one cohesive section of platforming: 10-15 seconds of play.  This is good because, by the last level, it became a bit frustrating.
Obviously from my "one sitting" remark, it is not a long game.  The entire game, including reading all the short histories, took me between 3 and 4 hours.  Additionally, there is not a lot of replayability to it other than to mop up achievements if that's your thing or simply to once again enjoy the beauty of it.  I could see myself doing the latter someday, perhaps.
Adding some to the little length the game has, you will encounter asterisks along the main path of progress.  After touching these, you can read a short several paragraph summary of a topic about typography.  I found them interesting, but they are completely optional if they do not interest you.  There were occasional typos and word spacing issues, which seemed all the more evident due to the subject matter.  I also wish there had been better examples of each font discussed in the history, so one could better visualize the changes over time being discussed in the text.
I did encounter one bug that caused me to need to restart the game and repeat the very little progress I'd made.  But after that point, I had no further bug issues during the remainer of the game.
I think it's evident that I enjoyed Type:Rider and recommend it to anyone who enjoys platformers, is interested in typography, or just wants to experience a gorgeous, albeit short, game.

This game is a very realistic driving simulator. Drive soviet vehicles through mud, water and other terrains. Let's get to the review.
Spintires is an offroad driving game where you get behind the wheel of a number of Russian vehicles and drive them through all the mud you could possibly hope for. Using only your map and compass you have to navigate the rugged terrain in order to complete objectives such as collecting and delivering lumber.
+Great graphics
+Quite a few different trucks, each with customisation options and they are all quite different to each other, in appearance and performance
+Amazing mud physics, the deformation caused by driving through mud looks realistic and is excellent
+Several maps, all of them are quite different to each other and the vehicles available vary between each one
+The winch system is great and the power of it feels quite realistic
+Multiplayer, particularly with friends, is a lot of fun
+Driving controls are good, as are the crane controls (used for putting lumber in your trailer)
+You have to discover the different parts of the map so even if you don't want to do the main objective there is a lot to do on each map
+They did a very good job in making it difficult to judge water depth
+/-The majority of the gameplay comes from getting yourself out of the mud, personally I think it's fun but it might put some people off
-The camera controls and the camera itself are awful. The controls are very sensitive, when you zoom out it automatically zooms in making it very hard to see when using big trucks, it has a very strange centre, sometimes it pans by itself, you can only move it on the x-axis, it has awkward angles and it's difficult to get it at the angle you want
-The devs still haven't added a first person camera which was promised very early on after its launch
-The relationship between the dev and the community isn't great (see forums)
-Infrequent updates despite being promised regular large content updates
Verdict:
8.9
It's an amazingly realistic game that definetely deserves a buy, especially at the price listed.

The difference between common edutainment and Type:Rider is integration, and what a difference it is! This game offers fascinating information and easy fun. Not too difficult of a platformer, Type:Rider will make you learn, and that's not a bad thing.
NtK Before Review:
Video games are educational by nature, a byproduct of introducing someone to a new universe. Level one in many games serves as the first lesson in a line of explicit interactive lectures which often extend to the final level of a game. And those games which don't explicitly teach its students how to play often demand players' innovation in learning to play. It would make sense then, gaming and learning being so closely related, that games would make excellent educational tools. The truth is, however, that most educational games a more boring than a dump being flushed. And many popular games are just as boring in their in-game "lectures" on how to play as the boring lecturing teachers whom we accuse of not connecting with the students who play these games. What's the problem here? Why do games educate incorrectly and educators incorrectly apply games? It all boils down to gamification. I know that's a loaded topic, but I'll describe the essence of it in brief: Somewhere along the line that we call time, someone else caught on to the fact that games were awesome. They wanted to bring the appeal and motivation that games offered to the real world, so they extracted the elements that they perceived to be the essence of playing a game and applied them to business, education, research, and many other domains. Some say it works and others say it doesn't, but that's not the point. It's stupid regardless. People enjoy collecting the coins in Mario because that's what Mario does. But if you were told to write an essay and then, upon completion, you see a blip of a coin with a retro sound effect on a screen, that is not a game. Because that's not what Mario does and, in that moment, you are not Mario. The content and the task are dissociated. Dissociation was the problem from the start when the elements of gaming were separated from the game. Now take this issue to edutainment. Edutainers take what a game would be and add unrelated tasks, like math problems or multiple-choice questions, and expect students to learn more from it. They make no effort to immerse the players (in fact, these games often acknowledge that the players are external and claim that the main character "needs their help to solve the problem!"), they follow the poor practices of game design that the "lecture-y" games have, and they make the game about things that the subject is not about.
The Bullet Dodged:
Now these are the bad things that intentionally educational games tend to do. Type:Rider fantastically avoided such problems. It begins by telling me to move the colon (as a typeface character, not a large intestine. Also, the player is occasionally the first two dots of an ellipsis.) in a cave to navigate my way out using my thumbs (I played through the first time on a mobile platform). I see cave paintings, and I question the nature of my environment. There is a star nearby, so naturally I grab it and my questions are answered. A book zooms around the screen to reveal my environment are the pages of a book (makes sense why I'm a printed character now), and the page turns to inform me about cave paintings as communication and that the painting I saw was a real one. I am now rolling, on my page again, and I find myself struggling to make it up an incline. I find this incline to be triangularly shaped and an elongated pentagon hangs loosely-attached to the ceiling just beyond. I grab the asterisk at the top to learn that the background of crude carvings behind me were hieroglyphics, which make sense now because I was on a steep pyramid and the now-fallen pentagon actually resembles an obelisk, a monumental structure common to ancient Egypt. I'm not gonna blandly talk through the whole game, but the idea is that the content (learning about the "font" at the time and culture in which the pyramids were built) and the task (making it up a pyramid) were integrated. For the entirety of the game the environment is the subject material. My incentive to learn about the effects of the Catholic counter-reformation on printed works is that, immersed in the game, I am threatened by a firey stack of books, which also teaches me about history. Certainly, Type:Rider uses gamification in requiring the player to collect all the letters, ampersands, and asterisks, but recall that gamification isn't inherently evil, merely inherently dissociated. The incentivization is seamlessly integrated into the environment and content that collecting the items is part of the learning.
The Verd:
The art in this game is beautiful and reflective of the defining typefaces and printing machines of each era, and the music is subtly blended as well, so as to create some awestriking atmospheres. The only negatives to this game are suboptimal controls (uncoordinated at points, which is hard to ignore in the platforming genre) and the storyline is told in history, so I guess no insane plot twists (sorry ): ). There is a certain population that will refuse to find this good, and that's logical, just as not everyone will enjoy science class. Either way, the appeal or repulsion is caused by the scope of the content and not a lousy integration of otherwise crowd-pleasing content. An easily recommendable [7.5 / 10], Type:Rider is a surprisingly enjoyable roll through a side of history that tends toward banality under other presentation methods; it's an ideal model for what education-based learning should look like. This will definitely not be everyone's cup of tea, but I find it to be one darn great Earl Grey.

The Binding of Isaac.
Oh dear Lord, The Binding of Isaac.
Hell. Yeah.
This has got to be one of the sickest, most disgusting, horrifying, frustrating yet amazingly addicting games I have ever played. Once I found myself in the Basement, I found I couldn't escape, in more ways than one.
This game is HARD. Like, balls-to-the-walls hard. Hell, it took me a few attempts just to get to the second floor. And then it took me more attempts to get two more floors or so. And so on and so forth. The game is frustrating to the point not of breaking you, but making you want to keep going. You'll die, and I'll think "GAH! I ALMOST had it! ...Just ONE more try, I can do it!"
Of course, just trying again isn't a guarantee of further progession or victory. The floors you play in are randomly generated each time you start a game, so the experience will never be exactly the same twice. That's part of the fun of this game - just seeing what's in store for you every time you give it another go.
In these randomly generated floors I've been randomly rambling about, you may find many things: enemies to hurt you, items to help or hurt you, shops, secret rooms found by blowing up walls, secret rooms hidden in secret rooms, and some TWISTED boss fights. Seriously, the bosses of this game are some prime examples of this game's nightmare-inducing imagery. Most of them are also pretty fun to fight, or at the least, satisfying to beat. ("YES! IT'S GONE! I DON'T HAVE TO LOOK AT IT ANYMORE!") Really, there's just WAY too much content to go over. For such a seemingly small 2D package, The Binding of Isaac sure does have a crap-ton of content and replayability about it.
And for all of that, it's fun as hell. With the super-low price tag of five dollars and an extra three for a crap-ton more content, The Binding of Isaac and Wrath of the Lamb are MUST BUYS. If you somehow haven't bought them already, do yourself a favor and do so. Right now. Yes, now.
With all that said, ladies and mentlegen, I bid you adieu.
~Tyranno

The Meh:
-Mafia III definitely doesn't hold a candle to Mafia II or Mafia I but it's an acceptable game in the series. They cut out a lot of the great content that was present in the previous games like the garages, houses, and vehicle customization but I hear they are planning on fixing that in upcoming DLC (I think I hear EA cackling with delight in the background somewhere).
-They got rid of some of the immersive qualities I enjoyed about the previous games like lights, engine repairs, fuel, etc.
-Graphics are Meh. Beautiful in some areas and 2009-esque in many others.
-Vehicle damage was disappointingly simplistic. No satisfying glass shattering, bullet hole ridden, delicious crunchable  cars...
The Bad:
-Optimization leaves a lot to be desired. Graphical issues, framerate issues, weird wacky lighting effects (The trees are on fire and Lincoln Clay and his feral friends all have a radioactive glow). I'm sure these will be fixed with time.
-Lots of grinding to advance the story. Side missions, etc don't complement the game like they should. This is a game where 100% completion isn't something you want to strive for nor does it seem very rewarding. Serious lack of incentives. "Go here, shoot them" and "Interrogate this guy" over and over again. I have little desire to replay this game unless the DLC does some major overhauling
The Good:
-The gunplay, CC Combat, and stealth I feel is really well done. I had a blast utilizing the stealth approach and kick down the front door approach alternatively. Melee kills are well done.
-The hit detection and relative realism was also very satisfying. The bodies staying behind is a good touch. I also was impressed with the reactions from bullet impacts in various body parts (Shot in knee vs shot in chest vs shot in head - recoil, impact, and obvious wounding). All very well done and relatively realistic. It made every death "personal" not just business as usual.
-Excellent story, well written characters, and superb voice acting. Very atmospheric and gives you a feel for the time. *I got a little tired of the confederate flag waving redneck racist stereotyping though. It was as overused and overplayed as the Nazi's and middle eastern terrorist stereotypes. The bad guys felt very "cookie cutter" if you get my drift. The Italian mobsters were really well done though as you would expect from ths series. Tons of backstabbing betrayal and pure unadulterated greed. Scheming, lies, and deception abound. Mr. V was my favorite without giving away spoilers, always having your back and not p!$%ing and moaning like the others about every decision you make in the story. A true gentleman.
-I am really glad they overhauled the money system. In Mafia II I got really irritated that every couple of hours you would lose every penny you had due to some routine betrayal or another and I kept having to rebuild all the time. I still advise you to stash your money and utilize the free Consigliere service you get later on as often as possible. As far as I know, theres no limit to how often you can do that or call for weapon resupply.
I'll wrap this up by saying at the current time, you shouldn't buy this game at full retail price with the season pass. You won't experience a lot of the issues I had until it's well past the 2 hour refund window. I still recommend it as an enjoyable game and I'm willing to give the developers slack if they listen to their critics. I bought this game for around 40$ and think it fair but I will wait for the season pass to go on sale. Thanks for reading!

Shotgun Farmers could be the cream of the crop. That's probably the only vegetable pun I'll do, maybe.
I was surprised with this game as I went into it thinking it might end up being a lazy asset project. To my delight it seems like the developers are putting in a lot of effort to make everything from scratch along with creating some decently enjoyable gameplay.
The game plays like a regular arena shooter for the most part with one "groundbreaking" difference in that you harvest vegetables to both regain ammo and pick up new weapons. It's mostly a gimmick because it functions similar to arena shooter pickups, but the spawn locations are more random.
The gameplay is currently a bit limited with only a handful of weapons. Hopefully some more get added in the future as the game leaves Steam Early Access.
That being said, the core gameplay is solid, runs well and fairly enjoyable. This is the type of Early Access project that just needs additional maps, weapons and items to be a great and worthwhile experience.
The art style is cute and nice to look at. I dig the cartoonish characters and maps. They had a vision in mind and were able to create it.
One thing I would like to see updated is some more music during matches or sound going on. It can feel very quiet during matches after the initial music is done.
The playerbase is rather small right now, you will most likely need to be involved in their Discord to get a full server.
Overall, with enough watering and sunlight from the developer, Shotgun Farmers could end up being a great little niche indie shooter.

Before I say why this game is bad, I'm just gonna say I beat the game multiple times on multiple difficulties and got all the upgrades in a very short time, so I'm not some whiny loser who can't get beat the game and cries in a review about it.
Anyways, the combat is bad. Hack and slashes are all about exciting combat with a variety of enemies that could kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you don't really know what you're doing on higher difficulties, but that is not the case in this game. You can spam basically whatever the heck you want, sheathe your sword, then do a massive amount of damage to bleeding enemies. Not really what I would call exciting or execution heavy by any means. The most functional form of combat is nothing but guard-cancelling your slashes, which is awfully boring because the enemies are designed so poorly that you can do this to literally anything, including the bosses.
The story is non-existent. Not really a problem if you're just playing for the gameplay, but for those who do want a story, this is not the game for you. You kill some random enemies that are apparently demons and you're chasing down this girl  who was apparently your best friend and you end up fighting her twice. Real great story. I personally don't care, but this is not a game you buy for the story.
The level design is weak. It's basically a generic survival-mode where you fight a few waves of enemies that are supposed to get harder with each wave and then you fight a boss in the end. This wouldn't be too bad if there was a lot of enemy variety and it was actually progressed in difficulty, but unfortunately, it's just the same enemies over and over for each level.
The length of the game is way too short considering it has little to no replay value. Anybody can beat this game under 2 hours. Not much to say about that.
TL;DR - Buy the game if you want to waste a couple dollars or something you'll play for 2-8 hours, then never touch again. If you're really bad at hack and slash

But it sucks.
I am a HUGE fan of all of the Fallout series, even when they were beind developed by Interplay. With the release of Fallout 4,  my love for the series came back. So when I went on Steam and found this game, I was very excited, then dissapointed.
I can sum this game up in two words that any professional gamer like myself would automatically stay away from: mobile port.
The game is a good concept: running and establishing your very own vault set right in the Fallout universe. But it lacks in many places, the biggest I think is keeping your interest in the game. There's been points where I just stare at the screen for (I kid you not) ten minutes straight without anything other than resource icons appearing. Not only is the game lacking in design, but like most other mobile games, there are the dreaded, microtransactions.
If the word "microtransactions" didn't set off some kind of warning, then nothing is stopping you from playing this game.
Besides the fact that there are microtransactions, they're used in the worst of ways. You can pay money for a couple things like Nuka-Cola quantum, which can be used (to my knowledge) to buy these weird lunch-box things. And guess what these lunch boxes have in them? Nuka-Cola quantum. Usually less than what you paid for the box itself. It's little things like this that just make this game unplayable for me, but I think that if this game went a little faster, more things happened, and the microtransaction were removes completely, I think it would be a decent game. Not a great one, but one that I would play if I was waiting for something or on a plane.
I hope that this review was helpful! this was one of the first reviews I've written on Steam, and I hope that I conveyed my message clearly. Thanks for making it this far! You now known not to play this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game.

Don't be fooled by the trailers. This game is surrounded in controversy, mainly due to it's main developer David Prassel.  Among a long list of nefarious acts, Prassel has been accused of stealing elements from other games, laying off employees without paying them for work, and manipulating message boards to deflect negative criticism towards the game. In addition Prassel tried to rebrand the game formerly known as "Dino Beatdown" into "Dino Horde" to increase Metacritic scores; claiming it to be a sequel when it's more of a content update. Even if one were to ignore the game's depraved upbringing, the game with it's comically short T-Rex arms fails to grasp the lofty claims and over-hype created presumably by Prassel.
Ignoring the game's heavy influence from Halo, the gameplay revolves around a stereotypical group of "space marines" defending bases against swarms of prehistoric predators, which in of itself sounds okay on paper. However, within the first hour of playing, any seasoned gamer with a critical bone in their body will start to see the game's inherent flaws emerge. The game which marketed itself around commiting mass dino-cide features a surprisingly laughable AI that would make a Stegosaurus roll in it's sedimentary grave. The dinos tend to path in a completely linear fashion towards the player which makes "Dino Horde" feel more like "Dino Queue" which really brings the atmosphere in the game to extinction. Taking high ground will often result in dinosaurs running around in erradic beelines as you frantically spray at them with shoddy hit registration until they die. Don't worry about the hit registration though, because all of the basic ground dinosaurs can be run down inside of invincible ground vehicles such as the Wartho- I mean "Gladiator" combat buggy, making firearms completely pointless outside of killing large dinosaurs. No seriously, I ground dinos into lizard burger for an hour and was awarded top score for being the most unskilled player on my team before I logged off in bitter apathy.
I tried giving this game a fair chance, I really did. I tried looking past Prassel coddling his "baby" like an overprotective parent, his apparently questionable business practice and his deplorable attempt at dodging Metacritic rating, Underneath it all though was only the husk of a game, a grand idea with poor execution, and unfortunately it will not keep the interest of experienced gamers. Don't get me wrong, this game can be a fun waste of time with friends, but you should be laughing WITH the game, not AT it. Until someone can nail the "dino defense" game on the head, my dream will remain fossilized in amber until it's DNA can be extracted and brought back to life, which sadly will most likely not be anytime soon.

If you're expecting a solid and interesting thirdpersonshooter, look elsewhere, the gameplay -while functional- is the standard modern shooter fare:
cover based shooting
bloodyscreensoreal
annoying squadmate that gets in the line of fire
press X to stealthkill
carry only two weapons at maximum
blind fire and hipfire near useless
wait for your squadmate to open the door for you
help your squadmate over the fence
shoot explosive barrels
etc. etc. etc.
The game doesn't even try to hide that it is uninspired, it has no gimmicks at all, the mechanics never evolve, it's just a shooting gallery from start to finish.
So if you're coming in from a gaming perspective, stay away. Because this game is nauseatingly generic and wants to be a movie really bad, it has that nasty framework that people are so fed up with these days, i.e: "corridor-shooting gallery-cutscene-repeat"
But here's where things might get a bit controversial: if you come in from the perspective of a movie fanatic, and review the game as if it were a movie, this game is actually pretty neat! It turns out that it works pretty well as a pseudo-movie.
and since i didn't go in expecting a good game, and just wanted to see how the game handled that striking neo-noir theme its got going on. it actually didn't disappoint in that department.
The cinematography and level compositions are gorgeous. Gritty city decay contrasted against neon-spangled streets, all viewed through a wide angle lens camera with deliberate digital artifacts such as scanlines, noise, low bitrate, screen tearing, bokeh, light bleed, chromatic aberration and dynamic range fluctuations. the acting and pacing is on hollywood level and the soundtrack and sound design has a real sense of space and depth. It's field recordings of city noise interwoven with eerie electronic patterns and feverish soundscapes of pulsating drone.
I personally think that it all is meant to convey the mind of lynch, and how he is hungover, miserable, confused, disorientated and detatched from reality.
Definitely something to check out if you're into neo-noir movies. if you can bear the gameplay that is. Its atmosphere felt reminiscent of enter the void or trainspotting, and if compared to games i would say i felt a bit of the hotline miami and max payne mood.
That's all folks! Pretentious hipster and wannabe critic signing off~

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is an open world action game where you hunt orcs in an effort to defeart the evils that lay in Mordor. The movement is smooth and the combat has weight and is incredibly fun.Hunting and fighting orc captains and warchiefs incredibly fun and the nemesis system adds a new element to gaming, an element that allows you to truly forge your own story through interactions and fights.
Middle-earth: Shadow of War is an open world action game where you mindlessly grind for hours on end for petty loot that's barely worth the effort. The movement is smooth, but the combat has no weight to it and the systems from its predecessor are butchered. Grind for hours to get skill points that you use to unlock watered down abilities from the previous game that aren't anywhere near as good as they once were. The nemesis system, while upgraded, has no impact on the gameplay whatsoever, making one wonder why it's even in this game. Oh, and the lootboxes. Shadow of War's progression has been slowed to a crawl in order to incentivize you to buy them. If you ignore the lootbox system then have fun wanting to blow your brains out grinding for days. There's also the issue of the true ending. In order to unlock this you basically have to grind for literal days, or buy a ton of lootboxes.
In short, Middle-earth: Shadow of War isn't very good. It's a watered down sequel that could have been good if they decided to actually improve upon the foundation its predecessor layed. The other glaring issue is the lootbox-based progression system. If you don't gamble for those items you might as well stop playing. Don't buy this game unless you can get the gold edition for dirt cheap. Do not recommend.

Oh damn I hate to write this. I loved Shadow of Mordor for what it was: orc-killin' simulator. I expected something similar with Shadow of War. No great strides, just more of the gory fun I got out of the first one. Oh how wrong I was. Let's start with some positives. The voice acting kills it (I'm looking at you Bruz and Ratbag!). Everything is beautifully delivered from the cast. Couldn't be happier with the performances. And...that's where it ends.
I have fallen through the earth 6 times. I have run across rope bridges countless times only to get to the end and then run in place forever. My favorite stabby stabby orc stealth kills look like they were animated by a computer animation undergraduate. When trying to escape a tough combat I run to a wall to climb up and out of the way. What happens? I roll into the wall. Again. And again. And again.
Story quests have a habit of making it really hard to do them. Not talking about "it's a tough fight" or anything like that but, case in point, the balrog chase. You have to hit icicles to slow the monster down during the chase. Missed an icicle? Just reset. You're done. The balrog gets so close that no icicle will even hit him so game over. I don't mind tough gameplay but one-miss-failure-states aren't fun.
The long and short. I really had high hopes. I loved the stabby stabby of Shadow of Mordor and was willing to do more of it in War. They just didn't bring their "A" game. I didn't get into the microtransaction debacle here. It is hardly a thing. You can earn chests just by doing vendetta missions. If you want to throw money away over digital nothing then be my guest. God, pitching canon aside (which SoW readily does) this could have been something special. While not perfect, SoM delivered, at the very least, pretty solid gameplay. Bugs? Yeah, there were some in there, but they can't hold a candle to this trainwreck. Rarely do I write reviews for any game I play, but I must say this game and its plot rank among my favorite. Perhaps even knocking Dragon Age out of first. I finished the game in about 10 hours through the past 4 days. However, with any game, there are good and bad points.
The Good:
- The plot development seems slow at first, but after the first few acts you'll find yourself gripping your seat.
- If you've played Shadow of Mordor, the Nemesis system offers a unique alley and enemy system that makes gameplay enjoyable.
- Consistent morality for our main protaganist, Talion. Many games cannot keep a character straight and the fact that he was kept in check thrilled me.
- The graphics, while not on the same level as the Witcher 3, are very enjoyable and offer a realistic twist to the Tolkien world.
- You do not have to be a Tolkien fan to enjoy the games. In fact, I do not care for any of his books but both games hold a place in my heart, as do the characters.
The Bad:
- Game bugs are really what hurt this game. At times, it's random crashingings, freezings, screen flickerings, or the infamous audio issues. Some can be resolved permanently or temperarly, but this is worth mentioning.
- The plot is a bit dry at the beginning, and I looked more forward to the battle scenes than the actual dialogue. After Act I, though, it picks up and I was able to enjoy it more.

I want to keep this review short. This game is a f***ing visual masterpiece. Hotline Miami is a violent 2D top-down shooter drenched in color and chaos. In case you think 5.8 hours isn't enough, I've played over 10 hours and finished the game on my friend's account before purchasing my own copy.
This game was designed to thrill and frustrate you. The gameplay is extremely fast-paced and will test your reaction speed. It's relatively easy to pick up, but it's difficult to master since weapon choice and position are significant elements. Prepare to spam the respawn button because it's a guarantee that you will die several times. It can get repetitive eventually, but an interesting mechanic is the mask system. These masks either buff or debuff your character depending on the mask and provide a different experience, but ultimately these are completely optional.
~8/10
I personally love the art of this game because it fits in so well with the 80s setting. The pixelated art style serves as a great throwback to the old 8-bit and 16-bit games during that time. Honestly, I wasn't really interested in picking it up because the faces in some cutscenes reminded me of those poorly drawn flash games in Y8 which I really disliked, but it was really the colors that drew me in. The neon-soaked world of 1980s Miami was reflected best through the color palettes found in the UI, characters, and backgrounds. This game is worth buying purely for the a e s t h e t i c itself.
~9.5/10
The soundtrack is filled with slow chiptune beats that are great to listen to when you're high as well as fast-paced electronic tracks that will keep your blood pumping. I love the soundtrack because of its great variety and for the overall immersion it brings to the user. As soon as you boot the game, you get hit with trance music and as soon as you get in on the action, you get hit with a rapid succession of beats that go on loop until you clear the level. If anything will keep you going after several deaths, it's the music.
~10/10
I'm trying to keep this as spoiler-free as possible. You're a murderer inflicted with a mental disease. The protagonist, Richard (the name of his original rooster mask), is conflicted with three mysterious personas all wearing animal masks and questioning him on his understanding of the events that have occurred in his life and how it shaped him. He seeks to understand himself and make sense of the relationships he has formed with other people. It's a really dark yet gripping story that delves into themes of the psyche.
~9/10
I don't really need to delve much on this. Hotline is a PC-friendly, low-spec game that will only take about 600 MB or less space in your hard drive. This game will run perfectly on almost any computer with Windows XP. Additionally, if you are playing on a Alienware computer, your keyboard's color scheme will shift between shades of pink and blue (my favorite colors) and flashes red when you kill someone, which looks visually epic.
~10/10
Compared to its sequel, Hotline 1 has a better, more organized plot and its gameplay is less repetitive, making it the stronger of the two. If you do want a more challenging experience, however, get the sequel which provides even larger maps and ties up the story.
~Overall 9.5/10

When I first read the reviews regarding this game, all I saw was panties or its Japanese derivative "pantsu". I come back about two months later and still see "pantsu". You must be asking "They made a game about panties then?" and if gameplay footage of this game is an indicative about anything, it's that this is not a game about panties.
What is it, then? I hear you asking. It's an arcade-style action game that not coincidentally features a female protaganist. Who wears a short skirt. Don't my words as being conservative or anything. I am merely trying to help you understand how this "pantsu" thing started. So panties are not what you will exclusively get to see in this game. Most of the time, you will be saying "HOLY ****!" or "There are so many enemies!" or shouting at your mother why you are vociferating. She will come over and say "It's just a game." and you will want to beat the daylights out of her. But I digress.
What we have here is a fast-paced action game with a female protagonist with a story that could not care more about itself even if it tried. So this is a story about a girl, a blade-templar, named Misa tracking down and killing her classmate, Suzuka, who is possessed by a demon sword and popping up monsters all over. At first glance, you would think "That sounds like every other fantasy story." And you would be right. The writing for this game is simply uninteresting. How did Suzuka come in possession of a demon sword? Who are the blade templars? Is there no way to save Suzuka? All these questions flutter about inside your head and there is no answer for them. At least, in the game.
But the story is not the charm of this game. People who love it, including yours truly, love it for the high-pace and high-action. It feels like a Devil May Cry game. Or something out of a Devil May Cry game. Though DMC has so much more substance in comparison and has a story and lore to go with it. The combat is challenging. The crowds are not overly aggressive as long as you can put some distance between you and your targets.
My first disagreement with this game, though. is how you have to rely on upgrades to get you through the game. I mean, you can survive until the last boss without any upgrades to health but eventually you will have to take them. Boss fights are a little bland for my tastes. You can't take them head on. They have too much range or are too spammy for you to take advantage of anything.  That is if you wish to get unclose and personal. That is it, really. I would have liked it if you didn't have only one viable method of fighting a boss. It's always space, holy tec full charge, space, holy tec full charge, bleed, zanshin. It ends up being repetitive than fun.
Now for the big question: Is it worth buying? Well, if you are well-versed in action games and like the adrenaline pumping into your vein or simply looking relieve some stress. then you will like this game. But if you don't like repetitive tasks, don't like action games, there is a good chance you won't like this game. If you are looking for your entry into the genre, I suggest you seek something easier.

A beautiful and informative game about a fascinating subject? Well, technically, yes; it certainly is very pretty, and highly informative - not much of a game to be spoken of, though.
OK, you'd have to be an idiot to look at the screenshots and expect complex gameplay mechanics - but the clumsy movement controls which underpin everything you do and the overwhelming simplicity of the minor puzzle elements leave this a good distance from being genuinely entertaining.
But, if it's beautiful and informative, is that enough in itself, despite not being entertaining? Well, to put it bluntly, no.
Admittedly, it would be difficult to relate the history of typography and printing without heavily depending on the player simply reading through pages and pages of information - but the way the information is gradually fed to the reader is desperately poor for 2 reasons.
Firstly, the way in which these pages are unlocked. In each of the different themed zones, along your way to collect all the letters in the alphabet you will also come across 6 asterisk signs. When you collect one of these, you have about a second to hit the enter key - upon doing which, the game is paused and the new page presented. If you miss the tiny window of opportunity, you need to wait until you come to the next asterisk, and then read through 2 pages. So, if you're in the middle of a precarious situation (as will very often be the case) you feel forced to pause the game, knowing full well that when you return you will have to desperately wrangle to avoid tumbling to your doom and having to restart the level. Does enter have any other function throughout the game? No. But it's inexplicably disabled outside of this tiny window, so you can't roll on to a safe location before you stop to read the text. Of course, you could just unlock all of the pages and read them from the main menu afterwards - but the connection between the interesting information and the threadbare game is already so weak, to completely seperate the two begs the question why you're bothering to play in the first place.
And then, the second problem with the way the information is presented - and the absolute killer blow. The frequent clumsy translations and outright mistakes in grammar and punctuation are unforgivable. I got through about 30 pages, and nigh-on all of them included at least one error. I recognise that the developers don't speak English as a first language - but to release a product that expects players to read through several dozen pages of text, and not have a competent native proofreader go through it is ridiculous.
If you think this game might be for you, I'd urge you to reconsider. Get one of the many excellent comparable indie games such as NightSky, and pause it every 30 seconds to read a few lines from Wikipedia articles on typography. The game will be infinitely better, and the articles not so jarringly crammed with obvious errors.

This is a strange game indeed. It is an educational game like Math Blasters or... (OK that's the only educational game I remember playing as a child), but for people of any age instead of just children. I like that it teaches a rather niche and not necessarily important topic, typography. I got the game because I had always wanted to know more about typography, so this was the perfect chance.
The gameplay itself is incredibly simple, as one might expect of an educational game. You take the role the colon - yes you are litterally the colon, this guy right here ":". It is a simple platforming game. The catch is the platforms are letters and objects having to do with the history of typography, like the printing press. This gives the levels a visual theme and separates them from other platformers, but as the typography of the letters can get quite complext, this can lead to some unweildy platforming. Some parts are genuinely difficult to get through because of the odd platforms.
During the levels, you collect orbs that give you pages of text on the history of typography. These can interrupt the gameplay, so I preferred to read them all together once I had completed the level. This is where the learning of the game comes from. The information is well-written and interesting. In fact, it was the reason I completed the game. After a while, the gameplay does get rather tedious, I'd say about 2/3 of the way through I wanted to stop, but I kept going because I wanted to catch up with the history of typography up to the present day. I will say though that I find the early history of typography more interesting than the recent history, but that's subjective.
Overall, I'd say get this game if you're interested in the subject matter. Needless to say the gameplay alone doesn't carry it, but if you want to learn about typography there are certainly worse ways. I honestly wish there were more games like this, that taught narrow subjects in game form. Of course this game is certainly not the perfect way to do so, as it could benefit from more interactivity with the material, but it's a good start.

If you are not one to be offended by the game's graphics/subject and you are a fan of top-down shooters or real-time roguelikes, you should definitely pick this game up.
The game plays a lot like the dungeons in the original Zelda on the NES.  The difference being that levels are randomized and there is a metric ton of items you can find which will enhance Isaac's abilities.  Combat is controlled similar to games like Smash TV or Total Carnage where you can move in one direction and shoot in another.
To me, one of the game's most defining features is how Isaac's appearance and characteristics vary wildly as he obtains new items.  By the end of a playthrough, you will often be a completely different character from your previous attempt.  This bolsters the game's replayability by having items which significantly change the way Isaac attacks.
The expansion for this game, Wrath of the Lamb, adds a ton of new content to the game and is really recommended if you enjoy the base game.  Although it should be noted that it adds significant difficulty to the game, so you should probably play the game first before you purchase the expansion.
It should also be noted that this is a Flash game and can run sluggishly.  There is a remake of the game in the works though that will do away with this nuisance.  There are also some tweaks and mods that can improve performance of the game, though I have never used them personally.
All in all, for the price of this game, you will likely get way more than your money's worth out of it.  Its the kind of game you can use to kill 15 minutes of boredom, or you can get caught up in the addiction of trying to reach the bottom floor and spend several hours trying to defeat Mom.

I've had my fair share of The Binding of Isaac and what I can say for certain is that this easily falls in my favourite games list. At first when you get into the game nothing really makes much sense, items, goals, levels, story - it's all pretty confusing. But after 2-3 hours of playing and after a bit (20-ish) restarts you'll see that everything is well executed with infinte replayability in mind.
Items are the most helpful and most weird aspect of the game, maybe the only thing that can compare to their weirdness is the story. Every item has its own effect on Isaac's stats and his visual appearance. I can guarantee that at the end Isaac will never look human. Items are randomly generated, like the levels, and add tons of variety and make sure that every run you do you'll get a different experience.
The story is something that most people will probably ignore, or will not notice at all, but it is there. The end game cutscenes are the key component and after a few replays you'll get what it's all about and will probably want to find out more, to which I say that you should pick up the DLC for the game. It finishes the story and fills in some missing parts.
The DLC is awesome, since it adds even more variety to the game, but be warned that if you're new to The Binding of Isaac and if you haven't put in a bit over 10 hours don't buy it just yet, because it makes the game a lot harder and might leave you struggling at the starting floors again. But aside from that all the new items and the new trinket system involved really help the game feel even more genuine and diverse.
In conclusion, I'd just like to state again that the game is awesome and well worth the money. It's a good option to have when you want a fun and new experience and only have an hour to spare. When you get into the game it's gonna be hard to put it down. So why wait, start your experience now!

**Binding of Isaac**
Story (6/10):
BoI's story is simple; a boy is stranded in the basement of his home, chased by his abusive Mother who believes it is God's will that her son must die. In all honesty, the story is not very important to the game, and is not a focal point.
Gameplay (8/10):
BoI plays like a standard 4-directional shooter, introducing a gameplay style that is easy to learn, but difficult to master, so to speak. The game introduces numerous enemies, and staggering amounts of upgrades and items that the player must use to utilize throughout the game. Combined with an unforgivingly hard difficulty, the average player should be prepared to die. A lot. Unfortunately, the game sometimes is hindered by its forcing of the player to only shoot in the cardinal directions, since enemies come from all sides.
The game's ability to randomize the levels/powerups through each playthrough gives you motivation to continue to play, and feels satisfying throughout.
Visuals (8/10):
The game has a cartoony, Flash presentation, similar to Super Meat Boy, that is pleasing to the eye. McMullen paints a dark picture of Isaac's basement, introducing horrible creatures and disturbing imagery that is not always as cutesy as the main character. The game is obviously not trying to be a graphical powerhouse, and it works.
Sound (7/10):
Solid, suspenseful music, combined with apt sound effects, give me no complaints about this aspect of the game.
Replayability (10/10):
BoI's entire purpose is to be replayed, over and over again. Games are very short, either because the player dies from the game's brutality, or finishes the playthrough (only takes an hour or so). Usually, a playthrough will unlock new items, reveal new strategies for the player to use, or provide some other incentive for the player to try again. The game tries to be addicting, and succeeds immensely. It's hard to put this game down once you pick it up.
OVERALL:
BoI is successful in what it tries to do; make a rogue-like arcade shooter with RPG elements that allows for many quick plays, that incentivize the player to keep going. It's a real treat to play.

Supremely touching story experience featuring well written realistic characters that are easy to relate to as well as excellent voice acting performances. Without going too in depth I highly enjoyed the stotry and characters, and there are some wonderful life lessons that this game will remind you of very bluntly and effectively. For what it's worth the choices in Life is Strange felt far more weighty and meaningful than any other Adventure/Choice game of this style, again mainly looking at Telltale but Until Dawn comes to mind as well. Compared to the aforementioned titles I felt that this game does a much better job of getting you in the main character's shoes as you feverishly try to rewind and rectify you and your friends problems in life. The rewind time gimmick makes you obsessively feel the need to have everything play out perfectly for Max and everyone around her and it's easy to get engrossed in the world and feel empathetic towards the cast as the story unfolds.
If you're a sucker for a good coming of age story as I am then do not miss this game, it's one of the best I've seen in the medium and I'm truly glad I decided to experience it. Racial profiling would have been great if it was in more depth. Getting randomy stoped in the street, or pulled over for no reason. Making you feel more on edge and tense.
