Hold On I'm Comin', to New Bordeaux, A modern city with traditional Southern Values. Right from the get go, the in-game documentary (which runs the course of the game) is used as a framing device to introduce the city of New Bordeaux (a fictionalised New Orleans) and the protagonist of Mafia III (Lincoln Clay) to the player, this is a smart move as these are clearly the games two strongest elements, and this exceptionally strong opening sets a tone which is mostly maintained throughout the entirety of Mafia III.
The year is 1968, and Lincoln Clay has just returned from the Vietnam war to reunite with his adopted family (The Black Mob). Very early on Lincoln's family are betrayed and killed by the Italian Mob and Lincoln sets out on a plot of revenge, which is the main setup of Mafia III. On paper it seems like very ordinary, unremarkable stuff however Lincoln Clay is one of the most interesting and multi dimensional characters in modern gaming, with an excellent story arc and sense of character development (including PTSD, and justification of violence).
The setting has also been done completely right. New Bordeaux itself is full of pedestrians having topical conversations, who will run to the nearest phone if they see you commit a crime. Shop keepers and business owners will get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if you go behind the counter (or other restricted areas), while some establishments are "Whites Only", and will call the police if you stick around regardless. Mafia III handles the subject of Racism in a very realistic manner of the time and should be commended for doing so. This combined with phenomenal voice acting, The layout of the city and the topical Radio Stations (with loads of great music of the time), make New Bordeaux feel a lot more convincing and alive than other video game cities, making it a joy to drive around, and almost compensate for the lack of a fast travel system.
Now lets get into the actual game play of Mafia III, which is what (as the player) you will be spending most of your time on. You take over each district in the city, one racket at a time by going in and killing everyone in the racket. There are two rackets in each district but before you can get to the rackets you need to do 3-10 smaller missions of a similar nature to gain intel on your target and/or draw the crime boss out. This seems like a sound idea in theory and works just fine the first 3 (maybe 4) times, then you realise there are 9 districts to take over, by the 5th district I knew exactly what I would be doing and how to do it without even talking to the mission givers first. The actual combat is Mafia III is functional, but really nothing special. It can be fun to go in stealthily and pick off each enemy one by one, but at some point it doesn't really make a difference as nothing is particularly difficult about shooting from behind cover (played on hard difficulty), sadly these mechanics are no where near as tight as something like Gears of War or even Uncharted, making it feel like a bit of a chore. Sometimes cover snapping straight up doesn't work, where cover switching rarely will. The stealth is a little better which is why I preferred to play mostly that way, though the AI is extremely dumb, and occasionally broken, sometimes seeing you behind walls, and a massive pile of corpses won't send alarm bells ringing.
Once you take over a district you have to assign it to one of the games 3 under bosses (which are excellently acted, all be it with little character development), Including Vito Scaletta from Mafia II. If you don't assign the districts evenly then they might turn on you and you have to take one of them out, however you can't get the best upgrades in any category if you choose to keep them all alive. I kept them all alive as it felt like the right thing to do, but kind of don't see much benefit either way. It's not like any of the Upgrades are really essential, The game is generally quite easy with just the basics you get right near the start of the game.
One thing all of this does add to the game is a (maybe artificial) sense of scale. The story continues to unfold in documentary like snippets, and although it seems mostly predictable, there are some great set-piece style story missions which take great turns, making all of the lead up to it feel like it has paid off, and like you are really taking over a city from the Italian Mob. A part of me feels that the game may have worked better with Only the big story missions as mandatory, with the rackets being optional, though that would have caused some problems with the narrative and taken away from the sense of build up (and resulted in a much much shorter game). The story really starts to get interesting round about the halfway point, including conspiracy theories and political themes, however it never feels like the Lincoln's fate is uncertain, it does give you some choices that effect the ending in meaningful ways.
There open world-iness feels just as formulaic as it would in an Assassin's Creed or Far Cry. There are wire tap boxes which unviel a part of the map including enemies and collectables. The collectables are fun to collect and feel like great virtual suveneirs, however you would be missing absolutely nothing (other than a sense of achievement) by not bothering. The Driving is at least pretty good, allowing fine control of the vehicle even in tight situations, I had a lot of fun just driving around the city listening to the great soundtrack Mafia III has to offer.
There are also an array of Technical problems which hold Mafia III back from being the game it should of been. Some side missions seem straight up broken (with trucks/boats not spawning), with some story missions breaking and requiring me to restart at a checkpoint. The framerate is nowhere near where it should be at any point in the game with dips to the 20's in some areas of the map. The game also straight up crashed to desktop a handful of times, with no error message. The textures are also of a very low quality for 2016 which make it look like a last gen title, though the game does have some excellent use of motion blur combined with Bokeh Depth of Field, as well as nice lighting effects at times.
Overall Mafia III is a great game with lots of good points, including some of the best motion capture performance and acting in a video game to date, coupled with an excellent portrayal of the American south (and the state of the Mafia) in the late 1960's. However it is sorely hurt by technical problems, and a very repetitive mission structure, stopping the game from reaching it's full potential. This is a real shame as the things it does well, it does really well.

My first review on steam I think.
Im a huge fan of the first Mafia game. It is one of those few games I played from the beginning to the end many times. The second Mafia game had a very nice story, but gameplay wise already felt it was missing something the first one did perfect. Still a very enjoyable game though.
And then, we got the third version. I tried my best not to watch any trailers or gameplay videos and thankfully succeded in this. Therefore the hype only got to me in the week of release. I have all the gameplatforms at home, so doubted for a long time for which platform I wanted to buy the game. At the one hand, console is easy plug and play, but on the other hand the PC ususally has more graphical options. Then there was the issue of Mafia 2 having problems on the PC. But I decided to take the risk.
First: The PC version is really not good. I have a moderate PC (it was really high end a year or two ago), with two R9 290X cards and a decent i7 processor. This PC runs most games at high or ultra settings on 60 fps, but has problems running Mafia 3 at 30 fps at normal settings. And then it still does not really look nice. There is something with the graphics that makes the game look really....off.... somehow. Next to the peformance issues, I came across quite some bugs with cars driving with open doors, cars sinking through the ground, and other strange things.
The gameplay of mafia 3 is really average. The gunplay is nice, with every weapon feeling a bit different and a nice selection of weapons to pick from. I went with the silent approach in the missions, and the silenced weapons really helped with that.
Other than the gunplay, there is really not much to it. Sneaking is quite easy, with really easy enemies, you can pull towards you one by one with a wistle. And if you do happen to screw up, you just shoot your way through the end of the mission with no real penalty.
The driving is decent, but with lack of traffic rules you had in the first two games, there is no real challenge. Where I started the game driving nice with the rest of the traffice, I soon turned to high speed racing throught the city with no concequences. The cool thing about the previous mafia games was that you could get pulled over for speeding or hitting other traffic.
Then the story. This is the one thing where I liked the previous maffia games the best. The story of those games were wonderfull, and I have really good memories to them till this day. I have to say that I like the old italian mafia setting of those games a lot. The setting of mafia 3 did not really apeal to me, except for the music in that era. But, when i started Mafia 3, I really like the way they told the story. It had a really nice movie kind of story telling, with good looking cut scenes and a well thought off plot development. however, halfway of the game this story started to go to the background and the repetative mission structure got the upperhand. They got back to the story to the end of the game, but it never really got to me anymore. Then there is the srange way of putting choises in the story. You conquer districts of the city and have to give these to one of your three luitanents. I tried to keep everyone happy till the end, which I was able to do. So there was not really a lot of options in that area. Then, at the end of the story, they suddenly put in three or so choices which decide the outcome of this story. Somehow, this feels kinda rushed. They developed the main character quite well, you know why he does what he is doing, end then suddenly you have to make the choice of who he is and what he is gonna do. Feels strange.
All in all im dissapointed with this game. The mafia franchise is really dear to me. And this game is just not living up to the series. I enjoyed it, but it is really not a top notch game.
ps: sorry for my English, not my first language.

This game is the best I've ever played when looking at story telling and involving the player himself. Yes, there is Telltale's The Walking Dead out there, but in my opinion it didn't even come close to the experience of Life is Strange. I don't want to know how long I've been sitting in front of my screen just contemplating wether it'd be better to drag the mouse to the left, upwards, to the right or downwards. I'm so glad I took the opportunity to buy this game as I saw it was on sale and didn't miss out on the best game I've ever layed my hands on. Now, I love BTD Battles to death, don't get me wrong. I've played Flash and Mobile/Win 10/Steam (they play just the same) quite a bit. But there are a few things that really need to be fixed in this version that the devs know about (unless they live under a rock or something) but won't fix. Let's get to pros and cons, shall we?
Pros:
-Replayability, for obvious reasons
-Good for all ages and skill levels with its family-friendliness and its battle arena system
-Many fun gamemodes
-A very nice tower selection
-Solid graphics, most other TD games tend to be too realistic or absolutely terrible looking, this game finds the sweet spot between them
-Decent matchmaking
Cons:
-Game balance
-"Downloading Vital Data" bug
-Need to pay to enjoy the game to its fullest (I'll overlook this myself due to my love for BTD, but for others this can be a huge annoyance)
The pros speak for themselves, so I'll talk about my cons.
Fist of all, the "Downloading Vital Data" bug. This bug causes you to be completely unable to play the game due to the loading screen getting stuck at "Downloading Vital Data" forever, and happens seemingly at random (and not to everybody), sometimes staying for days and other times requiring a simple close-and-reopen to fix. This has been around for a long, long time, and makes this game very difficult to play on PC for some people. I haven't heard of it happening on Mobile.
Secondly, game balance. Many will disagree with me here, but I just feel like some towers are absolutely ****ing useless and others are winning the "best tower" race by a few thousand miles. Here's some examples:
Dart Monkey - cheap, extremely good early and mid-game, requires zero support until round 22
Spike Factory - slow, not that good at any point in the game compared to other towers, requires a lot of support
Banana Farm - gives a massive head start on economy, can be sold to defend a rush, counterrush, or rush, usable on all but one map to its fullest extent
Bloonchipper - combos well with many other towers, can destroy entire Ceramic bloon layers with just 2 upgrades and entire ZOMG layers with 4, and can almost infinitely stall any amount of bloons with a large enough amount of x-4 Bloonchippers (just fix this already ****it, it's not hard)
These are just 4 examples. There are many, many more.
There are only really 4 mid-tier towers, which are the Ninja Monkey, Monkey Apprentice, Sniper Monkey and Ice Tower. They perform well, but need support from other towers, just not too much. They're examples of very well balanced towers. Other towers are either quite a bit better or quite a bit worse, and it makes it so that higher levels of play boil down to one or two different strategies, with the rest being unable to keep up with the best of the best.
Paying for faster-regenerating battle energy (battle energy being a huge part of the game) and more battle energy is already showing a little bit of pay-to-win. You can still beat energy-buyers, don't get me wrong, it isn't like buying a $1 in-game money tower that has infinite ZOMG and bloon popping power. It's still a bit of an unfair advantage. There's also the fact that you can only enter 1 club room every 24 hours without the $6 pass, and the fact that you can fully upgrade a tower for $6, making it somewhat unfair to new players who get matched up with you because of your 5/2 win-loss record. I'm not saying this game is pay-to-win, but when you need to pay to get the full experience, it's not good.
Overall, I have to give this game a negative. If they put a little more thought into game balance and micro-transactions, I would definitely change my mind. Heck, even just nerfing the Dart Monkey and Supa-Vac would make an absolutely massive difference. But as it stands, this game's downsides, despite there being few, make this game quite a chore at points.

I would recommend this game with a warning: it is beautiful, immersive and instructive,
. It ranges from frustratingly bad to game-breaking awful.
.
Typography is an art, and this game could be a wonderful guide. With the help of Arte (a german-french tv station known for its quality and cultural sensitivity), the developer managed to create an "edutainment" game with great visuals and pedagogic value. You will learn a lot without realizing it, all the while having the direct representation (the font) around you and the moody music goes well with it.
All of this is true until the penultimate level where things go horribly wrong. The concept of the game is a platformer where you are a colon (yes, this one --> : ). A wobbly, bouncy, inertia-crazy colon. For the most part, it is easy to forgive the approximation of controlling the character (pun intended) with strange physics. Then, when you are required to do precise jumps and control your trajectory, the game becomes rage-quit-inducingly hard. You are at the mercy of the physics engine, hoping it decides to launch you where you want to go. Some sequences have required more than 50 tries, and I'm not talking about trial-and-error: there is nothing to learn, sometimes it will work, most times it will not. Deal with it.
It's a real shame because it is the only let down for an otherwise great game. Check the forums to see if the issue has been adressed since the writing of this review.

I like this game. It felt meta towards the end, a comment on video games in general. The entire time I listened to Kane and Lynch both complain about the game, the killing, the mindless drudgery and the feeling of "one last job" I felt the same. The gameplay is terrible, I fought to the end of each mission, massacring police and gang members to do the same in the next area. To do the same in the next. Then the next. Rarely mixing it up with an escort mission or turret segment.
Towards the end the pair orally ask when it will end multiple times, pleading for it to be over and I started to feel the same. Relief at the end of a mission, a sigh at the beginning of the next. "When will it end?" shouted Lynch, as he prepared to fight yet another wave of Shanghai's police.
Three and a half hours from the beginning, a cut to black and the end of the game where I felt relief the same as Kane and Lynch. It was over. There was no triumph, no lessons learnt, and no achievements; just a temporary escape until the next game. I think that was intentional, an artistic move on the part of the IO Interactive to induce the same feeling that the pair go through on missions, to highlight something about video games and gaming culture.
That said, I still can't recommend it because it's three hours of shooting down corridors at waves of enemies. Artistic statements and interpretations only really end up working in games when the gameplay is good in the first place. This was a massive chore from start to finish.

10/10: An engrossing roguelike that feels like an old SNES Legend of Zelda dungeon full of Cronenberg's nightmares.
A delightfully morbid dungeon crawl, courtesy of Edmund McMillen. With procedurally arranged dungeons, challenges, extra characters, and scores of pickups to unlock, you never replay the dungeon quite the same way twice.
Some would call this a roguelike, but the first game that comes to mind for me is Zelda: A Link to the Past due to it's use of hearts, keys and a bomb slot. Combat is ranged, in the sense that you cry at your enemies to damage them, and as a result some fightst are reminiscent of bullet hell games. Enemies consist largely of the deformed, parasitic, infested, and sometimes even biblical varieties, and are varied enough that even somewhat similar enemies have noticeably different habits.
I liked to explore in this game, since the shops stop appearing after a certain depth and I used bombs primarily to check for secret rooms. It's cool how repeatedly beating the game opens up even deeper levels, which provides a steady increase in challenge as you play. Totally worth the price, along with the Wrath of the Lamb DLC.
The only gripe that comes to mind is that they use arcing shots sometimes, which doesn't show up great in the 2D style used here. Be careful and keep your distance with them if you're trying to obtain the no damage achievements.

Now the real review, because after 2 1/2 months I was finally able to play the game (woohoo?!)
I finished the game today, took me about 37 Steam-hours, probs a bit more than I really actively played.
I did every story-mission and every side-mission but didn't collect every piece of the collectibles.
I like the story quite much, how it is told with the cut scenes, though the first mission with it's many breaks was annoying.
Sadly, the story-missions and the optional missions themselves are not very unique and get repetitive pretty fast.
##SPOILER##
Only the last mission or more it's ending was disappointing. This drama-blabla, let's have a drink and tell stories wasn't necessary. A shot in head after the first drink would have suited Lincolns character way better.
And then you don't even see the body after you look out the window....
##SPOILER END##
So let's make a pro-con-list:
Pro:
- The story and how it is told
- The music (if you like it)
- some nice small details (like the radio gets bad in the tunnel)
- The collectibles (though finding them isn't really a quest anymore like in Mafia II)
- The money collector, car delivery and weapons guy are a cool feature
- I like the weapon and car handling
can't think of any more points, so here is the cons:
Cons:
- Technical realisation
- Clothes in "in-game graphics" cut scenes have a life of their own and are shaking around
- Cars tend to hang or crash on curbs, rails or transitions in the street (like at bridges) or even still get stuck in walls
- low to mid-range systems barely get playable FPS, especially while driving
- Repetitive story and optional missions
- The dumb AI, shooting them down is mostly a walk in the park
- non-skippable end credits, WTF
- though they showed me that there were quality testers for this game, which I found funny
- no real car tuning, all cars you own get the performance upgrades automatically, the rest is only cosmetic
- car sounds are way worse compared to Mafia II
- don't know what the Deluxe Edition including the season pass got me extra, so I consider this extra money spent, wasted....
So all in all a good story realised pretty badly.

Let’s get the obvious out of the way first - the PC version (at the time of writing) is a bit of a mess. Framerates are all over the place (regardless of settings), the lighting seems broken and crashes are pretty common. However despite these issues I thoroughly enjoyed the game. For starters I really dug the late 1960s setting and the characters. New Bordeaux is nicely detailed and the various districts have a distinct atmosphere. Driving through the murky Bayou feels different compared to the bright lights and neon of Downtown for example.
Like the earlier games in the series the story is a standout element of Mafia III. The writing is consistently good even if it falls into cliche at times. It is helped by some solid voice acting and characterization and the faux-documentary style storytelling is a nice touch. The plot itself is a typical revenge story but it is told with enough flair especially in the beginning and towards the end. I must say the ending is really satisfying and I loved the unexpectedly outrageous mid-credits revelation.
The combat is some of the best in an urban open-world game. It’s fast, fluid, weighty and brutal. The combination of stealth and shooting is pulled off really well. Stealth is borderline broken in how effective it is. The AI can be pretty dumb and easily exploited with the “whistle” mechanic which allows you to pull enemies away from groups one by one. I personally didn’t mind it too much because it’s fun and given the huge amount of combat encounters in the game the dumb AI is actually is a good thing. Switching from stealth takedowns to shooting once you’re discovered feels natural and the gunplay itself is quite satisfying.
Mafia III has been getting a lot of negative press for it’s gameplay structure which to be honest isn’t terribly different from that of most open-world games, especially Ubisoft ones. You essentially must take over every district in order to reach the ending. This involves a sequence of repetitive tasks - talk to NPCs, cause enough damage to the rival gang’s racket and draw out the racket boss to take him down. Then do this twice per district to unlock a “main mission” to take over the district itself. This is basically the whole middle portion of the game. The main missions themselves are great with some standout moments, unfortunately they are too few and far between. Even the side missions involve the same activities repeated a number of times until you finish them all.
The entire experience could have easily been condensed by reducing the grind needed to unlock a mission. I finished the game at around 35 hours, 10 or 12 of those could have easily been shaved off if it was a tighter experience. I personally didn’t mind the grind too much because the combat was always engaging and driving from place to place felt great. Cars handle quite well on the simulation setting and listening to the amazing soundtrack made driving a very relaxing and enjoyable experience.
There’s also isn’t much to do apart from fighting and driving, there are collectibles to find but they don’t unlock anything or even give you any achievements. The game could have also used some kind of customization options. Being able to change Lincoln’s clothing would have been nice, though I hear customization will be coming as a separate update. I just wish it was in the game at launch. I also liked how the game handles money and upgrades. Money didn’t run out of uses halfway through (like many games) and I was buying weapons and upgrades right up to the final mission. Assigning your territories to your Lieutenants is also a neat mechanic and gives you some interesting choices to make, though it doesn’t take a genius to figure out the best approach for doing it.
Overall I’d say Mafia III is worth playing. I believe it will be looked upon more fondly as time goes by. The technical issues can be patched but the game’s repetitive structure is something players will have to live with. Don’t get discouraged by the lukewarm response, gamers and critics have become jaded over the last few years. This is a perfectly good game, just not a great one.

Here’s the thing, I played the game then finished it, then checked my personal trusted gaming media & review sources like the crew from
, re-experienced the game then come to this point eager to share my thoughts.
It is not until several further observations that have put me into to reviewing this game.
But here we go, I spent a lot of hours in this game and the more I played the game then finished it the more I identify its strength and weaknesses especially after playing more hours of Shadow Warrior 2.
One of the most noticeable comparisons between Shadow Warrior 2 and Mafia 3 was the quick access to areas or some would call it fast travelling.
With simple commands, you will be able to fast travel from one area to another in Shadow Warrior 2 but in Mafia 3 you can't. You need to manually travel from one point to the next and does not have an option to at least teleport to discovered areas. I think had they made that fast travelling system in the game I would have seen the game a lot better than right now.
But that’s just one of its issues. However, I should acknowledge on where the game shines.
The presentations, music, dramatic acting performances, gunplay & stealth hit most of the spots in this game. Mafia 2 left me with strong storyline between Vito and his Best friend. Mafia 3 got me immersed the setting and I felt like I was there until the end. I was also amazed on how the actors performed excellently well on their assigned roles especially their dramatic pause effect in hopes that the audience would build some dread or some sort of impact between pauses. I love it!
However, I need to address the negative issues here but I hope I won’t disappoint the readers for these are all based on my experience with a help of other things that opened my mind to conclusion.
As mentioned, I didn’t like the feeling of driving myself all the way from point A to B in the game, had they at least give us the option to fast travel I would have viewed the game differently. I know that its predecessors also didn’t have the feature but it would have been a lot better that this instalment was the game to finally introduce it. I mean, the map is huge and at least they could have put that in the end just to keep me interested to play more and not waste additional time by traveling from multiple areas.
Knowing that I was expecting a story focused game just like Mafia 2 did when in fact it did but the balance between doing almost the same thing on missions to each district can get boring & the excellent experience on stealth and combat gameplay wasn’t enough to cover up the flaws. So, it can be a bit of a mixed bag there and to add on getting all the collectables in-game can fall into a chore especially when you discovered that you missed one all the way from where you are up north to the bayou down the south. Indeed that ZTGD from N4G Podcast said that it may take around 30 hours minus the side quests and extras you do in-game to finish it and that may very well be true because 50% or so from that game-time will contribute highly to travelling from one point to the other.
Okay, let’s go back to the good stuff, in terms of improvements from the last Mafia 2 there are a lot to mention. But to name the things I like the most is that they finally put a lot of things in the map than just typical traffic obstacles for you to avoid just like in Mafia 2. When we’re talking about conveniences, they nailed a lot of them down despite the travelling system as one of them.
Specifically, you can call in supports for a car or a caretaker to transfer your money to the bank so that you won’t lose 50% of them if ever you get killed…etc.
So I think that I know where the developers are coming from by putting that feature to call in supports anywhere and time.
The stealth mechanic works so well for me to the point that I don’t want to easily blaze myself towards enemies every time I go in mission areas. Plus the executions are brutal and satisfying especially when they’re done in stealth.
And one of the major things I really like in the game is that you’re not going to take over the place alone, you will need to work with three underbosses and each has perks to aid you in-game whenever you assign them to certain rackets or districts in the map to take over.  However, if you won’t balance their share, you may find yourself losing one or two of them and will end up being your enemies in the game and you will have to take that underboss down. But to ensure their loyalty towards you, you can optionally do their loyalty missions and even do side missions to other three underbosses who are loyal to corresponding three underbosses you mainly assign to. But however, that will cost extra travel time and that’s the only major issue with the game.
I think it helps to contain the excitements and truly understand the differences when identifying first impressions to a full-scale view.
I mean, it’s normal to get hyped on things but we should also acknowledge their faults especially when we discover them afterwards.
I really love this game regardless the imperfections it holds. However, only when passed my excitements I finally open myself to its obvious flaws and honestly, it needs to be addressed.
I personally love this over
even though it’s not as “open world” as it is. It’s because of the story telling, the clear goal on what to do just to get there and the things you need to get there. It was a long but satisfying journey to me in the end but at the same time I cannot ignore nor welcome one of its major flaws that hinder my interest to do all the repetitive side quests at the end and that sadly killed my interest to go further and just get done with the game main campaign.
Am I recommending the game? Yes, especially when you’re a Mafia 2 fan but it’s true that you don’t need to know much about Vito to play this game because he felt more like a supporting character and seems to aged a lot because of how powerful the protagonist is but all characters were great.
You know what? I like Vito more than Lincoln, it’s sad that they didn’t put enough details for Vito and what happened after the ending of Mafia 2. I guess we’ll never know…
The story and setup of the game is actually very sensitive and tackles racism in the United States of America with racial wars, the Vietnam War and assassinations of actual personalities like JFK and Martin Luther King.
However, I won’t recommend this game if you’re not willing to spend some half of the game-time travelling from one point to another.
But I thank the ones who made this game possible; it’s indeed a huge step up from the previous game despite the imperfections and lack of wide customization on cars and apparel.
Replayability? Possibly especially if you want to see different outcome of the game like killing some of your underbosses and take over their territories or check different endings.
In the end I enjoyed the game but I guess that it's not going to be one of my personal GOTY contenders because the mechanic and technicalities of the game killed the concept and awesome idea of this game. It’s a shame that I didn’t end up loving the game more but maybe, just maybe if the devs would tweak at least the traveling issues I just might get back to it and who know, I would probably do all those fetch quests in the game.

EDIT - 06/03/2017: Still no word from the devs on ANY updates or patches AT ALL for over a year now. It has almost certainly been abandoned with dozens of major issues still rampant. I would stay away if I were you.
Below is my original review of this game, which was negative to begin with:
First of all there have been no significant updates to this game in MONTHS, last few updates added a couple of new trailers and maybe one or two new trucks, while completely ignoring major issues with the game, like not being able to save your multiplayer game, save deletions, crashes and very bad stability in a lot of user's sistems.
Second, game gets boring after 10 hours due to lack of any other objective other than "Get logs from here to here". It also suffers from an over-sensitive damage sistem, example: touch a tiny rock with the bottom of your truck at 5mph, get 24 damage (this is bad when most veicules have a max of 500hp and there are tiny rocks EVERYWHERE) and when it's not the tiny rocks it's the small twigs that get you.
Decent graphics and amazing physics make this game very realistic in terms of mud behaviour (most of the time at least), for example: if you only take the same route over and over the terrain is gonna get harder and harder to move in due to the mud getting boggier and boggier.
Soviet era trucks and military offroaders, what's not to love.
Good level design.
Fuel consuption sistem makes it a lot more realistic.
You can knock down (some) trees.

This game is just amazing. Not only does it teach you about orbital dynamics and the physics of space travel, but it also actually does it in a way that doesn't bore you. It actually interests you in real life space travel, makes you research rocket designs on Google to use for your Kerbal-version to make it better and more efficient, and keeps you tied to your chair for hours, all without a great storyline or beautiful cutscenes or big explosions (this is the only game I have that I don't want to see any explosions in). The Kerbals are beautifully designed little green man that talk "Kerbal" (backwards spanish) and make funny expressions whenever your spacecraft spontaniously disassembles itself. The music is great and very calming (although there are moments when it doesn't help) and the overall art style looks good, even though it's nothing too impressive.
My overall opinion: I would definitely recommend buying it for 20 bucks or less, or even for the full price if you informed yourself and know that you'll be investing a lot of time into it!

Wasteland 2 tries to sell itself as a revival of the original Fallout games, but all it does for me, is makes me grip my head and wonder why. The game doesn't capture the magic of the original Fallouts for me.
My first big issue with the game, is that you can select your squad at the start. I dislike this, because I enjoyed looking through the wasteland of Fallout 1 and 2, searching for someone to help me alongside my journey. Instead, in this, the units are just kind of there from the start. It doesn't feel right to me.
Next big thing, is that if a character specializes in a certain combat skill, they will get a great weapon from that. If you pick heavy weapons, then one of your characters will start off with an LMG. The entire point of an RPG, is to make you feel like you've accomplished something, but I felt like from the start, I had this giant badass on my team who could kill anything.
In Fallout 1, if you play the game the way it was intended, you won't get armor leather armor, until about 5-12 hours in. But in Wasteland 2, I can run around with an LMG saying, 'time to die' and killing everybody within 1 or 2 hits.
EDIT: I'm fine with having a party or squad at the start of an RPG, but I don't think it fits in something that is trying immitate the original Fallout games. I also dislike it when my squad can kill everything, far too quickly.
In the starting areas of Fallout 1 and 2, you can still die. In Shady Sands, there's the radscorpion caves. In Vault 15, you have Mole Rats. In Klamath, you have the Trapping grounds, that are filled with Geckos.
Final thing, is that I feel like I can't be my own character, because whatever I choose to play as, I'm still working to become a Desert Ranger. And you could say that, "In the first two Fallout games you had to find the water chip or the GECK." You weren't kind of strapped to that one mission. You went from place to place, learing their stories, and becoming a member of their communities, and it all happened naturally. In Junktown, you had the Killian vs Gizmo situation. In San Fransisco, you had the Shi, Hubologists, and Brotherhood, all of which didn't like eachother. And you were forced to decide who would take control of San Fransisco, all for a side mission.
So, in all, I didn't put much into the game, but from what I've played, I didn't enjoy it.

NS2 one of those games where even after hundreds of hours, I feel like I still kind of suck at it - but darn it, I'm still having lots of fun!
It is an excellent game - maybe simple in concept, but beautifully executed. The alien side is novel and fascinating, and challenges you to think outside the box with tactics. On the marine side, you feel a hint of horror genre as you attempt to wreak righteous vengeance on the aliens invading your space station.
Crucially, this game gets almost every aspect of its game mechanics right, in places where most other FPS-RTS combo games fail. Matches are generally of a satisfying length,  progress and change over time, and have plenty of room for pulling victory out of the jaws (get it?) of defeat when you're on the losing side. Balance, while an issue in every RTS-FPS combo, is better than most in the genre. Asymmetry is utilized to great effect. Teamwork is encouraged by the game mechanics.
I do find myself switching to the combat mod at times when I get frustrated by permanently losing high-level characters due to a small mistake - I don't know if the learning curve can be improved or the frustation can be dampened but for now it's just par for the course, and makes it all the more thrilling when you pull off death-defying feats.

+ Saves and upgrades can be accessed and applied at any time in the arena, and effects are immediately applied
+ As upgrades are unlocked, combat becomes drastically more fluid and cinematic
+ In stark contrast to mobs that populate the waves of a given stage, boss fights are actually quite challenging, and are noticeably skill-dependant
+ Character models are rendered with plenty of detail and look generally adequate
+ Japanese voice-acting is well-done; feels very organic
+ Combat is generally very fun, fast-paced, and visually striking
- Camera is sub-par and operates unreliably
- Boring and uninspired environment and audio design
- Game quickly becomes repetitive and a chore to slog through; this is largely because each level offers little more than the last, and it essentially boils down to 'hack, slash, rinse, repeat' with nothing to break up the pace or keep one interested
- The game suffers an achievement bug; Steam achievements that have been unlocked during gameplay will remain locked in the Steam application until the game is closed (this is a problem because they will all share an idential time-stamp)*
- Plot is underdeveloped to the point that it may as well have not been included; utterly forgettable
- Enemy mobs are cripplingly generic and suffer from lack of variety; each stage is essentially a massive copy/paste of the previous stage, and 'upgraded mobs' share the same design with a different color scheme and slightly higher base stats
- Extremely short campaign (1-2 hours) and little else in the way of replay value, save for a drive to unlock all achievements, and a narrow selection of unlockable outfits
*While this may not affect everyone, a quick glance at the forums indicates that others are experiencing this issue

Altogether I can recommend this game on sale, or if you are a fan of good games with a rough learning curve.

Edmund McMillen is a freaking genius, Part 2. (For Redux version go
.)
'Isaac' is simply the best rogue-like I've ever played. Even with slightly more rogue-like experience under my belt now, I still love to go back to this game. It sets the bar freaking high.
Released just under a year after
, with a jumbo DLC expansion another year after that, the game plays like a top-down dungeon-crawler-shooter with randomised levels - no 2 playthroughs are exactly the same! (Unless you use a certain program that can pull the map seeds, but that's a different story.)
The base game itself was very good, difficult at first but gets slightly easier as you unlock the more OP items and collectibles. The DLC adds a ton more content. Not to say that the items take away from the difficulty of the game though - some levels with the new Wrath monsters (and quite a few of the old monsters as well) feel somewhat akin to bullet curtain-like games.
The only real gripe I have with this is that I cannot save my game mid-way! It's still a small flaw, and one that is corrected in its remake, '
'. :)
In the meantime, to circumvent this during super epic games, I recommend hibernating your computer with the game still running. Okay, well, my computer has survived the hibernation, but I'm not sure about yours...
Well, okay, one more gripe - the game engine is in Flash, which is laggy at times and hard to play. For the most part though I didn't have any problems or let that detract from the fun of the game.
If you can get this and the DLC for a cheap price, a must buy. It has possibly one of the highest ratios of time spent in game to money spent on game. (Excluding F2Ps, of course.)
In May 2015, an all-new hard mode (Edmund M has called it names ranging from "Trololololol hell mode" to "Florian's ♥♥♥♥ You Mod") was released for owners of the WotL DLC - and it is hard as heck. You'll probably spend a lot of time trying to beat this mode with all characters, even if you are a veteran. Getting it on a steep discount will give you a lot of hours worth of gameplay for your dollar, but even full price for both game and DLC is not such a bad idea - Florian deserves to be rewarded for his new fiendishly unfair eternal manifestations. I genuinely mean that. It got me to re-look at, and re-evaluate, an old game which I thought I was done with.

As a whole Fallout Shelter is a great game, It's a few years old now and updates like quests and weapons/clothing factories have made it that bit deeper and more playable. I've got probably 100 hours both on Android and I'm not far off the same on Steam. I've enjoyed all these hours.
Pros:
- It's great to jump on for 5-30 minutes once or twice a day, do the quests, check how your dwellers are doing and just generally play around in the Fallout universe in a different way.
- It's free. Also more importantly the pay to win side isn't needed. I've got over 100 Nuka colour sat as I don't mind waiting to start quests or for dwellers to level up alone etc. There is plenty of content for a free game and you don't feel like you need to spend money.
- It runs well, the graphics have a nice feel and look good.
Cons:
- Using a mouse can be painful at times. I think it's because it was designed and out first on touch screen devices. The amount of dead dwellers I've had from not being able to click on the healing or the amount of times I've raged from not being able to drag a dweller. it's not a huge problem and doesn't affect the game long term, just frustrating!
- It gets predictable at times, I guarantee that I'll have a Death Claw attack within five minutes of getting in game every time without fail. Again nothing major but gets a little dull.
- Achievements. If you're an achievement hunter, don't bother unless you're worth millions or have years of time. I'll explain as it frustrated me greatly as an achievement hunter wanting perfect games.
- Get off my land - Survive 50 raider attacks. After 60 dwellers you mostly get everything apart from raiders. This ends up in starting a new game to try and get them more frequently. IMO it should be stop 100 vault attacks. This way as you progress and get Ghouls or Death Claws you can carry on getting the achievement.
- Blast from the past - Find 20 legendary dwellers. Don't bother... I've done my 200 ish hours on both devices and had five. I should be due a couple more from the last quests but that totals maybe five after 100 hours. It's basically a case of waiting for lucky lunch boxes.
All in all the game is good, I've enjoyed my time on it and will log in once or twice a week for some time still. Maybe they'll update at some point and add more game time which would be nice. The bad points aren't huge and don't get in the way so I'd recommend this game.

Well that was certainly something different. It has been a while since Hotline Miami was released and it has build up a special kind of reputation for sure, but I was not expecting this. I always held to the belief that it's a good thing to occasionally play something outside of your comfort zone. Let's see if that holds up with this particular title.
For once I'll start with something that didn't wow me  that much because it's rather short – story. Now, something like story might be utterly redundant in a game of this type, but I disagree with that notion considering a good story, setting or background can add to any game. I liked Hotline Miami in that department for the majority of it because despite kinda barely being there yet also reinforcing the idea of our character's personality, so to speak, as the world and he himself both descent into madness. Or do they? Game never really makes it explicitly clear how much of what's happening is real and you'll go through some trippy sequences such as talking to three masked people who may or may not be there, repeated salesmen offering you things for free and as the world around you becomes more and more gruesome, seemingly commonplace. There's also a revenge plot within all of that which I didn't mind at all and goes with the '80s sensibilities of a badass nameless protagonist, if not anti-hero considering what you do over the course of the game, but what I did take objection to was the epilogue. In my opinion it was kinda tacked on even though it explains things such as who's making the mysterious phone calls and certain other seeming coincidences.
Let's dig into some of the unanimous positives now. Game was designed and plays like a charm, and I also probably wouldn't change much aside from adding greater effects to masks. But I jump ahead of myself. Operative phrase in these parts is: you're going to die. Fortunately, Hotline Miami makes it so that reload is achieved about as fast as you can press letter R on your keyboard after dying and there are no loading screens once that particular level has been loaded. Gameplay is frenetic and absolutely adrenaline-fueled as it requires you to rely on pinpoint accuracy... or does it really when you take into account just button mashing and firing aimlessly won't really get you far. You need to take a look at each level's layout, plan for enemy patrols, and whether you want to keep it low-profile with melee weapons or go guns blazing and alert half the map to your presence. Aside from few gimmick levels game usually gives you freedom to go about it however you want, but whichever approach you go with it feels absolutely great and reward with that crunchy and, dare I say it, visceral combat.
Speaking of masks they're how you can affect your character. Which you unlock along with new weapons that randomly spawn on the level following each death with your score – there are masks that can make you go faster, make guns have more ammo, make hitting enemies with doors actually lethal instead of just knocking them out, etc. There's nothing like clearing a single room in a second or two after you've gained insight on how the game runs and gotten over the initial shock. One iffy segment of the gameplay department is when the game throws a boss at you. These moments are rare, but you'll undoubtedly end up dying for a while not because you're thick or anything, but simply because you need that trial and error approach to beat them and they usually don't give you the time to ponder on what to do.
But the real gem here is the game's soundtrack which is absolutely outstanding and will get you hyped like few games do. Not to mention it really works with the whole “stop and go” approach that constantly dying generates and you never get that jarring feeling of songs switching around to match the game. Dennaton Games really went all out and got the likes of Perturbator and M.O.O.N. on-board for some great electronic pieces, or whatever wide genre of music this soundtrack as a whole would fit into. I know I enjoyed it profoundly and it even got me hooked enough to listen outside of the game which hasn't happened in... well, forever. Maybe I should branch out a bit as far as my music tastes go.
I've kept this long enough, with select songs from the game blasting in the background, so let's pop the big one – would I recommend Hotline Miami? That's a firm yes. You should keep in mind this IS one of those frustrating, peripheral-snapping games that will make you curse the day it was made until you understand its rules and get into the groove.
Hell, by the end I was almost playing to the music.

Mafia III is a difficult title to really detail or describe.
As a PC release, it's rough around the edges. More resource intensive then expected, limited in options and suffering from a few graphical oddities and other issues that only hinder the experience for some.
But, as someone who was a huge fan of the previous installment, I can say will complete confidence and honesty... Mafia III is fantastic.
Touching on issues, yes, performance is a bit disappointing. Yes, the lack of certain graphical options (LOD levels, water details, multiple AA options...) and even a lack certain UI options is a letdown.
And yes, the practice of breaking down the enemies rackets can become a bit repetitive.
But, I personally feel this is the cause of trying to shift what was a linear, mission to mission game to a full open world setting.
And a new studio that just wasn't fully sure of what to do with that open world.
But, I will say, I would rather they do something like this... as opposed to adding pointless fluff like playing darts or going bowling.
Or, going the MGSV path and offering a massive open world that has absolutely nothing to do in it.
Mafia III is a brilliant story. Amazing told, written and acted with fantastic voice acting and beautifully produced cut-scenes depicting Lincoln's dark, grim and depressing story.
And this is all wonderfully pin pointed with amazingly engaging story missions to key off each main section. Be it sneaking through an abandoned theme park at night, to gunning your way out of an underground fight club engulfed in flames.
And even so, the side missions were only as boring as you let them be. While you were doing the same thing in most cases, I found myself sneaking through one... going in guns blazing in another. Or even calling in back up on another and not lifting a finger myself.
There are options, you just have to remember to use them.
Mafia III is an amazing installment in a brilliant series that has always put story and characters first. And this newest title does exactly the same thing. And it's truly worth the time and energy to experience this story yourself.
So, if you were a fan of Mafia 1 and 2's storys, this game is for you so long as you can truly appreicate what is the main draw.
The DLC is really good as well.

I loved Mafia II, and played countless hours on my xbox back in the day. While it had its problems at launch, Mafia III is a great game, and everything I was hoping for. It has a great story, interesting characters, engaging gameplay, and is just pretty fun all around. The problems with performance and the 30 fps limit have mostly been resolved, the game lets you play with 60 fps or unlimited, and it runs pretty well on my upper-mid range rig.
The game does have a few issues, however; for example there are several bugs that have not yet been addressed, and they can really distract from otherwise great gameplay and story. Most recently, I encountered a bug that prevented me from destroying boxes of explosives as part of a mission, so I was unable to advance in the story. I was able to work around this by killing enemies in the region for what felt like an eternity, but it was still pretty aggravating.
Aside from the bugs, Mafia III feels like its missing certain features. For instance, there are red barrels scattered around a lot of the gun fight locations. When you shoot them, though, nothing happens, and it feels pretty unsatisfying since red barrels in an FPS game are generally recognized as a universal "this explodes" sign.
In conclusion, I'd say Mafia III in its current state is an amazing game, and worth checking out, but maybe wait until a few more patches are released or the game goes on sale. As an eager fan, it was worth the price even with its issues.

The Music Machine has to be one of the wierdest games I've ever played.  As you'll find from most other reviews it's a narrative story.  You walk around, click things, and read dialog.  There's a puzzle element to it which you can solve by brute force, or exploration, and a short (very easy) FPS segment which isn't meant to be taxing, but demonstrate a choice that you make.  The game itself is quite short: If you bump into the right things in the right order, you can easily finish the game in about 20 minutes. However, playing to explore can let it spin out into a few hours.
The other thing you'll read about is the 'art style', which you can see from the screenshots consists of a very heavy binarizing shader and a colour tint. I gotta say, I was dubious at first, but the style really works.  There is a point in the game where the 'style' is altered, and the change is beautiful and shocking.  In some ways, I wanted to go back to the orange forest, and don't ask me why... The game does that to you; you just don't know why you feel the way you do.
Playing through this gave me a serious sense of nostalgia for the 'old days' of gaming. Back in the old days of Freescape(tm) games (Kids, you have no idea how lucky you are to have graphics cards, haha), there were game makers such as "The 3d game construction kit", and they made games that were essentially 'worlds' made up of a very limited palette of geometric shapes and simple primary colours, with very rudimentary shading.  To get from one 'map' to another, you generally clicked or 'ran into' a black rectangle, which teleported you to another 'map'.  the maps tended to be smallish square 'rooms', or sometimes large open spaces with buildings in them.  Think "30 flights of loving", but without the texture maps..
This game feels very much like it was made with something like that, but heavily buffed up with some modern shading, and if it weren't for the nice music and interesting sunbeam effects in the woodlands, I'd have guessed it harked from mid-1987 or 1988.  The lovely atmospheric music, and the interesting (if slightly weird) story combine to make for a strange, poignant, playthrough which leaves you with a bitter-sweet taste in your mouth.   It has the benefit of not needing to explain too much before or after, so it can be as weird as it wants to be.  It's particular weirdness is in the 'relationship' between the two protagonists, and what transpires to be the reason why you're on this island in the first place (why is it always islands?!).
I really enjoyed playing this game, and went back to find the other 'endings' (although there's only really two, there are a few ways to get to one of them). It's not to everyone's tastes, that's for sure.  It ain't a AAA game, and although there is some 'action', it's not a heavy shooter or RPG. But for an indie game, it's as satisfying as they come.  If you like weird narrative stories and 'experiences' more than AAA shooters, this could be for you.

For five bucks you get a visually stunning, surreal adventure with roots in Lovecraft lore. Apparently, this game coincides with another one of the creator's games, The Moon Sliver and is supposed to clear some things up about it. I'd probably have to go back and check it out again to get a really god grasp on it.
Much like David's other games, this is surreal as hell and more about soaking in the atmosphere than challenging gameplay. Which is fair, because the most challenging thing you do in this game is find a way to bust some boards down.
Much like his other games, this has a story that feels written at the level to make you confused but not so much that you don't feel like the answer is right there. It probably requires multiple play throughs to fully grasp.
Regardless, the dynamic between the two characters, Haley and Quintin, is interesting. Haley is a thirteen year old who is posessed by the spirit of Quintin for at first unknown reasons. All we know is that Quintin holds a grudge and is searching for a satisfying way to kill Haley. They have arrived at an island, seeking a murderer who has apparently been pretty busy filling people with holes. It's a strange setup, but one that plays out pretty nicely as it goes on, and eventually deals with some loftier themes.
To say much more would be to spoil a lot of the surprises this game holds. While it may feel a bit obtuse in some of its themes, it's a pretty absorbing adventure while it lasts over its hour and a half- two hour run time. Check it out along with The Moon Sliver.

Overall, unless you absolutely cannot abide the framerate issues, I think Mafia III will be worth your time. Despite being 30 hours long, it is far shorter than most RPGs, so people looking for a good story without a lot of time may find value in the game's episodic pace and 1-2 hour long segments.

If Fargo produced the original Fallout, then either there were clearly better minds handling the design of that game or he's direly lost his touch.
Wasteland 2 drags on for about fifty hours, consisting of a number of quest hubs that all involve Faction A vs. Faction B and there's about three interesting ideas in that pile. If the game were cut down to a few standout quest hubs and a little more care were given to those, it might not have lost steam before the second act even starts. Many quests in the second act are just fetch quests and high level speech/utility checks strung together with some subpar dialogue by a bunch of unlikable faction members.
Combat's a fun, XCOM/Shadowrun Returns-ish style thing, all the way up until you hit the mid-point of the first act and realize the only way for the game to continue going down its path is for all of the numbers to keep increasing ad-nauseum. By the time you reach the second act it feels like someone gave up on figuring numbers out and just decided to make everything a too-lethal yet too bullet-spongey, zero miss slogfest. I enjoyed my kind of sub-par squad and had some challenges along the way, but a final dungeon preceeding a final boss fight that both consist of giant heaps of max-geared enemies to drill through made me give up and swap to easy just to get some resolution after the dozens of hours I'd invested.
I like the setting, and I clearly enjoyed a good chunk of the game if I managed to reach a point of sunken-cost fallacy in completing it, but spending entire sections of the game walking back and forth across giant, empty maps and clicking through boring dialogue in hopes that I'd get back to the good stuff didn't leave me with a good impression. I don't hate the game, but there's far better ways to spend fifty hours of your life, even within the scope of crowdfunded CRPGs.
Full disclosure, I backed this game during its initial Kickstarter run and only got around to playing through it over three years after its first release. All of my interactions with the Kickstarter side of things went fine, my impressions are completely within the scope of the game itself. While I technically recieved the Director's Cut later as an extra part of that, I paid a standard backer fee for the original game.
Wasteland 2's Kickstarter success was important for showing developers that such a model was possible, but maybe you should look into those offerings instead if you're craving a CRPG.
The Director's Cut appears to be the same game ID as the original release, thus showing my playtime for the original game and not my 53 hours played in the Director's Cut, for what it's worth.

This game is unlike anything you've played, unless it's Nuclear Dawn.
I bought this game due to the idea of being able to play RTS and FPS. Wasn't exactly what I thought it was as you can be either one or the other. It does allow for a commander in multiplayer mode and you have to actively work with your team to build new sort of "buildings" or stations. You issue the order, they physically have to go there and build it and possibly protect it. There are two opposing teams going at it at one time : humans and the parasites. Humans have their respective weapons, and you are able to choose what you would like to use from the ammo bin (once it's built)! Being the parasites takes a bit of practice to really hone control or get a kill. Parasites also come in variations as some fly, some are small and quick, some are used to build their own defensive systems. Unlike human upgrades (regarding weapons), beasts upgrade gradually when you choose to evolve them. You can get evolve points the more you successfully kill opponents. There are a lot of people saying the game has a steep learning curve (which is sort of does) but all the in-game players were more than willing to answer any immediate questions I had. The game becomes easier of course the more you play it. Do not be afraid to learn! Depending on who your commander is for your team, you can either have a great game or an okay game. One may ask who would I rather be, the beasts or the marines? To be honest, I preferred beasts at first due to the ability to climb about on walls and be invisible on creeps but over time I learned how fun it is to be a marine.
Graphics are absolutely impeccable on this one. Sounds are appropriate for the world the dev created. Makes you nervous when you start hearing things and you know your about to be attacked.
RATING : solid 8/10 - this is a must buy if it's on sale!
For future Natural Selection games : maybe have a few vehicle options (or fixed weapons placements). I understand the concept of one person in charge of a team, but the problem arises that no one wants to be the guy watching instead of playing. Maybe allow for a real-time planner?

'Isaac' is simply the best rogue-like I've ever played. Even with slightly more rogue-like experience under my belt now, I still love to go back to this game. It sets the bar freaking high.
Released just under a year after
, with a jumbo DLC expansion another year after that, the game plays like a top-down dungeon-crawler-shooter with randomised levels - no 2 playthroughs are exactly the same! (Unless you use a certain program that can pull the map seeds, but that's a different story.)
The base game itself was very good, difficult at first but gets slightly easier as you unlock the more OP items and collectibles. The DLC adds a ton more content. Not to say that the items take away from the difficulty of the game though - some levels with the new Wrath monsters (and quite a few of the old monsters as well) feel somewhat akin to bullet curtain-like games.
The only real gripe I have with this is that I cannot save my game mid-way! It's still a small flaw, and one that is corrected in its remake, '
'. :)
In the meantime, to circumvent this during super epic games, I recommend hibernating your computer with the game still running. Okay, well, my computer has survived the hibernation, but I'm not sure about yours...
Well, okay, one more gripe - the game engine is in Flash, which is laggy at times and hard to play. For the most part though I didn't have any problems or let that detract from the fun of the game.
If you can get this and the DLC for a cheap price, a must buy. It has possibly one of the highest ratios of time spent in game to money spent on game. (Excluding F2Ps, of course.)

You'll probably spend a lot of time trying to beat this mode with all characters, even if you are a veteran. Getting it on a steep discount will give you a lot of hours worth of gameplay for your dollar, but even full price for both game and DLC is not such a bad idea - Florian deserves to be rewarded for his new fiendishly unfair eternal manifestations. This game follows the mysterious events that surround Max, an introverted senior attending Blackwell Acadamy. Max has a vision of her town being destroyed, and she gains the ability to reverse time.
As Max, you can interact with other people to find information and influence the world around you. Every choice counts. Some choices can mean friendships or rivalries, and not just between you and others. Your choices can tear your town apart if you aren't careful. Thankfully, Max's time travel ability allows you to change your choice really quick if you don't feel comfortable with your choice, but often times you won't feel comfortable with either choice. The time travel also allows you to learn info you can use to go back in time and talk about a different subject with someone, and maybe learn even more or gain access to something useful. I will warn you now: PAY CLOSE ATTENTION TO EVERYTHING, AND BE VERY CAREFUL WITH YOUR CHOICES! It's easy to feel like you can do whatever you want because of your time travel ability, but one faulty choice and you'll end up regretting it. You literally have the power to either save lives, or lose them. I 100% recommend this game if you enjoy mysteries, choice-based games that influence the story, and story-rich games. Okay, but certainly nothing to be excited about. I'm a fan of the original Wasteland, and what I loved about the original was its open world, its delightfully unbalanced gameplay, and the wackiness.
Wasteland 2 heavily restricts your movement at all phases of the game. Combat is brutally slow (let us skip animations, or run them at 8x, please), and the weapons have been given the dreaded 'balance' treatment. The side quests were unmemorable, and the main story was just okay. Skills have been balanced too, unfortunately--adding tedium.
The thing that makes classic 90s RPGs (and Wasteland, which was ahead of its time) amazing are their open worlds. Hopefully Wasteland 3 recaptures that magic. Wasteland 2 did not.
(I certainly didn't play this for 300 hours; I left it open idle for days at a time while working through it. My true time played is somewhere between 20 and 40 hours.)

I don't know why people dog on this so much (see what i did huh huh, no? f*ck you then) from the reviews i read beforehand and from just having played the first game this is much better than i expected, much less jank than the first one, i really enjoyed the shooting in this.
This had to have influenced Max Payne 3 as well from an aesthetic perspective. For some reason which isn't explained in the game, there is an documentary style guerrilla filmmaking gimmick used in this, where when you run the camera shakes behind you violently like Paul Greengrass is the cameraman. There is also this terrible filter used throughout the game where the faraway image is compressed and when you move around or things explode you can clearly see compression artifacts...purposefully done to cement the fact that you are viewing this on a really bad £200 handheld camera. This is never even explained in game from a storytelling point of view, like seeing the police or someone watching the footage back. It's just one of the worst if not THE worst design decisions i have ever seen used in a game before. There is even this pixelation that occurs when you shoot or shotgun enemies in the face, like they do on tv when it's too graphic to censor it or they want to blur someones identity (again unexplained).
Max Payne 3 had a blurry drunken effect every so often throughout the cutscenes which was a mistake but nowhere near as bad as this. One thing i noticed is that both games removed being able to use grenades which annoyed the hell out of me, i miss using grenades! you're taking my fun away.
There is an option to turn off the shakycam in the game if it makes you feel nauseous, i kept it on because i was already used to it and it looked weird to me when it was turned off.
Story wise i still don't understand why Kane & Lynch continue to work together, especially after what happens to them halfway through the game. After what they were put through why would Kane continue hanging out with Lynch? There was talk of them making a movie out of this property and if that ever happens i really hope the writing is 100 times better than what they used in the games.
If you can get past those decisions then the actual gameplay is fun and the level of detail used in recreating Shanghai where the game is set is second to none. It really feels like you are in Shanghai and there is a nice variety of locations throughout the city, but the best ones are in the first half of the game, with more warehouse style bland stages towards the end, with a peak again at the end with a shootout at an airport. The graphics are a huge step up from the first Kane & Lynch.
The game is really short though, i completed it in 3 hours (it's meant to take 4) but i did play it on the easiest setting to start with. Multiplayer seems to be dead, i couldn't get into any games, but apparently there is a bot mode where you can play against AI.
I would recommend this if you can find it dirt cheap like i did and are a fan of shooter games, and cover based Gears of War style gameplay.

I was immediately suspicious when I saw Life is Strange compared to Gone Home. But thankfully, this comparison turned out to be very superficial, because Life is Strange is actually a good game.
The plot uses familiar settings and ideas (high school, time travel) mixed with some new and original ones (photography) to create something very fresh and interesting. It's weird in that it sprawls all over the place but it does flow rather smoothly to each new idea and near the end of the game I was thinking "how did I get from the start of the game, to this?" The story is also quite engaging and uses that to introduce some powerful moments to the players, especially major character deaths.
But the story isn't without its problems. The dialogue starts off a bit shaky and cringeworthy. I felt Episode 5 kicked the player around a little more than necessary to get the point across. The ending was also somewhat of a letdown. **Minor spoilers here**, all the choices you've made up until now and all the characters who died from your choices - it becomes meaningless at the ending (perhaps except for a few actions leading to a slightly more intimate moment in one ending), where you're always given the same two options to choose from.
Max's character, while being mostly believable, feels a bit all over the place. You do get a sense of overall character change at the end but throughout the game, she changes frequently from low self-esteem to sarcastic to innocent and thoughtful to bitter and hatred.
The gameplay is about as good as a game like this can get. The player is rewarded for exploring different areas and objects, and the dull monotony of walking around is broken up by puzzles, thrilling action, tense moments and strongly emotional ones. The rewind mechanic is used well to enhance the gameplay, adding another dimension to your thinking. There is a stealth part near the end that makes sense conceptually, but gameplay-wise feels a bit "ehh". Thankfully, it doesn't drag on too much.
Overall, Life is Strange definitely has some bumps, mostly at the end, but manages to create an engaging plot with unique ideas that's skilfully intertwined with gameplay that doesn't feel boring or monotonous. Basically, it does everything that Gome Home did with mediocrity or failed miserably at, and I'd give Life is Strange an overall 8.5/10.

I'll start by saying that I really enjoyed Shadow of Mordor so I was going into Shadow of War with high expectations.
This game is just AWESOME, I find the combat to be so fluid and enjoyable that it just never gets old. Hunting down Orc captains and making your own particular enemies is just as fun as it was in the original, plus there is a much larger variation in the types of Uruk-Hai that you encounter.
The storyline is okay, it's interesting enough to keep me invested and there is a really nice balance between doing main quests and then running off doing your own thing. There are plenty of recogniseable characters from the LOTR universe so the entire experiencew is very nostalgic.
The new ability of creating orc armies from the captains that you defeat is fantastic, leading to some really interesting and often hilarious relationships with your minions. It's also worth mentioning that the skill tree has been extended since the first game, so you really start to feel like a force of nature as you level up.
The gear collecting is a nice touch but it still doesn't feel 100% right somehow, perhaps I wish there was a larger number of unique cosmetics that you could obtain. The loot boxes have no place to be in a single player game, but you DO NOT NEED TO BUY THEM. The game is completely playable without spending money on microtransactions, they are simply there for the players who don't want to grind for the gear and orcs.
Overall, if you enjoyed the first game or are looking for an open-world beat-em-up then this one packs everything you need into a Tolkein setting.
