Well that was certainly something different. It has been a while since Hotline Miami was released and it has build up a special kind of reputation for sure, but I was not expecting this. I always held to the belief that it's a good thing to occasionally play something outside of your comfort zone. Let's see if that holds up with this particular title.
For once I'll start with something that didn't wow me  that much because it's rather short – story. Now, something like story might be utterly redundant in a game of this type, but I disagree with that notion considering a good story, setting or background can add to any game. I liked Hotline Miami in that department for the majority of it because despite kinda barely being there yet also reinforcing the idea of our character's personality, so to speak, as the world and he himself both descent into madness. Or do they? Game never really makes it explicitly clear how much of what's happening is real and you'll go through some trippy sequences such as talking to three masked people who may or may not be there, repeated salesmen offering you things for free and as the world around you becomes more and more gruesome, seemingly commonplace. There's also a revenge plot within all of that which I didn't mind at all and goes with the '80s sensibilities of a badass nameless protagonist, if not anti-hero considering what you do over the course of the game, but what I did take objection to was the epilogue. In my opinion it was kinda tacked on even though it explains things such as who's making the mysterious phone calls and certain other seeming coincidences.
Let's dig into some of the unanimous positives now. Game was designed and plays like a charm, and I also probably wouldn't change much aside from adding greater effects to masks. But I jump ahead of myself. Operative phrase in these parts is: you're going to die. Fortunately, Hotline Miami makes it so that reload is achieved about as fast as you can press letter R on your keyboard after dying and there are no loading screens once that particular level has been loaded. Gameplay is frenetic and absolutely adrenaline-fueled as it requires you to rely on pinpoint accuracy... or does it really when you take into account just button mashing and firing aimlessly won't really get you far. You need to take a look at each level's layout, plan for enemy patrols, and whether you want to keep it low-profile with melee weapons or go guns blazing and alert half the map to your presence. Aside from few gimmick levels game usually gives you freedom to go about it however you want, but whichever approach you go with it feels absolutely great and reward with that crunchy and, dare I say it, visceral combat.
Speaking of masks they're how you can affect your character. Which you unlock along with new weapons that randomly spawn on the level following each death with your score – there are masks that can make you go faster, make guns have more ammo, make hitting enemies with doors actually lethal instead of just knocking them out, etc. There's nothing like clearing a single room in a second or two after you've gained insight on how the game runs and gotten over the initial shock. One iffy segment of the gameplay department is when the game throws a boss at you. These moments are rare, but you'll undoubtedly end up dying for a while not because you're thick or anything, but simply because you need that trial and error approach to beat them and they usually don't give you the time to ponder on what to do.
But the real gem here is the game's soundtrack which is absolutely outstanding and will get you hyped like few games do. Not to mention it really works with the whole “stop and go” approach that constantly dying generates and you never get that jarring feeling of songs switching around to match the game. Dennaton Games really went all out and got the likes of Perturbator and M.O.O.N. on-board for some great electronic pieces, or whatever wide genre of music this soundtrack as a whole would fit into. I know I enjoyed it profoundly and it even got me hooked enough to listen outside of the game which hasn't happened in... well, forever. Maybe I should branch out a bit as far as my music tastes go.
I've kept this long enough, with select songs from the game blasting in the background, so let's pop the big one – would I recommend Hotline Miami? That's a firm yes. You should keep in mind this IS one of those frustrating, peripheral-snapping games that will make you curse the day it was made until you understand its rules and get into the groove.
Hell, by the end I was almost playing to the music.

I'm very surprised at how good reviews this game has gotten. The controls are very messy. The same button is used for fighting, lighting torches and picking up stuff, which means that you'll repeatedly do something silly in the midst of combat. In order to pick something up you have to stand on exactly the right spot, which means you have to shuffle around looking for it. If there's a torch nearby, you may not be able to pick something up at all. Also, enemies doesn't drop loot immediately, so you have to wait around for a bit.
There're also quick time events that kill you and force reloads, mini games with unexplained controls and some glitchy or just plain ugly animations (mixed in with generally decent graphics).
The story's fine, as far as I've gotten. Presumably that's what keep people playing despite the gameplay issues. Personally I'm more interested in gameplay than heaps of cutscenes.

Budget Bayonetta
Take this as a positive review when the game is on sale. Competant Bayonetta/DMC clone that unfortunately is not deep enough or long enough to be worth the full asking price. There isn't much game here. Expect to fight lots of the same enemies in the same octogon of playable area. The gameplay is fun, but not very deep and frustrating when it shouldn't be. Your rolling has no ability to push enemies or go around them, because their collision data seems to be a giant square around them. Because of this, getting even almost surrounded means death. Even slower hack-n-slash influenced games like Dark Souls and The Witcher have much better and reliable rolling.
Despite this, there is fun to be had in the gameplay, at the very least during levels. Bosses are another level of frustration.
Bosses have extremely frustrating collision and hitboxes, and beating the bosses involves memorizing where the damage zones for their attacks are, because they don't actually correspond to the effects at all. Most noticeable on the stage 2 boss, whose punches seem to project a damage aura anywhere in front of his body. If you play enough, you realize that the vast majority of these attacks can only be avoided when rolling in 1 direction, so the difficulty comes from finding out which direction this is. Try rolling directly into attacks first, as this seems to be the only way to beat the lock on tracking everyone but you has.
Will entertain you for an afternoon. Don't pay more than $2.50 or it's not worth it.

As it has become mostly the norm for horror games (and even movies) to contain jumpscares, so much a lot of people expect jumpscares from horror games and find games without them not worth in that category. However, jumpscares does not equal horror if the atmosphere and interactions the player makes is not effective nor put in any context. Due to this, jumpscares can easily become stale when you play enough games with jumpscares or watch enough movies that uses jumpscares to scare.
The Music Machine (and well all the games by this developer) goes away from jumpscares and focus on how the atmosphere connects the player and how to envoke a sense of fear. The Music Machine excels at this with how unique each element seemingly connects. It is difficult to say which came first: the color choices, the enviornment, or how the story progresses in each place. The story/writing has improved as you explore. Despite noticing some flaws, it is not really disengaging from the plot and noticing how the characters change with only dialouge. Overall, this has come a long way from Fingerbones and definetely extends on The Moon Silver in the best way.
There's not much I can say without repeating myself or giving away the story. I recommend this game if you really like atmospheric games or if you are open enough to not be more engaged in automatically classifying this game as horrible because of no jumpscares; but instead more engaged in how this world can mess with you.

Sorta In-depth Review:
I'd highly recommend this to people who are fans of things such as Ninja Blade for the Xbox 360 or the Dynasty Warriors series. This game is very beat em' up-y and of course this means things can get a little repetitive after a while. However, the game does a very good job at fixing this by allowing you to buy/upgrade new skills with the points that you earn from beating up said enemies. The best part is the fact you can keep whatever points you make when you die, so you can upgrade your health/katana gauge/etc. as much as you need until you're finally beefed up enough to take down the big bad that's troubling you.
The controls require you to have a gamepad or usb controller of some kind, because there's so many buttons that do so many things. If you've played (and beat) this game with a keyboard alone, kudos to you.
The story is pretty decent. It gives you a set goal to accomplish and that's basically it.
The soundtrack is really nice to listen to, and I didn't find myself growing tired of it.
The voice acting is pretty good, but I wish it had more variety and blended in better with the clashing of swords, robot arms, lasers, and the BGM. Hearing "hoo ha hoo ha hoo ha hyah hoo ha hoo ha hoo ha hyah AUGHGHGHGHGHGH" does get a little irking after a bit.
Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10. I've had a lot of fun with it so far and I hope to see more titles from this developer in the future.

'Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae' is an action game that, at first, seems to be very basic and rather boring in its' repetition. You're placed in a circular arena, fighting off waves of baddies that progressively change their colors and patterns. You have your genre stables of jumping, blocking, dodge rolls, and of course your light/heavy/flashy attacks. And at first, it's more than enough to get you through the first five waves of enemies.
And then the first boss drops in, and kicks you in the teeth. Not because he is very difficult, but because you don't know how to play this game yet.
Upon defeat, you learn of the location of the Upgrade station - which was in the pause menu the whole time - and buy a couple new skills. At this point, the game begins to show what it truly is.
Instantly evolving from a simple mashing game, you start to understand the importance of maintaining your Katana meter, which allows you to perform powerful attacks with your sword. You learn to apply Bleed status to as many people as possible before delivering the Coup De Grace, which is also your main healing method. You also start to dabble in Just Guard, Counters and Flourish timings, if not for survivability, but for flashiness as well.
MKH is a game that, to me, has managed to feel like a new experience every time I get a new skill, or upgrade an old favorite. It's very short, taking around an hour or two to clear, but it's something that I found to be very fun to replay several times.
For the asking price, this game is more than worth it. I just hope to see a sequel with so much more added to it. If you enjoy Devil May Cry's take on action combat, then you'll likely feel right at home here.

Well that was certainly something different. It has been a while since Hotline Miami was released and it has build up a special kind of reputation for sure, but I was not expecting this. I always held to the belief that it's a good thing to occasionally play something outside of your comfort zone. Let's see if that holds up with this particular title.
For once I'll start with something that didn't wow me  that much because it's rather short – story. Now, something like story might be utterly redundant in a game of this type, but I disagree with that notion considering a good story, setting or background can add to any game. I liked Hotline Miami in that department for the majority of it because despite kinda barely being there yet also reinforcing the idea of our character's personality, so to speak, as the world and he himself both descent into madness. Or do they? Game never really makes it explicitly clear how much of what's happening is real and you'll go through some trippy sequences such as talking to three masked people who may or may not be there, repeated salesmen offering you things for free and as the world around you becomes more and more gruesome, seemingly commonplace. There's also a revenge plot within all of that which I didn't mind at all and goes with the '80s sensibilities of a badass nameless protagonist, if not anti-hero considering what you do over the course of the game, but what I did take objection to was the epilogue. In my opinion it was kinda tacked on even though it explains things such as who's making the mysterious phone calls and certain other seeming coincidences.
Let's dig into some of the unanimous positives now. Game was designed and plays like a charm, and I also probably wouldn't change much aside from adding greater effects to masks. But I jump ahead of myself. Operative phrase in these parts is: you're going to die. Fortunately, Hotline Miami makes it so that reload is achieved about as fast as you can press letter R on your keyboard after dying and there are no loading screens once that particular level has been loaded. Gameplay is frenetic and absolutely adrenaline-fueled as it requires you to rely on pinpoint accuracy... or does it really when you take into account just button mashing and firing aimlessly won't really get you far. You need to take a look at each level's layout, plan for enemy patrols, and whether you want to keep it low-profile with melee weapons or go guns blazing and alert half the map to your presence. Aside from few gimmick levels game usually gives you freedom to go about it however you want, but whichever approach you go with it feels absolutely great and reward with that crunchy and, dare I say it, visceral combat.
Speaking of masks they're how you can affect your character. Which you unlock along with new weapons that randomly spawn on the level following each death with your score – there are masks that can make you go faster, make guns have more ammo, make hitting enemies with doors actually lethal instead of just knocking them out, etc. There's nothing like clearing a single room in a second or two after you've gained insight on how the game runs and gotten over the initial shock. One iffy segment of the gameplay department is when the game throws a boss at you. These moments are rare, but you'll undoubtedly end up dying for a while not because you're thick or anything, but simply because you need that trial and error approach to beat them and they usually don't give you the time to ponder on what to do.
But the real gem here is the game's soundtrack which is absolutely outstanding and will get you hyped like few games do. Not to mention it really works with the whole “stop and go” approach that constantly dying generates and you never get that jarring feeling of songs switching around to match the game. Dennaton Games really went all out and got the likes of Perturbator and M.O.O.N. on-board for some great electronic pieces, or whatever wide genre of music this soundtrack as a whole would fit into. I know I enjoyed it profoundly and it even got me hooked enough to listen outside of the game which hasn't happened in... well, forever. Maybe I should branch out a bit as far as my music tastes go.
I've kept this long enough, with select songs from the game blasting in the background, so let's pop the big one – would I recommend Hotline Miami? That's a firm yes. You should keep in mind this IS one of those frustrating, peripheral-snapping games that will make you curse the day it was made until you understand its rules and get into the groove.
Hell, by the end I was almost playing to the music.

Well, another "well done" game. This is a 2D Jump&Run, more action-oriented than the Trine series. The story isn't bad, the voice acting and humor is excellent, especially the dialogue between Dust (the main character) and Fidget (his sidekick, basically). There's also the talking sword, but that one is more like the wise guy in the background
Some reviewers considered the boss battles to be "underwhelming", but I tend to call it something like "they aren't intended to stop you from continuing in the game".
If you want to die a lot then this is generally not the game for you, as Dust is clearly superior to anything he encounters. And since you can level up in any area you can also be "overlevelled", especially if you keep repeating stuff to find the last secret or something like that.
And despite being mostly a one-man job (programming, graphics and levels), each of the 5 chapters has a very distinct look. So while your fighting doesn't change much during the game, and your equipment is not reflected in your character look, it still doesn't get boring.
The Steam trailer is kind of stupid, as they changed the intro to some talk about the 4 elements and dust and steam, just to get "Steam" into the trailer, which replaces most of the previous intro that explained what "tide" Dust is going to turn. The story isn't that confusing, and it never deals with 4 elements or something like that.

Duck Game is one of those games that brings me sheer joy every time I play it. No matter how much I play, it never gets old. Never has a game been so goddamn funny, enjoyable and just plain fun for me than Duck Game. Often described as a mix between Warioware, Towerfall and sometimes Smash Bros., Duck game is a multiplayer game where up to four ducks are pit against each other in pre-made or player-made arenas. Rounds are short and you die in one hit. And yet, the sheer amount of crazy stuff that can happen is so immense that the game manages to feel fresh even after playing it for hundreds of hours. It rewards skill, yet if you're not careful, you can get yourself and your teammates killed quickly, whether it's your fault or not. It's so fast paced that there's almost always something new going on. It's just pure, unadulterated fun.
So, why the hell don't you own it yet? It's $13, go buy it already and have one of the most hilarious multiplayer experiences imaginable.

Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days is the worst video game I have ever played.
The story begins with Kane and Lynch in Shanghai trying to scrape together a gun running deal.  Before the deal goes down, Lynch drags Kane to go settle a grudge match with some guy for some reason.  The duo accidentally kill a girl who happens to be the daughter of some government bureaucrat with enough money, power, and influence to not only control his own gang, but the police and even the Chinese military.  His goons pursue Kane and Lynch.  Kane and Lynch get caught and tortured.  What follows is the most gruesome, unncessary, and tasteless sequence in an already awful game, in which we see our lovely protagonists running around naked and covered and blood.  Then they get captured again, get taken to the villain's building, and decide to kill him while they're there, because why not?  After killing him, they escape, and the player is left wondering what the point was.
Because having a shallow, pointless, and disgusting plot wasn't enough, the game also features a shallow, pointless, and disgusting graphical gimmick.  The entire game is designed to look like it's being filmed on a handheld camera.  This makes no sense in-universe since nobody with a camera is actually following the duo around.  The result is shaky cam that would disgust Paul Greengrass, horrible looking lens flares, and a generally disgusting visual aesthetic.  The effect is amplified when running, and will make you want to puke as the visuals go out of focus and shake wildly.  Just charming!
The gameplay is built around simple, co-operative third person shooting.  It's about as standard and bland as it can get.  Headshots instant-kill enemies that would otherwise be massive bullet sponges.  You hide behind cover (which feels miserable).  There are the mandatory "stealth" sequences that don't actually work.  A turret level.  Shooting down helicopters.  Pretty much all of it is standard to the point of being boring, or it would be if not for the horrific AI.  The enemies are both dumb and dangerous, featuring absurdly good aim (despite the guns being horribly inaccurate when you wield them) and bricks for brains.  They also have a tendency to only peek out of cover for a fraction of a second at a time, turning the game into an obnoxious whack-a-mole clone.  The terrible AI is made even more obvious in coop, since the AI will only ever target one player at a time, and will instantaneously snap between the two.  Because of this, it's not uncommon to sneak up on an enemy only to have them abruptly spin 180 and kill you.  Getting killed is also very frustrating in coop.  You can mash E to stay alive longer so they can come help you up, but the timer is really short and mashing E appears to make absolutely no difference in the amount of time you can survive.  In addition, the E key is used for pretty much everything, so it's not terribly uncommon to try to pick up a friend and find your character instead picking up a fire extinguisher.  While mentioning multiplayer, I should also mention that my experience was extremely laggy.  This could have been my connection, but I think the game just has bad netcode.
A terrible story, hideous visuals, and awful gameplay are capped off with glitchy animation and showstopping bugs.  Numerous animations look quick and jerky.  When you open doors to proceed to the next room, the animation just cuts midway through.  Later in the game my friend and I began to experience characters getting stuck on geometry, massive frame-drops, garbled video, and outright crashes.  The game barely feels functional at all.
Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days is the worst.  When the game isn't glitching itself into unplayability, it's merely disgusting and unpleasant to experience.  9/10 pretty ok.

The Binding of Isaac is an incredibly deep and entertaining game that will bring you many hours of entertainment for such a small price tag. Binding of Isaac uses bullet hell and stick shooter mechanics that make the game really simple to pick up and play, but learning all the intricacies and mastering the game takes quite a bit of time. Even though this game takes a while to fully master, every minute I spent with it was incredibly enjoyable (with quite a few exceptions; more on that later).
The game’s depth comes from in its use of RNG to randomize almost everything. Room layouts, floor layouts, item drops, enemies, and bosses are all randomized, making every run different and unique. Enemies and bosses have a lot of variety in attack patterns which requires the player to learn different techniques for avoiding and killing each of the different enemies. When combined with random room layouts and random combinations of enemies, every room presents a fresh challenge.
The wide variety of items that you can potentially come across during a run also adds a considerable amount of variety and spontaneity. A good number of the items offer basic effects like range up and damage up, but the majority of the items have very distinct effects. Every item reacts differently with other objects, which leads to a significant amount of variety in the way your character moves, looks, and attacks during each run. Experimenting with different combinations is fun and keeps the game fresh, and learning the good combinations from the bad ones takes quite a bit of time.
The learning curve may be tall, but it isn’t steep. Any casual player can pick up this game and gradually get better until they have the game mastered. The rewards are spread out evenly enough that you continue to unlock new items, characters, and floors at a steady rate, encouraging the player to continue progressing. Towards the end of the game, unlocks slow significantly, but the idea of earning 100% is enough motivation to continue at that point.
This game is also noteworthy because it has managed to transcend typical levels of unfairness and set a whole new standard for stacking the deck against the player. RNGesus punishes all heresy quickly and efficiently. This game has a considerable number of opportunities to make your day miserable, and RNGesus will not hesitate to seize any and every opportunity to punish those who displease him.
Even though it can and will be incredibly frustrating at times, I highly recommend this game. The feeling of triumph you will experience when you accomplish some of the tougher challenges in this game is a feeling that a game hasn’t been able to give me in a while. The $7.98 price tag is an incredibly good deal for the amount of entertainment you will get out of this game. 10/10 would suffer again.

All of David Szymanski's games contain thoughtful, interesting narratives. The Moon Sliver is the best of them. It's an experience I won't spoil here except to say you should play that before you play The Music Machine.
Or not. The Music Machine is billed as a "follow-up" to The Moon Sliver, and that would be more accurate than to say "sequel." You could probably play either first and still appreciate them both, but you'll get more out of The Music Machine if you enter the experience prepared. I would have been very confused without at least some grounding in Szymanski's catalogue.
To avoid giving anything away, I'll simply say The Machine Machine reminds me of Stephen King's The Dark Tower series, or maybe even David Lynch's film Inland Empire, in that it incorporates the creator's earlier works without necessarily invalidating or permenantly modifying those earlier experiences. Do I percieve allusions to A Wolf in Autumn in TMM as well? I'm not entirely sure. Fingerbones also? Maybe.
This is a walking simulator, so just know that going in. All of Szymanski's games are interactivity in service of a story, whereas most games contain story in service to the gameplay. If "games as art" doesn't turn you off, this is a good purchase, even with its short length. (It can be completed in one sitting.) You're playing for the narrative and especially the atmosphere.
I look forward to purchasing anything Mr. Szymanski creates in the future.

Games like The Music Machine don't come around very often.  When they do, it seems that even many of the people who would enjoy them feel reluctant to give them a try. Sometimes a game looks a little too strange and people (at least, people like me) get anxious about the idea of wasting their money. In the hopes of addressing some of the fence-sitters, let me simply say that The Music Machine is the best horror game I played in all of 2015.
When The Music Machine begins, all you know is that you're a spirit controlling the body of a young girl. To say more could constitute major spoilers, but even from this fairly unique premise, the story takes some unexpected turns. Speaking of story, the plot of The Music Machine is tenuously connected to the plot of The Moon Sliver, David Szymanski's previous game, but The Music Machine is not a sequel and either game can be enjoyed without having played the other.
Depending on how often you stop to take in the view, accompanied by a genuinely excellent score, you'll likely spend two or three hours exploring the various monochromatic areas of the abandoned island, and it is in this exploration that The Music Machine shines. Almost every object can be examined and doing so will usually trigger a short conversation between the two main characters. The dialogue is superbly written and you can even keep walking around once a conversation has been initiated, unbound by the object you were examining.
When a game is this short, a discussion of its length is unavoidable, which is why I feel I need to mention that the length of The Music Machine is absolutely perfect.
When a game can be completed in a single sitting, it's story stays fresh in your mind throughout it's runtime. Arbitrarily padding a game like this to extend it's length would only lessen the experience in the long run. Keeping a story succinct means it never gets dull.

* Played this game for 136 hours, but overall did not enjoy it enough
* In later parts of the game you have to reconfigure your skill extensions way too often (drain regains arrows/restores full health/takes over orc, etc), which in itself is bad design, made even more annoying by the how deep in the menu this is hidden...
* As in many games these days you are required to spend too much time decluttering your inventory (destroying useless weapons/armor/rings)
* Combat is easy most of the time, until things suddenly get messy
** Especially against certain stronger opponents game makes it hard to recovcer, in the few situations were things go downhill
** Opponents learning your attack patterns would be fine, but them becoming immune to every attack during combat is ridiculous. Most of the time they are dead long before that, but if it happens, you face a sort of super opponent, who will block e.g. an ice attack coming from his back, even if he is engaging another opponent...
** Blocking attacks was strangely sequential-hit-and-miss for me: Either it worked fine multiple times in a row, or it failed time and time again. Maybe had something to do with me streaming the game into my living room - but that very small lag should not suffice to create this effect...
* Splitting all stronger opponents into one of two categories with regards to ranged effects is imho a very bad (and quite frankly puzzling) game design decision:
** Takes ranged damage => already dead
** Immune to _all_ ranged effects (including pinning foot, arrow fire damage, etc) => 70-80% of your skills become completely useless => your tactical options are severely limited
* Shares the same camera problems as its predecessor (combat becomes annoying if camera is in a "bad spot")
* Conquering strongholds is done very poorly gameplay-wise: Once you have all or most chiefs on your side and defenses are therefore disabled, taking the fortress is like taking candy from a baby, apart from the arena fight in the stronghold's throne room, which can be annoying
* Dragon-riding controls are close to broken, i.e. do not work well at all
* Alas: etc
On the plus side:
* Cut scenes are fantastic, cinema quality, and a real treat after every successful mission
* Basic combat is still enjoyable, as in the first game
* Liked the story

6. Excellent writing! Combining with the perfect story and talented voice actors, all dialogue is EXTREMELY well-written, though it's hard to prove without spoiling some of this gem.

When it is finished, and if it had greater support and a better reception it could become the next multiplayer game on the PC. It does not come cheap however and is not honestly worth the investment yet.

Never played this game but steam say that I actually did so instead of judging the game here's a cool way to make skinny guacamoles with homemade baked tortilla chips :
Skinny Guacamole:
2 medium green sweet peppers
2 medium fresh poblano chile peppers
1 bulb garlic
1/2 teaspoon olive oil
2 roma tomatoes, seeded and chopped
1 serrano pepper, minced
2 medium ripe avocados, halved, seeded, peeled, and diced
1 teaspoon lime zest
2 tablespoons lime juice
1/2 teaspoon salt
Baked Tortilla Chips:
Corn tortillas
Olive oil spray
Salt
For the guacamole:
Preheat oven to 425° F. Line a 15 x 10 x 1-inch baking pan with foil; set aside. Quarter, stem, and seed the peppers. Place pepper quarters, cut sides down, in the prepared pan. Cut off the top half inch of the garlic bulb to expose ends of individual cloves. Leaving garlic bulb whole, remove any loose, papery outer layers. Place bulb, cut end up, on a double thickness of foil. Drizzle with the oil. Bring foil up around bulb and fold edges together to loosely enclose. Place foil packet on the pan with the peppers.
Roast peppers and garlic for 20 to 30 minutes or until pepper skins are charred and garlic cloves feel soft. Allow to cool about 15 minutes. When garlic head is cool enough to handle, squeeze garlic paste out of the individual cloves.
In a food processor combine roasted pepper quarters and the garlic paste. Cover and pulse until combined, but still slightly chunky.
In a large bowl, combine tomatoes and serrano pepper. Add roasted pepper and garlic combination and stir to combine. Add diced avocado, lime zest, lime juice, and salt. Gently toss to combine.
Serve immediately or cover the surface with plastic wrap and chill for up to 1 hour.
For the chips:
Cut corn tortillas into wedges and place on a foil-lined baking sheet. Spray lightly with olive oil spray and season with salt, to taste.
Bake in a 350° F oven for 8-10 minutes or until lightly golden brown.

One day, a few months ago, Steam suggested that I looked into a little game called Fingerbones. I looked into it, thought "eh...it sounds somewhat interesting" and I gave it a shot. I did not expect to be as immersed into Fingerbones as I was. I enjoyed it so much that I looked to see if the creator, David Szymanski, had made any other games. Thankfully, not only had he made two more games, but they were also cheap (and on sale to make them even cheaper). I then bought The Moon Silver and The Music Machine, downloaded them, and forgot all about them until I saw them in my steam library the other day and decided to pick them up again. Worth every penny. Especially The Music Machine. Of the three games, I feel that I most enjoyed The Music Machine. One thing that I really enjoyed was the progression of David’s work from each of the games. Not only have the games increased in scope and scale (from Fingerbone’s setting confining you to a singular house, then the island of The Moon Silver, finally to the multiple worlds of The Music Machine), but David’s story telling also, while still very strong in Fingerbones, has gotten better as the games progressed as well. Also, damn this game is pretty. The different color themes of the different world in The Music Machine sets a distinct tone for each world, and I actually was not sure what I would think of the heavy orange and yellow theme of the island. However, after the game began and I saw the sun through the trees I knew my previous assumptions were wrong. The story also tackles some pretty interesting content as well: revenge, loneliness, controlling anger, forgiveness, and even divine beings. Not only that, but the soundtrack for this game was also amazing and utilized perfectly to provoke specific emotions in the player during certain parts of the story. Even though there is a save feature in The Music Machine (unlike its predecessors) I really don’t think it is necessary because the story will engross you to the point that you have to finish the entirety of game in one sitting.
All in all, The Music Machine is an extremely good game. It is visually beautiful, the soundtrack is not only beautiful but used perfectly in setting the tone and emotion of the story, the story is intellectual as well as intriguing, and has built off of the successes the games predecessors (Fingerbones and The Moon Silver).

As most of us, I bought mafia III with visions of shooting gangsters in my head. While the shooting gangsters part was true there where many things left out or unpolished in the experience.
Let's break this down one section at a time.
TL;DR at the end
Missions: Easilly the games weakest point. Now we all expect a game like this to have lots of shooting, that's not the issue. The problem is after playing through one or two rackets the originality of missions is practically gone. The missions break down as follows: Get information from this guy, Steal X, Kill these guys, destroy X, kill/capture this guy. Infact after playing through the entire game I can only remember one mission being somewhat different. There is a stealth option to let you mix things up, more on that later. However I will say that most of the missions never feel like you are diverting from lincols goal. Every missions having a place a long the way to kill Sal.
Side missions: Some of the side missions are where things get more interesting, such as hunting down vito's hitlist. However these missions are just about as bland. The only saving grace being the conversations with the underbosses. These make the characters come to life more and give you a feeling of being closer to them. One of the very few occurances for the underbosses in the game.
Other things to do: There isn't much beyond collectables. You also can't use your money for anything but weapons, supplies and upgrades. So you not only never change your cloths throughout the game but you don't do anything else. No getting yourself a new suit, upgrading your car (all car upgrades are passive to cars in your garage), new paintjob, getting a bite to eat to regen your health. Infact you don't even use your money to bribe anyone. This destroys the whole mafia illusion simply changing the story to a revenge plot with the mafia bit being a side line.
Gameplay: One of the most satisfying things to do in Mafia III is shoot people. Unlike most games they will react to bullets hitting them, their bodies moving from the impact and shear pain of a bullet going through them. Most enemies don't feel like bullet sponges.
Now onto the stealth. The game offers a stealth option. I will say that stealth can be good fun but it is still unpolished. For example if one enemy sees you there is a good chance even a bullet in what you think is in time would stop everyone from being alerted. The AI is also rather dumb with stealth.
During the game one of your goals is to make enough money to afford taking out Sal. However the only thing you can ever spend this money on is upgrades to lincoln, guns/gun upgrades, car upgrades. The enemies in the game also never get harder which makes most of the guns pointless. You could pick out the two weapons you like using the most and get through the game. I used the silenced m1n1 and the blackburn pistol through the majority of the game with no problems.

The weapon veriaty itself is also lacking. Many weapons only being slightly worse then the next or whole guns being rendered pointless by them being so close there is no point. Infact one of the supposed "best" pistols the clipper.44 is a reward from burke. This gun is actually worse then one I can buy earlier one and for cheaper (unless the clipper was given to you). Shotguns are also dissapointing. Enemies will get knocked back by them but not only do they fire slowly they also have a much shorter effective range then actual shotguns. Unless you are up close and personal they won't help you.
Story/characters: The game shines it's brightest with it's story and expertly voice acted cut scenes. Through these cutscenes the characters and game come to life in a way gameplay doesn't. Not just story wise but also graphically, which is a bit of a shame, would love to have seen the whole game look as good as the cutscenes. The way the game tells it's story through a documentary style fashion is a nice touch.
The characters themselves are good, except for some cliches such as clay's quest for vengance changing him into more of a two dimensional protagonist.
Setting: It's obvious the devs spent alot of time recreating a 1960's new orleans type feel. Every part of the game feels authentic to the time period, even down to the uncensored racial slurs. This I have to commend them for, making a game with this kind of commitment in a world where people seem to always find something to complain about.
Glitches: In one word, ragdoll. Enemies will sometimes get stuck in a sitting position after death, with nothing holding them up. My favorite is when I pull a freshly knifed enemy to the side to chuck him and he decided being a part of the door/wall is more his style.
I will also mention there was one instance of an enemy in a car seemingly being bullet proof. Turns out when an enemy leans out the window to shoot you his hit boxes stay the same as if he was sitting in the car. Remember, aim for his♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ apparently.
In conclusion the game had a very strong start but by the end I was left feeling unaccomplished. If I was able to return the game now, I would. While I still think it's a good game it doesn't deserve 60 dollars. Maybe 20-30 at most.
TL;DR
Good- Solid shooting, great story, fantastic setting
neutral- graphics are a bit sub-par but still looks great, about 20 hours long.
Bad- Some unfortunate glitches, bland repetative missions, weapon veriaty, money only spent on guns/upgrades

Natural Selection 2 is an interesting breed of a game, in which who play an RTS/FPS depending on you role. Although it may seem complicated, it is very easy to learn; however, to master the game takes time, effort, and skill. Unlike most FPS's, NS2 will force you to have great skill and teamwork, this is not meant for the lone wolf.
With it's balanced system of weapons, maps, and tech, NS2 provokes players to use different skillsets. They are tasked in the elimination of the opposing team, to destroy all ways to the map. This is the RTS thing I am talking about, a single commander will help a team by accessing tech and strategy to win game; however, everyone else playing is in an FPS mode, so they will not always do what the commander wants.
Overall, there are some flaws (mainly issues in running), but the actual gameplay is solid as is. If anyone is bored with normal multiplayer experiences, this game is a new take on an old genre. It is extremely refreshing for what it does, I give NS2 a 9/10. Good luck and happy gaming, I will see you on the battlefield.

I'm sort of a fan of idle games myself, the thought of a game playing all by itself with you just stopping by to collect a couple of things is half decent for me, even if it seems like play-to-wait games nowadays are one of the many problems of the game industry.
Now, this game....Well, I'm looking at this from the eyes of a person who isn't really that savvy when it comes to Fallout, but who's got an interest in the setting of the series nonetheless. (So, I know little about the plot other than basic stuff and whatever I've seen in the games I have played so far.)
This game isn't all that bad. It starts slow and painful, and I do agree that the whole "Wait for♥♥♥♥♥♥to be done" hurts the pacing and the general enjoyment in this game. It would've been better if they fleshed out the combat and building aspects of this game, got rid of the sit n' wait, and made this a paid product. I'm totally up for that, the idea doesn't seem that bad. Being an idle game, this is one of those games that you play for 20 minutes - an hour or so each day, and then you just move on with your day, and that is kinda bad, there are times when I just want to do another quest or explore another place, and I realize I can't because I have to anywhere betwee 2 hours and a day for my dwellers to reach their destination....Or you can use the premium currency of the game, nuka-cola quantum. Yep, that's pretty much the hook, take it at a snails pace, or cough up some cash. And it hurts me that a fairly interesting game gets reduced to that.
I wouldn't recommend spending money on this game, though; As far as I know, lunchbox/Mr Handy/Nuka Cola purchases only affect a single vault (AKA save file), and if you lose that vault, like for example, a bug (More of that later), or just a standard game over because all of your dwellers died, your money is gone with that save file.
And even if you think you can handle it and you're 100% sure that you want to spend money in this game and that you aren't going to lose all your dwellers to some catastrophe, this game is still a bit buggy. It has never happened to me personally, but people have lost their files in the past, with all of their hard work deleted, and yep, that's right, even purchases. And even if you don't suffer from said dreaded vault removal bug, there are other bugs here and there, like losing the progress of your objectives, and that one has happened to me at least 10 times. From what I understand, the chances of your save file getting corrupted are reduced if you don't tab out of the game when it's loading your vault after a quest, and I've done my damn best to avoid disturbing my game while it's loading, and so far, my objectives haven't been fiddled with anymore.
That being said, the combat in this game is a bit lacking, your dwellers attack automatically, and the only things you can control are who they are shooting at, how much damage your are going to inflict with a crit (When you get one), and when to use radaways/stimpacks, kill every enemy in the room, loot, move to the next one. Rinse and repeat. A 2-D Fallout game would work if combat was a bit more fleshed out, IMO. Now and then, you get to choose dialog options in a quest, but as far as I know, your choices rarely matter. In some cases, the enemies will/won't attack you based on your dialog choices, or might/might not give you an outfit/weapon or come with you, but other than that, there's not too much to it.
The enemy selection in this game is still relatively small, you get radroaches, mole rats, radscorpions, feral ghouls, raiders, deathclaws, and that's about it. When you send a dweller to explore the wastelands (Basically, you just wait for hours and they will find goodies and deal with enemies, but it's only text based) they mention mirelurks, dogs, yao guai and super mutants, but they do not appear physically in the game. So, your worst nightmares are going to be the radscorpions, feral ghouls and deathclaws, and as far as I know, the first two aren't all that threatening in the main series.
I personally like the artstyle, it's pretty much the retro style that you see in the trailer of Fallout 3, with your dwellers pretty much looking like Vault Boy. I like the visuals, and I think the Power Armor, as scary as it is in the main series, looks rather cute in a way in here.
TL;DR
It's a nice game if you like idling, it's one of those games where you check what your vault/dwellers are up to daily, and then you move on with your day. It's fun, I would give it a try, but I would recommend not spending money in this game yet. With its dreaded vault wipe bug, and purchases only applying to a single save file, it feels like you aren't getting much out of your cash. Plus, everything can be obtained in game, even if it's a bit grindy.

I just finished this game, and here's what I got to say about it: This game feels to me like a Grand Theft Auto game that was written by smarter people but had a lower budget. The best parts about this game are in the use of setting and time period, along with some good dialogue and characters I bothered to remember and care about (especially Vito, Father James and John Donovan). The gunplay was fun too; the enemies are dumb but that makes it fun to mess around with them as you constantly relocate to different cover.
The problem is that while the narrative parts and main missions are fun, the rest of the game relies on a repetitive loop of 'smash rackets and take em over'. All the side missions are really simple compared to everything else. To the game's credit, it doesn't make you finish every single side mission to progress, but the side missions were so unimaginative and unvaried that it felt like they were made by a different team.
Another problem: No fast travel. The city is kinda small and it wont take you more than 8 minutes to go around from A to B if you were driving at top speed 24/7 like me, but still, this was a baffling design decision.
That said, I personally believe that this game is worth finishing. I liked Lincoln Clay, and I sincerely hope that there's DLC that either involves him or John Donovan, the best/worst CIA agent ever. If you're willing to go through some repetitive missions to soak in a simple but memorable revenge tale, buy this game. Wait for a discount if you don't want to pay the full almost-sixty dollars, but I will say that everybody who's played open world crime games should experience this game just for the characters and vibe alone.

Mafia III is such a frustrating game. The story is so well told, with strong and very well defined characters, aided by great acting and impressive facial animations. You look forward to cut scenes unlike most games. My favorite characters are Father James and Donovan, who steals every scene he's in. There is also a ton of great music from the era. Unfortunately the game gets pretty much everything else wrong: it's as repetitive as people have been complaining; you have around 12 targets whose rackets you need to take down before facing them, and in order to do that you have to pretty much do the same missions over and over again. Not only that but the main target is located in the same place a previous mission took over, adding to the repetition. Only the main capo missions add much needed variety; they are the strongest missions in the game (the capos are also very well characterized and acted). Shooting is pretty mediocre (it was stronger in Mafia II) and stealth is an option but AI is very dumb. It also looks pretty dated and ugly, and is very poorly optimized. There are a ton of collectibles in the game but, if you can believe it, there are no achievements for collecting them all, which is really absurd.
Obviously a great deal of money was invested in the making of this game and no doubt there was a lot of heart involved in its creation, so it pains me to say that this one is a pass.

Update: I will keep everything that I've written about the game, as I think it is important for people who have no to little experience with that particular genre of rpgs. The game gets a recommend with caveats from me, BUT READ TILL THE END BEFORE YOU BUY IT. Also note that I play the Director's Cut, but cannot post my review for it on it's page. Instead, I need to do it here.
INITIAL REVIEW
I've started my long journey into Wasteland 2 and can already see that it isn't a game that a wide audience can get into.
I've played my share of kick-started rpgs and know and understand perfectly what I am up against; it isn't that big of an issue for me and I will keep playing, as it was made after one of the most iconic rpgs ever. That, however, doesn't excuse the poor beginning of the game. RNG is bad during the first few lvls. You have the game throwing things at you that can one shot you while you're still figuring out the UI. Most of the voice acting is subpar; it would have been better left without. Many of the initial characters you interact with are kind of bland and emotionless.
I understand where this is coming from, and again, I will play the game and keep the review updated. It's not uncommon for games like that to have issues at their beginning. But when it comes to recommending a game to another person, one has to take into consideration the fact that Wasteland 2 sets a high bar for newcomers, who better have low expectations. Know anyone like that? The first few hours into the game won't feel pleasant.
UPDATE
Wasteland 2 is a very rough gem, but one that begins to shine somewhat if you spend enough time with it. It's experience will range from bad to good to bad, and you will need to tone down on your expectations for real if you want to play this game. The pleasant surprise here is that if you're wondering where the Fallout from Fallout 3/4 ran away, you will find most of it here. That said, this is not a game that a lot of people can comfortably get into. It has some needed steps you need to take if you want to enjoy this post-apoc adventure. First, if you have no previous experience with rpgs, it wouldn't be that much of a problem, but if you have no previous experience with the classic Fallout or Wasteland games, you may find the going tough, even if you've played many of the d&d based games for the PC. Without exception, I would suggest that you begin the game on the lowest difficulty for about 5 to 6 lvls(maybe even more), until you can pump up some combat skills up to scratch. The initial RNG is too punishing. As you progress in the game, you will be able to take on the higher difficulties, up to the highest at about lvl 25, in my opinion. Also, play slowly, talk to everybody and be sure to check everywhere as currency and supply is kind of limited and you will benefit greatly the sooner you move into higher tiers of weapons/armour. There are some especially beneficial places in the world that reward the wayward explorer.
Graphically the game is nothing to write home about; some find it ugly and I am in no position to argue, but personally I am ok with it. It's enough for me in the year of 2017, and I like how this game presents its world. For a newcomer the adjusting might be difficult. Be warned.
Sound and music are up to scratch for the post-apoc environment, with some tunes being very atmospheric. The sound design is nothing exceptional, almost bare-bones, but again, it is enough to be functional.
The real strength of Wasteland 2 is that it stays true to it's roots. It's a difficult game(part difficulty, part purely bad design); an indie title developed with a particular niche in mind and it is a very good successor to its original. It uses a lot of the quirks, positives and gimmicks of the classical post-apocs and that feels refreshing in today's environment. The design of the game is ESSENTIALIST, if not, almost BARE-BONES. You have to keep in mind this is a KICK-STARTED game with a small team behind it, supported mostly by fans of the old Wasteland/Fallout. That does not make it entirely bad(or good), though. One might wonder where the stealth is, for instance, but sometimes designing additional features like that may ruin the game instead of adding to it if not enough time is dedicated. I think that the devs have taken a decision to stick to what is old and functional, rather than try and add something that they may not have had enough time and money to properly develop...or they were just being lazy. Instead of an open world, you will get an over-world map in which a representation of your party will travel around, discover new things based on your skills and go from zone to zone. That was and still is a neat and clean way of doing things, not necessarily inferior to the newer and more expensive features. Instanced game world is sometimes preferable. In my opinion, devs need to start thinking hard when going open world vs instanced.
The main story gives you clear objectives and you will never get lost.
Pre-combat positioning is crucial for almost every encounter and you will have several options as to how to approach most of them, including SOME boss fights. This is kind of sad and annoying in the same time, because for some encounters the lack of precombat positioning, or even worse, the game changing your precombat positioning or putting you in scripted scenes(♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥), will make those encounters unnecessarily difficult, not to mention, ruin your immersion or role-play. Save often; this is a tip given to you by the devs themselves. In spite of the limited features of combat, the tactical options available will keep it fresh for one playthrough. Consumables and explosives are rare(save med and surgeon kits), but have significant impact. You will learn to be conservative with them and get the most bang for your buck.
And without spoiling any of the actual fun you may get out of the game, that is everything I will say about it. I don't want to talk about any specific skills, scenarios, builds, weapons, ect. ect. I find the game to have enough variety so that people can express themselves in the world as they see fit. Just remember, spread your skills across the entire party.
One more thing that I think the modern gamer needs to see is: this game combines its seriousness with its unique and funny quirks in a way that is very refreshing to see in 2017. I mean, how many other games you've seen that would tell you on a loading screen that ''Explosives can turn the tide of any battle, but remember: they are expensive and heavy, just like my ex-wife.'' Wasteland 2 is full of stuff like that. Go and play it, even if it is only for that.

I'm sort of a fan of idle games myself, the thought of a game playing all by itself with you just stopping by to collect a couple of things is half decent for me, even if it seems like play-to-wait games nowadays are one of the many problems of the game industry.
Now, this game....Well, I'm looking at this from the eyes of a person who isn't really that savvy when it comes to Fallout, but who's got an interest in the setting of the series nonetheless. (So, I know little about the plot other than basic stuff and whatever I've seen in the games I have played so far.)
This game isn't all that bad. It starts slow and painful, and I do agree that the whole "Wait for♥♥♥♥♥♥to be done" hurts the pacing and the general enjoyment in this game. It would've been better if they fleshed out the combat and building aspects of this game, got rid of the sit n' wait, and made this a paid product. I'm totally up for that, the idea doesn't seem that bad. Being an idle game, this is one of those games that you play for 20 minutes - an hour or so each day, and then you just move on with your day, and that is kinda bad, there are times when I just want to do another quest or explore another place, and I realize I can't because I have to anywhere betwee 2 hours and a day for my dwellers to reach their destination....Or you can use the premium currency of the game, nuka-cola quantum. Yep, that's pretty much the hook, take it at a snails pace, or cough up some cash. And it hurts me that a fairly interesting game gets reduced to that.
I wouldn't recommend spending money on this game, though; As far as I know, lunchbox/Mr Handy/Nuka Cola purchases only affect a single vault (AKA save file), and if you lose that vault, like for example, a bug (More of that later), or just a standard game over because all of your dwellers died, your money is gone with that save file.
And even if you think you can handle it and you're 100% sure that you want to spend money in this game and that you aren't going to lose all your dwellers to some catastrophe, this game is still a bit buggy. It has never happened to me personally, but people have lost their files in the past, with all of their hard work deleted, and yep, that's right, even purchases. And even if you don't suffer from said dreaded vault removal bug, there are other bugs here and there, like losing the progress of your objectives, and that one has happened to me at least 10 times. From what I understand, the chances of your save file getting corrupted are reduced if you don't tab out of the game when it's loading your vault after a quest, and I've done my damn best to avoid disturbing my game while it's loading, and so far, my objectives haven't been fiddled with anymore.
That being said, the combat in this game is a bit lacking, your dwellers attack automatically, and the only things you can control are who they are shooting at, how much damage your are going to inflict with a crit (When you get one), and when to use radaways/stimpacks, kill every enemy in the room, loot, move to the next one. Rinse and repeat. A 2-D Fallout game would work if combat was a bit more fleshed out, IMO. Now and then, you get to choose dialog options in a quest, but as far as I know, your choices rarely matter. In some cases, the enemies will/won't attack you based on your dialog choices, or might/might not give you an outfit/weapon or come with you, but other than that, there's not too much to it.
The enemy selection in this game is still relatively small, you get radroaches, mole rats, radscorpions, feral ghouls, raiders, deathclaws, and that's about it. When you send a dweller to explore the wastelands (Basically, you just wait for hours and they will find goodies and deal with enemies, but it's only text based) they mention mirelurks, dogs, yao guai and super mutants, but they do not appear physically in the game. So, your worst nightmares are going to be the radscorpions, feral ghouls and deathclaws, and as far as I know, the first two aren't all that threatening in the main series.
I personally like the artstyle, it's pretty much the retro style that you see in the trailer of Fallout 3, with your dwellers pretty much looking like Vault Boy. I like the visuals, and I think the Power Armor, as scary as it is in the main series, looks rather cute in a way in here.
TL;DR
It's a nice game if you like idling, it's one of those games where you check what your vault/dwellers are up to daily, and then you move on with your day. It's fun, I would give it a try, but I would recommend not spending money in this game yet. With its dreaded vault wipe bug, and purchases only applying to a single save file, it feels like you aren't getting much out of your cash. Plus, everything can be obtained in game, even if it's a bit grindy.

“Follow protocol and we’ll all make it out alive,” says a boss character in one of Hotline Miami’s later missions. It’s a perfectly reasonable thing for him to say to his henchmen. All who hear him probably think it’s good advice, wisdom dispensed to survive an impending attack by you, a relentless killer. So they follow orders and do what they’ve been trained to do. Some stand with guns, some patrol rooms with knives, and all are ready to slash and shoot and murder the intruder in a bloody font of insta-death. Yet none who heard the order appreciate its irony. They don’t comprehend that by following protocol they follow the game rules that you've learned to overcome, and that by complying with their boss set themselves up to have their brains splattered against the wall and organs spilled across the floor.
Dennaton Games’ Hotline Miami is stuffed with moments like this that stir up identity and purpose into a neon-lashed, ultraviolent, self-aware skewering of video game conventions and the nature of entertainment. Lynchian scenes of surrealist intrigue pop up right at the very beginning as masked figures ridicule you about events they never explain, immediately and succinctly establishing a sense of distrust. The nonstop flux of pinks and purples wrapped around the edges of every playable area, the grainy waves washing across the retro visuals and sublime soundtrack where reverb bleeds from fat synths over electronic beats aren’t solely for style, but mesh perfectly with the sense of worming paranoia established through the dialogue, amplifying Hotline Miami’s lonely, dreamlike qualities, where nothing is necessarily certain aside from the promise of a gore-splattered spectacle when a stage is complete.
To compound this sense of distrust, every mission is based on a lie; a phone message asking you to kill for false reasons. There are a few explorable non-combat spaces and each feels like a tease. You have an apartment with an old video game console on the ground. You pick up pizza boxes and VHS tapes and eventually gain a roommate and you can never interact with any of them in a significant way. They are all background elements. They are initially framed as non-essential. The only way to truly interact with the world is to kill. Such is the case with many games, yet few call out the inanity of it so bluntly.
Before a mission begins you put on a mask. Each confers gameplay bonuses and further obfuscates your identity to place emphasis on what you do, not who you are. The overhead perspective serves a similar dual purpose. It enables you to look across vast stretches of each playable area where enemies wait behind doors and breakable windows to kill you in a fraction of a second. The perspective allows  you to plan how to move, from which angle to fire a shotgun or toss a knife or stun an enemy by opening a door behind him just as he passes then proceed to wreck his face against the floor. The perspective also dehumanizes your targets by presenting them as only heads and shoulders and weapons, an effect strengthened by their pixelated appearance. It’s not until they’re dead and their bodies sprawl across the ground in full view with blood pooling about them that they feel human and, maybe for a moment, you feel a twitch of remorse.
Yet whatever regret you may have over brutally and relentlessly murdering is immediately neutered as Hotline Miami flashes a giant score bonus over each fresh corpse. Kill multiple people quickly and you’ll build combos. With enough speed and efficiency and recklessness you’ll amass higher scores and unlock more masks and weapons and receive better ratings at each mission’s end. The gameplay is kind of stealth but mostly quick action. You wait around hallway corners for an enemy to walk away then sprint around the corner with a crowbar, break his head, toss the crowbar at the shotgun-carrying enemy in the room’s corner to score a stun, throat rip the guy who just wandered in then pounce on the still-stunned foe to punctuate the spree with a burst of gore, and in those moments of blood-soaked success feel a rush of satisfaction because it could have gone so horribly wrong.
Hotline Miami doesn’t only share the same audio-visual themes of Nicolas Winding Refn’s Drive (the director is specifically thanked in the credits), but also the same kind of startling ease of transition between life and death. In general, if you get hit, you die, and if you hit an enemy, they die. The game auto-saves after you change floors of the buildings you assault, but each floor needs to be cleared without making a mistake. Resetting is quick and encouraged, much in the same way as Trials HD or Super Hexagon. Mess up and you can instantly return to the action armed with more knowledge of enemy positions and map layout. Even after you learn everything about a stage, when you respawn enemies may move in a slightly different way and they may not carry the same weapons, so memorization alone won’t result in success. There’s always an element of chaos in the action that parallels the puzzling tendrils of the story. Stringing together a continuous combo throughout a stage often requires frantic improvisation and prevents the action from suffering from too much predictability.
More depth is added through the way Dennaton handles sound. Bats and crowbars are quiet, but guns draw attention. You could run into a room and try to cut everything apart with a shotgun, but in a populated stage it’ll bring in others, some of whom may flatten you before they’re even visible with an unavoidable burst of bullets. To get around this you can target an enemy before entering a room, you can silently fling your weapon to temporarily knock him out, which may give you enough time to punch a patrolling enemy, steal his weapon and murder them both without alerting anyone else. Getting better at effectively juggling these variables, managing sound and line of sight and speed, is a rapid, noticeable process, and the sense of reward for efficiently cutting down all lethal threats is significant because there’s room to slay with custom style.
As the body count rises, the sense of disconnection with the tragedy of what’s happening onscreen grows. You crave more kills to again feel that rush of just barely surviving and seeing those big, flashy numbers burst across the screen with Peggle-like splendor. You begin to think more and more like the serial killer you’re playing and find delight in the purity of the task, not the implications. Yet for all the ways Hotline Miami seems to needlessly pop skulls and spray blood, it does so for a reason.
It’s hinted throughout the early non-combat scenes that bookend missions that at first seem so disposable. Violence begins to infect what initially seems to be a wearying, comically dull routine where you run errands following a successful killing spree. Even as the world around you is corrupted by the grotesque and shop owners carry on disturbingly reasonable conversations with corpses bleeding at their feet, you don’t react. You proceed as usual, mission to mission, a process suggestive of a far deeper and troubling psychosis, again thickening the layers of dishonesty in Hotline Miami’s presentation and strengthening its motivating sense of intrigue. Direct and implied lies are piled up until fantasy and reality are inextricably bound, and Dennaton finds ingenious ways of integrating interactivity and story development to keep you directly involved in the process. While the characters rattle the bars of their virtual prisons, driven to discover some kind of truth under the apparent pointlessness of their missions, Hotline Miami’s hyperactive pacing never slackens as it continually offers the same solutions to all the existential issues raised: keep killing, keep playing.

Wowser. A story-telling masterpiece, from start to finish. Unbelievably well-written and smartly executed, Life is Strange will pull you into its incredibly gripping tale. Like a good book or TV series, you will not want to put it down. Not since The Last Of Us or The WItcher 3 have I experienced something that has sparked such an emotional response. Be warned, this is an 18+ game, and it will touch upon themes that will make you feel uncomfortable, sick, happy, sad, hateful. It puts Telltale games to shame. You will look at the store page and probably think this is just another teenage drama walking simulator, but it's so much more than that. It takes time to pick up the pace, but like any good story, it needs to build up its events leading to its inevitable conclusion. It manages to craft a deep story with layered characters to near perfection. Life is Strange proves again that the videogame industry can push the boundaries of story-telling even further.

If this is not enough to get you to buy the game, the gameplay involves you solving numerous puzzles using a time mechanic, but that's all I can say without spoiling one of the best aspects of Life is Strange. The puzzles are very unique and challenging, but never unfair. Graphics are ok, considering the art-style is a kind of water-colored paint. Playing this game feels like walking through an art museum.

In short, give this game a try. If you like a good story, you will not regret this. It's mature themes might hit you personally, but it will surely make you think about your life and the people around you. No game has ever made me cry, but this one came so damn close.

I've only been able to play survival mode so far but have been having a blast doing so.  It certainly requires team-work, especially in the final waves, to take down the hordes of bigger dinos before they smash your base.
Credit based weapons and augments are available between waves though in some cases getting back across the map in time can be difficult if you happen to be stuck on foot.  There is also a teleport device available by pressing 5, but if you've burned it up and it's on cooldown, hopefully you are paired with other players that realize this and stop to pick you up in one of the multi-seat vehicles.
The amount of upgrades available really let you customize your class uniquely from other players.  I played medic in all matches and each time was different.  In one case I was able to get an augment that allowed me use of other class' weapons, very cool.
The controls were something I still fumbled over with at the end of the night (even after remapping keybinds).  Keys 1-4 seemed to have no visible use for changing weapons, althought 4 does bring up high-cost weapons like turrets once purchased, and 5 brings up a teleport device to return you to base quickly (found completely by accident on my part).  Scroll Wheel does little to help with weapon switching as it will only cycle your primary and secondary weapons.  For the case of a medic, there is a 3rd healing gun which I had to bind to Mouse3 just to have fast access to it.  Quick switch on Q had me repeatedly bombing my team with grenades.  Out of habit from other FPS games, I've become accustomed to subconciously hitting this to go between primary and last used secondary which never included grenades.  In this game however, grenades are looped in.  I'd like to see them removed from the quick switch cycle.  These are minor adjustments the devs can make if other players felt the same way I do.
Lastly, the AI of the infantry dinos (raptors) seems like it could use some work.  They are way to easy to take down in packs as they come at you line up in a row with no signs of deviating when being shot at.  It was effortless to rack up killing sprees and higher on them.  There were also times entire packs of raptors would run right passed me with one of my teammates firing on them; not very raptor like.  The larger dinos seemed to have more intelligence as they would knock me away from the group often and keep us divided by distances.  I would see the T-Rex target snipers by hurling rocks, so I wondered if the devs spent some time tuning them with actual objectives.
Other than these minor encumbrances, this game is fun and I look forward to playing more.

So I've just started playing this game on a mac (2.9Ghz i5, GTX 660M 512, 8GB RAM) which lies in the medium-spec range for this game and it is frankly nearly unplayable. Even on the lowest settings in a small window this game has continual stutter and input latency, so much so that surprisingly I can't find it in me to continue (considering I have been playing games on a 5 year old dual core laptop for years now).
The tutorial was very badly put together - while it showed all the aspects of gameplay, it was a staccato of hints that continually broke the action and limitations on what the player could do (you could only do combat actions which were expressly commanded to you) which seems strange when a player is trying to learn about the control scheme.
The gratuitous nudity which starts off the first cutscene was unneccesary imo - alluding to his encounter the night before would have been sufficient, while Geralts clothed form highlights the inequal bias in the developer's use of the naked body (which is sadly a product of our time in which nudity is fine - as long as it isn't a man). This view is supported as one of the top 25 mods on the nexus is to cover up the offending article. I feel I must state that I am in no-way a prude but I think that games should be forward looking, and can be even if they cover material set in bygone ages.
The kings narrative in the opening siege scene is quite frankly boring and had to skip through much of it (which I never do in a frist playthrough) and while I have only just started and don't feel compelled to continue. I'm just glad I got this during the 80% sale.
Perhaps my views have been influenced by the sub-optimal performance of this game on a relatively powerful computer, because it does have interesting combat and character progression and I would have liked to have been drawn in by this game. Perhaps I will attempt to play this game in the future, but for now farewell.
