There is art, and there are games.  Type:Rider is the former and not the latter.  If one were to call it a game, one would have to admit that it is an extremely frustrating game due to the unresponsive controls, especially when jumping.  Making the problem worse is the "wall jump" mechanic; pressing towards a wall and jumping will let you wall jump the other way. . . but the nature of the controls is such that you'll often wall jump to the left when trying to leap a single step to the right.  There is a Tetris-inspired level that is especially terrible because of this.
On the other hand, the game is extremely beautiful.  Stark iconography on top of distinctive level design mixed with an environment-specific soundtrack make for a pleasing experience (except when you have to jump).  The exploration of the history of typography is also fascinating; and for me, a little sad.  Seeing the thousands of years flit by with ideas replaced by ideas causes one to both be humble and to reflect.
--- Two Circles ---
This is the story of two circles that rolled together through time. One always rolled on the ground while the other rolled in the air above, floating directly above the first. Which did which?  It does not matter: sometimes it was one, sometimes the other. What is important is that they were two that went everywhere as one, for together they formed a Colon.
How they met I do not know. All I know is that it was during a time of great experimentation and exploration. Renaissance
the period of rebirth, when beauty and the civilized soul were discovered once more. Chiaroscuro
the bold contrast between light and dark. Sfumato
without boundaries, edges like smoke. These words and more defined a new world that seemed to dawn brighter than the sun. And as a Colon the circles delighted together
in the hope, in the glory, in the splendid possibilities of the coming future.
"Shall we keep going?" asked one. "Of course!" the other said excitedly. The two circles rolled forward together with eagerness and ease.
Time passed - as it does - and the world changed - as it does. What did not change was the demand for a Colon, for there were always new lists to enumerate, new words to define. But for the first time a darkness fell over their service. Heretic
an individual whose beliefs run counter to those approved by the authorities. Inquisition
a tribunal with widespread powers and prerogatives to root out undesirables. Auto-da-fé
the public penance of apostates prior to the execution of their sentences.
"What is this?" one asked. "What is happening? Has the world always been thus? Have we been blind for all this time?"
"It will pass," the other said, hiding the uncertainty in its voice. "It must. But only if we keep rolling forward. Together." So they rolled onwards through a world that seemed increasingly unkind
colonization, conquistador, pandemic. But instead of retreating, the shadows lengthened even further
guillotine, coup d'état, manifest destiny. And the circles found that they no longer rolled as easily as before.
Then came the decades of constant war
the Somme, the Marne, Stalingrad, Dresden, Hiroshima, Auschwitz. Blitzkrieg
a bolt strike whose electric speed throws the opponent into panicked disarray. Ethnic cleansing
the destruction of a group of people based on racial or cultural criteria. Unrestricted warfare
a strategy conducted with the understanding that civilian targets and military targets are one and the same. And the lists of the dead, a
followed by a series of graven names that never seemed to end, a list incomprehensible and nearly meaningless by virtue of its very scale.
The circles rolled on, together still, but now in silence, slower and slower.
There came the day when the circle rolling on the ground stopped and realized that something was different. Confused, it looked all about, and the change was so obvious that it could not understand it at first. The space above was empty, suffocatingly empty; and what did that mean?
Recognition came slow, but once it did the circle felt half-drowned with terror. It quickly retreated, searching behind until finally found the other circle. The other circle was motionless and sunken into the ground.
"Up," the circle urged, "up."
There was no answer.
"Up," it said again, "up!" and now it could not hide a quaver, the crack that revealed fears it did not dare voice.
For agonizing moments, silence. Then, a whisper: "Leave me."
"Leave you?" The circle could only laugh, the idea was so ridiculous. "How? I cannot."
"You must. I am too tired to go on. I have seen too much and I do not wish to witness any more. I want to stop. A Period marks an ending, does it not? Very well; leave me and let me become a Period. Let me end."
The frightened circle was left speechless. It wanted to plead, chastise, cajole:
But it could not. For in truth it understood how the other felt because it, too, felt that way. And the exhaustion it had denied for so long suddenly descended like a shroud. "I, too, will stay then."
The tired circle laughed. "Two circles on the ground. One too many for a Period, one too few for an Ellipsis. What will we be?"
"We will be two circles waiting together." The circle's voice, hesitant at first, started to grow bold. "Perhaps someday we will be a Colon again; perhaps someday a third will join us and we will continue as an Ellipsis. But I do not intend to let us end. I do not intend for either of us to become a Period. If, that is -" The circle stopped, scared to say the next words. But it was necessary. "If you will allow me to stay by your side."
For long moments the other circle said nothing.
Then it rolled over to the circle and touched it once, ever so slightly. And that was enough.
I do not know what became of the two circles. I hope that they found their strength eventually and rolled onwards through time. I hope that they found new beauty to celebrate, new wonders to lighten their souls.
But hope is less than a shadow of a dream. I know that it is just as likely that they lie in the ground still.
However I do know that wherever they are, they are together. I know this because my heart tells me so, and I do not wish to believe that my heart can lie. And that is comfort enough for me.

If you don't cringe at the thought of a game based solely on exploration, then you could safely quit reading this review and go buy The Music Machine now. This narrative psychological horror adventure is easily one of the better examples of the genre.
It is very difficult to explain how eerie and yet strikingly beautiful the monochromatic artstyle is, because neither the videos nor the screenshots do it justice. Simply walking within this world is a fascinating experience worth the tiny pricetag. Accompanied by a brilliant soundtrack and a minimalistic sound design that highlight the atmosphere, you will for once actually not mind wandering aimlessly around and staring fascinated at the shadows of the trees and the patterns on the walls.
And yes, you will occasionally wander aimlessly around not knowing what to do next, so some patience and some observation skills are required. Thankfully this is one of the few walking exploration games that is mostly accessible, even if you aren't a great fan of the genre. Despite my best efforts to become confused on where I was and how to proceed, I was most of the time pleasantly surprised when I accidentally stumbled onto what turned out to be the obvious next step.
I am very unwilling to divulge anything about the story, because I was glad to have read very little about it before playing. The game introduces its characters through small snippets of dialogue that pack a few shocking punches yet are often quite entertaining in their oddness. I especially appreciated how beautifully tight the dialogues were despite (and sometimes because of) their occasional melodramatic crescendos. Suffice to say that, if you don't enjoy playing games that are trying their best to make you profoundly uncomfortable, this may not be the game for you. The Music Machine revels in the existential perversity of its world and the troubling dysfunctional relationship of its (surprisingly well realised) protagonists. It is ultimately a story of two broken people that are almost too engrossed in their personal dramas to be actually shocked by the horror of a world crafted by perverted supernatural entities. And despite its occasional flaws (that include some pacing issues and also some glaring typos that are hard to excuse in narratively driven games), I was very intrigued by the well-rounded and well-explored story, enough to try and uncover both endings.
All in all a very interesting game, unique, memorable, intriguingly written and visually stunning. If you're at all curious, don't hesitate.

Set in a grim, post-apocalyptic world, Wasteland 2 is an RPG with an old-school design. It is full of stats, skill-checks, turn-based combat and quests.

- Graphically it isn't that impressive.
tldr; Very meaty, old-school RPG. Solid but unspectacular.

First and foremost, while I write this, I only have 3 hours played in this game. Having said that I feel I've played enough to write this review.
This game can be quite fun. Provided you are in a balanced server ( not always the case ) and you not only have a Commander that knows what they're doing, but also your team is working together to win. This doesn't mean you can't learn anything from a round where the teams are stacked against you, just that you more than likely will not win that round. No problem though, you can find a new server in no time. Also some servers seem to be "Rookie Friendly" so that helps.
If you're really interested in learning how to play I'd suggest playing the "Training" ( Tutorial ) the game provides at the main menu, after booting up the first time. It's not so much for some one who hasn't ever played an FPS before, but rather to learn how the teams ( Marine or Alien ) work, along with weapons, upgrades, what your Commander can do for you, etc. However, if this is your first FPS it will teach you how to play as well.
You might find at first you'd rather play Marine because it is familiar to you, that's fine. I did. However playing as Alien has it's benefits too and can be quite fun - whether you like to ambush your enemy or rush them like a rhino, I think you'll find an alien ( given the scenario ) where you can do such things.
All in all, despite my small amount of time playing, I'd say this game can be a lot of fun. It might take a little bit of time to get the basics down or do some server browsing to get in a game that's balanced and every one is ready to win, but that's really not a big deal. Also, this game does have a bit to offer in the Workshop, so if you find yourself wanting a new crosshair for your rifle or shotgun, make sure to check out what's offered!

In the game you steer two (invisibly joined) dots through landscapes, inspired by history and fonts. You collect letters, asterisks and ampersands. Every asterisk unlocks a page about history of typography. The two dots can only move left and right and jump, but as they are two connected dots, it makes for a - sometimes frustating - challenge to overcome typical platformer challenges, like moving letter-shaped platforms, barriers, pitfalls etc.
The game is rather short, it took me abut 4 hours to beat all the levels, collect every letter, unlock and read all the educative material and beat the secret level. Considering the price of the game, that is fair.

There is a second story going on which is only slightly interesting, but pretty much everything is explained to you in detail by a character you meet halfway through.  You do not discover anything by yourself.  There are a few notes laying around for you to read in the first level but they don't tell much.  You will be walking around in mostly empty areas with nothing interesting to inspect, no clues or anything like that.  Just boxes and crates most of the time.  There are a few "puzzles" but they are insultingly simple.
Some of the environments are interesting to look at or a bit creepy, but calling it "psychological horror" is a HUGE stretch.
I got this game for $1.79 so it's not a huge deal but to be honest it's not even worth that.  There are flash games that have a better story, prettier environments, and better gameplay than this.

Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae is a 3rd person hack n slash/brawler/spectacle fighter/katana simulator with a name that almost no one outside of Japan can pronounce or even translate. So instead let’s just stick with pantsu may cry because you basically play as Vergil, the level format is similar to bloody palace and like the 4th game most of the budget and development time went into the combat system and nothing else.
The story is… there… occasionally, you play as Misa, a sword priestess cutting down waves of demons as she tries to catch her classmate who has been corrupted by the demon sword, that’s about all there is to it. There’s nothing interesting about the plot but it’s so simple and very rarely rears its head that it never becomes a detriment to the game.
The combat on the other hand is the sole reason to buy this game. Misa’s move set revolves entirely around her katana, her hand to hand attacks charge up a bar that allows her to use standard katana attacks as well as more powerful attacks with more range that have to be charged. The stand out superstar of this combat system however is her sheathing mechanic.
If you’ve watched enough anime in your life, you may be well aware of the cliché of sword fights where the finishing blow only appears once the winner sheaths their sword. Pantsu may cry translates this trope wonderfully into gameplay, if an enemy takes enough damage they start flashing red, Misa can then sheath her sword causing them to take more damage as well dropping health and spirit money that is used to upgrade her combat. As well as being as flashy as hell, it’s quite useful for staggering enemies as well as getting health without going through the effort of killing enemies, in fact enemies/bosses that would previously block Misa’s attacks without staggering can be stunned and juggled once they start flashing red which provides players an opportunity to go ballistic on an enemy that use to be a pain in their side.
There is no level design, you fight enemies in waves on a circular platform with an environment that occasionally change between fights, but just like the story that just means it doesn’t interfere. Most of the enemies and bosses are petty uninteresting with the exception of Suzuka, Misa’s classmate, who makes a great final boss with a fairly deep move set with attacks that have similar starting animations making them difficult to telegraph.
My one gripe with the combat is that there is no lock-on, so with no real method to focus on a single target, some of Misa’s attacks will go in a completely different direction than intended, also some attacks don’t string together, there are times when there’s that awkward pause between combos because the attack you inputted requires your katana to be sheathed, it’s an unnecessary nuance that convinces you to switch between hand to hand and katana attacks but it’s very minor and might not even be noticed on a 1st playthrough.
This game doesn’t have the depth of other hack n slash games such as Devil may cry and anything platinum makes, but it’s a £7 game that lasts around 4 hours and it’s great to play in between games. I hope this sheathing mechanic carries on to other games and I’ll gladly recommend it to anyone provided they’re aware that the combat is the only part of substance to the game.

is the sibling game to go alongside with
, David Szymanski's previous game. Combined together, they form a most beautiful, sorrowful yet elegant story. When I finished
, I felt a bit blinded to a deeper truth behind the happenings of the game. After I played
, everything falls into its intended place to portray a scene that I won't soon forget.
As the game starts, our "characters" arrive a forested island on a day break. We meet Haley and Quintin, the 13 year old girl and the 34 year old vengeful ghost that possessed Haley's body to find a satisfactory method of killing her. We soon find out that Quintin dragged Haley there to go after a murderer with conflicting ideas in mind. We start exploring the island while witnessing their exchanged dialogues. The more we explore, the more we learn about them, and the truth of this beautiful yet uncanny island. Suffice to say - to avoid major spoilers - something's really off, maybe something beyond human comprehension.
The whole game is designed in Unity engine, with the sole usage of monochromatic scenes: the contrast of a single lush color over black shadows, and voila! I present you the most beautiful, strong and eerie atmosphere ever! Forged with a fleetingly eerie narrative and accompanied with thrilling background sounds and music,
promises a sublime experience for 2 hours. The scenes that we encounter feel right out of a strong acid trip, with cosmological symbolisms under. Details within worlds are crafted to be wondrously allegoric, as mental associations of the human mind with an alien interpretation. If this is not art, I do not know what it could be.
The character contrasts between Haley and Quintin are done masterfully, if I may say. Their perceptions, expectations and world view are presented as sharp conflicts in written dialogue with nuances so tender, even though there is neither voice acting, nor visual character design - since this is a first person camera game - they come alive as characters. This is incredibly hard to accomplish since there is nothing else beside a written narrative to enact them. You suddenly find yourself worrying for Haley, or wishing the best for Quintin.
Let's talk about the gameplay. It takes the tried tradition of WASD and your mouse, nothing complicated. There are some very basic puzzles and a story for you to witness. There is no actual combat element common in horror games. Only an elaborate narrative and exploration, so yes, it can be categorized as a walking simulation with some adventure elements. The horror of the game is carefully crafted with an atmospheric expectancy of "something ominous about to happen", and yes, the ominous happens... Don't worry, the game saves your progress automatically when you quit.
For 2 hours,
invites you to take seat, and ask questions. Ask about religion, about society, about morality, about dynamics of power for men, and creatures beyond. What is creation? What is beauty? What means to be alive? I bet you already have your own ideas anyhow, but you might get surprised on what this gem has to offer you.

When you mix together a great two-character drama based entirely on dialogues, a bunch of rather empty walking simulation levels, and a visual style that murders your retina… you get The Music Machine.
The Music Machine is a walking simulator exploration game with a hint of Silent Hill style suspension horror and a great dose of character drama between the two protagonists: Haley, a 13-year old girl, and Quintin, the ghost of a middle-aged bachelor who now controls her body on the intent of killing her. To do so, they travel to a derelict island, where they find a strange temple organ which teleports them to a few desolate alien worlds.
Their banter is the high point of the game. It not only manages to tell their backstory without resorting to long plot dumps, but it is also a good tool to keep up the suspension. Unlike the supposed plot about the heavenly world builders; it feels like their story is cryptic only to mask that it makes no sense.
For a game, The Music Machine is… not pleasant. The starting island is hard to navigate and you may miss half of the dialogues by accidentally stumbling up on the way forward. The alien worlds are thankfully short, but they are empty. And finally, the visual style may look especially great on storefront images, but actually seeing this two-colour high-contrast style in motion will physically hurt your eyes.

I have very mixed feelings on this one. I didn't play the first Wasteland back in the day, but I did grow up on Fallout, Baldur's Gate, and the other big CRPGs of the 90s and early 2000s. Consequently, I was a Kickstarter backer for this along with the likes of Divinity: Original Sin and Pillars of Eternity. I'm very fond of those sort of in depth CRPGs and really want to like this game. Unfortunately, I don't think Wasteland 2 holds up as well as its Kickstarter RPG bretheren.
Party Creation and Skills
Simply put, character creation is way too fiddly, with little room for interesting options. Attributes are pretty poorly balanced with some obviously superior choices. There are a ton of skills available, but they're just not very interestingly done. Many of them are extremely similar and feel like they could have been easily consolidated without losing anything. Each one is pretty much completely isolated from both the other skills and from the character's attributes and the only thing that matters is whoever has the highest skill. Consequently, in the vast majority of cases it simply doesn't matter who has a given skill, just that someone in the party does. Characters end up having little personality because I could just as easily swap almost any of the skills around and it wouldn't make much of a difference at all. Compounding this is the fact that with seven party members and a bit of planning it's not hard to cover pretty much every important skill. There's a perk system, but most of the benefits are minor at best and most characters will probably grab the same good ones anyways.
Consequently, I'm left feeling like I didn't actually make any interesting choices or tradeoffs, I just did a bunch of busywork to ensure I'd be able to do everything during the course of the game.
Exploration
I feel like I spent most of the game waiting for my guys to run from one side of the map to the other. All of your skills effectively amount to opening containers or enabling environmental objects. So, most of the exploration amounts to talk to an NPC, exhaust their dialogue options, and either fight someone or open the container that has the thing they need while running back and forth over areas that take way too long to traverse. There are a some interesting choices and options scttered throughout, but they're limited.
I had a hard time getting into the setting. It tries to balance grim and gritty gruff military men with guns in a horrible world with wacky, mostly 80s pop culture non sequiters and just didn't quite work for me. Everything just ended up feeling kinda isolated and inorganic. It doesn't help that a lot of the humor is purely referential. For example, early in the game you might come across a character named "A Boy Named Sue". Everyone very conspicuously points this out in their dialogue, but the writing never actually does anything else with it. It doesn't add any interesting characterization, there's no twist, it's just the game saying "hey, we listened to a Johnny Cash song!"
It also doesn't help that there are a ton of minor annoyances that build up over time. For example, finding the item you need for a quest can mean opening the inventories of each of your seven party memebers and carefully searching for it among the largely nondescript junk you've accumulated. It's the kind of thing that's not a dealbreaker in itself, but contributes to a feeling of overall frustration.
Combat
Everything else could be easily overlooked if the game had a good combat system. Unfortunately, it just doesn't come together very well. I had just finished an XCOM game when I started my playthrough and Wasteland 2 suffers quite a bit from the comparison. For the most part your guys are limited to pretty much just moving and shooting. The presence of cover complicates things a bit and aimed shots, explosives, and skills add a slight bit of variety, but the vast majority of the time you're simply moving into range of an enemy and shooting them.
There just isn't a lot of room for strategy or thinking. It pretty much amounts to throwing the stats of my guys against the enemy and seeing the result. That could still work if there were a more interesting character building system behind it, but that falls flat as well. When I won it didn't feel like I played much of a role and when I lost it didn't feel like there was much I could have done differently.
Conclusion
I really, really want to like Wasteland 2 a lot more than I do. I love the kind of CRPGs it's harkening back to and on paper the game does a lot right. But, if I'm being honest I spent the latter half of my playthrough just kind of wanting it to be over. I still have high hopes for the future of the franchise (enough to have backed Wasteland 3, in fact), but I'd have a hard time recommending Wasteland 2 to any but the most hardened CRPG veteran craving an unapologetically old school experience. Pillars of Eternity and Divinity: Original Sin do a much better job of capturing the spirit of those classics while providing a more modern experience.

A masterpiece for fans of the CRPG genre.
Full Disclosure: I backed this product on Kickstarter and have been playing it on and off for over 3 years.
I finally got around to dedicating a solid chunk of time to Wasteland 2 and exploring a great deal of its content. At over 100 hours played (for some reason steam says 12.6 hours) I've experienced most of what the game has to offer.
This game is a true call back to old school CRPGs. The atmosphere of the game is fantastic- the wasteland is a mess and it feels like the world after nuclear war. I love the graphics and artwork in the game as well.
Combat is the strong point in this game. Developing a squad, figuring out the skills and weapons that compliment each other, and the tactics for each battle make the game better.
Problem solving: There are many ways for most quests and problems to be solved in the game. Some only have one solution (e.g. a skill check), but those are the exception rather than the rule. Your choices impact the ending of the game (think Fallout 1 and 2 style). Each way you handle quests can impact other quest outcomes or paths down the road. The game is purposefully ambiguous and it is not always clear what the outcome of your choices will be. This is a strength in my opinion.
Exploration:
Excellent. You are rewarded for taking risks and exploring more.
Difficulty:
Brutal start up difficulty. This game pulls no punches and throws you in the deep end up front. Make the wrong choices for your squad and it can be worse. I list this as a con because I am writing this review from the perspective of the average gamer. There are no tutorials, no wading into the shallow water here. Personally, I loved this! I spent a good 10-15 hours tweaking my skills and characters through several playthroughs before I got a mix I was happy with. I really enjoy doing this, but for many it could be a turn off. There is a very steep learning curve with this game.
Voice Overs:
The dialogue system as far as your responses and the detail is great.... but voice overs are terrible. The main villan is one of the worst. The actor constantly says different things than the text in game.
Character depth:
I found the characters early in the game to be really fleshed out. As you progress, the depth of characters diminishes, until very late in the game. To me this made some areas feel far more developed than others.
Dead end quests:
I found that I got caught in many quests hitting a dead end because I failed a skill check or killed a character that became relavent later on. Not an issue for me, I think its a plus, but its a warning for others.
Overall this game is a classic.... it mirrors the old classic CRPG genre magnificantly. This game is a masterpiece for fans of this genre.

Alright so I have not done a review for a game before however I will try to be fair in my review of this game.
I will try to keep a specific format and there will be a tldr at the bottom.
Middle Earth Shadow of War has been one of my favorite releases of this year. Being a fan of mature and realistic fantasy, especially Lord of the Rings, this game holds a lot of both fun and appreciation for the effort that went into it. I will seperate this review into six categories, in chronological order; Game design/gameplay, world design/exploration/progression, story(spoiler free), art, music/vibe, and economy. For each of these I will list off the pros and cons that go with them;
Okay so Game Design. There is a lot to talk about in the games design, from combat with both the main controlled character and that of the orcs on the sides of the player character and the enemy, as well as the games most marketed feature, the nemesis system.
Combat in this game can be fun, however it is not without flaws:
-Pros: As Talion combat can feel very unique. You have several different ways to fight and you really rely on the enviroment. The learning curve is not too heavy, and at most difficulties you will be scanning the environment around you to combat different orcs. This awareness of your surroundings and your ability to adapt and capitalize on a variety of different mechanics and tools at your disposal makes combat feel a lot more interactive and appealing to continues with. For orcs vs orcs combat may vary based on the intelligence of the ai for that orc and their own skills, and finding orcs who excel at either form of combat or even both definitely blends well with other parts of the game. Combat never overly bores me, but it still has its flaws;
-Cons: The main issue of having fun with combat as talion vs orcs is that after a good while of gameplay, most orcs are all the same. There are six different archetypes of orcs, and it does get rather repetitive. It is better that it should be simplistic in this case, and for certain there should not just be 10s of types of orcs you all have to be aware of how to fight, but after a while all you have to understand is what that orcs specific strengths/weaknesses are and how to generally fight them. This isn't too great of a detriment to the fun of it, but combat with orcs will certainly just end up repetitive over time and you won't be really playing the game for a unique plethora of enemies to fight, you'll likely be playing it for the nemesis system. Orc versus orc is not really an exception either, in fact in orc vs orc I would argue is even less varied. Combat varience is not the games strongsuit and as I said not what most people will play and stay for, instead it will be for the most marketed attraction of the game, the nemesis system;
-The nemesis system, if you've not heard, can be generally explained as 'your enemies and allies will remember what you do and react accordingly'. Among the things this game accomplishes well, the nemesis system is certainly one of them. Using a complex series of ai this system allows a sense of realism and immersion with the orcs in the game, having their reactions to the things you do give a sense of personality. For the pros of the system;
-Pros: The nemesis system in game allows you to find orcs you really like and forge a bond with them. Not many games can boast of a relation between you and the npcs in them at a level of depth such as this, and its a breath of fresh air for innovation of game immersion in the industry. Most people play with this system in order to try and get different orcs of different personalities whether by using the 'shame' mechanic or 'cheat death' mechanic. Definitely a system many would love other games to have, though the complexity of the ai required to create such a system does rather limit it to larger developers.
-Cons: Repetition, that is that after a while, mostly concerning late game, you will find that there unique orcs, names, and personalities are far and few between as most spawning will probably be similar to others you have already found. Frustration can also be a very big thing since if you lose an orc you really liked, and they don't respawn, it is very annoying.
World Design/Exploration/Progression: The game itself is very large, and the design of the world is of course based off of Tolkien's own, yet not every part of it holds up to such a standard. Exploration is not what you seek in this game and the progression system is, while not being too bad, is not the best either.
-Pros: The broader world of the game definitely looks and feels nice, there are parts where it looks good and finding your way around the five different maps can be cool. The game does not have too high of a learning curve and the progression system is fine, certainly not terrible but nothing which feels too rewarding or fun TO progress through.
-Cons: The maps, honestly, are not that varied. You will not be looking too intensely at every detail of them, care for exploring any hidden parts of it, or really spend time caring about the place you are in beyond another area to play with the nemesis system in. As for progression, after a certain point you are only getting skills you don't already want in your build and won't likely use often, meaning leveling up doesn't feel rewarding after the point you have all you want out of it, and progression can require a lot of grind and time.
Story: For those who care for the story of a game in Lord of the Rings, you may be disappointed in some ways. This game certainly holds true to the Lord of the Rings and respects the series, however the writing may fall flat in some areas.
-Pros: It feels like LotR! This game, as I said, definitely respects the series and the writing, while not being done by Tolkien, is still decent enough that you can be engaged with the games story. You will likely enjoy several characters and how they act and the story is indeed appealing to follow.
-Cons: Where the story falls flat, however, is in the predictability and development of some characters. I will not downright say that the story is bad, especially on the basis of it being a different righter, but there are for sure several stereotypes or predictable actions which some characters take. Character development mostly centralizes around Talion as well, so that other side characters really don't get used well, and I do understand that others do not like how some end up. Regardless the story is certainly fine and it holds its own as a good part of the game.
Art: The game looks very nice and is not too bad looking at low settings, but machine requirements can take away from the experience for those with low end computers.
-Pros: It can look very pretty and very realistic, especially with the 4k resolution pack(free) and you will likely not be disappointed with the look of the game.
-Cons: You can still play with a poor graphics card without lag, but to actually get high end graphics you need a really good one, so don't expect the game to look too good with a low end machine.
Music/Vibe:(gonna shorten it from here)
-Pros: Good atmosphere, nice to listen to
-Cons: Nothing outstanding, some tracks repeated from first game
Economy:
-Pros: Nothing too hard to grind for and no hidden percentages/terrible rng in place, not unfair
-Cons: Lootboxes exist, and while it certainly isn't pay2win as most lootbox orcs are not viable or interesting, they are still very unneeded and greedy.
TLDR: The game is fun, and for those who have enjoyed the first one they will enjoy this one, however it falls flat in several places and is riddled with flaws. If unsure don't buy for the full price, but if you have the money and its on sale, go for it, its not a game that will hurt most people to play.
Lastly, I trimmed a lot of fat in the review, and couldn't say everything, but I hope you found this review helpful! :)

It's a perfect 6 really.  Your average, boring open-world game.
The story is actually decent, if basic.  Lincoln is a badass character, but he might be a little too badass for his own good.  At first, the game is about taking down a ruthless mob boss, and Lincoln makes it very clear that he doesn't just want to kill him:  He wants to take down his entire organization, and claim it for himself.  ♥♥♥♥ing awesome right?  That's what I said when I heard it.  But it starts to get a little sarcastic when you find out managing territory is actually ♥♥♥♥ing annoying.  It's kind of hard to still want to kill the Antagonist when I'm busy managing the emotions of the three school children I'm divvying up my territory to.  This is the problem with a lot of open-world games, a story with no sense of timing, because it is second fiddle to the sidejobs the player is compelled to complete.
It's kind of like that Rick and Morty episode where Rick sets up a service to uncurse the Devils items, and then gets bored when he actually has to deal with Employees 401k's and♥♥♥♥♥♥  Except you don't get to light your store on fire in this game if you want to kill the mob boss.  You have to deal with at least one person getting progressively more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off as you don't give them territory.  And that person will most likely be Cassandra, because...
...The AI is awful, and you can take down an entire compound of 20 people with the sawed off shotgun, before upgrades.  Once again, Lincoln is too badass for his own good.  What Cassandra offers is gun upgrades, which you don't need.  Ammo can get tight, but that's about it.  You can always have ammo delivered to you.  So there's really no reason to give any territory to Cassandra other than you like her, and she is certainly more likeable than the Irish ♥♥♥♥ to your left.  But he gives explosives, and those CANNOT be found in other places, and are actually critical to some missions, so he gets to stay.  And Vito is the only actual Mafia looking guy in the game, so you obviously want to keep him around.
We have to ponder:  What do you call it when a game gives you multiple solutions to the same problem?  Hopefully you call it freedom, but sometimes that's just a fancy word for Easy.  Because it doesn't matter if you are going stealth, loud, explosive, or decide to just call in Vito's guys.  The game is pretty easy, and the only penalty for dying is losing half your cash, and Vito can deliver a banker to you on demand, so there is actually no punishment for dying.  I was even interrogating someone at one point while literally, not figuratively, literally 30 cops showed up.  What's the point of High-Nooning it if I'll just respawn with no heat on me?  This isn't Freedom, it's just giving you more tools to distract you from the fact that the game isn't even a game.  The only Freedom you could have is giivng up territories, and one of those options is basically picked for you (Thomas Burke, the man with the explosives).
And by the way, what is up with divvying up territory at all?  Because if Lincoln is the badass that can take an entire territory down by himself, why the ♥♥♥♥ does he need anybody else?  It doesn't seem worth it considering the percentage Lincoln gets from them.  Casssandra's starting income from her territory was something like $30,000?  $700 of that is for Lincoln.  Alright, now he really seems too badass.  Maybe he should get into something more obvious, that actually makes money, like boxing.  Or, I don't know, maybe let the Antagonist keep the territories, because you make a lot more from finding money in enemy territory than you do from actually owning the territory (apparently your guys ♥♥♥♥ing suck at making money).
None of that would be bad, of course, if killing bad AI was fun.  And I love stealth games, and most stealth games have horrible AI, so clearly I don't mind it.  But, for me personally, the only fun way to kill someone in this game is with a shotgun.  I don't know how, but they ♥♥♥♥ed up the shooting in this game, and Mafia 2 was praised for the way the environment reacted to the shooting.  Not this game.  Tommy Guns feel like pea shooters, and pistols ARE pea shooters.  Explosions are severely disappointing.  Even the "Brutal Takedowns" are ruined by the camera being shoved into some corner of the room.  The only thing that's fun is a shotgun, because it sends people flying, draws blood, and makes a hell of a sound.  Sniper Rifles are semi fun, but the big battles are mostly indoors.  It's not like you can go on the roof of a lot of places, even.
It gets worse:  Every territory has the same activities to take it over, and everytime you want to take it over, you have to go through an unskippable cutscene with some guy you'll talk to twice in your life, and it goes a little something like this:
"Oh, that Racket boss?  Yeah you'll have to do some stuff to get him to come out and stuff.  Why don't you break his stuff?  Of course you need to find out where his stuff is.  Interrogate his guys, particularly this guy, cause he's head of stuff."
You can't skip it.  You just have to sit there and listen for what you already know you need to do.  Then, you will go and kill people, sometimes blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, and you will wreck the Racket bosses business until they come out of hiding.  And they always do.  Thing is, they come out of hiding in a place you already were...
Yes, most territories have a large building with 20-something guys in it, and it is part of the Racket you are trying to take over, so you raid it.  You will come back to this exact same location with the exact same guards and fight through them, again, to get to the Racket leader.  This game was already repetitive enough.
If you were not on board when I said the drive of the story is killed by the gameplay, maybe now you can see how all of this adds up to your indifference of actually killing the Antagonist.  I didn't finish the game, guilty.
I could go on.  I could go on about how there are items unlocked with "favors," and you can do all the missions labeled favors, only to find out those weren't the favors they were actually talking about.
I could go on about how there are sidemissions to increase the income of your men (and in-turn, your income), but they are completely based around driving across the entire map and nothing more.
I could go on about how the blood comes in tiny, little, poorly-detailed spurts that would feel at home on a ps2 game.
I could go on about how, at no point in the game, do you ever feel like you are running your own organization.  And it's not because, as one reviewer said, "You're some black guy."  Lincoln could've been a very compelling character to run things.  It's because Lincoln doesn't run things.  He just picks who does run things.  The Scarface Videogame had more of an ownership feeling than this game does.
You don't even feel respected.  Hangar 13 has done a great job of showing the prejudices of the time.  Lincoln isn't just a token black character.  People talk to him differently.  They think of him differently.  There are shops that still say "No Colored's Allowed," and you can actually get in trouble if you are in them for too long.  But it's a little strange when you own half the city and you walk into a shop and they are like "What the ♥♥♥♥ are you doing here boy?"  Really?  You don't remember me killing everybody in the compound across the street?  Lincoln Clay?  Everyone is talking about me?
But this was a perfectly average 6.  A game that tries to be nothing more than driving to point A, to shoot guys A, before you move onto point B.  The shooting isn't great, but it might be comfort entertainment for someone who just wants to unwind.  But a game this repetitive and pointless, with little unlocks along the way, leaves you asking "Why did I play 20 hours of this?"

Time passes by so fast when you're having fun. And for me, this game is the kind of "this makes me want to smash my keyboard in anger, but I still want to play it!" fun. Difficult, but oh so rewarding when you complete it.
As the game is always generated randomly, you never know what bosses you will fight, what items there will be or what monsters will try to chase you down. Sometimes you can have a real lucky run, with powerful items, easy monsters and bosses that you can manage well. Other times the game simply hates you, giving you the worst upgrades along with the harder bosses. Some monsters will really play out unfairly on the screen, chasing you into a corner because your character took pills that made him walk too slow, other times they are shooting more projectiles than you can avoid.
The dungeons are also generated at random. You never know what you can expect behind that door. Is it worth the risk to perhaps find a reward? Maybe there will be some of those monsters you really hate. When you are at low health, it becomes even more important whether you want to risk getting killed by monsters or go to the boss room and hope for a somewhat easier challenge.
As the game is so random, it allows for a lot of replay value. You never know if you will have an easy or hard run. You never know what items you will have, so you can only make the best of it. You can't really prepare for much other than finally encountering mom. Oddly enough, I found the original encounter much harder than the one added in the expansion. It seems a bit backwards that the new content is much easier than the old.
I also find that the more you play this game, the more you eventually unlock, which leads to a lot more challenge and a lot more replay value. It keeps me going despite my moments of pure hulk rage. Some of the items you unlock can sometimes even make the game easier, depending on what items suits you better. Personally, I like the little dolls/characters that follows you around and adds their own shooting along with your own character.

It isn't really the story that moves the game along, but trying to survive in the dark world of evil monsters.

This game is a very satisfying 2D sidescrolling ARPG. The fact that one guy created almost everything in this game by himself is really impressive. For a $15 game, people should have no issues getting at least 10-20 hours of gameplay. This game has a great and unique art style, which is one of its strong points. The combat plays extremely well, and I ran into no issues using the mouse and keyboard. Some fights can be a little easy by spamming the parry ability, but the combat still requires you to dodge, and use your companions abilities to take on larger groups of enemies.
The voice acting was off in a few parts, and done really well in others but nothing that affects the quality of the game. There is a system where you can collect materials and a blueprint, and take them to the Blacksmith to be crafted which is cool, but I didn't take too much advantage of it.
There are a lot of side missions, which helps flesh out the story/game, but I found the quest log a little weak and thought it could've been more descriptive. Each time you level you're able to put a point into your attack, defense, max health or your companion which helps her abilities be stronger. It's an easy system and works well.
Overall, highly recommended game that has a lot of exploration and content.

The Music Machine is a deeply troubling and disturbing experience presented in an excellently handled style. For a horror veteran, maybe the horrific implications and actual creepy scenes will be unfazing, but for a softie like myself, it really hit me deep a couple of times. Of course I won't spoil anything here, this is a purely story-driven game afterall, but I can say this much: There are no jumpscares, just scary environments and scenarios.
The story revolves around two characters... kinda: Haley, the 13-year old girl who you are controlling, and Quintin, the ghost of a 34-year old man that Haleys father pumped full of lead after Haley excused him of molesting her... when in reality Quinint rejected the "love" Haley showed for him. And now Quintin's ghost possesses Haleys body and tries to get her killed. This is why he brought her to an island where horrendously deformed corpses have popped up multiple times, corpses full of holes. Quintin wishes to seek out the one who caused these injuries and leave Haley in his or her professional hands.
Quite a messed up setup. But the strangest thing is: Haley and Quintin still lead calm conversations, and Haley still shows affection for Quintin. There seems to be little hostility between the two... besides Quintin's very clear intentions. And so this pair of deeply troubled and hurt characters uncover the secrets of this strange island, and believe it or not, it gets even weirder. But any more info would be spoilers, so I'll leave the rest for you to find out.
The surreal and disturbing story of the game gets supported by a very surreal and unusual artstyle. A 3d world consisting only of a single colour and heavy shadows. For the first few minutes I thought the stark contrast would be a bit weary on the eye, but my eyes soon adjusted to it. The style also brings the benefit of being not very taxing for your computer, so you probably won't have to worry whether your computer can handle it or not, it most likely can. The biggest downside I could see for the game is its length. I beat it in 90 minutes, and after you beat it there is pretty much nothing else to do. It's up to you whether you think that time is worth it for the price. I found the game intruiging, and while it's a bit hard to define whether I enjoyed it or not, it definitely left and impact on me, and it will probably stay with me for a while. The story might not be for everyone, I can imagine that the horror aspects won't be effective for everyone, all I know is that it worked for me. A good friend of mine who is a horror veteran also played through the game and enjoyed it so much that he bought it for me and forced me to play it, so I think that even if you don't get scared by it, you will still get your money's worth.
TL;DR:
Pros:
-unique unsettling story
-interesting and relatable characters
-visually interesting and disturbing world
-pretty much any semi-modern pc can handle it fine
Cons:
-takes only 90 minutes to finish
-little to no replay value

enjoyed this game. As many others have said, the art and music/sound effects are superb; combined with the underlying premise and developing story, they create a frightening environment. Even during a second playthrough (not long after the first), I

list of areas for improvement, I have absolutely no hesitation in recommending this game. Seriously, just buy it, even if for no other reason than the experience of moving through such a trippy environment. It's well worth it!

Absolutely amazing game, unlike most team fighting games, this game has 2 teams that are completely differant and yet balanced. Fantastico:
+ tight controls and fluid gameplay
+ fun boss fights

Lame:

Less simply,
MKH is a very straightforward hack and slash game. There's no exploration to speak of, no weapon to wield other than your trusty katana, and MKH's story doesn't really try to do anything beyond creating a reason for you to cut some dudes. But you know what? That's all okay. MKH does the hack and slash in "hack and slash" well.
Expect to fight legions upon legions of varied opposition, and don't expect them to be all that easy to dispatch. Because of the difficulty of these fights, the game's sense of impact, and your flashy moves, cutting into MKH's enemy hordes is very satisfying. However, the composition of a horde only switches with each new wave, and each wave lasts for quite a decent amount of time, so fighting normal baddies is prone to becoming a stale experience.
Fortunately, the boss fights, which come after every five waves of typical baddies, do a good job of breaking up any monotony. These fights are easily the highlight of the game. They're the kind of fights where, even if you win by the skin of your teeth, you will want to retry for a more convincing more flashy result. They're so much fun to play. Be ready for boss fights that will test your reactions, timing, and adaptability. In particular, the fights with the main antagonist, Suzuka, are a complete blast to play.
MKH is a short game as it doesn't feature any extra modes or content, but, if you love a challenge, the game is highly replayable thanks to its multiple difficulty settings.
In the end, MKH is a super solid game. The controls are tight, the action is fluid, and the enemy encounters demand that you devise some semblance of a strategy to face them. If you're a fan of hack and slash games, give MKH a try.

If you want a deep, intricate story set in the LOTR universe, move on.
If you want a tactical game that involves having to plan out a course of action and doing it all perfectly, move on.
If simply having microtransactions in a game causes you to break out into hives, move on.
If you didn't like the first game, probably move on.
Still with me? OK, good: Shadow of War is a fun game. It takes Shadow of Mordor's nemesis system and improves it beautifully. Every single bit you liked and plenty more you wanted, it's all in there. This is by far the best orc-recruiting game on steam. Arguably, its one of the best sandbox open world games on steam. Also, you can ride dragons.
Shadow of War is to, say, Dragon Age as Just Cause is to GTA. It is somewhat of a mindless game, combat is an affair of few buttons but it feels so absolutely awesome. I'm not really one to care about deep stories or basically having to use more than 10% of my brain, and Shadow of War is right up that alley. It's not a bad game for that!
Yes there are microtransactions but they're not ever needed. You get legendary orcs from them, but you can also just.. get the orcs by playing the game. Just as quick too, as the ones they dump on you aren't all that and more importantly you dont have any attachment to them. You will grow to love your orcs in all the flavours they come in, from the guy who's screaming about god knows what, to the guy who can only say one word, to the big tough one who plays a lute.
The downsides? The story missions suck. It takes a while to get going even though you have almost all your key abilities at the start of the game. It's a bit expensive. That's pretty much it.
Overall, FUN/10

Alright, so I've gotten a lot of people asking me what I thought about this game, so allow me to just answer everyone here and now, all at once.
Game Score: 4/5
I'll start by saying, yes, this game does not stay true to its roots with its feeling and gameplay.  The game plays much more like a GTA genre game.  It does not really have any of the true feeling and authenticity of the older entries of the Mafia game series.  This is why I gave this game a 4/5.  This single issue was indeed enough to drop this game a full mark in my books because this series was always known for making you feel like you were actually a part of the mob and make you feel like you belong in the game.  This game does not do that, it attempts to though by revealing a couple of characters from games past (I won't spoil who), but fails to capture the magic from games past.
What this game fails to do, it does make up for though.  It is very crisp and does infact introduce a very intriguing story for gamers to divulge in.  I found the story-line to be very indepth and involving.  At times the side-missions do seems to be repetitive and senseless, but what game does not feel like that at some point nowadays.  It is very hard to introduce things today that gamers have not seen, or that developers have not thought of, already.  What the game does do though, it does very well and I applaud them for that.  I would go more indepth, but I do not want to risk spoiling the game for even casual browsers of the reviews.
My final words:
If you loved the older Mafia titles for the story and story alone, this game may not be for you, as it does stray from its roots and the story that older gamers have come to love.  On the other hand, if you enjoy Mafia for it's gameplay and don't mind being opened up to a different style of Mafia gameplay/story, then this game will not disappoint.
I will warn any viewers, the game does infact use a lot of racism, but I feel it is very critical to creating its atmosphere and it does infact use it to paint a very realistic and deep story.  It really does suck you in and you can easily blow afternoon after afternoon into this game and realize you have only chipped the tip of the iceberg as to the story of this rabbit hole.
I hope their next installment brings them back to their roots, but for now, we must wait.  Still a very worth-while title if you know what to expect when you walk into it.

Kane and Lynch are back in this sequel and it is improved. While the story still doesn't deliver, the game is a big improvment from its previous version. This tyme around we play as both main characters from the games.
Everything was repolished and improved in this sequel. The enemy AI is not good here, however the damage you take from getting hit have increased and the game will throw tons of enemies at you all the time. Now you need to be careful not to get hit, because 4 to 5 shots from an automatic gun will take you down on normal difficulty. The graphics have increased drasticaly and the good cover system is back with even more destruction.
It is obvious that the sequel has the same concept as the previous game, but this time around the overall story and feeling of the game is much darker. You will find really disturbing scenes and crazy new ideas the developers used to make a great experience.
Don't worry about multiplayer, because this time around it works. However you won't find many people playing this game. But once you gather a group the multiplayer mods are really enjoyable. Such as cops and crooks.
The different levels of difficulty and new achivments will make you want to come back to replay some levels you unlock. However, one of the annoying aspects of the game is the camera system. The default camera system is aweful. It will shake a lot when you run or fire the weapons, they try to make the game more realistic but it just gets extreamlly annoying not to be able to shoot your enemies because of it. Thankfully there is an option to tun off this shakey camera system, which improves the gameplay a lot. This time around the weapons have some good weight and feel good to fire. Alhtough they are not very accurate and one can't simply click the mouse button like crazy, they still feel good to use.
Overall this sequel is an improvment over the first game with an even darker feel and good combat. The game is still short but fun.
Good:
- The mood of the game and overall feel
- Improved difficulty
- Voice acting and characters
- Great Multiplayer (if you can find a match)
Bad:
- Shakey camera system, even in cutscenes
- Censored head shots and nudity (with pixels)
- Again the game is too short (4-5 hrs. to finish on normal in Single Player mode :/)

There were enough negative reviews of this game floating around to make me cautious. Yet the combination of a bargain price in the sales and the 2-player coop mode were sufficient to make me part with my money. Given what I'd read and heard, my expectations were pretty low, predicting something along the lines of Payday with a little more in the way of storyline and set-pieces.
There is very little about this game to recommend. One of the key features seems to be the gritty handicam perspective, which tries to make the game look like one long amateur video, replete with back angles, shaking and the pixelation of exposed genitalia and gunshot wounds.
Unfortunately it's something of a marmite move, since the movement makes a lot of people feel confused or even nauseous. Turn off the dodgy camera options though, and you get to the meat of the game which is... patchy at best. The majority of the time you find yourself playing a kind of
. Sadly the mallet you've been given has a mind of its own, making the whole thing feel like a training programme for Imperial Stormtroopers. Perhaps 90% of the game you'll be standing at a corner pointing your gun at another corner waiting for an enemy to pop out so you can fire a bullet into a nearby wall and perhaps make him jump. A few magazines later and you might have cleared out enough enemies to progress to the next area, which apart from the slight scenery change will be nigh on indistinguishable from the previous section. Interestingly, whilst you're lucky to hit a barn door from ten paces, if you throw a gas can or fire extinguisher in front of you, you'll hit it no matter where it lands – even if it bounces completely out of sight!
That's just one of the many moments in this game which make it feel completely unpolished.
, which isn't unusual for an action shooter, but still jars with the gameplay. Enemies occasionally spot you from a country mile away, firing at corners before you appear, shooting through otherwise opaque objects. At other times they completely ignore players only a few feet in front of them, presumably because the scripting sequence hasn't been activated yet. The player characters will randomly call out 'It's this way!' even though both players are nowhere near the route, which happens far more often than in should. In an action shooter like this one, good level design should provide players with the semblance of freedom and openness, whilst subtly leading them towards the path they're supposed to take. In Kane & Lynch, the
. That's when the game isn't use crude and clumsy invisible walls to prevent players from interfering with an NPC's orchestrated death sequence.
One of the main reasons I picked up this title was for the co-op mode, but this offers little in the way of variety. Many of the game's locations feel claustrophobically narrow, and apart from a few two-man doors,
. It's possible to go down in this game, in which case you can either get straight back up again (presumably that bullet to the temple didn't hit anything vital), or you're told to press E, which appears to do absolutely nothing, as it's your partner who's the one to get you up. Even were they in a position to do so, there's barely any time to react, and some levels specifically split up the two players making this mechanic entirely useless.
Maybe it's something to do with the German translation of the game, but it felt like many of the buttons displayed didn't do what they claimed to. Even where the controls do what they say on the tin,
. Trying to get into cover often feels like tossing a coin as to whether your character will press his back to the exposed side of a box. There is no jump key, so hurdling over obstacles is generally limited to very specific areas (and confusingly involves the cover key). Even picking up weapons and ammo can be something of a headache, as moving around a fraction can mean the difference between replenishing your supply of rifle ammo and swapping it for a different peashooter.
Perhaps this game's only saving grace is that it's soon over.
, during which time the virtually non-existent plot cleverly unfolds, going from being vague to hazy. To be honest, I can't see any reason why you would want to play it any longer than that!

This is a quirky little game that focuses on the history of fonts/written text. Sure, it sounds boring on the surface, but if you give it a chance, it really ends up impressing.
You play a colon (not the body part) that can roll around sideways or flip around. You have to navigate through various levels, which are separated typically into 4 parts each. The whole level is focused on a particular font and timeline, ranging back from the beginning of time, to the most recent fonts. You collect letters as you explore, from A to Z in order. Also strewn across the maps are asterisks - each one presents a 'page' of a book that introduces a couple of paragraphs of interesting information. You don't have to read them, but for a game of this nature, it would make sense to spend the time learning a little about the fonts of which you are reading at this very moment. I'm no history buff myself, but I definitely got some neat information out of it.
On top of the learning experience lies a robust and intricate platforming game. As you travel onwards, collecting letters and asterisks is fairly straightforward, but there are also some ampersands lying around that are somewhat hidden. Nothing too elaborate, but enough to make you pay attention to the levels. That said, the level design for each timeline is very well done - lots of various jumps and platforming mechanics abound. Some may say that the controls aren't that tight, and that is true - at times it can be frustrating; I found a few moments where the colon just didn't want to make it over a ledge or out of the way of something - but I have played much worse. For a game that charges less than a typical meal, its nothing to really complain about. The music in this game is also pleasant and fits the tone of each timeline.
The game features a few achievements, most of which are standard fare, but one of them is downright evil ('Desperado'). It will make you work for it, but the relief afterwards is worth it. Surprisingly enough, this game comes with trading cards, so if you like those, then that's a big plus. Overall, the game took me a little over 3.5 hours to finish - but that was with getting every single achievement, and I did skim the history pages a little. If you took your time, you could probably get at least 4-5 hours out of this.

Type:Rider looks genuinely interesting and it had my attention back when it launched on iOS.
Unfortunately, after having completed it, I'm afraid it fails on its two major goals: being a good game, and being a
learning experience.
Type:Rider is a simple platformer based around Typography. Every level is crafted from different letters (all themed according to a certain era and associated fonts).
You play as ' : ', and traverse several different time periods, learning a little bit about each one.
First off,
. As you can probably see from the screenshots, the game looks unique, and there's no argument there. Despite having a very simplistic foreground, each background gives the levels a very distinct feel, and often fit the font and time period. If nothing else, the game was a treat to look at.
The
was pretty great as well, mostly fitting the rest of the levels. One big issue though, is that whenever I alt-tabbed, the music stopped (even after getting back to the game). Well, I alt-tab a lot. And that quickly became a big problem, as I was playing mostly with no music. It would be nice to see that fixed.
Nonetheless, from what I've heard, the music was great!
No complaints so far. Still regarding presentation, I must say that the
was awful. This was an almost straight port from iOS, with big icons and way more navigation than it needed. Besides, the settings tab was almost hidden and while limited it had enough for the game it is (separate audio sliders and resolution options for the most part).
Now that I'm done with presentation, let's see why Type:Rider fails as a game.
This game is for all purposes, a platformer. And you play as ' : '. Despite looking cool, thematically, and working well, it's still a very clunky way of doing a platformer, and it makes it very easy to get stuck in a corner between the two dots. BUT, since the game is about typography, I'll let that one go.
The game starts of waaay too easy and slow. Every level seemed just like going in a straightline, jumping above a ponctual hole. Despite getting much better as the player progresses, it's still a game that hardly provides any real challenge. It's literally a walk in the park. You're walking around looking at the backgrounds, and collecting extras (I'll get to those in a minute).
It's really cool that the levels are made of letters, and it contributes for the whole theme of the game, but overall, there could be anything in place of those letters, as they're simply patformers for the player to walk on.
In each level there are 3 things to collect. Letters (
), another special character (
), and
.
The
are acquired naturaly throughout the levels, requiring no additional action from the player. The special
is the hidden collectible in the game, with 1 present in each level (each with 5 stages).
Both of these "extras" provide absolutely nothing aside from achievements and an "Aa" badge in-game. I don't even know why they're there. The only thing requiring a bit of exploration to find (and it's very little, to be honest) is the &, and even that provides you with nothing. I've only missed 1 on my playthrough, and I easily found it on my second try through the level.
Then, there are
. Each of these is also in plain sight, but they offer a page of information about the font and time period of the level. These are way cooler. I understand that they're supposed to be found by the player, but all of this makes the
.
There are some environmental hazards and tricky jumps in later levels, but even these barely feel a part of the theme, and the challenge they provide is questionable.
The main challenge in the game is controlling the at-times infuriating ' : '.
So, as a game, this is just a very bland platformer, clearly designed for iOS with very short and easy levels, plus a transvesti of exploration in the form of collectible achievements.
Now, the way more interesting part of the game and why it made me play it. The theme and learning experience.
Typography. That's a weird theme that they chose, isn't it? And yet, it's a very visual one, making a game the ideal medium for it to be taught on.
Well, unfortunately, Type:Rider fails as making the
a learning experience. Despite the levels being very unique, thematically and feeling coherent with the theme and era, they provide little to no information.
Simply playing the game naturally will teach very little, leaving only a vague idea of the particular font's origin and timeline.
Sure, there are a couple of pictures of the style and machinery used in the background, but it's not very substancial overall.
The way they tried to make it a teaching experience, was through collectible pages. The big problem here is, after you've collected them, you'll need to pause the game to read them. And that's pretty much it. It's almost like "Hey, you've collected this *! Here, have a wikipedia article you can read! Learning in-game is fun!". Well, no, it's not. It's just like reading a wikipedia article with the advantage of having the information a bit more streamlined.
And that's not the point of educational games! Not at all. The mechanics are supposed to be the learning vehicle itself, complemented by its aesthetic. Not just making a pretty game with pages of text forced into it.
Maybe the point of it wasn't to be the teacher itself, but to simply plant the seed of interest. Make the player interested in typography, and then tell him to go do his own research. Then again, this is not the way to do it, in my opinion.
I didn't become interested in typography by playing the game. I was interested in the game because it had some apparent innovation.
My conclusion regarding this. I think Type:Rider has an awesome concept, that I absolutely share and support. But, I think it missed its target in many core areas. The game itself felt very separated from the learning experience (visuals and music are
).
I like the idea, and I do not regret having tried it, but I would not recommend it to anyone, unless they were interested in it as a concept as well. And if that's the case, go ahead.
There's a huge gap between gameplay and information. If you're looking for a great game, pass this one up. If you're looking for a completely different and innovative experience... not quite what you're looking for.
It was fairly interesting, sure! And it did give me some curiosity about the subject. But I don't think this is quite what they were aiming for, and it will not appeal to the majority of people.

Type:Rider is a puzzle platform game designed more of an educational experience to introduce you the history of typography than to provide a thrilling and testing game experience.  As the aforementioned educational experience it's really interesting, purely as a game it can be frustrating.
You control two balls, a colon(?), inexorably linked across 10 levels, one intro, 1 hidden and 8 main ones representing the various ages of typography each with a font theme appropriate to the era.  From Gothic to Time, Helvetica to Pixel, each level has it's own unique idenity and all are very different, thankfully never feeling grindy.
On each level the goal to collect the entire typeface, A through Z, 6 or so asterisks' and a hidden ampersand.  Apart from the sort of hidden ampersand, you really won't have to go out of you way to collect anything.  None of the levels are difficult, you are meant to experience this game, not be challenged by it and with the fine ambient music, levels are a joy.  Each main level is split into 4 parts, two collectable platforming sections and 2 puzzle areas.  These puzzle areas range from Arkanoid and Peggle clones to shifting a third ball around through typeface to open a door, all doors requiring a third ball, key, to open.
As a game it is let down by frustrating controls, the wall jumping doesn't quite work right.  Jumping is also an inexact science and once you get to the final level there are sections that really deserve better controls.  This game isn't Super Meat Boy, but a little more time was needed to finesse the gaming.
It's definitely worth your time, a couple of hours, at a decent price, but I can't help the feeling that if they had made the control and physics more predictable, it would have made a better game.

Type:Rider is a casual platforming game that leads the player through time by observing the style of text used for each part of history.
Although I do not recommend buying this game, there's much good to be said about the game.
-The art is fitting and also interesting
-The same can be said about the music
-The idea of this game is unique
-The gameplay changes up a bit every once in a while so it doesn't feel redundant
To elaborate, the background art and music are very nice and each level has its own style that reflects the font and the time period. The player rides across letters and collects the alphabet in each font. It is something that I have not seen before. Also, each level has its own interactive objects that reflect the time period and font, like (Possible spoiler alert) the printing press machines for Times New Roman, or the tetris part in Pixel (End Spoiler Alert).
Now here's the major issue: Everything was done well except for the platforming. The character is a colon (:), which is also unique, but controlling it is not fun. It's frustrating. It feels as if the center of balance is opposite where it's expected, which makes the character either spin when it's not intended and also make it hard to get up a ledge when one end is sticking off. In fact, when both dots aren't on the ground, it's hard to move around at all unless the player is trying to flip end over end.
As I played it, I did learn some interesting things. However, I never truly felt like I was in control, but rather the game did its own thing and when anything cool happened it was more of a fluke than me performing a stunt. The commands I input didn't  exactly transfer to what I was intending, and I felt a slight disconnect with the gameplay the entire game.
I have no issues with the game being short (2.2 hours to complete all the levels for me, acquiring almost all the collectibles), but I do wish the programmers and the level designers spent a little bit more time on how the game felt as it was played. It'd be nice if the player could move and jump through the level smoothly if they knew the controls rather than jerking to a stop on most landings or falling in the gaps of the capital W because the letter's really big and the player just finished racing down a slope and just jumped when they realised the ramp ended.
Overall, I do not dislike what the game designers have done, but I do wish they could have focused more on the player so that this game has everything a good game needs: good art, ideas, and gameplay. And I feel that the designers failed in the gameplay aspect, because the game makes the player wonder why it's so hard to move, and despite the extraordinary art, despite the extraordinary ideas, there is no compensation for the frustrating gameplay.
