I've written two sections. The second section is aimed specifically at those who have played The Moon Sliver. So potential spoilers when you get to the part.
Although it's described by players and the developer alike as a horror game, I personally don't agree. (Though obviously, genre specification is inherently a subjective thing.)
It's an exploratory, narrative-driven game. I wouldn't call it as scary as much as it's surreal, and at most, unsettling.
You're in a strange environment (in part due to the dichromatic visual style), and as you explore and proceed, the world becomes increasingly stranger. The story follows the same pattern. It starts off weird (you play as a ghost who's puppeting the body of a young girl, and looking to kill her), yet ultimately moves into even more fantastical directions that's much more vast in scope than I had expected from the start.
I enjoyed the tale immensely. Much of the tale is conveyed through the internal dialogue between the two characters (the girl and the ghost who's controlling her) and they are a rather interesting duo imo. It's a short game (1 hr average I think for a full playthrough) but the way the dialogue develops feels both natural and informative, allowing the player to learn more about them while figuring out the craziness that's happening in the game.
The pacing of the game and story is as good as the character development. The second 'half' feels like it snowballs a bit too quickly, especially near the end, but I think that's inevitable given the number of...environments that the game has. Not saying it was not enjoyable nor satisfying, and that it seemed rushed, or that the dev should have fleshed out the latter half. The pacing just caught me off guard is all.
And besides, the final sequence IS good: the one area of the game that I would call horror, and it's very effective. It's an excellent wrap up for the story, the characters, and the game as a whole (followed by a great epilogue-y sequence that I won't spoil).

So overall, I did very much like the game. The story and characters were both engaging, and the environments were all creepily alien and oh-so intriguing. I felt for their characters during my brief time with them. I felt dread whether I was exploring small claustrophobic corridors or vast, desolate fields.
Again, I treat it as narrative-driven, exploratory game. So there are only a few puzzles, and they're all very simple. But I liked that; they didn't bog down the experience of the narrative.
And relately, one small detail that I liked was the ability to pick up most miscellaneous objects. Without spoiling much, this interface IS useful for some of the 'puzzles', but what I liked was that for the most part it, such movement was useless. I know it sounds silly but that was part of the reason why I liked Amnesia: The Dark Descent. It just felt more immersive, and as enjoyable to me as the random descriptions you get when examining random objects. It adds just the right amount of interactivity to augment the player's engagement with this world.
There were even times where I was pointlessly doing X trying to figure out obstacle Y...but it didn't bother me. It felt organic; my trying to find my way through the game.
Now for those who have played The Moon Sliver. I'm sure you're wondering about its relationship to the game.
Rest assured, even though TMM functions well as a standalone game imo, it manages to, in the process, expand, clarify, and enriches the backstory of TMS. And it's very satisfying. There is one particular detail in TMS that I was disappointed was never explaineds/shown explicitly. And it's there, right smack near the end of TMM. But if you never played TMS, it wouldn't be as poignant, but it would still be relevant, and would not stick out.
Gameplaywise, it's much more of a game than TMS, and I think it's a good thing. It does so without sacrificing narrative quality. E.g. Having an inventory screen did not detract from the experience.
The way the story is conveyed is different, but I think both games are interesting in their own right, and they both kind of stem directly from the games' unique settings (conversations with a ghost versus a person looking back and reminiscing).
I think pacing is better in TMS, but I'm 90% sure that's just due to the order I happened to explore things in TMS.
As I stated in the first section of this review, there's more interaction in TMM, and that's good for it as a game. If you liked TMS, there's a high chance you'll like TMM, as a whole, if not just for the tie-ins alone.
It's twice as expensive, but I think it's twice as long (same length for me, but I got lost in TMS for like a half hour lol).

Following the dev's games from Fingerbones to TMS to TMM over the past week (lol), I'm definitely looking forward to the dev's next entry in the genre (A Wolf in Autumn, I believe is his next project). And probably outside the genre as well, just to see what sort of stuff he cooks up next.

And if not, I'll at least look at the soundtrack, cause the music has been awesome. I normally don't acknowledge music in games usually, but when I did in these titles, they were quite mesmerizing stuff.

This is a review for the DC version of the game.
This game, for what it promises, is not even a shadow of what Fallout 1 and 2 were. Aside from the extreme RNG dependency, this game doesn't offer that much. Boring activate-this-object side quests, with little to no thinking required or a minimally decent story made most of this game feel empty and boring. Obvious character progression.
Pros:
- Individually interesting settlements
- Big party that allows for one or two interesting combat encounters
- Many companions available in the game
- Difficulty levels (mostly affects combat)
Cons:
- Awful and unjustified performance (this game runs at 30 fps dropping down to 5 fps on the same computer I play The Witcher 3 at 30 fps 1% lows)
- Never delivered on their mod-support promise (and probably never will)
- Mindless boring quests that rarely require thinking or planning
- Obvious and shallow character progression
- Full of bugs, crashes, glitches
- Gets stuck on loading screens (seems to be their "top priority bug" since 2014, according to dev's posts on forums)
- Wildly incompatible character portraits that ruin the little immersion you can force yourself into as soon as you see an indian with a geisha portrait (really, why even bother including those?)
In the end, this definitely didn't live up to its hype. It's a mediocre tactical RPG with a generic storyline, bland combat and a really shallow character system.
This definitely doesn't even remind me of old Fallout games.

Absolutely worth a play if you enjoy this type of experience.

I came into this, expecting a poor-man's Counter-Strike. To a certain extent, this is true. You certaintly won't be finding any originality or anything fresh in WARMODE. What you do get, however, is a decent, small (in terms of filesize), quick to pick up and relatively easy to learn FPS. The community isn't the greatest. Anyone with any prior FPS experience WILL get accused of hacking by the large collection of 10 year olds who have came over from CoD. However, the community is easily ignored, especially given that there isn't in-game voice chat (not that this makes too much of a difference). The game does have some issues, asides from the problems with its community. One of the most blindingly obvious problems it faces is it's netcode - it's appalling. There is NO consistency in terms of what it takes to kill enemies as a result - some times you can 1-tap enemies in the head with your AK, at others, you'll be left shooting a full magazine into them, only to have them 1-tap you, instead. The netcode also leads to there being some stupid incidences where you hit someone, but the game simply doesn't register it. However, perciviering with the game will lead you to discover that WARMODE is a fun game, with some great mechanics borrowed from both Counter-Strike and Call of Duty. This leads to a rather entertaining shooter, with the best features of both of the titans of the FPS genre, although some of these features are rather half-baked and poorly implemented.
Overall, a fun game. It does have its issues, but, being an early access game, I'm sure these issues will be solved over time. Devs, sort the netcode out. Players, give the game a try. It's not as bad as a lot of other free-to-play FPS games out there. And, yes. It does have skins.

I am really loving this game; the sound effects are great and the visuals are fantastic. It has the potential to be a 'dream' offroad trucking game. BUT, there are of course a few issues:
1. The mud is WAY overdone, ridiculously so, to the point where if you see a big muddy area ahead you might as well just quit the level and restart and take a different route (especially if you're pulling a traliler). Even nice grassy areas turn to mud under your truck, where it should be solid ground, and your rig will sink to the chassis. The winch is a cool feature but it really seems like nothing more than a mechanic to allow you to play at all - because you'll probably need it every few meters, winching from one tree to the next just to keep your truck moving. The mud is great if you enjoy a truck swimming simulation, because most of what you do is more akin to swimming than driving.
2. Small rocks and logs (even piles of branches and twigs) pose too much of an obstacle and can even stop your massive truck in its tracks.
3. Simply too few vehicles and too few maps at this time, plus the lack of ability to select map to play based on what trucks are in it, or the ability to choose which trucks to use or to put additional trucks into a level.
Other than those things, I'm really enjoying this game so far!

I don't usually recommend games that are physically painful to play, but Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days has managed to defy the odds and gain my love.
I'd like to preface this review by saying that I have not played the first game, Dead Men, in the series, but I am fully up to date with the story and many of the gameplay elements. The first one never drew in my attention because of certain mechanics it used, but this one did.
Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days is the second instalment in a third person cover based action shooter game series focused around the stories of two guys. Kane, and Lynch. Kane, a man with a questionable past and morals (who was the main playable character in the first game) has come to Shanghai to visit his... partner, Lynch, a literal psychotic with who he has worked with before, in order to do some business with him. I won't help into too many details, but as expected, things go bad really quickly, and you're thrust into a non stop action thrill ride that will either make you violently ill, or wanting more.
What do I mean by this? Well, if you've played the first game, you'll know that it was a fairly normal feeling third person shooter, in which you played as Kane and focused on his story. Now, the focus is put on Lynch, the psychotic. And boy, the game sure does feel like it was made with you actually controlling a psychotic. If Dead Men was a Kane focused normal third person shooter, Dog Days is a Lynch focused psychotic trip.
The way this is accomplished is mainly by the visuals and camera, which I feel is one of the biggest draws in the game. The visuals in Dog Days behave as though the entire game was being filmed by someone with a camera. There are visual artefacts, intense glare, and blur/pixelation effects used throughout the game. When you get shot, you might see your screen go fuzzy in some areas. If you see a bright light, you might get intense glare. If you shoot a civilian in the face, you might get a pixelated area where their face should be. These are all really neat features and really help to make the game feel like a video. While these have a relatively minor impact on gameplay, there is one more effect that is always in use that may make or break the game for you. The screen shake.
The screen in this game is ALWAYS shaking. And I do mean ALWAYS. Even when you're crounching behind an obstacle, the screen is still shaking slightly. Sprinting make the camera shake like you'd expect someone sprinting with a video camera would. You get shot? Shaking. You need to run? Shaking. Getting into cover? Do you even need an answer? And considering this game really is non stop action with hardly even a minute of relaxation every now and then, the screen is going to be shaking more than wet dog that's had 50 cups of cold coffee in the snow. This shaking, along with the other effects, can make the game more difficult to play, and can make it difficult to see enemies sometimes, it is also the cause of many headaches from many people, and it's clear to see why. And yet, I absolutely adore this feature. Once again, it really helps with giving the game a gritty feel, and a sense of speed and urgency. Everything is always moving so fast, and Lynch, being a psychotic, obviously has a harder time dealing with it than most people. He's in constant pain, and to a degree, you feel this as well.
Speaking of fast, by god is this game fast paced There's no collectables or anything to slow you down, and the game in constantly RUN AND SHOOT COVER AND SHOOT RUN AND SHOOT COVER AND SHOOT REPEAT FORVER! The game can be pretty difficult as it doesn't take much for you to get killed, but you also regenerate life fairly quickly and this works really well. Since you play as Lynch for the majority of the game, you always have the computer (or other player) controlling Kane, who is with you for almost the entire game. You can't give him any commands or whatever and he just deals with things himself, and he can't die, so there's no reason to pay mind to him. But the banter between the characters in game is really enjoyable and he doesn't have any negative effect on the game at all. The game is build around having these 2 together and it does so well. If you hate having an extra character constantly tag alone, like Ashley is RE4, Shiva in RE5, or Alyx in HL2, I assure you, the game works really with both of these characters and you are still in complete control the entire time. No waiting for the other character, no inventory management, no revival, or anything like that exists. At least not in single player. In multiplayer, a revival mechanic does exist, but not the other stuff.
However while the game is really fast paced, naturally, the game is also over really fast. It takes only 4 hours to beat the main campaign, and I'm counting deaths. If you managed to beat this game without dying (extremely difficult even on normal difficulty and probably on easy, I'd say I died about 100 times on my first playthrough, and don't worry, there's VERY frequent checkpoints) then you're looking at maybe 3  or 2 and a half hours of straight gameplay. While this is a con, the game is VERY jam packed and never has a dull moment to lengthen it out. It also have several extra missions that you can play alone or in multiplayer which add a few hours. I also feel the game is very replayable, as there are no skills trees or anything to worry about. This is a game that starts fast and keep going.
The story, while nothing particularly noteworthy, does at least draw you into the feelings and thought of the 2 main characters, who are still totally jerks, but ones that you can't help but feel sorry for.
Music that shows up now and then isn't very noticeable and very forgettable, but isn't bad, and sound effects are fine for the most part. There are some glitches in the game, like the screen going grey and not showing the game, but these are rare and usually fixed just by restarting the game. The weapons feel pretty good to me to be honest, but some seem to not like the sound of them. True, they don't feel overly strong, but since you're shooting 90% of the time anyway, I feel that they feel strong enough. Some of the guns also feel as though they have little to no accuracy to them (except the shotguns, which have a pretty good range for most videogame shotguns) but these weapons are quickly replaced by much better guns with better accuracy. In general, the gunplay feels quite good, covering works fine (most of the time), and it's a joy to play.
Sometimes, it also feels like the game hates you, as some parts are incredibly difficult, even at the start, and the ending really seems to come out of nowhere and leaves you asking "was that it... seriously?", but to be honest, I feel this is very refreshing, and sort of goes along with the struggle of Lynch through the game and his deranged mind.
All in all, Dog Days is a fantastic game, but one that most people will not enjoy. I feel as though a game like this will never be made again considering the reception it got, so this is one of a kind. It's sick, twisted, sad, and psychotic, just like Lynch. And I wouldn't have it any other way.

Gave the free 1st episode a try.
The lipsyncing is horrible and the controls are annoying. In addition the shots when you are not controlling you character are really badly framed - someone should take a 101 photography class. The 3rd person view really doesn't do anything for the game. A classic 2D point and click approach would have been way better from a pure story telling perspective.
I like the idea of changing your choices though, but I just couldn't get over interface issues and the very simple puzzles. These puzzles are just there to progress the plot without any real puzzling at all. It is usually the simplest form or fetch quest requiring no thinking. You are not really interacting with the world you are more or less making choices like in Telltale games - though they matter here how to story will progress. Sadly the plot of this so called "story rich" game is paper thin.
On top of it the writing is just bad. Adult males out of touch with the worlds shouldn't try to write teenage female centric chracters as it ends often in cringe-worthy dialogue and character actions.
Basically this is just a computerized game book like the branching-path books of the 70s. And this is exactly how the rewind feature works. You don't like the result of a choice? Flip a few pages back and take another branch.
I can see how this game appeals to a certain audience, especially to a 20 something audience who never were exposed the 70s game books and fide this nearly 50 year story telling way fresh.
If you can overlook the horrible lipsyncing and badly designed interface but what an simple emotional story told where you can see how different choices play out over the story this might be something for you. And for 5 bucks on sale you can't do much wrong. But in any case before consider buying play the 1st episode and ignore the praise the game gets and form your own opinion.

Type:Rider is a beautiful game about the history of typography. It is obvious that much love and care was put into its visual aesthetic. Each level is a collage-like smattering of gigantic letters, mixed in with the imagery and visual artistry that we associate with that era in history. For instance, the Clarendon level explores the evolution of slab serifs in the 19th century, throwing you into the Wild West among mine carts, wanted posters, and a bounty hunter’s roving crosshair, out to end you. The Futura level explores the “function over form” design of the Bauhaus School and the experimental typography of many modernist movements, littering the level with the colorful deconstructivist shapes of Malevich and Arp. The music and sounds of each level are also lovingly composed on top of that. There’s a great deal of visual and auditory pleasures to enjoy while playing this game; it’s just too bad that playing it for the gameplay is an experience that starts with disappointment and ends with frustration.
In keeping with the theme of type, your player character is a colon (:) that rolls and bounces about each level to collect the 26 letters of each font’s alphabet and asterisks which unlock different facts in that level’s book. It’s a creative idea and the colon was probably the best choice of punctuation mark around which to design.
Despite the strength of the idea, the bottom falls out of the entire execution very quickly. Sometimes you will just not roll fast enough, weighed down by being awkwardly long and flat. Jumping can be a nightmare as the colon’s physics can seem random and capricious, causing you to restart certain sections over and over again because it decided to bounce this way instead of that way or jumped from the wrong end, sending you backwards into a hazard.
The levels seem to have been designed and tested with a placeholder player character instead of this unwieldy one. Sometimes you are expected to land flat on the dot of a giant “i,” but the square is simply not long enough to hold you, dropping you to your death over and over until you land it just right. Some of the more challenging sections in the game involve passing moving hazards in a rhythm – certainly possible for a character that takes up a square hitbox, but infuriatingly difficult with the character you have. Neat level design such as rogue pixels in the Pixel section or the smashing pistons of the Times section are regrettably remembered as design flaws because of this shortcoming. The game consistently presents you with a nice amount of “game” for what is basically an edutainment title, only to immediately give you too much “game” and ruining the flow of something that should have been enjoyable and relaxing.
It’s also disappointingly evident that the game half and the educational half were worked on by two different teams. I’ve already mentioned the easily recognized love and care in the visual design. However, the facts you pick up about each historical era of typography read, at best, as lazy rehashes of a Wikipedia article. The worst are the entries that just throw a bunch of names and dates at you without truly looking at the importance and influence of those people and events. There’s a distinct lack of discussion about the design benefits of each font. Typos are almost ubiquitous and most are glaringly obvious. Did no one proofread this?
Type:Rider is such a beautiful game to look at and listen to; it’s a shame that I can’t honestly recommend it since all that looking and listening would have to happen while attempting to play it. The game design is not lacking in interesting ideas, but they could have been less lazy in testing them. The first line you see in the credits sequence tells you that the game was created by Cosmografik, with their company name kerned incorrectly. Surely there was room to try harder.

It's pretty. I learned some new things. But I have never been this angry at a platformer. I love brutally difficult platformers. But when it's just pure luck that's getting me killed because there's no way to tell what will happen if I dare to jump, no.

August 22nd 2017: W2 Review by Tandberg_J (steam account name)
Summary:
“The absolute dream for fans of the classic style of Fallout 1, and Fallout 2, and it's still a good game even if you are just casually familiar with Bethesda's Fallout reboots.”
This review is for the Director's Cut Edition, which in 2017, has been mostly debugged, and is very stable. I play on a PC for the record, and can't comment on the console ports. But, I've played and beat the original PC version as well, before the director's cut was released, so I've seen the game's development and refinement. (I recommend learning how to edit your save game files, [they are plain text .xml files,] as this allows you to avoid some glitches that might affect your game in purely mundane minor ways, and you can avoid little annoying bugs like not getting credit for a small side quest) Also, you can edit your characters and give them some clothing and aesthetics that are not available in the vanilla game. But this is optional of course. Also there is a huge mod scene for this game, which I can't really say I've tried.
Use the wasteland 2 Wiki and online strategy guides often, as they will lead you in the right direction. It's not cheating or spoiling, use the guides as needed, as this game is so much a sandbox, that the guides are more like suggestions for strategies than they are “How to beat the game.” This is NOT a linear game. Of course, it has an ending, and two world maps, but how you get through them is completely up to you. And of course, every local will factor into the final ending depending on what you do with the people there. And also of course, there are ways to fail and end the game early, NOT including just getting killed in combat.
Now, here goes the formal review:
I am a hardcore fallout 1 and 2 (refereed to as F1&F2 hereafter) fan from back in 1998, which was the year I purchased F2. Then, later that year, my friend and I bought him F1, so we played both religiously as teenagers that summer. We beat them both, but kept playing because of the replay experience. Honestly, the Bethesda Fallout Games, with "Fallout:New Vegas" being my favorite of the three, NEVER lived up to the quality and fun of the original Fallout Games, which as most know, were developed by Brian Fargo and the crew at Black Isle Studios, and published by the behemoth Interplay.
(FO3, FO:NV & FO4) are the only AAA Bethesda reboots of the Fallout Series of Games, that exist at the time of this writing, and I know there are many people who share my opinion about the original F1&F2 being superior to Bethesda's rebooted games. This review is written for this crowd, which is the crowd that is old school and shares the love of classic 2D Fallout. Still, if you are more of a modern Bethesda Fallout fan, I invite you to play Wasteland 2, and experience some of the old school good stuff that inspired Bethesda to buy the damn franchise, trust me, you will like it!
At the very worst, you will be challenged and pushed harder, and put out of your comfort zone, in a nuked out hell, in what's left of The Earth. That is not to say that I didn't purchase and enjoy all three Bethesda Fallout Games. They just weren't a true “Fallout Game” to me.
I never played Wasteland in the '80s, and I only knew of the game when I played F2, because I had read online that "Fallout" was the spiritual sequel to Wasteland. I've played all the “Fallouts.” I played Fallout Tactics, which was kind of disappointing. The only “Fallout” game that I haven't played is “Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel” which was a game that was released for the PlayStation 2 console in 2004.
So, having played all but one of the AAA all Fallout games, and completing them multiple times, with different characters, I can say that "Wasteland 2" is an Old School Fallout Fan's ultimate dream game. Because Wasteland 2 (Hereafter refereed to as W2) was able to be crowdfunded and released with no big name corporate publisher, it is basically everything a fan would want without the generous helping of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t we see so much in the Bethesda Fallout games. Gone is the patronizing, annoying use of nostalgic imagery for the sake of keeping the franchise "looking like" Fallout, while changing the game mechanics. Gone is the whitewashed, predictable story lines that don't touch on more mature and morally complex themes, because Bethesda wants maximum profits, because they need to market to teen demographics. Gone are the silly 3d first person graphics, that don't add to the story line, and are too realistic, but fake enough to raise an eyebrow, and just pollute the immersion. Gone are sputtering frame rates that jar your experience. W2 may have old school graphics, but they are just like the ones in Fallout 1&2. They are old school, minimalist, gritty, and damn post apocalyptic looking. Just like Fallout, Even the GUI in the game is made to look like a bad 1980s computer system. This makes it very immersive.
A key difference between the Wasteland Universe, and Fallout Universe, is this: Instead of the 1950s retro futurist setting of Fallout, Wasteland has a 1980s retro futurist look. So in W2 you don't have all of the 1950s influenced music and style and imagery. In W2 all the 1950s stuff is replaced with 1980s style cyberpunk music, cars, dialogue, clothing, etc.. This is the key difference between the franchises, and I find that other than this difference, the two game universes share too many similarities to even name.
As merely one example of many game play systems that W2 has reverted back to in “the old school way,” W2 returns to our old favorite system of having two weapons, pictured in a gray box at the bottom middle of the UI, and the player, being able to switch back and forth without a cost to action points, can use the two weapons. Also, W2 returns to purely turn based combat system, which, to fans like us, is refreshing. Like the good old days, you get to meticulously plan out each round fired, decide when each enemy is shot in the legs and crippled, and decide when each packet of drugs, or mystery medicine, gets IV'd into your veins. While Bethesda's Fallout's “V.A.T.S.” system was a nice try to bring this turn based combat back, I didn't feel it was a proper replacement for turn based combat. And in a game like W2 or Fallout, I prefer turn based combat. If you don't feel this way, perhaps W2 isn't your game. But that said, maybe you would like W2 as it will pull you out of your FP shooter comfort zone. I think the veteran fans will all agree, that combat in classic Fallout and Wasteland games is best when it is TURN BASED ONLY.
In wasteland 2, you create not one, but 4 player characters that you get to control like they are your own character. (Think “Baldur's Gate” here people) No one of the 4 characters is more important or in control. So it's different from Fallout, in the sense that you get to role play 4 unique people, that you create abilities, character portraits, and backstories for. And out of the 15 or so NPCs  you'll meet in the game that can join your party, up to three of them can join your party, making your party size swell up to seven playable characters. This doesn't include characters that are merely following your party, even animals and mutants will follow you at times. I've seen up to 11 creatures and characters on my screen following my 7 PCs. Even goats and cows have been in tow. I once had 6 cows following me around, so chew on that!
Also, welcome back to the game that plays from a top down view. Technically W2 is a type of isometric view, yet with a slightly oblique projection (Like Fallout 1&2), which allows some walls to be seen better from certain angles. We will just call it isometric, for simplicity's sake. But that's not what is the most important thing about W2. The view is just like F1&2 which is a huge plus.

Great game but flawed game mechanic slightly ruins it for gamers seeking a real challenge.
I have beaten the story on gravewalker difficulty and have taken out a fortress with enemies 20+ levels above me and vastly outnumbered.
You just roll around for an hour and nothing can kill you. During your god-mode rolling you dish out 1-2 sword attacks, shoot some arrows, shadow strike/dominate, summon drake/graug and use might spells. Okay, some fights you need to be fast and well-timed because when you do attack you are vulnerable and in gravewalker, 1 hit can kill you so it still offers some challenge.
A little damage at a time adds up and eventually the enemy bosses will die but you will be spamming roll for a looooooooong time. It's almost like a spacebar tapping simulator.
Game is still a blast though, especially in the beginning. So, I am still thumbing it up as it is a phenomenal game. Unfortunately, that one god-mode rolling mechanic kind of ruins it a bit.
The most impressive thing about this game is that after almost 40 hours I haven't heard one repeated speech from an orc captain. The randomised orc speech and personality is truly a remarkable achievement.
Also all the negative reviews about microtransactions are silly. I already beat the game on the hardest difficulty without spending real money. I didn't even grind followers or items. You can purchase silver war chests with silver coins from simply playing the game. 2 orc followers cost you 1500 silvers and playing the campaign earns you up to almost 100000 silvers. The game definitely looks and sounds nice, to begin with, and it has some really interesting ideas in it, but that's about as far as it goes.
The game is an arena shooter built around a series of rather gimmicky mechanics, which more or less take over all the shmup elements.
The controls are very unintuitive and irritating. The dubious decision to use both the keyboard and mouse, as well as the extreme discomfort of reaching over to the number keys, really hurts the game, and it feels like it was designed exclusively for left-handed people. Often, getting the controls to do what I want is the hardest part. This alone will probably be a deal-breaker to most shmup fans.
I like the idea of having large open levels between the bosses, but they feel empty, tacked-on, and devoid of action, and most of the time one only needs to see a small part of them to progress anyway.
The bosses are interesting and are probably the best part of the game. On one hand, they are exciting and colourful and each one offers something new, but some tend to overuse annoying puzzle elements while others lack intricacy, and it's not uncommon for a boss to use the exact same attack for more than 15 seconds at a time.
There are some good things in it, but it mostly feels like just another janky reinvention of shmups for reinvention's sake.

Note that this is a review of the Director's Cut, which I completed in about 40 hours but doesn't seem to show here.
While the visuals may feel off-putting at first and the outright excessive amounts of skills and junk loot can get overwhelming, Wasteland 2 ends up being a pretty fun and compelling post-apocalyptic RPG.
There are a diverse set of places to visit and people to meet/help/kill, and a wide array of weapons and challenges that you can respond to more or less how you like. I enjoyed dealing with the story quests and occasionally breaking into places to bypass problems, and there were a few pretty neat characters among the bland ones. The ending sequence was quite well-done, with a few genuinely surprising moments capping off story points from throughout the game. Combat feels suitably weighty and sometimes chaotic, and there are plenty of weird tidbits scattered throughout the wastes.
Overall a good and enjoyable game, though it does have some typical CRPG flaws - voice acting was inconsistent, there was way too much loot to manage, and narrative quality was inconsistent too - some of the characters or scenarios lacked imagination and relied too much on tired tropes, even though others were fun and interesting.

Let me start off by saying I've been playing Bloons ever since I was very little (around 6 years old). The first Bloons game was one of my favorite games at the time and each installment after that brought me much joy. Each and every installment of this game is great in my eyes and this game is no exception. A multiplayer Bloons game would've been a dream for me back then and it's still hard for me to believe that the series had made it this far. Of course, we still have a product to review here, so let's get to it.
Bloons TD Battles is the first Bloons game to focus on cooperative/competitive play and it really does a great job of doing both. It started out as a mobile game, and unlike most mobile games on Steam, this one is a really great PC port. The gameplay itself is smooth, getting in a match takes a few seconds and you will likely find yourself addicted to this gem quite quickly.
All that being said, there are a few flaws with this title; to start off there is no apparent "EXIT" button; this isn't a big deal, but it would definitely be a nice touch to be able to exit the game without having to alt-tab out. Another thing is the "In-App Purchases" this game has. Most of them aren't really that big of a deal, but one thing that kind of bugs me is the fact that the "Cobra" monkey costs 5,000 medallions, which is very difficult to work up to if you don't plan on spending a penny.
In conclusion, I'd rate this game an
out of a possible
. It features very addictive gameplay, only a little bit of pay-to-win and a great title that'll have you hooked (given you're a fan of tower defense games!) I would definitely advise you to download this title if you're looking for a game that's easy to pick up and learn, runs well on older computers and allows you to take it on the go.

Seriously!? How does this game have overwhelmingly postive reviews? Who is playing this game and actually enjoying it? Are you all 12 year olds that haven't been alive long enough to understand what makes a good game and a good story and think this is acceptable? Because that is the only explanation as to who is giving this game good reviews.
First of all right off the bat the lip syncing is absolutely awful. You think that in a heavily story driven game this would be a detail to put some effort into, but no, its like playing something from the 90's. Which brings me to my next point. THE. STORY. IS. AWFUL. and THE. CHARACTERS. ARE. A. NIGHTMARE. Who wrote this? Some babyboomer who thinks this is actually how teenagers speak nowadays because he's out of touch with reality? Everything they say is so cringe worthy and not even the cringiest of modern teens would say half of this stuff. It's like they took every single cliche highschool moment and every single cliche  highschool character, put them all in the same story and thought "Yeah...this is a good idea." None of the characters are likeable at all and you don't care about any of them. They either talk about random pretentious $h!t that I've never even heard of or they start in with the cringiest of teenaged angst. It's vomit inducing!
Next is the gameplay. Remember when video games were meant to be fun? When was playing a game where you do daily house hold chores that I have to put up with on a daily basis in real life considered fun? I understand in these story driven games that their has to be filler somewhere between the good stuff but the problem is NOTHING HAPPENS. The whole thing is so damn boring. Their is more action in my daily office job in real life than this whole game. How is this good? I was straight up lied to in the trailers. I loved games like Heavy Rain and Beyond Two Souls and I was promised with something similar as well as splashes of Stephen King and other interesting supernatural stuff. But instead you just get the average life of a teenybopper who happens to be able to rewind time. Which btw the time mechanic's only purpose seems to be so that you can change your mind about decisions instead of having to restart the game. It's a glorified shortcut for indecisive people. I thought it was going to start off slow but start really delving into some supernatural stuff but it's just a cringy teen movie. Who wants to sit through that? Everything is just super awkward and bad.
So in conclusion I ask again, has the world gone mad? This many people actually liked this? I guess mediocre garbage is what passes for good nowadays, and their are just more and more brain dead people nowadays coming out of the wood works and eating this crap up. This is why horrible games are being made in droves today because people will buy them. Why put in any effort when you can copy and paste cliche crap and people will eat it up? I'm in my late 20's so I guess I'm stuck in that weird generation that is young enough to remember days of highschool nostalgia and the corny things I used to play and watch but also old enough to not be so gullible and demand higher quality out of my games. I'm smart enough to know what makes good characters and their development and, unfortunately, this is not it. Too bad too, because it looks like someone had an outline for a decent idea and then gave it to the worst writers in history. I guess I'll just wait for bigger and better things coming in 2018. Glad I only wasted $5 on this crap.

A brief 2D action platformer art installation. It's a mobile port. Pretty. Excellent sound design. Challenging and inconsistent gameplay. You play as a colon, platforming on various fontfaces. Fun, but frustrating. I enjoyed the concept and experience, but recommend it only casually.
The art is bright, colourful and interesting. The sound design fits in excellently to the context of the fonts as does the aesthetic. Manufactured fonts get a factory them whereas pixel fonts get a digital theme, etc. I really appreciated the lazorcat and general concept of the bonus level even if that level's gameplay was infuriating and unforgiving.
At times, it's hard to tell when and where you can jump. It often feels like you aren't really in control as you will fail, but not know why. It seems cruel, unfair and random as a result. The camera and level design make for a lack of visibility of your enemy in some few instances as it's hard to not fail when you can't see what you're doing. These failings are especially evident in the bonus level which is the only scrolling level of the game and does not have the checkpoints that made some of the previous levels more bearable.
The game rewards your progress verbose wall of text chronicling the history of the font types. If you're into that sort of thing, it's interesting and you can learn some stuff, but otherwise, it's a lackluster offering.
Most of the achievements are simple things like "beat the game" and "find the hidden nick-nacks" which are all relatively easy if you're thorough enough. Beating the bonus level is fairly challenging as is beating the western levels in one run without dying. There's an achievement for posting to social media from the game, but all you need do is click on one of the links to get the achievement - you don't need to post anything.

The bosses can be challenging at first but you quickly learn the attack patterns and it becomes easy, the only one I died too in the entire game on my first playthrough on normal was the second phase on the last boss. The combat feels fluent however their is a very limitied amount of combos to use and upgrade, making it feel very repetitive after a while.
The audio in his game is terrible, highly recommend playing music or listening to something else while playing this game... The sound effect of hitting an enemy sounds like hitting an enemy in a 90s Super nintendo game. The voice over is good but nothing special. Their is only one song per stage that just loops over and over again.
You are a blade templar sent to hunt down a fellow blade templar who has gone rogue and has been drawing power from a demonic sword. Thats about it.. Their is no real back story between these characters, their is no story progression or anything of the sort until the end. But even the ending was basic and gave no story.
For the most part I love hack and slash games, however this one felt worse than X-Blades.. WIth very limited combo moves and the small amount of upgrades available, this game got repetitive very quickly. Basically kill, kill, kill, kill, fight a boss, next level, rinse and repeat. This game could have been a lot better if the developers put some effort into it. The state of it right now just seems lazy and a way to make a quick buck off school girls and panty shots. The only good thing is you can fly through it in a couple hours.

**This is a product review for the Director's Cut version, in which I have spent 38 hours at the time of writing. But I can't place a review there.**
The atmosphere in this game is amazing, each settlement you visit is a unique location tied to a back story. Characters often have a history themselves, knowing people from other settlements and having an opinion about them. The game itself however, is very bad. It crashes often during loading, looks like it was made in 2008 and it has a large amount of tediousness connected to the gameplay as well as things that are just not very well thought out. I bought the game because I like XCOM and I wanted to have a similar game in a different setting that could run on my Linux computer. But I was wrong, this game was nothing like XCOM and it didn't even work that well on Linux.
Pros:
* Good atmosphere.
* Settlements are unique and exciting.
* Plot twists!
* Simple graphics (which is a pro for me since it means it ran on my computer just fine).
* First run took about 38 hours.
* The end is pretty cool, all the friends you made gather to defeat the common enemy.
Cons:
* Frequent crashes during loading of locations.
* Achievements didn't work for me.
* One of my characters had the 'Raised in the Circus' quirk and had to run around in a non-removable clown costume the whole game.
* There are a lot of useless skills that you only need once during the whole game (or not at all). In addition, you might find followers that have overlapping skills with your core rangers making your first runthrough very inefficient.
* Invisible walls of radiation block you from going to certain areas in the overworld.
* Characters will gladly shoot through walls for you.
* You can't walk through allies. So I had one melee character with high initiative which was often stuck between other rangers. This could have been avoided by allowing allies to move past each other on the same square.
* Sometimes you finish a quest before talking to the quest giver, who then promptly gives you the reward. Or the other way around: someone assumes you heard about X before when you didn't even talk about X.
* You can't throw away quest items. You can buy multiple rad suits in the beginning (which I did because I thought the bonus stacked), but then you can't dispose of them since they are quest items. Same goes for items for quests that have been finished already.
* AFAIK during an ambush you do not spent AP but you can still get the Slayer perk  (no AP spent) triggered, which seems useless to me.
* Often the quickest solution to a quest is just to shoot everyone. The quests often involve a lot of walking around clicking on things which make them really tiresome to do.
* The enemy can surprise you before you can surprise them in most cases.
* In the end you need to have your whole squad specialised in one specific skill in order to be able to defeat the game with ease, which is a shame.
* Combat gets repetitive, even with the different types of enemy squads you encounter.
* If you free aim a shotgun you have a better chance to hit multiple enemies (or less allies).
I bought the game for 10 euro, I wouldn't recommend buying it at any higher price because of the bugs. Most notably the crashes made the game really hard to play. I'll be looking forward to seeing what Wasteland 3 brings, and I hope they will fix the issues in this game.

I only have 50 hours on steam but in total ive played this game for around 180-190 hours. This consists of the closed and open beta.
This game has seen alot of changes since I started playing Paladins in December 2015, the game has changed in a way that I do like but also kinda hate.  When I started playing you could almost call paladins another game, since it was level based back before, basically when you had gotten a few kills and level`d up you could choose from 3 different cards that would affect one of your abilites. However now this have been completely scrapped, the game has now alot of different gamemodes, its siege, payload, survival and CO-OP..
Siege: Two teams battle to capture a point to so have a payload and push it to the enemy base, first team to 5 points.
Payload: One team gets to push the payload all over to the enemys spawning area under a timeperiod, the other team will try to stop them, after the time has ran out, teams will switch roles.
Survival: Survival is a gamemode where the two teams only have one life per hero to kill the enemy team as fog all around you gets the teams closer to the middle, last team standing wins, first team to 5 points.
CO-OP: CO-OP is basically as you team with other players to fight really hard AI with different changes to either their abilites, toughness or damage, if you get 5 points you win.
Now as ive described the gamemodes ill go over the things that I really dont like about the game
- There is always some sort of balance issue in this game, there is always a characther that is better than some of the other ones.
-Constant changes to quite important stuff, like recently when they added a essence system which got alot of crap for players which later resulted in that they gave us players a crap ton of essence and a disenchant system to get essence to buy legendary cards.
-Going for a match and then there is that last guy/girl that doesnt press the ready button.
-Quite toxic community, not really helpfull.
-Hi-Rez isnt really good at customer support
From these things that ive mentioned. i really like the game, id just really like to keep the game the way it is now, not do drastic changes to either make the game worse than it already is. Stay free 2 play as much as possible.

After about 15 hours I've decided I can review the game based on what I've seen.
Shadow of War is yet another semi open world action adventure game. I say semi open world because there are loading screens for each zone you need to go to and each zone is fairly small.  Gameplay consists of going to each zone, doing a few quests, then taking out the stronghold there with your army.  The issue with me is, gameplay gets tedious and boring rather quickly due to the repetitveness of it.  You do the exact same thing in each zone. Take over a bunch of orcs, level them up, attack the npc stronghold...rinse...repeat *yawn*.
I honestly dont think other players are even doing the online assaults because my strong hold has never been attacked. I dont see how it even fits in the context of the setting. If i was an orc player, then yes, i'd understand. Anyway, i honestly couldn't care less about attacking other players bases.
The loot crate gimmick is just dumb. Pay real money to get in game gear which really does very little for you since you get really good gear anyway from quests. Just play the game you paid for people...dont give these publishers any more money.
In the end, it's a decent enough game. The setting is great as is the story. I enjoyed talking to Shelob and seeing her in human form as she is pretty hot. Dev's did a great job creating her backstory from what little was given in Tolkien's books.
So in conclusion, I'm recommending it only if its on sale. I got it for 50% off and don't feel cheated of my money.

Not sure where to start with Mafia III, I have been a fan of the series since the original and to be honest usually when i see lots of very negative reviews I avoid games at least until they are patched and playable, however I decided being a fan of the series that I would give this a shot for myself, people had complained of it being badly optimised but I figured since I have a powerful machine that I would give it a go.
(i dont like giving pc specs, but to give an idea as to what to expect performance wise, i run a gtx 1080 with i7 4790k / 16gb ram)
The game, unfortunately is not optimised as well as it could have been and this definitely should be something that shouldnt be happening but still does, its finished for console means just get a quick fix and send it to pc players.. On average with graphic settings on high (i took down some things that seemed to cripple fps for no apparent reason as visually it got no better or worse) I was getting around 60-80 fps.. when driving this would occasionally drop to 50 or very rarely down a tad lower for a split second.
The sheer amount of glitches currently is killing it for me, this is stuff that should have been erradicated in beta rather than selling pc users a beta version, I'll be finished the game at this rate before you get around to patching it..
The graphics in honesty are sub par given the age we're in, weird that dev lets it go out the blurry vision, within a few days of release the SweetFX modding guys did their best for this to make it look presentable and I highly recommend using their mod to fix the blur / overall GFX like HDR etc..
Performance aside, I just wanted to get a good feel for the story and I will admit I really enjoyed the game from the start, I'm a huge 60's music fan and the soundtracks are nothing short of superb, in fact its what really made the hairs on my neck stand up as what happens to lincoln near the start is met with paint it black from the rolling stones. The game and story itself seems pretty good and I enjoy the feel of the game.  Some people complained it lost its mafia feel because of the speed limit and stopping for red lights or having to get petrol.. I'll hold my hands up and say I was never a fan of those features in the original games so it was of no great loss it was gone.
The AI is bad, playing it on max difficulty doesn't make the AI smarter, it just means 1 bullet rips through you harder.. AI watches you murder their friend as they stretch and don't care.. The workers in the factory are happy to continue just doing their trade as I walk around slaughtering their bosses without a care in the world (using the silencer or silent takedowns). When dealers are giving a girl a beat down, I shot the guy in the head and then the girl stands up and goes to call the police..
Story can feel a bit repetitive, go to new district, there is 2 rackets.. do the same thing and take them down, no real story behind any of the rackets just go there, rough up that guy who spills the beans within 1 punch and give it to your colleague of choice.
Weirdly enough, after all this I still find myself actually enjoying the game and I think I am nearly 40 hours in, feels like I am close to completion and I've been doing every side mission I could find so far. However.. there is 1 major niggle, the wiretaps... the god awful wiretaps and having to collect those green dots on a constant basis, it totally rips away from any enjoyment stop starting all the time to pick up these silly little things..
On that note so much more couldve been collected or picked up, but instead the devs just thought, keep plopping in those little wiretap things and make that the only thing needing collecting aside from some old playboys and hotrods.. You totally overdid the wiretap thing, make it only 1 instead of 3 requirement and cut half or 2 thirds of the green dots out the game..
Overall I would recommend it on the basis that the dev team pull the finger out, fix the glitches.. fix the poor optimisation and fix the performance issues. I also would only recommend it at cheaper price, I found this for £20 online and would probably be resentful if i had paid £39.99 which is the RRP

I have to admit that Type: Rider really got my attention just after beating the tutorial. I was expecting a mere platformer but I found out it to be something more. I actually had no clue what this game was about and that's why I decided to play it on a hunch. I'm glad I did so. Type: Rider offers you basic and simple platforming gameplay, you move and you jump and that's it. However this game introduces you to the history of typography. The history of typography is told by books, each book refers to a certain font and a certain timeline and each book represents a different level which is then divided in 4 sublevels. By acquiring asterisks, and by this I mean ingame collectibles in the form of asterisks which can be found on each level. Besides that you can also collect each letter of the alphabet on each font that is told on a specific book. The books range from the early  writing of the cave men, to the egyptian hieroglyphs, to the medieval times and then to first languages that were introduced in computer programming. One thing I found particularly detailed was that on each level the music is adequate to the timeline in question. Visually I found Type: Rider to be really appealing but that may vary from person to person. It is certainly not your average game and you should only play it if you have any interest in history, otherwise it might get boring. I also think that if you have a kid you should let them play this, I think it would probably interest some young ones by learning on a new way. I highly recommend Type Rider!

Now this is how you make a sequel. Just so you know, I was not a huge fan of the first Witcher. The world and the story were all interesting and well made, but the gameplay was just bad overall, and the game was quite boring for a lot of the time. Now that we got that out of the way, what do I think about the Witcher 2?
The fine folks at CD project have improved nearly everything from the first Witcher. The biggest improvement is quite clearly in the visual department. This game looks simply gorgeous. There were multiple occasions when I just stopped doing whatever I was doing, and simply wanted to look at the beatiful visuals. Also the nudity department has gotten far more extreme this time around. We both know this is the info you really wanted to see matey!
The 2nd massive improvement is in the gameplay. I actually had fun playing the game. The combat is not total♥♥♥♥♥♥anymore, but I still can't exactly call it good.I heard from many different sources that this is a really hard game, but personally I don't exactly agree with that. It is challenging from time to time, but mostly because the game does throw in some pretty uneven fights. Boss fights are a good example of those, and I didn't exactly like many of those. They can destory you with few hits, but on the other hand you can kill nearly all of them by using the same tactic over and over again. Overall, the combat does get better later on when you learn the tricks of the trade.
The alchemy is far less complicated this time around, which is a big + in my book. However, you can't drink potions in the middle of fights anymore. This is a bit weird to me, because it was possible in the first game. How are you supposed to know when you are going to need those potions exactly. Do I need to take a quick look into the future??? The controls feel much smoother overall which is another big improvement. The dialogue system has also seen some changes this time around. There are often many ways to get through a dialogue segment.
Even though most of the gameplay was improved, the developers did make few really stupid choises. For some reason they have added quick time events into this game. They happen so rarely that they will most likely catch you off guard, and in most cases they lead to an instant death. OH THE JOY!!! Another weird choise is that stamina and magicka have been combined into 1 thing, vigor. It just seems a bit weird to me. Blocking attacks takes a part of it away, but rolling doesn't. How does that work exactly.
Now on to the story side. I might sound like a broken record by now, but I found the story in this game to be a bit better than in the first game. A lot of suprising twist and turns and difficult choises just like in the first game. The characters are also a strong part of the game. A lot of old people return, and a lot of new people show up. Witcher 2 still has the branching storylines mechanic from the first game, so you can play the game a 2nd time and see a totally different take on the story. Also the choises that you made in the first game carry over to this one. I wish that more games did that. The story did seem far shorter than it was in the first game. I was looking forward to chapter 4 and 5, and then all the sudden the epilogue begins. I was quite disappointed to be honest. They did wrap up the story quire nicely in the epilogue, but a lot of question still remain, and they will most likely be answerd in The Witcher 3. The mission desing, also seems a bit more varied this time around. Less random errands and more cool stuff. Me like! The enviroments seemed more varied as well. Plenty of little things to find and see, but I do wish that the game was a bit more open. I suppose Witcher 3 will grant me that wish.
So what is my final verdict. I think that the Witcher 2 is a great game, that all rpg fans should consider trying out. The story is still the highligh of the game, and it is 1 of the better stories in recent fantasy rpg's(not sure if it's fair to say that because it is based on a book series but meh). Improved gameplay and missions make the game FAR more fun to play, and exploring the detailed world is still enjoyable. The game does still have some issues here and there, but I still think that it's a very solid game. This game made me real hyped up for Witcher 3.
Edit: So yeah, Witcher 3 happened and it's absolutely fantastic. What a way to end a series

Alan Wake is one of those games I'm willing to call a ''work of art'', celebrating fiction as a whole. I mean that in the least pretentious way possible as the game doesn't take itself too seriously. It manages  to tell a serious story however, while at the same time not being afraid to have fun with the campiness of its setting and characters. The story that's delivered, and the way its delivered, are superb.
The game tells the story of Alan Wake, a writer whose wife misteriously disappears on their vacation to the small, secluded town of Bright Falls. It's up to Alan to find his wife and unravel the mistery of the town.
As you might have guessed, Alan Wake is a horror/thriller, and an episodic one at that. I get that alot of people dislike the episodic format, but this game does it the right way. It feels natural and isn't overblown by any means.
It falls more into the latter category, as the game apparently tries not to scare the player, always panning the camera to show you where the enemies are coming from. This may add to the cinematic value of the game, which is already huge as it is, but it lessens the suspense some people think it already lacks. This isn't the only instance where the game does this, but I won't mention anything else, lest I tread into spoilers territory. The visuals, atmosphere, sound design and the design of the environments are on point, which may get you to feel dread at times, but there's no moment where you actually feel

As I said, the visuals of the game are on point, and they all look great even on the lowest settings, all these years later. They are very easy on the eyes.
The gameplay some might deem too simplistic, even uninspired or too easy, but I feel that this is not the case (as long as you're playing on Normal difficulty at least) and that it fits the theme of the game perfectly.
The only real gripe I have with the game is its ending. Its confusing, but not entirely in a good way. Leaving things open ended is not a bad thing, but here some of the key plot points are left unexplained on purpose as they are planned to be sorted out in the sequel. The issue with this is, that we may never have a sequel, even though its been worked on multiple times in the past. Even the developer's current project, titled "P7", is confirmed not to be Alan Wake 2. To fully get the idea of what happens at the end of Episode 6, you will need to do some research outside of the game.
Some may like this, but I usually find endings like this one to be unsatisfying until they're fully understood.
Even though it may be too late to get it now, as its
not for sale anymore, Alan Wake is definitely worth playing through. It's a shame we might never see a sequel, but then again, it's worth keeping in mind that Alan Wake's development roughly took around 9 years to complete, so I'll be holding onto hope at least until 2019.
This game however, is a must own for every fan of the thriller genre (horror fans might find slightly less to work with here), episodic and narrative driven games. Even if this review isn't able to help people decide whether or not to get the game now, I'm happy that I still have the chance to add my two cents, as Alan Wake is undoubtedly one of my favorite games of all time.

'The Music Machine" is a short, unsettling trip through a surreal world. If you imagine "The Scream", meets cubism, you're getting pretty close to the idea.
The game is very story driven, enhanced by the stark, two-toned environment, eerie music and some very creepy sound design. The gameplay mainly focuses on exploration and simple puzzle solving, allowing the player to gradually put together who the two main characters are and how they came to be in this strange place.
While it's not the scariest game I've ever played, it does create a good atmosphere and there were definitely a few areas that elicited the "aw hell naw" response before I soldiered on in. The last level especially, in my opinion. The environments were varied, some made use of enclosed spaces, harsh lighting and impenetrable shadows to ramp the "nope" meter up, while others used colour, sinister items and bizarre architecture to wrap you in a steadily increasing feeling of dread. The dialogue between the characters was also occasionally used to add to this, with reassuring statements such as "I feel like someone's watching us."
The soundtrack blends in and builds tension slowly without you noticing so it can ramp it up occasionally to make you crap your pants wondering what's going on. In the absence of music, the dull, reverberating ambient noise is often worse and if you're playing with headphones, every creaking floorboard sounds like the crack of doom. Right behind you.
Despite all of this excellent atmosphere, I also felt a little bored at times, after exploring an area for a while and becoming used to the ambient noise pattern, there wasn't much else that happened. Some of the mechanics, such as the ability to pick up and throw objects, were barely needed and added some confusion as to what I was supposed to be doing in the earlier levels.
I understand it's a walking sim, but there wasn't quite enough dialogue or creepy events at times to fill the long walks, and the dialogue itself - while it had its moments - mostly alternated between feeling awkward and out of place and then like someone had thrown a psychology textbook at my face. I love psychological meaning and metaphors worked into game stories, I really do, but after the fifth convoluted, God-complex filled note I eventually got lost. The concept of the relationship between the two main characters is very original and contains so much potential, but I feel it wasn't executed as well as it could have been and got lost as the story progressed. In the end, I think I got a pretty good idea of what the game was trying to convey, but it was not an easy or overly enjoyable process in that area of the game.
Overall, I did enjoy "The Music Machine". It was genuinely scary at times, the design works well with the theme of the story and despite its flaws I'm always happy to see more contributions to the psychological horror pool.

The story focuses on Haley (a 13-year old girl) and Quintin (a recently deceased 34-year old man who is possessing her). Listening to their snarky banter is entertaining, and the writing is excellent. I don't want to spoil too much about the story/situation they encounter, but suffice to say it is

highly recommend this game.

I didn't have any clue what I was expecting when I bought this game from the summer sale and the only thing I knew of this game was from trailers a few years ago. When I began playing this game I realized I had no goddamn clue what I was doing, even after playing the tutorials, since the tutorials leave out a lot of finer details that everyone should know. When I started my 1st multiplayer game I was incredibly confused, I tried to play it like aliens vs predator, just trying to rack up my kills and I thought that was the way to win, but I soon realized killing things is just a side objective in the game as everyone respawns very quickly and you wont get far by just killing aliens and marines. After I realized that the game plays out more like a RTS game where the main targets are your enemies structures I actually began to contribute to our team by playing as a support class. After that initial haze of confusion I began to have a lot of fun with the game itself. Most of the mechanics are very well polished and balanced, although if your team has a poor commander prepare to lose, since the commander is the person who orders you to push, builds structures and assists you on the ground. Therefore it goes without saying teamwork is a huge part of natural selection 2. You have to communicate with your team and you need to coordinate your attacks, otherwise your team will be a complete utter mess, you really can't go solo'ing in this game like in most games, since you will be annihilated in most situations if you do.
Both of the teams are very well distinguished, in both combat, buildings and overall gameplay. So you really have to develope new techniques depending on wich team you are playing on. There is also a fairly large community of players playing this game around the clock so you wont have any trouble finding company either. It is really a great game as long as you have a mic. I have olny played it for 20 hours as of now, but I am sure it will provide many, many more hours of entertainment.

It's like DarkSouls but without having to run all the way back to where you died and go through the by bull**** enemies again. Since there's checkpoints and not a ten second loading screen after dying, then likely you won't end up breaking your controller or keyboard.

(Review for Director's Cut version - single playthrough ~50 hours)
Pros:
The writing is absolutely phenomenal.  The overarching plot isn't really anything special, but the major locations you go to are very creative and inspired.  Comparable to or even surpassing FO2 or New Vegas.  Some of the best writing I've seen in years, to be honest.  And there is a lot of it.
The setting is cool, if unoriginal, and it's pretty open ended.
You level up a ton, so there's a pretty constant feeling of progression.
There's lots of hidden stuff and easter eggs and generally clever references.
Mediocre:
Combat is ok.  It starts to get repetitive, just due to the lack of options, and you approach every fight pretty much the same way.
The character generation and progression is pretty bland.  It's pretty much entirely just increasing your % chance for good stuff to happen (combat hit, crit chance, unlock door, disarm trap, etc.)  Perks are cool, but none of them feel gamechanging or worth building a character around, like they would in FO2.
You'll be using some skills ALL THE TIME, and nearly all of them simply result in you getting more money/ammo.  By the end of the game, you will be drowning in them, and there's really nothing that comes along that makes it worthwhile.  BUT, every once in a while, you'll find a quest item or somesuch, so you never feel like it's safe to just skip all the locked chests.
Cons:
Your party is just a bunch of random dudes which you create, with no personal storyline.
You determine your characteristics right away, but then you encounter additional party members pretty soon who can overlap with your own skills, meaning you just wasted all those skill points.  Pretty frustrating unless you play from a guide and know that is coming.
There's a lot of borderline worthless skills, except for a couple instances where they are super critical for quests. (I'm looking at you, Toaster Repair.)
The first few areas (~5 hours worth) are pretty bland, combat heavy, and will remind you of Fallout Tactics.

I purchased this game in very early access, back when Kerbin was the only planet and there were only two engines to put on your rockets. I've spent hundreds of hours playing before porting the game over to steam, so that time is not reflected in the reported hours played.
The premise of the game is simple: Explore space.
There are different game modes to accomplish that feat. There's a sandbox mode where you have access to all items and can build any rocket you can imagine. There are also science and career modes that each have progression and require the player to make small steps toward the goal of exploration. Personally, I prefer to play sandbox mode. But the other modes are pretty well balanced and give more well-defined objectives for players who tire of the sandbox.
The reason this game is fantastic is the real rocket science and physics that happen in the background. Now that doesn't mean you have to do math or understand Kepler's laws to play the game. Ultimately most players, myself included, just put together a big rocket and hit GO. However, the most ambitious among us can do the real calculations to determine the size of their rocket, the amount of fuel they need, the burn times, the engines, everything. The real physics is what makes this game so amazing to me. Anyone who plays this game will walk away with a substantially better understanding of how rockets work and of real-life space travel. I even describe this game as educational, and highly recommend it to anyone in STEM fields and absolutely recommend it to children who hope to enter STEM fields.
The other huge benefit of the simulation-like physics becomes apparent when the player reaches their own goals. I can still remember the first time I managed to land on the Mun. It felt like I had really accomplished something spectactular. Like I made a leap for mankind. It was a feeling I have never experienced in any other game, and I doubt I will ever experience that same feeling again. It felt real. Like I was a part of a real mission to land on the real moon.
I cannot recommend this game enough. The incredible sense of accomplishment gained from the first time you make it to space, get into orbit, land on the Mun, and reach other planets makes this game absolutely worth it. Not to mention the game is very fun and allows for an extreme amount of creativity and problem solving.

Hotline Miami is a 2D shooter about a guy who receives mysterious phonecalls that are methaphores to incite carnage on a targeted group of people. He also gets visited by people wearing animal masks who interrogate/intimidate him.
PROS:
+ Dynamic gameplay; there are many different ways to complete a level, both harsh, silent or berserker-like
+ Brutal, merciless storyline and combat; this game is certainly not shy of gore or extreme violence
+ A selection of unlockable animal "characters" which all have a unique skill
+ Trial and error: each level features multiple hazards and obstacles which are conquered mainly by just trying out the best way a few times
+ The gameplay feels surreal in an odd and eerie but satisfying way; a sick mindf*ck of a game, in a good way
+ "Get your butt down and learn the physics" mentality: one difficulty only
+ Great soundtrack (available as DLC)
+ Fair price
+ Trading cards
CONS:
- Some levels and bossfights feature no checkpoints and are dragged on for too long, which means a
of restarting, which very rapidly deteriorates the fun of the game (keep in mind that most attacks are a 1-hit-kill), which is a honest shame considering that I find this game done very nicely
- I really cannot let out that this game is relentlessly frustrating at times, especially when you have a bad time coping with adversity and having to start over
have to watch/skip the cutscene each time
- The game is a little short
- A small list of minor complaints and technical flaws that don't really need individual cons:
• the hitscan/frames/boxes are quite wonky and the gun accuracy is a bit bad
• some animal skills don't seem to (always) work
• certain sounds are much louder than the other sounds, meaning momentary earrape or having to turn down the volume taking away the majority of the sounds too much
• the volumes can barely be configured and the menu is not available in-game
• there's no "continue" option; you have to load chapters individually (they do go in order after completing the selected chapter, however)
A "refreshing" game because it's something different than what most games are. It's not an easy game either, so if you are up for a challenge in a fast-paced 2D shooter, take it.
My rating: 7.5/10

A friend and I both purchased this game during the last big sale, eager to co-op and see what the game was like.
I liked the found footage sort of thing the developers had going on with the game and the cutscenes. I felt the little touches like loading screens reading as "buffering" was neat, Then we enter the first cutscene. The graphics seemed fine, and the story started off simple enough: Kane's in China and helping out Lynch with an easy job. Suddenly, the bullets start flying as we opened the door to the apartment to see a chinese man in his underwear wielding a gun, beside him a young woman whose naughty bits were tastefully censored through large pixelated mosaics.
It wasn't until gameplay started, where the man shrugged off a dozen gunshots and promptly teleported away that I realized what I was in for.
Kane & Lynch 2 does something you don't see very many modern shooters incorporate, and that's fantasy and magical elements. You don't just fight gangsters, crooked cops, and the chinese military, you also fight against an assortment of wizards, chronomancers, and straight-up terminators. Alongside your standard enemies, you'll run into opponents who seem impervious to bullet fire, or having the capability to blink between reality as they teleport from one point to the next (some even phase through walls or cover!). Their ability to deny the laws of physics adds a new element to the gameplay, along with bringing another level of difficulty that I find refreshing in this genre.
On top of that, Kane and Lynch also gain the ability to weave spells, however to a much more limited degree (for example, you can only teleport very short distances and in order to trigger the two of you need to hit the button prompt beside a large enough door).
If delving into the mean streets of China and getting involved with the occult is your sort of thing, then I'd wholeheartedly recommend Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days!
