This is a wonderful tech demo with a lot of potential, but this is yet another game that was released before it was ready.
First off, the good points.
The game engine is impressive and does a good job of simulating the vehicles as they navigate the terrain, including fording flowing rivers with currents.
Graphics are quite good for the most part, including a full day-night cycle.
Vehicles can be customized at garages and the game has the logistics to necessitate fuel trucks and repair trucks.
Unfortunately, this game also has some fairly major flaws that prevent me from being able to recommend it at the asking price.
The camera is terrible. There's no first-person cockpit view (there's not even drivers in the trucks) and the 3rd person camera position is weird which makes it hard to see what you're doing with the larger trucks.
There's only one game mode and a handful of maps. The maps themselves are tiny (square KM or so), and the only reason they feel as big as they do is that going anywhere requires a fair bit of effort due to the insane amount of mud you have to drive through so you'll be moving at walking speed in 1st gear with 4WD low and lockers 90% of the time or you'll get stuck.
The whole premise of the challenge maps feels contrived as well. You have to haul lumber from an arbitrarily placed lumber stockpile to the sawmill on roads so bad they really are just mudpits. The sawmill is surrounded by trees. What is so special about these particular logs that someone is willing to risk big expensive trucks fording deep, fast flowing rivers?
Garages and fuel stations are placed with respect to the challenge so you end up with strangely placed buildings surrounded by mudpits that make no sense for anyone actually wanting to turn a profit hauling logs.
There is no free-roam mode, so this handful of maps is it for in-game content. There's enough to last for a few hours, but I was pretty disappointed when I learned this after buying the game.
In conclusion, this game still has a lot of potential and is still (slowly) being updated, but don't pay full price for it at this point. I got it on sale for 75% off and that's about the right price for this game.

So... I've been waiting for this for a little over a year now, having played Mafia I on the PS2 and playing Mafia II later on the PC, you can say that yeah, I am a pretty big fan of the Mafia games. Both games had magnificent stories, a thrilling idea and it was your classic rags to riches mobster story that feels like Goodfellas more than waht this game felt like.
Mafia III in my opinion is one of those games that you just have a bit of a hunch on. After Mafia II, I thought to myself in all honesty that this could not be topped. And I was half right. This game is flawed, for some it makes the game disappointing, others overlook it for the sake of their own entertainment. People clearly don't like repeditivity, but some do.
Lets just get into the list of what I personally liked and didn't like
-The Soundtrack and the Original Score: The soundtrack in thsi is a brilliant selection of Jazz, Rock, and a lot of other genres of music from the time period. Let me just say, it is entertaining to hear Marvin Gaye, or James Brown, or for most, The Rolling Stones, Hendrix etc. The Original score gives me a good amount of feels during certain scenes where I just listen to characters talk. I really dig this soundtrack more than I would GTA V's soundtrack for example.
-The Story: Despite not being your typical Italian Mafioso story, this still is in my opinion a good story to follow along too. Jesus, it's written like a real crime doco you'd see on the CI Channel here in 'Straya, and I love this game more for it. I enjoyed hearing all sides of the characters speak about my flawed but interesting protaganist, I even applaud the fact they didn't shy away from the racism theme, and the brutality factor of the era the games set in. This game shouldn't have had the name Mafia IMO, because the game is barely about your typical Mafia, it's a Revenge story. It also reminded me of Sons of Anarchy on ocassion for some reason.
-The Characters: Okay, lets get this out of the way, we all know and love Vito. But personally? I find interest in the other two secondary characters. They both have their reasons, their stories for being involved in the situation they find themselves in, it's a shame they didn't get just a wee bit more screen time, or even better loyalty missions (Vito's was more akin to your typical loyalty mission). Other than that, even Lincoln was an interesting character to follow in my opinion, his heritage being an interesting mix, but also hearing of his morals and service record in 'Nam is what made him interesting
-The Setting: It is a rare opportunity in my opinion to see a city like this. Of course, we know it's a fictionalised New Orleans, but having no knowledge of the state, I couldn't say for sure how accurate it is to the real place, I have yet to go (This part is subject to change whenever I get a chance to actually go there). I love how the Bayou looks like it's set on fire sometimes, tis a shame however that the French Ward is not as lively as it seems, but nonetheless it is still a pretty sight to behold.
-The Gunplay: Okay, straight up, I love old weaponry. It's just something I got a thing for, so when I got a chance to handle the weaponry of the 60's, I can't say I wasn't pleasently surprised by some of the choices. This is kind of an issue too, but we'll get into that soon. But mainly, I just liked looking at em, and they felt like they kick nicely.
-The Repedivity (Hear me out): Okay, this is my good and bad point. I didn't mind the repedivity, I always made it entertaining one way or another. I just shoot up the joint when I have too, but I do have a problem wiht this too. This is a minor point personally.
-The Repeditivity... Again: I will admit and agree that most fo the tasks are quite repeditive, and I wish that there was more variety in the tasks that were put in the game for the sake of progression. The main story missions I will admit were okay, but some really should've had more of an epic impact rather than just the same animations, or the same ways.
-The Game length: I realise that I basically farmed the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game and I finished it quickly, but in my opinion, I wish that it had more missions from the past akin to Mafia II (maybe see Lincoln in Nam doing his thing, seeing his runnings with Sammy in the golden age of Lincoln's life). Hell, I could've had a few more epic feeling story missions as mentioned as well.
-The Graphics: I am no graphics ♥♥♥♥♥, I cannot lie about this. I personally would prefer games be cell-shaded because I personally enjoy the more 'unreal' type approach to certain games. People can argue that the Mafia series has strived towards a heightened sense of Realism, but still, it's just a matter of opinion. However, I must agree that the graphics defintely could've been better than the final product has shown. I am glad that they did fix the framerate issue that was first gathered upon by this game. I find it that it is unfair however to compare this to the likes of Arkham Knight's issues, I can understand but at the same time, at least they got the 60 frames out ASAP rather than waiting longer than Day 1 for it.
My final thought is that this game had potential to be like the previous Mafia games but with a new twist, however, it kind of debauches the Mafia namesake in terms of not being truely about the Mafia. Yes, the Italian organised crime syndicate known as the mafia is in it, but they aren't the stars, their the villains which is fair enough. I give this game credit for not shying away from what the 60's was for those of a different culture or ethnicity, the rampant corruption of the sixties.
I personally do not like rating, because thats what people go off rather than reading reviews. But I give this game the equivilant of a B+. It's flawed, yes, but if you don't mind repeditivity, and play it for the good writing and acting, and even the more exciting moments, I think you'll get your moneys worth.

Overall I'd say this is a game worth getting. It may not be worth $60 but it's still strong and I don't feel bad that I spent money on it.
PROS:
- The Story:
This game has one of the best stories an action game has had in recent memory. It's nice to play as a Black War Veteran Anti-Hero, it's a direction that hasn't been taken in many games in the past. It also features a cast of interesting characters (at least the ones of any significance to the story). Without spoiling too much the high point of the story is definitely the confrontation at the end between Clay and the villain; it is realistically one of my favorite moments in any video game. The story isn't perfect, it isn't as good as Mafia II's story and is sadly spread too far and few between by an abundance of repetitive (and unskippable) story missions that don't actually progress the plot. Overall though the story and characters are so well written that it has to be a plus.
-Combat:
Combat is definitely improved in this game over its predecessors. The inclusion of the stealth and brutal execution mechanics are key points which make this a fun game to play. Nothing is more satisfying than brutally stabbing a mafiosa repeatedly in the face and then taking out his startled friend with a close range shotgun to the gut that sends him ragdolling back through the air.

There is also a great amount of flexibility in the combat tactics you can use in the game. Stealth, going in guns-a-blazing, and any mixture of the two are all valid and useable combat tactics in MAFIA III. It also is really rewarding to stealth through one of the racket missions just to sneak up on the man in charge and grab him before he knows what's going on. I do need to make note that the AI is pretty stupid, especialy when it comes to the stealth; they will often times look right past you and you can make them throw caution to the wind with a simple whistle to draw them to an area where you can stealth kill them with a simple press of the 'Q' key. The flexibility doesn't just come in tactics either. There are a wide range of weapons and explosives to choose from. Although it is kind of lame that you have very limited ammo supplies (even with the upgrades) and additionally can only carry two weapons, one small arms and one large arms weapon. I found myself often times dropping the extremely overpriced weapons I had bought purely out of the lack of ammo supply.  Regardless of these small issues the combat definitely felt improved over Mafia II.
- Exploration:
Exploring New Bordeaux in Mafia III is a lot of fun. Each area feels pretty different from any of the others which is crazy considering there are 10 different areas in the city. While exploration isn't very fruitful, aside from gathering collectibles (see cons), it is still enjoyable for explorations sake. If you want to be rewarded tangibly for exploring you may not enjoy the exploration but if you just enjoy virtual site seeing you'll have a good time.
-Soundtrack:
The soundtrack is great. While I prefered Mafia II's soundtrack (jazz is my jam), the use of classic rock songs at specific points of the game was great. Also the twangy 'bayou' music that plays during a lot of cutscenes and at the title screen is also great. It does a great job at establishing the setting and the subtle changes depending on actions are both articulate and well executed. I also enjoyed the brief moments where a jazzy song would come on, usually while checking out the map, but that is just me.
Intermediate:
These are topics that weren't really positives but weren't really negatives either
Difficulty:
I beat the game with relative ease on the hardest difficulty. It seems rather unbalanced to be quite honest. There were certain parts that were extremely difficult and others that were a breeze. These moments were generally outliers though, most of the game gave a challenge but not a frustrating one. The way the health and armor worked were also pretty unbalanced and annoying. Fully upgraded you have four health bars, but getting shot with a shotgun puts you down to about half of a bar, and then only that bar will refill unless you use medicine (which is extra annoying because the game insists on making medicine hard to come by when you need it and expensive to buy for how often you need to use it for it to be effective). Similarly the armor that you spent $3000 on would disappear after a shotgun shot and pistol shot combined. While it may be helpful in a few situations on the whole it doesn't really do too much. That being said, this was only really noticable at certain times. The challenge was generally pretty fair (except for two particular instances) and definitely made it difficult to try and storm in on an area guns blazing if there were many people there. As I said earlier I beat the game on the hardest difficulty, and while that wasn't the most difficult of accomplishments it is certainly better than many modern games I can think of that are just so frustratingly difficult on harder settings.
Driving:
The driving in Mafia III feels pretty meh. A lot of the nuiance that existed in Mafia II was scrapped. Speed limiter was totally removed. One  improvement though is that while the driving AI is still stupid, they look like geniuses compared to the drivers in Mafia II. One really annoying aspect of the driving is that you will often hit something and die but it isn't consistent. Sometimes you can get in a head on collision at max speed and live, others you hit a twig in a boat going 3/4 of max speed and die. This is definitely annoying when you make a lot of progress in a mission just to be set back to the last checkpoint for something stupid. I do have to say that driving really fast and with lots of drifting does feel great in this game, possibly better than it does in Mafia II. I should mention I was playing with the realistic driving settings on.
Cons:
Repetitive:
By the end I was pretty much bored of doing the same old racket missions over and over again just to get to the Story missions in between. That being said it was worth it to grind through for the story. Nevertheless, I wish that they could have used more original ideas than the very common, go here, kill this person or destroy this stuff approach. Racket missions also completely lacked story elements. At first they were fun but you have to remember, there are 18 rackets to take over. It gets old. Also I should mention that all the side missions (Vito's were actually pretty cool but that was because if you played Mafia II you had a little insider information as to what was going on and you had motivation to do it) were ♥♥♥♥ing awful. Burke's specifically were terrible. Stealing multiple of the same car was so god damn annoying. Same thing with the missions you were given to boost rackets. There's only so many times you can steal a boat full of marijuana before it gets old.
Lack of Immersion and Customization
In Mafia II you had to buy guns and clothes at stores, could store and customize cars, had to fill up cars with gas, and coulld stick up stores. It really sucks to come to Mafia III and see all those things gone. Lincoln is stuck in the same outfit the whole game (aside from story missions where a specific costume is given for the duration of the mission) and while he has stored cars, they are all unlocked and have to be called in, you don't have a garage that you retrieve them from as previously done. You also buy all your guns and ammo and upgrades from the back of a van that you call in which takes away from the Immersion as well. Empire Bay felt like a real city, New Bordeaux really didn't.
Collectables:
They have no achievement or even in game benefit for collectors. They're in the way.
Summary:
It plays very much like Saints Row 2 but more serious and story orientend than goofy and without the immersive factors that Mafia II had previously brought to the series.

Best walljumping umlaut simulator of 2013.
But, to be more serious: this is a platformer with occasional puzzle elements. As platformers go, this one is extremely easy. As a work of interactive visual art, it is gorgeous (as befits a game about typography). As an educational presentation, it presents the history of several significant fonts, as well as a condensed history of typesetting in general.
For each font, there is a set of levels as well as a book explaining its origins and historical significance. Scattered across the levels are collectibles which each unlock one page of the history book. While you are given the opportunity to read a page immediately after unlocking it, all of the reading material is entirely optional.
If you play the game as intended, your time is spent alternating between gameplay and reading. Aside from teaching you a history of typography, the pages also provide context which clarifies the meaning behind the various objects and images that form the in-game terrain and backdrop.
Personally, I think the educational aspect could have been improved by using voiceovers during gameplay to present the information from the pages. Using voiceovers would avoid breaking the immersion of the platforming gameplay, while still allowing the player to review the information later via the pages if s/he so desired. (Therein lies the idea for a Let's Play or longplay video...)
Overall, while I wouldn't call this a "gamer's" game, it is still an enjoyable experience, especially for the amateur typography enthusiast.

good, but that's where the qualities stop. For some, that might be enough for buying this game, because it works the same way someone would buy Crysis: for graphics and gameplay. However, The Music Machine fails at everything else, with a subpar story enough to make me embarrassed of the awkward writing, a gameplay based on walking (more on this later) with some stuff "patched" in to make it different from most. Of course, that doesn't work.
Keep reading, I promise I won't spoil the story.
Okay, let me get started with the good things. The Music Machine looks good. It's not good on graphically impressive, but it is interesting and enough to make you check out the game. Some places looks really cool, and the art style focused on simple colors doesn't put a strain in the eyes. For that, I give the game my points, the last section right before the credits looks really, really nice.
Even though there are only a couple of tracks, all the songs are really nice and beautiful. Nice work has been done here, and together with the graphics, the game had everything to be really good, but everything else overshadows these qualities. The music is moving, sometimes unnerving, and they can pass the feeling really well.
I can tell just by the OST that whoever did the songs, really loved what he was doing.
Before that, the game runs really well. It didn't drop below 60fps in 1080p at least a single time, so that's  something worth to note.
Other than that, the gameplay relies too much on walking. That can be something if you have actually something to do other walking from place to place. In this case, it remembers me a lot of Proteus, but these two games are two different things.
The Music Machine also features an inventory system. To be short, it's bad. There's a lot of spaces in there, but nothing you can fill them with. On my playthrough, I picked one single item, which I used two times. Other than that, two pages with numbers to progress with the story. There is one item you get at the end of the game, that feels like something placed because the writer didn't know how to finish the game. It's terrible and completely breaks the immersion.
You can also pick objects from the game, but I never found any use for that. Actually, there is one time you need to pick boxes to get them out of your way, so you can interact with something. Makes me wonder why so much effort for something that didn't add anything in gameplay. I picked boxes, rocks, wood; nothing was ever used. You can't stack the boxes to reach somewhere higher, because you can't jump. It's actually frustrating because your character feels like a slug even when running, but mostly because you are stuck to the ground.
That is where everything goes from bad to horrible.
The writing is simply off. Awkward, with characters I can't give a damn about, and full of "smart" moments.
It's bad. The game tries to be smart a lot of times, and I felt like reading some fanfic from a 12 years old boy after reading Lovecraft for the first time.
The characters are full of little jokes and collaboration as a comedy duo, and it completely breaks the immersion. Are you on a place that looks unnerving as hell? Well, because your character thinks something looks like a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
There's also something greater in the story, and let me get this straight: it's the worst part of the whole game.
The last part looked cool and actually got me a little cautious, but the writer didn't know how to finish his story, so he just ended the section with a half-hearted conclusion.
In the end, the only thing I could save from the story was... nevermind, I can't even remember most of the game. And I just finished it.
It's hard to tell what the developers were trying to do with this game. Something with so much potential wasted on awkward writing and design flaws. You might not feel ripped off if you get this in a bundle, but at least be sure you have something else you want from that bundle, because this game is nothing special.
The Music Machine is surely a forgettable game, and that's a good thing. It's not buggy enough to make you hate the game and tell everyone to not buy it, it's that kind of game you just say "nah, I thought it was bad" and move on.
I'm sure I will sleep and The Music Machine will just feel like a dream after I wake up, and it will just become another game in my Steam library. One of those I click just to see the screenshots.

It's easy to take fonts for granted. After all, hundreds of them come preloaded in even the simplest word processors, allowing for uninhibited freedom for formatting whatever we might need. But what most probably forget, is that it didn't use to be like this; those fonts came from somewhere, each a painstaking creation designed with a specific use in mind, which have nonetheless endured for generations and are now being put to use for far different purposes.
In many ways Type:Rider acts as a sort of mini history lesson to the legacy of fonts, a subject far more interesting in execution than on paper. From the earliest known texts to modern computer code, it's surprisingly fascinating to see the evolution of printed text and how various fonts came into being. There's a special place in my heart for games that can be both entertaining and educational, and this is certainly among the best I've played to date.
If you're shaking your head thinking there's nothing you'd rather not do than read over history descriptions while playing a game, it's worth noting that it's entirely optional to do so. It's never in your faced or forced upon you, but if you are planning to dismiss this side of the experience you'll be left with an otherwise rather bland and clumsy platformer. I was able to look past many of the weaker aspects of the game because I found the artistic and academic elements to be interesting in themselves, but those looking for even an average platformer are likely to come away disappointed.
This falls solely on the controls, a terribly clunky lesson in frustration as you attempt to maneuver a character that seems to like nothing more than to flip wildly out of control at the worst moments. Most levels make up for this by being relatively simple to traverse, but on a handful of occasion more precision is required which proves truly aggravating. The secret level being the most difficult and featuring no checkpoints only adds insult to injury, making me wonder why the developers chose to add such a challenging segment to a game that seems designed to be a relaxing an accessible experience.
Type:Rider is far from a perfect game, maybe not even a good one, but it is a unique and interesting endeavor to give a little background on a subject I'd never have bothered to look into otherwise. For those who can appreciate it more as an art piece than a traditional platformer, it's an intriguing slice of edutainment the strength of which lies in its excellent aesthetic and nontraditional source material, and not its gameplay. Anyone already bored reading this review should go ahead and pass on it, as there are dozens of other games that will be a far better fit for what you're after.
If nothing else, I doubt you'll ever look at comic sans quite the same way again.

Wasteland 2 makes for a pretty decent experience purely from a gameplay standpoint.
The mechanics are great, feels like the old school Fallout games but much better and more modernized.
Building your characters up is fine, lots of options in how to do it, though it feels like there's too many "wrong" ways of building them, with some weapon skills being far better than others, or some skills like disabling alarms being mostly useless compared to stuff like lockpicking or computer hacking.
The combat itself is fun, not much else to say there. Takes some getting used to the mechanics of it, since it's very much an old-school inspire game with a lot of things on the interface to deal with. It's also a decent challenge, enough to keep you on your toes from start to finish, particularly in your first playthrough.
Everything else though... the game doesn't look great from a graphical standpoint, and I at no point cared about the story, the dialog, any character outside of the four that I created. If you're looking for a good narrative experience, look elsewhere, and the game feels like it's gonna age like milk because of how it looks.
Worth picking up on sale I'd say, but might be worth waiting for the third game that's coming instead, which is bound to look and play better, and maybe have a story and characters worth giving a damn about.

It's effectively more of the same. If you like SOM, you'll like SOW. The sequel has all you'd expect from a successor; better graphics, new abilities, improved gameplay etc. If you're a newcomer but familar with Assassin's Creed, then simply think of that but with a Lord Of The Rings reskin. If you're not familar with either the first game or the Assassin's Creed franchise, then for around £30 I recommend picking this game up. It's a little bit of an open world / sandbox.
Those are it's good points. Time for the bad.
- The story isn't exactly something that'll blow you away. Not terrible, but clearly there to weed you through learning different combat mechanics, learning new abilities etc.
- It's very repetitive. Fortunately the combat is slick with enough variety to try out a few things or simply enjoy the spectacle, but it all boils down to run here...kill orcs...rinse, repeat.
- The controls can be very sluggish. You stick like glue to practically everything, and sometimes you may want to jump one way but end up somewhere else or crawling a wall or GRRR. Also, using the mouse slider by default to allow you to sprint faster is a poor design decision because A) Not everyone has a (functioning) mouse slider, and B) Not everyone has one of the mouse sliders where you can just let it continue rolling after pressing down a button. It looks clunky repeatedly having to flick it up to move at a decent enough speed.
- It's grindy. Not too bad in the early stages but you can see why they introduced...
- Lootboxes. They have no place in a single-player only game. I'm not as up-in-arms as most peope are about microtransactions as they do have their place in the industry (IE. Free-To-Play games and / or cosmetics only), but for this game their implementation is wholly inappropriate.
For that point, and that last point ONLY, I'm rating the game a thumbs down. Not because it's bad (IT ISN'T), but simply because I can't condone a business practice that is hostile towards customers.

Disclaimer: I played Wasteland 2 (WL2) (not the Director's Cut), a fair amount of my play time, was the game being left on overnight, there was also a substantial amount of save-scumming with the Weaponsmithing skill.
I supported the vanilla version on Kickstarter, and I have to say as a long-time Fallout 1/2 fan, this game definitely scratched that itch. Is WL2 a perfect game? No. But it is a pretty fun turn-based tactics RPG. The tactics end of this game is solid. The cover, crouch, range, and ambush aspects add to combat experience. The inventory management during combat has just the right amount of Action Point (AP) costs.
The weapon balance is good, but it could have been better. Melee attacks (Brawling, Bladed Weapons, Blunt Weapons_ are not all that great with the exception of just a few weapons - mostly they are a way to use up APs or get rid of enemies that have already closed the distance. Assault Rifles and Sniper Rifles are definitely the most useful combat skills. Other weapons have some good uses (Shotguns against enemy clusters or Energy Weapons against robots and heavily armored enemies), but are mostly there to give you multiple ammo types to draw upon. It would have been nice if the weapon balance or enemy placement necessitated more variety in team weapon skills. The non-skill use of explosives and rockets launchers is satisfyingly effective but balanced with their high costs and weights.
The role-playing game (RPG) aspect of this game is not as good as Fallout. Perhaps if WL2 had talking heads like the original Fallouts (as may change with WL3) the character dialogue and story-telling aspects may have seemed more important. As it is the dialogues seem occasionally interesting, emotional, scary, or funny, but you rarely gain much of an attachment to any of the characters. The single word buttons (with the actual sentences showing when the mouse hovers over them) is convenient but makes it seem like a quick minigame. Only on rare occasions are the consequences of using Hard♥♥♥♥♥vs. Smart♥♥♥♥♥or Kiss♥♥♥♥♥skills in conversations apparent. Most of the time it seems like just a different skill to get the same thing. Also most smaller quests in only have 2 solutions (jerk or helpful). It would have been nice if was a greater variety (using all of your skills) for more quests.
And that is what this game is really lacking in most - VARIETY. In random encounters, it is always fighting one type of enemy. It would have been nice to intervene in Wastelanders fighting off raiders instead of just the aftermath. Or 2 factions fighting each other. Or hidden treasures. The last fighters don't even flee, and there isn't an easy way for you to escape most random encounters - once entered. There are few times when diplomacy or stealth can actually help you avoid ANY fights. So keep in mind that this game is heavy on the combat. The death animations also are limited and often don't seem to relate to the attacking weapon. There is a lot of variety in scenery, but very little interaction with it (other than cover in combat).
Also I know I am in the minority on this, but I really appreciated how with Fallout 1 / 2 the developers included a gore switch and a language filter so that I could play in the presence of younger family members. Other suggestions would be the have more tags on the inventory items. There are a lot of Junk items that are not Quest items, but are either valuable to a certain vendor somewhere or are useful to resolve some obscure quest later on in the game. They should be labeled as Useful or something - but the game either assumes that you will hold onto at least one of each type of junk. Also when using the Weaponsmithing skill if your character has a 10/10 in that skill shouldn't they be able to get the parts them want from the Strip For Parts option instead just xx% chance for each.
Lastly it would have been nice if there were more challenging combat encounters. The game is really difficult for a novice - especially if you don't check walkthoughs to optimize characters (APs are crucial) and if you don't know the best weapons to choose / modify. Once you know how to do those things, the game is a breeze except for a few "boss fights". Now if it seems like this review too negative, I hope that it was mostly constructive criticism and I only do it because I care. Good game. General Vargas, I salute you.

It's OK. not great but OK.
Graphics are an improvement, Nemesis system is a step up, voice acting and story are also improved. There's more human interaction in the first two hours here than there ever was in the entirity of SoM. Combat and stealth feel a tad downgraded, Navigation is improved aside from sticking like glue to things to the point where you'll glitch on a ledge.
The game is a grindfest from act two onwards (The point at which you can start taking over the fortresses) It's quite clearly designed to be a grindfest and it feels like you can't really do anything other than focus on building your army. I want to explore, I want to finish quests but it feels like if I don't focus on building my armies then I am going to regret it later which you do as when you reach a certain act the strength of your strongholds becomes the most important thing in the game and in order to build them up to an acceptable level you have to grind and grind and grind to earn in game currency.
This in game currency is used to buy chests to unlock orcs and orc training to improve your forces and why is it designed to be such a grindfest? So you'll eventually cave and purchase "gold" with real money to shortcut the grind.
What's worse is that this IG currency is also used to buy upgrades for your fortresses which get pretty pricey (up to 7500) which can be a grind in itself by design to further "encourage" you to spend real money.
Microtransactions in a singleplayer game are terrible but the ones in SoW are by far the worst I have ever seen. They are very anti-player.
Here is how the "loot boxes" work. There are different kinds. Silver, Gold and Mithril. The silver chests (lowest grade chests) are the ONLY chests you can buy with currency you earn in game. In these chests you will get two orcs of varying rarity and one orc training. These chests cost 1500 in game currency each.
The gold chests (Which contain four orcs and two training items) and the Mithril chests (Same amount but all 100% legendary grade) you buy with "gold" and how do you get gold? By paying real money.
So they lock all of the good stuff behind a pay-wall basically. Spend hours upon hours upon hours grinding currency to buy measly little silver chests at 1500 each or drop money on some gold and just buy the higher grade chests. There are gold chests you can "earn" in game but these gold chests only give you gear for your character and give you nothing for the meat of the game which is the armies.
These microtransactions really can ruin the experience. They intentionally made the main mechanic of the entire game (Main as in you NEED these fortesses to progress through the story) a massive grindfest while locking things behind a pay-wall to try and force you to spend even more money on a game you just dropped a hefty amount on just to play.
Take the microtransactions out and it's an "OK" game that I could reccomend getting on sale. With them in here though? Don't even get it on sale. Very anti-consumer, disgusting practice. People gave the developers an earful for their practice and rightly so, people recently went batsh!t crazy on EA for what they did (again, rightly so) but what these guys are doing is so much worse in my opinion.
You drop £45/$60 on this game and they have the audacity to take the main mechanic and draw of this game (the army system) and lock things behind a ridiculous grind and a pay-wall.

This is a wonderful tech demo with a lot of potential, but this is yet another game that was released before it was ready.
First off, the good points.
The game engine is impressive and does a good job of simulating the vehicles as they navigate the terrain, including fording flowing rivers with currents.
Graphics are quite good for the most part, including a full day-night cycle.
Vehicles can be customized at garages and the game has the logistics to necessitate fuel trucks and repair trucks.
Unfortunately, this game also has some fairly major flaws that prevent me from being able to recommend it at the asking price.
The camera is terrible. There's no first-person cockpit view (there's not even drivers in the trucks) and the 3rd person camera position is weird which makes it hard to see what you're doing with the larger trucks.
There's only one game mode and a handful of maps. The maps themselves are tiny (square KM or so), and the only reason they feel as big as they do is that going anywhere requires a fair bit of effort due to the insane amount of mud you have to drive through so you'll be moving at walking speed in 1st gear with 4WD low and lockers 90% of the time or you'll get stuck.
The whole premise of the challenge maps feels contrived as well. You have to haul lumber from an arbitrarily placed lumber stockpile to the sawmill on roads so bad they really are just mudpits. The sawmill is surrounded by trees. What is so special about these particular logs that someone is willing to risk big expensive trucks fording deep, fast flowing rivers?
Garages and fuel stations are placed with respect to the challenge so you end up with strangely placed buildings surrounded by mudpits that make no sense for anyone actually wanting to turn a profit hauling logs.
There is no free-roam mode, so this handful of maps is it for in-game content. There's enough to last for a few hours, but I was pretty disappointed when I learned this after buying the game.
In conclusion, this game still has a lot of potential and is still (slowly) being updated, but don't pay full price for it at this point. I got it on sale for 75% off and that's about the right price for this game.

Hotline Miami is a game that makes me question my sanity. Sure, they're little men in white coats, but every single stab, slice, or bludgeon is just another point in the scoreboard, just an objective needed. I enjoy it, I think. The game plays like a fever dream, a bad trip, with trance-like music (my favorite tracks are "Crystals" and "Deep Cover"), moving camera angles, and irrational scenes. Is the narrator's friend a video store employee, a pizza store employee, or a barkeeper? Does it matter? Hotline Miami makes you wonder but it never forces you, because it's not important who the main character is, nor what his story is about. Its about the killing. Don't feel bad for enjoying it, because it is good violence.
With any enemy attack killing you, the game brings a visceral realism to the entire experience. Of course a single shotgun blast will kill you, I start questioning games where it doesn't. You're one man against a whole lot of (admittedly stupid) men. Weapons can and will kill you and you have to be the smartest, the fastest, and the most skilled. I can't help but feel a giddy pleasure when I execute a large amount of people in a short amount of time. The controls are fluid when you're running and smashing people in the head with a melee weapon, but clumsy and hard to use when trying to pinpoint aim a rifle to take out other mobsters. It feels intentional, because a gun feels like cheating, almost. Part of being a spree killer, which you undoubtedly are, is to be gritty and makeshift. What's more satisfyingly homespun than throwing a glass bottle at a man's head?
In terms of combat, I'm confident in saying that this one handles it better than the sequel. Wrong number makes melee a breeze, because most weapons you have are way faster than they should be- just holding down the swing button and running straight at them is horribly efficient at decimating a small army of people wielding lead pipes. No sell in this one: you have to plan, because weapons can be slow (with the exception of the incredibly fast knife) and you have to take enemies by surprise to have a chance of not getting brained by a golf club. Guns are also largely unneeded- and mostly impractical. Shooting a gun just sends every person in the area running at you and you only have limited ammo to kill them with. Instead, throwing a knife (which might not always kill the opponent but nonetheless knocks them down) is a good way to deal with ranged foes.
There's a couple of bosses in this game. I won't spoil the last one, but the first one- who you see more of later, is a doozy. I've never felt more like playing a real person than when a single slice from your opponent will end your life, and the only way to win is to evade, evade, evade, until they give you a chance to smash their head open. My hands hurt after that portion and the NUMEROUS times I had to retry it, but it was never frustrating.
Hotline Miami's tone is something I adore deep in my heart and it's almost hard to find something quite like it. It's hot and sweaty, gaudy in its psychedelic influence, and the blood and gore feels out of place yet it belongs so utterly within the crowded miami mob bases. The music is all techno, which is something I thought I wouldn't enjoy, but damn, do I? Each one is made by great artists (who I tracked down and bought albums from because YES) and picked perfectly by Dennation to match the level they're intended from. Particularly of mention is the later level "Clean hit", which has a portion where you have to sidle along a building and crawl from window to balcony. The music playing during this moment, "Hotline", made it feel like a heist caper- so perfect was this moment that I still try to recapture that feeling, even if the levels are downright short compared to the second game.
The top down 2d feel never feels like it could have been better in another format, and indeed, this game practically reinvigorated the top down shooter as it is. Pixel graphics are basic yet provide a perfect lackadaisical tone to the violence, making it brutal and graphic but never overly so. The face sprites are one aspect of the thematic game visual, though, that I don't quite appreciate- yes the game is gaudy and feels like a trip to the red light district and it's a nice change to see people who aren't afraid to make ugly sprites- but do they really need to look quite like that? I'd have liked it just a bit more if the faces looked more normal, but that's just a nitpick. As it is, they have a lot of character and I can respect the decision.
All in all, this is the best game I've played recently that I thought I might not like. God, it's so good, I want to be playing it more instead of writing this review. The levels are all mostly the same and it's like a drug trip, no matter how much you know you'll be getting the exact same thing you want more. I recommend this game a whole lot. Play the sequel too but beware that it's just not as good.

Shadow of War builds on the previous title and the use of the Nemesis system with an array of new abilities, powers, and missions. In that sense, the game has a lot of promise. It does, however, have a fatal flaw. Whereas in the previous games, you generally picked your targets, in this game, your targets are largely pre-set, and proceedurally generated. This means that the difficulty curve is all over the map, where you might be playing for a while, hit a very, very difficult fight, spend hours grinding through it, get better at the combat system, overcome it, and then be greeted by a return to enemies that are now beneath your skill level.
I'd suggest that you consider picking this game up on a sale, because it has some fun innovations, but overall the quality has declined from the first game because of how all-over-the-map the difficulty curve is.

Natural Selection 2 (NS2) is a FPS/RTS Hybrid that pits aliens vs. marines to destroy each other's base of operation.
If you want to play a game that requires skill and communication to execute an effective attack on an enemy base/position then this game is a LOT of fun and it is for you. Honestly one of the best moments of a game was one in which the aliens were losing yet one player kept coordinating attacks on the marines, gathering eight aliens to a marine base only to have us all die, and respawn only to do it all again. These moments are always the best, even when they don't work out. There was a real sense of comradery in that game due to one eager player.
Let's face it the best moments in a rts is when you get your entire army together to storm the enemy base. The army that you built by gathering all the resource points and have been spending on fantastic upgrades such as:
Aliens- better speed, armor, invisibility/stealth, visible hit markers and position, more energy for attacks, giant rhino tanks that knock marines to the ground (onos), phasing death-scythe beasts, and kamikaze aliens. A herd of onos + gorge healers = Game Over Man, Game Over!
Marines- grenades, shotguns, armor, firepower, flamethrower, grenade launcher, mines, jetpacks, exo suits, and double exo suits. Flamethrower + Jetpack = If it bleeds, we can kill it.
If you want to be a "one man army" like many FPS games then by all means, go play one of the dozens and dozens of FPS clones. I still do on occasion.
Some general tips to do well if and when you first get this game-
General - be polite and kind, do not blame others. Listen and follow directions to the commander, he/she can see a lot more than you can and can help you if you're playing smart. You will die a lot, it happens, don't let it discourage you. The learning curve on this game is steep, but you will get there. And for god's sake stick together and communicate with your team. Listen closely for any and all footsteps. And have fun
Aliens- (skulks mostly as this is how most will play for a while) use the walls and ceilings to ambus marines with your team. Do not run at the marines face first. Be minful how loud you are when you move and hold shift to silence your footsteps at a reduction in speed.
Marines- Always have a buddy, the aliens always do. Use your distance to your advantage as aliens have to run to you, use long hallways to shoot from a distance. Switch to your pistol if you need to reload yet are still under attack. Watch your teammates backs as they build/repair structures and buy a welder to patch your team's shields and repair damaged structure.

I am only 2.7 hours in at the writing of this review, but already I can tell you that this is well worth the $15 I paid for it, perhaps even the full $30.
The physics engine is amazing. It's fun watching the chassis flex and the sides of the carriage flap around as you trundle along, or seeing mud clump up on your tires while you are digging "trenches" in the ground. I can use real-life tricks that have succeeded in getting me out of muddy/snowy parking lots in real life on scenarios in-game, to the same effect.
If you like spending 15 minutes trying to think your way out of being stuck in a mud hole, then you will love this game. If you don't have a tremendous amount of patience, though... This game is going to *punish* you. In 2.7 hours of gameplay, I have managed to get into a bit of a cycle:
- drive halfway across the map to get lumber
- drive halfway across the map again to refuel at the garage
- get 1/2 to 2/3rds of the way to my destination
- lose patience, roll over
- swear
- return to square one
It's definitely a challenge; not an impossible challenge, though. I eventually managed to swear and giggle my way through all the levels.
On top of that, there are achievements that are challenges rather than chores and also a tremendous amount of "modding" going on, so this game has as much replay value as you want it to.

PROS:
- The Story:
This game has one of the best stories an action game has had in recent memory. It's nice to play as a Black War Veteran Anti-Hero, it's a direction that hasn't been taken in many games in the past. It also features a cast of interesting characters (at least the ones of any significance to the story). Without spoiling too much the high point of the story is definitely the confrontation at the end between Clay and the villain; it is realistically one of my favorite moments in any video game. The story isn't perfect, it isn't as good as Mafia II's story and is sadly spread too far and few between by an abundance of repetitive (and unskippable) story missions that don't actually progress the plot. Overall though the story and characters are so well written that it has to be a plus.
-Combat:
Combat is definitely improved in this game over its predecessors. The inclusion of the stealth and brutal execution mechanics are key points which make this a fun game to play. Nothing is more satisfying than brutally stabbing a mafiosa repeatedly in the face and then taking out his startled friend with a close range shotgun to the gut that sends him ragdolling back through the air.

There is also a great amount of flexibility in the combat tactics you can use in the game. Stealth, going in guns-a-blazing, and any mixture of the two are all valid and useable combat tactics in MAFIA III. It also is really rewarding to stealth through one of the racket missions just to sneak up on the man in charge and grab him before he knows what's going on. I do need to make note that the AI is pretty stupid, especialy when it comes to the stealth; they will often times look right past you and you can make them throw caution to the wind with a simple whistle to draw them to an area where you can stealth kill them with a simple press of the 'Q' key. The flexibility doesn't just come in tactics either. There are a wide range of weapons and explosives to choose from. Although it is kind of lame that you have very limited ammo supplies (even with the upgrades) and additionally can only carry two weapons, one small arms and one large arms weapon. I found myself often times dropping the extremely overpriced weapons I had bought purely out of the lack of ammo supply.  Regardless of these small issues the combat definitely felt improved over Mafia II.
- Exploration:
Exploring New Bordeaux in Mafia III is a lot of fun. Each area feels pretty different from any of the others which is crazy considering there are 10 different areas in the city. While exploration isn't very fruitful, aside from gathering collectibles (see cons), it is still enjoyable for explorations sake. If you want to be rewarded tangibly for exploring you may not enjoy the exploration but if you just enjoy virtual site seeing you'll have a good time.
-Soundtrack:
The soundtrack is great. While I prefered Mafia II's soundtrack (jazz is my jam), the use of classic rock songs at specific points of the game was great. Also the twangy 'bayou' music that plays during a lot of cutscenes and at the title screen is also great. It does a great job at establishing the setting and the subtle changes depending on actions are both articulate and well executed. I also enjoyed the brief moments where a jazzy song would come on, usually while checking out the map, but that is just me.
Intermediate:
These are topics that weren't really positives but weren't really negatives either
Difficulty:
I beat the game with relative ease on the hardest difficulty. It seems rather unbalanced to be quite honest. There were certain parts that were extremely difficult and others that were a breeze. These moments were generally outliers though, most of the game gave a challenge but not a frustrating one. The way the health and armor worked were also pretty unbalanced and annoying. Fully upgraded you have four health bars, but getting shot with a shotgun puts you down to about half of a bar, and then only that bar will refill unless you use medicine (which is extra annoying because the game insists on making medicine hard to come by when you need it and expensive to buy for how often you need to use it for it to be effective). Similarly the armor that you spent $3000 on would disappear after a shotgun shot and pistol shot combined. While it may be helpful in a few situations on the whole it doesn't really do too much. That being said, this was only really noticable at certain times. The challenge was generally pretty fair (except for two particular instances) and definitely made it difficult to try and storm in on an area guns blazing if there were many people there. As I said earlier I beat the game on the hardest difficulty, and while that wasn't the most difficult of accomplishments it is certainly better than many modern games I can think of that are just so frustratingly difficult on harder settings.
Driving:
The driving in Mafia III feels pretty meh. A lot of the nuiance that existed in Mafia II was scrapped. Speed limiter was totally removed. One  improvement though is that while the driving AI is still stupid, they look like geniuses compared to the drivers in Mafia II. One really annoying aspect of the driving is that you will often hit something and die but it isn't consistent. Sometimes you can get in a head on collision at max speed and live, others you hit a twig in a boat going 3/4 of max speed and die. This is definitely annoying when you make a lot of progress in a mission just to be set back to the last checkpoint for something stupid. I do have to say that driving really fast and with lots of drifting does feel great in this game, possibly better than it does in Mafia II. I should mention I was playing with the realistic driving settings on.
Cons:
Repetitive:
By the end I was pretty much bored of doing the same old racket missions over and over again just to get to the Story missions in between. That being said it was worth it to grind through for the story. Nevertheless, I wish that they could have used more original ideas than the very common, go here, kill this person or destroy this stuff approach. Racket missions also completely lacked story elements. At first they were fun but you have to remember, there are 18 rackets to take over. It gets old. Also I should mention that all the side missions (Vito's were actually pretty cool but that was because if you played Mafia II you had a little insider information as to what was going on and you had motivation to do it) were ♥♥♥♥ing awful. Burke's specifically were terrible. Stealing multiple of the same car was so god damn annoying. Same thing with the missions you were given to boost rackets. There's only so many times you can steal a boat full of marijuana before it gets old.
Lack of Immersion and Customization
In Mafia II you had to buy guns and clothes at stores, could store and customize cars, had to fill up cars with gas, and coulld stick up stores. It really sucks to come to Mafia III and see all those things gone. Lincoln is stuck in the same outfit the whole game (aside from story missions where a specific costume is given for the duration of the mission) and while he has stored cars, they are all unlocked and have to be called in, you don't have a garage that you retrieve them from as previously done. You also buy all your guns and ammo and upgrades from the back of a van that you call in which takes away from the Immersion as well. Empire Bay felt like a real city, New Bordeaux really didn't.

The Music Machine is a surreal and eerie voyage through nightmarish landscapes: exploring and easy puzzles slowly give you a glimpse of the story behind the worlds you find yourself in.
-the graphics are simple but very nice: the use of two colours for each level really adds a sense of surreality and dread
-the world you explore are well crafted and pretty original
-very nice and eerie soundtrack
-an interesting story, albeit some of it is left to the player's imagination
-both characters are quite interesting and interact in a believable way
-game doesn't refrain from bringing up very dark themes in its narrative
-pretty linear
-very short
-a few typos here and there
-inventory system seems more like an afterthought
-no replay value unless you want to experience the funny easter egg level
The Music Machine was a very interesting experience, its landscapes and story truly evoke a sense of dread and some of the themes can be downright crude.
I didn't have "fun" per se while playing it but then I feel fun isn't what the game wants to offer: ultimately the basic gameplay is there just as a mean to let you experience its story.
And said story is a very good one: perhaps it'd have been better suited to a short story book format rather than a game and its surely disturbing and cryptic enough that only a certain audience will properly enjoy it.
Still, if you feel like you're part of that audience, this game is a worthy experience and a fine example of how nuanced horror narratives can be: due to its short length and linear gameplay I'd recommend snatching it up on a bundle/sale if you're interested.

The first time I played Wasteland 2 was when it was initially released and filled with bugs. After a couple hours I lost interest and uninstalled the game. Fast forward almost three years later, and I decided to fire it up again and test out the new "director's cut". And I'm glad I did. As I am taking summer courses and have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of free time, this game is perfect. I've always been a fan of the Fallout series and of post-apocalyptic games in general, so W2 fit right in.
My favorite feature in W2 is the party system. When you begin, you can completely customize up to four Rangers, choosing from loads of skills and weapon proficiencies. On top of this, as you progress through the game, you can recruit up to three more companions who can switch in and out of your squad as you see fit. Each companion has a unique skillset and adds their opinion on what is happening around them, adding depth to the game.
Next is the complete freedom of choice. Each encounter can be played out differently. Each quest has multiple sides you can join. Or if you want to just kill everyone, you can do that too. (Red Skorpions..)
The game really took off for me when I reached the second chapter, in an entirely new area. At this point, I had a seven-member killing machine that left corpses of the wicked and grateful smiles of the innocent behind it. This new area is ten times more of a mess than the one you leave behind, and the difficulty noticably ramps up. But so does the fun.
The only weak points I can think of are that using skills are a bit slow, navigating the map can be frustrating, and the first area gets boring after a while. Other than these issues, the characters, locations, and story are enough get you addicted almost right off the bat.
I'll give it a 9/10. Essentially it's a slower, more complex XCOM game. If you're a die hard turn-based party RPG fan like me, buy it, you won't regret it. If you're on the fence, just wishlist it and wait for a sale.
But either way, don't hesitate, because the wasteland needs you!!

The other reviews here are fairly old (for a game with active devs), so I just want to clear some things up. There are more than two servers. I only played about an hour and found games in a few seconds every time I started the game. I also have yet to encouter any hackers, but take that with a grain of salt, as I do only have an hour played. There are skins, but you have to pay real money for all of them, and as far as I can tell, there is no drop system. The graphics....leave something to be desired to say the least. It seemed as though my avatar had a perpetually broken arm, but as long as he kept shooting, who cares? There are graphics options but they are painfully barebone: resolution, overall graphics quality, anti-aliasing, and a few other yes/no switches. In terms of gameplay, I think that the moniker of "arcadey counter strike" is justified. You do buy weapons with money gained from kills, but obviously you respwan after every death, so the tactical money management of CS isn't present here. The guns themselves seem rather unbalanced, but I'm sure the devs will adress this. Heashots do pay off, and recoil is a thing, but moving while shooting is a much more viable option. To be honest, the reason why I will continue to play this game is potential. The devs honestly seem genuine in their care for the game. They are performing daily/weekly maintenance on the game and adding new features each time, according to the update logs. In conclusion, if you want a counter strike where you can relax, and simply go for kills without having to worry about tactics, I would consider this game a win, especially if you take into account that it still is in early access. I for one am looking forward to seeing how this game will develp over time.

is a truly rare gem in the open-world genre. I do not understand what many of the critics are thinking in panning it as repetitive, limited, or not up to the standards set by the GTA series, etc. I'd say in response that those things are it's greatest strength.
does not attempt to be the greatest make-your-own-crazy-fun-by-being-a♥♥♥♥♥♥simulator, which is what the GTA series seems to me most of the time. If you want to have a gazilliion mini games within your game or get your jollies wandering around smacking useless NPCs in the face with an inflatable♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ well, go play something else.
This game has a laser-sharp focus on an engaging story, which is doled out in effective dollops via lovely cut scenes. You feel like everything you're doing in the world is all about reaching your objective: paying back the antagonist in the only currency that really matters in the end.
I think the racism is a little overdone. In this game nearly every white person is a near-rabid racist and every black person is an innocent doe-eyed victim. But it's not as horrible as it could have been, and I suppose overdoing the importance of racism is just the flavor of our age. So at least it isn't as bad as it could be.
What really keeps bringing me back, however, are the presentation values and the game mechanics. First, this game is
, I mean jaw-droppingly, heart-achingly beautiful. I've posted screenshots of sunsets that look to me more like impressionist paintings than a video game. I just love walking around and looking at things. It reminds me of the limited time I spent in New Orleans, only better without the blazing heat, humidity, and bugs.
The audio effects and voice work is nearly as good as the video, but the soundtrack... well, the soundtrack brilliantly captures the whole spirit of the age. It takes me back to being a little boy when much of that was still played in my parents' house. The soundtrack alone would justify buying the editions of the game that have it.
And the game mechanics, while maybe a little too forgiving at times, are brilliant, truly first class. I originally disliked being limited to a mere two weapons, but it forces me to choose intelligently. And of course I can always pick up whatever my enemies drop, which is handy in protracted fights.
I think the stealth mechanics are pure perfection. You can actually screw up a little without an enemy immediately going from bored to shooting endlessly at you. And when you do screw up too much and somebody opens up on you, only his nearby buddies come to his aid. It doesn't feel like they're all part of an enormous hive mind that immediately commands every bad guy in the whole bloody game to start shooting precisely at where you are.
You can break line of sight, get behind them for ambushes, lay your own traps with noise-makers and such. I don't think I've ever played a game like this before with such wonderful stealth mechanics. And then as you progress in the game, stealth isn't your only tool. Once you can call in some muscle, well, your likelihood of surviving by going in guns a blazing goes up considerably. And it's a blast.
The only thing I haven't much figured out yet is evading the police. Some story missions force you to try to evade them, and in those it seems like they have an infinite number of patrol cars, and not just behind you. No, I'm getting better at shaking the cops behind me. But when around literally every turn there's another roadblock and multiple patrol cars, well, you're just screwed.
Fortunately it seems like the game only lets you fail so many times before you just go on with the story. I'm not sure I'm entirely happy with that, but it beats the hell out of being stuck for hours until you just get lucky.
So here's the bottom line. If you buy an open world game to do everything
experience the main story, then
probably isn't for you. But if you're ready for a mature, gripping story with lots of action and fun, set in an absolutely beautiful game world, stop reading and get to buying already.
UPDATE: So I've now spent over 54 hours with the game, and I have found one thing that has become increasingly annoying and one thing that's more of a minor irritation. For sake of thoroughness, I thought I'd update the review accordingly.
First the minor irritation. The game is a little inconsistent in the way missions go down. Most of the time you show up and talk to somebody, Donovon for example, and new markers appear on your map and you can go pick and choose what to do. The initial conversaion just unlocks things.
But on rare occasion, talking to someone kicks off the mission itself and you suddenly find yourself in a situation for which you might be badly unprepared. I won't give away anything significant, but it happened to me yet again last night and was very frustrating. There was basically no way to complete the mission with the way I was equipped.
There's no way I can find to determine what's going to happen, so really what this means is that you've always got to go into every conversation loaded for bear. Or be prepared to abort the mission, wait for the lengthy re-load, and such. Like I said, a minor irritation.
The more major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ that takes some of the shine off the game for me, is how Sal Marcano sends hit squads to kill you from time to time. The concept itself makes a lot of sense, and I see how that could be some thrilling game play. But to date the execution of the game mechanics has been horribly flawed.
Almost every time this happens, I'm running down the middle of a street or locked into an unskippable animation (e.g., wiretapping). The cars full of enemies spawn so close to me I can literally see them pop into existence in the game. And when this happens while I'm in an unskippable animation or in the middle of the street, eight thugs open up on me at point blank range, and I can't even draw a gun before I'm dead.
It's basically the game's way of saying **** you. You have to wait for the painfully long reload, re-buy your flak jacket, and get on with what you were trying to do. It's a badly broken feature that needs fixing.
UPDATE REDUX: Another update to my review after spending another dozen-plus hours with it. The thing that I've wondered about since starting this game is how so many of the reviews slag it for falling short of the GTA series. So I spent about a dozen hours with
because I really wanted to see how it compared. The point of this update is to try to say something useful for those players.
First, I think I finally "get it" where the GTA series is concerned. I've not been able to stand the previous entries in the franchise, but I see how GTA5 is genuinely entertaining. But I remain surprised nevertheless at the people complaining about how
doesn't hold up. I think it holds up quite well.
The key thing to understand, like I said earlier, is that it's far more focused.
tells a wonderfully touching and engrossing story, and it does this in pretty much everything it does. It makes me care about Lincoln Clay and all the choices he makes. In contrast, GTA5 doesn't make me care about any of the characters I've met (at least so far), it just makes me wish they'd shut up and stop dropping N/F-bombs every other word.
Seriously,
comes off as
by comparison, and that's really saying something. I feel like I'm just wallowing in stupid when I play GTAV, whereas I love the world of New Bordeaux in
. Of course I do have to give it to GTAV where it's deserved: it is without question the most involved, hugest, most interactive open-world game of its kind. I've never before seen a game where I can wander around playing golf and doing so many other things.
But I just don't care.

These dogs need putting down.
The Good:
* Better weapons
* Your partner is actually useful in a fire-fight
* Graphical Engine is better but doesn't have a lot to do.
* umm.. didnt crash?
The Bad:
* Still violent but somewhat toned down in language and action
* Shaky-cam everywhere.. because movie!
* Dumb loading screen with a buffering logo.. because movie!
* Continual lens flare, motion blur & pixelation.. because movie!
* Censored blur of body parts.. because movie?
* Cover system so poor its best not to use it
* Guns sound limp and seem less accurate, except shotguns
* Diverse environments replaced with samey grubby alleys
* Story is non-existent and copied from 1 element of K&L1
* AI is dumb and predictable
* 4-5 Hours long for story mode
Background: Playing 1&2 back to back for the first time so mostly comparing to the first game.
Impressions: You can see huge missteps everywhere in K&L2.
1) Cinematic Misunderstandings
Cinematic leanings of the first game are magnified in all the wrong ways that people who don't understand the language of cinema fall into and add elements because you have them in this sort of film.
POV shaky-cam everywhere when people are just talking or having lunch and the POV is not of a person but some nebulous floating camera. Couple this with lens flare and blur and its a recipe for motion sickness. The buffering logo as the level loads is obnoxious, who likes to see a buffering logo.. and it might be a joke but it often stayed on 99% while the dialogue finished long after it had read the game into memory.
Gone is the plot and character progression replaced with mundane streams of generic enemies and a vague goal of not dying.
2) Game mechanics
The cover system is broken in the same old way since enemies can still shoot you through walls it's  better to crouch a foot off the wall and then you take no damage.
Continually tells you to flank but enemies face forward until you shoot. Similarly as you move around cover the ninja like senses of the cops track you through walls 90degrees ahead of them.
Recommended for: Boarderline recommended for those looking for a violent but rather weak FPS.
Conclusion: 5/10. Weak sauce, play K&L 1 and forget this ever happened.

Following the magnificent games in the franchise, especially Mafia II, we were hoping for another great and captivating story. What we got is an impressive and rather unique storytelling that keeps pushing you and asking for more. Characters are strong, impressive and the game surely doesn't hold back on this part.
Nemesis system that 'debuted' in Shadow of Mordor is back once again, although in a different style and magnitude. Unfortunately, rather than using that system up to its full potentional, Mafia III unfortunately overstayed its welcome and stretched a bit longer than it should've.
Gameplay is very satisfying and enjoyable as well as driving, but arguable AI will often leave you unsatisfied with missions layout and their objectives. You'll often find yourself in a position where it's either too easy or quite challenging to take down a simple mob due to rather strange and problematic AI structure.
Soundtrack is on another level and developers nailed it, from opening songs, to closing ones, from driving in a car to just randomly playing a song after a certain mission - this game has it all, and it showcased its soundtrack amazingly.
Customizing is very lackluster, so often you'll end up spending your money on refilling ammo, bandages, buying weapons and such.
Altough the game sets a great base and has a great core overall, performance issues such as numerous bugs, low draw distance, often FPS drops will make you think twice before purchasing this game at its full price.
Score: 7/10

So far it's been quite underwhelming. I'm a fan of the whole Mafia series and this one has a an interesting setting and a fresh take on the Mafia theme, but Mafia 3 disappoints. The game seems unfinished. Why?
1. The graphics issues - choppy frames, mirror-like glitches appearing out of nowhere, plastic-looing cars, lighting and colour changes - have still not been resolved, and we're talking post-patches.
2. The world. For all of its linearity, I loved Mafia 2's game world. This is one of my favorite RPGs of all time, but is certainly one of the best of the last few years.  It isn't an open-world explorer like Skyrim - the Witcher throws you deep into a tale of political intrigue, clashing mages, threatening dragons, and racial (meaning Dwarvish and Elvish) tension.  The universe and backstory are fleshed out through maps, books, and an admittedly sometimes annoying bard narrator and you play a key role in the rise and fall of the many kingdoms of the game.
You play Geralt of Rivia, a semi-superhuman mutant with magical, alchemical, and sword-combat abilities.  You kill monsters for hire, but soon get dragged into  tale of assassination and war.
Though this is story-driven, it isn't completely linear as the 3rd act plays near completely differently depending on what factions you align with and much like Fallout games, the decisions you make influence in minor ways how the game plays out as well as the end video sequence.
The Witcher III looks kickass and is coming out this year.  Pick this one up so you'll be exposed to the excellent backstory and universe!

Since it's free and on sale this weekend, I'll go ahead and put my two cents in, which is to say that I highly recommend this title to anyone at all interested in RPGs.  Ok, I'll admit it - fatansy games aren't my favorite genre, and I tend to skip over most titles where magic is the primary component. To be honest it was the "adult content" that first caught my interest in the game - not that the sex and nudity isn't far tamer than what you can see on any given web site, I just wanted to see how far a video game would push the envelope on this kind of stuff. The game looks amazing, with some of the best graphics out there - a little too good, if you turn on ubersampling, which very few systems can handle well.  The story is rich, complex and engaging, and well-told throughout, with incredible music and excellent voice-acting.  You would do well to play through the first Witcher game if you want the full backstory, but it's not strictly necessary.  Finally the magic system is well thought-out and easy to learn, which is great for someone like me who doesn't play a lot of fantasy games.  All in all, if you're a hardcore RPG or fantasy fan, this is definitely a game for you.  If you're on the fence about either, this game is a great introduction to the genre.  For this price you simply can't go wrong.

Type:Rider is a relatively straight-forward platform designed around the concept of showcasing the history of printing and typefaces that came about from that.  You control a simple two-wheeled vehicle that can jump, allowing you to drive and manuever throug the abstract levels composed of structures made mostly of characters in the given type face. The goal in each level (about 8 of them, centered around the major innovations in printing), besides reaching the end, is to collect the 26 alphabet characters in each level as well as lore markers (which opens up brief articles about the specific period. There's also a hidden amperstand (&) character in each level that's more a challenge to locate and get. Levels are well designed with great visuals (taking a page from Limbo to have clear distinction from foreground and background elements) and several dynamic features.  The gameplay is otherwise rather easy - plenty of checkpoints, no life counter, and save for a few places on the last few levels that require twitchy controls, simple-enough puzzles. It took about 2 hours to complete all the levels (not full collectio) though the last bonus level is not as forgiving.
It is not a must-have game, but it is a game that has been lovingly put together for a specific purpose, and one of those that I'd recommend at a sale price, or if you are interested in the history of print to start with.
