Hotline Miami is a game that makes me question my sanity. Sure, they're little men in white coats, but every single stab, slice, or bludgeon is just another point in the scoreboard, just an objective needed. I enjoy it, I think. The game plays like a fever dream, a bad trip, with trance-like music (my favorite tracks are "Crystals" and "Deep Cover"), moving camera angles, and irrational scenes. Is the narrator's friend a video store employee, a pizza store employee, or a barkeeper? Does it matter? Hotline Miami makes you wonder but it never forces you, because it's not important who the main character is, nor what his story is about. Its about the killing. Don't feel bad for enjoying it, because it is good violence.
With any enemy attack killing you, the game brings a visceral realism to the entire experience. Of course a single shotgun blast will kill you, I start questioning games where it doesn't. You're one man against a whole lot of (admittedly stupid) men. Weapons can and will kill you and you have to be the smartest, the fastest, and the most skilled. I can't help but feel a giddy pleasure when I execute a large amount of people in a short amount of time. The controls are fluid when you're running and smashing people in the head with a melee weapon, but clumsy and hard to use when trying to pinpoint aim a rifle to take out other mobsters. It feels intentional, because a gun feels like cheating, almost. Part of being a spree killer, which you undoubtedly are, is to be gritty and makeshift. What's more satisfyingly homespun than throwing a glass bottle at a man's head?
In terms of combat, I'm confident in saying that this one handles it better than the sequel. Wrong number makes melee a breeze, because most weapons you have are way faster than they should be- just holding down the swing button and running straight at them is horribly efficient at decimating a small army of people wielding lead pipes. No sell in this one: you have to plan, because weapons can be slow (with the exception of the incredibly fast knife) and you have to take enemies by surprise to have a chance of not getting brained by a golf club. Guns are also largely unneeded- and mostly impractical. Shooting a gun just sends every person in the area running at you and you only have limited ammo to kill them with. Instead, throwing a knife (which might not always kill the opponent but nonetheless knocks them down) is a good way to deal with ranged foes.
There's a couple of bosses in this game. I won't spoil the last one, but the first one- who you see more of later, is a doozy. I've never felt more like playing a real person than when a single slice from your opponent will end your life, and the only way to win is to evade, evade, evade, until they give you a chance to smash their head open. My hands hurt after that portion and the NUMEROUS times I had to retry it, but it was never frustrating.
Hotline Miami's tone is something I adore deep in my heart and it's almost hard to find something quite like it. It's hot and sweaty, gaudy in its psychedelic influence, and the blood and gore feels out of place yet it belongs so utterly within the crowded miami mob bases. The music is all techno, which is something I thought I wouldn't enjoy, but damn, do I? Each one is made by great artists (who I tracked down and bought albums from because YES) and picked perfectly by Dennation to match the level they're intended from. Particularly of mention is the later level "Clean hit", which has a portion where you have to sidle along a building and crawl from window to balcony. The music playing during this moment, "Hotline", made it feel like a heist caper- so perfect was this moment that I still try to recapture that feeling, even if the levels are downright short compared to the second game.
The top down 2d feel never feels like it could have been better in another format, and indeed, this game practically reinvigorated the top down shooter as it is. Pixel graphics are basic yet provide a perfect lackadaisical tone to the violence, making it brutal and graphic but never overly so. The face sprites are one aspect of the thematic game visual, though, that I don't quite appreciate- yes the game is gaudy and feels like a trip to the red light district and it's a nice change to see people who aren't afraid to make ugly sprites- but do they really need to look quite like that? I'd have liked it just a bit more if the faces looked more normal, but that's just a nitpick. As it is, they have a lot of character and I can respect the decision.
All in all, this is the best game I've played recently that I thought I might not like. God, it's so good, I want to be playing it more instead of writing this review. The levels are all mostly the same and it's like a drug trip, no matter how much you know you'll be getting the exact same thing you want more. I recommend this game a whole lot. Play the sequel too but beware that it's just not as good.

The Music Machine is a pyschological horror walking simulator with a heavy emphasis exploration in the forms of exploring the game world and exploring the narration of the game.
In this game you play as a 13 year old girl named Hayley, who is currently posessed by the ghost of an older man named Quintin, who is trying to find a satisfactory way to kill Hayley for causing his untimely death. You start on an island where multiple people have been murdered recently, banter back and forth for a while, and then explore and uncover the secrets of the island, as well as uncover the secrets that lay beyond the island.
To be honest, I didn't know what I would expect from this game and throughout the game I was surprised by quite a lot of things. I experienced a lot of feelings of discomfort, tension, and the sense of unsettlement... and at times was creeped out and overwhelmed by how intensely I felt these feelings. I was also surprised at the fact the game explores the issue of the damage that false accusations can cause. At one point, I didnt know if I would be able to keep playing because of the feelings I felt. This, to me, is a lot better than the other genres of horror games, to me this is REAL horror.
+The two tone colorization of the graphics add a lot of this unsettling, almost bleak aura that permeates throughout the entire game. However, is also adds a lot of frustration when trying to identify items of interest.
+The Music Machine has a very beautiful, but haunting soundtrack, that when mixed with the subject of the game, and the style of graphics, adds a lot more depth to the game. The music itself is not overpowering in any way and helps add immersion for me.
+This "walking simulator" has a sprint button. I state this because movement at times can be very slow, and the sprint option gives this a step up from other walking simulator style games.
+The game has a save feature, that while being clunky at best, is another step up from previous titles by the developer. I would like to note that towards the end of the game the save feature would not function properly for me. However, you can easilly get by with not saving the game due to its length.
+The premise and subject of the game, to me, are very unique. The subject of false accusations is something that is not touched often, and this game explores that subject in such a way that it makes you think for a while.
+The game has puzzles, and though they aren't challenging, are very fun and work well with the game. It is very refreshing to see a game developer to blend two game types and execute it in a way that functions very well.
-There are some minor grammar and spelling errors that I saw right away in the opening dialogue. This to me was very disappointing, since this is a narrative driven game.
-There is no voiced commentary, you are stuck reading everything. While this isn't particularly important to me, I know that some people do not enjoy reading as much as I do.
-I didn't feel a strong emotional connection to the two characters right away, and at times I thought their relationship was very odd, and not in a good way. I only started feeling a stronger connection to them as characters as the game progressed. I also feel that their backgrounds could have been expanded upon more, as there were quite a few things I found interesting about them.
This game is very short, taking such little time to complete, depending on how much the person explores. However, I feel the price for this game is very agreeable because it has some of replay potential in it and it is such a unique game that has not been disappointing to me.
This game has been a very pleasant surprise to me, and while it has some minor flaws, has been one of the best psychological horror games that I have played in a very long time. It has a very interesting premise, graphics and an atmosphere that stand out from other games within the genre, and was clearly made with care. I would have no problem recommending this to anyone who enjoyed horror AND walking simulator games. I am rating this an 8/10.

This is one of the best games I've ever played.  It simplifies space exploration enough that anyone can learn how to do it, while giving everyone a working knowledge of exactly how rockets move.  You can certainly just throw a few fuel tanks together with a capsule on top and a rocket at the bottom, and manage to flail your way into space, but it's so much more rewarding when you figure out how things really work.  The first time I landed on the Mun was a tremendous rush.  The first time I docked two space station modules together in orbit was a tremendous rush.  The first time I put together a spaceship that could take three Kerbals to Duna with a lander and rover, and return them to Kerbin, was completely worth all the time and effort I put into the prep work.
I've always been a fan of NASA and space in general, and I always figured that the stuff they do is hard work, but until I played Kerbal Space Program, I didn't realize just how much I didn't know about how hard the work is they do!  Knowing what I've learned with this game, I can much better appreciate how amazing it is when folks at NASA send their probes out on looping solar orbits to get gravity assists from the other planets, and I understand why they have to do it that way.
Once you've gotten the basics down, you can take a look at the official forums, check out some mods.  It's a very mod-friendly game, and installing a mod is basically drag-and-drop.  There's mods for everything from simple data readouts, to visual upgrades, to simple life support, to new rocket parts (both from science fiction and actual proposed near-future technologies), to historicaly accurate recreations of actual rockets, to the full on Realistic Overhaul mod group that's the ultimate hard-mode.  You can mod the game to exactly the level of challenge you see fit.
But even without mods it's a fun and often challenging game.  The only downside to playing Kerbal Space Program is that you will never be able to watch a sci-fi show or movie without wanting to yell at the screen about how unrealistic it is.
tl;dr: Stop reading reviews and buy the game, it's awesome.

Let me preface with this, Alan Wake is a wonderful, story-driven game. It has horror, thrills, suspense, mystery, atmosphere, and the pacing to draw any story-driven buff in. It's just a shame that expiring licenses are the culprit to removing it from Steam. I have heard that Remedy Entertainment is going to attempt to renew the licenses, something they don't have to do. That shows how much they care about a game now nearly a decade old. I wouldn't hold your breath, however. It would seem the only other way to get this game are through "other means", unfortunately, since I do really think this game is worth price to this day.
Anyway, let's begin.
Pros:
+ Story - The story in this game is one of the best, if not
story I've played in a video game. And this is coming from a gamer who has played video games for nearly 20 years. If you can ever obtain it, whether it be on Xbox 360 or on PC in whatever way possible,
play through the main game and its two episodes, that being The Signal (Special One) and The Writer (Special Two) for the full experience.
+ Characters - The characters in this game are exceptionally well-written, especially Barry Wheeler. He has some of the best and most amusing dialogue in the game. I find him to be amusing because of the way he talks, as well as the fast talking he does and in the manner of which he expresses himself.. This not to detract from other characters, however, as Alan Wake is a compelling character despite him being a bit of a jerk. The characters of Bright Falls make you feel as if this is a real town, and make you feel at home there.
+ Musical Composition - I have to say that both the Orchestral Score and the Licensed Music fit well into the game. Petri Alanko did a wonderful job of making the music flow and match with the situations that Alan is put in.
+ Atmosphere - My God. This game has one of the BEST atmospheric content I have ever seen. The way the dark forest and town feel, along with the thrilling scares the game provides, it's unlike anything else, and unlike the M-Rated games that rely on gore and graphic content to be scary. In certain instances, I will say some of the Shadow People are indeed scary and intimidating. Especially when you first meet with the Shadow Version of
. The other thing that is creepy is the voices of some of the Shadow People, especially when you can't see them and they're stalking you in the forest.
+ Graphics - I know graphics don't make a game, but my goodness are the graphics really, really good. I would say they even hold up today, 7 years later. And the effects when the trees are blowing under high wind, as well as that type of wind that the Shadows emit, it's great.
+ Sound - The sound design is wonderful. From the loud wind, creaks and other strange noises. And the creepy Shadow People harassing you with their voices while they be stalkin' your behind.
+ Narrative - The way the story is told is great. From the perspective of Alan Wake in the game, the story makes it hard to discern whether what is happening is a
, making him as well as you the player, question his sanity.
+ Pacing - I personally thought the slow, even, and easy-to-follow pacing was just fine. That is how you know Remedy Entertainment wanted to really take the time to develop the characters, the story, and the game in general at a good pace.
Cons:
x Repetitive Enemies - The enemies you fight, that being Shadow People, are all you fight in the game. Well, that, and the occasional object that flies at you.
x Uninspired Combat - The combat isn't that great, and even Remedy's previous Max Payne games did better. The combat is not bad, per se, just nothing new was brought to the table.
x Lack of Unique Weapons - Not that there is anything wrong with the Revolver, Flare Gun, and Shotgun, I could have felt they could have had more weapons that made sense for where Alan Wake was.
All in al, I thought Alan Wake was one of the best games I have ever played, and I don't state this lightly. Because of the few drawbacks, I award this game a personal rating of 9.90 out of 10. I would like to say again, I highly suggest you play this game and its two Specials. Thank you.
- Michael

I like this game. Really, I do. An ineresting idea that adds nuance to combat, atmosphere and story-telling, cheeky self-aware humor, very clever framing, and the best part: the whole thing is a love letter to Stephen King set in Twin Peaks. Though it bears mentioning I am a very story-oriented player, and it's only because of this that I find this game enjoyable at all. The supernatural mystery/thriller is a genre I think is very under-utilized in the medium, and this one gets the pacing of answering questions while asking new ones done perfectly. As a complement to the story (also like Twin Peaks) it has a tongue-in-cheek sense of humor about itself rarely seen in serious games. There are some cliche story-telling devices throughout, some are commented upon (the narrator acknowledges one of his realizations of what he has to do next makes no sense, like it usually does in these stories), and some are actually retracted from the plot almost immediately, just as you've had enough time to say, "Really? C'mon." To me, these, and only a short list of technical pluses (more on that later), are the only reasons the game is worth playing, and not very good in general.
First, there are only a handful of enemy types, and though your first encounters can be pretty tense, a few hours in they're not much more than a nuisance. To stun enemies and make them vulnerable you have to point your flashlight at them for a few seconds before you shoot, but there's barely enough battery power to do this to one or two enemies, which then still require a few shots to take down. This being survival horror, that in and of itself is not a bad thing, but the frequency at which you need to change the batteries (ammo/mana equivalent) to sustain the effect is just annoying. The power does refill slowly, but why you need batteries brings me to my next gripe: the flight is even worse than the fight. Often times a whole group of enemies will come into view, and if you run out of batteries you need to retreat or hide for the power to refill. Once again, totally legit device, obnoxious to use. If there's not anyone behind you, gaining distance annoys you by sprinting being for two short a time with no HUD to let you know, only a few seconds tired from sprinting is enough to get NPC to catch up and hit. The sprint button and the dodge button share a key, which makes for some awkward close battles, for which you hve no melee weapon. Health has no power-ups, and though it does slowly refill, can only be gained at checkpoints. Playing cautiously can lead to just standing around waiting for the bar to refill.
These things said, I love a couple of things abou this game that I had never seen before about its presentation. Another self-aware jab, the game is broken up into a handful of "episodes," complete with "Last time on Alan Wake..."opening, which I found perfectly clever conidering the tone and atmosphere. Most impressive of all, the lighting effects surpase any game I've ever played and saves a bit of tention and alertness that would otherwise have died three hours in. The way shadows and environments in the dark respond to your light captures EXACTLY how they feel in real life when you're already scared. Several times, I even shot at trees or bushes because I just caught what I was sure was an enemy in the corner of my eye. And even after enough time spent to beat it, I still can't tell if the devs intentionally made them to look more manacing or if it was just me, which is exactly what makes it brilliant.
All in all, though I like this game quite a bit, I can't recomend it in general because the gameplay elements were just as weak as the story is strong. If you're in it for a story, consider it, but it's certainly not one you just HAVE to have. It's just okay.

It's no masterpiece.  I believe we are all aware of this... But, to be honest, I didn't find it near as "awful" or "worst game ever" status as most "reviews" would make you believe.
Let's start with one of the highlights: the scenery. Good god, this game looks the way a crime shooter game should look.  It's gray, it's shiny, it literally makes this the better-looking iteration of Shangai I've seen in a video game. The lighting in the game is very good as well. Yes, the "filmed with a phone" look can get tiring, but, honestly? I even got used to the running, which I believe it's what made most people sick with this particular aesthetic.
Second highlight: the sound design. No epic music, no rock and roll, just a superb ambient music soundtrack that helped making me feel the desperation these two scumbags go through in this game. Highly recommended soundtrack.
Overall, the art direction in this game is superb. Regarding its flaws, this is something no one will take away from it.
Now, the story:
It feels like Spec Ops: The Line without the twist. It servers its purpose, but nothing else. Now, the characters, we could argue all day long. No, they're not complex, and no, they're not even memorable, but I'm sure they don't want to be, either. They are both psychopats, there's no question about it. In the middle of a shootout you can listen Lynch trying not to lose control over himself, trying to count to ten, and by the end of the game, you can notice the paranoid feel over him. Now, Kane, he's no strange to being crazy. Most of the time he seems the more reasonable one, but there's a point where you can see he's not.
. And if there's other debatable aspect on this game, is your partner's AI. Yes, he gets in the middle of the shooting because he's a friggin bullet sponge, but he PROTECTS you. More times that I can count I see an enemy shooting me from an angle I can't reach, and he takes care of him.
Sadly I can't say the same thing about the enemy's AI. They're dumb. And they're bullet sponges as well. I don't believe the shooting is THAT bad, because it even feels the way these two morons would shoot guns, but the hit detection on the enemies is crap. Sometimes you empty half a clip on the enemies, and not only a fully armored SWATlike, but enemies with a shirt and a short absorb the bullets like mofos. It's even funny that sometimes you shoot them instead of falling, it gives them a boost so they move to other place. Add to this that they spot you no matter what. By the second "stealth" section I ddn´t even bother and started shooting like hell.
Yet, I played through it with no regrets. There are a couple of levels that I actually enjoyed A LOT. Specially
Level design is a bit "off" (says the one who never designed a level in his life), but some mechanics, like destroyable cover and throwing fire extinguishers that knock enemies if you hit them in the head, are great. Speaking of the latter, the "shooting the whatever you just threw to make it explode" could have use some more polish. It's so random and impossible sometimes that when you are able to shoot something over 3 walls, it's ridiculous.
A few bugs here and there could have frustrated me, but nothing too crazy. Haven't tried the co-op yet, though, so no idea of how it plays with a buddy.
I got it for like 2 bucks, but I think it can even be worth up to $7 for singleplayer only. I wasn't sad when IO cancelled its 3rd installment back then, because I enjoyed Hitman: Absolution so much and loved they were going to focus on that, but now I do feel kind of sad. With better gameplay, it would've been the anti-shooter to hold the crown until Spec Ops came out.
TL;DR: Play it, at least to enjoy the wonderful art direction.

The first game finished so badly (one of the ending anyways) that it had to continue with Kane & Lynch 2. Thats a good thing, right ? Nope. Not here.  The story uses the same overused theme thats been done in movies and games since the beginning of games...revenge. Its predictable from start to finish which is kind of boring if you think about it. Theres no more character dept and Kane stops Lynch from learning more from each other right from the start, Personally I think its the biggest mistake that the devs made.
For the gameplay, I have to be honest what impressed me the most are 2 things. First is the enemy AI...It's brutal. If you take cover and don't look around you, the enemy will come up to you and ♥♥♥♥ you up. That is impressive since most AI will just stay behind cover and shoot you endlessly without anything more to do.
Second is the cover system. Far from perfect but at least this time I press C to activate it so in a very wierd way...its works. Since Kane & Lynch : Dead Men, the cover didn't work almost all the time.
The game forces you to change weapons since enemies don't use all the same weapon so its possible you'll run out of ammo for a specific weapon so you'll have to change. I personally don't mind that because it forces you to change strategy to kill your enemies (don't snipe with a shotgun) and you have to think about ammo conservation as well.
Level design is the most absurb thing besides the story of course. What you see is only Shanghai city...its the same view you get from room to room, to buildings to ... well everything looks the same. So level design is just really bad, boring not appealing at all.

This is a mature dark fantasy game with rich lore and adult themes. The first game had a rhythm-based combat system where you would click the attack button in time to perform successive attacks in sequence. This game drops that and goes for a more traditional combat system that utilizes slow-heavy attacks and light-fast attacks. Both games are forerunners in combat animation but there's a certain meatiness to the combat in The Witcher 2, you can really feel the blows that land on your opponents.
It takes about 40 hours to get through one playthrough of the story, but the large choices that you have to make throughout the story have lasting consequences in shaping the world and lend heavy replay value to this game. The only thing that would make this game more interesting to me is if the developers put time into designing an investigation system into the game, which makes you dig into the lore of the world a bit more in order to solve problems.

I've been a bit of a fan of David Szymanski's games. I stuck The Moon Sliver in our indie games of the year list, while the story wasn't the most original, and it didn't look the best, the way it told its story was fascinating. Fingerbones was rough, but its story unique and oblique, just about as dark as anything else in gaming. The Music Machine mixes cues from both games, it's dreamy, vague, and eventually, unremittingly bleak
Like the two previous games, The Music Machine is a narrative exploration game, a 'walking simulator' if you will. You play as a young girl, possessed by a vengeful spirit, who puppets her around with the ultimate aim of killing her in the worst way possible. The game commendably pitches this against a light hearted tone, the girl is playful, the relationship between the two is more familial than murderous. It helps soften the characters, making them likable and relatable, something that can be undermined to brilliant effect later on.
This is true of the world too. Szymanski's games have never been lookers, but with The Music Machine he's used two tone colours, setting black against colour, to create a striking and at times beautiful world. The large swathes of abyss black create doubt, in a world so threateningly desolate they could be hiding anything. The structures become peering obelisks, the simplicity of the world unsettling, it's something that's grounded in the narrative, and if it's a deliberate attempt to draw from limitations, it works brilliantly.
It's fair to say that The Music Machine is an original story. There's a moment, or a representation of a character, that I'm less sure lands, it's unique certainly, but in what is otherwise quite a heavy game, and a heavy moment, it just falls on the comical side of absurd. Not that comedy has no place in the game, The Music Machine has its fair share of humour, usually as part of a very well written script. As mentioned the relationship between Hayley and Quintin is superb, they bring the barren world to life, it's a very natural relationship, despite its origins. It's also a parallel for the structure of the game. The light-heartedness, the sense of wonder, eventually becomes undermined, you suddenly realise that the impish threat that had seemed no more than a curiosity has begun to loom over you. Each new area carries with it the threat of the unknown, but there was a point where the game had become genuinely unsettling. That said, one of the possible endings is a little fluffed, I got it out of curiosity rather than malevolence, meaning it lost a lot of its intended impact.
The Music Machine takes a very grounded issue, the damage of a false accusation, and then throws it in to a surreal high concept world. It's a unique story, the reveal of the what and why of the music machine itself is an old-fashioned kind of horror, and depending on your choices it can explore the darker side of humanity, resentment, and revenge. As usual for anything from this genre it’s not for everyone, it’s not jump scares and gore, but it’s a fantastic story. unique and quietly unsettling

Just finished this game up with 115% completion status. I love this game, and not because it has furries in it. Yes, the visuals look amazing with loads of color, and the sound design is pretty nice, too. But what hooked me in was the gameplay.
The combat feels so good, especially when you get to stringing high triple-digit combos amongst your foes. It felt similar to the Batman Arkham games, which also have amazing combat. Exploration is also well-executed and rewarding. If you haven't played a Metroidvania-style game, this game pretty much encourages you to explore places you been to before to seek out newer rooms and areas that were previously unreachable, though I have managed to reach said areas before I was suppose to. It wasn't by the means of cheating or third-party apps, but just using the trademark Dust Storm in mid air.
The story was kinda unique to me, though I don't know if it's been done before. Maybe parts of it, but I wouldn't know. I'm not gonna spoil any of it, though the ending kinda had me a bit sad, but I won't say what. Dust and Fidget certainly made for a good duo, especially with the comic relief Fidget provides, though some of the humor can be hit or miss.
Overall, amazing game. It's definitely worth whatever price it's going for (sale or not), if for the gameplay alone. I want more games like this, especially since there aren't many Metroidvania-style games on PC. Hell, if that were to be "Another Elysian Tail," I would get it. But yes, if you like great combat and any of the two game franchises that I bunched into one word, you owe it to yourself to get this game like right now.

A great little atmospheric platformer Type:Rider is, taking you through time and introducing many of the important type faces in today's world to the player as you go along. Gameplay isn't particularly challenging so if you're looking for some hardcore platforming, look elsewhere. Having said that, for trophy hunters and completionists, you may have to open your eyes wider and explore the surroundings to get all the collectibles.
The selling point here is the experience and level design. Like I said above, the gameplay isn't challenging but some of the puzzles and mechanics involved in the level design are indeed very cleverly done. Even if you do not bother reading through the collectibles you find, you still feel like you learned something. Great visuals and music as well which mirror the setting and era of each type face.
I managed to 100% the game in around 4 hours without consulting any guides, so yeah, it's not on the long side, but more importantly it doesn't overstay its welcome. Something unique and quite unlike anything I've played before, so I give Type:Rider a resounding recommendation on my part!

This game is among the few games that I call one of my favorites.
This is a 2D action-platforming game with RPG elements, much like a Castlevania.  In terms of some of the RPG game mechanics, there is a great potential depth that could exist, but does not exist (in crafting mostly).  Combat is mostly too easy.  There are harder difficulty levels, but the ease lies in enemy attack behavior and comboability.  The movelist for the hero is not huge, but combos and variety is very fluid and smooth.  Platforming works very well and treasures can be tucked away interestingly.  There was nothing to frustrate about the game, although some optional easter eggs would be difficult to discover without a guide.
The aesthetics and setting though, for me, is what sells the game experience. The game environments are wonderfully vibrant and detailed.  The music accompanyment is excellently ambient and dramatic, and I will be buying the soundtrack as soon as I am able (a HIGH mark from me).  The sound from this game really gives it a wonderful sense of presence, inspiring tension and reverence and melancholy.  The story of the game is none too original but neither is it trite, being robust enough to not overreach its aim or come off as flimsy.  The game is fully voice acted and also very well done, giving the characters a great sense of personality, and no voice actor is too overbearing or too weak, and really made me just fall in love with some of the characters for their quirks and personality.
I love this game.  It was a wonderful experience for me, and I hope that if you buy it, that you will love it too.
Plagued by the abominable physics that serve as a key game-mechanic, the only redeeming qualities are the full picture of the history of typography it offers and the beautiful accompanying levels.
See that "KARMA" achievement? You will get that in no time.

A bird's eye view shooter, Hotline Miami is an extremely addictive game: if you like colorful enviroments and intriguing mechanics this game will surely hook you up.
You have very little room for error once inside the enemy facilities: you must find your time to engage your opponents, paying attention to every detail (ex. enemies can see through windows, so if they carry a ranged weapon they will be able to gun you down from there) but the biggest threat to your success is that every death, you respawn from the starting area with everything set back as in the beginning.
And dying is very easy: enemies only need to strike you once or twice at best, be it with melee weaponry or guns. However at the start of every level the player is provided a set of masks, from which you can choose one: every one of them has got a special power that the player will choose basing himself on the situation.
The price isn't anywhere high too, so no excuses: grab this game and have fun!

I finished The Music Machine just minutes ago. I have no idea what to say. I have pieces of what might feel like ideas, such as; I wish it had been longer, more. But in reality that might have been the worst thing, that it is actually beyond improvement in its present form. I wish I could have SEEN better, that perhaps I missed important things simply because visability was compromised. But again, the 2-color pallet created a mood no other game I've played has come close to expressing, and that color scheme was very important to the ending of the story. And since I completed the story three times (once alive, I think) I must be mistaken.
Unlike its predecessor, The Moon Sliver, TMM had a save feature, although it somewhat awkwardly involved exiting, then re-starting the game, and toward the end did not function (for good reason.) The controls were simple, the "puzzle(s)" was/were organic to the story in a very good way. The characterization was brief but adequately ambiguous (but I wished to know much more about both of them, nay, ALL of them). I wish the story had allowed for more exploration in one specific area, but that might have been superfluous, thus bypassed (leaving this player wanting more. Always a good strategy.)
As far as a recommendation, all I can say is if someone found The Moon Sliver intriguing, the same will be true for The Music Machine. BUt if they wish to play TMM looking for answers to TMS....good luck. If they want to spend a couple of hours in some unique landscapes, they've found that game. I might have liked more clarification, more connection between the two stories. But that's just me, and probably wrong. I haven't been the one to live with this story for an extended period, so I must trust to one who has.

While it may not be the most flashy game, or the most cleanly cut, there is a certain elegance to blasting away droves of Dinosaurs with a minigun. In the survival and conquest game modes the game excels and forces you to make tactical decisions of how to balance your budget on weaponry, augmentations and vehicles. The combat side of the game is great fun with varied enemies attacking you all at once and the appearance of larger dinosaurs to force you on to the defensive and for a change make you run. There are also 7 vehicles that offer a variety of firepower to turn the tide of the horde and work really well in the open air environments.  Unfortunately there are some problems with the game.
First of all the AI can occasionally be a bit off, with the flying dinosaurs of a wave getting stuck on cliff faces and one of the larger dinosaurs that looks like a crocodile can be shot at and circle strafed around without it being able to hit you. Secondly there is no real variation in the environment where you fight dinosaurs. It's always outside on a large expansive map. There are buildings where you buy your equipment, but you never fight inside them, even when capturing an objective you're merely stood out in the open. This proves a problem in the other game modes where you are vs. other players. You fight in large open environments that feel empty without the many dinosaurs (although they do sparingly spawn) and it becomes very dull chasing someone around a map instead of the fun and frantic other game modes. Rampage is a game mode with a nice touch, you can play as dinosaurs as well as humans, and have to capture of defend some eggs. The problem is the dinosaurs have very limited attacks and no power ups or any changes, so the game simply throws the money managing tactics of the other game types out of the window. These problems limit the replay value of the game, and it does become very possible to get bored of it.

I'm going to preface this review by stressing a fact; this game is about typograhy. Now, if that doesn't interest you, so be it. But if it does, everything about this game is wonderfully crafted.
Type:Rider is beautiful, historically appropriate, and surprisingly challenging at times. Maybe all three aren't so important to you but surely one of them is. The levels are very well designed, both in layout and aesthetics. Because you control two spheres as opposed to one you have to get used to that odd dynamic (this can be difficult and frustrating at times though). The game teaches you about each type and related typography facts--but not forcefully; you can skip that altogether if you're not interested. And some levels are just plain hard. Clarendon (if going for the achievement) is one. Pixel is definitely another. (The secret level Comic Sans is also a little tricky.)
Is it worth the full price? For me, yes. But for many, I would suggest to wait for a sale. If you enjoy the game Nightsky, I'd say it's worth it. Also, if you want to play the hilarious Comic Sans level at the end: worth it.
Entertaining, playable, addictive, and hey, you can't beat the price.

The Music Machine
Walking Simulator
David Szymanski
David Szymanski
is a story-driven walking simulator developed and published by David Szymanski, creator of The Moon Sliver.
The game is about a teenage girl and the ghost of her friend who is trying to find a way to kill her. They go to an island where several people were recently murdered, and they discover some kind of church, with a mysterious music machine that travels through dimensions and different places.
The story is really good and the dialogue between the two characters is really well written. The strongest point is the atmosphere, which feels both relaxing and haunting.
Developed in the Unity engine, the game has a really artistic style: every environment has a different color, and that adds to the atmosphere. The lighting effects are also very good, and the places you explore are all very big and fully explorable.
The game is a "walking simulator", which is basically a game that mostly requires you going from point A to point B. However, there are some puzzles that break (in a positive way) the exploration. The game is non-linear, and you might have to go back to a previously visited place to find an item that you might have missed.
There is little to no challenge: the puzzle are very few and not hard to understand. The core of the game is not to challenge the gamer, but to tell a compelling story and to deliver a worthwile experience.
The atmospheric soundtrack really helps set the tone of the game, and I recommend buying it. There are also sound effects that further immerse you in the game.
This is entirely subjective: if you like this kind of games, you will come back to fully explore the environments, read all the letters and better understand the story. Others won't see much reason to come back.
Overall, this is a great and fresh experience, with an interesting story and beautiful environments as well as a great soundtrack. However, if you don't like this type of games, don't buy it.

As a graphic designer, I am an admirer of great typography.  This game, with its subject matter and beautiful style, was easy to take a chance on.  In the end: Is it informative?  Very.  Is it beautiful both in terms of audio and visuals?  Extremely.  Is it fun?  Not really.
For me, the control (especially jumping mechanics) just never felt quite "right".  That is easily the biggest source of frustration in the game.  While some sequences are downright inspired, others are grit-your-teeth annoying.
The informative nature of the game and the actual gameplay seem at times to be at odds with each other.  For example, unlocking an informative page gives you a prompt to view it immediately - while I recommend doing this since the visuals and audio in the portion of the level you are in will be tuned towards this piece of info, it halts the gameplay and can break the pacing.  In addition, occasionally the game will destroy you as soon as you return to the gameplay and cause you to have to replay the small sequence again.  It feels like a punishment for doing what the game is designed to have you discover.
In the end, I just can't recommend the game.

Type:Rider is a game focusing on the history of writing, but with a focus on typefaces, as the printing press is introduced early on.  Collecting asterisks (*) in the levels reveals a different page on font history from the Stone Age to modern computer fonts (as well as a bonus level for Comic Sans).  The gameplay itself is a platformer, devoid of enemies (save an off-screen gun trying to kill you in Clarendon), but having you navigate platforms and hazards.  Each level is based on a font, and has a distinctive style like a water level for Garamond, an artsy theme for Futura, and 1920s for Times New Roman.  It's not for everyone, as some wouldn't be interested in the history of fonts, but I got it because I began to notice things I took for granted growing up (namely Helvetica, and on that, see the documentary of the same name).  It can be completed in a few hours, but i feel they were well-spent.

I think the biggest problem with ME:SoW is that it can't decide if it wants to be a stealth game or a hack and slash game.
In the previous entry in the series you couldn't really go toe-to-toe with enemies, even quite late into the game. However with this game you can do so pretty much from word go. *However* all the skill animations are geared towards stealth play. Have you ever noticed how in games like Diablo or Path of Exile the game doesn't stop to play an animation when you use a skill? That's because it breaks up the combat. In ME:SoW OTOH combat is *constantly* being interrupted, either by seconds long killing animations or by boss orcs introducing themselves which, during the fort defense stage, can involve up to 6 different long unskippable introductions. I don't care about your boring life story dude, I just want to kill orcs.
Then there's how the game's structured. If it had stopped at about the third way mark when you'd done all the quests and about to do the-quest-from-which-there's-no-return it probably would have been fine. Instead after that's done you have to defend your forts (of which there are only 4) about 20 times. It gets real tedious real quickly, and honestly the pay off for doing that grind is kind of a let down.
A more minor gripe I had was that I found the control of flying mounts to be very unintuitive and difficult. Where it stayed close to the original game it was fun, but then I have to ask myself why not just replay that game? So it's a no from me.

Let me just start off by saying that especially if you get it on sale, this game is really worth playing. It's pretty cheap even at full price anyway. For me it's like spending a day at the arcade or something.
Pros:
- Graphics are nice (better than most screenshots you'll see online if you crank it up in settings, and it can probably take third-party enhancements but I haven't tried yet)
- Lightweight program (it's like 249 MB on disk, doesn't consume a lot of RAM either)
- Quick action (all stages are like arenas, enemies just come to you in waves)
- Surprisingly challenging (I'll go into detail later)
- Beautiful character designs
- After a few skill upgrades you can be chaining combos like crazy, and that's just plain fun (if the game had only this to offer and had uglier graphics for example, it still would've been worth the sale price for me)
- Combat against bosses requires intelligence and quick thinking. You can't just hold your block key and think you can safely tank their attacks. I'll go into more detail below.
Con:
- Not a lot to do (it's really just enemies coming to you in waves in a few arenas then a boss to end that stage)
- Controls take getting used to, and are marked by symbols in-game instead of their corresponding keyboard/controller mapping
- Camera control and angling isn't very good except in the boss view mode, which you can use against regular enemies, but it requires constantly pressing a button (can't toggle). Because of this, you could get hit by grunts from behind (though it's arguable that this adds to the challenge and can be a good thing for some; nobody can see behind them IRL anyway)
- UI isn't polished, and there are translation inaccuracies
- Lots of buttons to press; you really need to customize it to something that's comfortable for you or learn the default well
- You can't remap existing moves (some are inconveniently placed, for example movement key + basic attack will cause you to do a flip kick, which isn't good if you accidentally do it when you wanted to do a basic attack)
- The challenge might cause a lot of frustration and ragequitting
I have more cons than pros but I still recommend it. I'm playing Hard mode now and the good mix of combo chaining and challenge due to high punishment for mistakes is keeping me in the game so far.
On the challenge of this game, I thought at first it'd be a simple fighting game like the Musou games from KOEI (Dynasty Warriors, etc.). Just make sure you hit first and complete your combos and you're good in Musou. No such simplicity in Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae. Even against the grunts you need to watch their movements and time your blocks and dodges. Bosses have a variety of moves, the damage of most of which can only be avoided using certain means (some moves are unblockable and need to be dodged, some moves can't be dodged and need to be blocked). You have the learn their moves and how to counter them, including what kinds of attacks work best for certain situations. You certainly can't spam combos, button mash, or sorta turn your brain off during fights. This will keep you on your toes.
What's funny is that with boss fights whenever you get killed, you'll probably be thinking like "man I saw that move, I could've dodged that hit!" Then you retry. For me it's just the right amount of frustrating challenge that keeps me coming back.
Will the game get old eventually? Yes I think so especially once you master the movements of enemies. But for now it's a wonderful distraction, and by the time I get tired of it, I feel like I'd already gotten my money's worth.

Here is my first review of a game on steam, english isn't my mother tongue. Sorry for the mistakes, I'll maybe update it later to give a french version too.
I've played the game without controler, only with my keyboard. Done this review after finishing the game 100% except deathrun.
A Pixel Story is probably one of the best games i've played so far. I had it on my wishlist for two or three months and I finally decided to buy it as I was looking for an hard 2D plateformer. The game in itself isn't super hard to finish (I mean, in a first time); even if there are some passages where you can find a bit more of difficulty. The story is hilarious (lot of references) and the atmosphere was wonderful. As a fan of the genre, I've found exactly the same feeling than when I played Crash Bandicoot on my PS1 when I was child (atmospherically speaking).

Witcher 2's great in all fronts, graphics, gameplay, story, lore, charecters and so on. The action-RPG's a unique one, having been developed by CDProjekt Red, a Polish dev company bringing us a real prideful offering as to how a western action-RPG presents itself on the global stage.
Unique in what regards?
Positive:
W2 has plenty of choices in the story arc, even outside the main forks in the road such as Roche's path, or Iorveth's path, there's certianly multiple ways to handel meeting up with bosses, and other key plot points. There's ways to close/not initiate certian mission b/c of xyz, so I sugest watching the "Changing Locations" vid from the devs on the multiple stories. W2 is indeed practically 1.5 games in 1.
The dialogue trees fill a convergence in the emersiveness and gets away with some pecilular takes on the cast's rogueish attitudes, Geralt picking up on chicks, the dice minigame, midevil slang, such as bugger, wh0r3son, ba$tard, all terms you don't really hear in the modern Americas, but used in Scottland, the UK, and such, however b/c this is a myere'd and dark time, synergysticaly it all plays to the story.
Negative:
The combat can be handled via simple mash to progress, however if you get into the rolling and dodgeing, you can fine tune your fighting tactics. Geralt's the archetypical battlemage w/ rather straightforward skilltrees for wizardry, and alchemy, however his swordplay and dodgeing whilst in combat are his coup de' grass. The skilltree progressions are linear, un-complicated, and arguabley a bit of a toss. Wizardy allows you to throw spells at a one shot per meter rate in battle, giving enemies status effects such as catching fire, while the alchemy tree has you crafting interesting potions that, unfortunately, can only be used just before the battle commences.
The weapon/armor progression system's unique in an unfavorable way in regards to the story's tendancy to branch meaning you can miss a NPC needed that would have given you quests, or items, or even find yourself in custody, or in a dundgeon, and if you didn't explore it just right, you will lose your confiscated gear.
W2's submenu's and UI are still difficult to nagivage, and aren't user friendly, however they're mods to it.
Witcher 2 has a modding community as well, w/ game dev's even adding to the combat w/ advances from Witcher 3.

I have a feeling I know what you're thinking about this game, "It's about fonts! How more boring can you get? Plus it's an android game so it's probably crap." But while some might find Type:Rider boring I certainly found it entertaining.
Type:Rider is a 2D puzzle-platformer, where you travel through the history of typography. You play as a colon, and believe me that's not as discusting as it sounds, rolling through different puzzles, in the form of different styles of lettering. Along the way you'll come across different locations with icons that will tell you the history behind the font the puzzle stage is made up of, which you can choose to read or not. It sort of felt l was playing through a museum exibit about fonts. And while that may sound boring to some, I learned a lot of interesting things about the history of typography that I didn't know before, and I still had fun with the game.
One other thing I really liked about Type:Rider is the style of it. Being that it's about the different types of fonts it should have a sense of style to it. The way I could describe the look of this game is, imagine an idea for a PIXAR short film got mixed with Limbo with just a dash of Element4l mechanics. I just found myself getting really sucked into the game, the great soundtrack especially helps.
One downside of Type:Rider is that I was expecting the puzzles to be a little harder. I mean most of them are still challenging, but the only rediculously hard level was the secret one you get at the end of the game. I have to admit I was a little disappointed in that regard.
Overall I liked Type:Rider. Even though it has it's downsides I thought it was a really creative and original idea, and they executed it well. If you'd like to learn something new, or like puzzle platformers, you'll probably like this game. If you're just looking for a puzzle platformer that's a bit more challenging like Limbo you might be disappointed and want to give it a pass.

I played this game as long as I did only to complete all achievements… With that being said, I'm going to help you get them all.
Note: There is “almost” no way you can earn all 35 achievements without paying (or cheating). I was able to get 34/35 by with some patience and allowing the game timer to run overnight and during the day.
I’m only listing a few of the non-obvious achievements, or, some difficult ones with tips that might help you get them a bit faster. Keep in mind to check your vault in the morning and at night. Should take several weeks to complete them all.
QUEST ACHIEVEMENTS:
---Big Pharma (Collect 100 stimpacks…)
---Decorator (Collect all pieces of 4 themes)
---Survivalist (Complete 60 quests)
The key with these is to constantly have dwellers on 3 quests at a time.
TIME-CONSUMING ACHIEVEMENTS:
---Fashion Statement (Collect 20 legendary outfits)
---Armed and Dangerous (Collect 20 Legendary weapons)
---Interior Designer (Craft 1 of every room theme)
With these, keep x1 outfit and x1 weapon being made at all times. They must be legendary and keep in mind what type of SPECIAL is needed to make it go faster (This depends on what you are making.) Also keep the crafting room themes going at all times as well.
THE TWO HARDEST ACHIEVEMENTS:
---Get off my lawn (Stop 50 raider attacks)
The reason I’m stating this as a hard achievement is because if you progress too fast, raider attacks become very few and far between; Raider attacks depends on the quantity of dwellers you have.
1-39 dwellers = Raider attacks.
40-79 dwellers = Raider, Ghoul attacks.
80+ Dwellers = Raider, Ghoul and Deathclaw attacks.
With this being said; 70+ hours in, I stayed steady at about 190 dwellers and completed all but the Blast from the Past and Get off my lawn. I was at 37/50 attacks and I was only getting attacked by Deathclaws. I saved my game, made a backup and evicted all but 39 dwellers. I got attacked by Raiders 3 times within an hour. (changed the game to Windows mode swapped from Chrome to the game every 10 min) A pain I know – but I recommend staying around 30 dwellers until you get about 40 Raider attacks, then I’m sure you’ll get them all later
---Blast from the Past (Collect 20 Legendary Dwellers)*
OK, honesty time here. At about 75 hours in; I was about to give up hope. I had two achievements left, Get off my lawn and this one. Also, at this point, I didn’t spend a dime on the game. I researched how to get legendary dwellers and, besides earning 1 or 2 from quests, you can get them ALL from lunch boxes. So I thought to myself “Self, you threw down 75 hours of free play, buy a few lunch boxes” – However, $5-$10 bucks doesn’t get you much, and what lunch boxes it got me… didn’t help. So I “obtained” a save file with 9999 lunch boxes and went to town opening- with  9999 lunch boxes, clicking to open them for several hours and BAM, 485 lunch boxes later, I got the achievement. So this means: (from my own experience)
485 / 20 = approx. 0.04% drop rate per box
485 * 5 = 2,425 cards (there are 5 cards per lunch box)
2425 / 20 = approx. 0.008% drop rate per card
The reason I’m saying all this is because if you plan on buying lunch boxes just for this achievement, then you may want to rethink it. I also feel cheap “cheating” to earn achievements, but♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bethesda has earned enough of my money over the years. They can take one for the team; I sure the hell did with Fallout 4

This was another game that I Kickstarted and then let linger for years before actually playing, hence the late review.
Wasteland 2 is overall a pretty good game that could have been pretty great. As one reviewer said, in many ways it's the game that Fallout 3 should have been -- much more a spiritual successor to the earlier Fallout games than F3 was (although F3 is a great game in its own right). So why do I say it wasn't great? Well, the experience was marred by a few serious flaws that became more serious and irritating as the game continued on.
First, the game is buggy as hell, and this is saying a lot for a game that came out three years ago. There are a lot of things that don't trigger properly, causing you to either find weird workarounds or say, 'Oh well,' about not being able to quite finish that side-quest or sub-plot that you worked so hard toward. The game gives you an extra smack in the face at the end when it summarizes a bunch of things about various characters you met in the game, often spelling out doom for people you saved because the game never quite recognized that you saved them. (Although this did work in my favour once, when the game claimed that a dead character ran away and had his "happily ever after" with his wife.)
Second, as your characters become more powerful, there will be increasing numbers of things that you can't do Because Plot. There will be things that you can do in every case but the important ones, when your ability will inexplicably just not work on the target you wanted to use it on, which can be extra frustrating when you worked hard to get that ability just for that reason.
Third, the pacing and difficulty are both very poorly done. There are areas where even if you're playing on the easiest difficulty, you're dominating like mad and then there's just a giant difficulty cliff, after which you're dominating like mad again. And the smooth overlapping of one task with the next falls apart in a few key places where you're just left with little or nothing to do. Couple that with poor hinting, bugs that can cause task markers to not appear, and show-stopping bugs, and the game will have you hitting up the internet for guides increasingly frequently as it goes on, even if just to confirm that something's a bug.
Lastly, the UI and graphics could have used a lot more work. The use of UI elements is inconsistent, and a good chunk of the "I can't X" posts on the internet turn out to be resolved by, "Oh, you have to do it this totally new/different/unexpected way instead". Many key quest items don't look the way you'd expect. The succession of rad suits is so terrible and easy to screw up I'd just call it broken. And there are many instances where targets or even movement waypoints are obscured by the terrain making them almost impossible to click on no matter how you rotate the camera. Additionally, the game is only even vaguely playable zoomed out, but there are a lot of things you'll only notice when zoomed in, and you'll frequently hear the "I noticed something," sound and not be able to determine what caused it. Oh, and the system of having to design a 3D character model and then also pick a portrait from a terribly small list is awful and leads to almost none of your characters' portraits looking anything like the characters. (Oh, and while I'm complaining, the changes from one gender to another when putting on the same item of clothing are semi-random and often vaguely eyebrow-raising, with the 'female' version almost always bearing no resemblance whatsoever to the item's description).
The fact that, despite all of that, I'm still giving it a thumbs-up, and that should tell you a lot about how strong the rest of the game is and about how strong a game this could have been with a bit more polish. It's engaging, challenging, has a compelling storyline and lots of interesting locales, and is often hilarious as all get-out. It also took me about 64 hours to complete, which makes its price (about $50 when not on sale) pretty reasonable, if not quite the best deal possible. But given that it's been a GOTA edition *and* a Director's Cut, I still expected it to be closer to what it could have been than what it is.

There's a very snarky, self-aware sense of humor that pervades the game, which I appreciate, especially since, if played straight, the game would probably be pretty grimdark and depressing; a tone that wouldn't mesh nearly as well with the aesthetic and mechanics as the fanciful, winking humor does.
I'm pretty forgiving of the fourth-wall breaking because those references largely come from the "comedy relief animal mascot" character, and that archetype is pretty well known for breaking the fourth wall.
Dust is a great deal of fun, and the art style is truly delightful.  Absolutely worth the time and money to play.

Ever dream of a pixelated puzzle platformer adventure in a universe full of parody? A Pixel Story gives you just that and grants you control of a magical hat that lets you leave it somewhere and then teleport back to it in order to traverse a fun filled land. None of these traversal puzzles feel like mysteries. You'll always know how to solve them. Its just performing them requires timing. The teleportation puzzles go from easy to timing perfect jumps and warps to make it deeper into the game. You don't start with the hat, or even clothes for that matter. You'll quickly obtain the hat once you get it back from a seagull that steals it. As for the clothes, you're given those pretty quick.
There's a good sense of size and scope when the camera pulls out to show you how big an area is. A Pixel Story is almost MetroidVania-esque, because it feels like an open world, but you won't obtain any abilities to get to new places outside of using your hat. The game is split into sections each with two "worlds." To travel back between these sections, you can warp back to your bedroom where you can leap between the sections as time periods. You're not allowed to have your hat in the first section, which is a shame and a missed opportunity. Each world has a theme everything from a bland grassland, to a lava pit and even the Bat cave. The game makes a lot of parodies of Batman, Gordon Freeman, and even the Terminator. These comical cameos are pretty entertaining and shocking to see. You'll give a crowbar to Freebird and see a bat signal only to have it fly away. There's a lot of comedy, charm and dialog boxes here. In fact an over abundance of dialog boxes when nothing needs to be said. You even have a helper that consistently appears with tips or even to talk about pancakes.
The graphics start out pretty basic with retro aesthetic and minimal colors, but get better as you progress because the game has you traveling through different eras of video game history. Everything continues to look more detailed. The backgrounds start to stand out more and more from simplistic to rich with beautiful fidelity. Your character stays nearly identical from start to finish. He consists of only a head, body, feet and hands, but no arms. So he's similar to Rayman, but feels like a country bumpkin with his magical red hat, overalls and the fact he starts out helping farmers, moonshiners and even a KFC Cornall whose band plays in instrumental "What is Love?" Again this game takes liberties with its parody.
The game amounts to collecting enough gems (memories) to get transported to the next world. Each world has eight gems that you'll find either by looking hard enough or completing a quest. There are a lot of quirky characters that give you quests, the silly thing is they'll ask you to accept it or not. Well why wouldn't you accept the mission? Then you'll have to obtain an item and bring it back to them. Of course between you and the item, you'll need to flip switches, jump on moving platforms, and springboard yourself from point A to point B. It feels like an old school role-playing game with this many fetch quests.
A Pixel Story plays pretty simple on your keyboard or 360 controller. Other than your menu, there are three major buttons; a jump, a leave your hat and recall your hat button. Once you leave your hat, you can teleport back to it by using the same button. Using the teleport leads to more interesting jumps such as at the height of a jump, leaving your hat, then with your next jump, immediately teleport at the start of the jump to appear at your hat and jump higher. You'll use that mechanic a lot with spring boards or even to save yourself from falling into a bed of whirling gears. It doesn't get more complex than that, but it becomes about angles and hat positions as well as your warp timing. If you ever leave your hat somewhere and travel out of sight, your hat gets its own little window to show what its doing.
Your hat hovers in the air when you leave it, so its a good way to get over and under moving platforms or even get through shifting walls. The further you progress, the more tricks each world will have, such as gravity platforms that will hold your hat to them as they move. So the platform can take your hat through gears and you can teleport to your hat. Its a nice twist. Later, springboards get replaced by bounce wire. If you walk on it, you won't bounce, but if you fall on it, you maintain the height of your bounce. You can then use your hat jumping technique to increase the height of each bounce. Its a good way to keep things interesting late in the game.
There are no enemies, its all one hit hazards that kill you. Its still a forgiving game, because with every death, you'll respawn at your last checkpoint. These checkpoints are quite frequent and they even allow you to fast travel to previous checkpoints. This makes any backtracking a breeze, but I didn't feel like there was any backtracking except when I wanted to find all the gems. Your map also shows you where your objective is and you'll unlock sections of the map as you visit them. Even if these maps are somewhat big, it doesn't feel like there's all that much exploration. There are still secrets like walking through walls.
As you go through the game, you'll find coins scattered here and there. These coins unlock special challenge rooms. I took one look at each insane room and left. Each one seems to be a single screen full of cannons, conveyer belts, grinding gears and everything else you can imagine. You wind your way through to get a gem at the end. There are no checkpoints, because then you'd never be able to make it back to the door. At least these are optional. I know there are a lot of hardcore players out there, but I would have much preferred a bonus room or something more interesting than something as intense.
Some switches are timed so they turn into races for you to do what needs to get done before the switch resets. It puts pressure on you in what is otherwise a relaxing go at your own pace game. Once you get toward the end, you'll get pushed to act fast when there's a death beam following you up a vertically scrolling Recycling Bin.
There are a few moments that break up the puzzle platforming, such as taking a dive down a chute full of gears. At first you're following someone down that warns you when things are coming. Soon enough he breaks off and you're on your own. You'll have to weave your character down narrow corridors lined with deadly metal. That's a good way
While the game didn't feel like the game has many issues, I noticed specific worlds such as the Forest and the Bat Cave had lag or slow down. I assume from the detailed backgrounds. Turning my resolution down helped, but it was still noticeable even with V-Sync off. It did also crash to the desktop once in the six hours that I played, but the game auto saves pretty often just in case. Sometimes death forced me to get the coins I had just collected, other times it didn't. There are several grammar errors in the hundreds of dialog boxes, but I'm probably guilty of that as well.
A Pixel Story is a fun little game in the early worlds before it gets more difficult than fun. The challenge is never out of reach though as long as you put some effort into your timing. A good way to see the difficulty is to look at the achievements and see how drastic the drop off is between the achievements. The real enjoyment is from the surprises that come from cameos. I'd like to thank Tom for gifting me this game.

A Pixel Story is a very enjoyable game that puts a great spin on a traditional platforming genre. I love the Pixel-styled artwork as well as the numerous computer-related humor and gaming references throughout. The music is awesome, too!
Some of the level progression can be quite difficult, but it's not like they throw you at a wall from the beginning. The level design teaches you as you move forward, both giving you enough to learn how things work, and still able to rack your head around some obstacles. Their extra Challenge Rooms are definitely a control-breaker.
I don't think it shows much of it in the trailer video, but later on in the game it isn't just jumping on platforms anymore. There is a lot of timing and thinking involved to move on ahead. They really introduced some cool concepts with the teleporting ability, and I found myself enjoying the different parts.
I wish they integrated the story a bit better. You gain background story by collecting the Memory in the game, but it's usually just flavortext inside the menu. You can essentially progress through the game without ever reading any substantial storyline. NOTE: I've only played the beginning area, so that might change later on. But if you DO read it, it reveals quite a bit of history and story in the game that does open it up to more than just jumping around on platforms.
I don't play a lot of platforming games, but this is definitely a fun one. A bit difficult at times, but definitely satisfying.
8/10, I would recommend to any platform loving gamers out there.

I don’t think Mafia 3 needs any real introduction. I’m sure most people will have played the brilliant first Mafia game or the second also-pretty-good Mafia 2. The Mafia games have always had open cities with rather linear missions, but Mafia 3 wants to change things up and let you choose which mission you want to tackle and in which order. So, did Hangar13 succeed in giving us the best Mafia game yet?

Sadly, no. By now you must have read several professional and user reviews to see that the game should be fun, but flawed. I can’t argue with this, but I always urge people to play for themselves and have an own opinion instead of just following the masses. Mafia 3 has some fun and good ideas, but sometimes the execution could’ve used a little more polish. I’ll get into this later on.
Let’s start with the story and the majority of the missions. As I mentioned missions can be tackled in any order you would like. This makes things a little less linear but unfortunately the majority of the missions is just copy-paste material, in a different setting or area. Although the story pretty much continues with each mission you do 70% of the time it comes down to killing enforcers, interrogating people, destroying properties, killing important henchman and finally taking down the ‘boss’. The sub-missions can also be tackled on in random order, and once the value of the area has been decreased to $0 you can choose to complete the other sub-missions (maybe for some extra cash) or just go visit the person who gave you the mission who will then give you the location of the boss. Boss locations can always be found in previous locations so there’s always a location you will visit twice. I found this to be a bit sloppy; you have this huge city and you can’t even find the time to put the boss in a different location? Anyhow, after having killed the boss you get to assign one of your three lieutenants to the area who will then bring in extra money (called kickback) and other perks, like having more health, or having the option to temporarily disable the telephone lines.
It all is quite fun to do in the beginning but later on it drags a bit and I truly hoped the game wouldn’t just be the same thing over and over again. But truth be told, it just takes too long before you’re getting more varied story missions and even then it still comes down to killing mafia members. Which is fitting, since it’s a revenge story but there’s simply not enough variety to make things fun and interesting for tens of hours.
All missions can be played in stealth or full, frontal action. The stealth part is something Mafia 3 does well, and at times it does pay off to do things completely unnoticed. If you do get noticed there’s always the chance that reinforcements will be called and all enemies in the area will then automatically focus on you, no matter where they are in the area or building. Depending on who’s still alive this might get you killed during later missions. Fortunately, the AI is hit and miss…
The AI doesn’t always notice your presence, especially from larger distances. Fair enough, this is to keep things fun, naturally. But at times they run past you, other times everyone knows exactly where to find you and at other times they have no clue, even though you clearly walked in their line of sight. Thankfully, this doesn’t happen extremely often, but it does take you out of the experience and lets you know you’re actually playing a game here.
And the music? Well, that’s something many of us will enjoy and will have grown up with. The music is just sublime. It ranges from The Rolling Stones to Sam Cooke to Creedence Clearwater Revival. It’s beautiful. It’s just that, despite the many tracks, you’ll hear a lot of the same songs within a small timeframe. It could’ve used a little more randomization, because I’m sure there are still some tracks in there that I haven’t even heard. Still, there’s a lot to love here.
I’m sad to say that I encountered two game breaking bugs in my playthrough – which isn’t a lot – but enough to mention them. Both were door related and the first one was actually in the very beginning where you take the money transport car and are then eventually supposed to go into a building. But, the door never opened. Same thing happened later on during a mission that I won’t spoil (it’s one where you finally get to do something a little differently). My girlfriend encountered the same game breaking bug during her own playthrough, on an entirely different system. I also encountered two bugs where I had to pick up a boat or vehicle and they just weren’t there, making the side missions impossible to complete. This is also the reason why I stopped playing these completely.
Like Mafia 2 Mafia 3 also features collectibles in the form of album covers, paintings, Playboy magazines and hot rod magazines. These are scattered throughout the world and I had a pretty hard time finding them but I wasn’t actively looking myself so I’m sure that if you go through the map systematically you’ll find most of them easily.

The audio and voice acting are both superb and contribute to making this a AAA game. The music is simply sublime and except for a few of the voice actors none of them can be faulted. They mostly deliver their lines perfectly and it makes the game truly more believable. Great job here!
As for the visuals. You may have noticed the PC release had some problems during the release; 30FPS, blurry visuals, et cetera. Thankfully most of these problems were fixed during the same weekend but it’s sloppy and unprofessional nevertheless. The reason why it had a 30FPS limit is probably because you need a monster machine to even maintain 60FPS and even with my GTX1080, 16GB RAM and i7 processor it still had difficulties running it at steady 60FPS the entire time, at 2560x1440. This is with most of the settings turned down (Medium or Low). Running everything at High in that resolution would’ve dropped the framerate significantly. I’ve tried dropping the resolution to 1920x1080 but since that’s not my native resolution is resulted in blurry graphics yet again, although with excellent performance this time around.
But technical issues aside; the game has a lovely art style with great atmosphere. There were a couple of glitches here and there, but other than that the game looks beautiful (the weather effects annoyed me at first, but I think they have been patched; I didn’t notice it the last couple of days I played).

Doing all of the side missions results in a game that will last you up to 35 hours or longer (depending on if you’re also grabbing the collectibles). Doing just the story missions will last you 20-25 hours. Replay value is pretty much non-existent. If you’ve played through it once you’ll probably never touch it again anytime soon, unless you’re going for the collectibles. But all in all this is really good value for what you for.
I guess Mafia 3 isn’t the sequel we all hoped for, but it does attempt to do some things differently. It succeeds in some of the areas while failing in others. I’m not sure if it’s worth the full price tag – also considering the technical issues the PC version brings with it – but if you like open world games with plenty of story and collectibles then Mafia 3 is absolutely meant for you. For all of the others I suggest waiting for a sale. €40 would be a solid and fair price at this time, in my opinion.

TL;DR:
A great puzzle-platformer that will delight as much as infuriate sitting at a great price point
Recommended 8/10
Synapsis:
You are a pixel from the classic game "Pong" that has fallen out of your original place in the game to a place deep in the system. You awaken to find a helpful robot named Search who informs you that you are the "Chosen One". You come to find out that this means you will be essentially repairing the system.  You do this, following a few tutorial puzzles, with the help of a hat that allows you to save your position and thus transport back instantaneously when needed.
The puzzle difficulties ramp up quickly normally showing themselves to be more infuriating due to precise timing  requirements and less about how much they boggle the mind.  You will me made to do a minimum number of puzzles to acquire colored gems called "Memory" in order to advance in the story. In addition, more challenging puzzles are available by opening doors with the coins you pick up along the way.
As I am writing this review I am, I believe, still very early in the game and enjoying it thoroughly. The puzzles keep me on edge and though the story is fairly cliche, it is keeping me interested enough to continue speculation of whats to come.
Like puzzle games? Like platformers?....If the answer to either of these questions is yes I can recommend you pick this title up. The price tag is great for what you get, having seen recent titles as good as this going for twice the cost.
