Mafia III is a strange beast. The story and presentation grabbed me at the beginning, but several crashes and some absolutely horrible AI interactions later, I put the game down. I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥because I felt like I had been burned. Then I picked it up again, maybe a week later, with adjusted expectations, and it's a game that I would recommend.
A few really good things:
+ Story - The presentation is innovative and the writing is superb.
+ Music - Awesome playlist from the 60's. Although, when you go into combat some generic, watered-down blues tracks play.
+ Melee - For as janky as this game is, the people in charge of animating the melee takedowns did a great job. They're violent as hell, and they do an awesome job adjusting to when you're behind a wall or whatever.
A few not-so-good things:
- AI - Wow. Really bad. But, once again, I changed the way I was playing and it's not an issue. I kinda speedrun takedowns and don't shy away from gunfights when they come up. That makes for some interesting surprises and some fun strategy.
- Grindy - Cause enough problems in x area to get to the local boss who is hiding in a back office in some building. Oh, and (this is crazy) you've probably already cleared that building and it's miraculously repopulated. Rinse, repeat. Yes, this would probably be unbearable if I was binging the game. It's not that bad when I log in a couple hours here and there.
A few whatever things:
Open world - It's interesting enough to look at. Many of the stores are the same. Whatever, there's definitely more depth here than Mafia II. The environment does a good job of providing a setting for the story.
Jankfest - This game has so many glitches it's funny. For instance, one mission I was supposed to rescue a guy in a meat processing plant. I show up, take everybody out, and find the guy. Awesome, time to leave right? Nope. Dude's chair that he was supposed to be tied to was missing, but the shackles were still floating in the air like he was still tied to it. It broke the mission. Fornutely, it was just a side one. After a while, you just need to learn to laugh at these. There's a lot of memorable jank moments to be had.
I would recommend picking this one up on sale. The story makes it worth it alone, and if you can embrace the jank of the entire experience, it's a lot of fun.

After "The Walking Dead" which is a pseudo-game focusing mainly on cheating the player into thinking that anything they do matters, Telltale-like games got into a personal black list of mine but since Episode 1 of Life is Strange is free, I decided to see what all the fuzz is about.
...Well, this experience only reinforced me in my opinion about Telltale games.
At least the lore of "The Walking Dead" was somewhat interesting. In this case we have the most generic set you can imagine - the main protagonsit is an American teenager in an American school. Yeah, it's just as bad as it sounds. The amount of clichés thrown at my face during only like 3 hours of gameplay made me cringe hard - and MC is sometimes even auto-ironic about it which sadly doesn't help. We have the shy, introverted but snarky girl, we have the mean "stars of the school", we have the rich kid who "owns the school" and therefore gets away with anything, we have the bullies (all footballers ofc), we have the bullied (fat), we have the rebellious punk-girl with blue hair, we have the corrupt principal... heck, we even have TWO janitors so we can fulfill TWO movie tropes - one is a paranoid, rigid Nazi and the other one is aloof, riddle-speaking weirdo who SURELY holds some FASCINATING secret. Ugh.
Even the main plot device - the ability to rewind time... You could think it's impossible to make it dull and uninteresting? Well, one day our protagonist, out of nowhere, suddenly discovers that she can rewind time. And then she was like "Wow, I can rewind time! Let's do some time-rewinding action amirite? Lol!". Yeah, it's THAT unconvincing and unrelatable. No questioning your sanity, no experiencing a mental breakdown, no asking "why"... Just like that. I suppose the reason of getting this superpower is somewhat explained in next episodes but the mere introduction of it made me completely uninterested in that (edit: scratch that, a friend told me that it isn't explained EVER. Wow, just wow, this is some fanfiction-written-by-a-13-years-old level of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t).
And now the best part... "Choices Matter"? Seriously, Steam users? How blind you must be to actually think that? All that your choices affect is one or two lines of dialogue and one scene. That's it. Heck, sometimes you're given a choice of two dialogue options and both of them give EXACTLY THE SAME answer. Yes, the devs are that shameless. What was the point of giving you that choice in the first place? To create an illusion, of course. An illusion of you having any control on what's happening on the screen. All this effort to make you think that your choices matter... All those "this action will have consequences" (guess what? It ♥♥♥♥ing won't), all this emphasis put on "decision-making" moments... It's all just lies and fraud. And those "overhelmingly positive" reviews are sad proof of how naive and easy to fool gamers are. This is why I hate Telltale and its clones.
The graphics are... "simplistic", to put it mildly. Another way to avoid putting an actual effort into the game. The facial expressions are way too rigid and robotic for a story-based "game". That's all.
To sum it up - during 5 hours of "gameplay" (aka watching things happening) I was looking for reasons for why is this game so highly appraised and I failed to find one. Well, maybe it's true what some say that it's all about female protagonist and waifuism potential. If it's true, then it's just sad. I don't care if next episodes are better or not - Episode 1 was supposed to be an introduction to the game in order to make me interested and hooked - and it failed its job horribly.

Stop. Do not spend money on this. Yes, I know, you've been looking around for some competitive multiplayer and you don't want to pass up the sale this time. Look, I know it's only three dollars right now. It doesn't matter. If you're thinking about buying NS2, then you probably have an internet connection, a mouse and a keyboard. If I'm right, then leave this place right now, and go play TF2.
You know that satisfying feeling you get from mastering foreign game mechanics and then using that mastery to murder other players to prove that you're better than them? That doesn't exist here. The kills in this game come from understanding cheap tricks like where to put insta-kill landmines or which combination of upgrades can give you an uncounterable character build in a given situation. So instead of that satisfaction when you defeat player in a fair fight, you end up getting a bitter victory when you realize your opponent had every odd stacked against him.
And that's the biggest problem with this game. There are too many no-win scenarios. There are few opportunities to match wits and abilities against other players because one person is a dude with a gun and the other might be some wall-crawling ankle-biter. It all comes down to an arms race of who can unlock the shotgun, the teleporting insta-death alien, the robot suit, or the giant alien on the box art. If "natural selection" were able to truly play out in this game, it would come down to flying jetpack shotgun soldiers vs. gorilla monsters.
Save your three dollars. Go buy some icecream and sit outside.

The Binding of Isaac: What is there to say about The Binding of Isaac? A simple yet, deep and complex arcade styled rogue video game. The Binding of Isaac is a joy to play and, is something everyone can play yet few will master. A wonderful blend of skill and just a touch of luck, you will descend deep into Isaac’s mom’s creepy basement, face a multitude of different enemies and bosses and pick up enough power-ups to blow up Earth and see what lies in the depths for poor little Isaac. For less than $10.00 USD you can own the original game and the expansion as well.  The game itself isn’t for everyone, as it is incredibly challenging and those without the will to persist will find themselves frustrated quickly. The imagery itself is also gross and if you have a gentle stomach, may wish to avoid the disgusting basement of The Binding of Isaac.  Overall, for the amount of content, the simple controls, and price there are only a few reasons why anyone would pass this game up. It is gross no doubt, and it is a challenge, but the rewards in the game are more than enough justification for this purchase. Plus you can’t just leave Isaac to his mother’s horrible whims can you?

I am writing this after finishing the main game and having rage-quit the secret level. This game takes you through typographic history in a way that is creative and visually stunning. The graphics and the music are phenomenal, and each chapter offers something new. Going into this I was afraid that each level would play the same but with different visuals, and I was happily mistaken. Each chapter offers a new twist with a new mechanic, and it will take all of your platforming skills to get through them. Because let me tell you, this game is hard. Maybe it's just me, but I found Type:Rider to be extremely difficult. Unfortunately I'm not entirely sure this was all intentional. The nature of your character, so to speak, means it's very easy to get hung up on corners and serifs. Have fun with the Pixel chapter. Jumping is also infuriating at times because of the wall-jump mechanic that's perhaps just a bit too touchy. And yet despite my rage I had fun playing this. Here's the thing. I love typography. I had fun scrambling across fonts, and I had fun learning the history of font. It's certainly not a game for everyone, but if this sounds like the kind of experience you'd enjoy then I definitely recommend this.

Imagine if the developers of
,
and
had an orgy and invited the guys who did
as well as the dude who created the Flashgame
and the guys who did
were spying on them through the window. If they all had conceived a baby that night, it would be
.
Nevermind that fact though, because the game wears its influences on its sleeve and isn't ashamed by that in the slightest. As you might infer from the line-up above consisting mostly of puzzle-platformers,
is obviously in the same genre as those.
You start your life as a pixel. But not just as any old pixel. You are in fact the ball from the legendary arcade classic
. But something is afoot in your system and you are violently ripped out of the game and through inter-dimensional portals you catch glimpses of other worlds you are about to visit. In a darkened room, shadowy figures initiate a sequence that gives you a humanoid body and you're let loose into the first world.
As is typical for modern puzzle-platformers made by people who grew up in the 80's and 90's,
boasts a retro-aesthetic. Or so I thought initially, because similar to
, the art-style changes over the course of the game. You start out in an 8-bit inspired world and after you beat that, you enter a higher resolution 16-bit world. After a third transition, bits don't matter anymore and the art-style has changed to one that is heavily inspired by
watercolor aesthetic. Similar to that, the music evolves as well, changing from simple chiptunes to more modern arrangements.
What doesn't really change - except during the final level - is the gameplay. Early on in the game, you are awarded with a hat (Gomez from
sends his greetings). This hat has a special power. It let's you use the hat as a teleporter. Meaning you can drop it anywhere in the level and with the push of a button teleport back to where the hat is. And that's basically it. That's your main mechanic outside of pulling levers, using jump-pads or just jumping from platform to platform.
Though as with any good game with a deceptively simple mechanic,
manages to pull out a lot of depth from it, and with that a certain maliciousness. The puzzles increase steadily in complexity and by the end there are a couple of brain twisters in there that don't make life easy for you. Or at least for me. If you are a better man than I am, you can also enter certain challenge rooms, though that name has to be the understatement of the year. Again, drawing from my pool of comparisons at the top, these challenge rooms take the
approach at game design, just throwing everything at you simultaneously, only it's even more sadistic than the adventures of Meat Boy the skinless one.
With all that talk about gameplay and aesthetic, I almost forgot to talk about the story part of
. Or better the lack thereof. Now there is a story that's being told, you're the chosen pixel to bring down the Operator of the System and set all the programs in it free. And over the course of the game you meet all sorts of different characters inspired by computers. Such as the Kernel, a rich philanthropist, or Search, your trusty partner and exposition dump. And he really is that, so very little is shown, most is told through lengthy dialogue or some background information from memory crystals you need to collect. But there's really not much to this world beyond that. We never see how or why the old Operator has been challenged by the new one, we never know the motivation of the current Operator. We're just the chosen one set to bring him down. We never learn who these shadowy figures at the start were that transformed your pixelly shape into a person. Or at least I never did. I assume to get the real ending, you'd have to beat all the challenge rooms and acquire all the memory crystals in order to unlock the final ending. So I at the very least will never find out, because the game is just too difficult for me to invest so much more time into it, and I would've liked it better if I'd have been give a bit more closure for just finishing the game and beating the final boss.
Outside of that, the game is chock-full of pop-culture references. You'll find a caricature program of Arnold Schwarzenegger as The Terminator and even a side-quest about a sleeping princess that turns out to be inspired by
. Though one that definitely put a smile on my face was a party where the band plays a chiptune rendition of Haddaways classic "What is Love".
If it sounds like I'm down on the game because of the lacking narrative, don't fret. Because all the other elements are fantastic. It's got a simple, easily understandable central mechanic and the puzzles are designed cleverly enough to provide plenty entertainment and challenge for a player and then some. Even though it lacks a unified aesthetic - given the fact that it changes with every new area - all the styles it employs are executed competently and the music that accompanies you on your adventures is really good. Since the game takes a lot of inspiration from a variety of different sources, as mentioned in this review, I can't call it innovative, but sometimes a game just doesn't have to be innovative to be good. Even an indie game. It's a really fun game and I can wholeheartedly recommend
to fans of puzzle-platformers that aren't stingy with presenting challenging obstacles for players to overcome.

Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae it's a little, actually VERY little, action hack'n'slash game (like Metal Gear Rising, Bayonetta, Devil May Cry and many more) centered on a samurai girl that tries to defeat another samurai girl (her best friend) possessed by a demon.
The game takes a very basilar approach: it throws you in some arena where you have to fight a number of waves of enemies in order to fight a boss and proceed to the next level.
This title is very short, the main story is composed of just 5 stages for a total hour count of about 4 hours, however the replayability is quite large 'cause there is a certain number of unlockables (costumes and difficulties).
The realization it's a bit rough: the main characters are realized quite well, however the stages are very plain and monotonous and there is a scarcity of types of enemies, but must be noted that the game is very fluid and delivers what it wants to deliver and it's actually a sort of gameplay tech demo (albeit a very good one).
In the end , if you are an aficionado of hack'n'slash titles you'll probably love this nice little game because of its gameplay, otherwise probably this isn't the right product for you.

If there is ever a game you had to play, it's this one. Games like these are rare, far and few inbetween. It treats you like an adult, and doesn't hold your hand. The story is believeable and plausible. With it's rich story comes some of the hardest decisions I have ever had to make in a video game, plus it really rubs it in when most of these hard choices have a timer behind them so you can't really sit there and think about what you're doing. Very much how it is in real life.
Oh, and the combat? Get ready to fight for real. The games combat system is some of the most unique I had seen and experienced. Like in real life ( I know I keep saying this but bare with me ), you don't charge headlong into battle like a mindless oaf. You prepare, you asses and you judge the situation. Much of that will happen during combat and before combat in this game. Preparation is paramount, and using your Witcher signs to the fullest is as well. Because you won't be able to pause during combat and equip an oinment for your blade or drink a point. You have to do this beforehand. That is, if you're playing on the easiest difficulty, then combat and it's horrors will be of no consequence. But, in truth, you are robbing yourself of what the Witcher is, if you decide to play it on that difficulty. Trust me, I have finished on both easiest and the normal setting, and they are worlds apart. In terms of combat atleast.
Main protagonist should also be mentioned. You play as Geralt of Rivia. Only THE most badass protagnoist to ever have lived. Trust me on this too when I say this. This man is the epitome of being a man you should not ♥♥♥♥ with. He is a professional monster slayer, augmented and tested, to be the very best at what he does. Also having super human strenght and reflexes help. Though I do have one gripe with it, you never get to see his super human strenght and reflexes in the game. He seems very ordinary in those two terms. I never really felt SUPER powerful, just skillful and really smart. Besides, I doubt even if I did see it , my opinion of him wouldn't change.
To wrap it up. This might be the most fulfilling RPGs I have ever played, until of course Witcher 3 comes out, and all who love the genre are doing a GREAT AND GRAVE injustice by not playing it.
P.S. If you're worried you will miss most of the story by not playing the first one, don't worry, the game gives you a short and sweet  " previously on the Witcher ". Although not shedding the light on most of what happened, I found myself rather ok with not playing the first one.

Natural Selection 2 is a game that pits 2 teams (aliens and marines) against each other in tug of war to destroy the other factions base. Each faction elects a commander to place structures and oversee the operation on the whole, while the rest of the faction's players play as the foot soldiers moving up and back against the opposing faction. Competing for turf is rewarded not only with positional advantage, but also with increased resource generation for use in upgrades and personalization.
The different abilities felt unique and the upgrade paths felt meaningful. It felt different playing as an alien and as a marine, and both had their fun merits. The aliens were quick and illusive, while the marines hit their marks hard and from afar. At the same time, morphing into higher life forms (aliens) or buying better gear (marines) felt meaningful, yet decently balanced.
The game seemed to often become a stalemate where there were chokepoints each faction could hold but not push the other out of. It would have been helpful if the game provided tips about how to push past or break these stalemantes in addition to all the information about what the weapons do.
Overall, it was a fun experience with some interesting (and enjoyable) twists on the usual formula. However, as far as team objective pvp shooters go, it's difficult to recommend this over options like the extremely polished, easier-on-the-gpu, free Team Fortress 2. As of this review, it seems to fall just short of standing on its own.

I was a kickstarter backer for this game and originally played it back when it launched. The game at launch was very buggy. I remember about three separate times when I had a problem with a quest but finished it anyway only to get a patch the next day that fixed the problem I had. I don't remember much of my original playthrough other than I stopped playing at the canyon of titan and decided it would be best to let the game incubate and then restart it some time later when it's been all patched up.
That was almost three years ago. Since then, they've released the Director's Cut edition complete with better textures and a new perk system. They've even moved on to promoting Wasteland 3. Surely Wasteland 2 must be in its finest form by now, right?
Guess not. Instead of having a bunch of minor bugs with unimportant sidequests, I have run into a game breaking one that prevents me from progressing the main story. My current campaign that I have invested 26 hours in has been a waste of time. I couldn't even get further than my original playthrough.
To be more specific:
But what if there were no bugs? Even then, I think the game would be OK at best. You start the game by creating four rangers. Its impossible to make characters that look good unless you really like the punk-ish, mad max "junkyard tribal" look. In fact, the game in general is kind of ugly and low poly in a bad way. Even for 2014 standards. Should I have different standards for kickstarter game graphics? I'm not sure. A quick search for mods to remedy this revealed only additional character portraits.
You can control seven characters total and the small bit of praise I will give this game is that the characters you can enlist along the way are all better looking and way more interesting than your four main rangers. The enlisted characters also allow unique interactions with some quests. Seeing how they fit into the world was always neat.  When characters lose all health, they go into a downed state. If they're attacked in this state, they're dead forever. Theoretically, you could kill off some of your four main rangers and have mostly enlisted characters, but the enlisted characters can leave your squad for story reasons so that's not the best idea.
The core component of the game is combat. It's fine. Combat is turn-based and takes place on a grid. Each individual unit takes a turn with the order of turns determined by the unit's stats. Its very similar to the pre-bethesda fallout games. You can put your troops behind cover to get aim and evasion bonuses, but what counts as cover seem inconsistent. There were also a few times when the combat grid did not properly fit inside a room resulting in the east wall counting as cover and the west wall being half a square off grid and impossible to take cover behind.
I think my biggest gripe with ideal bug-free Wasteland 2 is the skill system. Skills are things like being able to shoot shotguns well or pick locks. Each skill has 10 tiers. There are way too many skills for you to construct a team that can handle everything. That would be fine if it wasn't for the fact that some skills are way less useful than others and you won't know this until you are well into your first playthrough. I'm convinced that Wasteland 2's skills could be organized into a tier chart much like people do with characters in a fighting game. I found toaster repair and animal whispering to just not be worth it at all. I've never tried safecracking and I'm afraid safes are the same as toasters, just random high-value loot stores. It's also hard to know what spreading a character's skillset too thin looks like at first. From my limited experience, I would not recommend giving someone more than five skills but I can't be sure what that will look like by the time you reach the end of the game (*IF* you reach the end of the game). If five seems limited, it gets worse when you consider one or two of those skills should be a weapon skill. Maybe you can get away with having a pacifist utility character, I haven't tried it. I don't like the idea of missing out on the end of a side quest because I wanted to shoot a gun more accurately when I should have invested in computer science and wish they had separated the progression of combat skills and utility skills. It's important to be able to shoot the bad guys but finding alternate routes through quests using utility skills is fun! What if you could do important AND fun things?!
But I guess Wasteland 2 isn't about doing fun AND important things. Its about wasting your time with bugs.

Notice: My review states that I do not recommend this game because of inXile Entertainment's exceptionally scummy behavior during the "inXile vs The Alien Wasteland" incident (Google it for more details - basically, inXile used copyright laws in a frivolous way to bully a small indie developer). If you are in any way conscious about the future of game development, I implore you not to buy the game or any of the other Wasteland games. (If you are desperately looking for a post-apoc RPG, have a look at Underrail!)
To other reviewers: due to a Steam glitch, you have to review Wasteland 2 DC by posting a review to regular Wasteland 2. That also means you have to install and play that for at least 5 minutes too if you haven't already. (This is why it seems like I've only played a couple minutes - my real playtime is ~50 hours right now.)
For the sake of honesty, I am also going to write up a brief summary of the good and the bad points of the game itself. Wasteland 2: Director's Cut is a post-apocalyptic RPG about an American militia organization named the Desert Rangers who try to uphold law and order in Arizona after a global nuclear apocalypse, as well as the events of the first game (which, as explained very soon in the game as well, involved stopping a crazy scientist and a malevolent AI). You lead a party of four (or less) Rangers on a mission to find out about the circumstances of the death of another Ranger. This party can later gain up to three additional followers, up to a squad size of seven. These followers (of which there are plenty, so you'll have to make choices as to who you carry along) have the slight drawback that they can "go rogue", i.e. ignore your orders and do their own thing each turn (this can be mitigated), but are otherwise perfectly functional player characters.
Sounds like a lot to manage? It's not as bad as it sounds. The character attribute/skill system is simple enough, though it can feel overwhelming on a first playthrough. However, W2 DC does provide a default squad - you can roll with it on the normal ("Seasoned") difficulty level on a first playthrough and do alright (at least I did). The tutorial system is adequate and explores the various elements of the game well enough that you probably won't feel lost after the first 15-30 minutes. Combat may seem a bit punishing at first, but if you explore enough, the game rewards you pretty soon with a "crutch" follower, who is quite a bit stronger than your characters at that point and will help you get through the first few areas. (Though I also have a minor quibble here: this very same follower will eventually leave you, so if you thought they were a solid fixture on your team and rely on them for a critical skill, you may suddenly be left with a gaping hole in your team after they leave. You are subtly warned that they might only stay while your team are still greenhorns, but the warning is too subtle in my opinion. Most other followers do stick around once they join you, though, unless you make a choice that pisses them off big time.)
Speaking of choices, this game does have its fair share of "choices and consequences". Like most games that advertise this, this game does not deviate too much from its major storyline either, and the choices only have flavor effects or some minor gameplay effects at most. This does not mean the C&C system in the game is necessarily bad - I'm just telling you what to expect. Your choices do shape the world, even if not all of them have a significant effect on when and how you win the game. In keeping with the gritty theme, often you are forced to choose between two bad outcomes or may not be able to  stop a certain kind of evil at all no matter what you do, but at other times you can help the wasteland become a better place.
The various factions in the game are interesting, many of them are well-developed and have engaging characters. Unfortunately, the main plot is a bit too railroaded for my taste - the game is designed with the assumption that you are going to be a Desert Ranger through and through, identifying with them without question and opposing the main boss. There are some interesting nuances to the ideology of the main antagonists, but the game does not explore them sufficiently. There are alternate endings where you do not do what the Rangers expect you to do, but they are unsatisfying to say the least. The side quests are actually more interesting than the main plot IMO.
Regarding game balance, the game is balanced well enough that you can do a first playthrough on Seasoned (the default, normal difficulty level) with just the right amount of challenge, not too much frustration, but not too easy either. I think you might conceivably be able try a blind ironman first run as well, if you are so inclined - though I'd probably recommend  Rookie for that. The game is not a roguelike though, and it isn't designed for endless replayability - I think that there are about 2-3 playthroughs' worth of material in the game (provided you like it enough to replay it), and no more, so I'd advise against blind ironman play. One positive I'd like to note is that unlike quite a few CRPGs I've ever seen (the worst violator being Age of Decadence), this game - at least on normal difficulty - does not need extreme minmaxing to succeed, and you *can* start with suboptimal builds and still perform well enough. You can even branch out into a lot of non-combat skills and still be strong enough to be able to fight, and the game is forgiving enough that you can make drastic changes to your skill focuses over the course of 5-10 levels if you take your team in the wrong direction (my characters were around level 40 by the time they completed the game). For example, if you realize you desperately need the Lockpicking skill and forgot to take it on any of your characters, well, you'll be missing some containers for a while, but you aren't hopelessly behind and will probably still be able to max it out if you aren't too late into the game.
The interface and user-friendly aspects are generally good - there aren't a lot of really inconvenient/frustrating functionalities I've found, carry weights are not a huge issue, useless junk items that have no use other than sell value can be sold with a single click all at once... not much bad I can say here.
If you care about that sort of thing, the game is also LGBTQ-positive. Well, I haven't seen any T, but they might exist without you realizing it, y'know? There are quite a few openly gay characters though (mostly minor, but a particular married lesbian couple will help you out in the final battle if you help them out before). I've also found at least one crossdresser (in a town which is famous for its extreme sexual libertinism, to the point of being ruled over by a sex worker - and they are actually one of the nicer communities in the game, certainly compared to their main rivals) and hey, the game does technically allow you to have gay sex, though nothing is shown on screen - so if you're looking for smut, don't get your hopes up.
As a minor bonus, you can dress up your character in one of many different outfits found throughout the game world - this'll affect the appearance of your toons in the game world and on the character screen (though it's only cosmetic), and since any worn armor doesn't actually appear on you, this functionality isn't made obsolete as soon as you want to put some armor on. You can put really indecent clothes on your females, or have your men walk around in a pair of hold-up stockings, or even dress them up in a way that's actually intimidating and/or practical (but why'd you want to do that?!). It's a fun little minigame you can entertain yourself with while you are shuffling your inventory around.
Overall verdict: avoid, for reasons stated in the very beginning. If you do not care about punishing dodgy business practices, then I'll let you judge based on the rest of the review.

I have always been a BTD fan, I have been around the community for years and I wish to clear ALL the misconceptions.
Flash>Steam>Mobile
8/10
To begin, I notice that many, many negative reviews are on this game, 90% of these people have not played anymore than 1hr of the game, which frustrates me as it does not give a correct view of the game, for example if you play DOTA 2, and lose your first game and then make a bad review you have not experienced the game, as the game is far more complex than most people believe. Anyway back to BTD.
- BTD battles steam is literally a carbon copy of the mobile version with the addition of SOME hotkeys which level the playing field between mobile and PC. Although being a steam game, it has very limited settings which may annoy some more techy people such as myself, but it is bearable.
- Secondly, the 'pay-2-win' element of the game which countless negative reviews are complaining about is a very minor part of the game, as not only is the matchmaking fairly accurate but the grind to obtain these tower upgrades is very small, only taking about 10-20hrs to get EVERYTHING, comparing that to warframe where you need to put in a minimum of about 300+hrs in.
- Next, is the skill based area, this is the part which frustrates me the most, DO NOT EXPECT TO WIN IF YOU HAVE JUST STARTED, it is just like a MOBA, you are gonna lose a lot in the beginning until you learn the strategies and the physics behind the game, I was the same. Although balancing is a major issue in the game, it is not a problem as 90% of the time you will be matched with someone of equal skill level, and an equal amount of stuff unlocked.
- Fourth, is a simple one, there is no exit button. All you need to do is go to settings and change it to windowed mode, this allows you to fullscreen it with a border that has an exit button
- Fifth, this is another thing that really annoys me. Many people complain about losing to rushes, it is part of the game, you are playing on 'ASSAULT' mode for a reason, if you prefer late game, play defense, and yes defense is hard to learn but once you learn it, you can go late game every game. The concept is not that hard
- lastly, many people say that people put a lot of money in, you can transfer your data from the mobile version meaning people who have played 10,000 games can move to steam so, most likely they did not pay, and yes there are some people out there who do pay, but you most likely only be paired up with them if there is no one else available.
Now the comparison of the steam/mobile version to the flash version. The flash version has been forgotten by 90% of BTD players and for the more competitive game, it is the superior version. BTD battles flash, although worse graphics, less community, and no arenas, is a wonderful game, that boasts its amazing balance and physics which make the game a much more serious version compared to the mobile version. This is not suggesting which one is better because the mobile/steam version is targeted to the more general casual audience who just enjoys playing, thus the reason i am giving it 8/10 and not 6/10 because it is not targeted at the more competitive players. TL;DR: Bloons is a fun tower defense with multiple game modes and a varied amount of towers that I recommend played on the toiler (phone) and not on steam (PC... go play something with more depth!)
Bloons TD Battles is a port from your phone over to PC.  You can tell this immediately by the fact there is no way to turn down the volume after it deafens your ears.  You can either completely mute the volume or leave it on the default game setting.  You can either leave the game in full screen or a predetermined resolution windowed mode.
Outside of these poor options, Bloons is a really good tower defense.  Like all pay to win models, it suffers from having a ton of content that is restricted by a massive time investment or moderate (to massive) cash investment.  At the time of this review, I have 10 towers unlocked by can only use a maximum of 4 at a time.  Which allows me to use the wizard and any other random 3 because the wizard is OP in the early game.
There are random draft clubs you can play once, then can pay money to join later on.  In game currency can be wagered at predetermined amounts in best of 1 matches.
I recommend the game, but not on PC.  Play something with a little more depth on PC and play this game while your boss isn't looking at work.

Dust is obviously a work of love. The game's backgrounds and characters look fantastic and when they are put in motion the results are breathtaking, and with great music to boot. The gameplay is about as good as you can expect from an action-oriented metroidvania: level design is top notch, there's plenty of equipment and character customization and the battle system is incredibily successful and rewarding; its addictiveness is easily an accomplishment in and of itself.
The art style and the story might be a bit of a hit-or-miss, but this is a must buy if you have any kind of appreciation for platformers, metroidvanias, or games that just plain exude the ridiculous amounts of passion and dedication that went into making them. I couldn't put the controller down. (Oh yeah, it should go without saying this is definitely meant to be experienced with a pad).

Overall, I like SoW. Note that I haven't reached max level in the game and I'm not sure I'll invest the time to do so. It quickly started feeling like a grind and I started loosing interest. I had thought I wouldn't feel grindy until I at least hit max level. Side note: I received the game for "free" with a graphics card I purchased, which one could argue just shows how over priced graphic cards are...
Pros of the game
- Graphics are absolutely beautiful. I really like just running around sometimes taking in the view. Animations, for the most part, are really smooth. I ran very high settings on a 970 without issue. I've since upped to a 1080 ti and now have the game on ultra. My eyes aren't perfect and for the life of me, I can't really tell any meaningful difference from running it on the 970.
- Sounds are great. There's attention to little details like orcs complaining about their jobs when you're walking around your castle. Other than the obvious, I've not been surprised by anything in my surroundings because the game does a good job of making noises so you know when most enemies are around you.
- Decent variation in quests and what you can do. Want a mission to go take out a captain, you got it. Want to do a story mission that has a half decent plot, you got it. Want to raid someone else's castle online, yep, that's there as well. It's cool how they added several ways to enjoy the game, even if they are all centered around more or less the same concept.
- Stability and performance have been excellent for me. I've not had any crashes, freezes or bugs that I know. It's refreshing to see a game released and not be bombing and the company knowing it when they shipped it.
Cons for me, after 60+ hours...
- Animations > responsive play. While most all the animations your little fellow with do are cool looking, it becomes very frustrating after a while because you're wanting to go left and the animation for whatever you were doing is still playing through. Batman and that franchise suffered somewhat from this as well. I'm used to games where the animation either stops or flows more immediately into what you're wanting to do. I appeciate they wanted to show off all this, although at times, I feel like I'm playing a micro version of Dragon's Lair, back from the 80's, where you interacted with a story.
- Keyboard key overload - argh! Depending on what you're looking at, standing next to or maybe even the time of day (well, maybe not), the same key does a multitude of different things. Want to mind meld with that Orc, press E. Want to drop off that ledge and just hang, press E. Want to jump all the way off the ledge, hold E. The game, along with the animations, can be extremely frustrating because you hit a key in the heat of battle, start that cursed animation and can't stop immediately. When you have a fight with multiple captains and their minions, space bar might slide under big guys to avoid their power bit. Other times, against the same guy, space bar tries to jump over top of them. Or, if you get it to work when you want, space bar may lunge to the side to avoid an attack. It does make for some funny uh-oh moments. More than once, I'm standing on a ledge and wanting to jump down (remember that E key) and someone is below me, so pressing E instead has me jump off and try to dominate them. Fun times...
- Game gets a little repetitive after a while. I'm close to level 50 and not sure I have it in me to grind out to max level and then the grinding needed after that. At first, the variations in quests were cool. After a while, they are all doing something similar and along with the animation/keyboard issues, it's a little boring and frustrating, which is not a great combination.
- Price... So I got the game for free with a video card and if that hadn't happened, I would have waited for a GotY edition or something. I eagerly awaited the release of the game from when I first heard about it. Then I say how silly they went with the price. Seriously, $100 to get the game and a few extras? This whole DLC/season pack/whatever has just gone crazy. I personally don't purchase any game when it releases anymore. I wait for it to go on a big sale and still enjoy the same game some other person spent double the money on. While I may eventually purchase the DLC (when it's available), it'll be at a 50% or more sale before I do so. I can't imagine I'd get $40 worth of enjoyment out of DLC for a $60 game.
- I've been more or less pleased with not needing to get into the microtransaction ordeal, although I'm listing this as a negative. Read online and you'll find the real way to speed up your leveling is with boosters. I'm not sure what the point of these games is supposed to be. You buy a game to enjoy it, not speed run your way to max level in 5 hours and declare victory. At least that isn't my take on why I play video games. I don't like how some companies are trending on having you spend real $$ to get things. As if the $100 for full content isn't bad enough, here, take some more $$ so I can hopefully get a better orc for my little imaginary fortress. Vote with your wallet people.
I'm glad I've tried the game. I got my money's worth (considering I didn't specially pay anything for it) and I'm certainly glad I didn't pay full price for it. I would definitely buy this game on sale. It is fun for a while, although it became a grind before the end for me.

Alan Wake is an incredible mix of Twin Peaks, Silent Hill, and Stephen King (the Mist was the one I was thinking of while playing). I am not a hardcore survival horror fan, so when one comes along that garners hype, I'm always a bit reluctant and skeptical. With that being said, I really enjoyed The Last of Us, and this is up there with that.
This game strikes gets the perfect mix of making you feel vulnerable, and yet capable to deal with situations and the horrors that come your way. Movement and combat have the same philosophy. You can move fairly fluidly, but you're not Rambo (you're an alcholic writer after all). This means that you have to choose your battles wisely. Some baddies you have to face head-on, while others it's better to run in order to live to see another day.
As for the story, well, it's one of those dream-within-a-dream, what-the-hell-is-real kind of affairs. It can be cliche' and tropey at times, but overall the story keeps you interested to unravel the mystery (real, perceived, or both). The game's story keeps the tension building and gives you just enough answers to propell you into the next act. I couldn't put this one down. Beat the game is ~11 hours or 2-3 sittings. I had to know what was going on in Bright Falls.
Now that this is off of Steam due to problems renewing some of the game's song licenses, I don't know where you get this, but if you happen upon it, I say it's worth it. Truly a gem of the survival horror genre.

I recommend this game primarily for character action fans who don't mind something cheaper and with more of a novice's touch than they're used to. Certainly do not go into this game expecting Devil May Cry or Bayoneta.
The graphics are not outstanding, but they're servicable and a lot better than I'd expect from most Indie developers working with 3D.
The combat arenas are not very diverse, in that they're all the same, a giant circle with a number of different background locations to add a feeling of progress, but in a way that helps the game. You'll never find yourself fighting with bad level design, and the format of a pure circle is perfect for what the game is all about, pure unadulterated combat.
The AI of the game has a mild Platinum touch, specifically that enemies will not attack you if they are not onscreen, a trademark of Character Action games from the Japanese developers Platinum Games.
Otherwise AI has a problem in that all enemies follow the same movement pattern, that is they walk towards you in as straight a line as possible, then start to circle you once they reach a certain proximity. This leads to a problem where if you run away for enough time, all the enemies bunch up into one big clump, which is a problem as you are either looking at all the enemies, or none of them, making you either in for a real pounding from every enemy or completely safe.
Enemies have plenty of variety, starting off with basic faceless soldiers, then getting two Elite variants, then the introduction of more enemies that also get more complex and tough Elite variants. This leads to there being plenty combinations of enemies to keep combat interesting, you won't find yourself fighting the same encounter over and over.
The game is entirely devoid of a soundtrack, which does ruin the atmosphere a little, but perhaps no OST is better than a really bad one as is common with Indie Games.
The story is barebones and merely there to facilitate the existence of combat.
The game is very short, I have clocked in about 2.3 hours as of writing this, and I believe myself to be struggling with the last boss of the game. Though I am at the end of the story, the existence of an upgrade path, and I believe a New Game Plus type feature, in addition to the game's difficulty and pure focus on combat gives it a decent amount of replayablity.
Regarding difficulty, I have played the game on both Easy and Normal difficulty, I've found the game pretty challenging and enjoyable without being too frustrating, even on Easy difficulty. Bosses are somewhat reminiscent of Dark Souls, they feature large swings, and a somewhat difficult to predict movesets. Will the boss swing once and leave themselves open for a punish? Or will me attempting to punsih their swing cause me to eat a second swing? These are the kind of things you'll have to cope with if choose to play this game.
On the whole I definately recommend this game for action fans, so long as they're fine with playing something with little to no budget and an indie team behind it.

When I first laid my eyes on Type:Rider, it was for my job: I was reading an article about a new serious game on the typography history made for Arte, who is a cultural TV channel. It was first sold for Android and iOS but you had the possibility to try the first five levels online, which I did.
I fell in love with the game. I was considering buying it for my Android device when it was released on Steam. My reaction was "Take my money". I bought it. And I managed to get through the rest of the game.
Let me explain you the mechanics of the game: you're two dots travelling through levels concerning a font and its history. You have to gather all letters and & without forgetting the * representing a page of history. Indeed, as it's labeled first as a serious game, Type:Rider's aim is to "educate" you in that field. For example, you'll learn stuff about the monks who were copying documents during the Middle Age in the world Gothic.
Type:Rider is more a platformer/puzzle game than anything else. You jump, you make sure that the white dot appearing every two levels goes in its hole to open gates or finish the book (representing the world you're currently in).
First of all, the graphics are beautiful and adapted to the world you're currently exploring: the world Gothic contains gothic letters as "ground". Or the Ancient Greek part of the world Origins has a ancient plate background (the archaeologist in me is very happy to see Red Figure pottery used) from which water is coming.
Secondly, the soundtrack is very enjoyable to listen and very relaxing. It's also matching the world you're exploring. Even the two dots have their own sound when they're jumping.
I didn't really find some defaults in the mechanics. While it's true that sometimes, commands take more time than it should to answer, it's very rare. My major grief about the game is some letters or & difficult to reach and making my fingers ache as I'm trying to reach them by jumping and jumping and jumping.
For the texts, they're very well written and very understandable, at least, in my native language - I don't know how it was translated in English.
My conclusion is that the game is worthy of your time if you like that kind. You can try it before on the official website of Arte. But if you can, the mobile versions are cheaper than Steam (and I suppose that there is a valid reason behind that difference - Monster Loves You, another game, is showing the same pattern).

Definitely crosses over the "so bad it's good" threshold; a shame the storyline isn't more cohesive and the campaign a few hours lengthier because the actual shooting is some of the best out there and the game just oozes its own unique style. I also applaud the developers for having the integrity to set the game in Shanghai when so many other mediums these days are too afraid of offending that commercial market, and end up caving to the overly-demonized North Korea (Homefront, Red Dawn, Interstellar). You will literally gun down hundreds of Chinese cops, SWAT, army, and gangsters, not to mention a slew of accidental civilian casualties as this pair of dysfunctional, out-of-shape psychopaths shoot their way out of every conceivable situation. Many will find extreme discomfort in the hand-held camera style, distorted graphical effects and surreal soundtrack, but I like the way the art design gives the impression of an endless, feverish nightmare. Definitely not for everyone; fans of Michael Mann's filmography will feel right at home.

If there is ever a game you had to play, it's this one. Games like these are rare, far and few inbetween. It treats you like an adult, and doesn't hold your hand. The story is believeable and plausible. With it's rich story comes some of the hardest decisions I have ever had to make in a video game, plus it really rubs it in when most of these hard choices have a timer behind them so you can't really sit there and think about what you're doing. Very much how it is in real life.
Oh, and the combat? Get ready to fight for real. The games combat system is some of the most unique I had seen and experienced. Like in real life ( I know I keep saying this but bare with me ), you don't charge headlong into battle like a mindless oaf. You prepare, you asses and you judge the situation. Much of that will happen during combat and before combat in this game. Preparation is paramount, and using your Witcher signs to the fullest is as well. Because you won't be able to pause during combat and equip an oinment for your blade or drink a point. You have to do this beforehand. That is, if you're playing on the easiest difficulty, then combat and it's horrors will be of no consequence. But, in truth, you are robbing yourself of what the Witcher is, if you decide to play it on that difficulty. Trust me, I have finished on both easiest and the normal setting, and they are worlds apart. In terms of combat atleast.
Main protagonist should also be mentioned. You play as Geralt of Rivia. Only THE most badass protagnoist to ever have lived. Trust me on this too when I say this. This man is the epitome of being a man you should not ♥♥♥♥ with. He is a professional monster slayer, augmented and tested, to be the very best at what he does. Also having super human strenght and reflexes help. Though I do have one gripe with it, you never get to see his super human strenght and reflexes in the game. He seems very ordinary in those two terms. I never really felt SUPER powerful, just skillful and really smart. Besides, I doubt even if I did see it , my opinion of him wouldn't change.
To wrap it up. This might be the most fulfilling RPGs I have ever played, until of course Witcher 3 comes out, and all who love the genre are doing a GREAT AND GRAVE injustice by not playing it.
P.S. If you're worried you will miss most of the story by not playing the first one, don't worry, the game gives you a short and sweet  " previously on the Witcher ". Although not shedding the light on most of what happened, I found myself rather ok with not playing the first one.

Not as good as Wasteland 1 and not the spiritual Fallout 3 that many Fallout fans wanted, but it's a good role-playing game. In hindsight, as backers, we shouldn't have expected inXile to deliver an amazing game; inXile hadn't developed an RPG since the Interplay days more than a decade ago.
inXile learned a lot developing this game though. Signs of ambition are all over the game, with tons of reactivity from the start. But as the game progresses, you notice that many things seem to scale back in quality. There is less reactivity, and eventually the random radio chatter stops. This is more noticeable in California with the ranger HQ and the big cities. Santa Fe Springs has a relatively large map but it's never used. Hollywood in particular promises greatness if only inXile had more money and thus time. Quests can be tackled largely out of order with plenty of dialogue options to form alliances fake or real, but it's ruined by bugs or even perceived bugginess. It's definitely rough.
We already know Wasteland 3 will not try to be a 100 hour game, and is instead aiming for something along the lines of Torment: Tides of Numenera which is supposedly around 40 or 50 hours. Considering the original Fallouts and Wasteland were only around 20 hours each and how unpolished the later areas of Wasteland 2 were, I think this is a good idea.

To be put simply, it doesn't patronize the player, and it doesn't coddle their emotions.  This an RPG for adults who have seen the pro's and con's of this world and realize what it is, not teenagers who are trying to escape the notion of growing up and who overestimate their importance in the world.  It's not happy, it's not melodramatic, it's not moody, it is a fleshed out world with facts and tragedies all born out of the very nature of it's existence.  So to be put simply, it is a simply amazing story.  The tight action controls and easy to learn, difficult to master fighting are also a huge bonus.  As we all know, an amazing story on a game that's not fun to play doesn't mean much, but this is the whole package.  Add in the fact that CD Projekt RED have much more integrity than most modern development houses and this is a no brainer purchase.  Buy this game and enjoy it, and at the same time you're supporting future integrity in game development.

(NOTE: This review was done in the singleplayer experience - NOT COOP (However hopefully this review will stop you from wanting to even play this game with a friend))
This game............ sucks. It's bad. Like really bad. If you don't want to read my entire review, here is a summary:
This game is exactly the same as those hundreds of terrible greenlight horror games on Steam. It is not unique, it is boring and it is garbage. It's like a kid's first attempt at making a game, and it is laughable that the devs are actually charging $9 for this crap. When I've seen Happy Meal toys offer a more fulfilling experience.
If you want me to list out all the terrible things in this game. Here is a few:
1. The monsters. This is a joke. Remember how I said how un-unique this game is? Well, the enemies in this game are the most cliched and pathetic excuses for horror enemies I've ever seen. The game offers a huge selection of TWO enemy types. A mannequin (never seen that before: Silent Hill, Kraven Manor ) which you need to look at for it not to kill you (100% original. Not just like: The Weeping Angles or SCP-173). And the second enemy type is one that won't see you if you have your flashlight off (Which is like nearly EVERY HORROR GAME EVER). However, the game didn't even do that part right. At least in most horror games like Amnesia, you can turn off lights to lower your chance of being found. BUT IN THIS GAME, you can literally go up to the monsters and suck their d*ck, just as long as your light is off. They're completely static and don't even attempt to kill you.
2. It's stupid riddles. You're asked a total of I believe 12 riddles in this game in order to progress. Somewhat like a troll under the bridge sorta thing. However, this is honestly one of the laziest excuses at a bloody 'puzzle' I've ever seen. All the riddles you are asked, have NOTHING to do with the story. They offer NO explanation in the story, they offer NO personality of our characters, they have NOTHING to do with the game at all (other than to try to pad out your game time so you cannot refund the game). And the worse thing? They're all unoriginal. All the riddles in this game were completely ripped from online. The creators of this game didn't even TRY to create their own original riddles. They instead chose to steal them instead because their brains were rotted from Year 3's math homework.
3. The game is ugly. Visually it's gross. The game is too bloody dark so if your light is off you have no idea where you are going. The game looks like a collection of free-to-download assets all plunked down on a level editor. And the game uses so many stock-font choices it looks like the game was written using Microsoft Word 2007.
4. The story is non-existant. NOTHING, in the game, is explained. Nothing is resolved, nothing is revealed, nothing happens. What happened to that couple? NEVER FOUND OUT. Why are their monsters? NOT EXPLAINED. Whats with all the bodybags? NEVER ANSWERED. I'm fine with games leaving things open for interpretation. But there's a difference between leaving things ambiguous for analysis, and being too lazy to answer things yourselves.
5. The game is pathetic. This is how I feel about the game the most. It's pathetic. It's got pathetic graphics, it's got pathetic programming, it's got a pathetic story, the list goes on. The devs did not try. This feels like college students first attempt at making a game. WHICH IS FINE. But don't bloody dare to charge babies first game for $9. Which ironically is higher then the production budget of the game itself. If this game was free on Indie GoGo - sure. That would be fine. But the fact that this game made it on the Steam Page, really says a lot about greenlight.
I could rag on the terrible things in this game for dozens of more hours. Such as how slow your character moves, the fact that enemies can literally be placed behind a corner so you have no idea there is one up ahead and you die, the terrible overworld which offers like 5 locations, the lack of music or overall ambiance. But, that would be putting in more effort than the devs did to this entire game.
This game is a joke. For all those horror nutters looking for that hidden unique indie horror game like myself, move along. You've played this game before.
And to the devs, listen, I don't want to discourage you making games. In-fact, I want to encourage you to better yourself from this experience. Just please, try something new, try to increase your level of quality. I've got faith in you guys and I hope you can better yourselves.
Unfortunately, this game is bad and if you somehow couldn't guess it, I strongly DO NOT recommend this game. 'Stay FAR' away from this game.

is a 7 person turn based CRPG set in the fictionalized post apocalyptic world of the western border of the United States. Namely Arizona and the Los Angeles region.
The setup has you create a 4 person party using either pre-made characters or custom ones that you assign attributes and skill points to yourself. 3 additional NPC party members may be recruited through  throughout the game. I personally found nine. Though, through some reading I did after I finished there are some I never even encountered. This is one of my chief complaints, I fully understand why NPC's can't make up the whole party as there are numerous narrative reasons but I don't understand why you are not allowed a full 7 person custom party. It provides no advantage other than balancing skills throughout each person. Rather than forcing reliance on NPC party members for skills not attained or have high enough proficiency.
This game isn't the most friendly upfront, I say this to bring attention to the fact that the character creation has no direct classes and has tutorial missions up to 3-5 hours in that if not careful can result in full party wipes or at least the early loss of characters. Perma-death is a very real concern but with a nominal understanding of the games mechanics, (for instance the difference between field medics and surgeons) perma-death is rather forgiving. I, admittedly after restarting twice a few hours in, finally got a grasp of what was happening and didn't have anyone die my entire playthough. However, I had a number of very close calls.
Attribute points are assigned at the beginning of the game and only change very minimally throughout the entire playthrough. They, in essence are what makes the character more suited for certain skills. Skill points are what to pay attention to here as they are the ones that change the most from gaining XP and leveling. They're what you'll be directly using in game. It's not directly understood immediately but it allows for far more customization in your party. From shotgun wielding surgeons to charismatic snipers good at computer science, the game even allows for a space to write a custom bio for each character and use a custom portrait so long as it's 256x256 pixels.
, you wanted to. Additionally the game after completion exports these characters as “veterans” for use in other playthroughs.
I've heard a number of complaints that the world map random encounters can become rather monotonous in tedium. However, there is a very easy and lore friendly way around that aspect. The outdoorsman skill is your friend. Use it.
The game has a ton of optional side quests that really fill out the world and definitely affect the ending. That being said, I found the the main line end game a little lackluster, I didn't find myself caring about a large portion of the characters near the end game. It felt a little cliché and uninspired. Which is a little disappointing given the rest of the games content.

"Ashes to ashes...and dust to dust."
Expertly and exquisitely crafted over the course of years in the mind of animation artist Dean Dodrill, Dust: An Elysian Tail is a 2D Metroidvania action-RPG that does just about everything right - and impressively at that. The amnesiac Dust and his irresistibly cute buddy Fidget trek across landscapes of forest, flame, shadow, and snow, combining and unleashing Dust's unparalleled swordplay skills with Fidget's dynamic magical projectiles in a furious typhoon of combat against a range of foes and obstacles - all part of a journey seeking answers to salient questions: who is Dust, really? - and is there still a time and a place for a hero to save the world?
Each region traversed throughout Dust's 12-to-20-hour journey offers both platforming challenges to be navigated and mobs of monsters to be obliterated. Dust controls quite tightly, and all of his (and Fidget's) commands can be remapped as desired. Virtually all of the scenery in the world of Dust: AET is a rich delight, owing to its lush construction and ace visual design and demonstrating how gorgeous and appealing two-dimensional media can become. Also of note is the game's masterful soundtrack. Urgent strings, delicate pianos, and ambient synth pads are but a few of the pleasing instruments wonderfully woven into memorable melodies and soundscapes by Hyperduck Soundworks, working smoothly alongside Alexander Brandon (of Deus Ex fame). Rewarding side quests and imposing challenge arenas stand ready to be completed; fun cameos (by other indepedent game characters) and dozens of shout-outs to gaming and animation supply much-welcome joy between moments of surprisingly poignant sorrow. The game's cast is interesting, well-written, and voiced competently; consequent empathy with the hopeful villagers instills a resolve to aid their plight and answer their prayers. Each of the game's facets was created prudently and smartly - that it is an absolute blast to play seals the deal.
All in all, Dust: AET is one of the most rewarding games I've played in a while. It is, to its end, stellar. Congratulations, Dean: you *nailed* this one.

Fans of 2D platformer RPGs will find this game scratching itches they'd forgotten they had.
Storyline is just a touch generic (Isn't it always?), but it's told in a beautifully animated world by flavoursome and wonderfully voice acted characters, featuring plenty of humour along the way. Then the serious moments only seem all the more well done when you take a step back and realise how light-hearted and silly so much of what surrounds them can be.
Combat and items don't shine nearly as much, yet they're both robust enough to get the job done without feeling too mindlessly repetitive. Especially with the multitude of secret items and areas to come back for when you unlock your next key ability, which alleviate most of the grindy feel of the inevitable bits of backtracking.
Like most modern games, the length is nothing on the classics of old. But the price reflects that. So even though it won't last you as long as you'd hoped, fans of the genre should find it well worth the money.

However, this game suffers from 2 critical flaw.
1) THERE IS NO TARGETING/LOCKON SYSTEM. well actually there is one but it's only for the bosses.
2) TOO MUCH POSING.
Well now, let me explain how these 2 flaws will actually affect gameplay.
Without a targeting system, basically whichever direction you face is where your attacks will hit. This flaw does not affect your gameplay in Easy, Normal or Hard. I mean the waves after waves of enemies don't consecutively have a go at you non-stop. You could always adjust your camera direction to have your enemies in view. Well at least you have the time. BUT once you reach Very Hard or Inferno, that's when adjusting camera angle to keep your enemies in view becomes a ♥♥♥♥♥. Besides dashing around continously to avoid getting hit by the non-stop attacks of your enemies, you must adjust Misa's direction just to actually hit enemies. And take note, the time frame you have to adjust is about a split second, which you must at the same time release a combo of attacks before dashing off again.
As for the posing flaw, well I wouldn't call it a flaw. More like she poses too much after some giant combo attack. The developers probably thought, "Hey why not add in some cool poses whenever she does a combo attack so that she looks cool and all". The posing as usual doesn't affect gameplay much in easy, normal and hard. Unless you suck and mess up the combo attacks timing and leave yourself open to attacks since Misa can't actually move while posing. So how does this affect Very Hard? Well couple in together with the lack of a targeting system, having to manually target waves of enemies in a split second, your bound to not get them all during 1 of your big combo attacks. Which in turns come to you getting attack the next instant while your posing.
So unless there's some sort of update with at least a targeting/lockon system, I wouldn't recommend getting this game at it's original price. But if it's at a discounted price and you have the spare cash, then yea, why not.

The first hours have probably been the weakest part of that experience - you´ll automatically compare it to Mafia II and you´ll be missing some features. Only after having played the first chapters, you´ll see the missing features added in form of perks that you´ll unlock by advancing in the story.
As soon as you feel at home in the story and the city, you´ll be having a great time. The story-telling is well made and after some hours you might look forward to meet this or that character again (if they produce Mafia IV without Donovan, I´ll get a refund for the game ^^).
After 10 hrs you´ve got more weapons, more vehicles, more different missions and a bigger and more attractive map than in Mafia II. With the delivery system (weapons, cars and cash-deposit) and other clever new features they provide you with some nice extras. The only thing that´s not in yet: no change of clothes :O

But I am to lazy to figure out what the others have to complain about. Anyway: I´ve had plenty of fun with a game that´s got bad critics. It´s not the first time for me and still I´ve got funny feelings buying something lots of people don´t like. For those of you in that position: If you liked Mafia II and like music from the 60s, you´d better get this game (or wait for a sale).

Imagine this: you're a famous writer suffering from writer's block. Your wife brings you on a trip to relax, but it turns out she's trying to 'force' you into writing again. The two of you fight and you storm off. As you're leaving, you're wife gets pulled away by some dark force, and as you try to rescue her, everything goes black. All of a sudden, you wake up in the wreckage of your car, it's a week later and your novel has written itself...
The intro does an amazing job at pulling you into the game, When I first got this game 5 years ago I thought the graphics where the sh*t, but nowadays they're pretty so-so. That does not hinder the fact that the game itself provides an amazing psychological and paranormal mystery where you as the player is just as clueless about what is going on as the main character is.
If you are not used to the fps/over-the-shoulder view this game operates with, it can be pretty hard. Though, if you are used to fps or quick aiming in general, this game will provide sufficient difficulty without being too hard or too easy. For the love of God, this is one of the best games you will ever play!

One of THE worst games I have ever played in my life. What even is this?
This game is comprised of well, nothing. It's a 3 hour long game that's just a cover based shooter that is it. You go from room to room hiding behind anything you can in order to stay safe. You don't even need to come out of your cover because you can just fire around corners or over it with perfect accuracy.
There's also numerous problems with this game, there's around 10 weapons which range from useless or overpowered. However you do literally need to be on top of your enemy to actually land a hit as IO Interactive decided that all guns are accurate to about the length of a 15cm ruler. They tried an attempt at a 'real life' run mechanic whereby the screen shakes all over the place like a 10 on the ricther scale is going down, adding super DOF with large amounts of light effects and motion blur. Another brain fart mechanic was the jumping over obstacles nonsense where you have to crouch and take cover behind the obstacle you want to climb then wait for the jump prompt to appear. Really? Game assets are constantly reused, one car park level everyone had the same BMW in the same colour. Welcome to the lives of Kane and Lynch. One man is a psychopath who just loves the thrill of crime, the other a psychopath who blacks out in fits of murderous rampages when his medication wears off basically. The unlikely duo have one last deal to do in Shanghai before they stop their crime ridden lives to live in normalcy...of course this deal goes horribly wrong when a government official who is involved with the mob daughter gets shot by Lynch on accident and dies.
The games story is very much a crime drama, and if you're into that the story alone is more than enough to keep you hooked through the four hour campaign. Yes, the campaign is THAT short, though this isn't that bad of a thing. I feel like if the game were any longer it would have wore out its welcome. I say this because the gameplay is your standard third person shooter.
You take cover on walls, you can pick up weapons and ammo dropped by dead bodies, and when you get knocked down before death you get one more shot to get back up before you're down for the count. This is all fun and well even with the linear progression, but taking out one horde of cops, thugs, and scumbags after another does become slightly repetitive.
The game is more style over substance than anything with how the camera is. The camera works like a camera man is following you through the campaign filming every little thing with a grainy, somewhat low res camera. Kane and Lynch 2 does this very well, and it goes with the gritty graphics, story, and violence perfectly, though it can sometimes be a strain on the eyes.
Overall I recommend the game. If you like violent crime drama films you'll feel right at home with this game. If you're against a ton of blood and dead bodies all over the place...Well, you should probably stay far away from Kane and Lynch.

Main quest is takes too long. My full playthrough took over 100 hours and most of the time was spent on the main quest. While lengthy playtime is a good thing, having a lengthy main quest makes the game feel like a chore towards end. The game should have structured such that main quest only took 40 hours, while bulk of the goodies are in side quests.
RNG is broken. I was unable to open a 11% lock after over 100 tries. I am a math major. Statically, that's less than 0.0001%, while the game reports 11%. This could be a UI bug or RNG bug. If you read the forums, people report similar issue with weaponsmithing too, however I am not a big weaponsmither.
Non-combat progression feels unrewarding. Most of them end up feel like treadmills. While at the end of the game, maxed out combat skills make your characters feel godlike in battle (at least in normal difficulties), same cannot be sad about non-combat skills. The game would simply present obstacles (locks, walls, traps, etc) that has local success chance for even maxed out non-combat skills.
The worst non-combat skill is demolition. Instead of making max level demolition useful, the game would simply present you with 100 mines scattered on the path in front you. With 100 mines, it is simpler to pretend demolition skill never existed, as it is easier to just trigger them and heal with first-aid.
Quest item weights too much. Some of the later game quest items weighs 8 pounds each, and you need 7-8 of them. This either forces the player to maul all of them at once while encumbered, or forces the player to shuttle a portion of it just so they can loot other stuff.
Also since you cannot discard quest items, for quests with multiple solutions, quest items for path not taken would simply become hog in your storage.

Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae plays like a very simplified Dynasty Warriors where the main focus is just beating enemies up.  Using your sword skills, you fight rounds of enemies in an arena styled environment until you reach the boss of the level.  Repeat this again for more levels and that basically sums up the game.  There's a story but it's very simple and barely the focus of the game.  But the point of hack and slash games don't have to lie in story, it's in the combat although having a nice story is always a treat.
You start off with a very simple sword skillset and as you defeat more enemies you can unlock more skills or make your existing skills stronger.  Unfortunately the enemies aren't very varied, with many just being variations of the same types with more health and more damage with one or two new moves along with a different colored model.  This means that hitting enemies can start feeling like a chore as they become tankier and aren't as visually exciting.  The actual fun part of the swordplay lies in the counter system where perfectly timed counters deal massive damage to the enemies.  Because of the small window available for performing the counter, the first attempts will most likely end up in failure but once done correctly, it's immensely satisfying.  Even after finishing the game, I still find it fairly difficult to do.
Overall I would recommend this game with the caveat that you should like hack and slash games a lot and will find it more fun if you perform counters correctly.  Otherwise if you're looking for a Dynasty Warriors game, you won't find it in this.  Hopefully if the developers makes another game in the series, they'll expand the weapon types and the variety of enemies as well as create a larger, more interesting environment to fight in.
