Let's make this an honest review, alright?  I will not crack stupid jokes about waifus and pantyshots, and you, dear reader, will take this review not as my scores states, but by taking into account what I said here.
You see, this is not really a bad game. Its problem lies in the fact for WHO this game is. This game is, what I call, a "You Tube watching" game. The game is very short. A competent player can beat Normal Mode in around an hour or two at best. The enemies are not especially bright in how they fight and most of them can be beaten with one move -> Iai Slash. Once you get this to lvl 3 you can just hold the shoulder button and whack everything with Y. It defeats everything. Some bosses are cheap, but that is until you learn that every attack be Just Guarded. Pretty much till you get to the last Boss, you can dodge all boss attacks. At the last boss, you just Just Guard everything she does.
THAT SAID HOWEVER
This game is pretty good for zoning out. Like, you are watching a You Tube video with a lot of talking and not much going on the screen. Its as if you are playing an MMO, just for people that like Hack and Slash games. The game however is VERY SHORT. Seriously, not much content on. Like an Arcade game. You beat the game and leave it. Beat it again and so on. Like a NES title of the old times.
Can I recommend the game? No, I cannot. I got it personally because I like to fight something while watching long game reviews or when I listen to long talks on YouTube and such. I view a lot of movies that are mainly 30 minutes of someone talking and not showing anything on the screen. And this game, when set to easy, is perfect for this task.
I bought it for 2,50 on a sale. It is not a bad game, just incredibly short and for a niche audience. Requires not much skill nor effort to play. Ideal if this is what you are looking for.
Aside from all this -> During the one playthrough I made I encountered no bugs at all. ...well except for two annoyances, but these are not bugs. The camera will sometimes spaz if during a boss fight you dodge towards the enemy and hit their model, as if trying to pass throught them. Also, if you die and go to Upgrade menu - the game does not stop there. The enemy boss, even after beating you, will continue their assault despite the fact your character is dead and cannot be hit.
Consider this buy if you are looking for an easy, short game. Its fun to slash people. The moves look great and you feel powerful. But that is all.

I've had my heart broken several times in my life. Once, on Christmas Day 1989, I eagerly ran downstairs and gasped at the sight of what was clearly a crudely but lovingly wrapped skateboard. A skateboard that I had wanted ever since I had seen Marty McFly cruise through the streets of Hill Valley as a stowaway behind an unsuspecting SUV driver. A skateboard with a custom deck, with artwork that would cause my fellow skaters to shout "rad". A skateboard whose wheels would send me gliding across the streets as I headed for the nearest half-pipe. A skateboard of majestical proportion.
I grabbed it, and with shaking hands and a heart beating against my chest, I tore that festive wrapping as hard as I could. Through an intricate web of sticky tape, ribbon and ever expanding wrapping paper, I dug through. Years later, I wondered that this is what Andy in The Shawshank Rdemption must have felt like as he dragged hinself through the tunnels. My own redemption was in sight. My prize was near. Finally, the last shred of packaging fell away to the floor. And there it was... a plastic skateboard from the local store. With stiff plastic wheels. And a picture of a clown on the deck.
That's what playing ORION: Dino Horde felt like.

Once again I’m thrust into the world of making arms for money. Wait, what did I say again? Ignore that part. But here you are, making arms for the Motherland. It’s a simple premise of test and build and sell to expand and reset to be able to build better and faster… for funzies! Most of the time those types of games don’t interest me much at all. I’ve played a few games based on resetting to get a bonus and they just leave me with a bad taste. March of Industry is a great example of how to make that formula fun.
You’ll start out with simple, basic materials and will need to work your way up to the more advanced ingredients and weaponry as you progress through the ages. The ages thing does feel a bit tacked on, but I get what they were going for. It’s just so easy to work through the “ages” that it feels more like a “prove you can work with this” test to gain access to better materials. Would that have been better? I’m not completely sure, but I appreciate what they were going for. The interesting part of all of this is that you’re never given any specific blueprints. That means you’ll need to figure out which ingredients make which parts or weapons and then sell or make them into more complex parts or weapons. Maybe for some players the ages will take ages to get through, but I would like to give the players the benefit of the doubt.
You’ll probably get through the ages rather quickly if you’re going to sit down and plow through March of Industry like I mentioned. If you turn it on for only a few minutes at a time, it will be a different story. The longevity of this game looks to be in the achievements and mods. There are mods for new parts and weapons that you’ll have to figure out how to build as well as figure out if they are more cost efficient to build as opposed to other weapons that you already can build. Achievement wise, the two that will take you the longest will be discovering all of the blueprints first and then maximizing the size of your factory. Don’t cheat to find out what the correct blueprints are, that kills the point of this whole game. Test and see. After all, “Discovery requires experimentation.”
These achievements are going to be tackled together for my play-through. It only makes sense due to the abnormal amount of money that is required to maximize your factory’s size. I plan on building my money machines and then just experimenting on the side. What’s a money machine? Well, when you figure out what’s the cheapest to build and sells for the most, you can usually buy the 100 packs of the materials and have a series of conveyors taking those parts into machines that will combine them and then send the end product into an auto-selling crate. All very clean and proper. So I just have to make sure they have the supplies they need and then I can experiment on the side while the money flows in and out of my coffers. If only I could figure out how to auto-purchase ingredients… I’m sure it’s possible…
Score: Gewd/Tasty
While it may not do much, it does what it does well. I am enjoying the puzzle of figuring out all of the different combinations in March of Industry. I’m not sure why I’m finding this so fun… but I am and I’ll take it. It’s all about fun here on The Backlog and March of Industry delivers for me. Will it forever change your mind about a genre, probably not, but if you can catch a good sale and you like this type/style of game, you should pick it up because I’m guessing you’ll enjoy it.

Kane & Lynch 2 is another example of why the outside public believe gaming is aimed at an adolescent audience of monosyllabic thingy somethings.
The main focus of the game, being the story campaign, boils down to a 2.5-3 hour endurance of the two antagonists (Kane & Lynch if  you've forgotten already) cursing at one another, cursing at the triad, cursing at the police, cursing at the army and cursing at anyone else they feel like cursing at.
The actual gameplay is a rather rudimentary objective consisting of trying to shoot and trying to hide, "trying" is what you'll be doing, as the overrall mechanics just work, if they were more polished, the game would be much shorter and easier to play than figuring out which side to aim from or which gun shoots better.
Not only is it not a particulary interesting game of hide and go shoot, but it tries so very hard to be mature by gratuitously showing 80s style video nasty sequences, in its approuch to appeal to an audience who think acting in such a manner would be considered edgy; by saying some rude words and shooting lots of people.
An interesting side note would be the digital mosiacing of graphic scenes of violence, that for some reason is deemed to be too mature and gritty. Kinda of a dichotomy to the overall nature of the game.
The only few possitive things, one being the lead voice talent for Kane (Brian Bloom) and Lynch (Jarion Monroe ). The other being its unique approach to its visual asthetics, simulating digital video noise and video grime, bringing with it a documentarian style cinematography during its cut scenes which may be nauseating at times. But the immersive effect is often broken by the overall graphics looking poor and AI enemies missing key frames of animation when they move.
As a cultural artifact Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days is not something to be held with high regard.

This game could have been much better.
First of all, let me highlight positive sides of the game (potential spoiler here). It has intensity and is pretty atmospheric. You are not playing as some badass heroes fighting for just cause. Kane and Lynch were complete bаstards in the first game, and they remain being themselves in this sequel. And even those attempts of Lynch to save his girlfriend don't change fact: he and Kane lack pretty much every good moral side that any normal person has. This makes you feel the originality of the game, as it clearly doesn't have modern popular action game cliches.
But still, I can hardly recommend this game to anyone. I could barely follow the plot of the game, as it is unclear. Most of the time you are simply forced to survive in unending street gang and police gunfire. Graphically the game did not evolve even the slightest bit since "Dead Men", although there are solid 3 years between the releases of "Dead Men" and "Dog Days"; all they did is that swaying and shaking camera, as if an amateur cameraman follows every step of those two, shooting all the action on his mobile phone (it can be disabled in the options at least). Character control is rough, it lacks smoothness; try running around in co-op with your friend and you'll see. Cover system isn't great as well: you may get shot just because you hit "cover" at the wrong side of the cover itself, which leaves you exposed to enemy fire, and it takes some time to jump over to the other side. Leaving cover may not be always convenient, as the "cover" button has multiple functions depending on the nearest environment. AI is not smart at all, especially when in cover; you can simply run to the other side and shoot the crap out of your enemy while he won't be able to do anything about it, although this can be dangerous in the end, because there are usually lots of them; so, quantity over quality.
And yeah, the game is too short. I mean, you are able to complete the singleplayer within, literally, 3 hours. Same is about the co-op.
The game had potential, it just needed a lot more polishing. But alas.
It may be worth a shot when on a discount, though.

I'll keep this short, the game is a free to play, so it has what most free to plays have, in-app purchases (microstransactions),  energy (what most f2p games have to limit progression so that you keep returning).
however it also has a premium version too, aka club access/membership, this is bought through an in-app purchase of the Unlimited Club Access (which is a once off payment, permanantly offering access to the premium content that is otherwise only accessible [if at all] once every 24 hours).
Then there's a battery recharge in-app purchase which makes the energy regenerate 3x faster... making this f2p game act more like a proper pay to play game, what makes it different to many other f2p since usually f2p's don't include such an option.
The progression isn't stupid long, yes energy depletes fast and doesn't regenerate too quickly, but the towers you buy aren't too expensive, and after a week of playing you'll have some of the basics sussed, some f2p make the typical grind very exhausting and difficult, but this game isn't that bad, thankfully.
If you're someone who doesn't like paying for stuff in f2p games simply because you know that they charge way too much for what you get and would be more willing to pay if the game acted more like a regular pay to play title... then this game in my opinion has the best of both worlds.
I still think the membership cost and battery recharge is a bit expensive but then again, $16 something NZD or $7.49 each, isn't that much in comparison to the fun you could have, this is a casual game, great to play with friends, or against loners.
Yes it has it's flaws, but personally I think the games rating should be at least "very positive" not "mostly"... I was expecting it to be "overwhelmingly positive". P.S. There is no pay to win, so while the purchases can help you progress faster through unlocks or having energy, the winner will still be the one who plays better.

Let me start off by saying that this game kicks♥♥♥♥♥ Let nothing I say further along change that. It's got great combat and graphics, a solid, morally ambiguous choice system continuing from the first game, and the story, up until chapter 3, is great. The combat is just hard enough to get you engaged, and the world is filled with interesting characters and little details that add a lot.
It's hard to say whether this game is better or worse than The Witcher 1. It improves on a lot of things. The combat is way better. The graphics are amazing. There are no more recycled character models cropping up at 6 different places in the game. The level-up system makes more sense. The graphics are beautiful. The crafting system is a welcome addition. Oh, and the graphics are AWESOME.
I have two complaints:
1) At least when I played it, it was shorter than The Witcher 1 by about a third. This is due to a combination of a lack of side   quests, and a really short third act that I suspect was cut short due to lack of time or funding.
2)The story just wasn't as awesome as the first game. It's still better than most games, but it just wasn't as remarkable as the first's. This might be just because of the lackluster ending-- lasting impressions are important, and The Witcher 1's stellar ending is one of the things that make its story so great. Here's hoping that the "real" ending of The Witcher 2 turns out to be The Witcher 3.
Bottom line: If you haven't played The Witcher, get it-- the first game. If you have played The Witcher, then The Witcher 2 is ALMOST everything you were looking for in a sequel.

Witcher 2 is an RPG like no other that caters to the most mature and serious players in the genre. With absolutely zero hand holding and possibly the best cinematic storytelling I've ever seen, the game provides an experience like no other. When you play this game, you will never see halos or devil horns telling you whether the decisions you make are "good" or "evil". The game simply presents choices and consequences, so it is ultimately up to the player to decide what path they decide to take, and quite often the the lines between what is right and wrong can become muddled and even downright inconclusive to the player, making for some extremely thought-provoking scenarios and questlines. This is bolstered by the fact that the game has dozens of major choices throughout that, with each, will have a significant impact on the story, making for so many ways to play through the game.
As I mentioned, the game will almost never hold your hand. This means you will not have waypoints all over your screen telling you exactly where to go constantly. Often times, when undertaking quests, you will need to read over your journal or revisit certain characters to obtain information on where to go or what to do next, and use your intuition along the way. This type of approach gives almost the whole game the feeling of a challenge, rather than just a mundane routine. This along with other things can easily put off several people from this game who are looking for a more casual experience, as it is definitely a game for people who like to think and analyze. Possibly the biggest offput for some people may be the tutorial that the game starts off with, as it is quite bad. Getting used to the combat and inventory systems(which is also not the best at times) can be difficult, but if you can overcome that you are in for an amazing experience.

Friends (stylized as F•R•I•E•N•D•S) is an American television sitcom, created by David Crane and Marta Kauffman, which aired on NBC from September 22, 1994, to May 6, 2004, lasting ten seasons. With an ensemble cast starring Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Lisa Kudrow, Matt LeBlanc, Matthew Perry and David Schwimmer, the show revolves around six 20-30 something friends living in Manhattan. The series was produced by Bright/Kauffman/Crane Productions, in association with Warner Bros. Television. The original executive producers were Kevin S. Bright, Marta Kauffman, and David Crane.
Kauffman and Crane began developing Friends under the title Insomnia Cafe between November and December 1993. They presented the idea to Bright, and together they pitched a seven-page treatment of the show to NBC. After several script rewrites and changes, including a title change to Six of One and Friends Like Us, the series was finally named Friends.
Filming took place at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California. All ten seasons of Friends ranked within the top ten of the final television season ratings; ultimately reaching the No. 1 spot with its eighth season. The series finale on May 6, 2004, was watched by around 52.5 million American viewers, making it the fifth most watched series finale in television history, and the most watched television episode of the 2000s decade.
]
Friends received acclaim throughout its run, becoming one of the most popular television shows of all time. The series was nominated for 62 Primetime Emmy Awards, winning the Outstanding Comedy Series award in 2002 for its eighth season. The show ranked no. 21 on TV Guide's 50 Greatest TV Shows of All Time and no. 7 on Empire magazine's The 50 Greatest TV Shows of All Time. In 1997, the episode "The One with the Prom Video" was ranked no. 100 on TV Guide's 100 Greatest Episodes of All-Time. In 2013, Friends ranked no. 24 on the Writers Guild of America's 101 Best Written TV Series of All Time and no. 28 on TV Guide's 60 Best TV Series of All Time.

Just completed this game with about 77% game completion. So this game is a  beat-em-up platoforming game with RPG elements. Similar to YS-III or Castlevania.
The story was okay. It's very hard to take seriously when the game has semi-dark story but cute cuddly furry creatures. Nothing too deep or involved, but what can you really ask of a XBL Arcade game? There are a lot of loose ends and the story feels incomplete.
The platforming in this game is rather spot on any time you I fell into spikes I felt like it was my fault, not the games. I played this game on the Tough difficulty, dropping to Normal when battles were too hard.  I see myself 100% this game very easily. This is a very casual game on Normal difficulty.
This game kept my attention, that's something really important in a sea of unplayed, dust gathering steam backlogs. It was fun and entertaining to play and Fidget is just adorable. Dust is rather forgettable as a protagonist. Think Cloud Strife mixed with Sora from Kingdom Hearts 2.  If you like cute cuddy furry creatures with slightly dark storylines, give this game a go. I wasn't disappointed.
The background music in this game is pretty awesome. I suggest turning sound effects down to 60% so you can enjoy the soundtrack, otherwise it'll be completely overshadowed by the extremely loud sounds from combat.
The game has wonderful backgrounds, the scenery is just cool to look at. The characters and NPCS on the otherhand are rather bland and boring. Whether effects, cool blur, shine and lighting effects too! Though you may not notice when you're racking up 400 hit combos.
The negative... Combat doesn't have much strategy, once you find a combo that works you'll probably keep using it. (Likely just Fidget's Lightning Bolt Spam, a magic attack.) There is crafting but it's stupid easy to craft the best things in the game.
Don't play this game for the combat, play it for the exploration and finding stuff. You'll beat the main story in anywhere from 8-10 hours depending on your playstyle and difficulty. 100% items found in probably 13hours.
Even after hundreds of hours, there are still tons of things I haven't gotten around to completing yet. Worth every penny.

Yeah, I couldn't resist buying this at full price but if I wanted to follow the Ravenhearst story-arc, I needed it.
In MCF: Madame Fate, after freeing Emma's spirit from Ravenhearst, Madame Fate contacted you as she saw her own demise in her crystal ball - she needs you to find who among her employees wants her dead....
And you'll ask me: why is it tied to Ravenhearst? Because the storyline has a huge twist at the end, that will make you go back to Ravenhearst Manor in the fifth installement of the series.
You're now visiting a fair, along with people: you'll have a number of items to find in order to access to the future of the employees (doomed, doomed and doomed.... anyway). Each scene contains also beyond objects items (changing appearances) that will unlock special places where you can gain time - mainly if you're in the normal mode where you have a timer.
When visiting an employee, you'll have a puzzle of words to solve, each time different in the thematic. Then, there, you'll have to find specific items (5 clubs, 10 moons, 15 jelly beans, etc...).
And when you want to reveal their fate, well, you'll have a puzzle to solve - an elaborate one as sometimes, it's hard to see what to do.
As you understand, Madame Fate, while being in the first era of hidden objects games, has a tendancy to orient itself towards modern "hidden objects" games: beyond objects, puzzles, and hidden objects scenes in a scene.
However, I felt the game being long for a simple reason: you have many employees to check AND some objects are so well hidden that you'll need a magnifying lens to see them. Also, as the game is in English only, I had an hard time for the puzzle words (I don't know all the fruit in English or even the feelings) and for some items, like a dolly, where I was searching for a doll when it was something else (a tool used to carry boxes or crates). So in other words, Madame Fate isn't opened to everyone, at least on Steam. If you want a multilanguage game, you need to find it elsewhere or in retail.
Madame Fate's ambiance, however, is between cynism and dark humor. It's perhaps less creepy than Ravenhearst, the previous game, but there is still evil lurking around and the fair Madame Fate owned isn't the most joyful in the world.
Anyway, it's still a good game, a good moment to pass just to know the fate of the employees and who wants to kill her. I spent 10 bucks that I'm not regretting, however, you should prefer a discount on it, that will perhaps happen one day, as Ravenhearst and Return to Ravenhearst were during this sale!

I never would've discovered this game if the news of it disappearing hadn't come up. I got it because it's price was just too good to pass up: 100 PHP, which is around $2. But getting on to the game itself, at the time of this review, I have only played 5 hours and will update once I complete it.
So far, the atmosphere is creepy, I like it. The game doesn't rely on jumpscares at all, which is rare considering most horror I've played had at least a few jumps. Yet, the gripping story is just enough to keep me on the edge of my seat. Although, when the games give you the tip: When you're overwhelmed, run to the Light (paraphrase), I tell you, heed that tip. It'll make the game simpler and keep you from throwing your mouse, or controller, which is what I use. It makes it easier to dodge attacks from enemies. A slow-mo mechanic sometimes triggers when enemies pop-up, and at times you think you're safe, the game just takes a quick pause to make you realize, you aren't. When you pause the game, you can go into the options and set the graphics. Personally, my computer can't handle ultra, the fps just dips way too hard, but from what I saw, it had really good textures for it's time. Speaking of time, I feel that you could get a good 16-18 hours just on the main story alone. Now, I've heard the story was that this game cannot be purchase anymore on the steam store. A bummer. Sadly, I can't recommend it, because you can't get it anyway. But, there is a way, if you really want to. A bit illegal, but it's the only way right now. Or, you could also legally just borrow a friend's account. But if you have no friends, then look for a 2nd hand copy I guess. If you have an old Xbox 360 lying around, you could look for an old copy from some groups on facebook, since it's on there too. But, I do suggest the PC version because of the amount of graphical settings you can make.

I enjoyed my time with Mafia III. The game really set me in the mood of a late 1960s New Orleans. The graphics, the gameplay, the voice acting, all of it was generally great in the game. I only came across 3 or 4 crashes across my 25 hours of gametime, but the autosave always set me up where I last set up. My PC parts for reference:
Graphics: 8/10
I played with everything as high as it could go, with V-sync and Anti-aliasing off, and I got 40-50 fps on a gtx 970. The graphics of the game gave me a sense of where I was. New Orleans: flashy in the city, but also polluted. The advertisement signs looked like the late 60s. The brick buildings looked like the late 60s. Admittedly, there were some graphical glitches when I played, like a quick screen of blue, or random lines on the screen, but it was very rare. The colors in the city ranged from a huge bright color pallette to dreary colors, to washed out in sun, to dark with light pollution. The bayou country to the south was very pretty when it wanted to be, sometimes sun bouncing off of the water as you boat through the green marshes, to grungy swamp. Overall, it was pretty when it wanted to be, and it was ugly when it wanted to be, and it all worked.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
The gameplay is very solid. Whether you want to sneak around and whistle for your enemies to come close so you can rip out their juggular, to going in Rambo style and shooting everyone up with rifles, pistols, submachine guns, or sniper rifles, it all worked. The game is very generous with blood- stab him in the throat and see him bleed on his clothes, stab him brutally in the face and see his face be a shiny red, or shoot him up. It was solid and led to great times in game. (Also you can go up to any civilian and sucker-punch them- one of the best and hilarious parts of the game.)
SPOILER:
Settings-wise, white people call you a nig ger quite frequently, and black people will talk to you like a human being. In game, there are white people, black people, Haitian people, and Irish people.
The game contains a lot of cutscenes, and all of these are beautifully crafted. The detailed skin and clothes, defined mouth, jaw, and tongue movement when talking, eyes, and general movement all lead to a very good way of describing the scene. There is also some footage of Donovan describing events to a council that is projected like it was filmed on a late 60s camera.
Driving: 7/10
It has improved a lot since Mafia II. It is awkward to do at first, but you get used to it and it leads to some cool drifting. Each car was crafted to look like it was in that time era, and each look so good. And the little details make the game so much better- if you bust out the red glass on a brakelight, if you put on the brakes it is a white light. And most (if not all) of the cars are stickshift, and you can see visibly see Lincoln Clay shifting each time the car shifts.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game and I look forward to a Mafia IV in the late future. 8/10, and $60 well spent.

*Key provided by developer in exchange for an honest review.
March of Industry is a… I’m going with “factory simulator.” Your goal is to use the natural resources given in order to craft different weapons (and items to make weapons) for your glorious country, and make a profit. The game has that simple premise, but it’s actually rather difficult when you’ve just started. You’re not given the recipes, after all, but have to find out yourself via trial and error what to items make what.
The game gives you goals as you advance, be it in amount to earn or sell or what item to make next, and you are left to set up the machines and resources and discover what makes what and clean up the mess after on your own.
The controls are fairly simple as is learning to play it, the difficulty I feel lies in finding all the combinations, and then waiting for the machines to finish however many you need to sell to advance to the next goal. While I didn’t think some of the combinations were overly logical, I still kinda liked it.
The recipes you find are logged, so if you ever forget them, or go back to the game after a long while, you can always re-read what items made what.
The soundbits are repetitive and annoying, and yet they somehow added a sort of charm to the game. Don’t ask me why, after a while of having it open I just got used to them I guess.
The art is decent for pixel art, I rather enjoyed the fresh look that wasn’t cartoony.
At the end of the day, however, this is essentially a waiting game. And a rather short one at that.
Would I recommend it? Yes, but perhaps not for its full price, and definitely only if you enjoy the style of crafting/waiting/micromanaging game.

I entered March of Industry with the knowledge it would not take too long to proceed.  This wasn't a bother as the idea of the game piqued my interest.
Turns out, March of Industry was nothing like I thought it would be.  Automation?  Assembly?  Capitalism?  These concepts exist at the most basic level imaginable, and this is where disappointment kicks in.
March of Industry plays like a ‘Doodle God’ or similar style mobile game, where your aim is to take two objects and attempt to merge them together to make a new object.  This new object could then be merged with another object to make a new one, and continue this process until you’ve discovered all possible objects.  The manner in which you solve this puzzle is to place objects into a machine that either, by itself, converts to a new object – or merged with another object, converts to a new object.
The problem lies in the automation.  March of Industry claims to have automation of which there is almost none.  You must manually purchase your beginning objects, run them through your machines using conveyer belts, and then manually sell your end results.  The only automation that takes place is conveyer belts moving items through your constructed system.  Further automation improvements include the obvious: Automatic buying and automatic selling of objects.
March of Industry also boasts crafting of your weapons.  Crafting was already described above: put one or two items into a machine, new item comes out.  That’s crafting.  There are no timers, no extra machinery, no secondary steps, no real puzzle – just put items in a machine and see if something new comes out.  Didn’t work?  Try a different item or combination.
Capitalism?  There’s none of that, either.  There is no real sense of “profit” except needing to make money to buy more expensive objects.  Never does your money mean anything else.  Finally... play with your sound off.  Every time an object it produced, there is some sarcastic quip that is played *every bloody time* the item is produced.  Since the game driver is "make money," producing lots of items to sell is obvious.  You will drive yourself mad listening to the same audio clip over and over and over and over and over again.  The fact that there is no option to disable these, astounds me.
With major changes and improvements, March of Industry would be the Doodle God of the year.  Unfortunately in its current state, you’ll find yourself easily frustrated at the manner you play and the lack of sense of accomplishment as you progress.

Witcher 2 is an RPG like no other that caters to the most mature and serious players in the genre. With absolutely zero hand holding and possibly the best cinematic storytelling I've ever seen, the game provides an experience like no other. When you play this game, you will never see halos or devil horns telling you whether the decisions you make are "good" or "evil". The game simply presents choices and consequences, so it is ultimately up to the player to decide what path they decide to take, and quite often the the lines between what is right and wrong can become muddled and even downright inconclusive to the player, making for some extremely thought-provoking scenarios and questlines. This is bolstered by the fact that the game has dozens of major choices throughout that, with each, will have a significant impact on the story, making for so many ways to play through the game.
As I mentioned, the game will almost never hold your hand. This means you will not have waypoints all over your screen telling you exactly where to go constantly. Often times, when undertaking quests, you will need to read over your journal or revisit certain characters to obtain information on where to go or what to do next, and use your intuition along the way. This type of approach gives almost the whole game the feeling of a challenge, rather than just a mundane routine. This along with other things can easily put off several people from this game who are looking for a more casual experience, as it is definitely a game for people who like to think and analyze. Possibly the biggest offput for some people may be the tutorial that the game starts off with, as it is quite bad. Getting used to the combat and inventory systems(which is also not the best at times) can be difficult, but if you can overcome that you are in for an amazing experience.

If you're new to the game or starting fresh in the Steam version you'll soon realize that you will easily lose in the dumbest ways simply because either your opponent is a much higher level than you or because they have all of the good building unlocked. Since this is the case you are constantly having to use Dart Monkeys for camo baloons, Boomerang Monkeys for lead baloons, and using all of your energy to re-roll in vein that you either get a Bloonchipper, Cobra (which is easily the most broken thing about the game), or Monkey Sub. Either you can take days if not weeks to unlock them, while still needing medals to unlock all of their abilities, or you can buy each building for $4.99 each which is absurd. Once you run out of the initial 20 energy (which it takes 3 to roll each time) than you have to wait for it to regenerate. So Garry's Mod, it really isn't anything honestly, but that's what's so good about it.
Garry's Mod is a sandbox Source engine game, so if you've played games such as Team Fortress 2 or Half-Life 2 (or any other Valve sequel), then you should feel at home with this game.
The thing with Garry's Mod compared to other sandbox games (compared to Minecraft perhaps), there are no goals whatsoever. "It's a sandbox game, you aren't supposed to follow goals" is what you may be thinking, but a recognised sandbox game such as Minecraft does have overall goals such as the Ender Dragon. Garry's Mod gives you so much freedom that at times, you can't even decide what to do next since you can pretty much do anything you want without a single temptation of the game urging you to follow any rules or goals.
So what can you do in Garry's Mod?
- Sandbox: It's argueably most famous gamemode, sandbox is the mode that gives players so much freedom. With access to a seemingly infinite workshop, a player can modify objects, AI, vehicles, their own player model and more to however they may please. It's fun to see what you're able to create or do in this gamemode, but it really shines when you have friends to play with.
-- I won't mention every gamemode in Garry's Mod, but I will point out the ones I find most enjoyable from this point on --
- Prop Hunt: The gamemode that may be more well known than sandbox, prop hunt splits the players into two teams; the hunters and the props. The hunters goal is to kill the props with the props goal being to survive for the entire time limit. It's essentially hide and seek. While the hunters have access to a variety of weapons to hunt props, props are left completely defenseless except for the weapon of trickery, props can turn into any moveable object on the map being played on meaning they can appear so out of place, like a chair on a rooftop, or blend in so well, like a bottle in a fridge, creating a difficult challenge for the hunters. Intense, fun and very easy to laugh gamemode.
- Murder: Simple, a bunch of people are dropped onto a map, to explore and do whatever, however one of them is a murderer and their goal is to kill everyone, the murderer has one weakness however, a gun. One bystander out of everyone is supplied with a gun, loaded with a single bullet in the chamber and a long reload time. Better make that one bullet count, cause if there is a gun just lying on the ground, the murderer can easily take advantage of that. Don't expect to just know the killer is "xXProPlayerKidXx" however, everyone is given anonymous names to avoid identification and the murderer can turn into the victims they've killed. Careful, intense and teamwork oriented gamemode.
Overall, Garry's Mod offers so much to do to the player, with no restrictions on what they can or can't do, it really is a game you can't turn down.
It's been out for 11 years and still going strong, obviously, it can't be a bad game.

I enjoyed my time with Mafia III. The game really set me in the mood of a late 1960s New Orleans. The graphics, the gameplay, the voice acting, all of it was generally great in the game. I only came across 3 or 4 crashes across my 25 hours of gametime, but the autosave always set me up where I last set up. My PC parts for reference:
Graphics: 8/10
I played with everything as high as it could go, with V-sync and Anti-aliasing off, and I got 40-50 fps on a gtx 970. The graphics of the game gave me a sense of where I was. New Orleans: flashy in the city, but also polluted. The advertisement signs looked like the late 60s. The brick buildings looked like the late 60s. Admittedly, there were some graphical glitches when I played, like a quick screen of blue, or random lines on the screen, but it was very rare. The colors in the city ranged from a huge bright color pallette to dreary colors, to washed out in sun, to dark with light pollution. The bayou country to the south was very pretty when it wanted to be, sometimes sun bouncing off of the water as you boat through the green marshes, to grungy swamp. Overall, it was pretty when it wanted to be, and it was ugly when it wanted to be, and it all worked.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
The gameplay is very solid. Whether you want to sneak around and whistle for your enemies to come close so you can rip out their juggular, to going in Rambo style and shooting everyone up with rifles, pistols, submachine guns, or sniper rifles, it all worked. The game is very generous with blood- stab him in the throat and see him bleed on his clothes, stab him brutally in the face and see his face be a shiny red, or shoot him up. It was solid and led to great times in game. (Also you can go up to any civilian and sucker-punch them- one of the best and hilarious parts of the game.)
SPOILER:
Settings-wise, white people call you a nig ger quite frequently, and black people will talk to you like a human being. In game, there are white people, black people, Haitian people, and Irish people.
The game contains a lot of cutscenes, and all of these are beautifully crafted. The detailed skin and clothes, defined mouth, jaw, and tongue movement when talking, eyes, and general movement all lead to a very good way of describing the scene. There is also some footage of Donovan describing events to a council that is projected like it was filmed on a late 60s camera.
Driving: 7/10
It has improved a lot since Mafia II. It is awkward to do at first, but you get used to it and it leads to some cool drifting. Each car was crafted to look like it was in that time era, and each look so good. And the little details make the game so much better- if you bust out the red glass on a brakelight, if you put on the brakes it is a white light. And most (if not all) of the cars are stickshift, and you can see visibly see Lincoln Clay shifting each time the car shifts.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game and I look forward to a Mafia IV in the late future. 8/10, and $60 well spent.

Second, this game has poor optimization for particular builds of computers, don't let this scare you away, but if you are on the lower end of the spectrum when it comes to minimum requirements, you should check online to ensure your gaming experience will be satisfactory, I was decently ahead of the minimum requirements with a 2.9GHz dual core (AMD) and a Nvidia Geforce GT 240 with 1GB DDR3 VRAM, with 8GB of 1833 Mhz of "normal" RAM. I just finished playing the 5th episode 😭. It feels incredibly sad to say "Good Bye" to this game. While playing I had a chance to get to know every in game character, especially Max and Chloe. They've become like my new friends, we've been through so much together, and realizing that it's over now, it's hella tough.
I've seen a lot of great games before, but never did a game make me feel SO connected to its characters. And every time you need to make a choice, you start seeing everything you've been through before and thinking how to make things even better. But I think the most important thing here is not to overthink (I mean not to try to Google what consequences your choice is going to have because it kills all the excitement of not knowing). Just do what feels right and what your heart tells you even if you might be wrong. I guess that's the lesson I learned in here.
Other important things that make Life Is Strange my favorite game: The developers paid attention to the smallest details, some of them you don't even notice playing for the first time, but the fact that they're there makes me appreciate it even more. The graphics is hella amazing, you just have to see it for yourself :) The plot and the music complement each other in subtle ways, and I can guarantee you'll have at least several of the soundtracks in your favorites playlist ;)
The game's definitely worth its money and even more. I wish I'd be able to forget everything that happened in the game and start playing it from the very beginning, so I'd be able to feel everything with the same intensity I did during my first playthrough. But I'll definitely come back to it after some time just to do it all over again.
Dear Developers, THANK YOU so much for Life Is Strange. I wish you all the best and I'm looking forward to seeing more masterpieces from you.

The last thing I want to do is overhype this game. Part of its appeal to me was how the story's depth slowly and surprisingly increased over time.
That being said, this might be my favorite game ever.
During a transitional time in my life this game acted as a constant I could come back to. It was a show that swallowed my thoughts in a way that a real tv show never could. It was engaging to live this life that I never could have had, to empathize with this world I was never a part of but still feel the cultural weight of.
Not to say the writing is perfect. I think it's among the best writing in games, but not perfect. The game touches on a lot of different, very sensitive issues and I've heard mixed things from people to whom those issues matter. Some say it handled X issue well, but Y issue felt like it was written by someone who has never really experienced Y issue. I can't really disagree with that assessment but I don't think it takes away from the story as a whole.
This was a story that felt like it had real consequences, even if on paper it didn't really. You often don't know you made a choice of consequence, but looking back, you can see why what you thoughtlessly did mattered. There were moments where those choices hit me like a ton of bricks and I felt truly bad about the outcome I had created. The weight of it followed me for days.
But this isn't just a game of somber consequence. The twee aesthetic and soundtrack complement the lighter moments and general (2014) teenage feel. Reading Max's journal and texts help build a world of teenage angst and simplicity that offsets that fantastical elements well. I felt warmed by the soft moments in the story and disturbed by its darker elements.
The actual interaction with the story and world is very well done. I've never been much of a fan of point-and-click adventures or visual novels, but this game really showed me what people see in those genres. The unique mechanics are so well done that I think it sets a new standard for how adventure games should be structured.
The graphics are something I'm ambivalent about. The static environment design is very well done and the game's whole style feels very cohesive. I appreciate that there were trying to go with an easy to optimize look, but the characters suffer for it. The stares are often blank, the hands always look wooden, and the animations sometimes really distract from an otherwise great scene. This is something I really really hope they tighten up in a follow up game.
Regarding a sequel, all I can say is that I hope it has nothing to do with any of the characters here because this world has been chewed up narratively and all these characters have had the time they need to develop (with the exception of Rachel perhaps).

Fairly short, but the fun isn't in "beating" the game, it's in discovering all of the ridiculous recipes and then making absolutely ludicrous machines. I've played similar factory games, and most of them have a bit more content and a bit more explicit challenge, but also feel comparatively "sterile" (not to mention cost 2-3 times as much). The assembly lines in this have so many more possibilities, since it actually uses some rudimentary physics, and *really weird stuff* is possible.
I don't really feel like the point of this game is just to beat it... The goals are there just as a sort of tutorial to drive you forward in discovering the different tools available. I beat the game in like an hour, but I still ended up playing it for a long time after I beat it. I am all about efficiency, and making the most efficient production lines possible (using some really funky tricks) is the part I really enjoyed. I planned to just take a quick peek and make sure the game ran on on OSX, and ended up beating it several times over in a single sitting in my quest for production line perfection.
Disclosure: I received a free review copy of the game to aid with testing OSX compatibility.

The game is fun. It is very similar to the first game with a few differences.
The gameplay is fun but can get annoying later it the game. It feels like WB really wanted you to buy some loot boxes so they made the last act very long and tedicious. There are a lot of skill points to choose from and it changes gameplay a bit. There are many different orc personalities and classes which adds character to your armies. The orcs are a lot more memorable in this game. The fortress sieges and defenses are exciting at first but get repetitive very fast especially in the last act where you have to do 20 siege defenses in a row.
There are extra 'side missions' where you would locate an object from a 'Far Cry'- like fast travel point and then either collect it or do a minigame. For example, there are Shelob memories where you would have to find the right angle to see an image. These can get annoying when you can't find the angle right. There is also a fill in the blank minigame that seems out of place. The Gondorian artifacts come with a cool narration.
The story isn't special. I didn't feel attached to any characters. I can't tell you any of their names. Characters usually stick to a specific story mission branch and stay there. Once you beat that branch of quests, you will never see them again. There is a few twists here and there. I did enjoy the twist before the last act. In fact, the boss fights before the last act were cool. I personally think the game should have ended there with some other cutscene wrapping things up rather than making the player do 20 fortress defenses in a row. It get extremely annoying. I had to train my orcs to then defend then move on the next region and do the same thing there.
Steam says it took me 123 hours to complete the game, but in reality it was closer to 80 hours (I left the game running a few times).
TL;DR The game is fun until the last act where it is just a drag. The story wasn't anything special (I ignored it). Gameplay can get repetitive and frustrating at times. With the motionjoy driver (and the "betterds3" config tool) this game can be set up (using the mitsurugi_config.exe tool which you can find in the same folder as the game, you can find it using Steam by clicking on properties and opening the game files folder) to use controller instead of keyboard. You'll need to select the controller as "Controller (Xbox360 Wireless receiver for Windows)" in the mitsurugi_config.exe, even if you're using a Sony SixAxis (that's how the motionjoy driver makes the SixAxis controller appear).
Anyway, once you've configured the game to run using your controller, it's much easier on your hands (but still be aware of repetitive stress injury, this game is way too addictive, and so cute!).
The controls are well thought out, but there's quite a variety of things to learn so be sure to understand the tutorial first. It'll give you lots of ideas on how to get past the bosses. Pay special attention to how to recharge your health (the top bar). And don't forget to spend the skill points you earn to upgrade the power of your attacks (I got pretty far without realizing that, but it was very slow-going indeed!). Normal difficulty is probably sufficiently hard unless you've played these kinds of games a lot before.
Overall, this is the kind of well-thought-out fighting game mechanic that should have been emulated in games like "Remember Me" (which has an almost insanely-confusing gameplay mechanic compared to this jewel of a game).

First half hour, that I've spent, playing this game, was great, and I thought that I've found a true gem among visual novels. Sadly, after that, things got worse. Moments of good humor and interesting story-telling were drowned by frustration and disappointment, that comes not from writing, nor the plot, but game mechanics and the way they are used within the story. This is early access game, obviously, so there may be some changes until final version, but I will judge it for what it is right now.
It has interesting concept and it isn't overflowing with cliches, which is great.
Especially during Tymo's route. There are few moments when it feels like creators tried a little too hard (especially with multiple narrators - it wears off really quickly and becomes annoying), but overall, I had a few good laughs, and that's great.
Original, surprisingly likable, cute and funny. What's not to like?
I don't like this "trend" that started on app stores and slowly shows up up on Steam, with visual novels cut into pieces and sell separately as episodes or routes. I prefer this "early access" approach much more. That being said...
This is a 23€ game, with five (currently four) routes. From what I've seen (I've played three so far, some few times), you can complete single route in about an hour, sometimes even less, if you get bad ending. That gives us about 5 hour of gameplay, not counting the time that you will spend replaying the game, frustrated, trying to get the right combination of choices to get good ending or at least to not die. Oh, and time you'll spend gaining achievements, since most of them seem literally impossible to get (and I'm not referring to those from missing route). There is only one CG per route, so 5 CGs total. Plus, given the fact, that I know most of in-game music, it's probably royalty-free, although I'm not certain on that one. Either way, it's really hard to see how is it worth 23€.
Desperately, I may add. I think this game was intended to be replayed a lot, in order to unlock certain endings, but the problem is, it's getting very frustrating, especially considering that skipping isn't always working as intended and some (most?) outcomes are based on invisible love-meter. For example, on Tymo's route I found myself in a situation, where all of three available choices led to my death. I couldn't do anything about it, so I looked for help. Only thing I gathered from some older discussion, was "Tymo need to love you more". Uh-huh. So you're telling me, I need to replay the whole game, and then out of at least 10 choices or so, pick this right configuration that let me get through, but I don't have any indicator, which choice do what and I can only guess. Okay. If someone is patient enough to do that (or lucky to get it during first try), they will probably move pass this obstacle, but after that, I've decided to give up on playing further until there's some sort of guide or in-game indicator of this mysterious "love-meter". It just seems like massive waste of time.
Which isn't really surprising, but some games can pull this off well. Here, dying is neither dramatic, nor shocking, nor funny, nor in any way useful, it's a silly way of punishing you for choices that you had no idea could let to this outcome
. Death counter seems almost like a mockery. This is a visual novel and not "Dark Souls", seriously.
Isn't working right. Sometimes I wasn't able to skip seen text after reloading a file - I needed to wait for another choice. It's also slow.
Seriously?

Both of these routes were rushed and bland. There is some nice humor here and there, but not much emotional impact. Furio, with his "I loved you and you have not loved me back, so now that you love me, I don't love you anymore, because reasons" is particularly unlikable and I'm not sure if that was creators intention. Jan's route isn't out yet, but I'm not looking forward to that one.
I still have Einar's route to play, but I will wait with that one till the final version. For now, I cannot recommend this game, not only because of price, but also because of lacking content and frustrating game mechanics.

Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae is what I like to call a "supplemental" game. This is a game you would play while taking a break from another similar "main" game. Some people would prefer to play a different game, but I don't know. Juggling a plethora of games that represent dozens of different genres would turn anybody's brain into stale yogurt. Why take the risk when you can play something similar that's stil entertaining?
This game - which I'll refer to as MKH because acronyms are fun (AAF) - falls under the genre of arena-slasher. Typically a character-action game has some mode where you fight wave after wave of enemies (Bloody Palace, Lost Chapter, Tests of Valor).  When a character-action game is literally just that wave-based mode, it becomes an arena-slasher. These are pretty rare and tend to be doujin titles, like Croixleur Sigma (also available on Steam).
The plot to MKH is: woman kills stuff with katana. Each of the five chapters are divided into five waves. Enemies are rich in number but poor in identity. There are guys with swords, red guys with swords, yellow guys with swords, big guys with swords, robots, an evil schoolgirl, and maybe 1 or 2 other different types of enemies. However, this is a short game, one that you can slash through in less than two hours.
Not-evil schoolgirl (I already forgot her name) has a sweet sword and not much else when you start off. Upgrades can be purchased as well as new moves and powers. The #1 thing to keep in mind throughout is parrying. While it's easy to mash the attack button and slice evil to pieces, playing defensively is how you avoid getting your combos broken. More specifically, it's all about the parry. Blocking is fine, but it doesn't work on heavy attacks and tends to get broken by a continous assault. Timing the block just right allows NES to awesome her way through the enemy's attack and deliver a strong counter-move.
There are other tactics to keep in mind. When an enemy is struck enough times they'll start to bleed (turn red). At this point a few more hits are liable to kill the enemy, just before they die the player should sheathe their weapon. It's like that common Japanese maneuver where the samurai cuts a dozen people at once, but they only fall over and die after the sword's been sheathed. In this game it's just something you want to do to boost your skill-points & regain health, though it also does big damage to bosses. There are other abilities and skills to master, but it's better to get a feel for it while playing the game.
For the most part, MKH is a breezy entertaining slasher. It's satisfying getting those big combos while also deflecting numerous attacks coming from every angle. Keeping track of the action can be difficult though, and your sound has to be turned up to notice the enemies that inevitably attack from behind. Some more variety in the enemies and bosses would have been appreciated, but maybe it's just me. I've been playing Bayonetta 2 and it seems like every 10 minutes there's a new enemy to fight. Like I said though, MKH is a short game. 10 minutes in that game is at least 3 or 4 waves. New enemy-types would just get lost in the chaos.
Unlike the games it serves a supplementary role to, MKH can be enjoyed even if you only have 5 minutes of free-time. There's no sitting through cut-scenes or loading, nor does it take several minutes to get the action. It's also possible to save in-between waves, and you certainly aren't expected to play through the whole thing without dying. Start this game up, slash through a few waves, and put it down so you can focus on your main title.
All in all, this is a worthwhile pick-up.

So ive had rather short experience with previous Mafia games, i think i played hour or two the first game at my friends place and i played a bit the demo of Mafia 2, i wasn’t really super into them or anything, i thought them as average games – however i did love first Godfather game, because it had lot of cool stuff in it, but thats a other topic in itself. I guess the place to start talking about the game is the main character “Lincoln Clay” and i believe there was an intentional purpose to make him black to “sell” more diversity crap that leftist have been pushing a lot. When it comes to this stuff you have to look context too – the game takes place in New Orleans and there are lot of black people there whatever its Haitians and their voodoo stuff or just Afro-Americans so it does fit into the context, ironically a Hispanic is Lincoln’s voice actor so there is that…
Lincoln is a war veteran as it says on the bio and thats pretty much all they tell about him top of the fact he was raised by Sammy who is his adoptive father. He has his sense of humor and anger too i guess, but overall hes not that interesting character and doesn’t bring much to the table – i haven’t played Mafia 2 through, but Vito whose the main character in it does play a part in Mafia 3 and he seems to be lot more interesting character with more depth. There are no “oh thats so typical Lincoln” lines in this game theres nothing unique about him.
Putting that aside its a sandbox game and maybe your character isn’t that important so i can get that. In terms of gameplay the game has rather good vehicle driving engine and shooting is rather fluid, i would say better than GTA 5 even maybe, City itself is rather cool looking but there is not much you can interact with, you can kill civilians and shoot cops or raid places or do Side-missions. Oh yeah you do have collectibles that you can collect around the map, so there is that too.
The game took me around ~27h to complete, with some side missions not being done. So in terms of getting gameplay hours for the money, i think its rather good deal. While the game had some glitches and bugs at launch, they were patched out (Game is still a tad unoptimized i guess).

Great little puzzle game.  The controls and rules are easy to learn, and the puzzles are just the right amount of challenge.  The object of each puzzle is to get the 3 cubes to the exit square.  When you move a colored cube onto a square, it changes color to match the cube.  You can't move that cube onto the same square again, unless you use another cube to change it's color.  In addition, there are some pre-colored squares that can not be passed until you pick up a mini cube of the same color and carry it over that square.  There are various other blockades, like posts that drop with switches, and moving spheres that must be avoided.
If you enjoy puzzle games that require brain power instead of twitch skills, then this game is for you.

First of all I’d like to state that although I have clicked the ‘do not recommend’ option, my position toward the game is one of neutrality, neither dismissing it as unplayable nor condoning the exuberant praise that The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings seems to receive. The game has many redeeming features which shall be discussed shortly, however I feel as though there are just as many aspects that make the player underwhelmed with his/her experience. Secondly, I should say that this review builds upon my review of the original Witcher, which I have also reviewed on Steam, so I will be making a few comparative points in light of my disposition toward the first instalment in the series.
The Witcher 2 is driven extremely well by an engrossing narrative of political intrigue, racial prejudice and social injustice. Although the hybrid of Medieval and fantasy themes has been done before and is far from original, The Witcher 2 fully embraces the combination and creates a three-dimensional world with rounded and well thought-out characters that have their own individual agendas and follow them accordingly. There are a few plot twists along the way which I, of course, won’t mention, but these keep the narrative feeling fresh and engaging enough to continue playing til the end. I would say that the story, fresh from the pages of the original comics, is the main factor encouraging gamers to try this game.
Furthermore, we aren’t babysat. Nothing has been toned or dumbed down, which is preferable as too few games are made in modern times that have been made for an adult audience. We are shoehorned immediately into the action and I think that’s why the game puts many people off in the initial stages, claiming it to be unfriendly to new users to the series. I would argue this is a commendable feature however, as the harsh and merciless world of Geralt is directly reflected in the games content and contextual features.

The combat is far more engaging than in the original WItcher, due simply to it being more enjoyable. That being said, it is far from perfect. Battles range from being far too easy to far too hard far too quickly. We can quickly descend into the ‘trial and error’ form of gaming, constantly reloading previous saves in order to trial new ways of beating a difficult enemy. You can also only drink or create potions before a battle, not during it, which is more realistic I accept, but ultimately make many aspects of the combat frustrating. If I realise that a potion improving my vigor regeneration will help me win a battle in its opening stages, why not just let me drink one? The guise of this being ‘unrealistic’ simply makes alchemy and potion consumption frustrating; constantly saving, reloading and drinking potions before a known fight drastically effect the pace of the game and cause a stuttering experience that is cause for concern.
Perhaps the most disappointing characteristic of The Witcher 2 though is the world itself. I don’t mean its concept, I mean in its literal physicality. The areas you can explore are minuscule in terms of a 21st century RPG and the areas are quickly covered and recovered time and again. This makes the quests fairly limited, as there is only so much to do in a rather small gaming arena. Quests such as competing at arm wrestling, dice poker and brawling are irrelevant sideshows, yet if you take  these out you are only left with half dozen side quests in Act I and II respectively, and only a couple in the rather brief Act III. The overall longevity of the game is actually rather small, with a completed game taking between 16-30 hours (and that would be being generous). Essentially, there are a fair number of things to do in the world, but there really aren’t that many, certainly not deserving of high merit.
Quest exploration (in terms of the map and quest markers) is a rather touchy subject for both fans and haters of the series alike. Fans of this game state that the map and quest hints are intentionally cryptic because the game encourages you to explore yourself, and that we shouldn’t be spoon fed as gamers. Haters of The Witcher 2 point on the map and quest markers are totally useless, broken, and ruin the gaming experience completely. While I totally back the formers idea in theory, in practice the latter is nearer the truth. Quest markers as you approach them do sometimes teleport elsewhere without explanation, whilst the game map has no concept of ‘levels’, meaning that you may arrive at your destination only to discover that its several floors above you, a particular problem in Vergen. If the developers didn’t want to spoon feed the gamer and it was all about exploration and realism, why bother with a quest marker at all? Why, at the beginning of the majority of quests, does it tell us where to go? The quest exploration in the game seems to be a halfway house between attempting to help the gamer and encourage exploration, yet it ends up failing on both counts.
A problem with the critiques of the Witcher are of course, the critics themselves. Haters of the series have complained of a lack of fast travel. There is of course, no problem with that whatsoever. The developers have created a game that is very graphically impressive with some engaging characters, all of which they want you to experience. Removing fast travel will enhance the possibility of experiencing these things. Furthermore, the confines of the world itself is rather tiny meaning that fast travel is, for the large part, totally unnecessary anyway, as it does not take particularly long to run from one side of the map to the other.
One of my main bones of contention with the previous Witcher instalment was its ‘mature’ content. I stated in my review of that game that having maturity in the game does not make the game mature, and I think that unfortunately still applies to the sequel. I’m not sure if it’s because the translations from Polish to English are not clear enough, but much of the dialogue feels awkward, with characters using expletives, talking of♥♥♥♥♥♥and ‘ploughing’ for the sake of it. I think the developers could have included this content without making it so blasé, and it still seems as though the developers are trying to show off to kids and young teens. Nearly all dialogue refers to some obscenity and it becomes tiresome rather quickly. In fact, many of the characters are unlikeable because of this fact, most noticeably Roache and Ioveth. This does help serve the ‘shades of grey’ approach that the developers are going for, using a ‘lesser of two evils’ mindset, yet it is hard to play out an entire game without at least having a couple of likeable characters that we wish to associate with.  A positive note however, is that the ‘Sex Cards’ from the previous game have been removed, presumably because those who were amused or aroused by such content hit puberty and discovered internet porn.
Overall, the experience is okay and the narrative really is interesting. But the content of the game, although acceptable, really is not the experience that many exaggerated reviews on Steam that lavish the praise make out that it is. It has many issues that make it fall down. However, I would say that the commercial success of The Witcher 2 should allow the developers the funds to make The Witcher 3 into something special, reflecting an intriguing and exceptional storyline with equally impressive gaming content (for a change).
Please review and comment, any feedback is welcome and thank you for reading.

A simple game about monkeys popping balloons that has surprisingly alot of depth to it. Which is sort of a good thing and a bad thing. It's a 1v1 tower defense game where balloons travel on fixed paths with a variety of designs and lengths and players can choose a variety of towers which each have their own strengths and weaknesses while sending balloons to attack their opponent.
The game is great game but it doesn't have a great tutorial. Bloons TD Battles is a Real-Time-Strategy game which are notorious for their steep learning curves and the in-game tutorial provided does not teach you everything you need to know. It's best to try to lurk the froums (here or on the NK website) for tips unless you like losing your first 200 matches in a row just trying to figure out how to play the game.
Other downsides include the game being easy to hack so you can and will run into hackers from time to time, not the greatest servers so either you and your opponent can get randomly disconnected, and wonky matchmaking so noobs can get matched with pros and vice versa which doesn't always happen but can from time to time.
But past those issues, the game has alot of upsides to it. First and foremost, it's not pay2win. You can pay to unlock towers faster but everyone gets the same balloon attacks so you should always be able to stop your opponent even if it means being sort-of forced to play aggressively at the beginning. The card battles also isn't pay2win like HearthRoyale since all of the cards that can be bought are either trash or easy to counter. Other purchases are club access which are optional/alternate game modes, tower skins and bloon skins.
This is one of the most rewarding games I've played (and I've played for about 2 years before it was released on Steam). If you like fast-paced, interactive games you should definitely try this out.

After 58 hours playing this game, I wanted to write a review, but I couldn't because I installed the Director's Cut and it would only let me if I installed the original version. I like this game so much that I went ahead and installed the original Wasteland 2 to write about it.
Easily one of the best games I've played this year. This coming from a CRPG fan who loves Fallout 1 and Pillars of Eternity. There are few games today with this kind of mechanics and setting, and it is for me one of the best, of course not without its flaws and bugs, but none interfering so much with the experience.
Wasteland 2 is a party-based, tactical turn-based CRPG set in a post apocalyptic environment in a devastated Arizona (
). You have the option to highly customize up to four member of your squad or choose amongst pre-made characters. During the game you recruit several other NPCs to join your team. This game is not text heavy like Pillars of Eternity, it gives you a good deal of text to read, but very manageable. Working with the CLASSIC attribute configuration (Coordination, Luck, Awareness, Strength, Speed, Intelligence and Charisma), you are free to make dozens of different builds, from heavy artillery guy to tech expert to sniper doctor. One nice thing is that you find good use to most of the skills along the game, and most weapons as well are pretty useful (Energy Weapons are very useful later in the game, not so much in the beginning).
Choices in this game do not necessarily alter the course of the future, but it's very interesting how you can decide who lives and who dies, who deserves and who doesn't. This makes up for tough decisions and replayability in case you want to make different choices. One tip: Don't do a lot of saving and loading just to see different choices and take the best one; part of the fun is to be able to deal with the consequences of your acts. This is Wasteland, not the Wonderland!
- Tactical Turn-Based Combat is very well executed. The ability to split your party, flank the enemy, get behind cover and start some massive shooting is pretty exciting. Grenades and rockets are a MUST for the fun and also to get out of trouble! Many of the encounters are very well made and challenging.
- Choices! It'll generally come in the form of you between two gangs, groups or communities fighting each other and you'll have to decide to partner with one, promote peace or kill them all. You don't get that feeling that your choices affect the game in the long run, but the short term is exciting enough, and you can decide key points in the middle of the story.
- Tough fights! Getting into a fight with 10 armed guys and/or many robots and getting out alive is pretty satisfying.
- The mood and post apocalyptic environment are very immersive
- Narrative and dialogues are well made and fun to read, despite some bad acting from some characters.
- Music: Some of the music stick into your head (at least in mine) and they set the tone very well.
- Random encounters in World Map become monotonous, but they are usually good and not very long.
- Quirks and Perks system added to the Director's Cut version may add some juice, especially Perks that you earn each 4 levels; You choose Quirks in the character creation and pretty much forget about them (unless you chose the lightning bolt...)
- Poor character progression; There is not enough gear to collect during the game. Armor/clothes especially, the different looks you can get is pretty much the same you could've got in the character creation. Some characters may spend quite a while with the same weapon. You do not perceive individual character evolution very well. In the beginning you can use Safecracking skill to try and open a safe with 61% chance; 50 hours in the game you can try and open another safe - looking exactly like that one - with 61% chance and a much improved Safecracking skill. You spend points and in many cases your experience doesn't change.
- Player Characters lack personality. See Pillars of Eternity for example, where you have main characters with their own personalities and agenda, plus the ability to hire and customize other characters. In Wasteland 2, You can create your characters, but they don't have personality, only the later recruits do, and it's still just generally some stereotype. Some characters are fun and interesting; many are not, and you won't care about them very much.
- Bugs: You'll se them all around, be in the original version or Director's Cut; floating weapons in the hands of your characters, camera that always resets its position once you change area, delayed or mute voice dialogues and so on... none of them ruins the gameplay though.
Overall, excellent game for CRPG fans. Played and loved Fallout? Then get this game now!

Осилил этот небольшой шедевр.
Что мы имеем? Довольно-таки качественную изометрическую рпг с возможностью влиять на события в апокалиптическом мире, отыгрывая роль бравых рейнджеров. На этом бы и закончил, но некоторые моменты заслуживают отдельного упоминания.
Вообще, игра полностью пропитана иронией и отсылками к культуре мира нашего реального. Тут и Данте с Вергилием , и Сатана с Рэмбо есть. Конечно, они существуют в контексте игрового мира. Здесь вы узнаете, что американцы не высаживались на луну, потому что у земли нет спутников; подхватите сифилис, найдете парочку книг про андроидов, которым, возможно, снятся электроовцы; ракетой сотрете с лица земли пару группировок...или нет? - Выбор за вами, кстати о нем.
Представим ситуацию - есть две враждующие группировки > вы можете либо помирить их, либо помочь одной уничтожить другую, либо уничтожить их обе. И так всю игру. Не нравится персонаж? Дорогие цены? Пристрели к чертям этого барыгу и забери у него все, потому что арсенал не пропадет никуда.
Большой выбор оружия, модификаций, кастомизация персонажей, отличный звук стрельбы, эффектные бои, отличная озвучка, множество выборов, которые ВЛИЯЮТ на многое.
И минусы есть (куда же без них) - слабый интерфейс, слабые модели персонажей, слабая анимация, среднее визуальное исполнение, карта мира, пара багов, долгие загрузки. Критично ли это тут? Нет.
В конце добавили олдскульный приемчик, который приятно удивил.
От меня, пожалуй, 8.0 - и эта игра, которую стоит пройти. Не ради крутого сюжета, не ради перестрелок, но ради интересных моментов, которые Wasteland 2 вам обязательно приподнесет и заставит улыбнуться.

Despite being a huge fan of Factorio and having enjoyed Big Pharma (although that was a little repetitive) I approached this game with an open mind.  I had no real expectations that it would be anything other than a relatively casual factory/automation sim.
Unfortunately it really isn’t a very good game, which is a shame since it could have been something quite entertaining.
I’ll summarise my thoughts as a serious of pros and cons:
Pros
•	It’s fairly cheap
•	Very easy to get up and running in the game – it’s quite simple and self-explanatory.
Cons
•	Far too simple and the automation side of things is very limited.  Loading things into boxes only seems to work some of the time so I still had weapons spilling out onto the floor.
•	The sound effects are horrendous.  I actually ended up switching off the sound after a few minutes of playing.
•	The controls are very clunky, having to drag and drop things that have fallen of conveyor belts one by one isn’t much fun.  Would also be nice if the conveyor belts etc remembered which orientation you last had them in, although that’s just personal preference really.
•	Very, very repetitive.  Really it shows it’s free to play roots and from what I can tell it’s been switched over to a paid model with few changes.
TLDR:
Don’t bother with this game.  If you really have an automation itch that needs scratching wait for Factorio to come on Steam (or buy it from their website now).  Failing that if you want something less complex (than Factorio) get Big Pharma.
