Don't like my review? Here's a recipe for Fish and Chips:
Ingredients
For the fries:
1 gallon safflower oil
4 large Russet potatoes
Kosher salt
For the batter:
2 cups flour
1 tablespoon baking powder
1 teaspoon kosher salt
1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper
Dash Old Bay Seasoning
1 bottle brown beer, cold
1 1/2 pounds firm-fleshed whitefish (tilapia, pollock, cod), cut into 1-ounce strips
Cornstarch, for dredging
Let's Start!
Heat oven to 200 degrees F.
Heat the safflower oil in a 5-quart Dutch oven over high heat until it reaches 320 degrees.
Using a V-slicer with a wide blade, slice the potatoes with the skin on. Place in a large bowl with cold water.
In a bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, salt, cayenne pepper, and Old Bay seasoning. Whisk in the beer until the batter is completely smooth and free of any lumps. Refrigerate for 15 minutes. Note: The batter can be made up to 1 hour ahead of time.
Drain potatoes thoroughly, removing any excess water. When oil reaches 320 degrees, submerge the potatoes in the oil. Working in small batches, fry for 2 to 3 minutes until they are pale and floppy. Remove from oil, drain, and cool to room temperature.
Increase the temperature of the oil to 375 degrees. Re-immerse fries and cook until crisp and golden brown, about 2 to 3 minutes. Remove and drain on roasting rack. Season with kosher salt while hot and hold in the oven.
Allow oil to return to 350 degrees. Lightly dredge fish strips in cornstarch. Working in small batches, dip the fish into batter and immerse into hot oil. When the batter is set, turn the pieces of fish over and cook until golden brown, about 2 minutes. Drain the fish on the roasting rack. Serve with malt vinegar.

Well, like most other Indie games on my games list, I found this game to be an absolute blast; it is well worth the amount of money I spent on it. Granted, it certainly doesn't have the longevity of The Binding of Isaac due to the lack of replay value, but I still enjoyed every minute of it.
Anyone who enjoys the 'Metroidvania' games ought to feel comfortable with this game. It's a mix of Action-RPG, platforming and basic Hack-and-Slashing; the controls and game physics are nicely responsive as well. This game is heavily inspired by some of the older game franchises such as Castlevania and Metroid; this is readily apparent in its map system which borrows heavily from the Game Boy Advance Metroid games.
Fans of both old and recent games will recognise some conspicuous game memes and themes, and rather than feeling like it is a rip-off, it fits nicely into the game while giving kudos (or otherwise) to the original games themselves.
All in all, yet another excellent game for those who enjoy old-school games.

I bought this game last year in a sale without actually playing the first one, completed it in co-op with a friend in around 3 hours which is very short but worth it for the price which I have paid. I believe that many people were dissapointed with this game's lenght when they paid the full price.
The shooting mechanics are solid and fun, the action is great, the soundtrack is great too and atmospheric.
The game has a very unique art style, the whole game looks like a gritty amateur homemade movie shot by an unseen cameraman running after the player, complete with lens flares, distortions, blurs and even a shaky cam while sprinting which can be turned off. It's so bad it's good.
The game has a serious and mature storyline which gets kind of repetitive.
It basically goes like this:
"Kane, come to Shanghai, I need your help."
A few moments and dead bodies later...
"Let's get out of here!"
The environments are detailed and look authentic.
If I were to review this on release it would be terrible due to it's lenght but for what I bought it I really can't complain
The game takes you throught 3 hours of of non-stop action which follows the same routine: cover, shoot, run, cover, shoot, run, repeat.
The game ends just as it was warming up and the ending is nothing thats worth mentioning.
The multiplayer is pretty fun and a mode called 'Arcade Mode' is included which is the Fragile Alliance multiplayer mode in singleplayer which is pretty fun and adds replay value.
The co-op is fun and worthwhile and may add to the replay value if you want to play with a friend
Overall this game is recommendable only if it's on a sale, it is worth no more than £5 due to the linear short and kind of predictable story. But there are some memorable moments and fun gameplay as well as a great visual style. The game is like a gritty action movie, short but sweet.
Good to complete on a boring night, buy it on a sale, play with a friend.
An undo feature would be nice even if it was only for your last move. I can't get the music to turn off either, the check box does nothing.

First of all I’d like to state that although I have clicked the ‘do not recommend’ option, my position toward the game is one of neutrality, neither dismissing it as unplayable nor condoning the exuberant praise that The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings seems to receive. The game has many redeeming features which shall be discussed shortly, however I feel as though there are just as many aspects that make the player underwhelmed with his/her experience. Secondly, I should say that this review builds upon my review of the original Witcher, which I have also reviewed on Steam, so I will be making a few comparative points in light of my disposition toward the first instalment in the series.
The Witcher 2 is driven extremely well by an engrossing narrative of political intrigue, racial prejudice and social injustice. Although the hybrid of Medieval and fantasy themes has been done before and is far from original, The Witcher 2 fully embraces the combination and creates a three-dimensional world with rounded and well thought-out characters that have their own individual agendas and follow them accordingly. There are a few plot twists along the way which I, of course, won’t mention, but these keep the narrative feeling fresh and engaging enough to continue playing til the end. I would say that the story, fresh from the pages of the original comics, is the main factor encouraging gamers to try this game.
Furthermore, we aren’t babysat. Nothing has been toned or dumbed down, which is preferable as too few games are made in modern times that have been made for an adult audience. We are shoehorned immediately into the action and I think that’s why the game puts many people off in the initial stages, claiming it to be unfriendly to new users to the series. I would argue this is a commendable feature however, as the harsh and merciless world of Geralt is directly reflected in the games content and contextual features.

The combat is far more engaging than in the original WItcher, due simply to it being more enjoyable. That being said, it is far from perfect. Battles range from being far too easy to far too hard far too quickly. We can quickly descend into the ‘trial and error’ form of gaming, constantly reloading previous saves in order to trial new ways of beating a difficult enemy. You can also only drink or create potions before a battle, not during it, which is more realistic I accept, but ultimately make many aspects of the combat frustrating. If I realise that a potion improving my vigor regeneration will help me win a battle in its opening stages, why not just let me drink one? The guise of this being ‘unrealistic’ simply makes alchemy and potion consumption frustrating; constantly saving, reloading and drinking potions before a known fight drastically effect the pace of the game and cause a stuttering experience that is cause for concern.
Perhaps the most disappointing characteristic of The Witcher 2 though is the world itself. I don’t mean its concept, I mean in its literal physicality. The areas you can explore are minuscule in terms of a 21st century RPG and the areas are quickly covered and recovered time and again. This makes the quests fairly limited, as there is only so much to do in a rather small gaming arena. Quests such as competing at arm wrestling, dice poker and brawling are irrelevant sideshows, yet if you take  these out you are only left with half dozen side quests in Act I and II respectively, and only a couple in the rather brief Act III. The overall longevity of the game is actually rather small, with a completed game taking between 16-30 hours (and that would be being generous). Essentially, there are a fair number of things to do in the world, but there really aren’t that many, certainly not deserving of high merit.
Quest exploration (in terms of the map and quest markers) is a rather touchy subject for both fans and haters of the series alike. Fans of this game state that the map and quest hints are intentionally cryptic because the game encourages you to explore yourself, and that we shouldn’t be spoon fed as gamers. Haters of The Witcher 2 point on the map and quest markers are totally useless, broken, and ruin the gaming experience completely. While I totally back the formers idea in theory, in practice the latter is nearer the truth. Quest markers as you approach them do sometimes teleport elsewhere without explanation, whilst the game map has no concept of ‘levels’, meaning that you may arrive at your destination only to discover that its several floors above you, a particular problem in Vergen. If the developers didn’t want to spoon feed the gamer and it was all about exploration and realism, why bother with a quest marker at all? Why, at the beginning of the majority of quests, does it tell us where to go? The quest exploration in the game seems to be a halfway house between attempting to help the gamer and encourage exploration, yet it ends up failing on both counts.
A problem with the critiques of the Witcher are of course, the critics themselves. Haters of the series have complained of a lack of fast travel. There is of course, no problem with that whatsoever. The developers have created a game that is very graphically impressive with some engaging characters, all of which they want you to experience. Removing fast travel will enhance the possibility of experiencing these things. Furthermore, the confines of the world itself is rather tiny meaning that fast travel is, for the large part, totally unnecessary anyway, as it does not take particularly long to run from one side of the map to the other.
One of my main bones of contention with the previous Witcher instalment was its ‘mature’ content. I stated in my review of that game that having maturity in the game does not make the game mature, and I think that unfortunately still applies to the sequel. I’m not sure if it’s because the translations from Polish to English are not clear enough, but much of the dialogue feels awkward, with characters using expletives, talking of♥♥♥♥♥♥and ‘ploughing’ for the sake of it. I think the developers could have included this content without making it so blasé, and it still seems as though the developers are trying to show off to kids and young teens. Nearly all dialogue refers to some obscenity and it becomes tiresome rather quickly. In fact, many of the characters are unlikeable because of this fact, most noticeably Roache and Ioveth. This does help serve the ‘shades of grey’ approach that the developers are going for, using a ‘lesser of two evils’ mindset, yet it is hard to play out an entire game without at least having a couple of likeable characters that we wish to associate with.  A positive note however, is that the ‘Sex Cards’ from the previous game have been removed, presumably because those who were amused or aroused by such content hit puberty and discovered internet porn.
Overall, the experience is okay and the narrative really is interesting. But the content of the game, although acceptable, really is not the experience that many exaggerated reviews on Steam that lavish the praise make out that it is. It has many issues that make it fall down. However, I would say that the commercial success of The Witcher 2 should allow the developers the funds to make The Witcher 3 into something special, reflecting an intriguing and exceptional storyline with equally impressive gaming content (for a change).

For the first half of the game, it feels great, the world design is on point, the world feels alive, and the characters are vibrant and insteresting. HOWEVER, for the second half of the game the world space becomes becomes one flat piece of land, and the intricate quests are boiled down into one tedious and annoying fetch quest. Also it is worth mentioning that the combat falls short, enemies move way to far on their (and so do you) some weapons are downright useless, some are overpowered, and the AI is horrible.
The party system starts out great, like a lot of things in this game, you create 4 rangers specify their skills and backstories to make each character unique. After creating these characters they become mere interchangable cardboard cutouts, they atribute nothing to the story. The companions you can find throughout the wasteland help combat this, most of these NPC companions are useless though, most become useless halfway through the game.
The attribute system is a joke, if you try to create 4 diversed characters with each a unique set of skills, you will have a bad time. The only useful attribute is Intelligence, as it determines the amount of skill points you get with each level. All of the others are effectively useless and only determine if you can see something, swing something a bit heavy, get your turn first (sometimes), or shoot your gun twice instead of once.
Wasteland 2: Directors Cut added a system in which you target a specific part of an opponets body, each part would have different effects on the enemy if you hit them in that spot, however each part makes your chance to hit significantly lower, to the point where it is useless, it becomes either, you MIGHT be able to shoot this guy's gun out of his hand, or you can just straight up kill him. The sysytem is interesting on paper but is just garbage in practice.
Here's hoping Wasteland 3 doesn't fail in the same way.

As a hardcore LOTR fan I brought it to myself to 100% this game all achievements and all. Its got fantastic gameplay and the true beauty of the game doesn't lie in its story but the relationships, nemesis and encounters you make with the orcs of the world as well as its polished yet similar gameplay.
The story itself was interesting to begin with, but became incredibly lacklustre with a lot of non-canonical inclusions such as Shelob being a woman and other nonsense towards the end although it was quite an interesting twist.The story of vengeance alongside with Celebrimbor was much stronger in the first title and gave more meaning to hunting down the dark lord as opposed to this title. I felt more distracted by the gameplay which is a double-edged sword, I was into the mechanics and exploring the interactivity of the world but I felt very disconnected from the story as it progressed.
There were damn great moments in the game but I was disappointed at how they were utilised as the hype from the trailers made me excited for certain parts ie Balrog fight but although it was a cinematic beauty to behold it wasn't very in-depth.
Despite the shortcomings of story, though it was alright, the gameplay makes up for it. A large variety of skills and playstyles allows you to play how you want whether thats being an absolute brutal machismo orc slayer to being a deadly ranged predator. I liked the introduction of the different armour sets from rare, epic and legendary tiers as well as the weapons and runes. It added more to the RPG realm of things rather than just having the base stuff to compell yourself with the action.
Introduction of the runes which give you different ratings which range from increased health, increased weapon damage or increased rare loot drops and mirian (currency) really give each player a unique way to play their way and also adds replayability to those who don't mind grinding for the good stuff or trying out different play styles with said runes.
The vastness of the world and the regions are amazing. Unlike the last title, the game is split into 5 regions which have their own unique environment, orc tribes and of course story missions. It keeps the game fresh from boring out from the same scenery.
THE biggest addition to this game is the introduction of fortress defense and creating an army hierarchy for your orcs. Monolith do a great job making you feel like a powerful overlord with how you determine which orcs are captains to warchiefs and overlords of your fortresses.
Fortress defense is incredibly fun to begin with, especially given the magnitude of ways you can defend and conquer a fortress. Nothing beats the feeling of seeing Talion signalling the breach and your orc camptains and ologs go forth and break down the walls to slaughter their fellow kinsmen.
^ Following on from fortress defense the final act is an incredible grind fest and it makes fortress defense damn tedious. Its one of those, "really cool really awesome things that get too repetitive after awhile".
LOOT BOXES the ever controversial feature which may have potentially murdered sales for WB is in my honest opinion something to not even worry about. Sure, it was an incredibly selfish move from WB to garner more money from a single player game and I must say it does make the individual think whether the publisher has any faith in the game at all.
I was incredibly skeptical at first but to be honest, loot boxes are NOT essential in completing this game. They are simply there for people who are too lazy to enjoy and grind the game for their loot and progression and also a business tactic employed by WB. I repeat YOU DO NOT NEED to worry about loot boxes ruining the experience.
In conclusion, Shadow of War is a fantastic title and sequel to Shadow of Mordor which has greatly improved on the experience and gameplay from the first one. It has fantastic gameplay and features which are makes up from the lacluckster story.

Shadow of War is a game that's only fun in spite of itself. It's fundamentally stuck between being a power fantasy (having Celebrimbor inside you) and being a narrative about raising an army; as a result, the game suffers from some pretty extreme cognitive dissonance. For example, you're returned to level 1 and the various skills are seperated into 1 main skill and 3 upgrades, so even though you might've beaten Shadow of Mordor, you can't start the game with shadow strike (on the topic of skills, you can only have one upgrade applied to a skill out of three, I have no idea why you wouldn't be able to equip them all...) There's also a system where your weapons have levels, what this means though it that you start getting gated by numbers. It doesn't matter how good you are if you can be downed in one hit and it takes dozens upon dozens to kill someone else. That's not that you're starved for loot throughout the game, but juggling loot is positively boring and getting it is irrelevant. You're pretty much only interested in getting higher numbers as well, so often times rarity is less important than weapon level.
Also, it's pretty ridiculous that you can't recruit captains that are a higher level than you. It makes the process of building an army not only significantly more tedious, but it makes almost no sense. When I go into "Elven Rage" TM I can one shot almost anyone in the world. I've done the stronghold takedowns without any companion orcs and I didn't even notice a difference. It genuinely feels like they just wanted to stop you from having fun. It's this weird moment where the game strives to be more simulation than game and it's just frustrating. Like, having bodyguards is great! Yet you can only get those weak weirdos that you'd rather ignore and they can just get one shot by a higher level target anyways! You're literally better off bashing your head against the wall and it doesn't even matter if that's your strategy, because lore-wise you cannot die, so there are never any penalties for just trying something over and over until it works, and I promise you that it will work most of the time.
Now that we're discussing it, let's address the lobotimized AI which are in dire need of corrective eye sight measures (at least on normal), the frustrating combat system (can't combo those large ogres that they added! Do you love spamming dodge after hitting one attack? What about when you go to stealth attack an enemy, but the game highlighted the wrong target, so you now look like a fool in front of your vulnerable target). I will say that the combat is made more fun if you turn off all the incredibly intrusive UI elements, but then you realize how much the game relies on just spoon feeding you info through the UI.
Combat also suffers from so many animations being canned/magnetic. Trying to dodge out of the way? Nah, I'm pretty sure you tried to vault over the person who cannot be vaulted over. Trying to attack a weak, normal orc to build your multiplier? I'm pretty sure you were targetting that berserker ready to counter you. Wanting to execute that captain? No, player, I'm positive you wanted to waste your high-powered attack on a weak, unimportant orc. It just feels bad to target the wrong orc with no indication that your attack would miss. Of all the things to magnetically target in the fray of battle, why wouldn't your attacks go towards the most important target? All of your actions in combat are only contextualized with how they interact with a specific orc, so you lose out on a lot of freedom that you might come to expect from other games.
All that being said, the game looks amazing and the gameplay loop of killing orcs is super satisfying. If you thoroughly enjoyed Shadow of Mordor, then I think you'll have fun with this, but I wouldn't recommend anyone spend more than $20 on this. I got it on sale, knowingly going into something that's hampered by its design, and I still feel like $30 was a bit too much. Honestly, you'd be better off saving your money and using the time you would've spent on this elsewhere, but I'm still playing it for what it's worth, so take that however you will.
Also the fact that you have to manually locate points of interest after climbing to the top of a tower is just dumb. It just makes it even more tedious, especially considering you can locate things through walls/the environment, so you'll hover over a random part of a mountain to mark a collectible that's on the other side of it. It's almost insulting.
Speaking of insulting, they changed the parkour system, but arguably for the worst. I don't think it's up for debate that the climbing system of Shadow of Mordor was too easy to the point of irrelevance. In order to address this problem I just now prescribed to it, they added this ability where you just jump up halfway/the rest of the way up a climbing thing. It's nice cause it does save time, but I just wonder why they didn't make something more fun. They recognized that methodically climbing by just holding up sucked, but they just lowered the time you had to do it! You also have a double jump, but you can only trigger it after you jump off something, so it's more like a single air jump. All of the movement is stuck in this pre-fab hell and it's not just climbing either! Remember that eleven agility ability where you tap A to speed up after hurdling something? You move faster when you do in that Shadow of War, but it still ultimately restricts your fast movement to the randomly placed props around the world. I understand that building a large world to navigate is challenging, but instead of having this magnetic parkour/instant climb/only jump where we let you system I think it'd be better if they added a spiderman 2 style web slinging movement style or at least a Prototype/Hulk: Ultimate Destruction wallrun system. Anything to increase the fluidity of movement would be great, but like every other element of this game they made it function to the bare minimum standards, and even then it bugs out in funny/inconvenient ways. It's just disappointing.
It's not that I think the game should be harder, easier, or something else entirely. Going into this, I knew it would be worse because of all the lootbox stuff, but there are some design decisions that are baffling at best and malicious attempts at manipulating their audience at worst. Sure, it's not awful, but buyers beware (and have a good day!)

The Binding of Isaac is one of those games that may seem weird from the outside looking in, but ultimately this is a game that beneath it's initial weirdness is truly an amazing experience of a game. The basis of the game is discovery at its core, to see new things, try combinations you may not have thought to try before. The change between runs (for better or for worse) creates these new experiences, new challenges that can occur by circumstance ensuring that you don't always get a guarenteed victory, that each victory is earned. It's a game that is alot bigger than it seems at its core. The game is small, true, but it holds so much value in its ability to change each time its played that its worth coming back to, whether you're barely at your 4th win or you've attained platinum god! The game is by no means perfect, due to flash limitations it suffers in certain areas, but if you look past these things (most of which really aren't that big) you end up with a game that is spectacular! I highly recommend this game as one of my personal favorites. Try it out, and see what waits for you in the unknown depths below.

I got this game in a bundle, and was unsure whether or not I wanted to keep it. After reading numerous comments and reviews about MKH, I decided to give it a try - and was really happy to get a chance to play through it.
If you enjoy Japanese-themed swordsmanship with challenging technical mechanics, fighting mobs of enemies, and grinding for upgrade systems, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are fantastic - the detail in the different character models is very good, and the fighting special effects is well-done. The music and sounds are great, adding a high level of intensity to the brutal, fast-paced gameplay. The cutscenes are short but sweet, and add an anime-like feel to the narrative. Although fairly basic, the story is decent enough to keep you interested in the plot (although the fighting mechanic definitely is the shining gem for this game).
The controls can be challenging to learn - especially if you do not use a controller. The move list and tutorials are helpful, however, the default keybindings make keyboard play unnecessarily difficult. That being said, I completed several playthroughs without a controller (I will be attempting to complete it on the hardest difficulty with a controller, since keyboard play is far too brutal), so it is possible if you have no alternative. The learning curve is moderate to challenging because the later stages (and higher difficulties) really require you to utilize more advanced moves - like countering and parrying. If you cannot do this in the later levels (and/or difficulties), you will not get very far.
Each "level" consists of multiple waves, followed by a boss fight. Every enemy type follows a particular attack pattern that you can memorize and use to your advantage, adjusting your playstyle accordingly. For each kill you make, enemies may drop health or experienc orbs - experience is added to your total pool, which can then be used in the abilities store (you can access this at any time by pressing ESC).
There are a variety of things you can unlock and upgrade - in particular, improving your health and "katana energy" gauge (used to perform moves with your sword) is crucial to survival and chaining more combos. Improving your normal attacks will allow you to do more damage, refill more of your energy bar (hand-to-hand attacks refill your energy), and increase attack range, among a multitude of other things. You can also unlock a deadly counterattack, which is essential for defeating higher-tier enemies, and even bosses. Special attacks can also be unlocked and improved, however, it is entirely possible to complete at least one playhrough without further enhancing these things (it will just make it more difficult).
For achievement hunters, it can be both very fun and very lengthy to unlock every achievement in the game.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun, and technical players will appreciate the depth of the possible fighting controls and combinations. Definitely give this game a try.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game by Dean Dodrill (also known as Noogy). It is a metroidvania styled game with RPG elements. The game is very well done and that actually surprised me, since it was created by one man. The smooth and simple, yet satisfying gameplay had me addicted for several hours. The story isn't amazing, but it is pretty good and had me wanting to keep playing. The art style is very beautiful and hand-drawn. I have always loved when hand-drawn graphics are used in games. I loved the soundtrack and I still listen to it. The voice acting isn't the best, but is better than some games out there. As I mentioned earlier, the gameplay is very smooth, fun, and pretty easy to play. The game is basically a button masher, but there are also a couple combos you can use. It isn't a very hard game, though I'm sure it is difficult on Hard mode (obviously).
The story is a decent length and there are also side quests you can do, aswell as exploring, finding treasures, and finding the 12 characters from other indie games. I got about 15 hours from doing the story, some of the side quests, exploring, and level grinding (you don't really need to level grind in this game, it just helps). I personally hope that Dean Dodrill starts working on another game, and I'm sure it will be  just as good as this one. I fully recommend this game to anyone that wants a simple, yet fun game with a decent story. Even after beating the story, I still find myself coming back and playing this game. If I had to give this game a rating, I'd give it a 9/10.

Simplistic, straightforward gameplay that rewards and progresses based on your experimentality. Simply, you have resources that you put into "input machines" which become new resources. These new resources mix in various combinations with other resources with the ultimate goal of creating weapons which you can then sell. However, this isn't just about experimenting with resources, it's about efficiency and automation and your ultimate goal is to have a fully functioning factory that requires very little input from the player. Slap on a slightly, command and conquer-esque Soviet aesthetic and you have March of Industry.
Honestly, I find the core concepts to be a ton of fun and it's actually rather engaging and addicting trying to find new weapon combinations but there is just not enough content here for any type of extended play. Graphically, it's your usual 16 bit, pixelized look and the game becomes rather challenging rather quickly. Thankfully, the game isn't overly punishing and you should be able to rectify any mistakes you make without too much fear of having to start over. Then again, if you make a lot of mistakes then you've very little choice but to start your business all over again.
After extended playing, I've found there are a couple of negative issues. First, is the sound can get really annoying really quickly. If you sell items one by one, you have the "narrator" looping so you'll probably end up turning the sound off altogether anyway. Secondly, when resources get bunched up in your input machines, they get cluttered really badly and you have to select the resources one by one... which is sort of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ It'd be nice if the dev could add a double click feature which lets you select all of one resource in a general area or something. The worst problem is an almost complete lack of replayability. Sure you are suggested to restart your factories multiple times but what's the point? If I didn't enjoy the core game concepts so much, this would almost be a complete deal breaker.
All in all, it's simple and it's fun. 9.99 isn't a bad price but for the current content, I'd like to see that price go down to about 4.99 or there to be some additional content because the current version of the game can be beat in only a few hours.. Slightly recommended.

The two things that got me first interested in March of Industry was the theme and the gameplay mechanic. While the theme was kind of disappointing I had fun with the game. If you like assembling complex "machines" and games that rely heavily on crafting you should enjoy March of Industry. If after looking at the game you are interested in it I think you should enjoy it. With the ability for anyone to create their own materials and weapons there are a lot of possibilities for the game.
A couple issues keep March of Industry from being great though.
I wish the game gave you more control over how materials moved through your factories. Materials tend to get stuck in the conveyor belts too often. If you had more control over when materials would be released into your machines this problem could be solved. While this issue doesn't ruin the game it is kind of a hassle to keep unclogging your machines.
The other issue is that the game doesn't really have much of a structure to it. The game doesn't really have traditional missions. You pretty much just build assembly lines which get you more money to build more assembly lines. Once you reach a certain amount of money you can move to a new factory that provides an additional machine but that is the only thing that changes. If you can't get enjoyment out of making assembly lines without working towards a goal you might tire of the game kind of quickly since it can get repetitive at times.
If you like the game's concept and these type of games I think you will enjoy March of Industry.
Note: I received a free review copy of the game from the developer.

If you can get past the massive amount of information necessary to play this game, Natural Selection 2 is a game that will have you constantly asking yourself why this game hasn't caught on to a more massive community.
The game sets you up with two teams, you're either soldiers, or aliens, and your goal is to take out the opposing team's main base. Each team is led by a commander, or should be unless you're set up with a team of players uncooperating with each other. As the game progresses, you will be pitted up against the opposing team to gain ground. Gaining ground is the key to gaining resources, which in turn, can be used to level you up. Soldiers can purchase better/improved weapons, jetpacks, and even control big-body mechas. Aliens can use their resources to gain perks, or further evolve into stronger aliens. The commanders have a wide field of vision and can/must communicate at all times with the team, or risk getting overwhelmed and lose territory crucial to success. The Commander can also use their resources, along with the teamwork of fellow players, to provide more tools and other benefits to aid the team in taking control.
The maps are big and intricately designed. The gameplay is refreshing, which is in part due to aliens' movement options; their ability to walk on walls, through shafts, and fly. Which in turn, provides a unique experience for both players.
The game is great. The only downside is that the game requires more power than what some casual PC owners have (which is why the game hasn't taken over in the gaming community as much as we'd like). Also, this game definitely requires communication as you'll definitely need eyes all over the place. Getting overwhelmed is a very real possibility, and disadvantages can snowball into major one-sided games. I love this game, but just know going into this game, that communication and cooperation are a must.

Pros:

I have been a fan of this series for a while, so my bias is in favor of this game. While I feel they addressed this game very well I will address some topics that may want to be heard about.
Grinding:
While, yes, this game requires a decent amount of grinding to get all the towers (Paying for them just unlocks them quicker) the time grinding gives the player a sense of enjoyment of progressing through the ranks of all of the towers and also allows the player to learn at a controlled pace without overdoseing on all the tower upgrades.
Lag/Crashes:
Not much to say here. Some random lag spikes that really don't affect the game that much are just annoying more than a hinderence. Crahses are rare, but do need to be fixed.
Hackers:
Oh boy here we go. Now this is something BTD Battles has always had a problem with. Hackers will cause themselves to become invincible to your attacks which will then cause you to instantly lose unless they lag out. To try to combat this there is a "report player" button. However Ninja Kiwi should really try to put a stop to hacking if there is any possible way.
Overall a well structured game. Rating: 8.5/10

March of Industry: Very Capitalist Factory Simulator Entertainments; (Yes that is the full title) is a Unity Powered game and what I would call ‘fit-for-mobile’ which means it takes just a touch more than the average amount of brain power required to make beef stroganoff. Not entirely a game that plays itself, it requires some input from the player as they shuffle about purchasing resources from the shop to turn into ‘other’ resources which can be combined to make resources that… make weapons, but watch out for those traffic jams on your conveyor belts!
What makes what exactly is free for experimentation as you move between Copper, Tin, Vodka and of course ‘this is memes’ Potato Age (Think Age of Empires or Empire Earth but far simpler). For those who are not ‘in-the-know’ with this style of game, expect minimal to no hand holding throughout as newcomers are going to be dissuaded rather quickly by the underwhelming lack of information given through the wholly vast tutorial phase which breaks down as such; ‘Purchase Machine A; Purchase Resource A, Well you are good to go! Have fun!’. It does not help that the actual ‘HELP’ menu button consists of nothing more than the basic controls, a youtube/twitch.tv link and most bizarrely; the credits for the Developers of the game? Surely that could have been  set on a separate menu titled say.. Oh I don’t know.. CREDITS. So for first time users, be prepared to be very lost and confused. So anyway..
..You construct your Assembly lines by trading resources and weapons for cash which in turn is used to buy better equipment like conveyor belts, guard rails, resource processors and et cetera. You can also expand your work space by purchasing additional rooms. What this all breaks down into; is one massive rubix cube sort of puzzle that you solve over a prolonged period of time, but once you have solved said puzzle there is not really a whole lot else to do except to do it all again in New Game+, rinse and repeat. Now one could expect micro-transactions in a game such as this but the Developer seems to have had good sense by not only dressing an arbitrary puzzle solver in a post decedent soviet Russian theme but has skipped over the inclusion of an easily integrated micro-transaction system in a game that just screams out for one, altogether. So kudos for the sky being blue and not coloured in money I suppose, as they felt it was a necessary selling point on the Steam store front page, but $9.99 for the admission price of such a fundamentally basic game, this is still rather steep for all that it is and all that it is not. Look, it is not a horrible game by any means, there are far worse and the game does have a sense of humour that helps alleviate the otherwise mundane atmosphere of staring at 8 bit pixels for any great length of time, but this will inevitably fade and your eyes will glaze over as you hear the same regurgitated lines of dialogue over and over while playing for extended periods. NOW PERK UP, You are reading a review not playing this game but now you can sense the nature of the beast. It is recommendable on the basis that it is an interactive puzzle that has a unique if not isolated identity, but not much more than that. Is it satire? is it social commentary like Papers Please, Perhaps? but that is for another debate.
This is going to be a game for a very niche demographic of people who have little to do or a few minutes in between waiting to do something better. Now I must say… Congratulations for making it through my review Comrade, literary ingestion expanded Comrade! (Did I mention the incredibly obnoxious voice over throughout the game that grinds on your ears within the first minute that will never, EVER cease. Well now I have.) Now I am off to play something slightly more potato. Ha, I can finally meme. I feel dirty.

In terms of quality it's simply amazing as for an indie production. It's pretty original: a FPS and RTS crossover. Each team's commander plays an RTS game, the rest of the players are the units she/he commands. Well, in fact you're completely free to do what you want, so you can ignore the tasks given by the commander. Sometimes it's necessary as the situation changes so rapidly that no commander can react fast enough. Suggesting tactical or strategic moves to commander by the "commanded" troops is common. Because of the RTS elements the game is difficult at the beginning but the community is, generally speaking, forgiving and helpful so there's nothing to worry. You just need to learn a bit about game's mechanics (resources, different structures, etc.). FPS side tends to be very intense. If you're good in - lets say - Killing Floor or Counter Strike, you're good to go. Just follow more experienced players until you'll get the feeling for the strategic situation. And only then you'll start to really appreciate the game as skirmishes and your actions will gain deeper tactical meaning. Sometimes victory is secured only by a smart or skillful manouvre of only one player. Not necessary a commandr. Downsides? Well, I don't like to play as an alien because it doesn't feel like a standard FPS... But this diversity may be an advantage for someone else.

Just wasn't my cup of tea in terms of how they delivered it, I guess. Unskippable cutscenes and me getting the gist of a cutscene within seconds don't mix. Listen, it's just your usual cliché fantasy good vs. evil. The story isn't why you'd play a game like this, anyways.
Gameplay is my biggest issue with this game. I'm not awful at RTS or RPG games, but when it comes to real-time without a slow down or pause feature, you usually end up with a management issue *if you're not good at that kind of stuff*. Me, personally, I'm not but I still enjoy RTS games a lot, even if I'm not as good as others. Point is, the RTS and RPG sections in these games suck for their own reasons and it's probably because this game is a lot older and extremely flawed to the very bone.
The RTS sections are your basic Warcraft-esque format. You build buildings, you use your workers to slave away for resources, you slowly build up your army and buy the upgrades for each unit. My issue with the RTS in this game isn't the actual playing of it(aside from the horrible AI but that's not worth going into), it's the balancing around it and how the RTS sections are usually significantly more difficult than the RPG sections. The biggest issue I can point out for anyone is that when you alert an enemy, they run off to their base *BUT* unless you specifically dedicate yourself to white magic boons, you *cannot* catch up to the enemy because virtually every single ♥♥♥♥ing unit in the game having  same movement speed, which means if they start running before you can initiate combat and you're too early in on the map to have a sizable army, you're screwed. They're going to send group after group until you lose. No, I didn't find *any* hero up to the point I was at that had the movement speed buff. Aside from that, you end up building up a big enough army force to wipe out area after area because the AI is so bad and requires micromanaging(as in they don't every move to the exact spot you tell them to, they get lazy and stop moving just before the area you set them to move to) and it got pretty tedious for me. It's bad enough that you have to deal with relentless unlimited enemies, you also have to deal with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI. The upside to the game, though, is that when you leave a map and re-enter it resets, but this removes all buildings, units, and resets your map progress. Yeah, ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I had to do this for Godwall because that area is just stacked against you. My first army trigger was about 20+ enemies that came to wreck my whole base and you can't even afford to fight that many guys earlier on into the map.
The RPG sections are pretty standard and up until the point that I quit(Mulandir), it was pretty fun. You can have up to five(5) hero summon, plus your avatar(main character). The gameplay is pretty self explanatory(baldur's gate as a reference point). I, personally, found the highlight being skill and stat management since equips require certain stats and skills, unless you want to use the bare-minimum heavily underpowered level-requirement equips. Skills also seemed a bit weird since you clearly can't spec your character to use every magic and every weapon time but at the same time, doing combat + magic doesn't really work out well since the requirements for skill-ups go up faster than you can put up your stats. Some of the sections are extremely unbalanced, and this is why I quit where I did. Mulandir enters you into a place where you first encounter demons, and it's a ♥♥♥♥ing mess of a place. Overpowered gargoyles and medusas scattered all over the place and annoy demons with DoT damage that is more dangerous than the actual demons. I had found everything up until that point so I didn't miss any special characters, and items only help *slightly*, but my party got destroyed in under a minute in each encounter. It's just a mess, and this isn't the only place this happens either because the game only gets exponentially more difficult, to the point where in some RTS sections most of my units were more or less useless. Whisper is a big mess, too. So is the undead-horde segment before Whisper.
Problems with the game overall are just things like slow movement speed or slow unit spawn. The latter is the cause of the rune power mechanic, which is essentially that if you spawn too many units in a short amount of time, you'll run out of rune power and it takes *forever* to regen it. It's uh... Yeah, it's pretty ♥♥♥♥ing counter intuitive to a ♥♥♥♥ing RTS, huh? It's what made me lose so many maps too because the enemies *ARE NOT* limited. They are literally limitless, they send group after group until you lose or leave the map, that's it.
It's not a terrible game but it's horribly tedious, boring, and unbalanced/flawed. It got to a point where it just stopped being fun because it was just another slog of a game to push through. It's an old game, sure, but that's NEVER an excuse. For me, this was just a straight up bad game overall. I'm going to play the second one because *apparently* that's a lot better and improves on the first a lot. I didn't play the expansions, either. Get this game on sale or it isn't worth it, I'd say.

First of all I did not play the original Wasteland. But when I heard that Brian Fargo, who is responsible for the best games in the world (Fallout 1 and Fallout 2), wants to make a Wasteland 2 I was immediately interested. I bought Wasteland 2 but it waited a long time before I found the time to play and in the meantime a Director's Cut edition was published, which I received for free.
This game is not Fallout. But it is an awesome game nonetheless. It combines the RPG with tactics game (with more tactics element that RPG) but in a better way that Fallout Tactics did it. The game is hard. The combat is challenging and you always have less point in the skill that you need to use right now.
The plot is good with some nice plot twist at the end of the game. I was surprised as it all turned out. I enjoyed the grim future of the post-nuclear wasteland. People are struggling to maintain a decent life and you cannot help everybody. Sometimes you must choose who will live and who dies. And there are a lot of mad inhabitants (just as in Mad Max series and Fallout series you could tell that something in the radiations affects the brain cells). As I love a post-nuclear setting this was one of the best example of this unfriendly world.
The graphic could be better but for me it is not a major issue in a game like this. But it is done in a way to emphasis the dark world you are playing and that was done great. Personally I think that there could be more portraits. The sounds and voice acting are satisfying. Adrian Gordon wins the award for the best performance, he was outstanding. Just listen to his 'RAIN JERKS?!'. And last but not least the music. For me it was excellent. It caught the climate of the game perfectly. And I recommend to listen to the 'Cries of a Dead World' by Miracle of Sound (it is in the credits).
It is not the best game in the world but I rate it 9/10. Play it. Play it now!

Wasteland 2 is not, perhaps, a great game. A thousand tiny things swirl around inside it, each bothering me a bit; like the aribitrarily obscure solutions to some puzzles.
But whenever I play Wasteland 2, those problems melt away. I love it. It's one of my favorites, actually.
It's very much like the early fallout games crossed with Fallout Tactics (which I thought had lots of promise but didn't play well.) It's descended from Fallout's grandpappy, too, which makes for nice continuity nods if you played the C64 original.
Wasteland 2 is a squad based RPG largely set in the ruins of post-nuclear Arizona. Your squad of 4 Desert Rangers set out to find the meaning of mysterious radio signals, and uncover a sinister plot that could end the world a second time. In practice, the plot is a bit flimsy, but it provides a decent core for the weird people you'll meet in the wasteland-Pistol Packin' Priests being my personal favorite.
Besides combat, which plays out nicely, you'll need a wide variety of skills to traverse the wasteland-Conversational skills to talk your way to the better solutions, brute force to smash walls, computer science, toaster repair and so on.
I find myself having a hard time coming up with more to write. Please, if you're here take the time to watch the videos above. My time spent should tell you that I'm no casual when it comes to this game.
As much as I love it, the price is pretty steep right now. Wait until it goes on sale. It's good, but I don't think you'll get your money's worth at full price.

Ok, let me hit the thumbs down button and tell you why I really enjoyed this game.... ^^
I didnt really think Id ever be in a position where Id play a game all the way thru (of above single digit hours completion time), find myself really liking it, and then go and give it a negative review. Altho to be more accurate, a positive review really, with a thumbs down.
Shadow of War is almost the perfect example of how to do a sequel. You take your tried and tested formula, tweak it, add some depth, address some short comings of its predecessor, and you have got yourself a nice sequel! And they pretty much did it.
+Graphically its a step in the right direction. Incredible detail on actors and weapons, adequate everywhere else. A ton of options to tweak so you should be able to get smooth performance on modest systems. FYI Game ran brilliantly in 4K with even a notch increase on the res scaling, absolutely maxed out, spent most of my time in the 50s (capped to 58 for GSync), on an OC 1080ti.
+Gameplay - its more of the same from the first, with refinements. Getting around is a breeze, even leaping up structures is done in a snip. Combat is a near mirror image of the first, just some improvements to animations.
+Nemesis System. Easily the biggest improvement over the first. Named mobs are more interesting, and more deadly. Ambushes, betrayals, and more keep you on your toes.
+A huge range of options to tweak your journey - turning off hints, visual queues, various HUD elements, etc.
=Im not big on the Story in general, but even without being a buff I found it pretty flimsy.
=The Menus could do with some streamlining, ie getting into Army screen from map takes too long, an option to mass craft gems etc.
-As much as the mini intros/speeches can add more character, an option to disable them would be great. Being in the middle of an intense battle and having a string of 30 second VOs one after the other is irritating.
-The Fight Pits could *really* do with an "X2" and a "skip" option.
-MICROTRANSACTIONS.
-So good it needs to be mentioned twice, microtransactions!
Despite enjoying this game,
despite my opinion that what people do with their own money is their business, the way that MTs feature in this game is too devious to ignore. First of all, make no mistake, its gambling. Not sorta, but absolutely, gambling! And again, I actually dont care it exists or that some may want to do it. My issue is that they deny thats what it actually is.
what ultimately made my decision to give this great game a thumbs down, is some of the things up for sale. You can buy, with real money, XP boosts that tick down in REAL TIME. *NO* WARNING on the purchase screen (*there is a tooltip sometimes on the load screen that suggests to only use them when you can make the most of them - SSD/M.2 FTL?). So even if you "pause" the game to take a call, or you are watching a nice cut scene, or real life happens and you quit out - doesnt matter!! Tick tock, tick tock. That is just disgusting to me.
So. Great game, I recommend it really on sale and I implore you to refrain from using real money for any MT in game. They are not needed to complete the game and I would hate to support this particular implementation of MTs.

A lot of complaints about this game, but most of the negative reviews are totally garbage. Let me put this simple: if you enjoyed Shadow of Mordor, YOU ARE GOING TO LOVE Shadow of War. This game is an overall improvement over the previous one. Animations looks better, the skill tree have a broader range of situational and playstyle skills, graphics looks better, Nemesis system is improved, building up your army is a lot of fun and meaningful and you get to fight a damn Balrog!
The story has it's flaws, I can admit that, but in the end it all makes sense and you won't feel disappointed. In my opinion, they've should removed the chapter division and just follow the entire storyline as just one big act. This division is what is giving the impression that act 3 is rushed, because well... it is! But just because it was divided into this way.
Gear system is plain and simple and once you get legendaries sets, all you are going to do is to improve them completing some challenges, because other than the looks, everything else after you complete some sets, are expendable. But it is way better than Shadow of Mordor. It has more complexity and it is more meaningful, especially at the start of the game.
Microtransactions are the biggest trouble in my opinion, but you can always accept the EULA without checking the checkbox and disable the online features and the microtransactions. Or if you want the online features, you can enable it and just use mirians (in-game currency) to buy the silver boxes if you ever feel in need of some Epic level orcs into your army. But all of that is skippable and doesn't have a pay-to-win factor integrated, which makes it forgivable.
All in all, this is a fun and enjoyable game that is going to hook you in even after you've beat the game. Don't take it for granted just because of the microtransactions. I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥too, until I bought and played the entire storyline.

Also there seems to be a slight delay in responsiveness in the controls as to make blocking and time sensitive moves difficult especially when combined with the speed and lack of visual info telling you an enemy is going to attack. Doing combos is something I havn't quite figured out due to much of the above points.
It looks good for a budget title and its all pleasant ofcourse the shaders and shadows could be better but the models do look good and its generally visually fine. Story is beside the action and simply is there to guide you in between arenas while still offering some intrigue.  Unfortunately with some attacks and during some occasions the budget can really show as swords or attacks may occasionally pass through either the player or enemies without hitboxes coming into contact and at times getting hit when you felt you were not in range partially thanks to hitboxes and to the camera angle, especially during the final boss fight.
Its extremely difficult and it feels alot of that difficulty is from the clunky controls, animation, but also because of the very nature that it was designed to be pretty hard.  This isn't Ninjai Gaiden Sigma for sure but its an interesting title thats very fun once you get into it. Unlike most other games that arn't very good objectively this one is very fun to deal with the negative points and still overcome and win. Its a challenge thats actually fun to have a try at and there are uprgrades you can purchase to make the game a bit easier but its really only a bit. You really have to master the controls to get by but even upon mastering them it dousn't make the game easy.
The games also very short and dousn't over stay its welcome. If it droned on and on or was really any longer it would definetly stop being a fun game but thankfully its reasonably short and theres a decent spread of enemies and content throughout the game and a reasonable ramp up in difficulty.  Again its a budget title and Japanese. Its not exceptionally good but its a cozy game and if you can overcome the adverse controls I think most people could really enjoy this game for what it is.
What it isn't is a $40 to $60 game where the devs promise 10 hours or more of gameplay and all it is is repatitive junk thats not even on the same level as this game.
Its a short, $10 game with alot of replay value but its very repatitive but very challenging as to require you to get better to pass further on in the game and if you don't get better you simply don't move on.
One thing to remember is Japanese games are hard. Compare God of War to Ninja Gaiden Sigma/Black and most any other western to jap game. Dark Souls is another Jap game. And even if they arn't objectively good in many aspects these are all games that are regarded generally as good games even though they may have less polish than Western games. Its because of the real visceral challenges and the depth that you have to go into to beat or truly take advantage of the games design. Thats where alot of fun is in vidya, in depthfull challenge.
TL:DR Its not perfect, but if you work with it and do your part it can be a fun and very challenging game with enough depth to give you 2 or more playthroughs while still being a cheap game.

Absolutely gorgeous and incredibly fun! I haven't had such fluid, fun, and badass-feeling combat... ever. It's also just generally one of the best action RPGs I've ever played, with some of the most gorgeous graphics you've seen. If you're not a fan of the furry/etc. culture that the character design revolves around, don't worry... you won't even notice as you play (I'm not and I have enjoyed it immensely... the characters being animals actually adds a ton of charm to the game that regular humans wouldn't be able to bring) . You will feel like a combo-based-combat god even if you have no experience in the genre, but there is still a good amount of challenge. I highly recommend playing on the hardest difficulty (with the intention of trying to never die, i.e. true "hardcore" or "ironman" -type playing) right off the bat... it will make the game much more rewarding and the learning curve is really quite an enjoyable experience.
Some of the voice acting is the only thing I felt could use a little work, but it was only every now and then and you get used to it pretty quickly. For the most part the voices fit the characters pretty well, and the *entire* game is voice acted, so it's a minor issue.

This game is a fantastic blend of RTS and FPS with the players choice dictating how they play. The Alien and Marine teams aren't exactly equal as the Marines have more ranged weapons and the Aliens have melee and close ranged attacks along with two or three ranged attacks and also have a greater utilization of the map as they can climb walls and enter vents. The commander plays it like an RTS yet each unit is an actual player. It's a fantastic game that requires some team play and lets you really get invested in each match. You will soon find the team and weapons that suit you and you'll fit comfortabley right into the game. If you ever played Tremulous or Gloom, which are amazing mods based off the same concept as they were the first to try this split team dynamic, then you will certainly enjoy this updated version of the classic style of FPS.

The game has very nice graphics, that could be improved on, as well nice smooth controls when skulking around (pun intended) as you don't have to constantly hold down CTRL like in 'AVP' although you do find yourself stuck on little objects a fair bit ,and it is a challenge to sometimes get on the roof of a room however I'm not saying that is a good idea as you will have trouble getting to your enemy before you get shot, making it sometimes difficult to get away. Although due to the small objects that are included you can't easily 'blend' with the wall. You can, however, easily use the small pieces to do nice leaps from wall to wall to accelerate you.
That was only talking about the graphics and skulk though! As the aliens (or Karah) you can evolve into different types; flying, slashing, 'tank' and (the cute) support, allowing you to also evolve to the new types, each set with separate abilities.
The marines look like they have it tough but in fact they do not as the marines being equip with an arsenal of ranged weapons, along with jet-packs, allow them to dodge attacks and kill something before it get to them...usually.
It may seem that the game has a variation of 2 gametypes to play; fast and 'abusive' or slow and stealthy, but there is also a third variation. The commander! Without the comm (commander) you will be screwed, and without a good comm you will also be screwed, as a comm on either team are required to be able to place support structures and upgrade you. This means that if you are more of a good strategy, top down, player then you don't have to go looking for another game, honestly its like 2 games in one!
There's one major floor with some of the levels though; some are too wide. This makes it nearly impossible for the Karah to win. There are some rooms where the moment the marines capture it, the karah aren't able to even enter the room, as they are to wide open. There is also glitches in the maps that stop the comm from placing connection nodes called "cysts", these cysts are the Karah's way of 'transferring energy', where you are meant to be able to.
An annoyance is that sometimes you will get base rushed and that's the end of the game...no joke, once your base is attacked within the first 15 minutes you are placed in a permanent disadvantage. This problem is in many games, though, and can not be solved by devs. So nearly every player on this game has a mutual understanding not to EGBR (Early Game Base Rush) so it is currently quite rare to see a base rush within 15 minutes or so of a match starting.
Another major problem is the difficulty curve. Due to the fact that there is practically no training, trying to understand how to play properly and learn how to 'dodge bullets' is simply not possible. The training in the game is mostly just a movement tutorial as the bots are very...unresponsive. Although there is a video tutorial which helps when trying to understand the games mechanics.
In total NS2 is well balanced and if you stick with the game long enough it, will end up being incredibly fun. It only takes about 1 hour to fully understand the game... well for me it did.
I almost forgot to mention the loading times take about 5-10 minutes....

Have you ever thought about taking on the Hong Kong underworld in a quest for vengeance, money and lost love? Well then this might be the game for you.
This game takes everything the predecessor did and improves upon it immensely. The game play is much more responsive and fluid. The array of weaponry at your disposal really packs a punch adding to the heart pounding action you find from pretty much constant shoot outs.
The story is winding and epic, with many great set pieces and extended firefights. The environments are more vivid and feel alive. The whole game takes place throughout Shanghai, from slums to sky scrapers each level feels unique and feels totally different. The characters are much more fleshed out and defined, there isn’t a huge cast of secondary characters but this game is focused almost exclusively on the main duo and their exploits in a very short period of time.
I like this game and I had a good time working my way through everything. It is not the best game I have ever played but I did have a better time with it than the original. The one drawback is the sudden ending, but right up to that point everything was pretty solid.
I would recommend this over the original but I still can’t recommend this at full price. Pick this up on sale, play it for a while but don’t bother completing it as you will be left with a bittersweet taste.

Possibly one of the best cinematic stories in a video game delivered by a uniformly excellent cast (notably Alex Hernandez is standout as the iconic Lincoln Clay with Gordon Greene unforgettable as the tortured, conflicted Father James). The world building is original and memorable in its brutal depiction of late Sixties America culture and society. Cut scenes are deeply moving in places as the motion capture is superb in capturing the subtle nuances of the actors’ performance.
Developer Hangar 13 and its publisher 2K are to be applauded for the creative risks they take in a tough Triple A market – this is video game storytelling as art.
BUT! Like Mafia 2 (again great storytelling) the gameplay itself feels sooooo undercooked. This game needed another year in the oven. Despite some great flourishes in places, like NPC chatter and behaviour or sound design and music, so much of the game feels incomplete. The AI is dumb, downright terrible in places.  Many assets in the game world (particularly the buildings) look unfinished or simply ugly.  The mission design is samey, repetitive with no quick travel resulting in boring, tedious slogs across the generous map size.
Despite these flaws I’m playing through the game because I actually care about the characters and the story and on this basis it’s a recommendation from me – just keep expectations low for gameplay.

Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days is by far the hardest review I had to do. Not because it proved difficult to analyse or form an opinion of, but because it teases me with something that could have been great - yet is not. I don't like destroying a game I have a thing for, even though it's just on paper in the shape of a review, but there's no going around it. The franchise screams for a more flexible versatile game but instead I'm left with a repetitive hallway shooter.
Adam 'Kane', as ex-mercenary, and James 'Lynch', as felon convicted of manslaughter, form a crime duo to arrange an arms deal in Shanghai. However, sh¡t hits the fan and Kane accidentally shoots the informant's girlfriend. Unfortunately she turns out to have been the daughter of

mobster in
all of China, whom is not fond of his daughter dying from a bullet Kane fired. The game follows our protagonists through Shanghai as this crime lord throws in everything at his disposal as a means of revenge, which is a lot. From local thug to police officer, a few military companies to several special forces, this guy has them all in his pocket and intends to use every man to kill Kane and Lynch.
There really is nothing wrong with the writing, and reading about Kane & Lynch (either of the two parts) will want to make you play the games. The protagonist duo have a background together (as portrayed in
) which - coupled with their voice actors - look like cold hard m☮therfµckers. There's no other way to describe them. This is actually necessary to make their survival credible as far as the setting is concerned, and it does add up.
Though what doesn't add up is everything around it, with the partial exception of screenwriting: since the fundamentals of Dog Days is its hallway shooter mechanic, there isn't much freedom for screenwriting to begin with. The scenarios are heavily constrained to these mechanics and it doesn't take long for an observant player to notice that the intended storyline doesn't carry over as strong as it could have with different mechanics. The attempt is very admirable however, as even though some scenes are incredibly violent, they never feel forced or out of place.
The graphical quality is above average, though the used shaders and camera movement prove to be rather annoying over time. The bobbing, lens flares and shaders look great when only observed, but when you are in control of the camera yourself it quickly feels as if the game consistently misinterprets movements. There are glitches involved as well, though this might have to do with the fact that Dog Days is an older game and my newer hardware might not render some things correctly.
The sounds are too diverse to criticize in general. On one hand there are flat unconvincing gunshots, average ambience and mediocre soundeffects. On the other hand there's the convincing gritty voices of Kane and Lynch. While dialogue is well dosed, a great majority of the game still consists of shooting and as such there is little the dialogue of Kane and Lynch can do to make the game sound better in overall.
All of these assets could be worked with if it weren't for the repetitive hallway shooter mechanics. All details aside, this game is mainly about sitting behind cover, shooting people that are also behind cover, and moving up through the predefined path. The entirety of the game is played like this while every now and then a cutscene plays. The motives behind these mechanics might have to do with the developers intending to reach maximum cinematic experience by constraining the player, but when a game starts to feel like something that can be played on an light-gun arcade cabinet - graphics aside - a lot of players are going to conclude the game is boring without ever finishing the first playthrough.
And that's a shame because just the storyline, the strong characters being coupled with great voices, and the potential hidden in screenwriting makes this game a hidden gem. My conclusion is that it's definitely worth a play, Dog Days is truly different from a great majority of titles and a developer's second attempt to bring a franchise to life that is much more potent than the games are willing to show. While compelling story-wise, the gameplay itself will most likely bore you. In that regard it's funny how Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days is only three to four hours worth of playtime, because anything more would have been too much in its current form. Collectors will probably not mind putting down €10,- for this, and I would plead the same for gamers with a thing for mentionable titles. If you are on a tight budget and have no idea about what I'm trying to unveil with my review, then you wouldn't be able to appreciate the title(s) and it's best to stay away from the franchise.
I'm clicking the thumbs up for this game here because as broken as it might be: I admire the story, characters and voices, three things I value. Someday I will try the first Kane & Lynch and I'm also hoping the scheduled movie isn't going to ruin the franchise even more.

Usually I don't take games' story that seriously, and I don't really care about them.  But the thing that makes Life is strange a great game is its story and characters. It's gameplay isn't that great and even present in the game.

There are small details in the explorable levels that reveal small details about them.
Then theres the voice acting. Some characters voice acting are just on point, and some are unrealistic and just bad. Some parts of the game are nothing but cringy.
